One of the best games I have played in a while. The story was incredibly gripping, it was hard to pull myself away and I found myself thinking about the story constantly when I wasn't playing. The graphics are nice, and give the game a very cool, and (in my casual-gamer eyes) unique feel. I loved the atmosphere of the game, and with the great storyline felt very immersed in this game.
Depite being fairly linear it still manged to maintin an open-world feel incredibly well. It wasn't super long, but I feel the length complimented the game perfectly, not drawn out enough to be tedious, but still long enough to develop a great story. It has definitely joined my list of top games and I would highly recommend it.

I appreciate what the developers may have had in mind but there were more interesting story-telling avenues which could have been taken.

The world is beautiful but it feels baron, with virtually no wild-life, it could have held more collectable/interactables. I found myself searching every nook and cranny, to be constantly disappointed and unrewarded for doing so. They created this vast world for you to explore but failed to add any substance.

Despite these set-backs, most of the plot is well written. The dialogue between the two main characters was believable. engaging, interesting and at times exciting, it's easily the best thing about this game.

Finished my fourth playthrough. Yes, it (almost) ends the same way every time, but that's not the point. Playing Firewatch is like watching a favorite movie again and again: because of its atmosphere, its actors, its scenery. It doesn't have a lot of cutscenes, though. Most of the time, what you do and the way you behave is absolutely up to you.
I really liked the way dialogue options were presented. The different choices along with the timer really make you think about what to say next, and the conversation can take completely different turns.
You can also find some nice gadgets, like the camera or the turtle, which aren't really necessary to solving the game, but add a personal touch to your experience.
All of these things help you feel "at home"; it's your time in the lookout, your summer in the Shoshone.
But what makes this game so exceptional in my opinion is the way it makes you care about the characters – and that's amazing considering you hardly ever meet anyone. Henry and Delilah are not your typical stand-ins, but people with a real personality, and their chemistry is remarkable. The voice acting is superb, but like in a good movie, a good book, so much that's important is left unsaid, however you can feel it right under the surface. The only thing that maybe doesn't work for everybody is that some plot points might be hidden too good; it all makes perfect sense if you spend enough time in this world, but it's possible to miss some explanations when you rush through the game. Which you shouldn't, because it's too beautiful.

Firewatch is a single-player first-person mystery set in the Wyoming wilderness, where your only emotional lifeline is the person on the other end of a handheld radio. Yes, it's a walking sim.
So let's get the obvious out of the way first. Firewatch is a walking sim. No running and gunning, no arcade elements, some dialogue choices. I have to say I luv me a walking sim. And this is one of the best. Dealing with some personal troubles you take a job far away from civilisation, summer spent in the middle of nowhere, to clear your head and deal with current worries.
The game is short, at around 4 hours, during which you'll travel around the beautiful environments, deal with your traumas and uncover new mysteries while having only one other human to talk to, a fellow ranger - Delilah. I read a lot about this game, and I expected a good game and a poor ending. I got excellent game and ok ending. I understand how some poeple might feel everything is leading to a climax and then nothing happens, but to me the ending was in line with all of the game.
Anyhow, if you like walking simulators or adventure games in general this is one of the best walking sims I experienced. If you like the genre even a little bit and/or like slowly told human stories just play this. You will not be disappointed.
I liked:
* the graphics
* the story
* dialogue
* nails it in the atmosphere department
I disliked:
* nothing (alas I would love it the game was a little bit longer)
Get this if:
* you like walking sims
* you like good stories (normal human life stories)
Don't get this if:
* you don't like walking sims
* you expect more than 4hrs out of your game investment

Firewatch is a brillianty crafted game, with beautiful artwork and amazing voice acting. The storyline is engaging and the character development leaves you feeling fully entangled within their choices and lives. The game itself is a relatively small open-map, allowing you to discover areas whenever you desire (majority of which are not marked on the map which is fun). Throughout the game, tension rises and there were numerous moments were I felt very on edge. The ending was a little under-whelming after all the build up, but it was still an enjoyable game. It did however feel more like a teaser demo for something bigger. There is so much potential to develop it further and do more with the storyline, map and characters.
If you can get it on sale and enjoy exploring/storyline heavy games then it's worth a go

An intensely gorgeous game with solid mechanics (though, beware of man eating bushes! You just ight get caught if you're not careful), and a semi-intriguing story. The objectives are logical and it you have plenty of time to enjoy the scenery as you move along to figure complete your tasks. The resolution to the story does feels like it comes up short, however, all other componants are well-crafted, so I can overlook a slightly underwhelming ending.
The characters are mildly amusing. They do push the story forward well, but they don't have a decent conclusive ending. It feels as though it needed a more solid resolution. It was somewhat satisfying, but yet mildly underwhelming.
The mechanics were well polished. I did get caught on a shrubbery though. That was annoying, but fortunately the save points are more than generous so I wasn't set back after that mild inconvenience. I only encountered that one issue. I believe it's isolated and doubt I could recreate it. I don't consider it even remotely game breaking, but it si something that should be mentioned.
Walking was well-designed. Notably, in this first person game, you have a body, and when walking, you can see your hands. I did appreciate that touch very much. Additionally, the head-bobbing mechanics added a good finishing touch to the experience. It didn't feel like you're just moving a camera forward but rather a person.
You totally get the feeling you're alone. Even hearing the woman's voice isn't enough to shake the feeling of being along in this vast wilderness. The day time feels safe, andlike you're one with nature. Being out at night makes you wonder just what that sound was. Is it a bear or worse?
The graphics for the inside and outdoors were stunningly beautiful. The environment felt like a national park. There were man made paths that you could easily follow while still deciding to walk amongsts the trees.
You can't die, you can't lose!

What I really loved is the researching part of the game (although it's a huge shame you can only research one thing at a time) and mixing and matching the smiths' abilities to produce the weapons with the desired stats, and that's what this game really is about. The game is also very self-conscious and refers to other games A LOT, so it's impossible to finish it without laughing once.
tl;dr: Funny, a bit challenging, overall great. :)

Unlike other reviewers, I'm unfortunately not a backer from the Kickstarter. I got the game today, and as I play more the review will be updated as such. Anyway, let's jump right into the deep end here.
. I have
in my life experienced anything like it. The way the gaming industry operates nowadays is depressing. It's all rip off after rip off, but this is
much different. The feeling you get when you're skating around the city, mastering your routes and getting faster and faster than ever before is an experience I know well from games like the Tony Hawk series or Jet Set Radio, but it feels so much different on this game. In all other skating games, you're bound to the track, basically. You have quite a lot of freedom, but the route is defined. In Hover, you're free. You find your own damn route, and you take it.
The concept of the story is that you're in a city where games consoles are banned by the authoritarian leaders, and you're part of a rebel group that opposes them. I've ot played too far into the game's story, so unfortunately I don't know what it's like. One thing you'll have to understand is that this game isn't about the story. It's about the experience of skating. Once you get into the game and get past the short tutorial, you couldn't care less about the story.
The game's control system comes with mouse/keyboard controls and a default Xbox 360 controller mode, which I've been using and enjoying. It's fully customisable, so if you don't like any of the bindings you can change it. So far, the gameplay feel has been absolutely great, but it there are a few bits that annoy me. For example, when you're jumping from wall to wall, the camera angle makes it easy to lose youself and ruin your moveset. The first-person feel to the game is immersive, and I can imagine that it would be absolutely phenomenal on the oculus rift. I must add though, that the controls and gameplay takes some getting used to. It's not
steep, but there certainly is a learning curve.
The graphics of the game are lovely and appealing, but that's because they fit the styling of the game perfectly. The textures are pretty smooth, and there aren't many graphical bugs which I've found. BUT I'm not able to play the game well in high detail, an issue I shall be touching on soon.
Absolute eargasm. You just have to listen to it to undeerstand. It portrays the feel of the game perfectly whilst you're playing it, it's almost as if the game itself was perfectly tailored to the music style, or vice versa. There is more music scheduled to be added that's by Hideki Nagamura himself, the guy that made the original music for Jet Set Radio.
This is an early alpha game, and in some ways it really shows. The GUI, while nice in concept, feels rather jerky and unfitting, but this is a minor issue. The character colour-changing is a chore with the 360 controller, and I think a number of preset colours to use as well as the RGB sliders would go well. But the biggest and main issue is the optimisation. I have a rig that can run basically any game I want at Ultra settings and get 60fps, but I get less than thirty with high settings on this game. It's not a game-breaking issue, becuase putting it down to medium settings gets me 40fps which - with the game style - works fine. Putting it down to low settings get me around 50+ fps, but I prefer texture quality to fps personally. The developers of this game are very dedicated, and have stated that this is an issue they are working hard on to fix.
Now, do you like skating games? Do you like freerunning games? Do you like AMAZING music? Do you like addictive gameplay? Do you like enjoyable maps and landscapes? If the answer is yes to these questions, get this game. Although you might want to wait until the game is further optimised before you buy it. (I personally don't find it
bad. It just takes some getting used to).
There's a few features on the game I haven't tried yet, so the review will be updated when I do.
Controls take a while to get used to, but the game is very nice once you do.
A fun sci-fi parkour game that will remind you of jet set radio and mirrors edge.

It's not very often a Star Wars game (specifically this one) goes on sale. I remember playing this a few years ago when it first came out, just picked it up on Steam, too. Had loads of fun playing the campaign, lots of great memories from this game. I remember hugging the healing stations because I was worried I'd get killed during the next fight all the time.
You can play as different specialized Clone Troopers (i.e. Demolitions, Sniper, etc.).
This is actually one of those games where commanding your own squad is fun. The AI is decent (not perfect, but close enough). You can use turrets from fallen Republic Gunships and mow down enemies with it. All in all, a great game.. multiplayer wasn't that bad too. I had lots of fun dueling 1v1. One day, I was lucky enough to pull a direct headshot by bouncing a Wookie crossbow projectile off the wall on somebody. :D: Been a while, and I can't remember the name of the map, but it was an arena map called "Clone Training".
I give the game a 8.5/10. Although the game was pretty enjoyable, I remember it being short (a few hours only) and there were some brutal levels.. well, that's AI squad-based gameplay for ya. Anyways, you can listen to me yap all day, but this goes on my list of Top 10 SW video games ever released. It's on sale right now for just $3, worth buying if you're a fan of Star Wars.

Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army is a standalone game/expansion to Sniper Elite: V2. (You don't need to own V2 to be able to play this one.) It is built from the same engine as V2, featuring the exact same mechanics and gameplay yet features completely separate game modes. Unlike V2 which had 10 missions, this game features a series of 5 campaign missions that can be played in single player or up to four players in online co-op.
The story involves a "what if" scenario presented during the final days of World War 2, if Adolf Hitler were to deploy a secret last desperate plan to raise the dead as zombies through occult rituals and turn them against the allied forces.
While it is not a bad game in itself, fans of the original Sniper Elite V2 will be disappointed that the attention to detail that was given to V2 is not shown here. For instance right in the opening scene, we see Hitler giving orders to his generals in spoken English. That right there sets up the tone of the game. A goofy game set in an alternate universe that is not to be taken too seriously.
This time, instead of the 3 main tactics of Conceal, Plan and Execute, all you have to do is just aim your gun and shoot anything that moves. No subtlety is required. Enemies will not hide and take up defensive positions. The only thing they do is to stagger slowly at you in massive numbers. Mixed in with the standard zombies are a couple of special mobs such as zombie snipers with super jumps, tank-like machine gunner zombie bosses etc. Throughout the whole game, you just need to shoot at them and move away to avoid getting slashed.
This just makes every stealth and cover mechanics that was in V2 completely redundant. And because its made from the same engine, the mechanics are still there, but completely worthless as you will never need to utilize them at all.
Graphics wise, the game makes use of existing art resources used in V2, but this time overlaid with a bluish nightmarish tone, which admittedly doesn't look too shabby. Some of the graphics can be abit gory at times and you might want to make a note of that if you want to let younger children play.
Sound and music are appropriately creepy sounding. Well, as creepy sounding as you can get when you pump a growling nazi zombie full of lead. No complaints at all about this.
Overall Rating: 6.0 / 10
I can't help but feel that this game is a cheap cash in using the exact same engine as V2. I'm more then a little disappointed that the game mechanics which had been refined so well in V2 were basically abandoned in this game. Feel free to give this game a couple of points more if this doesn't bother you.
If you are looking to find a good zombie shooting game, i'd recommend either the L4D series or Killing Floor if you haven't already played them. If however you are looking for something new and don't mind a goofy fictional WW2 arcade shooting game with Nazi Zombies that doesn't take itself seriously, this title might be worth a look.

although i have clocked in only about 30 hours into this game i feel like writing a review for it.
ME is a very welcoming change in my library. as a fan of games like arma3,squad,killing floor and the likes this game is a nice step down in terms of stress and having to be on your guard if you follow my meaning.
ME is pure peace,slap it on with some soothing ingame music and let your inner builder get carried away. in real life iam the most uncreative person there is but once i start this game and it gives me the tools the ideas just flow. start with a humble abode and a place to store your materials quickly turns into "hmm, perhaps i could try my hands on building a cathedral or perhaps a nice looking library" and next you realise you have alot of unfinished builds started...and thats when you're hooked.
the game pulls you in and invites you to take a breath,gather some logs and start out your career as a medieval engineer.discover the vast landscapes to find a nice spot to build that suits your prefrences.mountainous areas,wide open plains or thick forest areas, this game has it all.
the learning curve in terms of building isnt steep at all and feels very intuitive. you dont need to grind for thousands of building unlocks and yet it is complex enough to keep you interested. once you have unlocked the crafting receipes you can build to your hearts contempt. in the medieval them era that is.
there is quite a few mods out there to enhance your experience though i have not tried many yet.
some things to consider:
if you are into hardcore survival gameplay, this game isnt for you. it does have a PvP mode and comes with (very easy to defeat) AI bandits,but there arent many things to keep you engaged in terms of action. however, once you enter a PvP server expect some fully functioning trebuchet's and catapults to come up against your castles. you will have to build them up from scratch though,understanding the mechanics and physics. the mechanic/physics in this game are quite deep and can make for some interesting contraptions.
expect lag on a server that has more than 6 players on it. these depend on the amount of mods hosted as well as how the servers are set up but you will get some lag.but its nothing game/immersion breaking.
so to come to a conclusion..if you are looking for a game to let your creativity go wild (medieval themed of course :D ) and just a chilled experience and a welcoming change in pace, or just like to build for the sake of building with some elements of survival..ME is a game to consider. i would recommend it highly. and the added physics as well as what you can do mechanically just adds to the fun and makes this game stand out from your other build to survive games.

An intensely gorgeous game with solid mechanics (though, beware of man eating bushes! You just ight get caught if you're not careful), and a semi-intriguing story. The objectives are logical and it you have plenty of time to enjoy the scenery as you move along to figure complete your tasks. The resolution to the story does feels like it comes up short, however, all other componants are well-crafted, so I can overlook a slightly underwhelming ending.
The characters are mildly amusing. They do push the story forward well, but they don't have a decent conclusive ending. It feels as though it needed a more solid resolution. It was somewhat satisfying, but yet mildly underwhelming.
The mechanics were well polished. I did get caught on a shrubbery though. That was annoying, but fortunately the save points are more than generous so I wasn't set back after that mild inconvenience. I only encountered that one issue. I believe it's isolated and doubt I could recreate it. I don't consider it even remotely game breaking, but it si something that should be mentioned.
Walking was well-designed. Notably, in this first person game, you have a body, and when walking, you can see your hands. I did appreciate that touch very much. Additionally, the head-bobbing mechanics added a good finishing touch to the experience. It didn't feel like you're just moving a camera forward but rather a person.
You totally get the feeling you're alone. Even hearing the woman's voice isn't enough to shake the feeling of being along in this vast wilderness. The day time feels safe, andlike you're one with nature. Being out at night makes you wonder just what that sound was. Is it a bear or worse?
The graphics for the inside and outdoors were stunningly beautiful. The environment felt like a national park. There were man made paths that you could easily follow while still deciding to walk amongsts the trees.
You can't die, you can't lose!

Back in the era of 56kbps internet connections, Half-Life (the original one) was a hit. Since then, it has always been a hit or, I should put it this way, a revolution of gaming. It has set the standard of gaming and shooters alike. However, there was one problem back then. Most computer games are designed for only one player, and multiplayer exists in terms of split-screen and turn taking. They require player 2 3 4 and other subsequent players to be there physcially. Online gaming exists only in the form of flash games on websites and yahoo! chess and stuffs. To be honest, online connection was never stable at that time, and you're pretty much done when your mom wished to make a call.
Then came cable and ADSL, which allows internet speed to go up to 512kbps or 1Mbps at that point, which is fast enough for most games, such as counter-strike. Good enough at that time.
Of course, most online shooters at that time (the pre-directx 8 era) are mainly team based and deathmatch games (team fortress classic and counter-strike are some examples), and little attention were paid to story-lines and co-operative plots when it comes to online multiplayer shooters. Most online multiplayer shooters are rounds and rounds of endless matches, of which some find them competitive while others feel that this type of gameplay can be rather mundane.
Then comes Sven Co-op. The most intrinsic idea of this mod (it's not a game, technically speaking) is to allow the possibility of having a multi-player co-op gameplay for the multi-award winning Half-Life shooter. It was this simple, yet in revolutionary for the valve franchise back than as multiplayer and story-based shooters had never mixed.
Soon enough, the community grew, and more players, custom maps and add-ons are added into the game. Sven coop has since been evolved and developed into a seperate branch of valve shooters - coop shooter - after gaining support and fame from half-life gamers. Till date, custom maps of all sorts, such as defense, maze and horde maps, can still be found lying around the corners of the internet.
That was more than a decade and a half ago. Today, we see Sven-Coop listed in our library again. Today, we celebrate this game which blended multiplayer and game plots together. Today, we can throw banana bombs in toon run, for free.

It's disappointing that, even as Generation X moves steadily into middle age, the games designed to appeal to the First Video Game Generation are still saddled with the campy, melodramatic conventions of comic books, B movies, and television.
Other than Kentucky Route Zero, Portal and possibly Dear Esther, there isn't much to recommend in the interactive experience category if one is a well-read, well-watched adult with little ingrained patience for complex control schemes and video gamey tropes.
I was really getting into Firewatch. There was some interesting meat there. Two strangers, separated by space, getting to know each other over the radio, possibly the subject of an unethical study, lonely, rough backstories full of mistakes and regret, good characterization, decent voice acting...
And then suddenly there was all this pseudo-thriller drammuh - property destruction, violence, missing teenage girls, a dead kid, a survivalist loner, and a bunch of strained emotive voice acting that sounded like two people trying desperately to overcome constipation.
Why is it that video game audiences demand Big, Dumb Thrill Rides? Firewatch could have been a really interesting, branching, gorgeous love story. Instead, it had to hang on to a rickety scaffold of Dramatic Conflict to sell itself to the perpetually bored, adrenaline junkie crowd and the games reviewers who pander to them.
I found the "thrilling" aspects of Firewatch to be a distracting annoyance from the gorgeous scenery and budding friendship of Henry and Delilah. The title's insistence on inventing stuff for the player to DO, spoiled character building and a setting that should have been allowed to just BE.
In the end, I was just pushing through the actiony, fetchy, double backy bits of the experience in the vain hope that there might be some kind of emotional payoff for the two main characters. There was, kinda.
I'm really don't mean to dog on Firewatch. I asks a fair price for a very polished few hours of time. It pushes the art of the possible further into adult territory for interactive experiences. It's the fact that it comes so close to greatness that makes it a bitter disappointment for those searching for something that isn't shootybang idiocy.

And there's a wealth of "background material" inside the game itself that can draw you into ths world and it's history.  And the choices you make throughout the game are remembered, both the good, and the bad.  You set the course.

TLDR: After a considerable number of playthroughs this game is easily one of my favorites in the RPG-zombie genre. Play it if you're a fan of survival RPGs with story, zombies, and base building.
While it certainly has its flaws, it is rather well made and features a fairly compelling narrative in addition to some engrossing turn-based gameplay and survival challenges that, especially on the hardcore setting, is still difficult even for expereinced veterans. On top of all this, it's also fairly true to the classic zombie lore of films and TV. There's no super-zombies, no 'special' zombies, and the later-game difficulty comes more from other humans--just as it should be.
Upgrading your shelter is rewarding and you get to see the fruits of your labor build up over time. Survivors whom you rescue grow stronger over time and you get to (somewhat) influence their growth, deal with their tantrums and moods, deal with allies who get bitten, and so forth. While the story is entirely scripted, there are a lot of events that trigger based on certain conditions, and that makes no two playthroughs exactly alike.
The biggest disapointment is the AI, and by extention the way zombie turns are managed by the engine. Most enemies will simply charge you head on, even though they have no chance to win, although there is simulated panic. There are numerous pathing exploits that make some of the harder missions too easy since you can't step over an incapacited body without killing it first. Worst is that some of the larger levels / larger zombie hoardes can take ages to resolve a turn or complete the level, making it a tedious chore that involves a lot of waiting.
Still, no game is perfect, and this one is better than most.

An amusing VN that throws anime style fanservice at you, yet even parodies itself by having a character comment on the ridiculousness of over the top fan service. Despite that being in your face at the start, it's really just a side-dish to the time traveling plot. I liked the story, though it had flaws. Some of Chrontek's plan doesn't make any sense and there are moments where the characters lose all sense of logic and I'm left scratching my head over where their intelligence has gone. Still, I enjoyed it overall. The plot carried some some surprising depth to it that one generally wouldn't expect while judging the cover. Questioning morality and putting a choice in your hands that I was genuinely curious to see how both options played out. The characters are cute, silly, and fun, and fit the plot well.
While the story is nice, imo, there is a lack of choices throughout the game that makes this far more a true "visual novel" then say an "Interactive novel" you might find elsewhere. However, I've also read some VN's that just provide an illusion of choice, making all of their options but one a simple "Game over", thus keeping you on a linear story anyway. At least Time Tenshi drops the pretense and just gives you the two options that matter for your particular story. As this is Silver Cow's first VN, the more linear nature of Time Tenshi is understandable. I personally enjoy more choices and hope to see more branching story arcs in the future as they acquire more resources to evolve their methods. As for Time Tenshi, it gave me a laugh and I look forward to reading the sequel! There is definitely a lot of setup for a continuing story here. I would recommend this to anyone that enjoys a read of silly psudo-science and, of course, a view of heavily endowed anime girls.

This is pretty much the game I've been waiting for since Mirror's Edge was released back in 2008. If you liked the idea of Mirror's Edge: Catalyst's open world but want to see it executed well with more fun, arcadey parkour and *proper* multiplayer then Hover is for you. While it is still only in alpha, I am having a tremendous amount of fun with it.
Hover is an open world parkour game (playable in single player or multiplayer) inspired by the Jet Set Radio series that allows you to race your friends and explore the reasonably large portion of the world that is currently available. When I first started playing the alpha (I backed the Kickstarter and started playing in February 2015), I wasn't a fan of Hover - the parkour felt a little awkward to use and it wasn't what I was expecting. However, after 30 minutes or so of running around the city and backflipping between grindable rails, it felt like second nature; it's fluid, fast and most importantly, fun. One of the coolest features is the fact that your camera rotates in first person if you do a front/back/side flip - not really anything that amazing, but it adds a nice bit of immersion to the first person aspect. You are also able to switch between 3 camera modes - first person, auto (movement is first person, tricks/flips are in 3rd person) and 3rd person.
One of my favourite things about the game is that there are actually different playstyles to use, something i've never really seen in a parkour game. As of the first alpha release, you can level your character to level 10 and increase your stats in 5 seperate attributes - speed, acceleration, jump, grind and hoverheat. While building your character in various ways is interesting and encourages different styles of play, the most interesting stat is "hoverheat", which allows your characters stats to temporarily increase by  building up energy from grinding on rails and doing tricks in mid-air. The higher the amount of hoverheat you have, the more your overall stats will temporarily increase, meaning you could be faster than someone with max speed or jump higher than someone with max jump skill. It's a style I haven't tried out yet, but I plan to give it a go after I level up my 2nd chracter to level 10.
While there is a decent amount of content right now (Lots of hidden collectibles, a mission editor, multiple races/escaping from police and 32 player MP servers) Fusty Games are planning to add in more cities, more mission types, more parkour moves, a story mode that includes parkour and stealth based missions and a soundtrack written by Hideki Naganuma himself.  Furthermore, the current online community is fantastic, which meant that I wanted to keep playing even with having completed most of the content. There's also a mission editor that allows you to create your own races to be completed around the city, something that adds a fair amount of longevity to the game.
If you've enjoyed the parkour in Titanfall or Mirror's Edge but fancy something more arcadey, you really can't go wrong with Hover. It's a fun game for a relatively low cost with a promising future (that doesn't look like it'll be dumped into release half finished) and I can't really recommend an early access game anymore than that.
Tl;dr Very fun game that plays like a mix of Mirror’s Edge and Jet Set Radio with an open world and multiplayer. Somewhat lacking in content/polish right now, but it’s still in alpha and I fully expect the issues to be ironed out.
: So I said I'd upate this review which didn't happen for over a year, but there's been quite a few patches since then. Fusty has scrapped the first city and rebuilt it completely, as it was the original city that caused the framerate issues. Since then, I have been able to play the game at 60fps on my desktop (i5-4690k, GTX970, 8gb RAM) and  haven't had any framerate issues.
Some new locations have been added too, including the E-cop prison, which gives you a taster of  some of the stealth sections Fusty plan to implement. While the movement feels a little too fast to be a truly precise stealth game, it's still fun and a welcome addition to the game. The other area that's been added are the Sewers, which is a sprawling area full of tunnels and races to complete. There's also a nice parkour course spiralling towards the top of the sewers which allows you to see the inside of Resistance HQ. My only real problem with the sewers (After briefly playing the update since its release last night) is that they're quite difficult to find your way out of. The main city district redesign has made it quite vertical, meaning it's easy to learn the layout of the city. The second district of the City is currently being worked on now, so there'll be an even larger area to explore (hopefully) soon.
There have also been extra characters added, all of which are good at different things; Greendy is much faster than other characters whereas Watabax gets a much higher boost bonus from hoverheat,for example.
I'd say my main problem with Hover right now is that it can be fairly difficult to learn the layout of the city due to how vertical District A (The main area) is. A map wouldn't help in this situation either, as it's hard to properly map out the district while accounting for the differences in height between areas. This could be helped if - when in the sewers for example - there were more environmental clues on how to leave the area or signs that made it clear as to where you were heading.
The animation NPCs have when bumped into is still quite strange and something that I hope is changed to make it look less jerky.
On the whole though, I have very few complaints about Hover; it's an early access game so there are things that still clearly need to be worked on, but it's a game I continue to have a lot of fun with.
: Each update to Hover has brought bug fixes, balance changes, more things to do and larger play areas. Each update has been positive and while progress is a bit slow, there's enough content here to justify picking the game up.

Name: Marlow Briggs and The Mask of Death
Developer: Zootfly
Genre: Hack and slash, action platformer, action adventure
Personal: Awesome, simply amazing, that was 7 hours of movies that ended climatically.
A simply amazing action platformer game with the titular Marlow Briggs taking helm as a badass guy on a mission to save the girl, kick the bad guys♥♥♥♥♥and all the while slaughtering hundreds of faceless mook that dares to even stand between him and his objective. I suppose you could compare this game to legends like God of War although it doesn't have the brutality associate with God of War so you won't be tearing your hair in frustration but instead can enjoy this game in peace.
Along the way witness the dynamic duo of Marlow and the titular Mask of Death as they trade banter while killing enemies, facing monstrous creatures and wielding terrible weapons.
You probably won't believe how beautiful this game is despite the fact that it merely clocks at 2gb something in terms of size, fauna has a beautiful sheen to it, enemies and environment has beautiful and varied art to them and you will visit many location each [barring the temples] has their own art style and colour.
It's awesome, its  beaty track that fits well with the game and doesn't sound out of place, especially when you face some of the bosses. It's great.
And here is where MBATMOD shines the most, you will wield many different [actually just four but they are all different in how they play.] weapons, traverse many different locale and best of all, fight tons of enemies all with satisfying combo.
Granted I don't actually know why its more important to string longer combos since  I don't actually notice any increase in reward but damn I would say its not that hard to pull off 100-200 combos by late game as your skill greatly outclass that of the enemies.
Enemies aren't dull dullard either, they will put up a stiff fight and unless you actually use those combos you will find yourself always running out of health and mana. Fun thing is killing enemies restore the meters albeit very very little. It's a fine system of risk of reward which is greatly enhanced by the fact that healing takes time and you can't just do that in the middle of a brawl with 10+ dudes so caution must be taken. One fun ability they give you in game is the ability to convert humanoid size enemies to your side by grabbing them and spamming the E button. Granted they do die quickly and are usually relegated to meatshield duty but I'll be damn if they didn't save my hide once when I got trapped in an arena with two hulking dudes and 2 never ending spawning enemies, which I proceed to convert naturally.
Did i mention boss fights are aplenty? Yes they are, and they are awesome, you will fight mythical creature, twisted monster and the demons of the underworld itself! Of course cleverly they disguise the mini boss fight as a tutorial segment to deal with the enemy type later.
So about controls, its very good and responsive. So far none of my button has mispressed. Although one issue with the game is the camera can be a backstabbing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ occasionally, It might swing behind you, in front of you or even block your off-screen view. I guess there has to be a con no?

I followed this game with great anticipation for a good chunk of time. After I had read about it in a Gaming magazine back in mid 2010 I was thrilled to hear about a Zombie game with base management elements. I have not been disappointed.
The gameplay is absolutly for the more hardcore zombie fans as it's clunky animations and turn-based combat system allows for some criticism. However it's good. It is worth 20€ for what it is.
The graphics are not to be amazed over but the quality of the smoothness when it runs is worth some degree. I have seen games with worse graphics that ran like a stick in the mud.
That said I love the attention to detail. If you are low on food and get a really good haul of it you will see in your pantry the massive amounts of food displayed. There will be close to nothing if you have close to no food. However have your stocks full and the pantry looks like a fully stocked super-market.
DoubleBear productions are worthy of some praise as the game kept me going. I have replayed the early-mid part of the game several times and I'm pleased. The options to craft your own backstory in the beginning is somewhat good but the dialouge options could feel heavy at times.
The cutscenes are nothing new or impressive as they just teleprot characters to an area to have them setup for dialouge. However the written story gives each and every NPC character. I was sure some NPC would be a minor leader but was not and some reactions of other NPCs were great. I personally loved tormenting the poor priest when he crossed my decision at one point by forcing him to do something he did not want to. That is great for immersion and for roleplaying.
However the sound is very simple but it works for the setting, it won't go down like a piece of art. However it works none the less.
The only true complaint I have is the RNG as it can sometimes ♥♥♥♥ you over and the AI system. So first things first. The construction and resource system. I do not like that certain upgrades feel so "limited" such as the garden part. I can easily imagine more outdoor areas get turned into growing areas. So there could be an update for that. The resources gained can vary very heavily sometimes and that can lead to weird situations when the need to upgrade is high. I have had the unlucky time of never being able to get the highest upgrade for the wall in one of my many playthroughs. The RNG does however what an RNG should.
The AI system can be very frustrating at times. I can setup a trap for raiders to stumble into a herd of zombies only to ahve the dead attack me instead. Same goes for raiders being so extremly dumb as they make continoues fire of thier firearms to attract over 100 zombies to the map. That♥♥♥♥♥♥is dangerous. They should know that and they should use firearms as a last resort. But the system does not allow it.
Overall, I love this game. It's one of the few good games that truly explores what an zombie apocalypse would be about. Yes there are zombies. But people are the biggest danger.
This is one of my "laptop" games, one of the better turn based games around.

This game sounded like a dream game: zombie apocalypse, base building and management, recruiting survivors, turn-based combat, survival narrative. I thought it would be a mix of Suikoden II, X-Com and Fallout in a Zombie setting.
But instead what you get is a shallow RPG experience, a base that doesn't really matter and which you don't really defend like you did in UFO: Enemy Unknown, one of the worst turn-based combat designs I've ever seen, and a whole crapload of tedium. The interface is also terrible.
In your base, instead of being able to access crucial menus to manage your base, you have to run around it for no reason just to access different menus. This is just tedious and adds nothing to the game. If I wanted to explore the base, I'd do it by myself. To view your character list you need to run around as well, because you can't view a survivor's data all in one place. You need to run to the supply room to check their inventory, to the cafeteria to check their stats, and you can only see their perks and morale level in the Goals menu. Why is everything so fragmented? What is the point?
Combat is a huge disappointment, and is hobbled by tiny rooms that are so hard to click around, a lack of proper hotkeys for player selection and reloading, stairs are particularly nasty as your people can only go through them one at a time and they are a teleport node instead of actually climbing them, so passing them completely isolates one guy to die to any enemies at the top. Worse, you cannot save while in the middle of combat. And the combat is so simplistic that it's even more barebones and basic than X-Com 1 back in the 90's. There's no saving action points to react to enemies, no cover mechanics, nothing.
The actual game idea is compelling, and playing through it can be fun, but the game really does its best to make it hard for you to play it.

It's disappointing that, even as Generation X moves steadily into middle age, the games designed to appeal to the First Video Game Generation are still saddled with the campy, melodramatic conventions of comic books, B movies, and television.
Other than Kentucky Route Zero, Portal and possibly Dear Esther, there isn't much to recommend in the interactive experience category if one is a well-read, well-watched adult with little ingrained patience for complex control schemes and video gamey tropes.
I was really getting into Firewatch. There was some interesting meat there. Two strangers, separated by space, getting to know each other over the radio, possibly the subject of an unethical study, lonely, rough backstories full of mistakes and regret, good characterization, decent voice acting...
And then suddenly there was all this pseudo-thriller drammuh - property destruction, violence, missing teenage girls, a dead kid, a survivalist loner, and a bunch of strained emotive voice acting that sounded like two people trying desperately to overcome constipation.
Why is it that video game audiences demand Big, Dumb Thrill Rides? Firewatch could have been a really interesting, branching, gorgeous love story. Instead, it had to hang on to a rickety scaffold of Dramatic Conflict to sell itself to the perpetually bored, adrenaline junkie crowd and the games reviewers who pander to them.
I found the "thrilling" aspects of Firewatch to be a distracting annoyance from the gorgeous scenery and budding friendship of Henry and Delilah. The title's insistence on inventing stuff for the player to DO, spoiled character building and a setting that should have been allowed to just BE.
In the end, I was just pushing through the actiony, fetchy, double backy bits of the experience in the vain hope that there might be some kind of emotional payoff for the two main characters. There was, kinda.
I'm really don't mean to dog on Firewatch. I asks a fair price for a very polished few hours of time. It pushes the art of the possible further into adult territory for interactive experiences. Absolute rubbish in every sense of the word. Where do I even start. Budget shooter from 10 years ago plays even worse than it sounds. Graphics are from 1999, not 2004 when it was released. You use the exact same bolt action sniper, pistol, and knife the whole game. Cannot pick up other weapons. The levels are super linear and look terrible. Bushes in the jungle block bullets and you can't move through them, basically making them blocks which makes no sense for a game called "jungle warfare" Enemies just run forward blindly or stand around while their teamates get shot. On the other end of the spectrum they always know where you are so if you try and sneak it basically will never work. Ammo is not picked up off bodies but in certain specific spots the developers chose. You face ridiculously high amounts of enemies each part where you just headshot them from far away, sometimes which doesn't kill them even though it hits them in the head. I got to a basically unbeatable sand level where all the problems of the game came together. The level is super linear and you cannot go through buildings or open doors. The stealth does not work. The game tells you to stay away from the streeets but there are enemies standing on it and you cannot go any other way but the linear way. When you shoot 1 guy 10 guys come. After having killed around 60-80 guys I just ran out of ammo on my main gun and pistol, and since the developers have no tents or buildings you could find ammo in since it wasn't on the street I just lost. My mo-ron teamate also didn't help, as he died one of the times I made it past the guys. Your teamate is worthless. He runs out into the open, never kills anyone (mostly because his sniper does absolutely no damage for some reason) he will not follow you sometimes. He also will stand there and take a ton of damage and then not use his medkits even though he needs to, for some unexplicable reason. The only redeamable features I can put is that this is in fact technically "a game" and that fun is too be had whenever your spotter partner says to sneak around or not engage with a group/area, and I just fire away and slaughter them all as if to say "fuuuck you" to my mo-ron AI teamate. That was the only fun I had. This game has negative reviews for a reason, trust them. 3.5/10

This is pretty much a game where you choose different dialogue options as part of a story that is told through a msn-like messenger. Starting up the game is like the sign-in screen for Windows XP, and as you choose between three dialogue options it may occationally say "Emily will remember that" or "You have chosen to something". However, your choices matter little in the end, or even during the course of the game the path of the dialogue always remains the same, Emily might say something different to a different choice but then she says the same thing after that response more times than not.
This creates an illusion of choice at first, the text about Emily remembering stuff and your choices making it seem like there is more to the game. I have replayed this game multiple times thinking maybe I missed something but no, it is a really linear story.
Incoming spoilers  at the next line skip in case you want to give it a try, HOWEVER it can get kind of heavy emotionally so I would recommend skipping this game for those with depression.
It's pretty much a mostly-online relationship though from the chat, Emily is met two or three times between chapters off-screen. The ending combined with the lack of choice gives a feeling of... hopelessness? If anyone has been overly invested in someone in a long distance relationship but drifted apart wishing you were close as you were before, that's what the ending is like. Perhaps the lack of choice resulting in the feeling of futility in saving the relationship was intended in some form of artful expression, however I personally couldn't recommend this game to anyone I know dispite it being free.

This game has made me tremendously sad. I am sad because I have finished it, and I weep for there are no more worlds to conquer.
Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is a rock-solid middling-to-hard Metroidvania platformer. A Metroidvania (or IGAvania, or exploration platformer) is an open world game that provides you with a huge environment to explore. As you travel through this world you gain strength, power, and -- most importantly -- special abilities that let you overcome obstacles you couldn't before.
The game opens with Scuttle Town being sold off by its childish mayor to the Ammo Baron, who plans to turn it into a military base. Shantae, the town's Guardian Genie, manages to defeat him, only to be arrested for attacking the town's lawful owner. While extricating herself from the situation, Shantae runs into one of her old enemies, a Tinkerbat, who's been possessed by dark magic. Shantae's nemesis, Risky Boots, warns her that the dark magic heralds the potential return of the Pirate Master -- the near-godlike entity responsible for the disappearance of most of geniekind. Shantae and Risky are forced to put aside their enmity to team up against the greater evil.
That's the storyline. The game itself is largely linear; Shantae and Risky arrive on a new island, encounter a series of comic mishaps, and in the course of exploration Shantae discovers the entrance to a "Den of Evil" (dungeon). Each dungeon contains enemies, puzzles, a boss fight, and one piece of Risky's missing pirate equipment -- these last items grant Shantae increased mobility, giving her a downstab, multi-jump, etc. Defeating each boss also unlocks the next island.
In true Metroidvania fashion, it's completely impossible to obtain everything just heading straight through the game. There are tons of hidden items and secret exits that can't be reached unless you come back to earlier areas with equipment from later ones; some of it is skippable, some of it isn't.
The first Shantae game was a decent length, with five dungeons and a large overworld, but the second game was pathetically short, with only two actual dungeons and a very short completion time, and since the second one has a PC release and the first doesn't, people assume it's characteristic.
Shantae and the Pirate's Curse again has five full dungeons, as well as a few overworld areas that are large and convoluted enough to serve as dungeons themselves. In addition to the usual heart containers, Shantae can collect "Dark Magic" from specific, well-hidden enemies; the vast majority are hidden in fair, guessable locations. (ROT-13 Spoiler: Fbzr Pnpxyrongf nccrne jura lbh penfu vagb fcrpvsvp jnyyf.)
Combat works well; Shantae has a lot of options, especially in the late game, and I rarely found myself blaming the controls. Aside from one boss (and anyone who's played knows exactly which one) fights are mostly about knowing what's coming and developing tactics to beat it, not raw dexterity or luck.
The platforming starts easy but takes the kid gloves off somewhere around the fourth island. While the later levels are full of one-hit-kill traps, you can nearly always see them coming -- and, in an innovation I'd like to see more of, one-hit-kills and falling off the screen don't mean game over. You just take damage and respawn at the start of the room, Zelda style. I haven't seen this in platform games before.
One pet peeve I have in platform games that let you explore in every direction is how it's often hard to tell whether falling off the screen means dying or just going to a new area. In Shantae, pits that will kill you are always marked with skull-and-crossbones symbols. No guesswork. I like it.
I refrained from using a guide until the last "clean up" sweep for missing hearts and magic, and got easily about 12 hours of gameplay. Since some of this time was spent searching and/or being stumped by puzzles, using a guide all the way through would probably cut this to 7-8 hours, respectable for a Metroidvania.
THE GOOD:
* Longest entry in the series
* Well-designed dungeons
* Characters are engaging
* Jokes are actually funny
* Good difficulty curve, decently challenging by the end
* Configurable keyboard and gamepad controls
THE BAD:
* Iffy replayability
* One deeply unfair boss fight
* No clues about certain collectibles
* Graphics a little pixelated for a modern game
(And yes, I know what the other thing people associate Shantae games with is. I enjoy it -- I'm human -- but I don't think it either improves or detracts from the quality of the game. Unless you've got some kind of hangup about women in bathing suits, almost all of this game is fine for kids -- the running gag in "Run Run Rottytops!" is a little over the line, but it'll probably just go right over most kids' heads.)

shantae and the pirate's curse is a 2d action platformer where players assume the role of the titular character, the adorable half-genie shantae. in this game, she teams up with her rival risky boots to save the world from a looming threat, the return of the (in case you couldn't already tell from the title) master pirate, who was defeated and sealed away by the guardian genies years ago.
unlike the previous game, which takes place in just one island, meaning a single interconnected world, this game is divided into different, separated levels, with shantae exploring five islands (not including the first one, where scuttle town is located) in a more or less linear way: the level design itself is fairly linear, but the player will often need to return to previous islands, either to perform some action that will allow the story to progress, either to get some collectible that was previously inaccessible and that you can now obtain thanks to abilities that have since been acquired; this way of organizing the world, making the player move back and forth between islands, is why shantae and the pirate's curse is considered a member of the metroidvania group of games.
the collectibles mentioned in the previous paragraph are divided into two categories: 1. dark magic, in the form of tinkerbats that have now mutated thanks to it and that you will need to defeat to seal said magic inside your lamp, and 2. squid hearts, which can then be melted in groups of four and transformed into extra health by the "squidsmith".
the aforementioned scuttle town, where the game begins and the town of which shantae is the guardian genie, will serve as a hub, to which she will often return, either to perform some necessary action (often in the form of interactions with npcs) or to acquire items and upgrades.
in each of the remaining five islands shantae will find a den of evil, a place from where the master pirate is obtaining the dark magic that is allowing him to grow stronger; these dens of evil bear a strong resemblance to the dungeons in the legend of zelda series: in each one of them you will find a new ability, which will allow you to explore previously inaccessible areas (both inside and outside the dungeon) and that will be used in some way to defeat the boss of the dungeon in question.
speaking of bosses, they are fairly easy to deal with: this game as a whole is not maddeningly difficult, but i wouldn't say it's easy either, so it comes as a surprise that the bosses fall so easily, at least if you choose to use the arsenal at your disposition. they pretty much will never be a problem, unless you are trying to get the no-hit achievements, but even then they won't be a huge headache. i don't see it as a big problem, but to some it might be disappointing.
shantae's main weapon throughout this adventure is her signature hair whipping, but pistols and a scimitar will be added to her arsenal as the game progresses; other weapons, which on the previous game used the (now gone, for story reasons) magic meter (like the pike balls) became consumable itens. controls are very tight and responsible, a pretty important thing in this kind of game (well, an important thing in any kind of game, but especially in games that ask for precision like this one).
the game's tone is very lighthearted and humorous, with a good selection of charismatic and excentric character, as well as some fairly funny moments; the anime-influenced art style, while obviously not as good as one that's purely anime, is nice too.
there are a few problems here and there: you can't check if you already got all of the collectibles in an island without returning to risky's boat (being able to access this info on the menu would have been very useful, as it can be hard to keep track of it) and a (considerably long) insta-fail stealth section, which is not a big deal once you beat it, but will probably get on your nerves the first time. additionally, it can be somewhat difficult to know what to do next in some points (funnily enough, i didn't really have any problems with this, but i can see some people hitting a wall that will keep them from progressing, which can be very frustrating, especially when this wall comes from the game not giving you much information), although i think this is massively improved over risky's revenge.
these complaints, however, are small when compared to the game's achievements, and i think it's fair to say shantae and the pirate's curse is a very good videogame that deserves to be played by anyone with an interest in the genre, especially considering how cheap it is.

in some ways it's also unlike it in a lot of ways as well. It's ultimately still a platformer and a skill-attaining game that opens up more areas, but instead of an overworld you are given stage select screens. And instead of magic you have pirate items.
The first impression I had when I started playing was that the game was confirming the magic is no longer a thing due to the events of the last game (Risky Boots' Revenge). Honestly Shantae's transformations were a big part of what I found to be entrancing about the previous game. The fact that it was gone for good left me feelign liek there was a little hole in the heart of the game that wouldn't
be filled by the new skills. And really they didn't fill that hole but they were still decent game mechanics.
Shantae's friends played a more active role in this game than they did in the previous game which I totally approved of. In "Shantae: Risky Boots' Revenge" Rottytops, Bolo, Skye, and Uncle Mimic were ultimately just there to exist - they did nothing and were as forgetable as any town NPC save for the fact that they had unique appearances. In Shantae and the Pirate's Curse they actually take part as plot devices throughout the story. They're more like characters and less like decorations - very enjoyable characters too.
On that note I was kinda meh about the whole teaming up with Risky Boots concept. When the only thing Risky does is sit at the dock and drive you from one stage to the other she becomes decoration. She does have her own part in the story of course, but she's given reasons all the time for why she cannot participate in anything which waters down the whole "teaming up" concept. I think a more interesting way to handle it would be to give Risky the pirate gear and leave Shantae some magic and transformations. It would have required different stage setups, but I feel it would have added something (pirate skills and a true teaming-up concept) without taking something (the enchantment of the transformations).

is just straight up stupid. It's a slow melee kick that does barely any better damage than the hair. The hair will do about 8 damage and can be spammed. The kick will do 10 damage but you'll take about a half second to do it. That's not even considering the button combo you have to do to pull it off. It is also shorter range if I remember right. You'll buy this to try it (because your curiousity will force you to) and then you'll never use it again. It's a badly implimented mechanic.
The level design - and the story surrounding each level - throughout Shantae was pretty cool all in all. It never took itself too seriously but it kept me enraptured all through the game. It even managed to make a filler boss battle feel like more than it was. The Shantae games seem to excel at this through sassy comedy and sexy-cute visuals.
I don't mind puzzles as long as they don't stop my progress. For the majority of the game this was okay. I was never hung up on anything long until the very last level. I'm of the belief that any game that has life bars or HP counts in them should stray away from including any instant killing factors (aside for bottemless pits anyway since that's just how it goes with pits). The final level is literally full of things designed to kill you in one hit. You'd probably think "well the last level is suppose to be hard, right?" and you would have merit to think this. But at the same time this game has you putting forth a lot of exploration and effort into finding heart squids to increase your HP. What is the point of this if when the final level comes you'll just die in one hit anyway? Is it challenging? Yes. It's also bad design.
Ultimately I did enjoy this game. The animations were sexy, adorable, and happy. The puzzles were mostly moderate or easy. The story was silly and fun. It didn't have quite the same flair as Risky's Revenge (the loss of magic really hit the alure), but I still recommend it.

If you like a game where you build up infrastructure and technical knowledge from raw resources, this is your game.  It is a lot like civilization and minecraft in different ways.  Like Minecraft Factorio has the player mine resources to build and expand your base/factory, and like Civilation there is a tree you research to get the next bigger and better tech.  The tech tree is  extensive and keeps you excited to see what the next effect will do for you.  Technologies fall into four broad categories(in my opinion) of production(product assembly, robots,  and mining), power generation and distribution(steam generators -> solar -> nuclear), transportation(trains, robots, and conveyers), and military(ammo type, turrets, lasers, rockets, atomic bombs).
There are multiple types of resources(stone, coal, iron, copper, crude oil, and uranium), most of which need to be refined in some manner.  I found refining crude oil to be a blast as it breaks it down into heavy oil, light oil, and petroleum gas which can be made into different products.  In turn you can crack heavy oil into light oil and light oil into petroleum gas if thats what you need for your factory at the time.  You end up researching the different processes in your tech tree to more efficiently break down the crude.  I personally found it exciting to see what new substances and products I could make with those raw materials.
When you first start out you will think that patch of iron you're sitting on will last forever.  As you progress, however, you'll find yourself eating through resources and needing to go out and explore for more.  In the process you will start building a train network, and let me tell you, it is a blast to watch your trains taking care of business and dumping huge amounts of ore into your ore refinery(They move MASSIVE amounts of material).  It's always fun to see what big patch of resources you can find, and who knows, maybe you'll find a nice rich patch of Uranium.
The one aspect of the game which I didn't enjoy was the enemy bugs that will attack you as your pollution grows.  I personally love the building aspects of the game and found fighting the bugs annoying and sometimes took away from my building time.  The cool part is you get to try out those new weapons you researched and assembled in your factory, or get to watch those new shiny laser turrets obliterate the enemy as they charge your walls.  I can forgive the annoying aspect of the bugs, however, because the developers did something extraordinary in the free play game to allow you to adjust how aggressive they are, or simply to turn them off.  Very few games I have seen with the level of control they give you over the enemies you'll have in a game.  I can't tell you how relieved and grateful I was that the developers added this control!
I will leave this off by saying that there are many aspects of this game which can become complicated and are lacking a good tutorial(the game is still in development).  I suggest going to YouTube and searching for Factorio tutorials to get the instruction you need to use certain parts of the game.  It's also a great place to get a bit of a review before playing.  Hope this helps anyone thinking about this game! Thanks!

Overall I feel this game is improving. Definitely a game that requires some creativity, but also a lot of fun.
Creative to survival conversion worlds are fun to make, castle sieges are fun, and creating challenges for players is also a lot of fun. Creative mode and Castle Siege are both quite enjoyable and often go hand-in-hand. Survival mode is currently not the best although improvements are definitely being made.
Devs tend to be responsive and fix issues (Obviously some things take longer than others to fix, but work is obviously being done).
That being said, it's time for the devs to prove their responsiveness. My message to KSH:
-Remove Food meter from survival mode. Make the food a healing/stamina boost item or something instead. This is an engineering game, and running around frantically picking mushrooms and pumpkins is boring and takes time away from building an awesome castle.
-Remove research tree. Instead just make more resource types, like space engineers has. The current research system is boring, grindy, and again simply not fun.
These could be made world settings as well, but these two mechanics are really what I feel like are detracting from the experience. Whatever sense of 'realism' or 'challenge' these mechanics are meant to create is completely offset by the frustration they create. A game that's centered on engineering should reward the player for their designs, and the food system doesn't do that. Even with farming, there are little options for creativity in design, and it takes a substantial amount of time to unlock the farming machinery in the equally frustrating research system. This time is, of course, made longer by the fact that the player needs to periodically go gather food to survive.
The current strategy I employ is in fact rushing the construction of a bed, then completely forgetting about food and simply building until I die, at which point I just spawn again and continue working. I don't think this is how the game is intended to be played, and certainly the constant interuptions aren't fun. Fix this. I would rather see "Removed survival meters and research tree" in the next update than I would "Fixed physics clang issues."
Still posting a positive review, as the game is genuinely fun. Just needs some work, which will probably get done, and that's the danger of early access.

YES! This game is way better now. I am writing this not long after the 0.6 update has dropped and I'm happy to see that two of my biggest complaints about the game (and many other annoyances) have been fixed. I still don't think this game is by any means perfect,
Though in my last review I was very close to giving it a thumbs up despite all its shortcomings, Now I am still nervous about giving the game a thumbs up despite its strengths. So lets start off with the bad stuff. Some of this stuff is complaints from my old review that have yet to be resolved.
-Barbarians (NPC enemies) are still dumb as bricks and easily defeated by standing on a wooden platform. Their spawn patterns have also proven to be annoying to me. I was attacked by several waves of barbs very early on in a surival game and died several times since I had not yet the means to defend myself. Yet later on when I was more well equipped, I did not encounter any barbarians. (They have useful loot, espeically in their weapons which can be melted down and made into tools.) This might have just been dumb luck on my part, however it would be very frustrating to a new player.
-It's still hard to make structures look unique. I still long to be able to whitewash castles. Decorating with small grid blocks (wood) allows you to do some sprucing up and you can make lavish and cozy interiors with a little enginuity.
-Flax is an extremely annoying resource. It's hard to find naturally occuring, takes a long time to farm, and 50% of the flax you farm will go back into seeds to produce the next crop. Fortunatley with this update it seems much less neccesary to tech up.
-Timbers/planks are now extremely annoying to craft as they take much more time in the inventory screen. I know this is in place to encourage players to use the new sawmill mechanic but getting the resources to build such a facility will be extremely late in a survival game. This can be circumvented by having a crafting bench and putting 7 logs in it; cuing the timbers you want and leaving the bench. The timbers will continue to craft and you can return in about a minute and have them.
Now the good stuff:
-The new biomes are excellent.( The lack of diversity in the world is actually a major complaint I had in my old review so I am happy to see this resolved) I haven't even explored all of them yet, but from what i've seen they're a huge improvement. I do wish the tropical enviroment were a bit more like a tropical rainforest rather than simply a grassy plain with a few palms scattered about.
-There are new sets of tools. Copper, Bronze, and Steel. This is a welcome addition. In my first few hours of playing, I managed to get hold of a Steel hammer (presumably the highest teir of tools being steel). It is incredibly powerful, able to build blocks very quickly, and well worth the effort that went into acquiring the resources to make it. I can't wait to make a full collection of every tool with every material and display them all using weapon racks.
-I haven't even gotten to try the mechanic blocks yet (survival player here). I will hopefully come back and update this with my thoughts on those. They seem like a very cool idea and it's nice to have something that the title screen video has been teasing us with for a long time actually exist within the game.
-The new quest system is vastly superior to the 'Sacrifice resources to learn to build new thing at the research table'. Like that you can choose what quest you want to do next; choose the things that are interesting to you. As the game is developed and becomes more complex, I hope that this is expanded on. It is also a great system for new players as it introduces the mechanics slowly and helps the player learn each step before moving onto the next.
-Also it seems like your character's ability to pull large carts has been improved. Some may find it a bit ridiculous that you can pull a cart with four fully loaded ore baskets at sprinting speed, but with the amount of grinding and back and fourth trips you'd have to do otherwise, I think you'll agree that its nothing to complain about.

Some people have had their stats blanked never to return to normal. That is a ton of time to put into a game, and have all the work disappear. The next thing is that the servers are hosted and not public. All of that said, I still love this game. The maps are big enough to feel big and use vehicles, but small enough to not feel like you are playing Arma/DayZ and just running around. I would like to first say that I liked this game. While I'm sure that many people scoff at VN's, particularly these kinds, they're also just looking at the cover for the game and making up their opinions from there.
I would not call this the best Visual Novel I've ever experienced. It is very abbreviated, it's plot feels very condensed and there's only two choices in the game near the very end. However, this VN has a lot of heart and charm to it, the characters are likable, understandable and charming, it has a decent amount of humor and is aware of itself.
When one of the characters, Kyo (The girl with the aqua colored hair) goes out to shop with Kenji (The protagonist) she wears what looks like a black lingerie slip, which is what she usually wears, and I thought to myself, don't tell me you're wearing that outside, and Kenji mimics my thoughts and questions how she can wear it outside as well.
It is not just limited to being aware of itself in humor though, it also tries its best to address certain expected aspects of a game like this. While it doesn't do it in a deconstructive way or analyze it too deeply, it does go out of its way to make it so certain cliches are presented as realistically as it can and tries to address certain qualities of other VN's that people groan at. This doesn't mean it doesn't have its fanservice but it's clearly not supposed to just be about the fanservice, I've seen VN's that are, and I can certainly say that the creators of this game were not going for that.
I recommend this game to people that want to support the creators. This is apparently their first game and I can see that they have potential to stretch out and get better at making VN's and that they do want to tell an interesting story while also having some goofy or fanservicy moments along the way. Most Visual Novels don't come over to America from across the sea and so I would be very happy to see more companies make them in my own country. But they need support to get to the point where we can get more complex stories and different genres. So please, if you want to see more VN's, give this one a shot, it doesn't cost much and its a pretty relaxed ride through the game.

Do you like boobs? Do you like really big boobs? Well then this is the game for you. There's plenty of boobs, but the actual storyline ends on a cliffhanger right when it starts to pick up, with only a message announcing a sequel to be released in early 2016 to give you hope of seeing more boobs. It's not nearly as bad as I've learned to expect from an American visual novel, but it is a mostly kinetic novel, with only two choices placed near the very end of the game that don't really have any lasting effects, and I was able to see everything the game had in less than 3 hours, so it's probably better to wait for a sale for this one. But at least the boobs were nice.

So...
The idea behind the story, as far as I have experienced it, is an interesting one. (But, I would have really liked if there HAD been, you know, similar interesting consequences to the time-travelling on Tenshi... Something unique could have been explored there, is what I'm saying.)
The quality of the art/pictures is pretty great, except for a few odd cases where the characters appear 'hand-drawn in a much lower quality'.
One thing of note though, as several people already mentioned :
The *severe* lack of choices, of being able to actually 'DO' anything- be 'involved' in the story. A lack of even simple ''artificial choices'', like being able to decide which girl to go talk to first/in what order you want to go talk to them(like in the beginning)... I seriously doubt this would have been something hard to implement, especially in such a game, yet it would have made a world of difference.
So, yeah, a game that is easy to like (especially if you are one of the MANY people with a soft spot/weakness for charming characters), but it really didn't have the weight it definitely could had have, if it had offered more real or artificial choices (and not just *barely* 2, right at the end, which really hurt replayability).
(Oh, and one significant inconsistency I found : In the beginning, it's said that Tenshi was at the hospital for about 2weeks, after the house burning/parents' death, to insure he was 'ok' all around, yet he later says to Michelle that his parent died '3 days' ago.)

I am having a lot of fun playing this game.  The girls look pretty and mature (as opposed to a lot of these types of visual novels where we have little/anorexic girls), the time travel theme is interesting, and the initial tragedy of losing your parents is a good hook to take the game seriously in the beginning.  I know it's more of a book than a game given a lack of choices, but it's good to read and look at.  I enjoyed the dialogue where Kenji (who you play as) enjoys looking at Michelle and doubts her sexy armor could actually protect. There are playthroughs on youtube if you feel you need to get more samples of dialogue.
