I played this when Steam first came out. My god, that was so long ago. In combination with Steam's launch populartizing HL1, so was Sven Coop. And it was really fun to play.
And quite a bit has changed, considerably.
Pros:
It's Half Life One, They hunger and several other mod campaigns merged into one, all of wich can be completed in single player (if you're really good at the game, most maps are forgiving though)
The playermodel selection is vast. From the HECU to being Boba Fett, you have a really nice selection of models to choose from.
Player colors, albeit limited, do exist. However, no neutral colors exist so no black/gray/white which kills off a lot of cool color combos.
It's free with no microtransactions and it never will have any.
If you own Opposing Force and Blue Shift, you can use the files in the svencoop folder to mount them on. And it does it flawlessly.
New HD (I mean REALLY HD) models, the look is extremely improved in comparison from the originals in 1999 and in 2004. You can chose between Software and OpenGL renders.
Heavily Optimized. Even if you own a potato, it will probably run about 30FPS on the highest possible settings.
Up to 32 players to go on a total massive rampage through various maps.
Voteban/Votekick/Votemap/Votemute to deal with trolls, squeakers, the average internet warrior in general.
Developers that actually care. Previously, I had joke that in the past 12 years I played this, they never added the Baclava HECU as a playermodel. They did in the first update shortly after the game came out (whether or not it is coincidental is beyond me but thanks anyway Sven Devs!)
Less than 1 GB in size yet it packs a huge amount of content.
Cons:
Like most gold source games, there's an Alias system. Which means you can use spoof names and freely troll and cause probelms and no one will know who you actually are on steam.
People can colide with one another, which can cause problems in terms of blocking doorways or breaking passages (that's what votekills is for though)
The Color system doesn't factor in White/Gray/Black, so the you're stuck with Red,Orange,Yellow,Green,Blue, Indigo, Violet and whatever colors are inbetween these.
All in all, it's an excellent game, most of the cons on based on opinion anyway. It's a good game to gather friends, and have a good time all in all. And it's easily playable by anyone, even if you own a rusty toaster. So Go ahead and download this game, have a blast!

No hours on steam because I started playing this exclusively through glyph, not knowing it was even on steam. I played the alpha, and currently have a level 30 in the game.
Despite the negative reviews here on Steam, this game really isn't bad. Playing this game with a friend or two is enjoyable, and it could be enjoyable for anyone who liked the click-and-kill playstyle of Torchlight or Diablo. Of course, this game doesn't offer the depth that Diablo does (it's a F2P MMO ARPG), and there's really no point in reading the quest logs or trying to follow the story (the voice acting is bad, and the story is just another fantasy do-gooder story). But there's a good bit of content to the game. Leveling is not that bad of a grind compared to other F2P games like TERA, and the zones change graphically and consistently. Each zone has something unique about it, which is refreshing, and there is a variation to the monsters within the game. The quests also have variations, changing from kill quests, to collect quests, to dungeons, and to doing A-then-B. But really, how much questing variation can there be in a top-down MMO?
It's also not "pay to win", like most people would find joy in whining about. You can either pay for XP-Gold boosts, cosmetics, and other items - or you don't. No one is forcing you to buy anything, and there are no things to buy that would up your DPS, health, or other stats over anyone who didn't buy them. Unless looking different is a stat. Like most other F2P companies, the creators of Devilian are trying to make a living from what they have spent their time and money on to make. It's mostly children whining about the inhumanity of having to pay for something that someone else has created for you to enjoy. Shocking. It's a growing concern that this is a hard lesson for children to learn. So, don't let the F2P model of Devilian turn you off from the game.
If you're looking for a F2P, Torchlight/Diablo-esque MMOARPG, then go for it. Devilian may not have the depth you want, but it may fill that gap for a while. I can't comment on the end-game content or the PVP, because I have not reached it yet, but I understand the game has an endless dungeon and heroic-mode dungeons, as well as PVP tier items and rewards - so the content is there. If you don't know what you're looking for, but enjoy F2P games, then you should also try Devilian, because it is one of the better F2P games that I have tried. The dungeons are fun, and you can even solo them if you want. Character customization is as deep as you make it, because there are cards you can choose to buff you character, and there are max-level "perks" you can put points in to (similar to Diablo 3's max-level perks). The skill-trees are interesting, and you can put points into multiple trees at a time, rather than being forced to pick from only one tree.
However, there have been server issues on the EU side that I did not experience (I have been playing on the US server), but I have heard of them. While it is a shame that these issues happened, please understand that this happened on the second day of an MMO's launch. While these issues are not great, fun, or acceptable - they happen. I've played MMO's for years, and I expect these things to happen, regardless of wanting them to. Please note that this issue shouldn't define the entire game as being bad, and please take negative reviews that are based solely on this issue with a grain of salt.

I've played quite a fair few MMO's in my time and one's similar to Devilian, so let's get started.
Devilian has the graphics and art for a modern day, MMO, top-down RPG. The music is quite nice as well, the enemies are quite well designed - bosses especially. The NPC's repeat the same thing when you talk to them, annoying but you tune it out eventually. It's also got a nice story to go alongside it that even has a bit of side story here and there.
Character skill system is nice, you're able to reset points freely so you can try out different skills as you want to mix things up. There's 3 catergories you can choose from each with skills and bonuses towards them, as you spend more points in each one that unlocks more skills and bonuses.
There are some bugs/glitches here and there but it's early days, it's not been out long but it's pretty stable for the most part.
Contrary to popular belief, it is in no way pay to win. There is an in-game store, yes, but it only has the following: 2 mounts, some pets, cosmetic items, exp/gold boosts, inventory/character/warehouse slot increases, appearance/rename changes. Overall, nothing that constitutes as pay to win. Leveling isn't even that difficult really, it slows down as is  the case with any MMO but that's common and you can just grind out dungeons or complete the quests.
Overall, it's nice to see this type of MMO again. It's early on so give it a try and if it's not your cup of tea then leave it and come back after some updates or just don't play it. If you like Diablo, MMO's and want to try something a bit new then give it a shot.
PS: There's boob physics if you're wondering.

I'm a fan of the 'Sniper Elite' series anyway so the Zombie version was a given for me.  There was a time when I wasn't too crazy for zombie games but I've become a fan of them over time and this sniper version gets addictive.  There's Steam achievements to farm for as well as Steam trading cards.
The graphics are the game's strong point.  It's an older game in the graphics engine area really but they've done a nice job of giving you an X-Ray look to head shots and critical blows that differs from other games (let alone zombie games).  There's a chase camera (the same as 'Sniper Elite' original chase camera) that will follow the bullet to it's target and upon impact explode in 'X-Ray' fashion that illuminates bones and tissue tears.  It's just such a nice thing to see happen to a zombie.
The game happens in waves as with most zombie games.  Weapons become available on the battlefield and there's different 'safe rooms' you come across in the game where you can reload or change weapons.
One of the 'must have' zombie games in my opinion.  It goes on sale enough so it's best to pick it up then.

I got this game in a bundle sale, for what, 3 dollars? 5 dollars? I've forgotten by now. I am not recommending this game, at 20 dollars or on sale. Maybe at 5 dollars it would be worth it... But the combat system is absolutely broken.
Combat works in this game turn based - portraits of characters/entities located on the map (which consists of pretty much a city block, 4 buildings or so). Your character moves/attacks, uses action points to use actions, perfectly fine. It works great.
But the long as ♥♥♥♥ loading times/switching times as you end your characters turns is just horrid. Lets say you have your small squad of 4 survivors out to scout. You go to a supermarket location, where since it's a super market lots of zombies are around. Standard zombie worldbuilding element, all good.
Until you kill, or try to kill, your first zombie on the map. If you succeed in killing them silently and in one turn, great! You can exit the combat mode and keep looting/exploring. Fail though, and the zombie will shamble towards you. Which would be fine, if the combat system didn't go through every single ♥♥♥♥ing zombie on the map, even if they're on the far edges. So you spend minutes per turn, not because you have to plan out your best moves or most efficient use of Action Points, but just waiting for when it's your turn again.
Story is ok, I have no problems with it. Could be better, but it's perfectly fine for a game. Graphics aren't the best, but eh. It works, and I don't need superb stuff. Portraits of characters (when you talk to them) are all fine, detailed enough.
Gameplay is just horribly broken though. I quit playing because 5 minutes per turn is dumb. And if you use guns/loud noise weapons, you will drag zombies in from the edges of the map. So you can get ♥♥♥♥ed in this cycle of "shoot zombie" "zombie dead" "more zombie from edge of map comes along and sees you" "battle mode triggers, zombie gets first turn and bites you".
It's enjoyable enough. I liked playing it. Until I went on three different locations with a ♥♥♥♥♥on of zombies. Then I just quit.  One zombie dead, two zombies dead, three zombies dead. Oh, end turn... five minutes later kill another zombie, and repeat.
Yeah. It needs a fast-forward option during combat. Except I got some issues with fps/client freezing (temporarily though) with the 20+ zombies at location. So I'd end my turn, then client freeze for a few seconds, then I wait for zombies to move around.
2/10 because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ combat system.

If anyone's interested here's an opinion from a veteran Jagged Alliance & XCOM player.
Dead State isn't linear but still it's is much a story & character driven game, so for one playthrough it can be a lot of fun. Maybe for two even, if you play the first game as a good & kind hero-type, and the second playthrough as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ready to rule all of the new world. Or vice versa. I liked the story, the background and how the characters and dialogues are written, and there are many good ideas being used here. And while it's not a 4x game, the map is still pretty big and has some interesting places to visit, and random encounters. Would be awesome, if the locations would change, so when you start a new game, you wouldn't know exactly where to travel beforehand.
Someone recommend Dead State as a Jagged Alliance -type of game... but can't really compare it with all the cool and awesomeness of the JA2. I mean RPG side here is fine with dialogues and decisions, but tactical side - not so much. The combat is fun at first, later not that enjoyable, and gets repeative after you learn some basic maneuvers how to deal with zombies. Although sometimes it's interesting if you're seemingly overpowered by numbers and one of yours is wounded or unconscious or runs away. Compared to XCOM though, the combat system and the enemy AI is pretty primitive - some good ideas are used here too, like several different modes for weapons. Still, it felt it never got really challenging. I was playing the famous XCOM Long War Mod at the time - so maybe because of this Dead State didn't give much tactical challenge. So, combat is good at it's best, but gets dull after a while.
Also, real time mode and turn based mode, they just don't sync that well - it's not terrible but not good either. Like: Shooting attracts the zeds, so the more you shoot the more zombies you have to deal with. But after the firefight you go on real time mode, and the zeds start to just casually walking upon you. So you have to keep an eye and go to turn based to prevent them just walking right next to you and bite. I wish this would have been handled differently. I mean you can work with the system, it's not hopeless, but it's cumbersome and gamey.
Still, I do hope there will be a Dead State 2, with some improvements in tactical game, as I would buy it. I can recommend this game too, while it's not great and lacks better combat, it's still interesting, compelling, exciting and fun at best, and in some ways original and enjoyably different to many main genre games, so for the price it's basically a deal.

Marlow Briggs is simply pure, dumb fun. This is a God of War/DMC cheap clone that at 5 bucks (or less on sale) is a steal. Self aware, absurd, and beyond stupid in the best, over the top, 80's style action possible.
+/- Graphics - for a budget title, graphics are really good. Lip synching isn't the best, bust graphics are bright and fun, matching the over the top atmosphere. Explosions about, and everything just works. Some environments are repetitive, and there could be more enemy variety, but what does exist really does feel like a nice jungle/industrial vide well. Overall pretty if not exceptional graphics. One note, probably due to budget, not all cutscenees are fully rendered, but instead play out in comic book style action frames. They look good and convey the action well, but would have been so much more epic in real time.
+/- Sound and voice work is mostly competent, if pretty flat. No stadouts here at all. Better maybe than what you'd expect for a $5 game, but nothing more. Explosions and combat sounds are good though. Again, nothing exceptional but fit the game well. Only thing would have made it better is if either Marlow, or the villian, Mr. Long, were better done to fully match the cheesy 80's vibe.
+/- Story is pure 80's cheese and I mean that in the best way possible. Everything is exploding, you are kicking♥♥♥♥♥and throwing puns, your mask sidekick mocks you when you die, and the bad guy absurdly sets up why everything is basically a deathtrap. This isn't a good story. It's clinche and dumb as hell. But it's fun.
+/- Combat, being the core of the game, is mostly well done. Learning to dodge and block, switching up between your varied attacks, and using combo's is the name of the game. We aren't talking Bayonetta or DMC level of complexity, but it works well. Movements are sometimes a bit sluggesh however, most noticably during some "challeges" where even on missed jump means instant death. Despite those "Challenge" sections, I found the game to be pretty responsive.
If you are looking for big, brash, stupid, 80's action movie style gameplay that is just fun. Look no further. For $5 bucks or less, you simply can't go wrong. Happily give it a 4/5 due to it just being stupidly fun and a steal when on sale.

I only bought this game 2 weeks ago and I've already logged over 100+ hours. As a long time player of Space Engineers (850+ Hours) It took me around the same amount of time to play just as many hours after first purchasing the game(s).  Both of which are incredibly satifying to the open-sandbox/survival genre, I've come to love.  While the survival aspects of the game aren't yet fully developed, and the game is still in early access I will re-write this review when this game gets its actual release.
So what is there to like:
- Crafting & Gathering
> There seems to be a fair balance between how long you spend harvesting compared to how long you can spend using those resources.  There isn't that much of a grind here, alternatively if you don't like that challenge there is a creative mode.
- Farming
> Plow, Seed, Grow, and Harvest Stages/ which can be sped up by making cool little carts to pull.
- Technology Tree
> Currently this is pretty basic, you give resources to get access to building certain blocks in survival. Some techs however can't be researched without another so it makes for a bit of a challenge when getting started but ultimately ends fairly fast.
- Construction
> With physical limitations and quite a selection of blocks you can sometimes get carried away before that tall tower of sticks comes crumbling down; better build it out of stone.
- Voxel Based
> The world is destructable and formable in, creative and survival; survival being quite limited to that of creative.
- Physics implementations
> This is appearently being over-hauled; but even currently it is quite unique. Using mechanics to your advantage... You can create working catapults, mangonels, and trebuchets, the last being the most fun (and dangerous).  Then there are many other creations, contraptions, and ideas to be experimented with, such as cranes, farm equipment, carts, and more.
Not to Like:
- The Videos shown in the Main Menu are decieving and many of the blocks shown there are no longer included in the game.
- Lacks Over-All Content; while there is much to do there seems like there could be so much more.
- The Introduction/Quest(s) in the game drop-off without much warning; although from that point it is pretty straight forward on what's left to do. Build and don't run out of food; even though there isn't much consequence for it and getting it is fairly easy to do.  Lastly it always seems to be taking up space in my inventory because you can't last more than a little while without it.
There is so much more I could say but the bottom line is would I recommend it?
Yes it is worth the current price if you enjoyed Space Engineers and like Sandbox Games;
If you're looking for Combat, In-Depth Survival, or Physics Simulators then No.

The last good Battlefield, plain and simple.
DICE/EA went on to copy CoD in every BF title starting here, however this is the game that got it right. Each successive title tried to blend weird action combat with the old BF style and it just didn't come out right. Here, however, the game design completely revels in NOT being Battlefield and it somehow succeeds in making the most entertaining modern BF experience.
For instance, the map design is much smaller overall, the prone stance was removed, jets and commanders aren't present, and the class count is cut down to 4. To most people, this seems like a straight downgrade, but what it does it make for a more fast paced BF experience while also keeping a lot of tactical play. Something like being sniped from very far away with an assault rifle or vehicle is minimized here (not removed entirely however, some maps are more open than others) compared to mainline BF titles and instead infantry pushes are much more important. I can't feel but mention the importance of the 'Rush' mode the game introduces. It's something that BF always needed. Instead of playing keep away with capturing conquest points, both teams have to play around objectives which makes the conflict happen.
There are a wide variety of weapons for whatever situation and style you like instead of a 'go-to' OP weapon that fixes everything (Carl Gustav aside). Each weapon is very satisfying to use with an impactful recoil and reload cycle; which comes to one of the most underrated aspects of the game: the audio.
Special care was taken in the audio of this game. I cannot even put it into words in a simple review, you just have to put on some headphones and hear for yourself. No BF title since has put this much detail into the sounds of conflict. Each gun has a distinct and satisfying firing sound. Every little thing in the game makes a noticeable sound which can and will work for/against you in situations. Rounds can be heard in the distance and shells ejected from a shotgun will echo in empty areas. The audio direction is simply engrossing.
The game isn't without its issues, however I feel like the issues it does have are present in nearly every BF title. Things like being sniped by ordinary weapons, vehicle abuse, explosive abuse, etc., all still very much modern BF problems and they're present to some degree here for sure, but not enough to commonly detract from the overall experience.
The overall player pool may be smaller now in 2015, but believe me when I say that you can still get a good round in from time to time. Check this out if you got a few bucks to spare and were let down by BF3/4/HL.

Got the game in a giveaway and well... Since I didn't spent any money, I can't say it wasn't that bad of an experience. I had 0 prior knowledge of this game before getting it and honestly it isn't too bad, but it has quite a share of problems. As I usually do in my reviews, I'll start talking about the problems it has, then move to the possitive points, that way you can judge by yourself if the game is worth it or not for you.
First and foremost, while I like parodies, references and such in video-games, this game just goes too far with it. 90% of the characters are references and parodies of something, some parts of the small amount of history are references, it gets old really fast. It just makes me remember games I could be playing instead of this, and some are even lame. Then there's the fact that the game is all about forging weapons and there's not really that many weapons from other games, just characters. The "Legendary Heroes" task you about making them a weapon from their original character but there's really not that many and some don't even ask for weapons. Gordon Freeman for example, instead of asking you to forge his trademark crowbar or gravity-gun instead asks you to build HL-3, which might make someone laugh but it just comes down as predictable to me by the point I had to do it. It could've also used more normal weapons that reference something or more weapons in some categories such as throwable and handguns, which have around 5 or 6 max while there's about 25 swords, daggers and staffs.
The game is also a bit grind-heavy in the later stages of the game. You'll be told that your next objective in the story is to reach, let's say, 50.000 fame, and when you finally manage it the game gives you a few lines of dialogue and sets you a new objective of 125.000 fame or so, then doing it all over again. And fame is not earned that fast, so you'll be stuck there building weapons over and over just to struggle and get through it.
There's also a small issue with freezing. Dunno why but at startup the game freezes after skipping the logos for around 10-15 seconds, then freezes again when loading the save, then freezes AGAIN when a random fate question pops up, it can't be that my computer is trash when I've managed to play motherf#cking XCOM 2 from start to finish 2 times already, that ain't MY fault.
Lastly, the story itself is... Well, nothing to write home about. With all the constant non-stop references you'd think the devs would make something to make their game memorable. Well, they didn't. The story is there because it might as well be. There's 3 characters in the whole story, 4 if you count a dog that won't ever talk or do something meaningful. Nothing really develops and the ending is both sudden and quite dissapointing.
Now, holy f#ck nuggets even I feel like I'm being a bit harsh. The game does have some good stuff, it's just hard to stop looking at the negatives at times.
The whole reference-overload stuff can have it's possitives, mainly the legendary heroes. There should have been more, and some feel forced, however I do like the idea a lot and getting to build something for once was a decent break from the generic farming for fame and money.
The art and graphics are also surprisingly good, characters look great and the music fits well with the whole theme. My only complain would be that the music was quite loud on my computer, was forced to change it in the options menu to the lowest setting and even then it sounded with the same strenght that most of my other games, which is really weird.
The gameplay is also entertaining enough until repetition starts to set in at the last stages. There's plenty to do and build. Just think of Game Dev Tycoon but about building weapons, you'll get the idea.
Lastly, the questions you get from time to time based on other heroes and games are actually a really fun idea and managed to make me forget the poor job with the overuse of references for a while.
Do I recommend this game? Well, it's a tough question. I do see good in this game, however for 15€!? No, not at all. There's better alternatives out there that are cheaper and don't drown the player in pointless references. However in a reasonable sale, I'd say it would entertain you well enough. The game has decent replayability and if you played at games like Game Dev Tycoon, then you'll know what you're getting yourself into, though this game is easier. If you haven't played that game, go look it up instead of this one.
TL;DR Edition: A decent management-simulator game that sadly drowns the player with references in a silly attempt of comedy instead of focusing in having an actually memorable history. However the gameplay is decent enough for me to recommend it, though at a big sale. 15€ is way too much in my oppinion.

Really brings me back to my childhood, one of my favorite mods ever finally has a home on steam as a standalone product, and it's completely free! Essentially Half Life levels modded to have co-op functionality, as well as custom levels created by the development team and the community. Playing Half Life 1 with friends is pretty enjoyable, but I think it's the faster paced custom levels that really shine. Well known favorites like the cartoonish Toon World return, plus some really wacky ones like this one map having me play in an RTS-like mode, commanding other players. There are team based competitions, puzzle solving adventures, tricky platforming levels, and more generic massive warfare shoot 'em ups. It's so fun to see what map is loading next, I honestly almost never know what to expect.♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is cool.
Why are there even negative recommendations? I'm sorry that this free game that's usually a nearly two decade old engine looks and plays somewhat ugly? The game is based off of Half Life 1, so there's no reason to think the game will look modern in any way, but the gameplay fun more than makes up for it. This game really takes me back, and I'm certain that you'd have a good time blasting vortigaunts with friends and strangers alike. Some of my most memorable, "formative" gaming years were over 10 years ago just running with groups of strangers opening fire on giant enemies in tandem while playing earlier versions of this mod, and I'm so glad it's back.
If you've never played Sven Co-op, you're missing out on a world of wacky fun.

Starwars is one of cinema's holy grounds. In the world of gaming, it's no pushover: but with gems like this, it really does cement itself as perhaps the most accessible science-fiction story ever.

With an intentionally claustraphobic HUD, blisteringly tense action and a smooth and sublimely easy - to - use squad command system, RC put's you straight into the action as the Republic's right hand, and you'll love every second.
Recommended to Starwars fans, as well as people looking for a little something different in their shooters!

Amazing game.  Buy it!  The writing is terse but perfectly composed:  you get to know these characters and care when they die, or turn against you, or become disillusioned with your leadership (yes, all this can happen organically within the game system).  This game creates a tremendous sense of atmosphere and freedom:  every place, however insignificant, has a story if you look closely, and the game throws plot events at you at a slow but believable pace that lets you explore and deal with the crises that emerge naturally from the dynamics of the world and your own play style.  This is one of the very few times I have felt like I do when playing a tabletop RPG with a truly excellent GM.  This writer knows what he is doing.  Plus... this is a very satisfyingly long game, especially given the price:  look above to see how many hours I've given this game and I haven't finished it nor can I guess how it might end other than... well... badly.  But that is the apocalypse!

Dead state the game with potential that just simply falls short.
When i first saw this game i thought it would be a great game with micromanagable features to make everyones experience different and in a way it is but there is so much that is missing in this game to make it really great.
First of all if you are buying this game hoping for a breeze then you are FAR FROM IT. This game is challenging. Not just challenging but almost unplayable at points due to the general difficulty right from the start. Now i played this on its base difficulty with no \"iron man\" or \"survivor\" options enabled and this game is still ridiculously hard.
Don\'t get me wrong. I love a good challenging game, it makes me feel alive and puts me to the test. But this game takes it way too far as after a good 9 hours gameplay i still feel so weak against everything. I had 3 fully equiped survivors out on a mission but we got stuck in a room and only one could fight at a time meaning that the endless horde of zombies waiting very politely outside the door ended up getting the better of me ONE BY ONE.
Not only is it hard when it is supposed to be but the features it lacks makes it even more fustrating. Want your guys to take cover behind an obstacle to avoid missle fire? Nope. Want to climb on top of a nearby building to escape a zombie horde? Nope. Want to simply trade an item within your shelter to a friendly survivor? Nope.
These are just many of the infuriating events that can occur to you and happened to me basically every event. However this game isn\'t all bad. If you feel inclined to challenge yourself to the point you regretably put a hole through your monitor than be my guest because this game has so much to it and can be so much more. I just think that for a \"survival strategy\" there has to be some element of strategy other than just luck and using the right weapon.
Unfortunately the good outweighs the bad for this one so i simply can\'t recommend :(

One of those frustrating games where ambition has outstripped ability to execute. The concept is great - managing a shelter of survivors of a zombie apocalypse - and there's a stack of looting, crafting and even diplomacy to do. It's often well-written, and throws up interesting choices.
Unfortunately it's all held back by the combat system. It's slow, it doesn't feel like there are many options (no overwatch/defensive stance), the bottlenecks caused by the narrow grid system are more irritating than strategic and the AI is really frustrating - just had a prime example where a human enemy had two zombies gnawing away at him, but kept shooting at my unconscious character until she died. Maps filled with zombies should be thrilling, but instead become tedious - even when 95% aren't involved in the current combat, the game torturously goes through every one each combat turn. That's 20+ seconds *each turn* of the game flicking through portraits with nothing happening.
It also has some dubious design decisions, such as requiring that your character be on every scavenging mission. Even if you have 20+ people at the shelter, and your character is best suited to leading behind the scenes, you must go out.
Not only does this discourage focusing on the leadership/negotiation skills, it means you're at a constant disadvantage as you have to either sacrifice a day of scavenging to rest or constantly have a character with half their HP.
Speaking of negotiation, it offers a lot of promise but is too reliant on hidden triggers. One example was when I had a heart-to-heart with a survivor and finished by asking him to ask how I was the next time we saw each other. I ran up to him with anticipation the next day...and only had the option of repeating that very same conversation. It made the whole thing feel empty and pointless. Likewise, a tense conversation with a militia leader over one of my survivors was interesting - but it fell flat when the exact same exchange was repeated the next time I visited.
Perhaps the biggest problem is the lack of a mid-game. Food and morale were never a problem for me after the first few days, which takes a lot of the tension out of the game. It just becomes a loop of exploration and looting, with the occasional interesting crisis or encounter. Not all that bad, just far from what it could have been.
That really sums up the game - it's decent enough, but could have been so much more. I still recommend buying it if you can get it cheap. It is still more enjoyable than many games, with a lot of content, and it's worth a shot to experience the positives; it's just depressing to imagine what it might have been.

Tyler Perry Presents: The God of The War (patent pending)
It's God of War for people that want the cover to fool customers into thinking it's a basketball game.
Run, shoot, dunk on ballas that can't step to your game. I think they wanted to make a franchise out of this, what with the character's name on the damn title. Too bad it's all mediocre.
The combat is of the button mashing variety. There are plenty of combos that take the form of a light and heavy attack, with combinations being strung together. The problem with that sort of combo system is that you can't expect me to remember all the 'XXXY, XXXX, XYXX, YXXY' combos. It winds up just being a button masher with a combo system that has too much to memorize for it's own good. You wind up memorizing three or so moves and just constantly mash those out.
It's boring as hell. Simplicity isn't bad, route memorization is. Metal Gear Rising had a similar set-up, but the memorization was kept to a minimum. The fun in combat lied in keeping your blue gauge up and getting those quick kills. The Arkham titles have an even simpler battle system, with the challenge being in continuing your chain of attack while thwarting enemies with properly placed counters. Marlow Briggs presents nothing unique or interesting in its combat. It's just randomly hitting buttons with the challenge lying in simply keeping your health gauge up. There's nothing rewarding in the combat itself.
Apart from the mediocre combat, the game has light platforming and puzzle elements. When you aren't busy fighting, you'll be traversing the level with fixed camera angles. The platforming is all pretty barebones and boils down to jumping across pits and pressing the action button when appropriate. Swinging from cliffs and walking across ledges would be a lot more exciting if there was any sort of challenge to it beyond pressing a button. The fact that the camera angles are fixed means that there's not even any challenge in finding how to proceed. It's all meant to look nice and tantamount to simply pressing right on the joystick while ocassionally hitting the B button to jump across the ocassional pit. Again, it's boring.
On the positive side of things, the game looks gorgeous for a budget title. I got it for 99 cents a few sales ago, and can't comprehend how such a cheap♥♥♥♥♥title can look so damn good. There's even some creativity in the way some of the cutscenes unfold.
Otherwise, it's all mediocre and completely forgettable. For a budget title it passes the time and is...not completely offensive, but if that's its only real upside then it really has nothing going for it.
Recommended if you are, plan to be, or ever will be Tyler Perry

A game I had a lot of fun with, but it has quite a bit of flaws. Having never played a Shantae and hearing it was a metroidvania style game, I was dissapointed when it turned out to be a mostly linear 2d zelda affair. The backtracking, unlike in regular metroidvania which makes exploring the world and unlocking new paths exciting and lore-richening, seemed like a tedious chore in this game. Almost like filler that they had to do in order for the game to be just a bit longer. The good thing is that the fast travel things you can buy in the one shop (yeah unfortunately there's only one shop in the very paltry main city) in this game are cheap.
Now some positives. The game plays and looks well, for the most part. The animations, music, and overall style of the game are on point. Usually I find that when a game panders towards an audience it is bad. At a cursory glance one look at Shantae almost looks like its pandering toward that harem big boobied fetish, and there's no denying that it is. Since the game is so tongue and cheek about the whole thing, and Shantae's dialogue is genuinely that of a cute character, I am down with it. It's not one of those visual novels that wants you to fap every second, the big boobs are there to be enjoyed in the background and in this case work as a fine character trait.
The dungeons, although entirely linear, had great platforming. Some rooms have you dying over and over to reach the goal, which I found quite challenging and awesome. The game starts out pretty easy, but about halfway through there is a major difficulty spike. Each and every boss in the game was excellently animated and a thrill to fight. All of the upgrades of the game got better and better, and by the end I truly felt like an OP character. This is how upgrades should be done, with each upgrade being a standalone good weapon, but also synergizing with the previous upgrades aquired.
And since this review, although I liked the game, pointed out some flaws let me just point out one small thing that annoyed me to heck. It doesn't affect the gameplay, it doesn't affect the enjoyment, it's just that when the score and the graphics and the gameplay and everything else has such high production value why does the pause menu look so crappy? Like they used they paintbucket tool on the regular blue setting and called it a day. I know pause menu's aren't the most exciting part of a game, but it always looked out of place.
Well anyway, despite the shortcomings and filler the game was cool. I'll pick up the next Shantae game if it's cheap and if it ever comes out. (At the time of this review the game has been in kickstarter hell for quite a bit of time.)

This is pretty much an improvement over Risky's Revenge in about every way. It's longer, more balanced, faster-paced, and in general just more fun to play. Though I'd also say it's still far from a perfect game.
A few things to note right off the bat; while this does have a metroidvania-style powerup system and shop and all that, the game map is divided up strictly into levels, each level being decently sized, but yeah there's no interconnected map here. The game does have an actual map system though, something that was sorely missing from Risky's Revenge. And as well you'll easily know when you've collected everything in an area since it shows on the world map.
The main game mechanics, Risky's various items, are much more fun than the dancing of the rest of the series. No more slowing to a crawl to perform a dance that's mostly only useful in a few select areas, this time you can pull any of your tools out at a whim and practically every one of them has uses both in platforming and in combat.
The pistol is, well, a pistol. You're gonna be using it for ranged attacks a lot, and though it's fairly weak compared to other weapons it's still plenty useful. The hat is mainly used for platforming purposes to glide through the air, but it's pretty solid. I do think it should pull out faster, there were a lot of points where I felt it was a struggle to use because of how slow it is to pull out (especially in one spot in the last dungeon that's waaay harder than it should be). The scimitar lets you bounce on enemies as well as break floor tiles below you, though you have almost no horizontal movement when using it, which would've been nice and allowed for some clever puzzles, but oh well. The boots are possibly the most fun item, letting you charge rampantly through everything, zoom zoom plowing through enemies, it's so much fun. Wish it was mapped to a button rather than to a context-sensitive timer, but it'd probably be horribly broken otherwise, I suppose. And the cannon gives you three extra jumps AND another aerial attack, allowing for safer fighting and pretty much breaking all the jumping puzzles in the game.
The icing on the cake is the mode you unlock after clearing the game for the first time that allows you to play through the game with all the tools from the start, speeding up the game quite a bit and allowing for some -fun- strategies against earlier bosses.
The bosses, then, let's talk about them. They're... a mixed bag. I like some of them, while some others are a bit... bad. The boss of the fifth island, for one, misleads you into thinking you should be fighting it with the gun since that's the most convenient weapon to use, but that is definitely NOT the weapon you actually want to use, you want to hair-whip it to pull it down to the ground, and... eh... I really don't like that boss because of the bad first impression it left on me. The boss on the sixth island is relatively easy, sure, but annoying since it's literally RNG and little else. I'm not really a fan of the movement RNG in these bosses in general, the third island boss, fourth island boss, and first phase of the final boss have it the worst in this regard, though maybe it's because I had to spend time grinding to no-damage kill these bosses, but it's a minor gripe. Overall the bosses are more good than bad though, in the end.
The enemies and combat in general are also pretty solid, there's a few that annoy, a few too tanky, a few too powerful, and the first area of the fifth island is just a huge pain because of rampant enemy spam, but in general it's balanced well with the platforming. There's a fair number of enemies back from Risky's Revenge, but plenty of new ones thrown into the mix as well. The platforming is also generally pretty interesting and creative, as are the few puzzles scattered throughout the maps. The exploration elements are there, too, even with the map designs, though some parts play out almost like an adventure game, trying to figure out where to go next or finding a specific item you need to progress the story, but poking around older areas with new tools tends to produce results most of the time. It's a very solid, enjoyable experience on the whole.
The game also looks great, the spritework and animations are lovely, the level graphics and background graphics are all nice, the character portraits look great. The game also sounds great, there's some reused music from Risky's Revenge but a lot of the original tracks are just generally nice and never really wear out, plus it helps that there's quite a ton of music in the game in general, 2-3 map tracks per island, multiple cutscene themes, a few boss themes, really no shortage of good tunes.
It's really hard to fault this game much, I had a few gripes with it but nothing that adds up to a major problem, and most importantly, it's fun. That's all I really need a game to be, in the end.

I'm not going to break my back defending myself because everyone who believes it won't have their opinion swayed, and everyone who doesn't doesn't need their opinion swayed. It's that simple.

Rich coming from me, but come on guys.
I'm not playing the pity card. I was in a♥♥♥♥♥♥spot, I already posted about that, but I've gotten considerable help and I'm working to better myself in every way I can. I've got two jobs, I'm moving out of my house shortly, and I'm pursuing other things. YouTube is over.

I know YouTube operates under a "guilty until proven innocent" mindset. It can be argued that my first two videos used this tactic, though I stuck to the words used by the subjects of my videos. The last good Battlefield, plain and simple.
DICE/EA went on to copy CoD in every BF title starting here, however this is the game that got it right. Each successive title tried to blend weird action combat with the old BF style and it just didn't come out right. Here, however, the game design completely revels in NOT being Battlefield and it somehow succeeds in making the most entertaining modern BF experience.
For instance, the map design is much smaller overall, the prone stance was removed, jets and commanders aren't present, and the class count is cut down to 4. To most people, this seems like a straight downgrade, but what it does it make for a more fast paced BF experience while also keeping a lot of tactical play. Something like being sniped from very far away with an assault rifle or vehicle is minimized here (not removed entirely however, some maps are more open than others) compared to mainline BF titles and instead infantry pushes are much more important. I can't feel but mention the importance of the 'Rush' mode the game introduces. It's something that BF always needed. Instead of playing keep away with capturing conquest points, both teams have to play around objectives which makes the conflict happen.
There are a wide variety of weapons for whatever situation and style you like instead of a 'go-to' OP weapon that fixes everything (Carl Gustav aside). Each weapon is very satisfying to use with an impactful recoil and reload cycle; which comes to one of the most underrated aspects of the game: the audio.
Special care was taken in the audio of this game. I cannot even put it into words in a simple review, you just have to put on some headphones and hear for yourself. No BF title since has put this much detail into the sounds of conflict. Each gun has a distinct and satisfying firing sound. Every little thing in the game makes a noticeable sound which can and will work for/against you in situations. Rounds can be heard in the distance and shells ejected from a shotgun will echo in empty areas. The audio direction is simply engrossing.
The game isn't without its issues, however I feel like the issues it does have are present in nearly every BF title. Things like being sniped by ordinary weapons, vehicle abuse, explosive abuse, etc., all still very much modern BF problems and they're present to some degree here for sure, but not enough to commonly detract from the overall experience.
The overall player pool may be smaller now in 2015, but believe me when I say that you can still get a good round in from time to time. Check this out if you got a few bucks to spare and were let down by BF3/4/HL.

I had a fantastic experience with Firewatch! Captivating dialogue and an immersive atmosphere really pulled me in. The game starts off as a relaxing stroll through the woods and gradually twists as you get caught up in a mystery. Am I being watched? I can see why some people wouldn't prefer this game over others, it's not the most adrenaline-rushing game in the world, but it's not supposed to be. However, there are definitely times in the story that my jaw dropped. At 50% sale £7.50 it was almost worth it for the 3-4 hours of entertainment but the last 45-60 minutes leaves that niggling feeling that maybe not quite. If this had been a movie, which it could just as well have been considering how linear the progress was and hom limited your choice of actions are, II would have hated to pay to watch the story at full cinema price but it would have been ok to watch on Netflix.
So in summary I suppose I give Firewatch a "meh, it was ok but I would wait until it drops even more in price." So recommend or not? Yes, I'll recommend it but only at a reduced price.

After a while you have everything automated, steel and iron is automatically mined and a conveyor leads it to a smelting machine which has coal coming in from one side, and the raw ores on the other side, and it outputs metal sheets. And then this feeds into another machine to make a few other components, and those are needed to make some higher stage components. So you spend the first several hours figuring out how to feed all your first level stuff into second level stuff and then into third level stuff etc. It is a puzzle that is quite interesting and it is addictive because you get so absorbed in this process and before you know you, you spent 5 hours building stuff.
The result though is that you now have a working factory that pumps out everything you need. You surround it by walls, put a few turret guns in each corner, and it is now safe forever. Late stages you build some big thing that require a lot of materials and a few more stages adding to your factory. Instead of one patch of ore feeding your factory, you maybe want to get a second one etc. But you are just repeating what you already did at the start, just adding more of the same.
The problem is the third phase. You now have an enormous factory pumping out everything, including end game gear. But now what? Some people seem happy to just keep tinkering, getting more and more resources to produce more and more stuff until your PC freaks out. But there is no goal or purpose to any of this and the motivation you had at the start to progress and build a good factory has all died instantly because you built everything. There really needs to be some long term end-game, but there isn't, and don't let anyone tell you that "this is what mods are for", because the mods in this game don't do anything like that. There are a few interesting ones that add planes and stuff, but there is still no purpose to any of this. You can fly around bombing the aliens but they never bothered you anyway and you get nothing from doing it.
If you can't get enough of Cities Skylines, Prison Tycoon, Rimworld etc. then you will probably love this too. Personally I find all those games fun for a few hours and then suddenly boring once I built everything I wanted. I also think that the dev team had a real lack of vision and drive with this game. It seems like everyone hyped the game so early, all they did was tweak what they already had and didn't make anything else. But it really needed some direction and end game content, and it will never get that now. It isn't in their roadmap, and they already made their money so they don't need to satisfy the minority who want more. So there are lots of unfinished ideas and things with potential but it doesn't get seen through. There are aliens that attack but there is no point to them. They are easy to defend against, you don't get anything from killing them, and vice versa. There is a pollution system but that only affects enemy attacks and once you have a few defences, nothing gets close to you anyway. So another feature with no point. And so on...

One of the BEST series out there. Wayforward creates some of the best games, Shantae being an OUTSTANDING Metroidvania.

Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is a classic 2D action platformer with metroidvania elements. However, compared to most generic modern platformers, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse distinguishes itself by the highest level of quality, with WayForward's pedigree in game development clearly visible throughout the whole game. Actually, this game is a part of an established series, being the third and latest installment to date.
The first thing you'll notice is the overall quality of graphics and animation, with the game being mostly done in awesome high-quality pixel art. Shantae also takes advantage of modern platforms by using high-resolution character sprites for dialogue segments. Everything looks even better in motion — the animations are surprisingly detailed and very smooth, so the fact that there are a lot of them in the game is a cherry on top. Shantae and the Pirate's Curse combines regual 2D pixel-art and modern visual effects, which look together better than you'd think. The game runs at 60 FPS, like platformers used to, and actually, should be played. Super smooth animations and super precise movement — eye candy and a soothing experience where the character moves exactly like you want them to.
Music and sound effects in Shantae and the Pirate's Curse don't fall short of the graphics, with the game featuring a large number of high quality and atmospheric music tracks, which greatly fit not only the overall game, but individual levels and characters as well. And since we're on the topic of levels, it should be mentioned that level design in Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is great, both in terms of visuals and platforming. It's clear that developers at WayForward are masters of old school platforming, employing challenging and interesting design, traps, secrets and everything else that makes this game feel like such classics as Megaman.
Every world in the game (seven in total) not only has its own visual theme and music, but is also designed around different types of platforming that you'll need to employ. Some levels feature platforming that is heavily influenced by games such as Megaman, while metroidvania elements present themselves mainly through the world being a bunch of inter-connected locations, presence of hidden areas and new locations slowly becoming accessible with new item acquisition.
Unlike previous games in the series, where Shantae used her magic, this time you're faced with the fact that she lost it (in the previous game), so she must overcome the challenges with various items that she'll come across through the game. Usually in a game like this items would be for unlocking / adding abilites, and weapons would be used for fighting, but in Shantae even weapons unlock new abilities to the player.
The game world consists of different islands that are unlocked after completing boss fights. These boss fights aren't that difficult, especially if you stock up on healing items, but fun nonetheless. Bosses are very large, and have a cool design, which comes in variety - a huge♥♥♥♥♥tank straight outta Metal Slug, a misspelled fire-breathing monstrosity Dagron, and of course, an abomination to your screen space in form of the final boss (true form only).
To sum it up, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is a joy to play, not only because of visuals and sound, but stellar level design and gameplay. An interesting cute protagonist also helps. For some reason people mostly missed out on this gem, with SteamSpy estimating sales at ~25K. But you definitely should buy and play this game, even if you aren't a fan of the genre.

Republic Commando has you playing the leader of a squadron of clone troopers through tons of missions and a story that is all its own. It's quite grand in scale, and one of the more intense and violent Star Wars games out there. But that isn't a bad thing, it feels very welcome, in the sense that it doesn't cause this game to feel any less Star Wars than it already does, as a prequel. It is still part of the non-canon, extended universe, but it is extremely engaging from start to finish.
The game has tactical combat in which you command different troopers, each with their own skills, weapons, and personalities. I just love to be in combat and hear them shouting, or command them to do something and hearing what they have to say. It honestly doesn't get annoying at all, it's really fun and welcome. The first person shooting is intuitive and fun, but the game has aged rather poorly as a PC title. The graphics options are quite limited and the resolution of the game was not quite built for widescreen monitors so it does take some getting used to, but it's all worth it.
+ Star Wars
+ Squad commanding
+ Squad members
+ Combat is fun
+ All the missions are interesting
+ Long game that doesn't get too repetitive
+ Challenging, but never too difficult
+ Physics and destruction
+ Star Wars soundtrack and SFX
+ Excellent voice-acting
- Star Wars prequel
- During the Clone Wars events
- Not canon, though better than any "canon" prequel material
- Resolution issues
- Hasn't aged too well

A casual time sink and click fest that's lacking depth and gets repetitive very quickly.
Having said that, the game has a unique art style, is practically all pop culture references and jokes, and is incredibly easy to pick up and play.
You run a weapons shop crafting supplying weapons to various hero's/market-places that you unlock as your fame increases. There's a back story as to how you got the shop, but I won't spoil it. Along the way, you hire/fire smiths, attract legendary smiths, level them up, improve your crafting equipment and purchase items for the shop that give passive bonuses, compete in weapons award shows to see which shop crafted the best weapons in various catagories, you search for new/rare materials, and research new weapons .... there's a lot to do .... but it all ends up the same way ... clicking.
I'm a little ocd, so I wanted to research all the weapons, find all the materials, win all the awards .... and things were going great .... I finally got the hang of crafting weapons in the right way, moving smiths from various work benches to other work benches to get the desired weapon stats .... I had more money than I knew what to do with .... and then I did something, still not sure what exactly it was, but I completed the final quest, which was just like every other quest, and the game ended ... it gave me an option to keep going, but there was no more research, no more awards, and I felt disappointed .... other than restarting, there was nothing else to do and I still have achievements to get, but I don't have the will to go through the whole thing again!
If you like simple management games like Game Dev Tycoon, then this game will probably satisfy you, it's well done for what it is, but if you want depth, Holy Potatoes doesn't have much, although there is DLC available.
Try to pick it up in a sale if the concept interests you.

This game caught my attention simply by having a weird name, then it captivated me by having an art style I reeeally loved!
When I saw what type of game it was I hesitated to buy it, yet despite that, my love for the colorful and cheerful artwork drove me to purchasing it. I never really play games with time and money management being the main mechanics, they're usually not my jam, that being said I have enjoyed this game quite a bit.
I've played this game from begining to end (literally just beat the game minutes before writing this) and these are my opinions of Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! Hopes this helps you out in some way. :)
Great Art, Great Humor, Great Times
Like I said I loved the art so that was the inital thing that drew me in, but with further research into the game I started noticing really quickly the references to other pop culturecharacters including Cloud from FF7, Gordon Freeman from Half Life, and even Kenny from South Park, all accompanied with shoe horned potato puns, and I couldn't be happier! If you have a good sense of humor, have a high tolerance for puns, and love you some videogame/movie/anime references, then I think you'll have a good time with this game!
Variety is the Spice of Potato Life
Not only will you be forging weapons for legenadry warriors, but you can enchant weapons, have your employees explore areas for resources, research artifacts to unlock new weapons, or even buy decorations to change up your shops look. Once you reach a certain amount of "Fame" you can travel to different regions unlocking more areas and legendary warriors! Pretty cool stuff.
Weapon Discovery
Discovering new weapons was pretty exciting at first, mostly becasue of the small amount of weapons you start off with. Though when you get farther in the game I started noticing that the only differences between one sword from another sword (other than appearence) were the stats, and not in any exponential sense, literally just a tiiiiny bit better than the last sword. I was expecting for certain weapons to have speacial abilities or to be favored by a specific customer or something like that, but nope, just a little better. If you get lucky enough to discover the best weapon of a certain type of weapon, than you don't need to bother researching the rest of them, unless your like me and just wanted to see their desgins.
Weird Pacing
Once I finished the game I ended up thinking was this game kind of had pacing issues in general. It felt like a slow start at the begining, mostly becuase of a learning curve. Then in the middle of playing once you get the hang of everything and start maximizing your sales everything feels good and it's like your actually running a succesful business. Then towards the end I guess became to good at my job and I ended having an abundance of money ( or $tarch as the potatos call it) putting a damper on the whole experience and making it more of a waiting game. On the brightside though there is a fast forward button which moves things along nicely.
In conclusion I would recommend this game, I had a lot of fun, I enjoyed the experience though I see no replayability whatsoever. I don't regret paying $14.99 at all, but if you are on the fence than definitly wait for a sale.

Fun idea for a game, but poor and simplistic execution.
Good:
- Turn based
- Base building/repair
- Rpg/stat based
- Graphics are simple, but consistent and pleasant to look at and have a "pastel comic book" feel. The game is not tiring to eyes.
- While weapon range is somewhat limited, it includes interesting choices such as handheld stun paralizers for example.
Bad:
- Very simplistic combat on squares. No hexes. Come on, Fallout 2 did it better ages ago.
- No aiming at specific body parts (come on, no head aiming in a zombie game?!)
- No terrain features other than "impassable" walls etc. If you thought about climbing on top of a car to fight off a horde, you can forget it. No taking cover from enemy fire behind walls, garbage bins etc.
- Very few and simplistic critical hits, status effects etc
- Very poor inventory management, including no handgun unloading (wtf?!)
- No trading items between party members in base (only in missions which makes it a pointless fuss)
- Similar as above = you can't enter party members character screens in base, so you don't even know how badly wounded they are etc.
- No sneaking
- Human opponents have dumb AI
- Guns have unrealistic short ranges
- Characters aren't interesting, neither friendly nor hostile humans have much of a persoanlity (except maybe 1 friendly character).
- Characters in combat are "activated" in a fixed "initiative" system, which makes for very poor coordination and cooperation between characters, as well as limits tactical options. I guess the devs thought it would make the game harder and more realistic, but all it does is make it more "automatic-move-and-attack-nearest-guy", and less of a "thinking man's game".
Final verdict: As a turn based game, the combat system is its heart and soul. Sadly combat is also the least polished, least complex and least enjoyable part of the game.
As a result the whole game falls flat on its face because of the shortcomings of the combat system.

Imagine this: You're a lone sniper (if not in multiplayer) in the middle of a Nazi zombie attack orchestrated by Hitler himself. That's on par with a low budget SyFy movie, right there!

They'll shamble, they'll moan, they'll come at you in hordes, and just when you're certain you got this thing by the balls, there's even tougher zombie variants to keep the game interesting.
But where the game really shines is the kill cams. If you've never played Sniper Elite, you're missing out on a killcam Skyrim WISHES it has. As bullets rip through tender zombie flesh, you'll be treated to an x-ray view of the horrible damage they're doing to your victim internally. Bullets will zip through kidneys, shatter bone, sunder hearts and generally give zombies a bad day.
Get this freakin' game already.

There are three AI settings.  People who complain about the AI might have missed this, because the hardest AI setting is like playing the dictionary.  If there's a person out there who can routinely beat the computer on the hardest setting, I'd like to meet them.  And no matter the AI setting, the computer's responses are lightning quick.
The game has windowed mode and a slick presentation.  The only thing you could want for with this game (provided you like Scrabble) is multiplayer.  You can't even do multiplayer on a local machine.  But the thing is, I own a very nice real life Scrabble set, and when real life friends come over, we use the genuine article.  But EVEN THEN I have this software open in the background because of the convenient dictionary included in the game that allows you to type in a word and have it judged as a valid Scrabble word or not.
So this game wins in every aspect for single player, and acts as a perfect "Scrabble Word Judge" companion for playing the  physical board game with real life friends.
Keeps your mind sharp, entertaining enough with just the bot you play against.

Terrible.   Lazy shovelware that is not worth playing at any price.
Game plays very slowly with animations between each turn. Does not track used tiles (you have to do this yourself, on paper).
No option to use the tournament wordlist (i.e., no swear words).  No option to supply your own dictionary.
AI is garbage.  Its only strength is perfect word knowledge.  It's easy to bait the computer into throwing away blanks and S's for low points.
No tools to help you improve your play, like a reviewer that recommends better moves.  Of course this would require a real AI.
No actual multiplayer.  Hotseat play is stupid and broken in a hidden-information game like Scrabble.
If you want to improve, there are better single-player  Scrabble programs and most of them are free.
If you want to play against many people, there are Scrabble games with real multiplayer and some of them are free.
If you want to play against people in your house, buy a Scrabble board.
If you want to spend $5-10 on a video game, there are much much better values for your money out there.

This is a meaningful commentary on the Nazi occupation of Poland. You start the game as an inexperieced, dumb polish horse. You are forced to balance your physical needs of hygeine, sleep, and hunger with the instinctive human drive to progress in life, be it in the growth of family or career path, in the midst of the oppresive uncaring populace of Nazi occupied Poland. The work explores the relationship between the body and unwanted gifts. What starts out as visage of whimsy and garish horse hijinks soon becomes finessed into a carnival of futility, leaving only a sense of dread and the dawn of a new understanding, the player is left with an epitaph for the edges of our human condition. We work, we eat, we sleep, bound by our economy and driven only by our dreams of progress. What starts out as hope soon becomes corrupted into a cacophony of distress, leaving only a sense of what could have been and the possibility of a new reality. This experience of beauty stresses the theoretical limits of the mind.

As I write I am desperately heading a scavanging party out into the wild once more.  It seems a blind foray hunting for meds, a dark sense of forboding as I know unless I track done a single dose of elusive antiboitics by the end of the day I join the hordes of undead.  Yet despite this it all feels irrelevant somehow.  Should I find that elixir I am still lost.  I am surrounded by one time allies who have grown to hate me - sometimes through bad decisions on my part but more often than not due to the cruel hand of fate.  With their ever growing sense of discontent they are sure to grow resentful and suspecious if I somehow buy another three days when so many of their loved ones have suffered the grim fate.  It feels as hopeless as the end of the world...which, of course, it is.
-----------
In short - I'm hooked.  This is not a perfect game but nor does it deserve the large number of negative reviews. OK, I've only come on board post-'reanimated' release, but it still seems harsh.  I suffer from the 'floating cursor' issues (note for devs - it is related to the graphics but not as simple as just the card - if I pull the interface to an old square VGA monitor the problem goes away; would also love to see scavanging without the main character to let them heal) but I feel compelled to try and work with it nonetheless...but only a minority seem to have this.  But it is immersive - when I'm playing, I'm in the game world and I have a taste of the pressures.  I feel the strain of the unresolved crisis - I know the right course of action but am unable to take it due to spent resources.  Initially put off by the archaic weaponry I expected from screen shots I instead find a mix - you'll have some gunfire but blended with other options.  So utilising everyday tools as lethal objects - as naturally they can be - is perfectly in keeping.  Hit someone with a crowbar and it feels as though it hurt.  The noise meter makes sense - a novel twist for an under utilised sense in turn based strategy.  Yet there is more than this.  There are characters which you will feel affection for and others you'll want rid of - just as in life.  You'll regret bad decisions - neglecting morale too much, spending too many parts on repairing a wall before I upgraded it, allowing too many of my ranks to become infected being mine - and feel a boost when fate smiles on you.
As far me I realise that all is indeed lost...perhaps time to restart without the option to allow the main character to become infected.  Three days in he picked up the strain and has gobbled meds ever since...to the detriment of colleagues.  Now the landscape seems dry perhaps it is time to start over after all...

Alright, the critics are blasting this game, so I feel the need to throw in my two cents.
It's not perfect. It took a couple pages from the Left 4 Dead series, took away the free movement, stuck you in a corridor, and left you in a rather monotonous "go here, kill everything" routine.
And I loved every minute of it.
I love zombie games. I know the market is glutted with them, but I like the different atmospheres. In Left 4 Dead, it was a B-movie feel, with the Survivors being heroes on a mission. Nazi Zombie Army keeps the campiness of the theme (c'mon, Nazi zombies!), but added a strong horror element that the L4D series didn't include. I've only played single player, so I can't comment on how the cooperative mode works, but being alone in dark areas, hearing the moans of the undead and the whispering of occult forces beyond your understanding was terrifying. What this game lacks in decent background music it more than makes up for in horror atmosphere.
The rounds you fire are affected by gravity and, at higher difficulty levels, wind and your own heartbeat. Even the muzzle velocity of your chosen rifle makes a difference for long distance shots. I think this is a nice change of pace from the usual "bullet goes here" system. The bullet time camera is a nice touch, but I recommend turning it down to Minimal, as it can get repetitive to have almost every shot go into kill-cam mode.
One refreshing twist was that nearly all of the Nazi zombies were the slow-moving, Romero-style shamblers, rather than the MTV Zombies that sprint. It doesn't sound so scary when you think you can mow several of them down with a submachine gun and trot to safety, but when you get backed into a corner while the creeping tide of undeath surrounds you, and only headshots are a sure-fire way to bring them down, you feel the panic set in. It is this horror setting that I really enjoyed. That, and I love campy zombie flicks.
I recommend this game, but I got it for about five bucks during the summer sale. Maybe wait until it's about ten bucks or less, then go for it.

The original Shantae was difficult to enjoy due to the restrictions of the Gameboy's screen, forcing you to play with a very small field of view. Risky's Revenge had confusing maps and slow gameplay that eventually turned me away from it.
But here we finally have what I can confidently call an excellent Shantae game. The gameplay is so much faster here and the world has been split up into different islands, making map navigation no longer an issue. And the music, man, I swear Jake Kaufman gets better with every album he releases. Rave in the Grave just blew my mind when I first heard it. It's so catchy. And I was really surprised when Scorching Dunes started out kinda generic, but then slowly evolved into a tune very reminiscent of the old Sonic games. And the tracks actually change a little bit on their second loop, keeping them from getting repetitive.
But of course, there are issues. The Monster Milk items, which greatly boost your attack power, make most boss fights utterly worthless. The only boss that I kinda enjoyed was the Steel Maggot, because it had mechanics that went beyond just using the item you got in that dungeon. You need a little bit of observation and trial and error to beat it.
Here's the problem with all of the Shantae games. Your most effective method of attack is a hair whip that can't be used while moving unless you're in the air. The devs then have to design the entire game based around that limitation. So levels are a lot of running, then stopping to attack, then running, so on and so forth. It's a lot like Castlevania Simon's Quest. Most regular enemies are no challenge and only serve to hinder your progress. (This is also why I appreciate the new pirate items so much. They let you speed through areas much more easily.)
Bosses are pretty much the same. They all have periods where they just stand still and let you hit them repeatedly, which is required because of the limitation of Shantae's hair. It's a fault by design and should really be changed for the next game, Half-Genie Hero. I should never get to a final boss and not be intimidated.
But hey, Wayforward isn't the biggest company out there. They did what they could and I think they did great. The art, the music, the characters, the humor, and the improved gameplay thanks to the pirate items make Shantae and the Pirate's Curse a memorable experience. I just hope that Half-Genie Hero doesn't squander the achievements made in this game and takes steps backwards.

In Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?!, you play a potato trying to make ends meet in an extremely cute and light-hearted world. The tone of the art, writing, humor, and gameplay all mesh very well together. The game is bright, friendly, brain-dead easy, and trucks exclusively in the two lowest forms of humor: puns and references. This is a game anyone could like, but few could love, unless you have a potato fetish.
I hate when reviews explain the very basics of gameplay, so here's a super-brief explanation of the core loop just so you can follow along: your goal is to make money by creating and selling weapons. You click on the weapon you want to make, your employees make the weapon, and you watch its numbers get bigger (a totally non-interactive process). Stronger employees make bigger weapons, which sell for more money. Weapons have 1-2 "Colors" (highest stat points). Match the color of the weapon to the color of the guy you're selling. Use the money to make more weapons, buy more upgrades, etc.
There's two large problems here. One: you don't make very many decisions - every choice you make is hardly a choice at all (sell your sword for $30,000 to the compatible guy or $100 to the incompatible guy). Two: Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! is so easy, so without consequence, that your decisions and strategies are largely irrelevant.
Every action you take - gathering resources, turning those resources into weapons, selling weapons, investing in your employees - increases your net worth. Playing well or poorly can increase or decrease the rate of success, but faililng is tricky. To go into debt, you have to make a point of hiring expensive employees (and the game limits your ability to do this as you progress) and have them do nothing but wait out the clock for months of in-game time.
I did this just to see what would happen; you get a friendly error message saying that your employees need money, and that you'll be covered this time, but next time it's game over. So I waited another month, and got the same message again!
Not sure if it's a bug or an empty threat, but either way it doesn't matter, because you would literally have to be AFK to ever lose at this game. As long as you're doing *something* and eventually converting whatever resources you get into money, you can't go broke.
Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! knows this, and tries to distract you with an impressive number of systems that initially make the game seem like a real management sim. Weapon attributes, enchantments, employee morale, random weapon quests, etc. But after you spend a little while thinking about each of these things, you'll "solve" them and they'll no longer be something you manage, just tedious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you have to do. When your employee gets sad, send them on vacation. When you need more (item), send your guy out to (location) and wait. Et cetera.
On the plus side, it's very polished, and the has a super fluid gameplay loop. I lost a night of sleep to Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?!. It's not insanely addictive or anything, but the progression is so smooth and rapid that you can easily lose track of time.
If you're a grown♥♥♥♥♥adult who wants more out of their gaming experience than pushing button until the smiling potato man tells you you win, give this a pass. But I admit that the cuteness would make it a solid fit for distracting 6-12 year old children, or 21+ year old children who still laugh at The Cake Is A Lie references in (current year).

The game provides enough challenge and plenty of gameplay on the medium difficulty. However, while my whole squad died many times, with the ability to call squad members to revive you with some Bacta when you die, makes the game feel less... Intense. You tend to notice this when you have to play through sections by yourself.
The characters in the squad are diverse with their own personality traits, and much banter occurs between them, making for some pretty funny moments.
They also move like a real army squad so Kudos to the designers.
The weapons system is fine and while you have a set number of weapons and only one 'loot weapon' slot, the real challenge is conserving your ammo.
Definately one to buy when it's on sale.
