After avidly playing this game for a thousand hours, I can easily say this game has a better storyline than any other game I have ever played. The game is filled with shocking twists and emotion-ripping moments that far exceed the quality of games like Skyrim or Fallout: New Vegas. For a meer five dollars you can get your hands on honestly the best single player game in existence. There are no limits to how you can create your horse's story in this masterpiece. You can become a mare whose struggling for work, starving, and in desperate need of a steady income to support herself, or a stallion with a family, working as a doctor, living happily in his homestead. You can custom build your own farms, travel to different beautifully rendered locations such as the beach, or a forest. To sum this all up in a single sentence, Pony World 3 is by far the highest quality singleplayer story experience you can get at this point in time, it has been put together perfectly with no errors or immersion breaking glitches anywhere at any point in the game, and is incredibly underrated.

Very crappy game for now. Tons of mindless achievements. A Blood&Bacon-like game without the fun.
Why it is so bad:
- Completely nonsensical (in one mission you have to gather wood??)
- Achievements are NOT FUN. Every dinosaur has a codename such as 7_22 and once you have killed it, you get the corresponding achivement. Which means every kill brings an achievement! It's like a joke which got repeated a hundred times, so that you are sick with it.
- Switching between weapons is PAINFUL! Why weapons cannot be assignated to the basic number keys?
- You start the mission with very low health so you have to run to the healing point before the wave appear.
- This is a wave-based shooter (just like Blood&Bacon). However each wave comes in... waves. So between two such subwaves you are just wanering around.
- Shooting at stuff is not fun at all, while it's all the point of the game. Seeing dinosaurs is incredibly difficult. I was aiming with the minimap.
What got me satisfied:
- No major bug.
- You can rebind keys.
How could it be improved (it's still Early access):
- I'd like to see the dinosaurs before they're eating me.
- The "Grenade" button does not work, and grenades seem useless anyway.
- "Using" crates to find more weapons/ammo is horrible. Crates should disappear once the weapon has been looted.
- Don't put this ugly message box with the red list of unlocked weapons at the beginning of each wave, it feels crappy.
- A better UI. Health should be more visible, just like ammo.
- The map is boring.
- A cool thing would be to have little quests. Such as "gather the wood" so that you can build a fence, then a tower; go destroy that nest of bleeding eggs in that neighboring area, so that you can start purging the planet out of dinos (which seems to be the goal); defend yourself against the waves of angry dinosaurs. Something with quests, upgrades, and coherence. Eventually a world map made of several small areas with different stuff to do in each.
- OR make it "Unlock the achievement" (that marvelous flash game with an elephant), but it means having real stuff to do, and some funny things to interact with on the map.
Easy 100% achievements, but the game isn't worth playing.

This was a really fun game, I played through the whole story and even played through almost all of the additional content, the fast gameplay and rewards kept me playing without getting annoyed or bored with the game.
Now first off the story, okay yeah it is kind of cool and also kind of lame basing the story on the Paramount War Arc, as this is seen as the most emotional moment in the anime, it is cool because it is nice to play out the scenario from the different perspectives but it is lame because it was such a cash grab decision on their point.
Now story wise it is exactly as explained, you basically play through the battle at Marineford from 4 different perspectives, Luffy, WhiteBeard, Akainu and Ace and each perspective gives you a different experience minus a few overlapping experiences.
The gameplay of the game is quite nice, it is a really really fast-paced fighting game where your first move could make the difference between victory or defeat, you need to skillfully dodge, block and use your guard breaking attacks at juuuuuust the right times in order to beat your enemy before they can beat you.
The online community of the game is basically dead, I only found 4 other people playing online but you only need to play 2 online battles (one ranked and one not ranked) in order to get all the online achievements required to get 100% if you're aiming for that.
The base game only took me about 4h 39m hours to complete while also playing through all the Wanted Posters took me an additional 9h to play this through, and yeah it was fun but I lost my urge to play it all through as they missions got really hard towards the end and the game just gives you an achievement for playing the first mission per stage and not for completing the stage so I had no motivation to 100% the wanted posters.
Anyways, the game was a lot of fun and I would definitely recommend this to all One Piece fans and fighting game enthusiast, however, I would not recommend this to someone who has never watched One Piece past this points as they won’t be emotionally invested in the characters and what is happening. 4.5/5!!!

When I recommend a video game, I tend to measure whether it's worth my time from the sum amount of fun and intrigue it produces. A game can be very intriguing, but not necessarily fun, and I can enjoy it immensely --take puzzle games, for instance, or Phoenix Wright. Vice versa, you have games like Team Fortress 2, where there's not much intrigue in story or setting but a ton of carnal fun. Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death lacks any 'umph' in either of those two elements.
Sure, the game can be occasionally fun. The game play is very Devil May Cry styled, quick, fierce, and sharp. The magic you get in the game, though limited, is quite satisfying, and the landscapes are generally pretty. Too often though did I find myself bored when I was chugging through the fighting segments, or struggling through some of the game's numerous mini-games. That's almost a kiss of death for a game centered around combat and platforming.
On the flip side, the game is only sort of intriguing. MBMD is just brimming with explosions, and it's sprinkled with a B-movie style humor that's actually quite charming. Only thing is, it loses its charm fast. Flat characters and a bland, almost predictable story keep this game from being interesting for me, and the flat voice acting and bland animation from everyone else beside the main characters just feels stale.
So for the most part, I really don't recommend this game. It's far from bad, but there's so much else out there that is worth playing more, unless you're really hungry for another platformer.

Sure, the first chapter feels dull and generic, with the lack of a proper introduction or backstory and a visibly linear design, but the game picks up on the second chapter and gets better on all aspects all the way to the end. The x-ray camera for headshots and vitals make it extremely satisfying to shoot through a horde of zombies. Causing exposed fractures and spraying brain matter all over the place has never been this satisfying.
The end was a bit disappointing, feels like a sequel hook, but not nearly enough to offset all the fun I had during the game. I can see this being awesome in multiplayer.
As Eurogamer Spain puts it: "This spin-off removes all the filling to keep only what's important: the sniper rifle, the x-ray camera and lots of stupid enemies."
Recommend.

(Originally played this title on the Wii U)
Platform: PC Windows
Genre: 2D Sidescroller/Platformer/Metroidvania
:
This is now the second game I've ever played where the protagonist is a female with her hair being her main power (The first one being Bayonetta). This installment in the main Shantae series from Way Forward Technology, just like the previous installments, offers much more than whipping your hair back and forth, Willow Smith style. A 2D platformer with a stunning soundtrack, Shantae and the pirate's curse is truly a blast to play and is arguably the best entry in the series.
:
Shantae is a half genie girl, belly dancer, and the guardian of Scuttle Town. Following the events of Shantae: Riskys Revenge, Shantae has now lost her Genie powers, but instead gets to borrow some of her former nemesis Risky Boots weapons to get by. When the mayor of Scuttle town sells the town for some chocolate to the military madman Ammo Baron, Shantae is forced to spring into action. Bigger problems lies at hand though, as Risky Boots confronts Shantae about the impending return of the Pirate Master, an evil tyrant who was sealed away by the genies of Sequin Land long ago. They reluctantly choose to work together and weaken the dark powers across the land by visiting many different islands and defeating evil creatures to prevent the Pirate Masters return.
:
Shantae's pony tail is something to be respected and it will be your main way of taking on the great variety of enemies that you will encounter. Whipping enemies as well as breakable pots makes gems drop which you can then use to upgrade your various items and said hair. Scuttle town acts as the hub town and you return there many times to buy shampoo for her hair, making your attack power go up and a silky cream which allows for faster whipping. A few damage upgrades are also available for new items that you will acquire as you progress through the story.
A 2D platformer with Metroidvania and The Legend of Zelda (Get item in dungeon, use said item on dungeon boss) style gameplay, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is certainly the best game yet in the Shantae series. Now that Shantae doesnt have to perform a dance (Although she is a very talented one) to transform herself into different animals but instead uses Risky Boots weapons and gear to get around, the pacing is a clear step up from previous titles. The dungeons are fun to explore and the platforming, while not being all that difficult, is still one of the best things about Shantae, mostly because of how perfectly precise the controls are. The dungeons also feature some thrilling boss fights at the end of each one, but I was a bit disappointed in the lack of difficulty and challenge most of them provided.
There are also Risky Boots army of small dark creatures called Tinkerbats that have been possessed by the Pirate Master's dark magic that Shantae can find in various locations. You can also find heart squids throughout the game that will increase your overall health. Just like in any Zelda game, trying to find all of these isn't all that compelling, with the somewhat lack of challenge that the game overall provides, but a few tricky platform sections and the latter part of the game will surely cause some unexpected deaths. The game lasted me about 10 hours the first time around and it also features a new game + mode, where you get to keep all your acquired items, but not upgrades and heart containers, and enemies do double damage.
:
The game looks gorgeous in all of its retro glory and is populated with many lovable side characters, witty dialogue and some great 4th wall breaking moments (many of them courtesy of the reoccurring character, the self-proclaimed filler boss Squid Baron), amazing 16 -bit animations and it's the small details that really made me take notice. Shantae, as mentioned previously, is a seductive belly dancer, and sometimes she might start to sway her hips side to side to Jake Kaufman's expertly produced soundtrack. Even when you are crawling on the ground or carrying Rottytops, Shantae's green zombie friend, who just so happens to have a thing for genie brains, Shantae is shaking her behind or stepping to the beat.
The music is upbeat and absolutely brilliant and accompanies each stage perfectly. Jake Kaufman further enforces my strong need for great musical scores in video games because they can really make or break your gaming experience. With Shantae and The Pirates Curse, its top notch and I certainly don't blame her for dancing.
:
Shantae and the Pirate's Curse offers superb animation quality, a downright awesome soundtrack and addicting gameplay that will certainly make you want to come back for more. It might not the best Metroidvania style game out there, but it is one of the most memorable and fun retro style games that i've ever experienced. Her hips don't lie and neither do I, so get this game, you will not regret it.

So I like this game. Like, a lot. I think I'm gonna be playing this for a while.
I did have an issue where the game crashed once, but otherwise it worked perfectly.
--------------------
1) The framerate stayed constantly smooth at 60 fps.
2) It looks pretty.
3) The loot system isn't super insane so you don't end up with like fifty things of the same chestplate right at the beginning of the game.
4) The combat is really fluid.
5) Hits feel impactful so it feels like you're actually doing something.
6) They know there are people who like WASD versus mouse clicking so they included both movement types. This isn't exactly innovative but it's nice they did it.
7) It's pretty easy to start a party, add a friend, and play together.
8) The classes aren't ridiculous like other fantasy MMORPGs.
--------------------
1) It can be intimidating at first, there's a lot of information that pops up suddenly when you're in town.
2) The enemies seem more like training dummies than enemies (at least in the lower levels).
3) The training area pretty much overpowers your character for the first town so it feels less like you're being involved in the game's progression and more like you're being taken for a ride.
4) The game can crash without real warning. I think I hit J when it crashed the one time it happened to me. I haven't lost any progress or items after crashing but some people have claimed to so be careful.
5) There's only four classes and each is gender/race locked. So if you want to be a ranged character either you're a female mage or a loli sharpshooter. That doesn't detract from the overall experience as much, but this can be a turn-off for some people.

--------------------
If you're not used to Diablo-esque games this can be intimidating, at first. But if you give it a chance and take it all in it can be quite fun, especially with friends. If you have a decent enough PC the game can look really good as well as run at a solid 60fps. The actual combat, however fluid, can be kind of boring. But it's always satisfying as a mage to send out a fireball and kill five crabs at once and see their bodies fly away in all directions. If you're a fan of Diablo 3, this game should feel similar. And for those of you who like Diablo but can't afford Diablo 3, this is a good free alternative.

Many of the other reviews have already said it: the game is more chore than fun--and that's further reinforced by a clunky UI and stale writing (not bad, mind you, just stale).
Combat--which might be expected to be the highlight--is generally dull and poorly balanced (on hardcore at least) with zombies/looters almost invariably sensing you from behind, with no stealth emchanism to sneak up on them effectively--and then even with a three-on-one in close combat the very real chance one of your members will take serious damage, as you whiff far too often from point blank range. Combine this with the sparse mechanics, like the noise level, which is poorly explained/clumsily executed (compare with Invisible Inc's alarm meter, or Thief's noise gem, both of which clearly and intuitively provide information while being stylistically coherent inside the game world) and you get a scenario where you can neither effectively sneak around and loot nor effectively tactically engage foes.
Base building and management suffer from an abundance of materials as opposed to a scarcity (not necessarily a problem, in and of itself), but it gives more of an impression of inventory management and 'finding x item to keep y character happy' as opposed to a struggle to survive, quickly lapsing into tedium,
Sadly, like so many other turn-based games of the same ilk, Jagged Alliance 2 came along over a decade ago and set the high watermark that so very, very many of these games have broken themselves against over the years. Kudos for the effort, but zombie games aren't exactly a scarce genre, and many of the others, from low-fi indie gems like Rogue Survivor or Neo Survivor, through mid-rangers like 7 Days to Die, all the way to high-gloss AAAs like Dying Light, pick aspects and do them better.
I don't think this is a 'bad' game, and I applaud the devs for the effort, but I'm really not motivated to play something this tedious when there's already a definite feeling that rewards for the invested time will be minimal.

I really wanted to like this game but in the end I found it very meh.
The graphics are neat and I do enjoy the artstyle but the game's story mode is where it falls flat.
The single player campaign takes place on a single island in one or two arenas that you can't really tell apart.
with the vast selection of Pirates that the game offers, you only get a very small fraction in story mode.  So much so that you will end up fighting the same characters over and over again.
To put it simply you will have seen practically all the fighters the game has for story mode after completing the first episode.
All the other episodes are the same fights all over again but this time from a different perspective.
This is kind of annoying since any fighting game that tries to tell a narrative these days actually changes scenery and doesn't has you fight more than just a handful of the playable characters.  Even Street Fighter 5 did a better job when it first came out.
So if you want to play as the other pirates and don't care about story mode.  You certainly can.  Once you make your way into episode 1 the other game modes unlock that allow you to level up the various pirates you can play as.  I really have no idea what leveling does since the enemy computers seemed to scale up with me when I did.
Some of the modes are online, flag battle and Wanted Vs.  Wanted Vs is kind of interesting since it's really just challenge battles that allow you to put together your pirate team which was kind of fun.
TLDR:  My overall impression of this game was very meh and by the time I reached episode 4 and was still fighting the same characters I already fought a bunch in the previous episodes I figured I had enough.  There are other better fighting games than this.

Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death is a third person hack and slash, action adventure that is probably the closest thing to God of War on the PC. It is fantastic game in general, let alone the budget price. It has over the top action, which means plenty of explosions and crazy moments like Marlow hanging from a helicopter and he needs to dodge left or right. The game plays great, the graphics are amazing. The camera will zoom out for you to see beautiful vistas, foreboding caverns and giant industrial complexes. There is a scope and scale to this game. You can be so tiny in a grand complex and you feel it. The game really shines with its gameplay diversity. You won't just be hacking and slashing. There are fun turret sections, plenty of not too difficult platform traversal, climbing, swinging, running from boulders, pushing objects, sliding down areas, working turnstile levers and even playing a top down vertical scrolling shooter. These other elements bring a lot of diversity to break up the brawling.
The story is simple and so bad its good. You're Marlow, visiting his girlfriend in a remote jungle, so she can quit her job working for an evil madman bent on immortality. To show her he means business, he kills you right then and there to kick off the game. Marlow gets killed with a magical artifact and the mask of Death resurrects him. So now with crazy magical powers, Marlow must save his girlfriend. The mask will guide Marlow along the way. There is a lot of humor between Marlow and the mask. Its not a comedy game, but has dabs of humor here and there. Marlow Briggs knows how implausible the situation is and doesn't always take things seriously. The mask is there to aide and taunt Marlow when he dies. To show the game's humor, the antagonist is named Heng Low. He makes some great announcements throughout the game, such as, "all personnel, go grab a gun. There's a nice reward for killing Marlow Briggs. You can use that reward to pay for the weapon rental." Oh and "All employees are fired, please avoid flaming death traps and bottomless pits on your way out."
The core game play is simple. You can move, double jump, weak attack, strong attack, grapple, block, roll in any direction with the right analog stick, use magic by pressing two buttons and change weapons with the D-pad. Marlow will get four weapons throughout the game. Each weapon has a different speed, range and damage, but for the most part they are pretty much the same. When he attacks he'll swirl around, causing beautiful death. Its visually appealing. There are four spells to earn. A fiery meteor shower in a circle, earth spikes in a straight line, frost to freeze a radius of enemies and a storm. Every enemy gives you experience to upgrade your weapon and magic levels. It seems like every spell depletes all your mana. Luckily each dead enemy brings you health and mana. There is plenty of mana, health and experience around each level. You just need to hold a button to absorb it, so if an enemy is around, they can keep you from getting them. Enemies can be grappled and thrown, but more interesting, they can be converted, making them fight for you! Your block can reflect projectiles if you time it right and you have magical projectiles of your own.
It is all a nice system, made even more enjoyable by a wide cast of enemies. The standard soldiers don't use guns, just machetes since this is a hack and slash. Rocket launchers that need you to reflect. Riot troops that need to have their shields knocked away with specific attack combos. Bugs that can be easily squashed. There are plenty of mini bosses that show up in the game. First they get their own fight, but then they appear later as common enemies. When most of the mini bosses get weak, you can hop on and control them. Not like the conversion, but rode. You can ride a giant scorpion and control it to kill enemies. You can ride giants the same way. The visual is better than the actual fun. I could kill the enemies a lot quicker without being on top of slow lumbering giants.
Speaking of giants, then there are the game's big bosses. The bosses so big that you're as tall as a single eye. Each big boss has many parts and they're quite memorable. Its all simple pattern recognition though so its easy enough once you figure out the pattern. The only problem is that you don't do much damage. At the end there is even a quick time event or mash the grapple button.
You have NO control over the camera. It is always carefully placed and follows you well enough. I only had a problem with that once or twice in the whole game. The load times are hid. I didn't notice one at all unless I came back to a save. Dying has a really quick reload time to the point its just a quote, then you respawn from the last frequent checkpoint. Its so nice to be back in the action.
To keep things interesting, there are challenges in the game. Things like you're sliding down a hill and need to move left and right. The challenge is collecting all the experience orbs! Don't collect them all? You can restart or just keep playing. You can kill all the helicopters in the turret section or the town down shooter section. It adds an extra level of challenge to what would be an easy game on normal (medium) difficulty. Even though the game stays the same level of difficulty, the later areas just take longer. Bigger enemies take more damage. Puzzles take longer.
Other elements in the game have players jumping between three mine carts to avoid obstacles. Floating with angels wings between platforms. Swimming through a swinging guillotine river. Climbing wall vines, killing worms. Inching with Marlow's back to the wall to avoid either falling or gears. Clinging to cliff sides. Dodging flaming wrecking balls. Turret shooting the pistons on a giant lava scooper as you ride around a cart. Getting chased by helicopters. Seeing giant scorpions get crushed by huge boulders completely unscripted. Escaping under a door by rolling just before spikes crushed the enemies in the room. Fighting enemies on a helipad as it flipped and flew through the air.  Seeing the giant facility Marlow is in was really mobile with treads.
It all feels like a high budget game in a lot of ways, but lacking in a few, especially the cut scenes. There aren't many animated cut scenes, but the majority of the scenes are fly around of scenes. Its like bullet time. You'll see a still frame circling around Marlow as he's hacked through a flame throwing soldier. As the camera swings around, it will reveal a helicopter. Then Marlow leaping from the copter, only to swing around and show Marlow slashing through an insect.  I'm happy that the cut scenes are the worst part of the game, especially since they're skipable. They spent the time in the animation, character models and gameplay.
The game is well worth the $5 price tag it currently has. I am shocked this game doesn't have a cult following or more popularity. Even with a 7 hour run time and not too much frills for any replay value, I think this could stand shoulder to shoulder with God of War. The diversity really kept me engaged. Nothing overstayed its welcome. 7 hours was the right time. Its best to leave players wanting more. Odd now Steam says that I only played 5 hours. Oh steam.

In a nutshell: I really enjoyed this game.
"Shantae and the Pirate's Curse" made me feel like I was back playing my old SNES. For a game made in 2014, it does an excellent job of capturing that classic old platformer feel and gameplay. But the appeal of this game doesn't end with the nostalgia factor. There's some really good humor in this game which makes for a really enjoyable play experience and the puzzles can get a bit tricky; not so much that they become a nuisance, but just enough to make you clever when you figure them out.
The characters were great and had a surprising amount of depth for a game that shows so much cleavage (pun not intended). There's a lot of character development in this game and, especially by the end, I found myself caring more then I would have expected about what happened to them and their relationships with one another. For me, this was one of the game's most endearing qualities.
On the negative side, this game does have it's imperfections, too. I mentioned earlier how this was a very loyal SNES-era style platformer and it is, in both the good ways and the bad. Playing Shantae and the Pirate's Curse reminded me why I would sometimes get so frustrated as a kid that I'd throw my controller at the wall. Things like timed jumps and frustratingly narrow gaps between spike filled walls, when not used properly, can easily become a nuisance which detracts from the enjoyability of a game. Shantae and the Pirate's Curse unfortunately succumbs to this pitfall. Long sequences that relied upon me timing numerous jumps perfectly - under threat of being sent back to the beginning over and over and over until I got it right- were aggrivating and the game would've been much better if they had been made so that you only took damage when you made a mistake, instead of being sent back to the beginning. The final journey to the big-boss was the most notorious culprit here, but there were other areas that suffered from the same problem. Forcing a player to replay long sequences over and over and over is annoyingly repetative and makes for a poor impression of the game as a whole.
Also, while I was able to get my Logitech Precision gamepad to work with this game, it required me to do some serious tweaking with some 3rd party software to get it to work and I was a little disappointed that Shantae and the Pirates Curse didn't include native support for it. "Shantae and the Pirate's Curse" is the kind of game that is really meant to be played with a controller (I briefly tried to play it via keyboard and I found it really awkward and hard on the fingers), so it's a shame there wasn't more effort put in to insuring that the game was more compatible with controllers.
But I won't let these minor frustrations ruin what was overall a really fun game! This game was well worth the money I paid for it and I will be eagerly awaiting it's sequel!

After having played Shantae: Risky's Revenge, I had already fallen in love with this series, and Shantae was already one of my 2 favorite video game characters of all time! For a single game to be able to do that speaks volumes about its quality. Now let's take this already flawless platformer and make it even better. What do you get?  You get Shantae and the Pirate's Curse.
HOLY COW!!! This game is incredible! It somehow managed to take everything the previous games did right and perfect it. The game mechanics, from hair whipping to hat parachuting to simple running and walking animations, are very fluid and wildly entertaining to witness. The pace of the game is never too slow because you're always getting new items, which each give the game a new level of depth. The various levels you explore are vibrant and colorful, or dark and forboding if it's a dangerous level, but the tone matches each stage perfectly and helps to draw you into the world. All the characters are incredibly loveable and fun, and the character models themselves are stunningly beautiful from an artistic perspective! The music is also ridiculously catchy!
I have tried, but I honestly CANNOT find a single problem with this game. The developers at WayForward have poured their hearts and souls into this game...and it really shows! As I have said previously on my review of Shantae: Risky's Revenge, this is a series that should absolutely be played. I can personally guarentee that you will not be disappointed if you buy this game, even at full price! Thanks WayForward Games for my favorite Half-Genie!

Don't worry about my playtime, I fully completed the game on 3DS originally, and liked this game so much I had to buy it a second time.
This is easily one of the best Shantae games yet: great controls, cute character art and vibrant world design, and plenty of collectibles to keep you playing for a while.
The only possibly negative thing I would mention is something potentially a little divisive.  If Risky's Revenge turned you off from Shantae with it's confusing world design that had you jumping between the foreground and the background to navigate the world, you'll be pleased to know that's gone for a more traditional, and much easier to navigate, single plane.  However, if you liked it, you might be disappointed at the simplification.
Shantae doesn't have her trademark transformations here, but they more than make up for them with some really fun gadgets that, among other things, let her rocket jump through the air, charge through obstacles, and shoot at faraway switches.

Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! Is an odd game, the title itsef is absurd. With exclamations, and a question mark you can somewhat see where this game is going. It is a simplistic "Management" game in which you order sentient potatoes to forge weapons for you, then you can sell them, as well as have the character explore to collect supplies, and enchantments. (Which allow for stat bonuses between the four attributes of the weapons:Accuracy, Speed, Damage, and Magic, Though they don't really have any affect besides how large of a payment you recieve.) The characters though rather limitedly written were rather amusing, the gameplay itself  was pretty interesting until you find all of the weapons, in which case you are just grinding until you reach the unsatisfying end of the game. The game is full of pop culture references, and to me they were used to an amusing affect. However, humor is subjective, so some, maybe even many of you would hold contempt for the writing. They definitely could've flashed out the game more, it just seems rather skeletal as it is, It is not a bad game by any means, it just feels as if it's lacking a few key qualities.
But, I am not an expert, and preference itself is subjective. So I reccommend reading the various other reviews, both good and bad, and consider their points carefully. I honestly enjoyed this game, but it did feel hollow. A better story, better variation in the potato puns, maybe try to find a way to flesh out the mechanics of the game so you don't slump into monotany near the end, and maybe a more intuitive way to upgrade various aspects of your characters, and equipment.
Would I recommend this game? No. Is it terrible? By no means, It just needs to be fleshed out.

This is my favorite game in the Battlefield series, and an improvement to the original Bad Company. The game's Frostbite engine allows you to destroy building walls, which changes first-person shooter game-play in such interesting ways. In Bad Company 2,  less is more when it comes to guns. There is a basic arsenal, with some gadgets. The more defined character classes seem to lead to more strategic game-play and teamwork. The character design is goofy, but this adds to the game and turned out to be somewhat iconic of the Bad Company spin-offs. The "War Tapes" audio opinion makes for great over-the-top gun fire and explosions. The maps on Bad Company 2 are some of the best (if not the best) in the series. The maps are more tailored for rush or conquest mode and were geographically diverse. There is a very fast turnover time between rounds and a simple load-out customization screen. The Singleplayer campaign is actually worth playing, just to listen to crap that comes out of Haggard's mouth.

SPOILER ALERT: DO NOT NEED FURTHER IF YOU HAVE NOT FINISHED FIREWATCH YET OR THINK YOU MAY PLAY IT LATER
I finished Firewatch about 1:30 a.m. this morning (spent 7 hours according to Steam, but part of that time was just me examining and reading/studying things). I've been reading the other reviews--particularly the negative ones--and can't really relate to much that was said (except maybe the price, although I purchased Firewatch when it was on sale). Aside from that, though, I didn't see any faults in the game, although it was short and the ending was kind of abrupt.
However, I've been thinking a lot about my experience...read some articles written by other people about the story...and I have a deeper...understanding? I guess that's the right word. Or maybe appreciation, like a work of art where the interpretation is usually subjective, particularly if it's abstract in nature.
For me, the storyline--while feeling like a mystery thriller most of the way through--was pretty unique. It was unique in the sense that it took a setting and characters that could have easily been based on a true story and simultaneously evoke that fear of the unknown. As the game came to a close it became clear that the fears and paranoia were unfounded, much like a lot of conspiracy theories in real life. It also brought childhood memories back of being afraid of the dark.
In addition--and this came to mind just a few hours ago before typing this review--I see parallels between the timeline of the game and the timeline leading up to Henry taking the job at the Two Forks lookout tower. Just like Henry felt an ever widening gap between himself and Julia as she succumbed to her illness, there was also a gap (albeit physical) between himself and Delilah. As Henry got to know Delilah over the course of the game I could tell there was an attraction and a desire to see each other. However, it never was meant to be as she decided to leave her lookout tower before Henry arrived, just like Julia who left Henry to be with her family in Australia. Physically he was able to go see Julia, but emotionally/mentally it was a great chasm. It was one of those "so close yet so far" scenarios; it's quite sad, actually...
Anyway, I liked the game and do not feel my money or time was wasted. Would I have preferred a more cinematic approach to the introduction?: Sure. Would I have preferred a happier ending?: Of course. Unfortunately, though, real life does not ever guarantee a happy ending, so in that light I felt the ending was apropos. A small chapter in someone's life--Henry's--ended and he had to start a new chapter. Whatever that was is irrelevant since, I feel, it was outside of the intent of the game, that being to cherish every moment you have with friends/relatives/significant other, both the good and the bad.

The game has solid writing but just about everything else about the game its underwhelming to mediocre to downright boring. It can be a trudge to get through the game and I found myself playing through long periods of boring and/or frustrating gameplay to get to short spurts of good writing. You see my playtime count? That is one playthrough, that is me being careful like you're supposed to and stretching out viable resources - what you're supposed to do. There are just far, far too many problems with the gameplay to list them. There's even major, recurring issues outside of combat and they too are too numerous to list. While the shelter functions almost perfectly you'll encounter glitches and bugs that make the game tiresome and even disrupt combat frequently. Aside from that bugginess there are a plethora of questionable gameplay decisions outside of it. Zombies are terrible enemies for an isometric RPG and don't work well as antagonists for numerous reasons. Tie in that the game is so glitchy with the turn order I can't tell if they're supposed to be fast zombies or slow zombies and the main antagonists of the first half of the game are just really frustrating to deal with. The game isn't well balanced for the second half of the game, which is further hurt by extreme bugginess. The writing is quite good but you only usually get exposed to it at the beginning of each day. While there is environmental storytelling in most areas, with even some events in progress, its not enough to fill the gaps.
The gameplay is just too much of a chore for me to recommend the game for its writing, which while good isn't so good its worth trudging through the rest of the game for. The game would've been recommended if it had the gameplay of a title like State of Decay but since 90% of the game is average to downright tedious and boring I cannot recommend it, not even for a Steam sale. I got it on such a sale for $9 and while I don't regret my purchase I don't believe I could recommend it to others.

Pretty fun game, if you can appreciate/stand a cheesy, over-the-top 80's action flick style experience (both in the humor and the game itself). It's a spectacle fighter with fairly decent gameplay, very good for the price point, I'd say.  Think God of War centered around Rambo's black cousin.
A lot of the attacks don't really feel like they have a lot of weight to them, especially with the Whip, because the enemies don't really react like they were hit or get staggered in any way. The attacks certainly at least look pretty though, and some combos feel very satisfying. Generally the combat system is fairly fleshed out imo. There are a lot of combos and each of the four weapon types has their own combo system.
My biggest problems with the game are the camera and the fairly frequent crashes. Unless I missed something you have no control of the camera at all. It generally gets the job done but often picks some angles that wouldnt exactly have been my first choice, and sometimes gets kinda awkward. And the game definitely has some stability issues. I don't know if it just hates my machine, but I'd say I crash probably once per 20-30 mins. The games usually fun enough for me to relaunch it and keep going though. But I do strongly advise you to make frequent saves. The checkpoint system is generally alright but doesn't to add more buffers in case you crash (or fall into a pit in a platforming section).
Other less major complaints would include a few turret sections that I didn't love but at least they weren't THAT long or overly frequent (think i've had 3 in a couple hours of gameplay), a few kinda annoying QTEs but again not that many or very long. I could have also lived without the audio-clips from Marlow's girlfriend but I think they can be skipped if they bug you enough.
The game does have some puzzle and platforming elements that you may or may not enjoy. Persnally I thought the platforming was just challenging enough to not be boring but it didn't get frustrating or overstay its welcome. If nothing else the companion makes a few funny remarks when/if you fail. The puzzles so far have generally been pretty simplistic and I could live without them but can also live with them.
Generally I'd say I've had a pretty good time with the game, and the positives have outweighed the few problems I've had with the game. The gameplay is pretty enjoyable and I personally rather like the humor with the banter from the companion, the villain, and the occasional 4th wall breaks. Got it on sale for like $1 and I definitely got my money's worth.. and then some.

But what does this game have that i missed in other MMOs? Here are a few things i find in some MMOs but never united in one:
- The combat system
For me, one of the most important parts of a game, it is straight up awesome. It´s not as refined as Diablo, but it´s quick, action packed and even with my horrible interent: accurate (concerning the hitboxes). It makes fun and made me completely overlook the dulled down quest system.
- The End-Game
I hate a level cap. The only other MMO i really played was Perfect World back in the day, so i guess that´s the reason why i can´t stand being blocked in progression. I never thought this was possible, but Devilian combines nearly infinite leveling with the end-game system other games like World of Warcraft offer.
The maximum level is 52 (at the point of this review) but once you hit that, you still have to level your Devilian-Form and your proficiencies, much like the Paragon-System in Diablo 3.
And yet you get an equipment score with which you may or may not enter in some of the later dungeons. Which brings me to the next point...
- The Dungeons
Very well designed layouts combined with awesome bosses make these stand out from any other game. Throughout your journey you will enter many of them, and even at the end, they stay relevant. Farming Heroic dungeons until your gear is ready to head into Hell dungeons just so you can farm that extra bit of Resistance-Essence, Setpiece of your armor, gem to level up your artifact or other materials to improve your character makes for an endgame i´ve never seen so diverse. There is a ton of stuff to improve on which means a ton of stuff to do. Way better than just to farm for one equipment piece over and over again...
- PvP
Now i don´t mean the normal PvP, i mean real PvP. Guildwars, Arenas, PvP areas. 20v20, 6v6, 3v3. I can´t believe something like this is missing in so many games. I just love going into Teamspeak with my friends and play together against other players. It´s not as well done as in Perfect World as there is no territorial system, but it´s still a lot of fun to be had.
I could extend this list but those were the most important facts on why i think this game deserves some attention. I will keep playing it, i hope you join the party...

So, what do we got here?
Another crappy Dinosaur-themed early-access game. This game is developed by the same guys who released "Dinosaur Hunt" - You should be warned.
In the current state there are the following "features":
- Two maps, one for the tutorial, and another one for the "campaign".
- The so called "campaign": Survive 10 rounds, called "days", and kill dinosaurs to succeed.
- Five weapons: Axe, Sword, Flashlight, Bow and Heavy Bow.
- Four different enemies: Raptor, Triceratops, Stegosaurus and T-Rex.
- Dozens of ultra-simple achievements (Press "W" to move forward -> Achievement unlocked!)
How is the gameplay?
Forget about the Axe, the Sword, and the Flashlight. The only useful weapon is the bow. You start playing on the only map (Achievement unlocked!), running in circles to avoid contact with the dinosaurs and shoot them in the head (Achievement unlocked!). If you're low on ammo, collect some (Achievement unlocked!). When its getting dark, pause the game and activate "Nightvision" in the menu (Achievement unlocked!). Try that with the other effects like "Colors", "Rain", or "Thermal Vision" - guess whats coming next? Right! Achievement unlocked.
Conclusion:
Running around on the only map and killing four kinds of dinosaurs with the bow. Beware, Triceratops and T-Rex need MANY arrows to the head until they're dead (There are headshot Achievements, of course).
Prediction for the future:
The game will stay in the early-access phase for the next six months. After these six months and a few changes regarding the gameplay the game will leave the early-access phase. To increase the profit, some DLCs will be released, like "Replacing-the-dinos-with-Aliens-stuff", "Adding-WW2-weapons-stuff" or "Replacing-the-enemies-with-Zombies-stuff", and the game will be another add to the "heartless ramshackled, never finished" game section.
Avoid!

For free.

A very satisfied action/platformer gamer who thoroughly enjoyed the GBC original release, this, and Risky's Revenge: Director's Cut.
Now that that's outta the way, on to the review.
On the surface, it's just an average everyday platforming puzzle solving game, however, the style and story are very well done and the variety of available sub-weapons and special moves adds to the fun.  I wish we'd seen the return of the belly-dancing transformations, but given this is a direct sequel to Risky's Revenge, I can see why they opted to leave the half-genie stuff out, seeing as she lost all her powers in Risky's Revenge.
Graphics: 4.5 - The colors are vibrant and the backgrounds vary from island to island.  Still, it's a bit dated, but for this type of game, it's not a bad thing at all.  This game is set to stand the test of time as it just looks good and easy on the eyes.  Be prepared for MORE BUTT WIGGLES!
Sound: 4.5 - the voice-over work was interesting, but I wish they'd run with it a bit more.  It would have been a bit more engrossing having at least the dialogs between main characters/villains with voice-overs.  Still, Shantae's voice is cute and lovable.  The music does the job well setting up the scenarios and scenes everywhere.
Controls: 5 - I'm using a 360 controller that's working flawlessly while I play.  The occasional ducking is a problem, but that's the CONTROLLER, not the game itself.  I fault Microsoft for that one because the d-pad, while great, is sometimes too sensitive and I find myself ducking and crawling when I meant to run forward.
Replay: 4.5 - Even if this game is short, I still find myself always going back to platformers and playing them again.  This is why Super Mario Bros. series has always stood the test of time. Still, I wish there were a few extra things to do during a 2nd playthrough. Short version:
This is a game about automation. If you enjoy setting up efficient systems that do all the tedious work for you, this game is gold. It is in early access and has been for a long time, but I've had 200 hours of fun this far and I intend to keep playing. There is also a lot of mods that add tons of content.
Long version:
Start out with nothing, build some basic machinery to extract and refine materials and expand your factory until you eventually have all you need to send a sattelite into orbit. Beware that the local, semi intelligent animals are not fond of pollution, leading to a war between you and nature.
Setting up and expanding your factory is the key part of this game. Finding joy in building complex networks and tuning it to achive efficiency is important, since there are few other ways of enjoying the game. There is a bit of combat and exploration, but without the factory you wont survive for long.
Some might say that games in early access are a risky investment (looking at you, TotalBisquit) and I would agree. But in this case I would like to say that this game is good as it is, so even if the developers bailed now it is still worth the money. Also, the developers are posting weekly updates on what they are working on, and they seem intent on keeping their good work up.
Regarding difficulty, there are ways to customize that before starting a new game. For new players there is a tutorial campaign, but I don't recommend it. Instead you should start a game where you've set the aliens to being not a threat (I don't think you can get rid of them enirely, but you can make them rare and weak) and play around until you get a feeling for how stuff work (or check the wiki).
There is great mod support for this game (you need to set up an acount at the Factorio website to get access to this). Some mods add things that helps with completeing the normal game. Some add completely new stuff that makes things more complicated. Some make the aliens stronger. I am currently playing with some of Bobs mods and ArchAngels mods, making the game f*ing complicated, but if there is something you would like to see in the game, there might be a mod for that already.
I have had some trouble with lagg, but that is probably because my graphics card is getting a bit too old and bad. otherwise I have not encountered any technical difficulties.

At first glance, and from popular opinion, this game will seem like an underrated, cheesily self-aware but still-enjoyable spectacle-fighter at a budget price. And it is largely those things, but it's still not far from being mediocre.
What the game has going for it is its cheesy, self-aware humor, and it did a great job of delivering on it. I smiled and got some genuine joy out of that aspect quite a number of times. I also enjoyed the set-pieces and technical-efficiency of the game. But past those, it's pretty much your run-of-the-mill CAG/hack-n-slash.
After the novelty wore-off for me (maybe 2 hours in), I started to get increasingly bored as I progressed because the combat just didn't deliver. It's your standard button-masher where victory comes relatively easily, and where "Hard" mode doesn't make the game more difficult, but more tedious (eg, less forgiving, so you have to be more liberal with dodging, damage-sponge enemies). Any time I got into an enemy encounter, and couldn't just run past them or quickly kill them by throwing them off a cliff, I would find myself falling asleep, doing the same attacks and dodges repeatedly until everything was dead.
Some other aspects that detracted were:
Overall, Marlow Briggs is beautiful, funny, and a very competent budget-priced game. But for those who have high standards for games in this genre (think: Ninja Gaiden II), it just doesn't hold-up.

Even being a fan of turn-based games, Dead State only scrapes being a passable game to play if you have nothing else to do. There are a few good aspects, though the negative aspects overrule a lot of the enjoyment which could be had.
Good Aspects:
- The micromanagement of each person in your shelter and prioritising finite resources is satisfying
- Unique survivor perks and characteristics which adds a bit extra decision making when deciding on a team
- The leveling up system is odd, but appears to function fairly well, allowing you to scale well relative to the dangers of the outside
Bad Aspects:
- Combat - At the start combat seems ok, but the further in the slower, more tedious, and painfully boring it gets. During each turn of combat, the queue of characters will cycle through the entire list of characters on the map until it gets to a relevant character/zombie/etc participating in that combat. With the larger, more zombie-populated maps, I was sitting up to roughly 15-25 seconds per round simply waiting for the queue to cycle to the relevant zombie. Plus, when a zombie is in the combat area, but unable to reach a player, it will stand there for 5 seconds or so, letting out a bored groan, mimicking my own, made worse again when 4-5 zombie were bottlenecked.
It may not seem like a lot, but if combat has as little as 4 or so rounds, I am essentially waiting triple or quadruple the length of time than is actually necessary to finish combat. And, the more you play and the harder areas you get to, the worse the issue.
- Descriptions - You will need to use Google. A lot. Descriptions of the various skills, leveling system, and user interface are very poor, meaning you will either need to have a second monitor with a wiki page helping you understand the basics for the first several hours, or you will be re-loading previous saves after realising you screwed your character up.
- Bugginess - While not the worst game bug-wise, there were many instances of characters occupying the same cell and making it difficult to issue certain commands, a few times I was attacked by 'invisible' zombies, which only appeared during the second round of combat, and there were a few crash to desktop moments, though I can forgive this.
In short - big problems, which could be quite simply fixed, potentially raising the score from 4/10 to 7.5/10.

Emily is Away acts as one of those free, short games which you always tell yourself you'd finish but fail to do so. At its core it's mostly a multi-choice game.
Here comes the days when there was no Facebook nor Skype but MSN with Yahoo!Messenger ruled the world. Players get to talk with a girl called Emily (just as the name suggests) and that's the main premise, but there are quite a lot of possibilities which you can brach into though it doesn't feel as many as they could be. The game unfortunately ends with you running out of questions to ask and all options being flooded with "Goodbye". That is unless you give up earlier than you should but that's about it.
There's also a little customization going on: you can change the avatar, text color and background. If you give yourself the right username you will be greeted with twice as many avatars, most of them easter eggs which branch into funny references at the start of each conversation but ultimately go back to normal. This is another reason why the game lacks replayability but I think it's also because there are so many choices to do it'd be painful to have multiple storylines for them all.
Among the surprises you get to experience is having your Steam friends included within the in-game friend list which is also quite funny since every profile has their own (I think random?) generated personal text. Currently I am unaware if it can use all of your friends or only those that are online during your play but nevertheless it's a lot of fun. Will generate a lot of reactions.
Overall it's a fun game which I advise everyone to try. It takes about one hour at most to finish and that is without unlocking every achievement. I also need to mention the fact that the game makes you press your keyboard whenever a choice is made as if you were typing, further adding to immersion.

Depressingly true to life.
The only jobs available are low-paying, demeaning, menial jobs, and require long hours just to afford enough basic necessities to keep yourself presentable enough to appear at work the next day. Everything that might be fun to do is closed by the time you get off work. Every possible opportunity to better yourself through education and exercise is also closed by the time your day job is done. The only things still open are the most banal of entertainments--your choice of empty, vapid pabulum on a screen, or dancing and drugs, to take your mind away from the daily grind.  Both of which only increase your "sociability" stat, which is useless for actually getting a better job. The jobs that require "sociability" are already taken by the pants-on-head moron who was in the same fraternity as the boss's clueless kid, and helped hold his hair back a couple times.
Even if the university, library, etc. were open into the night, there just aren't enough hours in the day to actually go to them. Once you've gotten enough sleep, eaten enough to survive, and worked enough to eat, that's it. The day is over. If you want to get more than that out of life, you have to start sacrificing necessities.
Soon you're showing up to work with less than 20% food, 20% sleep, and 20% hygiene, but no one cares; you're just another faceless drone who can't magically make the coffee machine spit out coffee any faster, nor figure out how to spell "Lundyynn" on the first try.
You scrimp. You save. You invest in your "garden" at home in hopes of generating some extra income selling "cabbage" out behind the convenience store. Somehow, through incredible effort, enduring sleepless nights, near-starvation, and bad personal hygiene, you save up enough to go to the university part-time. Finally, you think. This is the way out of this hole.
But as bad as the food-sleep-hygiene situation was before, it's even worse now. Power nap and power bar before work, and once again before class. Lather, rinse, repeat. Sleeping at night, the whole night? Eating full meals? What kind of madness is that?
But somehow, you do it. Bleary-eyed, gaunt with malnutrition, smelling faintly of sour dairy creamer and BO, you leave the university, flimsy paper diploma clutched tightly in one hoof. This is it. It's all been worth it, surely.
You check all the businesses in town, flinging job applications left and right. "Not experienced enough." "Nah, we'd rather hire someone from my son's fraternity again." "No, I think we're going to hire some guy who's 8 years from retirement age to fill 2 entry-level positions, instead." "What kind of degree even is this?"
In desperation, you return to the coffee shop and beg for your old job back. "Sorry, you're overqualified now. We can't possibly hire you, it's against corporate policy."
It's about then that your food, sleep, and hygiene meters all reach zero at the same time. You can't do anything. If you can even bring yourself to get out of bed, you just end up standing outside buildings, trying to will yourself to go in, to apply for a job, to just go see a movie again, even to just buy a meal. But you can't. You just can't. "Pony cannot do that because: unhappy."
It's then that you collapse in the street, broken, penniless, and alone; unable to die, yet unable to live.

Balance is not the strong side of this game.
I've gotten this game as a gift from a friend from the Monthly Humble Bundle, so far I've been enjoying it, but it has so many flaws. In fact, too many.
The story is really weak, it covers the Marineford arc, but you play it 4-5 times just with other characters every time, therefore you just replay the Marineford arc 5 times instead of going to the next arc.
The game in itself isn't balanced, the more you play and grind you can level up your characters, making them stronger. So instead of pure skill and mechanics knowledge you have to win by grinding more and more that it becomes ridiculous.
If you "main" three characters, they'll be the highest level, so you'll use them for pretty much all levels and it becomes stale real fast. You won't switch to other characters because they're low level.
Putting that aside, the story is extremely hard. Most of the fights are the same- Spam that one attack, after 3 minutes you get the enemy to half health, then he uses one move to delete 70% of your HP.
The only thing that made me play the game that much (Not sure if it's even considered a lot) is the side battles- The wanted posters. Basically you choose a team, and fight against groups of different enemies every time, it is kinda interesting, but even that becomes boring after some time.
Online- You have online to fight against other people (By the way nobody is on, so online is pretty much dead) and you have an online map in which you can fight and  conquer island- All with teams of other players. So the player who grinded more will win.
Now as for the DLCs, they should've been in the regular game, they really are really expensive. It pretty much doubles the cost of the game.
It lacks characters. Most of the fighters are only the big hits from the latest arcs- So you'll find Whitebeard, Blackbeard, Boa and Doffy. Ace, Sabo, Smoker and Buggy- Who are side characters but more important. Of course the straw hat crew, the admirals, and a few from the worst generation (Law, Kid, X Drake), as well as Jozu and Marco. But you won't find any of the previous arcs characters besides Enel. No Rob Lucci or others from CP9, no Arlong, Garp, Hody Jones and many others which made appearance through the series.
Now, it seems that the more important the character is, the stronger he is. Whitebeard for example will be extremely strong compared to X Drake, Which is just stupid as it limits your choice of characters even further.
One Piece Burning Blood isn't worth 50$. And with the DLCs- 105$. Definitely not.

Shantae and the Pirate’s Curse is the third and most refined entry of the series thus far, forming what is now called the “sprite trilogy”. In this installment, Shantae teams up with longtime series antagonist Risky Boots on a quest to tame an ancient curse that threatens all of Sequin Land. Bereft of her genie magic, Shantae must instead make use of powerful pirate items: Risky’s pistol, hat, boots, scimitar and cannon, to traverse the world. The overworld and warp points of the earlier games are replaced with a free-roaming stage select, where Risky’s ship takes you to each of the levels, and she can be talked to at almost any time to leave your current island and travel elsewhere, up to the very end of the game. Easily twice the length of Risky’s Revenge, Pirate’s Curse retains most of the advances made in that game and also brings back a number of elements not seen since the original GBC game, most notably, the bathhouse in Scuttle Town that lets your recover health for free. Also, reloading a save will refill Shantae’s health. Pike balls are once again consumables as in the original, and the storm puffs and fireballs are gone, but Risky’s Pistol provides unlimited ranged attacks and can be upgraded, like Shantae’s hair, for more damage. Shantae can use the hat to glide, the scimitar to pogo-jump enemies a la Shovel Knight, the boots to do a Super Metroid-style boost run, and the cannon to do up to three additional jumps, altogether making Shantae her most maneuverable self yet. The same great sprites seen in Risky’s Revenge are augmented with new character art, new music, and a variety of new environments and enemies that revisit those seen in Shantae 1. Other new editions include consumable items that boost Shantae’s attack damage, food items that drop off enemies and restore various amounts of health, and “pirate flares” that allow you to return to Risky at any time, so long as you are outdoors. Overall, Pirate’s Curse is considerably more challenging then Risky’s Revenge but not to the point of frustration- falling into a death pit or touching the spikes merely removes a single hit point and returns you to the entrance of the current room, and you can have a total of forty, and carry enough health items to render an actual game over a near-impossibility- thanks to the addition of auto-potions that trigger automatically upon losing all your health. It is not however, anywhere near as cheap as the first game, and for that I am thankful. If you liked the previous Shantae titles, Metrodivanias or platformers of any kind, Shantae and the Pirate’s Curse is a treat for your eyes, ears and fingers that should not be missed.

Marlow Brggs and the Mask of Death is hack and slash-esque platformer, with
minimal options for attack, and repetitive attacks.  There are also limited puzzles,
and a few turret sections.  The music, while respectable, was not used appropriately
to emphasize action or atmosphere as you progress through the game.  There are
leaderboards for those that enjoy them, and challenge areas that require a different
style of combat both to change up the standard hack and slash feel, and to offer
a harder level of difficulty for those looking to increase their leaderboard rankings.
The graphics look good, and the story is decent,
with eclectic comedic aspects that come off as more corny than the game was trying for.
The game doesn't take itself too seriously, which is good, but it has clung to certain
stereotypes such as "rescue the princess" that are overdone in many adventure games.
The level design is vast and impressive, but there is a certain suspension of
disbelief required in the physics.   Some may find no fault in a full on battle while
flying through the air, but most would probably question how the characters aren't
thrown to their deaths.  The platforming is where this game excels in content.
They are designed very well, and you will spend more time platforming through the world
than doing anything else. There is a major problem with the camera angle, however, making it
difficult to see distances when platforming, and seeing enemies due to the angle.  it
takes away from the immersion into the game, and requiring memorization of challenges
rather than going with the flow of the adventure.  I go more in depth into this
problem in the video for those that would like a visual example.
The combat in the game falls short of what it could be;  the weapons all
essentially do the same thing, with differences in range or speed.  As you progress
through the game, the enemies require more button smashing to defeat rather than any
tactics or response to their abilities.  There are spells in the game, but they all
cost an excessive amount of mana, couldn't be used often, and have little effect or
damage to the enemy, taking away from the fluidity of the game.
The game has good graphics, but has a lot of issues.  The story doesn't propel
you forward, and doesn't encourage an emotional connection.  The battles lack fluidity
and the camera view makes it more repetitive than immersive.  I never felt the game
was wasting my time, but I felt it was more boring than challenging.  You spend more
time platforming through the world than in combat.  If you expect more from games, then
good chance you will not enjoy this game, but if you are easily amused then this should
be good enough for you to enjoy.
For more details, see the linked video review, as this is a basic summary of
what I cover in my video.

Decided to write a small opinion about the game since almost no-one from my friendlist have it in their library.
tl;dr: I liked it. Really funny spectacle fighter/brawler game.
More:
It's a your-standard-generic-brawler game, like any DmC or Batman games this days, yet it offers a nice original story to it placed in Mayan ruins (or Aztecs, or Toltecs, or w/e ;)). There are small glitches here and there, the combat system is not as refined as in DmC, but it was a pleasure playing it.
You are a man who visits your Ancient South America (later referred to as ASA) linguist girlfriend and suddenly you are killed because reasons (not only monsters, but people as well don't like you in this game). However, the weapon you were killed with was possessed by some god of ASA and he recognizes you as The Spirit Warrior who will bring peace to this part of Earth. And so you get resurrected and have a scythe to get through hoardes of mercenaries, possessed mercenaries, ASA warriors and other monsters and gods from ASA believes.
During your progress you get more weapons (in total: scythe, rouge-like weapon - my fav, whip with a blade and warhammer with one side bladed) as well as learn some magic by defeating gods (fire, earth, ice and wind). Spells are summoned by using mana.
You replenish you health by collecting red orbs/masks and mana by collecting blue ones. Your abilities can by upgraded by collecting enough of yellow ones. However the upgrades are simple: each weapon and spell has three levels, and with each level you get more dmg with it, unlock 2 new moves and your health or mana base value gets higher. It's much simpler than in e.g. Darksiders: there you needed to think what to put your exp into, but here, as the weapons and spells are added to your arsenal in balanced manner, almost always you'd get one thing upgraded before having the other one obtained. With that in mind, the fight system is extremely expanded and the actions you get through sometimes are the typical Hollywood star Bruce Willis level of awesomeness actions.
The biggest issue I had with the game was the mana system. When you are fully upgraded you get to fire exactly 2 spells. But the mana bar doesn't indicate you in any way if you have enough mana to cast the spell, so you mash the buttons once or twice trying to see if it can work. As stated previously, mana is obtainable in form of blue masks (placed directly on map) or blue orbs (flying out of defeated opponent). As fights are mostly in closed area arenas with god-knows-how-much-opponents going to jump at you in next wave (if there will be any, who knows), you try to limit the usage of blue masks nearby. After you die two or three times to some bigger tank monsters and even start using the masks because why the hell not, you find yourself in a place where you need a smallest amount of mana to use the spell one more time, but it doesn't regenerate in time, and isn't replenished with inflicted damage, so you spend time and time until you finish the monster, and voila, blue f-ing orbs which you don't need anymore. And before next fight it is certain that more than one blue mask will appear.
Another problem I had were some mini-missions/challenges where you would slide down and had to avoid rocks, pits etc. Alice: Nightmare Returns had some similar sequences, but in here the time between when you push the jump button and when it is registered by the character in game was many times too big for me and I've spent countless times on some of those agility jobs.
And one smallest issue: the game needs some power to run smoothly. On my machine DmC was running 60fps on 1080p max settings while this one had to be changed to 720p and some of the graphic options needed to be disabled. I know that Unreal Engine which DmC was running on was tended professionally through years, and I have no idea what was Marlow Briggs build on, but I would expect a little more from the game fidelity.
Except of those two and a half points above the game was really nice: the story was addictive, the fight system, combos included, was sensationally developed and fluent, graphics caught your eyes and had some great sceneries and the music was always on spot. Also, your mask-god companion has a great sense of sarcastic humour and the voice acting for it is great, so you don't get bored.
Having in mind that it is actually a budget game (€5 without a sale) this is probably one of the best fun to price factor games you can get right now.

Don't trust my playtime on this, as I played many more hours while I was on vacations, with no internet connection. And boy, should I have instaled something else on my laptop.
Simply put: This game is boring and repetitive. It's one of those games where you feel like you're doing a script's work.
The concept is original: Instead of being a hero, you're a weapons smith who makes weapons for the heroes - there's no real action in the game.
However I wonder who thought a cool game could be made out of this concept, because this ain't so.
The gameplay consists on getting smiths and making them "forge" weapons. Certain weapon types level up some stats faster, and the smiths have different values for each stat as well. Heroes prefer different weapon types & stats.
Make a weapon, go sell it to a hero, get money, progress to next area and do EXACTLY the same process (all the game consists on this) with none to little story progress (For those who played: I made it to world 4, and I wonder, can that even be called story?).
You can also send your smiths to explore & find resources, which basically renders the shopping function useless as there's never any need to buy resources. There's also a research option which lets you discover new weapon blueprints using random stuff you find exploring. New weapons render all previous weapons of the same kind useless as basically they have the same stats ratio except each stat is higher. Really, if they just made different stat ratios on weapons of the same type this would already be better.
On top of all that there's some minor mechanics and random crap that you need to play around to keep going on doing the same monotonous task:
-Seasons: Spend money so it's not too hot or cold in the shop.
-Random events that offer multiple choices that could be both correct or wrong depending on randomness. Have fun enjoying the "nerfs" to the current weapon you're forging I guess.
-Move your dog so your smiths don't get too unhappy of working and need vacations.
-Town festivals and stuff? Never cared tbh.
The world/towns "system" seems to hint that something more interesting was planned for it, but it was quite a letdown seeing how simple it was (in specific how it prevents you from doing some things in some towns for no reason).
To sum this game up: Glorified and thus bad cookie clicker, except you need to do more clicking.
I have absolutely no idea how the heck this game manages to have good reviews.

The game is the type of game you'd whittle away hours at kongregate playing. If it was an online game, I would love the builds and the time taken to build up weapons and grind towards a goal... but as a desktop game it falls short.

That's all i got to add to others comments. Yes, the game is addictive, challenging and funny.

I BEAT THIS GAME IN 4 HOURS.
I got this as part of the monthly Humble bundle and got excited because it looked to be the One Piece version of the Excellent Naruto Ninja Storm games.  It doesn't give you any backstory, and the only voice language is Japanese but I just rolled with it and read the dubbing.  The pirates are attacking this base trying to save their friend, with the story being told in a mix of cutscenes and slideshows with voice over.
First thing, is that your characters level up when they fight, and they actually grow stronger as you go.  What this means is that skill can be replaced with grinding, and if you are good enough by the time you get to the end of the story mode, if you haven't wasted time doing literally the same fight over and over you get BS fights where you have to hit the guy 50 times to win and he only has to hit you 5.  Furthermore, once I finished the first chapter, the next chapter was a guy who died in the first chapter.
Turns out, you play through the same overall scenario (attack the Marine base to save your friend), but with a different guy, half the cutscenes re-used from the first chapter without anything new in the slightest.  Third chapter? SAME DAMN SCENARIO, but now you play as one of the bad guys, with fights that don't make sense because that guy LOST those fights in the first chapter.  Fourth chapter? Started off with something entirely new! Then in the second battle was BACK AT THE SAME DAMN SCENARIO, and the fourth chapter was THREE FIGHTS LONG, roll credits.
Over half the characters NEVER SHOW UP IN THE STORY MISSIONS.  The entire MAIN CAST? NOPE. The straw hat guy is specified to be from 2 years ago, as opposed to the main one you start with.  This implies that future story missions will be with the new guy, but that NEVER HAPPENS.  There's a bunch of contrived scenario one-off fights you can get and the stupidity of some of them boggles the mind. It's like: Hey, these three characters were all born in February! Go fight them all at once. I AM NOT EXAGERRATING THIS IS A THING THAT HAPPENS.
When it comes to the fighting I have no idea if it's balanced as the fact that characters have different levels (and you never see your opponent’s level so you’re not sure if you’re in too deep or you just suck until it gets ridiculous).  A lot of the characters have really cheap moves, and the AI fluctuates between dumb as a post and god-like reaction time.  Fights would start and by the third chapter, unless I started with the fastest move and then dodged, the guy I was fighting would do the exact thing to counter me.
There is a “Hey fight people to gain territory” mode, but again it looks like Character level matters because I ran into the same “I hit them with 12 straight combo attacks to take down one of their three teammates, but it takes 2 to take me down” BS.  Also, game design note, this Levelling up mechanic punishes experimentation because your new characters will be low level so you will get your butt kicked if you try anyone other than the character that you’ve been grinding with.
If you love One Piece, and you’re really only caring about PVP, AND you want to win because you spent a large amount of time grinding then through skill on a fair playing field, then this is the game for you.  If you like to win through skill, like a good story, and aren’t a rabid fan of the Straw Hat Pirates, avoid this.  It MIGHT be worth it at five dollars, but Fifty?  Hell no.  Also, 25 dollars for a few new characters (the "Gold Pack") Are you high?
