This is what I call an improvement!
If you check my profile, you can see that I played and reviewed an earlier installment of the series: Risky's Revenge. While it was lacking in some aspects it was cool enough that after the convincing gameplays I decided to jump back to the series. This is definitely more fun and polished game and I can easily say it is worth your interest with only few hiccups along the way. If the game is solid, then I'm more than happy to nitpick some issues for further ironing out for the next Wayfoward's game. Criticism makes excellence!
Game is notably faster than the Risky's Revenge. The previous game was pretty sluggish at times, but the improved controls, Shantae's speed and jumps in pair with good level design, help dictate a reasonable pace that makes you flow through the game with no noticeable frustrating moments. Graphics are in my favorite 16/32-bit Mega Man X4-rish style, that didn't really change after Revenge (with recycled sprites), but it still looks pretty nice, especially with the new locations. Bosses are definite plus. While not very challenging, they provide fun encounters. There are a lot of new faces as regular enemies which are good to see. Platforming? No complains there.
Music deserves an separate paragraph. Jake Kaufman did probably his best score yet. In my opinion it's far better than Shovel Knight's and provides tons of catchy memorable tunes that really "sells" the game. I would say that without this soundtrack, many locations wouldn't be as fun and atmospheric as they are now, since many of them are pretty generic. Mud Bog Island with Village of Lost Souls hidden within it is an great example of climatic location boosted by an amazing music. This stuff rocks.
The story. Characters are likeable and unique, scenes are full of humor and plot overall isn't particularly offensive, but...
Logic? Out of commission. Setups? Wasted potential. Lore? Barely touched.
It looks like the devs had a plenty ideas for funny situations and hijinks between characters. There are lots of mini character arcs that bring this thing together, but logic behind why scene A resulted in events in scene B is completely bizarre. It fits the convention and style, but for me it is something of a missed opportunity. Keep in mind that this is a nitpick and Shantae doesn't need a great story to be an awesome game, but I would say that this is an aspect for further improvement.
Upgrades. They are all powerful and really fun to use... unless we are talking about the Sword upgrade that is only useful for unlocking vertical shafts and nothing more. It gives no advanced mobility and is pretty weak against enemies. No sense in using instead of standard hair whip. Pistol and additional melee attacks also become obsolete really fast, but other upgrades are extremely fun to use and tinker with.
As for a completely minor sidenote, which doesn't hurt the game that much, but I would like to point it out... There is also a strange dissonance in level progression vs. classic Metroidvania mechanics. Shantae controls would really shine in level-to-level progression system (intro level shows this), but this series was very exploration heavy from the start. Game tries to bring the best of both worlds, but levels are not-seamlessly connected and they are overall pretty small, so there isn't as much exploration as in standard Metroidvania and there are not enough set-pieces as for classic platformer. You can really feel it, as the game has less adventurish feel and yet doesn't deliver as much level-specific excitement as Freedom Planet or Shovel Knight. Luckily, this is subjective and not very noticeable. It doesn't affect the enjoyment as much, probably thanks to the overall solid experience crafted by the devs.
The only proper negative that I can think of is the price. Content-wise, it offers a similar about of fun and features as afromentioned Shovel Knight and Freedom Planet, yet it's price tag is 5 dollars higher. 15 bucks is a perfect price for fun and enjoyment you will get from Pirate's Curse. It's solid platform game that is definitely worth your interest since it holds up a great quality on par with other genre representatives. If you are a platforming fan, then you are making yourself a disservice if you won’t put it on your wishlist!

Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, Sleepy Shantae, SLEEPY SHANTAE!

Well, I have a lot of good things to say about this one. For starters, I didn't play any other Shantae games other than this. But judging by the trailers for the other games, I can easily assume this is the best. This game came out last year on 3DS and Wii U, and just a few months ago was ported to the PC. Here's my review.
The game plays like your average platformer. You control Shantae, who uses her hair to whip enemies, although later she gets upgrades like a gun, etc. The controls feel very smooth and responsive. You travel through six locations where you have to accomplish certain things and then go to the dungeon of the world. This heavily reminds me of Zelda, especially considering there are chests, keys, items, puzzles, etc. There are also a lot of secret items throughout the game. You can get jellies, which you can turn into health, and there are also bats I think that give you dark magic (you'll find out the use as you play). Also, you can use money earned from defeating enemies to buy one-time items (spike balls, shields, potions, etc.) or permanent upgrades (faster whip, more powerful, etc.). One thing I don't like is that some items are hidden in places that you either don't see (so either you have to get to them by complete accident or by trial and error), or that look like you can get them but you really can't. For example, there is a section in the sand that has tiny platforms that break upon touching them. I got very frustrated trying to get it, only to give up and learning that you can get it, but only after getting an upgrade. If it was more obvious that I couldn't get it, then I wouldn't have to be frustrated.
Presentation-wise, this game has great graphics. They are in a 16-bit SNES style, although on top of that, there are full artworks of the characters in-dialogs. For some reason, WayForward decided to use a default font for the dialogs, which looks quite ugly and annoying if you ask me. The soundtrack? Don't even ask. It's f*cking amazing. The composer also made the soundtrack for Shovel Knight, Duck Tales Remastered, Contra 4, etc. There isn't full voice acting, only occasional words by certain characters are pronounced, ususally sound good, but can get annoying at times.
Well, this game isn't super long either. You can beat it in three hours easily. Do I recommend it? Definitely. It is a little expensive compared to other indies (20$), but I still think it's worth it. Buy it, you'll like it!

This is one of my "guilty pleasure" games I own, but not one that I'm afraid to admit to. I played the crap out of the demo on Xbox 360 (came pre-installed) but never bought it for that system. Years later and it's on a steam summer sale and I say "to hell with it, buy the damn game" and have not regretted it since. I may not get all the clones back, or all the secret action figures, or play on anything harder than easy mode, but I still love the game. If you are at all a fan of platform/exploration games pick it up!

Gameplay: The storyline is non-existent, which isn't the worst thing in the world. Unfortunately, however, there are no redeeming qualities to make up for this. There are a decent amount of game mechanics and levels to keep the total playtime up to 6 hours. The levels however are in no way challenging.
Visuals: It's pretty disappointing. It looks very unfinished.
Audio: It's not the worst audiowise. I can say that the sound effects match the disproportionate cartoon-like theme that they were aiming for. The soundtrack would get  repetitive as the amount of songs they had didn't match the playtime it took to beat the game.
Replayability*: There is none. I have no desire to go back and play the game. All the levels are the exact same and often times the "perfection" mechanics (collecting all of the X) can usually be done on the first run through.
*This varies A LOT from person to person, so only rely on this category from me if you've agreed with my other reviews' replayability sections.

I've loved turn-based squad strat games since JA2.  I'd still rank that as the top; give 2nd place to Silent Storm (up until they bring in the unicorn suits of rainbow bright), and give this one 3rd place.  Just finished my first full playthrough:
PRO's: Solidly done turn-based squad strat game.  It's got a base with lots of upgrades, tons of loot, decent selection of weapons, limited resources (ammo, grenades, fuel, etc), good character progression, zombie killing fun, base management, character interactions are fun, etc.  Basically it's got a LOT of stuff done RIGHT.
CON's:   Not as many different weapons or upgrades as I'd like (thinking JA2 again); approx 3-6 per ammo type (7 ammo types; maybe 20-25 weapons total).  The side stories are limited in content and usually amount to: bring character A to place B from their past; get special dialog, end of quest.  Not bad, but could have been made into much more.  There are a few bugs; I had about 8 crashes total over my playthrough, but with ample auto-saves you never lose more than the last 10-20 minutes.  Last and biggest complaint is the simplistic AI.  Dont expect you're enemies to Mcguyver up an ultralight and surprise you with an L-shaped.  It's just not there, still: what do you expect from zombies?
Still a postive experience; really recommend this one if you're a fan of the genre.

Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is a platformer game which was initially released on the Nintendo 3DS and WiiU. It's the third in the Shantea series. I haven't played any of the previous one so I was a little behind on the story here.  The game was released initially in 2014 and was ported to Steam in April of 2015. The 3DS release of this game was actually nominated for the best platformer and was also in the Top 10 games in the Nintendo 2014 survey of fans favorites
You play as Shantae, who is a half-genie. You goal in the game is to save everyone from "The Pirate Master", with the help of her what appears to be long standing nemesis, named Risky Boots.
Throughout the game you will find various different "pirate equipment" such as pistols and cannons, these items are all used at various points in order to progress through the story. You can also upgrade all of your equipment too to make them more effective. This game is said to be the biggest in the series in terms of how many locations are included for you to explore. We also see a familiar mini-map screen you will have seen in Metroidvania style games before. The actual gameplay is very Metroidvania too, lots of jumping puzzles, thought based puzzles, enemies, collecting jewels and gems to find and chests with equipment and keys in to find.
The game uses a 2D graphics engine, which I can imagine looks pretty good on the 3DS, however it does look like a bit of an emulated game on the PC. The dialog scenes look nice, but the actual in game graphics are very pixelated, granted some people enjoy that style so that may right be up your street.
I must warn you, this game is not easy at all. You will die, and die, and die plenty of times. It may even have you rage quitting at points that it is so frustrating, but you can't help but load it up again in order to move on. The difficulty curve is very up and down, sometimes you can be going through one level and think its actually quite easy, then all of a sudden you are failing countless times on a specific area in the zone. Being hard is not a bad thing at all; it's actually something I really look for in a game. I did have to revert to Youtube videos for hints on how to get past some levels though.
A full playthrough of Shantea and the Pirate's Curse took me almost six hours. Sadly I don't think there is much replay-ability to be had here; once you playthrough it the once - there is really no other reason to playthrough it again.
This is actually a well put together port to the PC. The developers have gone to the effort of adding full controller support along with a graphically helpful control screen to go along with it. I would highly recommend you play this game with a controller aswell; playing on a keyboard would be a disaster.
I would recommend Shantea and the Pirate's Curse; but not at full price. I think the six hours it took me to complete along with the zero amount of replay-ability means you should really be picking this up on sale. However I did enjoy playing it, it is in no way a bad game. I am looking forward to trying out the other games in this series now!

Okay so you have a pony and it walks around in a vaguely cute environment. Unfortunately everything that comes after that feels like someone sketched a vague idea for it out and then forgot to actually implement it. Instead you end up with a weird game which is "watch the loading bars." Want  your pony to work an 8 hour shift? Watch a loading bar for 30 seconds! Want your pony to enjoy a film? Watch that loading bar go! Feel like taking your pony to university and training in a new career? You guessed it! Loading bar! There actually is no content beyond loading bars to basically everything you do, not even tiny animations. I really cannot stress how devoid of content this game is. Even when you have an entire section of items called "Toys" barring two of them (which are also reused as the only two animation in the social interactions with other ponies) all that happens when you play with them is that the icon that represents them appears in a though bubble above your pony for a few seconds.
For a while I thought maybe the horrendous lack of content was because frankly little girls play this and all they want to do is decorate their home area, but in order to do that in any meaningful way you need money and lots of it and that means ... mmm loading bar based gameplay!
There are five minigames. They are probably the least child friendly and most unforgiving and at the same time unutterably dull mini games I have played in a very long time. With low time limits, no rewards whatsoever for a partial complete and ridiculously unforgiving collision detection on the one that requires dodging (getting hit sets your score back to 0 and makes you restart the level) I know plenty of adults that would struggle with these. Aiming them at small children just seems cruel.
Finally of course the game tops this all off with graphics glitches, instability and one area (The Park) where as far as I can work out the UI is displaced half way across the screen for everyone that runs it, rendering large portions of it inaccessible and causing problems for other gameplay elements that attempt to fit around it.
If you're totally desperate to play with ponies, not only are there better games out there but if you must have this one it's currently free in the Google Play store for you to have on your phone (where at least the UI works).
Oh and an honourable mention goes to the idea of having pony children. Searching across all the versions of this game has not allowed me to find out how to do this. It has, however, allowed me to find myriads of other people nearly all of whom are asking how to do it as well (It is actually a requirement for one scenario). I suspect it is a feature they forgot to add along with the rest of the gameplay.

Cloning Clyde is an enjoyable puzzle action platformer with native controller support.  The puzzles themselves vary in difficulty and all revolve around your ability to clone yourself and use your clones to manipulate certain puzzles on the gamefield.  My only   minor gripe about the game is the fairly low resolution graphics which on a widescreen monitor when stretched to fullscreen result in a lot of jagged edges on the screen.  The music is sparse and limited to flourishes and the intro screen, but I would still recommend this game to puzzle lovers who want a little bit of arcade action.  Platform arcade enthusiasts though may find the actual twitch aspect of the game lacking, and the enemies are really only their to delay the completing of the puzzles rather than representing a serious threat.  All in all it's a competent game though, and worth recommending to most Steam gamers.

Dead State is a RPG about surviving the zombie apocalypse in Texas. In terms of setting, the game nails it.  Since society has broken down you’ll have to turn your group into a bunch of scavengers in order to survive. This is a dangerous endeavor in Texas where firearms are plentiful, and some homeowners aren’t going to let you raid their pantries or medicine cabinets without a fight.
As leader of a rag tag group of survivors you are going to be in charge of determining who to take in, how rations are divvied up, what improvements to build at base with your meager resources, and how you will relate to outside groups like motorcycle gangs, militias, and remnants of the US Army. Sub leaders will emerge within your group whose council you will need to take into account. They may try to pull off a coup against you. Maybe you can accommodate them or maybe you can put a bullet in their head during a mission and blame bandits.
While I thoroughly enjoyed the setting, character interaction, and government game aspects of Dead State there were a few issues that might be major turn offs for some players. First off, it pretty much plays exactly like the old turn based CRPGs of the late 1990s. Think Fallout 2 with zombies. It also looks a little like Fallout 2 (as viewed through nostalgia goggles – obviously it is more attractive than Fallout 2 if you’ve played Fallout 2 recently).  I personally don’t like the art style because a friend pointed out that all the NPC’s have facial features characteristic of Down’s Syndrome (and now I can’t unsee that… thanks, bro). The lack of voice acting made Dead State’s NPCs feel a little flat. Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines’ NPCs were really interesting because of excellent voice acting coupled with great dialogue by Dead State lead Brian Mitsoda.  Also, be prepared for an assortment of bugs and crashes. I don’t know if there is anything game breaking you need to worry about but that could be a possibility.

What do you get when you combine Uncharted's Nathan Drake with Mass Effect's Garrus?  The mostly weak Kratos from God of War.  What do you get when you combine Mass Effect's Thane with Devil May Cry's Dante?  You get the superior Marlow Briggs, Baby!  Actually, Marlow Briggs encompasses little aspects from each character I've just mentioned, except for maybe Garrus who's inconsequential.  In fact, Marlow Briggs borrows a little something from each of their games as well,  except for Mass Effect.  There's even a bit from Tomb Raider thrown in.  All this is a good thing.  However, don't expect Marlow Briggs to be as polished as any of the aforementioned games.  Choppy transitions seem to be Marlow Briggs' biggest shortcoming.
There have been many sales offering this game for less than a buck, and that's well worth it!  Marlow Briggs set pieces, funny characters, and constant explosions make this game a blast!  Not perfect, but short and satisfying fun!

This is actually the first "God of War" type game I've ever played, and whatever the default difficulty setting is, it's really easy to complete without giving much thought to what you're doing. Now, bump it up to Hardcore and you're in for a challenge, except I'm now wondering if I had figured how to get the game to switch weapons sooner (Tab key doesn't work for me, I had to use the individual number keys), if it would've been easier. There is also a serviceable amount of platforming and puzzle-solving, though nothing any seasoned player will be stuck on for very long (with maybe an exception here or there).
Anyway, the game is fast-paced, action-packed, and has lots of explosions and goofball banter between the main character and his floating Mayan mask spirit helper, and just about every action game cliche that's been invented in the past decade - bullet time, QTEs, slow-mo special moves, massive combo attacks, mini-game sequences - you name it, it's probably in here. Once you're past the factory settings near the beginning and into the Mayan jungles, it becomes one feast for the eyes after another (screenshots do not do it justice).
The game frequently goes on sale for around $1-$3, and if God of War clones or action games in general are your thing, I can easily recommend it for that. Even the current store price of $5 isn't a bad deal for it, but since I found it easy, I imagine that people who are more used to playing games of this genre than me might blow through it quickly, even on Hardcore.
Rating: 3.5/5

So after a couple of hours with the game, I found myself not truly interested enough to finish. Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death isn't so bad or terrible that it isn't simply worth playing, but it's a very straight forward God of War clone that didn't keep me interested. The highest mark for this game is the comedic banter between Marlow and the mask - it will make fun of you for dying and Marlow will say a line that is clearly meant to break the fourth wall - commentary that is self-aware. I genuinely laughed when the mask berated me for having magical powers and then jumping off into a pit and asked if I was looking for enemies when I jumped into another.
All aspects of the game are standard quality for 360 era spectacle fighter, except for some jumpiness with some animations. One cool feature that I like are the frozen cutscenes, involving the camera moving around a scene frozen in time and will "update" as it passes things that obscure's your view. This has maybe been done before, but it was done well before and it was nice to watch these cutscenes.
Still, I found myself uniterested in continuing any further - many other games of this genre do it better, and the comedy and cutscenes are good, but not enough to keep me going. That said it is $5 as of writing, and it meets, arguably, exceeds that value if you intend on finishing it. If your time is limited to better games, I'd only bother if you're really looking forward to some occasional laughs. If you have played all the good spectacle fighters and still want more, then Marlow Briggs is an ok title to add to the list.

The best Battlefield. The map design is excellent; it prioritizes fun engagements above all else. Maps are largely built around prefab, destructible, 2-3 floor buildings, which buffer the flow of combat and compartmentalize individual encounters. This means that you can actually breathe and make meaningful decisions in between all of the twitch-based watch-every-corner assaults. You know that segment in every battlefield scene where two soldiers duck behind cover and banter, using the moment of calm to rest and survey their surroundings before leaping back out guns blazing? This game is all about that moment. Front lines move back and forth in a perceivable way, you can get caught in epic holdouts with your squad, and buildings take a LOT of damage before they collapse, with each blown-out wall potentially changing your tactics. And despite how dynamic things get, you never burn out. Because you can breathe.
Oh, and there are NO JETS, which means that A) Infantry can meaningfully engage every vehicle, B) no player has to  dedicate themself exclusively to countering air units, C) air units are easy to keep track of, and D) air combat remains cover-based and low-flying. The whole "battlefield" experience is much more tightly woven together as a result.

I was genuinely suprised at the quality of this game.  It's a platformer puzzler where you navigate your way through well-designed levels to find the exit, with the catch that to get past certain obstacles you will need to find or make clones of yourself, or mutate into different forms (bomb, frog, chicken, monkey etc.).
Once you have clones you can switch to any clone anywhere else on the level at any time.  There is very little combat or chance to fail, with just a few robots on each level you must destroy to open the exit.  You're not timed, but there is a par time on each course you can try to beat.  You also have the option of saving all your clones by exiting them through vents before you exit the level using your last one, and there are several collectibles to find on each level.  All of this is optional and tied to some easy achievements.
Dozens of fun levels, not frustrating at all and plays great with a gamepad.  A little too easy, though.

Story Gist
HP!AWS?! starches (huehuehue) out with an Agent 47 Potato named Agent 46. He is waiting for your potato, named whatever you want. Your grandfather, Batata is sadly mashed. You now own 0.01% of the shop. Agent 46 gives you a few blacksmiths so you can start your shop, and you get started with smithing.
'Game'play
HP!AWS?!'s gameplay is made up of clicking to either make weapons, sell weapons, buy items for weapons, explore for items you can use to research more weapons, or give your workers a vacation so you can make more weapons. Weapons are a big thing in this game. Forging is simple. The bottom of the screen says 'Forge', you click it, go to your category (dagger, axe, bow, ect) click the weapon, and hit 'forge'. Your smiths will begin forging their weapon.
Pros & Cons
Pros -
- Fun, easy to grasp gameplay for all.
- Simple, pleasant graphics. They're pleasing to the eye.
- 'Choices of Fate', sometimes a bar will appear and a question will appear. Two answers will appear. One will give you a benefit, one will not. Sometimes you'll get money, or a worker will be boosted for a while.

Neutral Things -
- It's quite repetitive. It's good if you enjoy this sort of simulator, like I do, but otherwise one will find it very boring.
- Just a peeve of mine, but the game's name is long. Not really neutral or anything, just annoying to me.
Cons -
- Lazy puns that could've easily been made by a 5 year old.
TL;DR
Overall, HP!AWS?! is a fun blacksmith experience, if you like that sort of thing. Blacksmith simulators are loved or hated, and if you love that sort of thing, then pick it up! If you don't, well then why are you here?

A wonderful game with stunning graphics, an amazing plot, and great writing.
Not so much a video game as an experience, with relatively little skill required aside from orienteering and map reading, this game takes you into the story of a man who travels to the middle of the woods to escape from his problems and instead finds problems there, of a different sort.  You journey through wooded hills, meadows, and canyons and soon find that you're not alone out in the woods, and something dark is afoot.  It takes a forest fire, and many long conversations with a mysterious woman on the other end of a radio, to realize that (slight spoiler alert:) the darkness comes mostly from within...

Firewatch is a unique story-driven game that has limited dialogue action and hardly any physical human contact, yet you have a strong connection with another person. This is a short game but it was a lot of fun. I don't see much replayability simply because how the story flows but there are different modes such as a free roaming mode of the environment that I have yet to explore.
This is a good, short, story game that is different from anything I have played before and I would recommend it to others.

I was pretty shocked to see that my original review of this game seems to have vanished -- it wasn't very flattering.  I can only assume it's MIA because now this is Dead State: Reanimated.
So let me begin by saying that I was an original backer for this game, and I have followed it's development closely.  It showed great promise and intrigue, and there appeared to be a great dynamic between the devs and community.  That was, until Christmas 2014.
In what was the most apparent and appalling cash-grab I have ever seen by any professional entity, Double Bear Studios knowingly and willingly released this game in an unfinished, buggy, crash-ridden state.  The flame war which ensued between the community and devs is the stuff that legends are made of.
I've hopped back to this game from time-to-time, in the hopes that it was finally completed in a halfway competent matter (again, great premise for a game and I love to support indie studios), but it looks like the project is finally been abandoned by the devs in a semi-working state.  It's still a POS final product, just not as big and stinky of a POS as when it was first released.
Pros:
Great premise of a game --  Walking Dead meets Jagged Alliance
Cons
Everything Else!
Game is still buggy as hell.  Don't even think about trying to play it on Windows 10.
Graphics and music are just okay
Combat is slow, slow, slooooooooooowwwwwww ... and equally boring.
Almost non-existent base building.  Some upgrades are available ... but .... meh.
Scripted locations and drops from scripted enemies.  Zero replay value because of this.  Almost zero percent random.
A few different endings ... but nothing really that special.  Nothing that would make a player want to go back, retrace his/her almost exact steps again while dealing with the bugs and crashes.
$30.00!!!!??  $30.00 for this POS buggy, game!??  Someone is seriously smoking crack if they think that's gonna fly.
In Conclusion:
I would suggest you don't buy this game.  Instead, spend a few hours reading through the forums starting at Christmas time, 2014.  The evolution of the flame war and the devs self-destruction of this game is far more entertaining and engrossing than the game itself -- and it's free.

Based on the latest release of - Dead State: Reanimated.
Progress through Dead State proved reminiscent of pre-millennial RPGs such as Fallout 1/2, Baldurs Gate and to a lesser extent, Vampire: Bloodlines. I'd consider this the highest praise I can bestow a game.
The creative minds at Double Bear were involved in the creation of such cult games and have succeeded in achieving the sense of wonderment I found absent both in Pillars of Eternity and Wasteland 2, both of which attempted the same trick of capturing the essence of these earlier titles. Personally, I found both PoE and WL2 shallow interpretations, with story, immersiveness and game mechanics triaged for improved graphics. I suspect both titles will be forgotten while the legacy of their predecessors will continue.
Given the teams behinds those particular titles were also involved in the creation of what I consider the "golden-age" era of cRPGs, I'd just about given up hope of finding another immersive isometric RPG. Maybe the real minds behind the greatest RPGs had left the business, died, or transcended to a higher plane of existence. Maybe, like myself, they were tired of the excreta being squirted out and trotted about as the "greatest RPG of all time" every few months. Maybe it was time to find a different hobby.
Thankfully, at least one of the minds involved in the creation of cult classic RPGs is still among us.  The sense of an expansive and hostile world awaiting exploration, the advancement of both your character and relationships within the base alongside combat that retains old-school strategy but boosted with modern animations is unique among modern RPGs.
The personal interactions are significant, with extensive dialogue trees that vary depending on your own actions and the emotions and morale within the base. Plus, there are a huge number of friendly NPCs, with 90% being unique and memorable. As an example, you can negotiate with a Vietnam veteran to kill his infected wife and join your base. You can either encourage his martial mentality, or relegate him to the kitchen. He can end up drunk and you can either admonish, mock him or give him time to recuperate. You can improve his mood with cigars and bourbon. You can encourage him to recover his old combat skills or serve the base more domestically. He can confront and threaten you if your leadership suffers, and you can either regain his support through negotiation or shoot him in the back as he leaves your room and insult him as he bleeds to death. Such extensive interactions are present with the majority of the NPCs within your base. This isn't Dragon Age type fluff, you aren't bored with slowly voiced over descriptions of the sexual preferences of Quinari princesses in the lands of make-believe. The topics of discussion are life and death, the answers are realistic, sometimes grim, and darkly humorous or a distraction used prior to a sneak-attack.
Yes, the zombie premise has been overdone. Yes, there are bugs (Fallout 2 and Bloodlines were also released in such a state). Yes, it can be hard to maintain morale and food in your first game. Yes, you may found the graphics not the greatest. If the screenshots are repulsive to you, this won't be your preferred game type. This game has depth and complexity, not 4D-quantum-parralax-10.1 reflective sunbeams accentuating the convexed-v-synced-bump mapped textures of the player characters rear end, each bun modelled with a 6-point physics skeleton for life-like jiggle as you waddle around. This isn't style over substance.
The Easter Eggs, such as the Friggin Chikin scratch card and bill-board signs, plus Dougs nerdy advice about attacking those crazed meth addicts with critical hits to their eyes is appreciated fan-service to those of us who immersed ourselves in such iconic RPGs almost two decades old. Dead State may seem out of place in the current horde modern RPGs, however it restores my faith that future RPGs can retain the same complexity, intrigue and challenge that made their predecessors so renowned.

Yeah, it's a God of War game. The parts that aren't God of War are clones of other games you probably know. However, I found it difficult to get bored because the game goes batshit crazy at a breakneck pace. It's laugh-out-loud exhilarating and heart-pounding hilarious.
It belongs to an elite class of games like Killer Is Dead and Monkey Island - while you're playing, the game seems to be having as much fun as you are.
You can tell that it was made on a shoestring budget - every unncessary corner has been cut, but no shortcuts were taken where it counts. Cutscenes are kept to frozen key frames, but those frames are gorgeous. The characters are simple, but fantastically acted. Combat's just God of War, but it's God of War done very right.
Issues include some minor control issues during platforming and some awkward camera angles, but these are the rough edges of an uncut diamond. Even when I got frustrated with repeating one section over and over again, I couldn't stay mad for long before a beautiful view and a great kill animation had me cackling with delight.

There are plenty of detailed reviews out there that detail this game's pros and cons, so I'll try to keep my review succinct. I managed to spend 48 hours playing this game, and I enjoyed them. I found the combat enjoyable, scavenging was fun, and upgrading the shelter was satisfying. But this game is not everything that was promised to be. Interacting with survivors at the shelter was a lifeless experience. "Crisis" events were very rare and sometimes made little sense. Crises also had little lasting imapct; besides a one-time morale effect, they were never mentioned again. Certain story and character arcs were clearly cut short. You will almost never be able to find a creative solution to a problem- outside of multiple choice crisis and story events, your choices will have little consequence. In the late game, you will likely have a glut of resources and will be able to simply go on cruise control.
This game had a lot a promise and only partially lived up to it, but there is fun to be had here. The 70/100 metacritic score is fair. I can recommend this game as long as you temper your expectations.

Let me share with you the tale of my pony, a tale of love, loss, and life.  On day one, he entered Ponyland happy, healthy, and ready to mingle.  He struck up conversations with various ponies around town and made multiple friends almost immediately.  However, this was not to last.
The trouble first began when he visited the pharmacy, and purchased a large dose of painkillers.  While in a drug-induced delerium he entered a restaurant and ordered 3 chickens, and a steak, which for some reason was labeled 'ship'.  Having only just sated his appetite for flesh, my pony discovered the hard way that inflation had hit Ponyland hard.  He grimaced as he paid his $650 food bill and left.
By this time, night was falling, and my pony had nowhere to sleep.  He wandered the streets by night, striking up conversation with passing female ponies, presumably hookers, until the early AM.  The next day, we traversed the town looking to apply his trade as a waiter, but nowhere he checked had any positions open.  In another drug-fueled fit, he spent $7800 on 13 sticks of bright red lipstick, marking the last of his initial funds.  He had to find a source of income, otherwise he would not be able to partake in any of the overpriced amenities Ponyland had to offer.
Another sleepless night drew to a close as another day began.  By this time my pony had not slept in 4-5 days, and his beauty, hunger, and happiness were drained to 0%.  Due to his purchase of lipstick, there was nothing he could do, as a crippling onset of depression took hold of him.  In a desperate ploy to boost his morale, he applied all 13 sticks of lipstick at once, caking himself in makeup.  This did not however boost his mood at all.  Having nothing left to do with himself, my pony tried to find work again, this time succeeding in landing a job as a barista at a coffee shop.  But this victory was short-lived, as my pony found himself too unhappy to work.  His income would have to wait.
Day 10 rolled around and still my pony had not slept.  My pony's sullen figure roamed the streets of Ponyland, looking for anyone to talk to.  At last he spotted a girl pony and struck up a conversation.  He roped her into a 13 hour joketelling marathon, after which he found himself falling in love.  As they watched the fireworks together, the light from the display illuminated a wedding ring on the pony's hoof (or whatever).  She was married already.  Devastated, my pony broke off all conversation with this harlot, vowing to never talk to a married pony again.
Day 15, and my pony had explored all parts of Ponyland, still battling his crippling depression, along with his abandonment issues.  FInally, while trudging along the beach, he noticed a lone female pony.  His thoughts raced to past interests and betrayal, but he didn't let that get in the way of talking with her.  This time, he noticed she was single, a good sign.  He repeated his perfect lady-game of telling jokes for 13 hours and watching fireworks until they were madly in love with each other.  He even considered asking her to marry him on the spot, but he was bankrupt from his lipstick binge and had no other gifts to offer her.  Dejected, he reluctantly left her and headed back into town, now more depressed than ever.
Two more sleepless and tear-filled nights passed and my pony found himself homeless, depressed, disheveled, and broke on the streets.  It was Day 17, a fateful day.  Still unable to participate in any fun activities or work for a source of income due to his unhappiness, my pony decided to call it quits on life.
Or rather, I decided to quit the game.
TL;DR this game is a fantastic real-life simulator.  Battle depression, bankruptcy, homelessness, lonliness, and insomnia in a quest for true love.  I only rated it down because  the menu clipped a lot.
Thank you for reading, and RIP my pony.

While the game isn't offensively bad and is okay if you get it real cheap, I wouldn't really recommend this for anyone to buy. At this time, I've only got ~4 hours and have only gotten to the third level, so maybe the game gets better later, but I've felt pretty much the same way about the game since my second or third attempt.
The game is difficult. As in the very first enemies you meet can easily kill you in one turn from ful health if you're not careful. The second enemy type I encountered was completely invincible from the front, which is an issue with 1-tile wide corridors. The third enemy type I encountered had a ranged attack that 1-shot someone from full health. Fighting these enemies didn't feel like I was overcoming some obstacle, but instead like I was tying to manipulate the game just to stay alive.
The levels can be a bit wonky as well. Some rooms and up completely unconnected from others, including the rooms you start a level in or the rooms an elevator is in. In one instance, this was a nice surprise as the room was filled with robots like a trap, but in all the other cases it was just a bit annoying.
The "upgrades" were not only few and far between, but also weren't neccessarily better than what you started the game with. About the only reason to ever switch to some of these is because you've run out of ammo or armor.
I'm also not a fan of shooting mechanics. You can only shoot forwards in a straight line, so it's near impossible to safely get multiple guns on the same target unless you form a conga line or in a nice open room. The "100% accuracy at max range" is an interesting concept, but the fact that everything past max range can't be hit at all leads to some wonkiness, especially with short range weapons. Also, you can miss with a grenade launcher. How do you fail to do any damage with a
? It
Finally, there is this wierd bug where you end a move between tiles, and it seems a coin flip which tile you start on next turn. The includes one instance where I was halfway between a tile that was in range of a robot and another tile just out of it's range, and I ended up not getting attacked as if I was on the tile that was too far away, but on the next round started on the other tile, which meant I was now sharing the tile with the robot. This bug is especially annoying in the few cases where it happens in the middle of a turn, becuase you have no way of knowing which tile the game thinks you're on until you move again, making going around corners or through doors a crapshoot.

Feels very unbalanced from early game onwards. I know half the fun of a rogue-like is wiping and having to start over, but you a need a few more hooks to make you feel like you're getting somewhere. Without some feeling of incremental progress I found myself just losing interest within 10 minutes of starting each game.

In a nutshell, Steam Marines is a turn based roguelike that puts you in command of a squad of four marines abruptly awoken out of cryostasis to deal with an unexpected assault on a steampunk spaceship. These fellas shoot robots and aliens, tear their spaceship up and of course gain useful experience from those educational activities. Their objective? To advance to the elevators that will take them deeper into the ship -because they're ordered to, no questions asked- and that pretty much sums the game up.
Before you get to see some action, you have to create a four-man squad choosing any combination of the five available classes. Each marine in the squad has a perk of your choice offering further customisation. The stats of both your marine and his starting equipment are determined randomly at the start of each game. As they gain experience by encountering and defeating enemies, the marines get promoted earning a stat point, a skill point, as a well as an invaluable talent. Upon her fourth and last promotion, the marine has the option of retraining; starting over as a different class, retaining stats and skills but losing talents already learnt. As far as items are concerned, the game doesn't boast that much of a variety. Armour protects from nasty stuff and occasionally provides some stats. Since they wear out with hits they are kinda expendable. Weapons shoot stuff - later in the game they can be modded into a laser guns and those, in turn, be converted to plasma guns (you tend to marry those).
In your turn your marines get to do various actions using action points. Then the AI moves all enemy units and - should you stay alive - you get to play another one. Moving around and changing facing is as obvious as it can be. Positiong is important since flank attacks hurt more and back attacks deal double damage. "Taking cover" is also important since standing in front of a door, even with a gun pointing towards it, might prove a bad decision. The line of sight is a couple of squares ahead and can be boosted by equipping the flashlight but having the flashlight on means that you can't use lasersights to improve accuracy. Guard is a very important mechanic since it is the only way of interrupting the enemy turn. A marine on guard attacks anything nasty that moves within her line of fire. Enemy movement has to be predicted and fire zones created in order to ensure the survival of the squad during the enemy turn. Now, marines interact with the spaceship's environment in an interesting fashion since they are able to, literally, tear it down. All walls can be destroyed to the player's best, or worst, interest. Once your turn ends, it is the time for the invaders to shine, one at a time. Enemies are plenty and offer a progressive challenge. Most of them have interesting abilities and feel nicely fleshed out. Α boss follows each stage comprised of five levels, each with a different twist thothough usually you want them dead before you get to see what fancy stuff they are capable of. The AI is fairly decent. Sometimes it plays a bit passively but offers quite a challenge!
Steam Marines is presented in 2D and will run on almost every machine. I find the graphics aesthetically pleasing though not impressive; there are prettier games out there. Not so much because the pixel art is mediocre but because the randomly generated levels lack elegance (gameplaywise too). Thematically it is best described as space meets steampunk. The concept is well executed but it could have been further developed. The synthesis of its two elements appears forced at times although I have to admit that the game feels rather original. Some little details that could make the whole concept skyrocket seem to be missing, such as variety in the features of the rooms that feel more or less the same.
The game is accompanied by minimalistic/ambient music that adds to the survival/isolation experience. Besides the track heard during 95% of the game, a main theme that sounds catchy to my ears is included, along with a boss theme that induces nail bitting symptoms; it gets the job done. The sound effects are decent and give off a retro vibe although they tend to get a tad repetitive, as the music. Overall nothing exceptional nor disappointing in the sound department.
Many people nag that the controls are clunky and the UI unintuitive but I beg to differ. Hotkeys mean the difference between fun and frustration. There aren't that many to remember anyway, most are pretty obvious. UI-wise I'm pretty satisfied as well. Everything is one click away and almost everything that needs to appear on screen as you play the game, appears. Nonetheless, many mechanics are hid behind a veil for sure. This rewards fans of trial and error and bothers those who want to have a clear overview of what's going on before they play the game.
The game, even on normal difficulty, is very unforgiving. A single wrong move can cost the life of a marine, even the game. Not that new marines can't be found after each level, but experienced marines are invaluable later on. However, given a solid knowledge of the mechanics, if engagements are approached cautiously, steady advancement is guaranteed. In a sense, the game is "realistic" as far as squad tactics application are concerned. Squad tactics applied here, also known as common wisdom, are often forgotten due to the seer amount of easy-mode games out there. You ought to advance in a formation with a steady pace, watch your flanks/rear and avoid exposing yourself, splitting up etc. In it's essence, this is a survival game.
Many people also nag that Steam Marines is unfair. Not once, at least on Hard, did I lose because of luck. Always, I mean it, it was because I made a mistake and those cannot be forgiven! Apart from enemy placement, which can always be dealt with proper positioning, the only random element is the to-hit "die", when not in the ideal weapon range. Luck is not a game deciding factor. Sure, there is a massive jump of difficulty from Easy to Normal but roguelikes are supposed to be brutal!
Definitely the game is far from flawless. The tutorial is lacking, leaving you with many things to find yourself while the manual well... There is no manual! Τhen there are quite a few minor bugs. For example, sometimes the enemy is not in the line of fire of a marine but the U.I. informs you how much damage you will deal to the enemy if you shoot. A couple of minor graphic or sound glitches are present here and there but nothing too annoying. Note however that the developer is active and always there to provide support at the forums! Finally, I have some issues with some of the thought process behind class development. For instance, Snipers can perma-lock bosses. On Brutal it is necessary sometimes even on Hard. Besides that, I think that one or two talents are underperforming and that wouldn't be much of an issue but, given the limited amount of options, I'd prefer every choice to be impactful. After finishing the game, a new-game-plus mode appears where you have the option of playing with your previous squad but there isn't anything new to see, I expected some surprises!
Yes, it tends to get repetitive and quirky but the overall experience is solid. It doesn't have that many elements to make each game feel unique, but what is offered feels rather special. How many  16-bit looking, retro, steampunk roguelikes are out there anyway? Until the 40hour mark I could play many hours straight and now, a game every now and then is always welcome! All in all Steam Marines is decent. It offers a challenging, turn-based, tactical fun that rewards careful planners. Worth checking out!

Shantae is a hair-whipping belly dancing genie. When she loses her magic, Shantae must team up with her nemesis, the nefarious pirate Risky Boots in order to save Sequin Land from an evil curse. As a pirate, Shantae gains new weapons to advance her quest, slay monsters, battle epic bosses…and hopefully get her magic back in the bargain! But can she really trust her deadliest enemy?
The third Shantae game is the biggest yet! Beyond Sequin Land lie cursed islands and labyrinths each hiding a new piece of Pirate Gear - Flintlock Pistol, Pirate Hat, Scimitar, Risky's Boots, and even a Cannon. Upgrade Shantae's hair and weapons or unlock advanced Fighter's Moves. Locate maps, return lost Heart Squids, collect rare loot, and laugh out loud at the weird, wild, and wonderfully humorous cast of characters. Incredible high resolution artwork, unlockable Pirate-Mode, multiple endings, and an unforgettable soundtrack make this one game you won't want to miss! - Recommended!

Shantae, the half-genie heroine of Shantae and the Pirate's Curse, is more than just an upstart in the Metroidvania genre – she's the new star. At a glance, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse may look like a game for kids, but it's actually very deep and expertly designed, appealing on a variety of levels from platforming and exploration, to music and visual style. I love the sense of humor, too – there are tons of outrageous gags that make both the good guys and the bad guys completely lovable.
More so than its predecessor, Risky's Revenge, Pirate's Curse feels like a platformer, with more clearly-defined levels (islands that you sail to) and difficult platforming segments that require multiple attempts to complete. There's a general lack of warp points within the levels, which can make for a bit of frustration when you realize that you have to go through an entire area again to pick up something you missed. Also, the whole game feels a bit too small, and I wish there were more support items to use (like the pike balls) to add more depth to the gameplay.
Problems aside, Shantae and the Pirate's Curse is the most fun I've had with this genre since the classic 2D Castlevania games. It's funny, stylish, and all-around an outstanding game that I heartily recommend.
(Rating: 8.5/10 “Excellent”)
Notes: I played Shantae and the Pirate's Curse with an Xbox 360 Controller for Windows. I recommend using a console controller like this for all platformer-type games, since it allows for greater precision control.

A fun and easy to play metroidvania that doesn't overstay its welcome.  The big difference between this and Risky's Revenge gameplay-wise is that the various animal forms are exchanged for pieces of pirate equipment that hit all the cues of a metroidvania; you have your triple jump, speed dash, hover ability, et al.
Stage layout and dungeon design are simple enough, but the "overworld" aspects of each island is a little too similar outside of their general theme.  The game is collectible friendly in that each level keeps a visible tally of how many hidden items are each level and how many you have already tracked down.  There's enough stuff to find to incentivize revisiting areas but not too many that looking for secrets feels like a slog or unrewarding.
The soundtrack is as nice and catchy as is most of Jake “virt” Kaufman's stuff.  The spritework is good and the game controls well.  Using the inventory/map is a little clunky, but not a big negative by any means.  Pirate's Curse is a relatively easy game, though it has a couple of areas that can be kind of a pain, like the stealth section and a final leg that's significantly harder platforming-wsie than the rest of the game, though it's not especially hard.
All in all, a nice little game that will take most people between 8-12 hours to finish but I can see it having a good bit of replaybility since once you beat the game you can start a new game with all of your pirate skills unlocked from the start, so you can triple jump, speed dash and so on right from the start. ♥♥♥♥♥♥like that rules and means I'll probably play this again some time in the future.
One last thing, if the idea of cartoon boobs drives you crazy and makes you want to make a forums post about it, pass on this.  There are tons of boobs everywhere but if you have any background with original property WayForward games, this isn't a surprise in the least.  WayForward loves boobs.  If you love cartoon boobs and metroidvania's, this is the game for you.

Hello Nerds and Nerdettes, I have spend some time researching this game and here are my conclussions. Below there is everything yu need to know in a writen format but here is a video in case you prefer to spend 5 min watching instead of reading
Game has been out for just over 2 years with first public build coming out on 19 of February 2015. And until now around 270,000 people bought the game with majority of the purchases happening in initial months. Currently there is about 7750 active players of the game and that number had risen from 4000 in September so we are seeing a bit of positive trend over last few months. Last but not least the game review scored has dropped dramatically from it’s original reception.
As always it is essential that people who buy early access understand that they buying an experience rather than fully developed product. It is implied that product will improve over the years but you must understand that the product may evolve in a ways you may dislike.
Okay with all the facts and this little introduction  in mind let’s look at a potential reasons in review drop and what that means to you potential customer.
First the description of a game reads as: Medieval Engineers is a sandbox game about engineering, construction and the maintenance of architectural works and mechanical equipment using medieval technology. Players build castles; construct mechanical devices and underground mining. There is an entire planet to explore!
What a time to be alive! I have always been impressed by the technological miracles engineers achieved with simple technology like rotors, ropes and powers of nature. We can easily imagine that people who bought into the product are modded minecraft veterans, Nerds and Nerdettes that enjoy tweaking their build, constructing impossible machines with clever use of simple technology. Modern day wannabe engineers who like a challenge that medieval times bring.
Here however lies the problem with the game. For first year and a bit game lacked a lot of direction developers were jumping from one update to the other with what felt like absolute lack of road map. Game started to drift away from it’s original purpose of engineering and machine building and more towards building design and multiplayer. After a while they started adding survival element. Of course survival elements and multiplayer are essential to keep game like this alive and challenging but slowly very focused goal of making engineering game shifted into making more general survival experience. This left many people disappointed as it wasn’t initial promise of the game. I think this lack of direction was a major factor in increasing disappointment and slow death of playerbase.
Medieval Engineer subreddit has stagnated in subscriptions as you can see in here:
and now look at what happen in other early access games with more focused development like Software Inc
for example or Kerbal Space Program
back when game was in early access or even Space Engineers
older sister game of Medieval Engineers. As you can see game struggles to attract new fans
I think major contributor to the state of a game is that team set themselves for a failure with weekly update schedule. Sometimes in game development you just have sit down and fix bunch of bugs, or code a major piece of work that will take small team few weeks to do. When you are pressured to release something new every week you end up focusing on minor additions rather than major patches. Even one of most recent updates is a door noise improvement. Is it nice that they tweaked it to be more natural? Sure. Is it important at this stage of development? Not so much.
Okay let’s now focus on positives since October time when Planet updates was released development feels much more focused and it gives out the impression that someone took a dev team together sat them down and decided on a game vision and has more consistent plan in achieving it. Still weekly updates disturb the flow hence door noise update etc. but it’s much better that it was prior to that. With the new focus we have seen increase in active players bringing back some of the old veterans of the game.
I am hoping that this focused direction will be consistent and will reignite the spark in the community and brings back more players, modders and content creators. From my brief chat with veterans of the game people who endured creation process of last 2 years it feel s it has been worthwhile experience and they feel game progressed
Okay so what is Medieval engineers really. It is Medieval survival game with focus on multiplayer and base building with some focus on machine building. If you want the game in a spirit of Life is Feudal you will have fun with Medieval Engineers. If you want a game about building new machines and engineering it gives you some aspects of it but not enough to buy on the merit of this alone.
Overall Medieval Engineers development is better than some of Early Access projects I have seen but game evolved a lot from it’s original form. Approach with caution or simply wait another year. As always with Early Access don’t buy the game on hopes on potential but it only if you like it in current format.
Nerds and Nerdettes my name is Feniks and I hope you had a great time watching today's Early Access Monitor and you are able to make better informed decision about the game. I am looking forward to your opinions in the comment section down below and hope for some good discussion. Have a nice day.

This game feels like a real wasted opportunity. Incredible visuals paired with brilliant voice acting, compelling character development. All it needed was a memorable storyline. At times the story felt like it was shaping up to become something interesting, but with each peak in the story came disappointment.
I understand that to some extent the developers have tried to maintain a level of realism within the story and it's characters, but I have to say that the majority of the key points in the storyline (and in particualr the ending) added up to what I would consider to be one of the most disappointing and lack-luster story of any game I've ever played.
After 4 hours of gameplay and really investing in the characters/story but still being let down more than once, all I was hoping for is a strong and satisfying ending that provided both closure and potential for a sequel. Instead, you are left feeling that all the decisions you have made throughout the game (which at the time feel subtle, but still significant to your character) have been completely pointless and that the developers have just simply ran out of ideas.
It really is such a shame that a unique game like this can possess such amazing visual and audio elements, but be let down by the actual foundation the game is built on, the story. Truthfully, there are 5-6 moments throughout the 4 hour story I can think of immediately that the developers could have changed to send the player deeper and deeper into the storyline and it's characters. By making the story more exciting throughout, they probably could have both extended the game's length (and therefore satisfy the player that think the game is too short) and vastly improved the ending, leaving the audience happy with the outcome but also longing for a second game to continue the story.

Now that my problem with Glyph has been resolved, I can fully review the game. As this is an MMO, I'll update this as I play, but as it stands, here is what my first hour and a half has merited.
- The cash shop, while it does have items that speed up progress, it's mostly cosmetics, and convenience items. From what I'm seeing, this game isn't Pay-2-Win.
- The game periodicly rewards you for playing and progressing in the story, which is quite nice. I don't mean from quest rewards, there is a seperate system that gives you items such as trumpets that allow you to talk in global chat. I like it!
- While not impressive by any means, as well as choppy animations, the game looks pretty alright. Certainly not terrible by any means. Models on the player characters look pretty good, armor looks nice, skills are flashy if not slightly dated looking. NPC models, especially mobs\monsters, can range from pretty awesome looking to blocky nightmares with bad textures. Overall, the game looks pretty good.
- While not extensive, you have a bit of room to customize your characters face, hair and so on before jumping in. It's always nice to see some degree of customization in a game!
- Combat itself feels fluid and fast paced. Bosses are fun to fight as they have telegraphed attacks, some being quite fast. This makes you use skill instead of facerolling your hotkeys. Another nice thing i've noticed is that potions are on a fairly harsh cooldown, which eliminates potion spamming to get through tough enemies.
- The form changing is rather nice, if you're having a hard time or are facing a tough enemy, for a limited time you can become a devil, granting you immense power and new abilities. This adds an interesting aspect to combat, and is pretty welcome.
- Oh yes, there is loot in this game, which is always a plus. Bosses drop items at the end of dungeons, on top of being fun to fight, this makes dungeon crawling a pleasure.
- While this game isn't graphically amazing, it seems to dip frequently. I have a GTX 960 and I have FPS dips seemingly at random. While it isn't game breaking, it can get on the nerves.
- Not very many classes, only 4, all gender locked. You have your Melee guy, your Assassin guy, your Mage girl and, oddly enough, your cannon toting short girl!
- A lot of sounds are your average cookie-cutter mmo sounds, many I recognized from other games, this doesn't come as a surprise in the least. Skills sound pretty good though, at least for the Evoker class. Music on the other hand is rather decent, such as the tune played during a part in a cemetary with zombies fit with the atmosphere and had a nice creepy vibe. My biggest issue is that one track will play, then there will be dead silence for 30 seconds or so. Voice acting is subpar, but an mmo with voiced cutscenes is rare, so I'll cut Devilian some slack here.
- There seems to be some lantecy issues, I'd find my movement becoming sticky randomly, only to be unnoticable later on. Also sometimes you'll just get disconnected out of the blue, which is problematic in certain situations.
- The UI is very meh. I've seen worse, however it suffers from a similar issue TERA Online does, which is opening your inventory will inexplicably freeze your game for a second. Also there's an issue with exiting windows, as half the time the X on the upper right corner doesn't even work, and some windows have no X to close them.
I will note that after a short session, this game began giving me a headache as well as making me motion sick, so I will need to play this is short sessions, which isn't a good thing. I personally blame the camera movement when running somewhere.
While this game is similar to Path of Exile, it feels more like a traditional MMO, with non-instanced areas. Think Battle of the Immortals, since this reminds me a lot of that game, albeit, more fun.
I would like to thank Kiwibird for their extremely quick reply, sorry I didn't see it sooner or I'd have given this a true review sooner! I can tell that this game has some good support.
If you enjoy games like Diablo, Pathe of Exile, or other isometric RPG games, I recommend you give this a try. It's pretty fun, and it's pacing seems pretty decent, and I think you'll have a good time!

TL:DR a good idea for a game but it got too grindy and boring after a couple of hours and started to feel like work
This is a pretty simple tycoon style game that is heavily influenced by Game Dev Tycoon. Instead of being a game studio making games, you have a weapon shop where you make weapons and everybody is a potato for some reason. You have four workstations and each has a different focus, being strength,accuracy,speed and magic. You assign your workers to the station that matches their skills, pick a weapon to craft and then craft it. Then you send one of them off to sell the crafted weapons. Thats pretty much the majority of the gameplay.
There are other things to do with your workers like send them off to explore the different available areas for materials and send them on holiday or training but the bulk of it is just crafting weapons. While the game is fun for the first hour or two it turns into a massive grind later on where it just becomes a process of researching and crafting weapons to sell to get your profits and fame up. As theres little else to do, that quickly gets really boring. It just got to a point where I couldnt take the repetitive grind anymore and stopped playing.
Good points:
-the game looks pretty good with its cute cartoon graphics and they fit the game quite well
-the game at least has a wide variety of weapons to research and craft
Bad points:
- the gameplay is just too repetitive and gets very grindy later on. It started to feel more like work than a fun game to play.
-I didnt really like the games humour and with all the pop culture references and memes it feels a bit forced
- this game feels like it would be better suited as a mobile game than a PC game

At first glance, it struck me as an interesting idea: playing as a shop owner, managing your shop, researching better weapons, etc. However, the actual execution of the game is extremely lacking. After about 2 hours of gameplay, everything is just a repetitive grind.
First off, all weapons from the same category has similar patterns of stat growths. For example, all Daggers have high speed and magic. Thus, there is a single "Best Weapon" in any category, and if you've already had that researched, there's no real purpose in researching the weaker ones other than for completion.
Secondly, the research mechanic is totally boring. They could have made an interface allowing people to "craft" certain weapons by combining relics, but instead they went for a no-depth waiting mechanic, where you just wait for your item to be done.
To add to that, the explore mechanic ruins the management aspect of the game. You never run out of materials anymore as long as you send your explorer out every month or so. There's no purpose in having shops around the world since your explorer gathers items for free. You end up completely drowning in materials that you don't really need.
Not to mention, some of the objectives require the player to gather a sum of money, and as soon as the player has that exact amount, the game takes it away from the player. One time, it left me completely broke that I wasn't able to pay my hired smiths on the payday.
All in all, the game had overcomplicated things that could have been simple (such as the general shop interface, the world events), and overly simplified things that could have been expanded and made interesting (such as the research, exploration, and general weapon-making mechanic). There are better games to spend your money on.

Surprisingly fun and well-made game. Extremely fast paced right from the start, with frequent check points so you never have to replay more than a few minutes of the game when you die. Graphics look good, with colorful and diverse environments.
The only major downfall is the frequency of MAJOR FPS SLOWDOWN, especially when you enter a new area or segment of one.The slowdown is particularly noticable during the 'avoid things as you go quickly forward on rails' levels. I did some googling and this seems to be a hit-or-miss problem, some players have no FPS problems at all, while others describe having the exact same issues.
PROS
+ FUN!  Extremely Action-Packed and Fast Paced right from the first few seconds.
+ Controls are accurate and feel great (with 360 controller)
+ Block puzzles are intuitive and don't require a guide.
+ Very frequent check points.
+ Short Shooting segments and on-rail events help mix things up.
+ Nothing feels repetitive or grindy. The game hurls you forward and never looks back.
CONS
- Annoyingly frequent frame-rate drops for some players, even on high-end PCs.
- "Freeze-Frame" cut scenes don't impress and it seems like the devs ran out of money to properly animate them.
- The 'mini-game' during the end game credits is horrendously frustrating. I'd rather just sit through the credits.
OVERALL: 8.5/10.  Get it on sale and be thoroughly entertained for the next 5-6 hours.

I never thought this game would be on Steam, but I'm glad it is. And even though I have not played any of its predecessors prior to it, I can positively say that this was a great introduction to a rather underrated franchise.
Storywise, it's pretty much like: "A great evil is attempting to rule over the land and you must stop it." I won't spoil what the rest is, but there ARE multiple endings.
Presentation: The menus are a bit simplistic, but they get the job done.
Art & Animation: Holy hell, are they FRIGGIN' AWESOME! just by LOOKING at the game you can see how much effort they put into character animations, especially in characters like Rottytops. The problem is some of the background can be a bit misleading. For example when I reached the part of Saliva Island with the Heart Squid (They increase your max health) behind stone walls, I thought that there was a secret room somewhere, but then I found out that the architecture on the upper-right corner was just background.
Performance: The game doesn't take much to run. Always a plus in my books.
Music: It's awesome, too! You got the pumping tracks of Tan Line Island and Scuttle Town, the dark and dreary Mud Bog Island and Village of Lost Souls, the cheery upbeat tracks of Propeller Town, the Tense Build-ups of the Pirate Master's Palace, and more.
Gameplay: Control is fairly tight, and thanks to a new update, a negative review has just been made redundant! The currency they use are called "Gems", but judging by the image in your HUD, they're Rupees. You can use them to buy Healing Items, Temporary attack buff items, Leaf Shie- I mean, Pike Balls, Pirate Flares which transport you back to the docks of an isand (Can't be used inside buildings/labyrinths), and Ability Upgrades/Advanced Moves (Like Jumping while KO'd in midair to recover.)
The upgrades are rather basic: Increase Damage and Speed with your hair, And damage for the rest. But the abilities are what sell it for me. ALL of them are used throughout the game: The Scimitar can be used to destroy blocks you can't destroy with your Whip/Pistol, the Pistol can be used to deal with distant enemies and switches, the Hat can be used to cross large gaps, the Boots to just speed through the entire thing while destroying everything in your way, and the Cannon, which gives you a Quadruple Jump (Cannonballs included).
Difficulty: It's a challenging game, but the curve is a little bit off. For the beginning islands, the real challenge lies in knowing what the heck to do, but then you enter Mud Bog Island and the challenge ramps up due to the sheer amount of enemies you have to deal with. Then you reach the final level, which is pretty much an obstacle course set to test how good you are with the abilties. Can you reach great heights with the Cannon? Can you maneuvre around Spikes with the hat? Can you dash to the end with the Boots? If not, you will be using at least 3 potions just for the entire obstacle course.
Replay Value: Unless you're a completionist or if the game is so good that you just want to play it again, there's not much replay value.
Verdict:
Presentation | 6.0/10 (Menus and dialogue boxes look simple, but it doesn't count much towards overall score.)
Art & Animation | 9.8/10 (The pixel art animations look amazing, the game is bursting with colour, and the character portraits during conversations are a nice touch. But some of the background can be a little misleading.)
Performance | 10/10 (Always ran at 60 Fps throughout the entire adventure.)
Music | 10/10 (The score is just plain awesome, nothing else needs to be said.)
Gameplay | 9.0/10 (Control is tight, abilities are useful, but the Hat can be a little clunky sometimes.)
Difficulty | 9.6 (The game is fairly challenging, but the curve is a little off, in my opinion.)
Replay Value | 3.5 (Unless you're a completionist, I can't see a reason to replay the game again.)
Overall | 9.4/10 (Apart from a few minor faults, and the fact that there's not much left to do once you beat the game, it's still a great game that every Metroidvania lover will enjoy.)
Misc bits of advice: If you played the original Shantae before this, once you have the Boots, charge into the left corner of the first room of the first labyrinth. You won't be disapointed.
Edit: I raised my review score because a recent update now allows you to change the controls, and gave Music/SFX sliders.

I've played a lot of turn based combat games in my time, some that you just can't stop playing, games that you can spend weeks playing and still have tons of fun. This is not one of those games. Zombies make constant, obnoxious noises every single turn, and they are so irritating that I've felt the need to turn off my sound on more than one occasion. The firearms in this game are far too underpowered to be of any use against anybody, living or dead. One of the worst parts of this game is the hit chance for a gun. I got a 0% hit chance with a lever action rifle from three spaces away, which is stupid. I'd also like to note that the hit chance system is complete bull, since even when you get a "90% hit chance" it's insanely likely that you will miss. The places you can go in this game normally have looters, which can range from one person with a knife, to twenty men with full armor and guns, yet there's no way to know how many looters are in a certain place without engaging them in combat, which, on many occasions, has killed me and my team in the first few turns. All these issues combined makes the game nearly unplayable.
By the time you realize how bad the game is, it's already too late to get a refund, so be warned, if you buy this game, prepare for severe disapointment and regret in not buying a better game.

I want to like this game.  I want to play this game.  Unfortunately, the game has different plans.
There's a mid-game mission where your small team raids a large biker gang base.
The first time through, I was doing well - getting through by the skin of my teeth, coming up with solutions to both biker attacks and zombies, playing them against each other.  Two women in plate mail I'd scavenged from a Medieval Times restaurant were wailing on everyone with swords and explosives while a Vietnam veteran made headshot after headshot and a veterinary student ran around bandaging the wounded.  I'd been at it for two hours without saving - the game doesn't let you save in battle, and isn't great at detecting when you're not in battle, so the whole map is essentially one long slog.  I was almost done but then . . . the game hard crashed.
Okay.  Fine.  It happens.  Like fifty zombies and gang members, that's a lot to calculate, I guess I can sympathize.  Second time through, let's try this again.
This time, I was betrayed by the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ way the game handles stairs.  The second half of this battle is arranged in such a way that, unless you are extremely lucky, one person gets stuck in the tiny space between the bottom stair landing and a nearby enemy.  The rest of the team, rifles in hand, sits around at the top of the stairs and picks their noses, unable to come down the stairs or affect anything on the first floor until a space is cleared - which it won't be, because the one person able to go down the stairway will, within a turn, be gunned down.  So your other three party members sit, helpless, as their friend slowly bleeds to death, because she's blocking the tiny space allotted to stairway movement with her heavily armored unconscious body.  This is after forty-five minutes of pitched, unsave-able battle, mind you.
This last I allow was my fault tactics wise, but, my god.  I had, essentially, a sniper at the top of the stairs, unable to help his friend six vertical feet away.
That said, rage aside, I can't bring myself to not recommend this game.  It's one of the best-written RPGs I've played in a while, and hits just the right combination of despair and hope with its mechanics.
I mean, I'm extremely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off.  I feel cheated of more than one long-fought victory.  But once I've cooled down, I know I'll try that battle again, and cross my fingers that nothing breaks this time, because I really do want to bring my little group of survivors through the zombie apocalypse to better times.
