As much as I love One Piece, I can't recommend this game.
I'll note first that I'm somewhat biased because of an issue that affects me as one of several players, but that the issue seems not to affect everyone. Online functionality is nonexistent, and worse, because the game tries to connect at the start of the game after the title page, the game 'hangs' on "Connecting..." for a solid five minutes, without you being able to do anything unless you want to turn off your Internet when you start the game up. Ultimately, not a good option. This problem has persisted for some players for months without a fix; the developers, in true fashion for Bandai, don't appear to care about their porting (see Naruto Shippuden UNSR and Tales of Symphonia on release, for example, as well as any of a dozen framerate-locked and/or controller-hating games pumped out), simply raking in the money from the 'One Piece' part of the game, as opposed to the game itself.
Now with that huge disclaimer out of the way, I'll delve into the actual gameplay.
Burning Blood is not balanced by any stretch of the imagination. It works on a point system, wherein you can choose playable and support characters up until a set limit, generally 9000. When a 2500 DLC-only character is brokenly strong in that 'spray and pray' spam manner, you know there's an issue right out of the gate. This is only highlighted when you see the version number - 1.9, at the time of this review - meaning that some of these characters are still broken after several patches. That's not to say that they don't try; while I wasn't playing at the time, Garp was apparently overpowered on release, and they have since nerfed him with at least a modicum of success (I hadn't gotten far enough in to play him, but I haven't found significant unfavourable discussion to indicate as such).
Other than that, the gameplay is... Stilted, for lack of a better word. The two-button attacks with an L-Button for 'specials'  is not terrible, even with the broken specials of some characters as hinted at above. However, it is very limiting, and any fighting game enthusiast will be disappointed with its simplicity, particularly when the combos are also near non-existent in variety. Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter, for example, are far better examples of the genre, both of which you can pick up for a price comparable or better to this.
Movement is even more stilted, which only entices more people to play the same 'spray and pray' characters as it is difficult to punish. This effectively means that you have two options for characters: long range spammers, and quick-dashing/teleporting brawlers. Some many find this a bonus, but I believe more people would quickly grow tired of the repetitiveness.
The 'story mode' only covers the 'Paramount War', otherwise known as the 'War of the Best' or the 'Marineford War'. It does cover it from multiple perspective, but even this is insufficient to save it from being woefully short. It does, however, have a 'Bounty/Wanted' mode in which you fight specific enemies with increasingly greater difficulty - several hours worth, in fact, but it does get a bit 'same-y'.
Unfortunately I can't review the online features for the reason listed near the top of this review, but for the people that are able to access it from the discussion boards, they seem to complain about the lack of people. Again, I can't comment more than that.
Given all of these factors, I could not possibly hope to give a positive review - in fact, I'm trying to obtain a refund at this very moment. If you are really into One Piece and you get lucky with accessing the online portion of the game - or if you don't care about multiplayer - it may be worth it, but unless you're a hardcore fan, steering clear and heading for MKX/SFV is a vastly better option.
Edit: Seems that even though a large portion of my playtime (around two hours of my four) was spent troubleshooting the connectivity issues, refunding is not an option. Congratulations on scamming me. =')

Good Points:
Makes use of one of my favorite gameplay balancing elements I call Vulnerability Periods. Basically before or after each attack or chain of attacks, the character pauses for a moment and enters a state where they can't attack, defend or move, with more powerful attacks having longer vulnerability periods. What I like about this is that it requires the skills necissary to recognize and react to an opponents vulnerability to know when the best time to use attacks, how to compensate for your own character's vulnerability periods so you know the right time to use each attack so you are not left vulnerable after attacking and to read your opponent's patterns so you can take advantage of the flaws in the execution of their attacks.
It's not just about raw power, characters can have uniqe abilities that can easily turn the tables in any battle if used properly.
All characters perform and feel uniqe.
Bad points:
The story mode can get a little repettitive and boring, and what's worse is that it is the only way to level up characters (I think am not sure)
It can be troublesome to learn all of both the basic and uniqe attacks and abilities, and there is no simple way of finding out about them.

Jotun is a beautifully hand-drawn game with a soothing soundtrack, unfortunately that is just about it that it has going for it.
The game is essentially divided in 2 parts repeated throughout the course of the game. The first part consists of 2 exploration levels. These levels are visually appealing but feel kind of lifeless. You go through these levels that are varying in size with the point of collecting health upgrades, abilities, and the item needed to progress to the boss fights. Every now and then your character will narrate and give details about her story and about the land, but I still never felt like I learned much about the Norse mythology surrounding these levels and the gods that rule them. Levels vary with their environmental hazards, enemy npcs, and puzzles but none of it is too challenging. Overall these levels just feel empty and not memorable and combined with the slow movement I found myself just trying to quickly get through them.
The second part, the fun part, are the boss fights. The boss fights are where the animations in the game shrine. The bosses feel and look big and each has their own animations and attacks that you need to memorize. This is where you can use your abilities to their max potential however they are still limited by the overall simple combat. This isn’t a too difficult game and unfortunately doesn’t have a lot of these boss levels when compared to other games such as Cuphead meaning once you beat them there isn’t much of a reason to come back unless you wanted to go through the game again on Valhalla difficulty.
Jotun is a simple but slow game that is saved by its hand-drawn visualization of Norse mythology. I would only recommend buying when on sale.

Dead State is a turn based game where the player has to manage a community of survivors during the zombie apocalypse. In theory, this should be my kind of game. I like fighting zombies, and I like turn based combat. Sadly, I don't like Dead State. Its not a terrible, broken game, I'm just feeling kind of ... bored.
The biggest problem is that I've discovered that zombies and turn based combat don't mix together.
I like turn based combat systems because of the tactical depth that they allow. I enjoy analysing what weapons and abilities my squad has, what type of enemies I'm up against, their abilities, the map layout and figuring out my plan of action. But zombies don't have abilities. No healers, no area of effect attacks, no teleports, no debuffs, no summons. They just walk up to the nearest person and bite them. Dead State has no special infected. Sure, there are some Human enemies. But they either melee the nearest person, or shoot the nearest person. There is no tactical depth. You can't even put your guys on overwatch. Nor can you control your companions' stats, because they auto-level up. Want to improve someone's ranged weapons skill? Well that guy is taking melee because screw you.
I just realised that all the other zombie games I enjoy - Left 4 Dead, Resident Evil, Dying Light, Dead Rising, Killing Floor, State of Decay - the action is real time, fast paced, and you're fighting through large hordes. Plus they all have special infected which keeps the combat interesting.
The other thing about Dead State that stands out to me is the poor sound design. Weapon sounds feel flat, the "arghs" a character/zombie makes when they get hit are dull, there's no voice acting for cutscenes and the music is too slow and quiet. I don't often comment on sound, I guess its one of those things that I don't notice when its done properly, but as soon as it goes wrong, its really obvious. I'm convinced the lack of exciting sound is contributing to my feeling of boredom.
I can't even motivate myself to keep playing Dead State, so I'm certainly not going to recommend anyone else to pick it up. Very disappointing.

Firewatch feels like the lull in the middle of some larger untold narrative. The choose-your-own-adventure style opening text unveils a backstory with more plot potential than the game's actual narrative, and the ending of the game implies consequences that have yet to be fully realized and could still conceivably come to a head if events were allowed to continue on. The main bulk of what you actually play is something of a muted thriller which morphs into an aborted murder mystery before abruptly ending. It's both more and less exciting than it sounds, largely due to the campy writing and clumsily disorganized structure of events.
Outside of the story, the game is a strange mash-up of early 2000s linear, corridor shooter design. You might imagine an open world, from what little marketing material there is, but it's actually just a well-crafted series of tubes that are surprisingly difficult to get lost inside of. All of the usual tropes are here too, inexplicable canyons, cliffs everywhere, heaps of impassable terrain, and mini-mountains shaping obvious paths around thick underbrush.
There's a surprising amount of gameplay here in sending out and answering radio hails as you hike along with a compass and a map as your guide, but this starts out about as challenging as it's going to get and becomes completely trivial by the end of the game. The term "walking simulator" feels a bit off here, as the game has got you doing a lot more than its competitors in that space, which is usually nothing, but it's ultimately not an irrelevant label either as you'll spend most of your time just hiking from one end of the game world to the other for arbitrary story reasons.
Really I wish I could recommend Firewatch, because the game is filled with the kind of potential I’d love to see fully realized, but the team behind it just didn't pull any of it off. It's simple, it's uncomplicated, and it ultimately doesn't give you much to walk away with. If you want to kill 4 hours doing something slow, then this is the game for you.
It just probably isn’t the game for most people.

Marlow Briggs is a budget God of War with some of the most frustraiting platforming I've ever experienced in an action game. Late-game platforming becomes impossible to judge without at least one or two pointless deaths due to preset perspectives. In general, the camera is not your friend, and you have no control over it. The fun combat devolves into slug fests agianst enemies and bosses with increasingly lengthy health bars.
I couldn't imagine throwing out combos with a keyboard, but your welcome to try. You will need near-perfect control of late game combos, and you will need combos to make any impact on late-game enemy mobs and bosses.
I recommend this game because the beginning is fun. The cheese-yness of the story and bad guy got old fast, and I really got sick of my companion mocking me for my failures. However, the combat is impactful and robust, even if the overall gameplay is nowhere near tight enough for what the game sometimes demands. The entire experience can be brute-forced, if necessary. Get this if you can on sale. Otherwise, go buy something else.

If you're into solving near-impossible puzzles, then this is for you.
In the beginning, i.e. after the tutorial and first few games, you will just die, die and die.
You won't know what to do with the things you find, no instructions.  You won't know what will blow up in your face or not.  You won't know which "monsters" are immune to frontal damage.  You won't know which of your guys to shoot and when to shoot.
So, you'll just die and die, however, you'll slowly begin to figure out how to put it together...then you'll die some more.
After your first 30 games or so, don't worry - they don't take long, you'll start to get past the first couple of levels, sometimes.  Every time you start to make some progress...you guessed it...you'll die.
Eventually, you'll start to move carefully, coordinate your squad, not over-extend, find some good stuff and know how to use it.  You'll get several levels completed, i.e. find the elevator, and just when you feel like you'll reach the goal...you'll die.  Did I mention this is all on "normal" difficulty; there are two levels of higher difficulty if you really like to die.
You'll love this game if you HAVE TO FIGURE a way to win, no matter how painful.  If you're looking for a point and shoot, boss fight, make progress game...this isn't it.  This is for you those guys who love to beat impossible games.

I really wanted to like Steam Marines. There's some pretty cool ideas at work here; turning Space Hulk into a roguelike. Unfortunately, it just falls short of almost every mark it wants to hit.
The random levels are entirely too random. Sometimes you'll spawn in a room with no doors. Sometimes you'll spawn in a room of nothing
doors. Sometimes you'll spawn on top of the exit! And on and on. Enemy placement suffers similarly, with you going from no robots to being completely surrounded in the space of a turn.
The UI is a mess. The tutorial doesn't tell you everything. And ultimately, what options you do have on a given turn are extremely limited.
This game has a great premise, and what's here is a promising effort, but ultimately I can't really say it's worth your time and money. It's not an egregiously awful game, it's just not really much fun.

This game isn't bad. It's had some turbulence with the porting process, and the online may be noexistent, but this is a good One Piece fighting game. If you're here for online, then don't buy this game, but if you're ok with playing the offline gamemodes then this is great. It has a very interesting fighting system that incorperates things like haki and logia reflex among other things. Game Content 10/10
There are many things to do other than the story. As you unlock more characters and support characters you can build and save your favorite comps. Additionally, you have Wanted VERSUS (Wanted Poster Battles) and Pirate Flag Battles. Only so many battles can be done per day in the flag battles, and the AI's you fight are generally pretty damn difficult. Furthermore, you can play versus with friends at your computer or online.
Online 8/10
The gameplay online has been overall splendid. Have only encountered 2 games where I encounter input delay and choppy movement, more than likely associated with the hosts connection.
Overall Rating: 9/10

For those who are into zombie-apocalypse games, this game is a welcome new addition. You survive a plane crash and are taken to a shelter which you must lead. The goal of this game is simple: survive. Every day will be a struggle - there are many threats in this apocalyptic world of Splendid, Texas. Not so splendid anymore.
The game is both a Fallout-like RPG as well as a turn based management game. You are in charge of managing a shelter which means gathering food, building upgrades such as fences to keep zombies out, finding survivors who may be able to help you get to safety, and dealing with crisis events such as a gang threatening to destroy your shelter. Each survivor has different areas in which they contribute to shelter management and it's up to you to manage the resources. In addition, there are conflicts and events that happen every day and it's up to you to deal with them.
If you know Fallout's combat system, then you will know Dead State's combat. All in all the combat is relatively easy - but there are a few encounters where you will literally be in war against a small army of guys equipped with military gear and assault weapons so don't take everything for granted.
The looting can get repetitive - it's pretty much kill everything, search containers, grab as much as you can and clear area. Combat is *usually* very easy, but there are modes this game has that will make it oh so much harder. And also, be very careful of what you say to fellow survivors. It takes just one bad statement to make them absolutely hate you. But this is a stressful time, after all. There's an achievement for rescuing all the survivors - some found randomly.
All in all, it's a good game, and I recommend it. 7.5/10.

Air Guardians captures the 360 degree thrill of air/space battles as you alternate between predator and prey in a ballet of missiles, bullets and space craft.  You must control your speed, angle and roll as you persue the enemy for an attack, then quickly alternate strategy to hectically dance your craft out of a missile lock before you take damage.  The ballet ends in either the completion of your mission or, if you take too much damage, your transformation into space dust.
The graphics are good enough to get the job done, but your enemies and allies are reused for all 6 missions so don’t expect too much graphical variety.  The sound of the bullets and missiles whizzing by your craft, or impacting into your craft, add to the atmospheric frenzy of battle.  Technically the control of your craft and weaponry all work very well and I always felt in control of the action.  There is only the hint of a story, but the combat is good fun for the hour or so the game lasts and a fair trade for the price of admission.

This is an amazing game.
...with a few problems.
I really love this game, between the massive factores you can make without even knowing to the awesome train networks you can create. Not to mention the story isn't half bad. The core mechanics of the game are all focused around building a factory and expanding to your liking. Speaking of which, brings up a good point. This game more or less gives a reason to expand upon what you have already done. To make new factories. However, the game doesn't go much into detail when you decide to stop this progression or when the progression itself is no longer. Because the game is based on how you act.
I mean we can launch rockets all day for white science packs, but it doesn't make a difference if we didn't need them anymore. I feel as if the endgame is lacking and is very crude. This I know because there isn't much to do during endgame, really you are just focusing on collecting the raw resources and waiting for things to be crafted. The progression is the best part to play and enjoy, the game does a very good job of this. These details I mention were small nitpicks but overall don't neccessarily affect the gameplay unless you plan to play the game a lot longer then it is intended to play. Like to the extreme.
The Following topics will be covered in this review:
-Multiplayer
-Singleplayer/Progression
-Mods
-Rating of this game
-Things I wish to see in the future.
MULTIPLAYER:
This experience really depends on the server and the group of people you meet, however I am going to partially genrealize my experience with other factorio players and maps.
I think the most basic way to say this is to say that the game plays itself to some extent while playing multiplayer, in terms of public servers. This is kinda the biggest flaw to multiplayer, as in, progression is too fast in multiplayer and you find a group of people who play on these servers split between two groups, three if you count griefers.
The first group is noobs. They don't know anything or they know little. Which isn't bad, it's just these players typically are newer, less experienced, and have little understanding on their draw of resources.
They tend to waste resources in the most easiest of ways without even knowing it, thinking that the base built by  10 or so people can support them. I feel bad for this group of players because the time they spent building whatever horrible thing they made gets ruined and placed over with a blueprint. It's not like the noob invested whatever amount of thought or time into something just for it to be deleted.
Which brings me to experienced players:
This is a group of players genreally speaking, who already have everything planned out. They're like the townhouses of the housing market. Cheap, cooker cutter, and built before. These players are very experienced and have spent litterally thousands of hours playing this game. Most of their designs are the same and they tend to argue about how oil is managed. They have a blueprint for everything. I am not saying experienced players suck, I am saying these players are suffering Min/Max sydrome. Something players/users do on any game to be the most proficient ever, which isn't bad but can take away from the creativity and thought of what is suppose to be a different experience every time around in factorio. Overall they tend to be nice, compentent people, sometimes they are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and think that they way they do it is better than the way you do it. Some of them think that playing without logistic network is more fun
Griefers: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who remove one random electric pole and half your factory is cut off and broken for biters to raid.
All this talk about multiplayer and how fast progression is drives to a much more specific point I've been wanting to adress. Player base online.
Servers in factorio are very empty and lack people. Some servers are chain servers that reset every two or so days so that players would be interested in playing constantly. These servers typically have regulars.
Another type of server that you definitley see empty with the exception of one to threee people are modded servers. Then there is the small servers that never filled.
There is also the servers that have already been completed and finished and that litterally have been running for a year doing nothing but moving trains.
Note: May make edits to change this, as I forgot to add certain things I thought were useful during the typing of this.
SINGLEPLAYER/PROGRESSION:
As I said before above, the game doesn't do anything when progression stops or slows down. It just functions, which doesn't give any neccessary reason to go beyond a point of satisfaction. This point of satisfaction can be anywhere, maybe you wanted to just be able to make lots and lots of steel for whatever reason, maybe you just wanted to collect base resources, maybe you just want to be far enough the tech tree to experience trains. The game does a great job with the tech tree in order to realize the progression, but it doesn't give you a need or urge to go and do it. This is genreally the role of the biters, but if you play the game with defai;t settings or nerfing them the game becomes easier. It isn't that motivating to start or to play when there isn't something there to make you fail if you don't do something. Atleast in my opinion. Single player takes a lot of patience and self devoation to move yourself along. Depending on the world you load, you can play the game for a while or in little to no time.
MODS:
Mods like bob's and angels, as well as 5dim and Yuoki really change how the base game works. To the point that it makes
the core game look VERY VERY Easy, this is not an understatement. Far from it. In bob's + angel's you have to harvest the ore, crush it, and then smelt the crush ore after removing the stone from the crusher. Tons of stone bi-product.
There are so many mods out there, that people have started doing modpacks.
Some mods are very overpowered while others are very indepth and worthwhile to learn. One of my favorite mods recently is the Yuoki Trains mod, they add a bunch of reskinned trains that are super expensive to make, however are not really worth it unless you are looking for cool looking trains. In such a case of upgraded trains, please refer to 5dim's train mod which adds upgraded versions of the train cars that have more storage.

♥♥♥♥ this Kyle dude who made this game......I mean seriously every single ending is sad & hurts my goddamn heart! THERE'S NO WAY I'VE FOUND FOR MY CHARACTER TO BE EVEN REMOTELY HAPPY IN THE END!! ♥♥♥♥..........If you want to get your heartbroken 6 ways to sunday play this game. If you don't want to get depressed for the rest of the month Questioning what you could've done differently to get Emily or Emma to love you....don't play this.......God I need to go punch a wall or something, feel manly.

Now maybe I'm just some sort of cold, heartless cynic, but this just provoked frustration if anything, and the comments of "oh so sad I cried into my waifu body-pillow for days" are bewildering. If you never got into AOL chat or whatever, then the presentation gimmicks, which are admittedly slick and well done, don't substitute for things like character development or meaningful player agency.
Basically, you play as some beta male who chats online with his e-waifu Emily. Like most sappy romances, these people seem to have no real problems, and all their relationship problems are caused by a ridiculous inability for the main characters to just talk plainly with each other. The game basically forces you to "love" Emily, I get that the character I inhabit has known her for a while, but you need to give me some reason to care about her. All I know about her is that she likes Coldplay, which is♥♥♥♥♥♥and I very much told her so, and that she's stubborn. Note that I didn't learn this through her action, but instead because she just told me that she was stubborn. Wow, 10/10 characterization.
No one seems to exist outside of their relationship with the player character. All Emily does outside of talk to you is get together with other boys to provoke clingy reactions from you, even though, again, I don't really know Emily. I mean, the game's only around a half-hour long and expects you to fall in wuv in five to ten minutes. Even the player is denied an ability to exist outside of his relationship with Emily. You can choose to have friendships with Emma and Mike, which are both ended abruptly offscreen. Basically, the story operates on a chapter structure, each separated by a year. So you have one conversation with Emily in 2002, one in '03 and so on. Yeah, I guess I might get attached to Emily if I have literally nothing else to interact with, and I think that's one of the tricks that hooked people. Isolating them, and thus forcing them to latch onto Emily.
This structure causes real problems, you simply don't have time to form a meaningful connection to this character, and every meaningful event happens in the gaps between chapters. You witness after-action reports, not events.
I get it, the story is supposed to be small and "personal" but again, Emily isn't a fleshed out character, and the main character is even worse! You know how I said this is like a sappy romance where people just won't communicate? Well, you're forced to inhabit the body of the most egregious offender of all. The game uses a conceit of "typing out" responses. Basically, you hit random keys after picking a dialogue option, and the character types the response out. Unfortunately, the gimmick gets boring, it's more of a narrative device as at times you see the protagonist type out a response, then backspace and rephrase, it shows indecision. TellTale's The Walking Dead did this once or twice, where Lee couldn't bring himself to follow through with a choice and it really hit me, here it's overused and cheapens the experience.
The protagonist won't ever openly state his feelings, but you can't steer him down any other path either. Other people thought this beta was really "deep" and that it took them ages to piece together all the game's meaning, but it becomes quite obvious by the start of chapter 2. We get it, people regret, and people feel sad about relationships. "Oh it was never meant to be, and it's, like, symbolism, of like, futility man." Wow, so deep. I get that, for the story's message to come across, you can't have a straightforward happy ending, but why can't any meaningful choice be made, just one? Like perhaps moving on from a relationship that isn't working. It's incredibly frustrating to inhabit a person, and have no ability to drive them towards a solution. Again, that's the point, futility and all that, but it just makes it seem like sadness is inevitable towards idiots who don't grasp basic human communication, rather than to me, the handsome stallion playing the game.
If this were anything but a "game" it would probably be forgotten as pretentious schlock. I guess no one else has played Shadow of the Colossus, or read actual literature, so any game that isn't about dude-bros shootin' dudes is suddenly a legendary modern art piece. To me? It's pretentious, and very shallow and manipulative schlock. For those of you who care about number ratings, 3/10, provoked genuine frustration while playing. Only reason I finished it was to try and understand the hype, and because it was really short.
Read Jayne Eyre instead.

An inescapable story of inevitable self-friendzoning. If you try to advance the story in a different direction by choosing a dialogue option to confess your feelings or ask for an honest discussion, your in-game character chickens out, deletes the dialogue and goes for something completely mundane instead.
Even if you try to choose Emma over Emily,

Strange how many reviews are "so sad, so friendzoned" or even getting annoyed with Emily, when the behaviour of the player character is so weak and indecisive.
It's a fun little game with a certain amount of replay value to explore the dialogue trees and unlock some fun secrets, but the main elements of the story are set in stone. Great for what it is - a cute little (FREE!) indie game that rides on nostalgia and some interesting observations on human nature.

This isn't a particularly intensive game, or one that really harnesses the impactive power of player choice. A lot of the options are limited, but in a way they feel contextually important. The time span is captured in the silly AOL era vernacular and the icons. While the game doesn't provide a lot of personalization, since not everyone will be able to relate to the options, there certainly is a poignant familiarity to some of the game endings. Since the game is free, it certainly isn't a waste of time, and the nostaliga factor was nice. One non-spoiler related issue I had was with the typing system. I found myself pretty irritated with not being able to predict what was being typed, since you have to basically smash keys to progress, but by the end of the game I valued not having full control over the typing options.

This is kind of like a friendzone dating sim told through AIM. As such, you have limited options for responses to Emily that railroad your relationship towards romance (or failed romance). So if you're not into women it's just kind of a strange game to play. It gives you the smallest of nostalgia trips (with avatars and song lyrics that call back to early aughts pop culture) but unless you're tring to get with Emily, it doesn't go anywhere-- the characters don't develop and our friendship didn't go anywhere because the theme of the game is supposed to be that you're interested in her. At the end, I felt like it was a total waste of time, but it was free at least.

The 'Now with Planets' update to Medieval Engineers turned it from a Early-Access Alpha into a truly playable game. The content of the game DOUBLED with the Farming update and even added a clear line of progression to the Survival game mode. I state this so that potential players reading this can get an idea of how much different the game has become in just a few months.
The Good:
Great little sandbox game. You can build amazing structures as well as devices to help you build or to demolish. For example when I am gathering wood, I use a cart that I designed to help bring it back, effectively quadrupling my inventory space.
Visuals of the game are pretty good. Looks clean but still keeping with a rustic feel. IMO it looks more 'Roman' than Medieval. But this might be due to the fact that the peasant's ain't got shtuff all over them.
Audio is pretty good. Sounds are clear and the music is soothing and ambient mostly. Barking deer is a bit weird. No they don't bark like dogs, they sound like deer but the noise they make makes them easier to find since they get a bit noisy when they get close.
Weekly updates either fix bugs, add new content for us to tinker with, both, or sometimes add major changes that impact the entire game. Its always neat to check back on Tuesdays to see what was changed.
The Bad:
As an early access game in Alpha, it lacks content. Its a sandbox game without any campaigns or scenarios. When you first load in, you won't know what the heck to do. You've gotta just pick a goal and go with it.
For survival, the little content in the game (establishing a base camp and farm to sustain yourself) is a bit grindy. Part of the game is simply trying to get yourself situated so most tasks are made easier by constructing mechanisms or simply building up raw resources and the containers to store them. This can get a bit grindy and monotonous.
I said the sound is good, before and I still stick to that. But I do have to be honest and say it still has some placeholder stuff. Again its alpha and that is just a polishing issue I'm sure will get fixed eventually, obviously a low priority.
The Ugly:
Peasants don't work. They are supposed to be little workers that help move stuff around for you. They broke in the Planet update.
Barbarians spawn... randomly. Even inside your claimed areas if there is a large enough grass area. This means they can even spawn inside your walls if you walled off a large flat area. They also can spawn nearly on top of you in some cases. They make for interesting foes, and even a source of materials (their weapons can be broken down for ingots), but I recommend leaving them turned off until you're established. If it was like in Minecraft where you had better control of when and where they spawn through ingame measures (like claimed areas restricting their spawn) I'd move this to a good feature.
I almost don't want to mention this last one as its probably going to be fixed very very shortly. But the Multiplayer has its issues. Players connected to a host will see interesting placement issues and other oddities. The most glaring issue, inventory desync was fixed four days ago so that is great. Reason I say that the rest will be fixed is Space Engineers just got a fix to its MP issues. ME will be getting that same fix very shortly, maybe even in a few days of this writing. So don't let this issue be the one to dissuade you.
Overall:
The game is great for what it is. The gameplay is solid. The bugs are few and far between. The game as an early access is doing quite well. The development team that was restructured a few months ago has done a phenomenal job. My biggest complaint is there's not enough of the game yet. But that is surely being worked on. I play ME just about every other day and my favorite part is playing it every Tuesday to see a new set of bugs squished and new content added.
If you're looking for a sidegame to add to your library, that will surely evolve over time to be something more. This game will do well by you. Its also a great game to hook up with a few friends on MP (even with the current issues) and work on larger build projects together.
I'm hoping in the future when all MP issues are resolved there will be more MP servers available for larger amounts of players to go head to head, Roleplay, or just dink around with community builds. It definitely has potential and I have faith that it will get there. ME has my recommendation.

This is a very hesitant recommendation. Steam Marines is a turn-based roguelike that tries to stand out by having the player control a squad of 4 characters (of different classes), instead of a single one.
It's also extremely difficult -- far too much so, to the point of imbalance.
I haven't played many turn based games, so my perception of the difficulty might be distorted. However, I will say that the gap between Easy and Normal mode is huge -- especially considering that there are also Hard and Brutal difficulties.
The game is pretty standard in its mechanics -- each character has action points that they use to move and attack, there's ammo and reloading, and position is crucial. The enemies follow the same rules, some with little quirks that make the game more interesting.
It's... solid. I enjoyed my Easy playthrough... somewhat. I'll get into it later.
The game has several issues that make it just an "okay" game, for me. Still, okay is fine, in this case. I do think the mechanics work well together, and a full playthrough is enjoyable. But that's about as far as I go, as someone who quit on Normal Mode.
It's hard to review exactly how I see the imbalance in the game, since it's heavy on numbers. Let's just say that enemies on Easy kill you in perhaps 2 hits, and only have 2 Action points per turn. They also have 6 HP. On Normal mode, they have 4 Action points, 12 HP and kill you in 1 hit. The actions points, especially, make a huge difference, as you need to be really far away from them to be safe. Plus the necessary reloading (that takes ALL of your action points), small rooms, and several enemies at once, make Normal mode infuriating. It's too easy to lose a character on the very first level. And there are 30 or 35 of them!
On Easy Mode, however, it's still hard to get through the first set of levels. When you reach the 6th level (second area), you have access to these Hulk suits that are incredibly overpowered, in comparison with the normal characters. After that, you can play through the game rather easily. Which is a huge problem, for me. The first set of levels being by far, the hardest. It's just a big wall that keeps most players away.
On my easy playthrough, I actually quit out of boredom. I understood the mechanics and quirks of the enemies, so the game got pretty formulaic. When you beat the game, you go into NG+. I beat that as well. When I started NG+2 I quit. It was simply not fun, anymore. I knew what I need to do everytime, it wasn't fun.
At that point, I tried Normal. I didn't get past the first set of levels... again. I could do it, but not without losing a character. There's an incredibly big difference between the two difficulties. It's just not fun, for me.
Then, there are other issues about its "rogue-like" label. It's always the same thing, essentially.
Character have 4 levels, with each one having a choice between 2 skills - a passive, and an active one. Always the same 2 for the given level and class. There's virtually no point in experimentation.
Some of the classes are also virtually useless, so your party won't vary too much.
Then, the worst of it, is that there are almost no equipment and weapons to find. Even when you do, it's purely numerical and provide absolutely no interesting choices. It's just a question of "this does more or less damage, accuracy, etc. etc.". If you take something like The Binding of Isaac, there are tons of interactions between the items, some of them drastically changing the game. In Steam Marines, there's none of that.
It also lacks a purpose, having a very monotonous pacing. There are 5 or 6 "zones", each with 5 levels. You find an elevator to proceed to the next level. Every 5th level, there's a Boss in the elevator.
It's always the same. Story is virtually non-existant, and the Bosses aren't very interesting, either.
Take FTL, for example, and there's a very clear threat and purpose in the Mothership fight. The whole game is a build-up to that moment. In this game, there's nothing resembling that. Especially with NG+, you can just keep going, without any sense of progress.
It's also far too long for each run. Even on Easy mode, is may have taken me 6 hours or something.
This is apparently a very, very negative review, despite the recommendation. Well, I really had big issues, especially being unable to progress on Normal mode. Maybe it's just not for me. But I still recognize some merit to its mechanics are the general idea. Perhaps it can appeal to veterans of Turn-Based games. For me, it seems imbalanced, lacking a good difficulty curve as well as pacing a variation.

A pretty simple store management game where you make and sell weapons. Decent graphics, a basic story to tie things together and full of pop/gaming culture references.
You start out with access to one area that has a few customers that want to buy your weapons. These customers are static and always want a certain type of weapon with certain stats. When you make a weapon, you choose what stats to give it by moving your smiths around to one of the four stations. There's a station for each stat: attack, accuracy, speed and magic (I learned them as red, blue, green and yellow because stats have no difference to you). The higher the stat a weapon has, the more money it sells for and the more XP the customer gets.
You can make new weapons by researching them (which consumes relics and uses a smith) and the new weapons usually have better stat growths, which leads to higher sale prices and customer XP.
Once I understood the mechanics it wasn't too hard to start a new game, follow the pattern/procedure I wanted, and repeat until everything was completed and I jumped ahead of the difficulty curve.
You don't want smiths to gain unused levels because it also increases their wages (at least until you have too much money to know what to do with it). I picked one person to be my dedicated explorer and another to be my dedicated salesperson. Also, to keep wages in check, I didn't upgrade the class of my explorer (because they were on constant exploration duty).
The simplest flow is to create batches of 3 weapons for customers in the same area then send your merchant to sell them all at once.
Eventually, everything flowed smoothly and the money came flowing in. My explorer gave me the materials, relics and enchantments needed to make great weapons, the weapons sold for a lot of money, and the money was used to pay for maintenance, upgrades and as a money buffer for the next world.
Other notes:
Worth a look if you like clickers and store-management/stat maximizing games.

First of all, i just played this game for an hour or so, so i know that my review is going to be very limited since i haven't experienced most of the game, but after just one hour i couldn't keep on playing because i was just getting bored and told my self that i could waste my time playing some other game.
Regarding the gameplay, Devilian is very similiar to games like Diablo, PoE, and Torchlight, beein an isometric hack 'n slash rpg. Move, smash some buttons to do the skills, kill the mobs, get the ocasiona loot, you know, that stuff.
The skills and animation aren't that bad either. I picked the chain-rogue like class (can't really remeber the name), and it had some really nice animation, with long chains and enormous blades coming out from my body. The gameplay itself didn't felt really smooth, it was always feeling like i'm moving a bit to slow than i should have done, always felt like my attacks were being delivered a fraction of second later than they should've done. I also had a dodge ability, with actually felt pretty useless since everytime i had to dodge an attack, the animation of my character felt to slow to actually manage to do it.
Also, while most of the MOARPG are usually instanced, this game actually had an 'open word-ish' map, which basically was just a slighty larger corridor than the usual dungeons that we usually see, and yeah, they were open world which meant that there were other players questing around you. And this, felt incredibly frustrating since being this an MOARPG, it's normal to clear big packs of mobs relatively quickly, so it was always a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to manage to do that 'kill 5 generic mobs' quest, since i passed more time looking for the mobs instead of actually killing them (same for gathering quests). Also, the quests itself were really really generic, 'kill x mobs, gather x things, talk to x' and so on, being also that, atleast in the starting area, the mobs were always the same but slighty bigger or of a different color, so it really felt like doing the same thing over and over again.
Around lvl 10 (or 11, can't remember exactly) you get acces to the 'talents tree', where you have to pick from 3 specializations, only that it isn't really a tree, but most like a branch, since you are forced to pick one skill, and then you have the option to choose from which of 2 aspects of this skill upgrade (like -2 energy cost, or +10 damage).
Around lvl 12, i got to the first dungeon, in which i felt no difference at all from the normal questing area: it was just a long map, where i had to kill a bunch o mobs untill i got to the final boss. It wasn't even harder that the usual, but actually easier since i had an npc helping me.
So yeah, i got pretty bored of the game. It's not really bad, it's just REALLY generic.
Othervise than beeing a 'I don't recommend this game' review, this would actually be a very 'meh!' review

While the premise of the game sounds good in theory, in practice it is overly cumbersome and vague.  Despite what appears to be a comprehensive tutorial at first glance, the workings and interactions of the game are more about randomness or “trial and error.”
Blessings/Buffs are not explained individually, requiring the player to waste them trying to figure out what they do.  Body parts/towers randomly stop working or lose connections for no explained reason.  Enemies can avoid almost every tower you place, leading to frustration and failure.  Some enemies appear that are never explained, resulting in the player having no idea how to combat them.
There are many nuances that have to be learned through “trial and error” or simply dumb luck.  Feedback about actions/choices or failure in general is almost non-existant.  Which can be very difficult to learn from during the hectic click-fest the game devolves to in short order.
Overall there are just too many fine details, odd memorization, and “trial and error” required to make this game understandable, and therefor playable, leaving the player more frustrated than entertained.

This is not a terrible game, actually it is a fun game to play and I like it.
It just does a terrible job at selling it's strengths!
The overall idea is nice, of course nothing new, but still I like it. "Tactical" Combat, Ressource Managment, Exploring, Survival, role-playing and npc-interactions in Zombie-infested apocalypse, if that is something which intrigues you, you may have a nice time with it.
But alot of the stuff put into it feels unfinished and/or falls flat when it comes to utilizing it's potential, especially the combat, which is sad, but it shines in other (very well hidden) aspects.
Combat in general:
The combat, one of the main parts of the game, since it happens so often, is lacklusting. One of the most often used tactics is being seen as early as possible, since enemies almost always got the first attack, so you want them to see you early so they first have to get close to you, spending their action points for moving, instead of attacking. Of course this tactic fails when it comes to human enemies with guns.
The lack of a stealth system is imo a terrible design choice. You can't sneak up on anybody/anything, at least not without initiating combat a few tiles away, so that you may have at least one (normal) attack on a chosen enemy, which wouldn't be that bad, if wasn't for the high amount of APs you need for your actions. At this point I can only utilize this "tactic" with my main char, since all other survivors are almost literally useless (too few APs, low skill values).
Also the special attacks are just not optimized. For example, there is an attack called flurry which executes as 3 attacks with 30% reduced accuracy, but on my Main char it costs 6 APs, while the normal attack costs 2 (reduced costs for high dex), so instead of using my APs for 3 attacks with normal accuray, I can could spend them on this "special" attack with reduced AP. Just wow, I am amazed.
As wrote above, generally enemies move/attack first (if you don't want to waste APs to "counteract" this). That also happens when someone reanimates as a Zombie (which is a cool mechanic in general btw). Ko'ed NPCs can and will be attacked by nearby Zombies, thus getting infected. They die and come back as Zombies. But why do they have to have the initiative then? They come back and can immediatly move and attack someone. Again imo another bad design choice.
The Gunfighting:
Mostly you wouldn't want to use guns, since they make too much noise, thus attracting nearby enemies (which is btw one of the good things about this game), but nevertheless there are moments you don't care much about noise, but how it was executed is just not good. Reloading takes an insane amount of APs, it's 7 (out of 8) for one of my fellow survivors, who was a Sheriff before the apocalypse hit. Okay, I get it, reloading just takes more time than shooting at something, but how translates this former Sheriff almost not being able to hit a human-sized (zombie) target less than 5m away to realism?! Not everyone has to be a good shot, but seriously?! Imo it would have been better if gunfighting was given some more love. The only advantage of using guns, instead of melee, is that you don't have to close the full distance to your target, that way saving some APs, but that's it. Attracting nearby enemies and the scarcity of ammunition are good mechanics/design choices, everything else...not so.
Inventory Managment and Looting:
It's tedious. Beginning with not being able to check the skills of your people while browsing your storage, but sadly not ending there. It would have been nice if you could change chars on looting screen, when not engaged in combat.
Another irritating thing is that sometimes the standard action on ko'ed looters(NPC enemies) is "attack", instead of "loot/search". Via right-click you change the desired action, but why it is sometimes loot and some other times attack, I still haven't figured out (see comments for update)
UI:
It lacks "Tool Tips", those informations you get about items, skills and so on in other games, also a nice addition would have been a clock display, speaking of, maybe it isn't necessary, have to figure out first, if time passes when exploring an area. In all else regards, it's nothing special, just essentials.
The used font also is a problem. On higher resolutions it's too small and the color makes it hard to
read.

NPC interactions:
Fleshed out well enough, even if it may not appear so at first glance (even some ingame days into it), but after some more time you'll find many possibilities to interact with NPCs in various, entertaining ways.
Stability:
On my system (which is quite stable I may add) the game isn't stable at all. 7.7 hours into the game and it crashed 3 times already, which is something I could excuse if it was a brand new title, because you can't rule out something like this on a diverse platform like the PC, but that shouldn't happen anymore after being for sale for month. (see comments)
Last words: It really isn't all bad, despite what you might think after reading this, at least I enjoy playing it, though I believe it to be shy of it's potential and and the price tag is just a tad too high imo. If you are into this kind of games get it for a reduced price when it is on sale (20€ would be okay I guess), though in my opinion you won't be butthurt if you bought it at full price, just don't expect a new standards setting gamechanger.

Anyways if you like either Tactical games, or zombies, or sandbox games, or exploration games, or shooting dem bad guys, or just scavenging your enemies bodies for cool new stuff then you must buy this game.
To simplify, this game is an strategically more detailed XCOM but with Zombies instead of aliens. Thik of it as "XCOM Enemy Unnown - Zombies Ultimate Survival Edition" if you will.  I mean freaking zombies, who doesnt love zombies.  Global defense isnt your goal, but Survival of you and your fellow survivors that matters. So build your Base Defense the best you can, keep your people safe, especially while you are out looking for weapons, food, fuel, water, a can opener..... (lol) etc, you get the point. Oh and zombies, I Mean Freaking ZOMBIES!!! DUDE!!!!!
Combat is tactical and turn based, youll want to weigh your options if you come across zombies or people. With zombies its a choice of "Do I wanna take em down quietly one at a time with my axes, knives and such in melee risking return/counter attacks or do I want to risk the noise and pull out my .12 Gauge Semi Auto Shotgun and get it done fast with no chance of them getting even near me.  Also using a party member as bait works well to, just dont use anyone you actually like because you can expect them to survive long enough that you learn their name but thats about it, hes gonna die in a mission/trip or two.
Now with humans its a whole other ball game, are they friendly or hostile?  Are they pretending to be friendly to get easy access on you with a nasty suprise later. They got guns!   Oh Crap!  but we are sneaking through a town full of zombies and we are to smart to fire our weapons and call the Zeds down on us all, buuuuut are these other people just as smart or will they open fire as soon as they catch you in the corner of their eye?
In total, there is a lot of fun to be had with this game, a lot of choices both in story and out of it. Suport this dev team, they do great work, and all of te content updates have been free, no BS DLC to speak of, they make it and just drop it in there for us to enjoy.

I really wanted to like this game. I've actually had in since it was in Alpha and just a one week demo. It's gotten considerably more content from then, but not much real polish. I like the idea of this game, but the execution of the design is rather clunky. First off, as people mentioned before, the interface leaves much to be desired. It's quite easy in the heat of combat to try to click on the HUD and accidentally move that character too far away to do anything useful in a single click. You are able to walk over dead bodies, but you're going to have a real hard time finding a spot that doesn't highlight the body to loot rather than the space below it to move on. Rotating the camera is necessary a lot of the time, especially when searching for hot spots where you can loot items, but a lot of the time it's in vain actually because there are usually very few places you can loot things from, although you do need to scour the whole map to find them. The turn-based/real time aspect is kind of weird in cases like where you're trying to break down a locked door. It goes into turn based for a second, makes noise, and the zombies in the area come to your location rather quickly. Like I appreciate trying to jump into combat faster but zombies aren't THAT quick. Another aspect that leaves much to be desired is the real time movement before combat. You can have up to 4 members of your team and they don't run that close together, they run sort of in a staggered formation that when you go into combat mode there's 1 person in the front that can attack and the rest are usually too far to do anything the first turn.

Firewatch is an unique experience. The story is all about the past of the character you play and the characters you interact with (wheter they are around or not). It is done beautifully, but also in a very liniar way. You can try to figure out who people are and what they are about, but you really only get bits and pieces of a puzzle, with a lot of missing or misleading pieces. Not every player is going to enjoy that.
But here is the thing with this game. The main protagonist, isn't you, but an average joe, who steers you in the direction he sees. I don't think this is neccesarily a flaw, but a lot of people will see it as such. A lot of players want to investigate and try to confirm their suspicions about this and that... but the character you play, just don't really go there. Sure he will investigate the obvious, but he doesn't think in between the lines and his dialog reflects that. He doesn't know what to make of most of the things he discovers.
I do recommend this game, but only to people who like the kind of story where you need to fill out the gaps and ponder upon what is really going on, in between and after game session. I also think you need to relate to the characters, in order to like this game. I, myself, loved the fact that I was playing an avarage flawed middleaged man, who had a rich and complicated life to look back upon. You are not playing a hero. You just play a guy, who gets into♥♥♥♥♥♥ and has a hard time dealing with it. So yeah, not for everyone. But an old fart like myself liked it :)

I succumbed to buying this on a whim due to friend pressure...For $1.  So, I entered with low expectations....
That said, what I found was actually kinda good.
It is the most random♥♥♥♥♥cliche mix of "Guy threatened your girl, you pushed back, he killed you, magic happened and now you can go get your revenge and save your lady".   And really, that's all the more you need, because god damn is it a lovely throwback of just mindlessly blowing s*** up and beating up dudes because, hell, because it looks cool.
It fills all the naughty cliches of some quick and silly turret sections, sometimes questionable checkpoints, and wonky difficulty curve at the end.   And yes, that difficulty spike is annoying---Going from playing whack-a-mole and one or two shotting everything, to 25 hits on basic mooks with fully upgraded gear being "standard".   But, if you can press on, it's still pretty fun and rewarding in it's own way to conqure the odds.
Filled with witty humor, some 4th wall breaking, and a trash talking God that thinks he knows it all leads to some amusing banter back and forth along your journey.   For every bad thing it does, it fills a few more throwbacks to just good old fashion, no-nonsense beat 'em up for the sake of beating them up fun.
It's a 5-6 hour experience, and you know what, for $1...Or even $5, it's worth your time if you want a bit of a throwback brawler to mess around in and then but back in the closet.  You too might be surprised by it.
Also, damn, for an unheard of game, it is dang pretty at times.  Screenshots galore for this one.

When I first saw this game I knew that I had to have it, so I did. The reason why I came to such a quick conclusion was that in the first videos of release they gave such broad and unbelievable promises that I knew that I couldnt miss out. Now the first problem you might have to my conclusion would be that promises are not always kept. To that I say, look at their other game Space Engineers which I also have and as far as I can tell they do keep the promises they make. So, lets get into the loves and wishes I have with this game. HPAWS is a semi-casual time-management and strategy game that is well put together and potentially addicting.
I said semi-casual, because there is quite a bit of room for strategizing in the beginning and middle of the game especially.  Making a great smith shop is hard work!  This game is more fun for the challenge, I think.  Towards the end, things can get a little easy or grindy seeming after you become a smithing GOD.  However, there are many fine elements in the game to keep your mind delighted, even if you get to that zen-stage of play.
This game is very well designed.  I have encountered no bugs that I can think of (as always, you can look up the specs on my profile).  The art is very well-done for 2D and the isometric potato-people have a cute factor that rivals games like Plants v Zombies.
For reference, I would say that this game is VERY similar to Game Dev Tycoon and if you enjoyed GDT, you'd probably get a kick out of this as well.  (Although I think GDT might be more challenging.)
There is quite a bit of light-hearted humor laced throughout the game as well, and the writing is actually clever, quirky and pretty damn good in the context of a cute little game like this.  There are also many potato cameos from legendary potato comic-books and potatoe mythology you may chuckle at as well.
Overall, I think this is a great buy.

I've been playing it since it came out for android and i'll be damned how the graphics chaged drastically when I transfer to the PC version the world map looks absolutely incredible it looks way more appealing than the mobile version but aside from that the mechanics in this game is not different from the other point and click style game out there but I gotta say this is good you're playing like a virus, there are different type of viruses ranging from a simple bacteria from a zombie virus.

The game is fun and involves strategy as well as some luck, a little mixture of the both - this means that if you win using a strategy, should you do the exact same strategy and exact same steps, theres a good chance you wont win again. I think this adds an element of fun to it, so you don't just copy strategies and instead "go with the flow". The single player is what you would expect - it's old, the game's been out for some time and I'm sure many people have already played it. The multiplayer is fun.
In multiplayer, there are 2 modes - Versus and Co-Operative, with the latter being the more popular. In Versus, you both go against eachother to see who kills the world the fastest, and in Co-Operative, you work together to kill the world. Co-Operative is the more popular of the two, with ~15-20 games happening in any instance, while Versus has ~4-10 games happening in any instance. Matchmaking takes from 1 minute to 8 minutes in my experience, most of the time around 2-3 minutes. You are able to chat with your partner, which makes it more fun in my opinion.
In multiplayer, you are able to choose "genes" for your "plague". You unlock a gene by random by completing 1 game of the gamemode you choose. Most of them have both benefits and drawbacks, for example, one gene called "Pharmaphile" is more effective in rich countries, while less so in poorer countries.
You are also able to choose the type of "plague", such as Bacteria, Virus, Bio-Weapon, etc. You unlock 1 by random by winning 5 games - not completing, but winning.
This game overall has a lot of depth to it and it's definitely worth the price, especially when on sale. Highly recommend, it's pretty fun.

Now maybe I'm just some sort of cold, heartless cynic, but this just provoked frustration if anything, and the comments of "oh so sad I cried into my waifu body-pillow for days" are bewildering. If you never got into AOL chat or whatever, then the presentation gimmicks, which are admittedly slick and well done, don't substitute for things like character development or meaningful player agency.
Basically, you play as some beta male who chats online with his e-waifu Emily. Like most sappy romances, these people seem to have no real problems, and all their relationship problems are caused by a ridiculous inability for the main characters to just talk plainly with each other. The game basically forces you to "love" Emily, I get that the character I inhabit has known her for a while, but you need to give me some reason to care about her. All I know about her is that she likes Coldplay, which is♥♥♥♥♥♥and I very much told her so, and that she's stubborn. Note that I didn't learn this through her action, but instead because she just told me that she was stubborn. Wow, 10/10 characterization.
No one seems to exist outside of their relationship with the player character. All Emily does outside of talk to you is get together with other boys to provoke clingy reactions from you, even though, again, I don't really know Emily. I mean, the game's only around a half-hour long and expects you to fall in wuv in five to ten minutes. Even the player is denied an ability to exist outside of his relationship with Emily. You can choose to have friendships with Emma and Mike, which are both ended abruptly offscreen. Basically, the story operates on a chapter structure, each separated by a year. So you have one conversation with Emily in 2002, one in '03 and so on. Yeah, I guess I might get attached to Emily if I have literally nothing else to interact with, and I think that's one of the tricks that hooked people. Isolating them, and thus forcing them to latch onto Emily.
This structure causes real problems, you simply don't have time to form a meaningful connection to this character, and every meaningful event happens in the gaps between chapters. You witness after-action reports, not events.
I get it, the story is supposed to be small and "personal" but again, Emily isn't a fleshed out character, and the main character is even worse! You know how I said this is like a sappy romance where people just won't communicate? Well, you're forced to inhabit the body of the most egregious offender of all. The game uses a conceit of "typing out" responses. Basically, you hit random keys after picking a dialogue option, and the character types the response out. Unfortunately, the gimmick gets boring, it's more of a narrative device as at times you see the protagonist type out a response, then backspace and rephrase, it shows indecision. TellTale's The Walking Dead did this once or twice, where Lee couldn't bring himself to follow through with a choice and it really hit me, here it's overused and cheapens the experience.
The protagonist won't ever openly state his feelings, but you can't steer him down any other path either. Other people thought this beta was really "deep" and that it took them ages to piece together all the game's meaning, but it becomes quite obvious by the start of chapter 2. We get it, people regret, and people feel sad about relationships. "Oh it was never meant to be, and it's, like, symbolism, of like, futility man." Wow, so deep. I get that, for the story's message to come across, you can't have a straightforward happy ending, but why can't any meaningful choice be made, just one? Like perhaps moving on from a relationship that isn't working. It's incredibly frustrating to inhabit a person, and have no ability to drive them towards a solution. Again, that's the point, futility and all that, but it just makes it seem like sadness is inevitable towards idiots who don't grasp basic human communication, rather than to me, the handsome stallion playing the game.
If this were anything but a "game" it would probably be forgotten as pretentious schlock. I guess no one else has played Shadow of the Colossus, or read actual literature, so any game that isn't about dude-bros shootin' dudes is suddenly a legendary modern art piece. To me? It's pretentious, and very shallow and manipulative schlock. For those of you who care about number ratings, 3/10, provoked genuine frustration while playing. Only reason I finished it was to try and understand the hype, and because it was really short.
Read Jayne Eyre instead.

An inescapable story of inevitable self-friendzoning. If you try to advance the story in a different direction by choosing a dialogue option to confess your feelings or ask for an honest discussion, your in-game character chickens out, deletes the dialogue and goes for something completely mundane instead.
Even if you try to choose Emma over Emily,

Strange how many reviews are "so sad, so friendzoned" or even getting annoyed with Emily, when the behaviour of the player character is so weak and indecisive.
It's a fun little game with a certain amount of replay value to explore the dialogue trees and unlock some fun secrets, but the main elements of the story are set in stone. Great for what it is - a cute little (FREE!) indie game that rides on nostalgia and some interesting observations on human nature.

This isn't a particularly intensive game, or one that really harnesses the impactive power of player choice. A lot of the options are limited, but in a way they feel contextually important. The time span is captured in the silly AOL era vernacular and the icons. While the game doesn't provide a lot of personalization, since not everyone will be able to relate to the options, there certainly is a poignant familiarity to some of the game endings. Since the game is free, it certainly isn't a waste of time, and the nostaliga factor was nice. One non-spoiler related issue I had was with the typing system. I found myself pretty irritated with not being able to predict what was being typed, since you have to basically smash keys to progress, but by the end of the game I valued not having full control over the typing options.

This is kind of like a friendzone dating sim told through AIM. As such, you have limited options for responses to Emily that railroad your relationship towards romance (or failed romance). So if you're not into women it's just kind of a strange game to play. It gives you the smallest of nostalgia trips (with avatars and song lyrics that call back to early aughts pop culture) but unless you're tring to get with Emily, it doesn't go anywhere-- the characters don't develop and our friendship didn't go anywhere because the theme of the game is supposed to be that you're interested in her. At the end, I felt like it was a total waste of time, but it was free at least.

Prophour23 is a top-down Tower Defense game where you play as an organism attempting to fend off assault from insects. It is free-form, allowing enemies to attack from any angle, and allowing the organs to be moved about on-screen at any time. It is, by design, rather obtuse and difficult, with the intent that a single playthrough will take a very short amount of time, and the player is tasked with surviving long enough to win the game (after some indeterminate amount of time). As an organism, you are to protect your heart, and can grow various organs (stomach, lungs, eyes, etc) through the use of blood.
There is a rather comprehensive tutorial for teaching the basics of the game, but it doesn't get into every aspect of the game - some organs will periodically cease working, there are other insect types you need to worry about other than those which were originally described, etc.
The art style of the game is very interesting, looking like an olde anatomy textbook. However, I feel that the game falls just on the wrong side of the difficulty curve for what they are trying to achieve. In many other "short, but repeatable, hard difficulty" games, there is some degree of feedback which allows you to determine what mistake you made which caused death, and allows for personal progression in later runs of the game. Prophour23 lacks any such feedback loop, which makes successive playthroughs a bit frustrating, as it can feel that the reason for failure is out of the player's control - it feels difficult for the sake of being difficult. There is nothing wrong with that, necessarily, but it's a sensation which most players likely aren't looking for, so it becomes difficult to recommend.
For people where that sort of difficulty sounds like fun? Have at - it's well constructed mechanically, for what it is, and the aesthetics are very solid.

The game looks exciting and I'd like to like it, but I can't help it. You grow organs in an illogical fashion: for example, lungs can be transformed into a stomach, or something like that, which is quite hard to learn. The plays also seem to turn into utter chaos really quickly for me. For no reason some organs may also suddenly stop working for a period of time, with a message like "Lung organs are numb". It just seems there are too many random elements and illogicalities for me to properly enjoy the game. Under the hood it must be pretty simple, but if it takes hours to learn a game that's supposed to be this simple, then I find there's something wrong with it.

Music accompanying is perfect. Dark drums in the background, a little nervous strings, and finally horns and trumpets once in a while. In menus it sounds like mystery, in game it sounds like threat, danger.
There is tutorial, that teaches basics, but still is leaving some advanced technics to be discovered by player himself. Or other kinds of enemies to be surprisingly spotted. Once again it has the spirit of medieval alchemical experiments with living creatures.
Then the gameplay itself. You may say it is some kind of RTS with very limited army slots. But I'd rather call it tower defense executed in a very unique way. There are no tracks for enemies, each kind of bugs that are attacking the heart of your creature acts differently. Most are in deed interested just to kill. But some are lonely voyagers, that actually reveal no interest in beating apparatus. Those might be even more dangerous than simple killers though.
Your task is to design a perfect creature, or better say organism, that will live against all threats attacking it. You use the blood that heart is providing to add organs, connect them, and tactically reposition them to where they are most needed at the moment.
Sounds easy? Yes, it is. It is the kind of easy to learn, hard to master game. Try to keep your creature alive for three days and you will see.

After having kickstarted then played through this game nearly three times in various phases of developement I'm amazed this title still sits as "mostly positive". I imagine that a lot of the negative or neutral reviews came in while this game was still in developement- the occaisional crashes, corrupt savegames, noise radius, and other issues have largely been hammered out (my last playthrough of over 120 hours contained none of these issues to memory).
This is a great game. Comparatively on the level of the first 2 fallout games - there's a deep crafting tree, a large amount of replayability from the skill tree/dialogues/npc interactions. You play as the lone survivor of an ill fated plane in Texas in the opening weeks of a zombie apocalypse engulfing the world. Boarded up in a school with a handful of other survivors from various walks of life it quickly engulfs the player in the tasks of figuring out basic needs in the new world (security, food, fuel, medicine) while also providing the unique challenge of managing your survivors' happiness and other needs.
There will be conflicts that arise both internal and external amongst your group and every NPC that you come across will stretch your party's abilities as well as its needs. As a result, especially on the harder modes- which is the best experience, in my opinion, you will be forced to make decisions regarding what new members bring to the group versus the resources they consume and potential conflicts they bring. The dialogue, of which there is a good amount of, is well written and each of the many NPCs have well written backstories, motivations, and unique needs.
Tied in with the NPC interactions are a series of events that occur- some random, others timed, that move the story forward as well as challenge your settlement. Ultimately, this is a game that moves past the traditional RPG/survival genres to ask the player how they would treat others in such a scenario. This topic is also examined in various lights by your NPCs with their backstories and actions.
Aside from being a well made, polished, and excellently written game there's one thing that I've cited as a reason to purchase this game- choice and causation. Rarely in games are there cascading events where one choice by the player leads to both scripted and unscripted outcomes that were unforseen. To be more clear, each playthrough of mine has brought about events and outcomes where "savescum" tactics would not work because your choices and outcomes were determined hours or days ago. This game provides a multitude of such occurances. It's hard to explain how glorious this is without having played the game suffice it to say that those that appreciate the "what ifs" will play through the game at least a second time.
TL;DR: Played through game 3 times since early developement. Worth the price at $60. Buy it if you have any appreciation for survival/rpg/writing. Watch for this studio's future releases- this is an excellent and so far, it seems, underappreciated game.

This game is fanastic, the Graphics are incredible, the controls are tight the hack and slash combo's all feel natural and aren't overly/needlessly complex. The Boss fights are interesting as are the puzzles and level design.

I recently played X-blades (which is terrible) and was shocked to find how much of a disaster the controls were, playing Marlow briggs feels as tight as playing Dark Siders or Devil may cry ( but not DmC that one sucked a big butt).
The whole game from voice acting, art style and writing are all meant to convey a certain kind of "cheese" but there are genuine moments of deep content and criticism of the videogame narative.
Have you ever played a game and wondered how workers in the factory actually got over these jumps and dodged the steam pipes and flame pillars? Well in Marlow Briggs the game explains that the workers in the ore refinery actually sabotaged the building by removing ladders, breaking platforms and turning the flames on. Making the level design actually have a place in the world, unlike a lot of games where only the protagonist could actually navigate them making them non functional or convoluted.
Small fourth wall breaking features and moments in the dialogue that poke fun at the narrative of videogames really help build a relationship with the main characters
