Marlow Briggs was surprisingly good. Let's be clear here. This game is a shameless,  complete ripoff of God of War in everything except that it takes place in modern times and features South American mythology instead of Ancient Greece. I chuckled everytime I came across a new mechanic that was lifted straight from God of War. The graphics in this game are really good for a budget title. The locales in the game are a bit generic. There isn't anything that hasn't been seen before. The gameplay is broken up somewhat by sections where you're flying a plane and the game plays out in the style of a top-down shooter. There are also sections where you are sliding down a hill and are going for the quickest time down it.  It took around 7 hours to finish the game. It really was easy. There were only a couple times I had to re-fight battles. I usually died from misjudging jumps.  If you are in the mood for another God of War type gaming experience on the cheap, then I heartily endorse Marlow Briggs.

I bought this game on a Steam summer sale for only a buck. The sale is over and the game's regular price is 5 bucks. Is it worth it's regular price? Absolutely.
This game is the closest that exclusive PC gamers who refuse to game on a console will ever get to playing God of War. As a huge God of War fan I can tell you that Marlow Briggs gets the job done as the combat system is near identical and feels just as good as God of War. I will say that the quick time events are much more forgiving in this game and they do not seem to be as well placed as they are in God of War. However the story is much more light hearted and humerous, so the game does not take itself seriously in the slightest which is good. If you get this game do yourself a favor and turn the music and sound effects down so you can hear the dialog durring gameplay. What I really like about this game is that it has added some variety to the God of War formula by having places where you need to shoot things down with big gun turrets and added rooms with moving obstacles to avoid while fighting enemies. Some of the game's cutscenes are a bit too dragged out with the whole Matrix like, slow camera panning scenes which only seem to slow things down, but every cutscene is 100% skippable if you feel the game is dragging which is a great feature. Also just like God of War, I felt the game was a little too easy on the normal difficulty so I recommend the hard difficulty to really heat things up and to make fights not feel so one sided.
In the end, wether you pay a buck or five bucks, you will have a good time. Isn't that what games are supposed to be about anyway?

I tried playing for a while anyway, so I played training, plus the first two of 6 missions.

Graphics were decent, I suppose, but you don't really see all that much, besides the ground from far away. (If you fly closer, it's pretty low res, but it's flight sim terrain, what do you want?) If this would be a mobile game, it would be nice for kids. But it is a PC game. The gameplay is repetitive, it feels like grinding. No depth to the story and other than the weird setting/names, no humor to speak of.

If you don't focus on the correct weapons, you're lucky to earn even half your salaries in month. Forget about any upgrades. The yearly contest that gives some much needed money, has competitors with weapons about 10-20x as good as yours' (me stuck at 100, tops, they at 2000).

I'm not entirely sure I can eloquently describe this game, but i'll try. "Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?!" is a management simulation game in which you play as a team of potatoes and operate a weapon shop, gathering or buying raw materials, crafting weapons in a glorious volcano of numbers and then selling them on to hero-tatoes for profit which you can then use to pimp out your workshop. Hey, that wasn't too bad after all.
Games like these are oddly compelling. Watching some numbers increase shrouded in a bunch of cute nonsense, hours can feel like minutes. I guess if you were playing this on a mobile device on the train for example that would be great, but I feel like there are so many better ways to spend your time with a powerful computer at your disposal.
I'm not saying this is a bad game by any means, In fact I think it's a good example of how this style of game can be done well. I just don't understand what the payoff is beyond watching your numbers increase. There is very little by way of interaction or skill on the player's part required as the game does a good job of spelling out for you exactly what you need to create at any given moment. It's addictive, I suppose, because you're given regular acheivable goals with immediate visual rewards (higher numbers, better carpets for your workshop, etc), which is very interesting to think about but ultimately doesn't actually have any real meaning. There is a story to uncover, but it's not exactly Shakespeare.
Yes it's cute, and I like that cute things exist, but is cuteness alone worth the price of entry? Or more pressingly the price of your time? You'll have to decide for yourself.
Also this kind of exists in the shadow of Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale, which for me is a very similar but superior game.

Pros:
+Amazing artstyle. Looks like an old cartoon. Every animated object is high quality and high frame rate. Static objects are beautifully painted, and landscape shots are stunning.
+Tight gameplay. Very basic but extremely effective. All god powers are useful and I just love the little animations when using them. Attacks are nicely balanced, hitboxes are precise. I had a bit of trouble aiming some attacks or cycling through powers while in combat, but that was probably because I was playing on keyboard.
+Good level design. Each area looks and feels special. Gimmicks are never explained but through environmental clues you can easily figure out what you are supposed to do.
+Setting. Norse mythology works pretty well for a game like this. Wish it included a bit more stuff, like Fenrir etc. but the progression is fine as it is.
+Mimir.
Ehs:
~The map. It's pretty cool, works as intended, but it just does not feel nice to use. I like how landmarks are only shown after defeating the area boss, but then again I feel as if it should be like that from the beginning.
~Area gimmicks. Some are better (like the Nine Rivers one), while some are... not (like Ymir's Blood). It feels like the devs ran out of good ideas partway.
~Balance. This is probably a personal issue, but I feel as if it would be better if it was easier to avoid damage but with more severe consequences if you get hit than the other way round, like it is in game. All in all, the game's difficulty isn't too bad, bosses can be beaten in a few tries if you found the powers in their area before taking them on.
Cons:
-Walking. Areas are WAAAAAAAAY too big for the default walking speed. Hell they even too big when you use the speed power. I guess it's to show how huge and godly the afterlife is, but JESUS♥♥♥♥♥♥does it become boring. In a game where exploring the environment is as important as in Jotun, areas that big are terrible.
-Too short. Looked as though there was more to it in the ending cutscene, but that was it and it left me a bit disappointed.
-The price. I got it for free from a promotion and I love it, but I feel that if I bought it for the current price I would be really disappointed by it.
-Not enough Mimir.

This fighting game is not about who can spam attacks the most.
It has a ridiculous amount of mix-up for a fighter of this type, with two kinds of guard break, sidesteps, and ranged attacks. Commonly, you'll be sidestepping a bunch of attacks when your opponent nails you with a powerful heavy guard break, which beats sidesteps, which you weren't fast enough to react in time to. If you expect a heavy guard break, you may rush in to attack, and then get countered by a side-step then attack. There's many counters and counters to counters. It's ridiculous how many people don't realize how deep this is, simply because they're so bad at fighting games.
I've been playing every fighting game under the sun for years, and this is the deepest I've ever seen a 3D arena fighter.
It's very tight and very strategic, once you learn how to play it. Just give it some time. Some systems, like the ability system or flash counters are kind of wonky, but it's all in all very solid.
I also like the way that hitting with raw special moves can often be more damaging than rushing in and hitting with a combo. This really encourages zoning and more measured play. It's not just a button masher. Also, you can get much more powerful combos if you start with the right move, rather than just using the basic combo.
The characters all play very uniquely, unlike some other arena fighters, like Naruto where you're just swapping out one special move, it seems. Some characters are very defensive, and have counter attacks and slower, bigger, more powerful moves. Some characters have devestating special move grabs. Some characters fight very well at range. Chopper can heal his allies. Usopp can lay traps. Almost all of the characters are really fun to play and unique, and because it isn't all about spamming combos, each of the characters can play in their own ways.
I really recommend getting into this game. It's the best 3D arena fighter to date.

There was a time when 3D Mark was relevant, back when developers pushed the absolute limits of graphics hardware with each iteration of their games. 3D Mark was a true benchmark in that it set the standard for a lot of devs to shoot for. In this day and age, however, most AAA devs shoot for what a PS4 can do while bolting on some features for the PC.
It's easier than ever to just get a current high end CPU and then you spring for either a GTX 1070 or a 1080 and enjoy your hardware for a few years. I don't recommend 3D Mark anymore. There is no special insight to be had, and for the purpose of reviewing hardware you're better off benchmarking actual games. The point of doing that is also greatly diminished as picking GPU companies is about like picking Presidents. You have two companies to pick from. During 3D Mark's heyday we had more than two different graphics companies (3dfx, nVidia, ATI, S3-hey now, Savage3D and Savage2k were pretty good, and Matrox). Each company had a different way of engineering things and 3D Mark was great at exposing their driver quality as well as their architectures. I bought this game when it was discounted heavily at the Humble Bundle Store. It had been very high (top 20ish or so) in my wish list because a adore the rogue-like genre. Although I had been very excited to try it, I was very disappointed with my gameplay experience.
If you like turn-based strategy games, rogue-likes, and the space theme, then you might enjoy this game. Honestly though, you should play Bionic Dues instead, a much more fleshed-out and well-done game. Here is my
for that game if you wanted some more info about it.
The aesthetics are okay - the amount of detail in the characters and background is decent. The sounds and music are also decent, however, I quickly muted the music in favor of my own.
The controls are easy to learn, however, the hotkeys (vs. clicking on each action) may take a bit if you are not used to using them - they are fairly intuitive (R to reload) though. There is a tutorial when you begin that teaches you everything you need to know. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with turn-based strategy games, and the lack of complex mechanics keeps the difficulty pretty reasonable (contrary to what I would expect from a rogue-like). Playing the different difficulty levels, however, seem to be scaled strangely - if you move from easy to normal you will find a large spike in how challenging the enemies are.
Gameplay consists of you moving 4 squadmembers through a randomly-generated ship floor - your goal is always to find an elevator to the next level. Before you begin, you can select different classes (engineer, sniper/scout, leader, etc) and a single perk (ex: splash damage, extra experience gain per enemy spotted) to better match your playstyle. Your characters can level up and select new skills and abilities, however, the pool is extremely small and lacks variety. I did not like this levelling mechanic because it meant that trying out the other difficulties had less incentive - maybe if there was an increased ability/skill pool or level cap for doing a higher difficulty it would justify playing new game +.
Combat and movement occurs on a grid-based system. Each character has a set number of action points (AP) each turn - you can use items in your inventory to refill some AP. Orientation is also important (and costs AP) - you don't want your character facing away from a door or chokepoint. Line-of-sight plays a big role in this game, meaning that enemies can sneak up on you if you are not covering all areas with your team (an enemy unit can be right behind you and not appear on your screen until you turn around). Shooting your weapon costs both AP and ammo, and reloading will take a large amount of AP - so a good tactic is to always have at least one squadmember able to fire (similar to overwatch mode in games like XCOM). You can have your members "wait," allowing them to fire during the enemy's combat/movement turn. This is crucial because your members are very fragile, and leaving them open to enemy attack can easily result in their quick deaths. The lack of depth makes combat fairly boring, as you will mostly be moving your characters, using items, and attacking - compared to other similar titles (Bionic Dues) that have different types of attacks and usable abilities.
Enemies will execute their turn after you finish yours, spawning and moving throughout the ship. There will usually be slight indications (noise, a small flash/effect) of general areas where you can expect enemies to be. You can spend AP to destroy walls, allowing you to take unorthodox routes and take advantage of line-of-site (you can often safely scout a room by destroying a wall rather than going through the door). If you break open a ship wall to space, you can also push enemies to their death. There is a small variety of enemies, making combat predictable if you play enough and understand each unit's strengths and weaknesses.
As you play, there are a large number of objects you can interact with - doors, crates, switches, etc. Each object may give you a random item, experience, etc. Items are kept in your inventory and shared by all squadmembers - which is good if you want someone to use a "restore x AP to all squadmembers," but only have 1 person with actions left. Once you exit the commander deck area (several levels), you can freely choose different areas of the ship to tackle (ex: armory).
Overall, the game plays decently enough, however, there are better alternatives (again, Bionic Dues) that I sincerely think you are better off trying those instead. The gameplay feels far too one-dimensional for a turn-based rogue-like title. Even after only a couple of playthroughs, you will probably be bored of the repetition (even if you are trying to go to different parts of the ship after the commander deck) - the lack of item/character/enemy variety further impairs replayability. It is probably easier to try Steam Marines before any of the more complex alternatives, however, I would still not recommend this unless you were dying to try it. I try not to mention price if I think it is unnecessary, but I would wait until this game is heavily discounted before picking it up - at a retail price of $16.99 I don't feel it is worth it.
Do not recommend.
Cheers,
DJSF

This game suffers from a series of issues.
1) The combat system is terrible. I mean it's truly terrible; this thing is somehow less fun, functional, and challenging than Fallout 2, which is 20 years old. This is further compounded by pisspoor A.I.
2) Where was the UX designer? The amount of glaring flaws in this game, flaws you'll notice within the first 5 minutes of gameplay, are astounding. Examples: Why are there no weight limit indicators visible WHILE LOOTING CORPSES, vision cones/agro ranges on enemies, range overlays for your guns, etc. Stuff that an intern UX still in college would be able to decipher.
3) Torque 3d. Because of how awful this engine is, you can expect crashes. Lots of them. The refusal to use other Engines baffles me, especially considering the Unreal Engine is free.
I had followed this game for 2 years waiting for it to evolve, and at it's finest moments.... it's playing like a vastly inferior version of Wasteland 2. It's saturated with all the concepts you know and love from games of the past, with none of the perks or joys from new age titles.
Base building: It's like a D+ version of X-Com's
Survivor management: It's a slightly better version of State of Decay's (since characters have personalities) with far less customization options
Turn-based combat: F; it's inexcusably boring, uninteresting, and slow-paced. Even for a turn-based tactical game, it's pitifully slow. I would go as far as to say it's the worst, most unintuitive combat system I have personally ever experienced (and I played Shadow Vault)
NPC interaction: It's very lacking. My choices, while phrased differently, seem wholly irrelevant and meaningless. Dialogue feels like a farce.
A few other things worth noting:
- I have no way to know what enemies are hard, and what enemies are not. They all look the same, but some hit WAY HARDER and have WAY MORE HP than others.
- It's ridiculously hard to see the "Loot is here" indicator; why a dull orange color was used, as opposed to like a dark green or red, I will never understand.
- Replay value seems non-existent. Want to win the game? Make a melee character, gradually ramp up to ranged, and walk through the game on cruise control.
- It's incredibly frustrating when you're fighting and 23 zombies have to move before you can. It's exacerbated by the fact that I can't turn up combat move speed to expedite the process.
I want to recommend it because I support indie studios... but I just can't. There are just entirely too many visible flaws in this game that suggest the lead designer either doesn't know what features are missing... or even worse, is not listening to feedback from his team about these absent features and mechanics.
You have to protect a beating heart from a louse invasion by growing muscles, "scream organs", and bones. It's gross and challenging. Best played in 5-10 minute spurts over days or weeks.

With a hand drawn art style and setting so out there and different, a soundtrack so maniacally obscure it's hard not to have your curiosity at least a little piqued. Amidst the droves of mundane and same-y indie games exists Prophour 23, a chaotic creation from the mind of a single madman and the only strategy game capable of effectively making your skin crawl. Strange, cryptic, surreal, and damn challenging. Aside from the hidden messages and symbolism of the oncoming and unknown forces of nature that lie within this tale of insanity, the concept is simple; protect your still-bleeding heart from the swarming masses of flesh-hungry insects.
A bizarre concoction of deep strategy and biological horror, Prophour 23 is an affair of critical thinking that requires more than a little bit of patience. Those looking to hop right in and start crushing bugs will be shocked to find their beating heart swarmed with the creepy little critters and devoured within minutes. Only a complete understanding of your body and the organs which keep you alive will be enough to maintain a healthy heart.
Your goal is simply to survive as many nights as possible throughout the infestation, and employing the use of different organs will be the determining factor. Scream organs and thorns connect to muscles and hands to create thorny barriers, while the boney rib-cages you can sprout create hardened lines of bone to redirect the swarming insects. Hands act as connectors for the organ to function while muscles give them their power to operate. It all sounds complicated, and it kind of is, but it's exactly the kind of game you have to "feel" out to really understand and that just makes each outcome of your terror filled nights of survival all the more surprising, strange and satisfying.
Placement is as crucial as managing the order you create organs in, not only will you think hard about where to situate your defenses, but whether to spend precious blood on stomachs to pump more blood or lungs to catch the blood and alleviate some of the pressure created by clicking droplets that spill from your pumping heart. The antagonistic insects crowd you from all sides at any given moment and the player is kept on alert at all times, with a warning arrow giving you time to adjust your strategy. As night falls, however, visibility is lost and the arrow is no longer seen.
Bugs begin to sneak in past the darkness and into your heart, the only remedy being the eyeball organs you'll purchase which when powered light up an arc in front of them. These are only a small handful of the organs you'll use at your discretion in this open-ended struggle of tactics and defense, and they offer a near limitless supply of possibilities in your strategy for each attempt. Every body part has a purpose, and thrives off of the existence of another body part. You'll quickly be constructing your meticulously drawn and pulsating ecosystem of bodily defenses with ease once you learn the delicate rules of how your organs react to each other.
Prophour 23 explores new territories untouched by the strategy genre that are strange, cold, and maybe even a little uncomfortable. The challenge remains spontaneous and unpredictable with new twists thrown at you each passing night, keeping the suspense and mystery high. The odd array of body parts fighting in tandem against the grotesque squirming parade of blackened insects that seek only to infest your organs is a sight I never expected to fixate my gaze on while deep in tactical thought, and it's effective in its gruesome distraction.
If you're tired of the usual fantasy and sci-fi tropes of strategy and tower defense titles, and want something that goes above and beyond the current offerings in the genre this is one worth checking out. When it comes to strategy titles with a penchant for detailed hand-drawn art and an intense and brooding soundtrack, nothing really comes to mind before discovering Prophour 23 making it, if anything, a totally original idea. Not only is Prophour 23 unique and original in design, but its strange mechanics and frustratingly cryptic difficulty keep you sufficiently puzzled and coming back again and again.

It is painfully obvious that there was not enough time devoted to play testing this game.
The controls are a mess. I don't exaggerate when I say that they are some of the most unresponsive I have ever seen in a strategy game, and they are a never-ending frustration. Free flash games on the internet have higher quality standards than this. There are also many random objectives and events that are entirely dependent on luck, and punish the player through no fault of their own. Units and power ups are poorly balanced, and the game seems to be more of a test of how well you can micromanage your units in a mess of crisscrossing lines without losing your temper than a test of strategy.
The one area where the game shines in its atmosphere. The music, visuals, and gameplay perfectly capture the feeling of loneliness and vulnerability from being under siege by an unfeeling force of nature.
Prophour 23 needs a patch to rebalance and fix the many issues with the controls, and I'm sad that it probably won't get one. There is a really good game in here somewhere, but it's dragged down by amateurish design and execution, and despite the great atmosphere and original concept, I cannot recommend this game as anything other than a weird novelty. If you want a satisfying gaming experience, then keep looking.

It's maybe tower defense at its core, but its done in such a unique fashion that it honestly never feels like that's what I'm playing. In fact, it feels completely different than anything I've played before.
There's a heart at the center, and then there's all the gross baddies trying to invade it. You're tasked with creating and connecting organs together in order to fend them off. Connect this organ to that one, now you've got a wall. That one to this one, now you've got a thorny ring of defense. The type of organs connected and even the direction you connect them from will result in different creations. Experimentation is key.
In fact with the "learn by experimentation" mechanics and overall presentation this game feels quite a lot like some creepy old science experiment you've gotten yourself into.
Tutorials are available, but there's much to learn beyond them, and at least personally I feel like finding out how all the organs interact with each other is a big draw of the experience. I'd recommend avoiding them as long as you can. (I found the sandbox mode actually worked great as a less stressful playground for finding out how things work.)
The game is frantic and fast. I die a lot, and quickly. But each time I learn more about how things work, and that coupled with the quick nature of it makes it very easy to fall into the "Just one more!" loop.
It's all a bit strange, a little creepy perhaps, and very engaging.

Management sims in a lot of ways live and die by their UI. How easily can I get the information needed to make a decision and how quickly can I implement a plan once I've made my choice? When done well a UI is something you never think about, a seamless extension of yourself. Other times it is like the UI of Holy Potatoes, a game I have to assume was ported from mobile devices due to UI design choices that make no sense otherwise.
But to back up a little bit and explain the big picture, in Holy Potatoes you run a blacksmith selling weapons to various questing heroes the likes of which most of us have played as in any number of RPG's. Your main currency beyond money is fame and fame is determined by how well heroes perform in the field while using the weapons you build. It's a decent concept for a game and there is a fair amount of depth later on as you manage 10 different smiths and their various needs. In the end though, Holy Potatoes is sunk by two key issues.
The first is difficulty. Simply put, the game is a cakewalk. You are presented with a series of missions to complete, one at a time by the game. Usually these involve increasing your fame or leveling up the heroes that hire you by giving them superior weapons. And occasionally the game asks you to hand over some money to the shady owner of your smithy. But there were times when I would complete an objective only to find the next three objectives were already completed. The best management sims show how difficult it is to balance the various parts of a major business, but even towards the end when the game becomes a bit hectic, I never came anywhere close to running out of money. And because there is no pressure there the entire game becomes a series of bars that need to be filled. And filling them is inevitable. The only thing making better weapons does is speed up the process.
But even an easy game can be fun for a while if the act of playing is enjoyable enough. Who doesn't love the occasional power trip or even a game where overcoming a challenge isn't nearly as important as making interesting narrative choices? But this game is neither of these things. For one the narrative choices you make don't seem to have any effect on the story progress, but more damning for a game this easy, you never get that sense of being all mighty because of an awful port job from the mobile version I'm just going to assume existed before this one.
I assume that because of the ridiculous way certain aspects of the game are designed. A key example occurs when you send out a smith to buy more components to make more weapons. You'd expect a menu to pop up that let you type in how much you want of each component but as far as I can tell there is no typing in numbers here. Nor can you hold down a button to have a number increase at a rising speed. No, to buy each and every item you must click on a button over and over, turning something that should be an automated process into tedium. I should be able to tell some smith under me to replace certain resources whenever my stockpiles drop below a certain level. I should be able to research multiple new weapons at once. I shouldn't have to click on an icon every time a smith returns from a job just to put him back where I left him.
Holy Potatoes is a game with potential and I'm curious to see if the recently announced sequel lives up to that potential. In the here and now, though, realize that this game barely qualifies as a management sim, considering how little actual managing you do.
Decent art design and audio work make the game easy to look at and listen to, but the referential humor is just lazy and none of it hides how many key features this self proclaimed management sim is lacking.

The easiest recommendation I've ever made.  Holy Potatoes is a cute fantasy management sim that does (almost) nothing wrong.  The style is colorful and interesting, the weapons and locations unique, and the individual smiths are all interesting characters.  The gameplay itself is tight and well-balanced, but limited.  The story keeps you on a fairly limited track, and you'll be following that path all game.  It drops a lot of gaming and fantasy references, which can get heavy-handed, but are still fun, and a bit quirky.
The two issues I have are the difficulty level, and the story.  I'd say it's close to impossible to find yourself in a losing scenario in this game - so long as you pay attention to when your smiths get paid and to when the rent is due, you're fine.  Even if you do mess that up, the game has checks in place to bail you out.  The problem with the story is that there just isn't much to it.  It's pretty flimsy, and the dialogue options are just for show.  In the end, the story just falls apart, leaving you wondering exactly what you just did.
That said, Holy Potatoes is fun and addictive.  Upgrading your shop and training your smiths keep you plenty busy between manufacturing weapons for adventurers.  It's fun for what it is, just don't expect a lot of depth.

Hard to say anything that hasn't been said by everyone else, but this scratches the OCD organised optimisation itch like pretty much no other game out there. If you like the idea of starting with nothing and ending up with a sprawling automated system of finely tuned production where everything is about finding that next bottleneck, fixing it, and then working on the next level of complexity, just to rip out half of what you've done when you find a different way of doing it that would be about 20% more efficient, this is the game to play.
Sure, there's monsters you shoot, and with the recent updates you can turn them from being "minor inconvenience" to "pain to stay alive", but the game shines in the way the complexity is steadily added from simply "mine stuff and turn it into other stuff having transported it on conveyor belts" to managing liquid production, using wires that turn stuff on and off with logical conditional statements, making new bases and building an automated rail network to send large quantities of stuff over large distances, then robots capable of carrying stuff through the air, then ... etc etc, every time you get a bit further you get faced with new opportunities, new problems, and new complexities to incorporate into whatever spaghetti network you've alread got.
It genuinely takes a long time to get through a game to completion, and even when you feel like you've basically seen it all some of the mods add huge amounts of additional layers and tiers of complexity (such as the Bob's mods collection).
Summary
It's like a dynamic and evolving randomly generated puzzle game mixed with a colony builder, where a single playthrough can genuinely take tens of hours (the higher level achievement for speed play is to complete within 8 hours of game time, which gives you some idea of how much there is to do). After a brief glance at the development logs, I have my doubts as to whether or not the developer will produce that any time soon. The game was in early access for at least a year, and I made a point of not playing it til after it was officially released since my backlog is already ridiculous as is. (I think I got it on a steep discount or as part of a Humble Bundle.)
In my admittedly brief time with the game, I found a number of irritations:
- Long (non adjustable?) delay after your squad members run out of action points before it switches to the next squad member. (Weirdly enough, you can adjust the enemy AI delay re: the length of time for their actions. It's a small quirk, but I knew if I played for awhile, nitpicks like this would drive me nuts.)
- Needs easier access to contextual info. It would be nice if I could just hover the mouse cursor over a tile to get more information. I don't think left click to focus does the trick, but I honestly can't remember.
- Enemies telegraph their location during their phase. (I was playing on Easy to try to learn the mechanics / interface, so I'm not sure if this applies to higher difficulties.)
I found myself wishing it had a user interface closer to something like Dungeons of Dredmor, which had excellent visual feedback and mouse support. Maybe the devs have to work around limitations of the Torque engine that they used to develop Steam Marines. Either way, there are better roguelikes to spend your time and money on.
There may be a fantastic game in here somewhere, but I doubt I'll put more than a couple hours into it out of morbid curiousity. Maybe I'm a masochist, but I find it interesting to see how badly a UI / mechanic can be implemented, which makes me appreciate all those little things I usually take for granted in other better games!
As it stands, I can't recommend it at anywhere near full price. The regular price on Steam is absurd, as I wouldn't pay more than $3 - 5 max and can't see it being worth more than a tenner if it ever gets proper UI updates. :(
Is it a rougelike? Or is it a tactical shooter? It's neither of these, and just a boring slog through levels, tediously opening up rooms and waiting for enenmies to come to you.

Steam Marines is a very fun and very difficult game. I enjoyed it a lot, despite the fact that I've only made it past the first section once.
Video Review:
What is it?
Steam Marines is a rouge-like turn based strategy game. It's gameplay most closely resembles the old Space Hulk board game (also the more recent games of the same name). Every time you start you get to choose four soldiers, each of which has a class and a perk. You then enter a randomly generated space ship that is infested with evil robots. Your goal is to fight your way to the elevator and get to the next floor.
There are five different decks of the ship that you have to go through. Each of these decks is divided into five levels with a boss on the final level. You always start on one deck, but you then get to choose where you go after you complete it. Each deck has its own asthetic and set of enemies that goes with it.
Throughout the game, your soldiers will level up, thereby gaining skills and abilities, as well as get new equipment. This adds good depth to the later game (and probably stops you from being completely curb-stomped).
I thought I might also note that if you have a less then four soldiers in your squad at the end of a floor you have a chance of getting a new soldier. You don't get to choose the class or perk, but this can at least give you a fighting chance if things don't go too well.
Pros:
-The game has a good variety of classes. In saying this, I mean that each class has a distinct role in the squad because of their specific weapon.
-The enemies feel equal to your soldiers. In my opinion, a squad turn based strategy needs enemies that are on a similar level to your soldiers. Without that, it would either be so easy that you don't have to think tactically, or far too hard. Steam Marines strikes a nice balance.
-There are distinct enemies. Through my journey I've seen enemies that are pure melee, pure range, ones that lose AP as you hit them, and ones that can't be damages from cenrtain sides. Each of these enemies needs to be dealt with using different tactics, which adds a good depth to the game.
-Each deck has a difficulty rating. You might think that this doesn't mean that much, of course they do that just makes sense. You're right, it does make sense, but the permadeath makes that addition all the more important. You will know which deck is least likely to kill you and thereby least likely to lose you all of your hard work.
Cons:
-The random generation sometimes causes problems. It is possible to enter a level on that levels elevator. One would think that that would be a good thing, but there is a problem. The boss on the final level spawns on the elevator. The first time I made it to level five I spawned on the elevator, directly next to the boss. This is an almost guaranteed loss.
-This con is not necessarily bad for everyone, but it still needs to be noted. The game is VERY difficult. I've played nine hours of the game and I only made it past the first deck once.
-The system for executing the enemy turns is flawed. Firstly, on default settings the enemy turn will last an ungodly length of time. This can be easily fixed in the settings, but there is a bigger issue. The game has a setting that, in essence, focuses on the screen as the enemies move. It will do this not only for ones that you can see, but also enemies that you can't see around you. This gives you advanced warning of where enemies are. Turning this off means that it will NEVER follow enemy movements. Your screen is also locked in place while the enemy moves. I hope you kept all of squad together, or you won't get to watch the action. (Man, that was long winded)
The game has some flaws, but overall I enjoyed it a lot. If you have played Dark Souls (and are hardnened to the idea of constant death) and enjoy squad turn-based strategy games then this game will hit the mark. It's a lot of deadly fun for $15.

First Impressions:
One of the strangest tower defense/strategy games I've ever played.  The organs act like your towers and do different things, though some have a symbiotic relationship that will make you think about where you're placing them and how you're connecting them.  Blood acts as your one and only currency, allowing you to build more organs.  It's got a rather steep (but short) learning curve...I highly recommend checking out the tutorials AND the sandbox mode before trying out the regular play mode.  "Prophour23" is most certainly a unique experience, one that will demand your attention and reflexes from start to finish.

No really, this game is mighty good fun. It sports some innovative tower defence mechanics and gets frantic
. No matter what you try, this game will mess with your strategy, but in a good way. It's quick to learn, and hard to master. Don't imagine that you know all the mechanics this game has to offer once you complete the tutorial. There's more to discover and some of it is nowhere near straightforward. Finding out how you can have the organs cooperate in innovative ways is really exciting.
Do yourself a favour and try to discover these hidden mechanics on your own. On your journey to understand how your body works, and how it can deal most effectively with all kinds of increasingly vile horrors, you will invariably die. A lot. You will die quickly, and you will die hard, and all the time you will be met by a completion factor of 0,00%. Seriously, I've played this for a day, and I'm still on 0,00%.
EDIT: After 13 hours and a bit I was finally able to beat this game for the first time, heart a-pounding, palms sweaty. Want to try and beat my score? PM me and I'll gift you the game. First come first take.

( Disclaimer : Review copy supplied by the developer )
The heart pumps the blood, blood feeds the muscles, muscles provide the strength to go on, the strength that gives voice to power, or the strength to breathe air, muscles are the fiber that connects and powers the organs, yet alone the organs are vulnerable. Thorns are the
metaphor for the immune system, and the bone walls the defenses that the body builds up over time to such attacks on the body.
When one wants to examine games as a potentiate for an artform, and this isn't me being all highbrow here, this is a good place to make a case study. It's -very- thoughtful. As a tower defence game it's good, there's some complexities here that will catch people unaware, true. A good case in point is the eyes. They - counterintuitively - must be connected to the muscles, not the other way around, to get the benefit they offer, thorns can be connected to the shout to duplicate the shouts effect, that's a useful trick as well. Placement and reaction plays a significant part, and at night time it becomes a hurried defensive scramble, trying to make it to the relative safety of the next day.
The game itself is split into two game forms, story, which takes place over three days and three nights, and sandbox, which is a more generalised "survive as long as you can". Both of which can be seen as a metaphor for the human body fighting off infection and disease. The former being a specific case where you're fighting to recover, the latter being "How long can you hold out". Both forms play exceptionally well, with the former rewarding a specific objective based approach, and the sandbox rewarding exploration to begin with, and testing out strategies for long term maintenance.
There's an extensive tutorial too, which I -strongly- recommend you delve into, because this game necessitates thorough study, it does away with a lot of the standard tower defence conventions and replaces them with a visual style and set of cues that you'll have to actively learn, as well as a build and upgrade system that operates in a world of it's own as well. Upgrades are less upgrades and more "evolutions" to different organs, each with their own distinct function. You'll need different organ combinations to perform different tasks and so you end up thinking more laterally than vertically.
Position is entirely fluid, with you able to reposition organs at will, with the heart at the center, and links being repositioned dynamically between connected organs (beware, they cannot reconnect if another connection or organ is in the way), so you'll need to think in terms of shapes and spatial connectivity. Setting up clusters that serve as defensive beacons for specific areas and ensuring that the heart is kept safe is order of the day, and there's an approach that will for a time help serve this function, but you'll be constantly improvising and adapting based on the messages relayed by the various maladies you'll suffer.
This is important because enemies -will- attack, from just about every possible direction, so you have to be able to reposition quickly and effectively, to be able to counter and adjust to their position relative to the heart (there's an organ that allows you to draw them elsewhere, but that will only mean that they make a beeline for THAT organ instead, you'll still have to defend that organ, or they'll munch that first, then they'll go for the heart right after).
The day and night cycle too, makes a vast difference, during the day, you have an arrow indicating where the next spawns will come from, during the night, that arrow is shrouded in darkness, and unless you have eyes connected to muscles (and muscles connected to eyes, in that order, to keep them powered), you're not going to see anything that's not directly around the organs themselves, and fighting blind is a very effective way to get killed in short order. Furthermore, the position of certain organs will directly influence what they actually -do-, the eyes are a particular example of this, with their position relative to the muscle they are linked to defining the "cone" they are able to see.
So. Yes. Do the tutorials, or you will be all at sea and you will die horribly.
In terms of presentation, the game is luscious for what it conveys, hand drawn illustrations on paper backgrounds giving the sense of a living book dealing with the anatomy under attack from infection and a representation of the various organs at work, with blood trickling down over the pages, it gives it a rather rustic charm that works exceptionally well. It's not the kind of graphics that will tax a system, and you can easily expect this to run on a simple laptop, but it does look easy on the eye, and it is easy on the ear.
As a metaphor for the stresses and strains of the human body - that's where this one stands out in particular, it's "more than" a game, in that sense. What you get from Prophour is going to be directly proportionate to what you put in, if you come to this game with an open mind, and a willingness to learn what it has to teach you, you'll come away with one of the most unique experiences on Steam to go with Take on Mars. It has taken a place in my curation list specifically because of the fact that as a unique experience, it deserves attention, and if you're willing to invest the time to listen to what the game has to teach, you'll get something very special from it.

The easiest recommendation I've ever made.  Holy Potatoes is a cute fantasy management sim that does (almost) nothing wrong.  The style is colorful and interesting, the weapons and locations unique, and the individual smiths are all interesting characters.  The gameplay itself is tight and well-balanced, but limited.  The story keeps you on a fairly limited track, and you'll be following that path all game.  It drops a lot of gaming and fantasy references, which can get heavy-handed, but are still fun, and a bit quirky.
The two issues I have are the difficulty level, and the story.  I'd say it's close to impossible to find yourself in a losing scenario in this game - so long as you pay attention to when your smiths get paid and to when the rent is due, you're fine.  Even if you do mess that up, the game has checks in place to bail you out.  The problem with the story is that there just isn't much to it.  It's pretty flimsy, and the dialogue options are just for show.  In the end, the story just falls apart, leaving you wondering exactly what you just did.
That said, Holy Potatoes is fun and addictive.  Upgrading your shop and training your smiths keep you plenty busy between manufacturing weapons for adventurers.  It's fun for what it is, just don't expect a lot of depth.

"Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?!" is a cute management simulation very very similar to the likes of Game Dev tycoon. You manage employees which specialize in certain traits (attack, speed, accuracy and magic) which directly contribute to the overall 'quality' of the weapon you are producing. You can level up the employees, train them, and fire them as well. To suit your needs, you can have them explore, research new weapons, and work towards your weapon creation. You can purchase upgrades to your office, but I found the selection to be quite limited. One issue I had with the game was the amount of required micromanagement the employees needed after doing ANYTHING outside the office (explore, train, vacation, buy/sell). I thought a better way of automatically assigning 8+ employees to default office spots was dearly needed.
The story is minimal, but the developers put a lot of effort into incorporating a parody of a lot of popular people and game characters into the game/story. This added a lot of enjoyable flavor to the game.
The aesthetics felt like a mobile game and a great deal of 'flashy' eye catching effects commonly used in mobile games were employed in this game.
The game unfortunately becomes monotonous after the second level-New area, explore, create weapons until you get more tickets, unlock new area, explore, create weapons until you get more tickets, repeat. This coupled with the lack of the much needed 'smart management' of employees gives this game a 7/10. It is an enjoyable management simulator, which the fun-ness factor wears thin after the first hour of play.

This game is by far the single greatest puzzle game you will ever play. A lot of people use the analogy "Time flies when you're having fun", and that's never been more true than when I play Factorio.
Whether I'm playing on my own and realising that I'm an hour late for Uni when I started playing the night before or if I'm playing Multiplayer with some friends, something that could admittedly use some work if other people don't know a whole lot about port forwarding, I can't sit and play this game for just half an hour, because each session will have a period of time where I just spend 20 minutes walking around my factory, watching it work, and following a line through my base, or driving around my train network and cursing when I crash.
In short, buy this game if you have any interest in puzzles. A significant amount of this game can be completed without having to engage in combat with the locals, and there are probably mods that rule it out entirely, but this game is worth every penny I've paid for it and more.

Totally worth paying the full early-access price, tl;dr this game is a complete treat. For me, this game really nails:
- Complex industrial processes with realistic crafting recipies (realistic enough at least, e.g. uranium might be lime green here but it sure has the isotopic separation and rarity of uranium-235 down pat. Also petroleum is so valuable and limited that it'll give you a serious "invade middle east" type itch).
- Well-balanced game progression and difficulty curve. Resources run out, technologies progress and the difficulty of organising increasingly demanding supply chains increase all at a satisfying rate... not unlike Civ's tendency to make you keep playing just one more turn.
- The mind-numbing number of logistical problems you need to constantly be on top of to feed your increasingly hungry factory. If you're not prepared, your factory will become a serious cluster♥♥♥♥ real fast.
- A nice circuitry system that allows you to further optimise your factory. Common uses of circuitry for me have been: automatic gates on railways that close when they detect oncoming trains, steam-measurement systems for my nuclear reactors that control fuel cell use, and of course simple custom alarms that let me know if a certain resource is running low.
- A delicious dieselpunk aesthetic that just bring back fond memories of playing 90's and early-2000's RTS's
- The aliens are so pesky that it makes you feel no guilt for enacting a nuke-powered genocide in the late game.
Other comments might be that it still needs to be more realistic imo (water being infinite and never requiring filtration is a little disappointing). Also the soundtrack is ok, gets a bit tiring at times, although the tracks "Beyond Factory Outskirts", "Pollution" and especially "Solar Intervention" are definite highlights.
Factorio is the best production line game currently. If you love to optimize workflows, setup your own production network, or exhaust your brainpower, play it.

A great One Piece game that looks gorgerous, but because of so many flaws and unfair mechanics I believe this is a game for really dedicated One Piece fans like me.
Games where developers are too incompetent to program a decent AI usually ships with AI system that cheats to scale the difficulty.
In this game, the game introduces "levels" that controls your attack and defense multiplier. It is only valid on the extremely short and uninteresting (even for One Piece fans) singleplayer.
The singleplayer only deals the Paramount War on different perspectives. No other arcs are covered at all.
This is probably the first fighting game that blatantly puts you on a terrible disadvantage.
The AI has far better attack and defense multipliers so you would take his 20% of max HP for landing about 8 ~ 10 successful combos whereas if you get hit by one of his attacks it will easily take 75% of your HP.
It's one of those games where the developers aren't competent enough to come up with a decent AI so they had to cheat the numbers to make the game seem at least difficult.
The balance here is a joke and a lot of mechanics such as Flash Counters and Unity Assists make this a casual fighting game at best.
If you're looking for a balanced/fair fighting game, do not buy this game.
If you're a huge One Piece fan, but has no friends/families to play locally, do not buy this game.
If you're a huge One Piece fan and have friends/families around to play locally, buy this game. You will love it. Despite the flawed designs and unfair mechanics, I had a blast only because I had people to play with.

When I think rogue-like, I think of a good, challenging (sometimes brutal), game that I can play in a couple of hours. I think of ascending difficulty where I try to find better gear and become more powerful so that I can attempt to defeat ever more challenging enemies until they kill me, or I manage to beat the end objective. Completing the game should be a proud moment that makes me want to brag to my friends that I finally accomplished it.
Sadly, Steam Marines fails to achieve most of this. The basic game mechanics aren't bad, and the first couple of levels were fun, but it gets sorely repetitive very quickly. Each area introduces new enemies, but they all do pretty much the same thing (except the bosses, but even they only have a minor twist to make them unique).  On the rare occasions when you find new weapons and armor, odds are your marines can't use it, or it will be worse than what you already have. Once you figure out how to beat the enemies, the game becomes very formulaic and more of a chore to trudge through each level. At normal difficulty, each level took about 30 minutes (that number can vary a lot). With 25 levels, it just takes way too long for a rogue-like.
When I beat the game, I wasn't jumping for joy. Rather, I felt myself saying "finally, it's done." I decided to raise the difficulty to see if it got better. The enemies were tougher and more numerous, but still did the same thing. The levels just took longer and longer to beat and felt more like a crawl. After a couple of levels, I decided I had better things to do than wait a minute or two between every turn while the computer made its move.
UPDATE: Changing the AI speed did help speed up the computer's turn significantly, but wasn't enough to reduce the tedium enough for me to want to play this game again. I got through a couple more levels and decided I'd rather spend my time playing something else. I do appreciate that the developers are still working on the game, so hopefully they'll be able to add enough variety to make me want to play it again.

This is my first review on Steam; have some strong feelings about this game and wanted to share.
PROS
- A zombie apocalypse game that doesn't focus on the zombies.
- Tons of survivors to interact with
- The Splendid, Texas school as an upgradable compound
- Nice top-down iso graphics. Old-school, but fun and 360-degree camera panning
- Addictive
CONS
- Too easy - I'm on day 30 and have a ton of food, high morale, and more supplies than I can shake a stick at
- Needs more/various upgrades to the shelter. As with "too easy," I'm almost done upgrading the entire shelter and soon will have nothing for my survivors to do except eat food
- Limited scavenging team ability. Your character must lead every team. I have a great fisherman in my compound, but he can't lead a team to the local lake and go fishing unless I'm there with him all day. A waste of time since he could be fishing while I'm killing zeds and bringing back ammo, fuel, or other depletable items.
- Poor zombie AI. Pull one zed, park your team 6 squares away. The zombie will walk right up next to you. Bash it on your turn. Lather, rinse, repeat.
All that said, I  continue to play the game as this genre appeals to me, especially without the 1st person blood-and-gore fest that most zombie/survival games have become. I love the strategy level game, the building of a compound, the interaction of characters... just wish it was a little tougher.
Still, a great game, though perhaps not at $30 yet. Try the demo first; you can play for 7 days - plenty of time to see the coolness factors. But keep in mind that by day 30+ there's not a lot left to do and gameplay becomes repetitive. Hope for more updates/upgrades/mods in the future, but I'll probably still keep coming back to it just because there's not much out there like it.

Dead State.  What really should be an indie darling hasn't quite managed to come into it's own.  Let me clarify: the game is interesting, challenging and, depending on your definition, fun.  What I consider the core issue is that it was built with the same engine powering Age of Decadence.  Why is this important?  Well, Age of Decadence is a rather unique RPG and it's engine was tailored for what it offers.  Since Dead State is a more traditional SRPG I don't think this engine choice has really done it any favors.  Add onto that a shoestring budget and you have a game that can't quite meet it's own aspirations.  Like directing a B-movie you decide where to sacrifice to realize your project and I fear Dead State may have sacrificed too much.
Before I get into why, I must explain why I recommend this game: If you are looking for a more classical take on zombie survival that takes its cues from pen and paper role-playing experiences with a heavy emphasis on character interaction there's a good chance this one is going to be memorable to you.  And for that alone I can give it a strong recommendation.  It isn't a bad game and it stands in opposition to every zombie game that focuses on little more than re-killing them.
So why the longer review?  Largely because my recommendation matters only if you understand at it's core it's a budget product and it shows through in every single place you look.  Combat, for example, is fine if you imagine it like a board game (it plays like one) and use your imagination, but everything feels so static many things would be more compelling in a book: "The zombie lunges for your throat!  Luckily you push it aside!"  The game is a very spartan affair with simple animation and a barebones audioscape.  While you undoubtedly get into situations that will feel genuinely tense: it's because the premise is done very well and not because it has compelling on-screen activity.
That may not bother you at all but for me it's hard to get past when larger issues arise in the continuity and premise.  Many things are presented so matter-of-factly, completely accepted and moved on from without any involvement from the player despite the emphasis on character interaction.  In a story-focused and character-driven narrative this is hard to overlook.  Take the very premise of gameplay: you run the shelter. Sweet, but while you very well may be a competent leader, it's handed to you with nary an objection or conversation despite being just some person they rescued from a plane crash.  The shelter is already established, everyone already knows each other and you are the total stranger.  Yet they immediately hand you the keys and let/ask you manage it.  You can literally ask people, "What can I get you to make life easier around here?" immediately after waking up from a head wound! You've yet to come to terms with the plane crash, let alone the strangers explaining everyone is now flesh hungry monsters who only want to kill and eat and your first activity is to get out of bed and build a fence?  Where's the character building here?  It's a classic case of reading the script and all the characters are in on it, this isn't a living intro: it assumes you know the plot of the game and provides an intro to hand wave off your history.  Nothing more.
Yes, this is somewhat moot once the game opens up A LOT in the following days and it hardly ruins everything but it strips a lot of personal motivations from you.  You might be the main character, but your motivations are not just at the behest of the writer: you're expected to co-opt them wholesale without the game bothering to give you a chance to justify them to yourself.  For example, if the shelter was being run so poorly you NEEDED to be the leader, or the previous leader was a scheming psychopath or even if you just STARTED OUT as a member of the shelter during their first night, fine, but there is at least one if not TWO or THREE characters with leadership characteristics there when you wake up and yet they concede their positions immediately.  I hate to get so caught up on this but it really did bother me.
I could easily dive into more criticisms like these but it really is a matter of engine and budget.  If you know the history of the project and engine, this is likely the best Double Bear could do with what they had.  It is a refreshing entry in both the RPG and zombie genres, framed from the perspective of the people surviving and their relationships, but its presentation makes it feel ten years out of date and the mechanics don't make up for that.  While I recommend it, you need to know what you are getting into beforehand.

I know these things. I have stress tested my PCs with programs such as Prime95 and AIDA (both free, by the way), which put severe stress upon components. Never had a problem. 3Dmark crashes when starting. 3Dmark crashes before starting any test, on the settings. 3Dmark crashes at random times. Futuremark's solutions have been tried, and failed. Seeing how the PC is stable both with games as well as other intensive stress test, I'd call this a waste of money and a failure. To add insult to injury, Futuremark has released a single DX12 benchmark as paid DLC, even for owners of the full, for-pay version. Perhaps they should devote more time to fixing bugs than milking the benchmark with dlc.

This is an amazing game.
...with a few problems.
I really love this game, between the massive factores you can make without even knowing to the awesome train networks you can create. Not to mention the story isn't half bad. The core mechanics of the game are all focused around building a factory and expanding to your liking. Speaking of which, brings up a good point. This game more or less gives a reason to expand upon what you have already done. To make new factories. However, the game doesn't go much into detail when you decide to stop this progression or when the progression itself is no longer. Because the game is based on how you act.
I mean we can launch rockets all day for white science packs, but it doesn't make a difference if we didn't need them anymore. I feel as if the endgame is lacking and is very crude. This I know because there isn't much to do during endgame, really you are just focusing on collecting the raw resources and waiting for things to be crafted. The progression is the best part to play and enjoy, the game does a very good job of this. These details I mention were small nitpicks but overall don't neccessarily affect the gameplay unless you plan to play the game a lot longer then it is intended to play. Like to the extreme.
The Following topics will be covered in this review:
-Multiplayer
-Singleplayer/Progression
-Mods
-Rating of this game
-Things I wish to see in the future.
MULTIPLAYER:
This experience really depends on the server and the group of people you meet, however I am going to partially genrealize my experience with other factorio players and maps.
I think the most basic way to say this is to say that the game plays itself to some extent while playing multiplayer, in terms of public servers. This is kinda the biggest flaw to multiplayer, as in, progression is too fast in multiplayer and you find a group of people who play on these servers split between two groups, three if you count griefers.
The first group is noobs. They don't know anything or they know little. Which isn't bad, it's just these players typically are newer, less experienced, and have little understanding on their draw of resources.
They tend to waste resources in the most easiest of ways without even knowing it, thinking that the base built by  10 or so people can support them. I feel bad for this group of players because the time they spent building whatever horrible thing they made gets ruined and placed over with a blueprint. It's not like the noob invested whatever amount of thought or time into something just for it to be deleted.
Which brings me to experienced players:
This is a group of players genreally speaking, who already have everything planned out. They're like the townhouses of the housing market. Cheap, cooker cutter, and built before. These players are very experienced and have spent litterally thousands of hours playing this game. Most of their designs are the same and they tend to argue about how oil is managed. They have a blueprint for everything. I am not saying experienced players suck, I am saying these players are suffering Min/Max sydrome. Something players/users do on any game to be the most proficient ever, which isn't bad but can take away from the creativity and thought of what is suppose to be a different experience every time around in factorio. Overall they tend to be nice, compentent people, sometimes they are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and think that they way they do it is better than the way you do it. Some of them think that playing without logistic network is more fun
Griefers: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who remove one random electric pole and half your factory is cut off and broken for biters to raid.
All this talk about multiplayer and how fast progression is drives to a much more specific point I've been wanting to adress. Player base online.
Servers in factorio are very empty and lack people. Some servers are chain servers that reset every two or so days so that players would be interested in playing constantly. These servers typically have regulars.
Another type of server that you definitley see empty with the exception of one to threee people are modded servers. Then there is the small servers that never filled.
There is also the servers that have already been completed and finished and that litterally have been running for a year doing nothing but moving trains.
Note: May make edits to change this, as I forgot to add certain things I thought were useful during the typing of this.
SINGLEPLAYER/PROGRESSION:
As I said before above, the game doesn't do anything when progression stops or slows down. It just functions, which doesn't give any neccessary reason to go beyond a point of satisfaction. This point of satisfaction can be anywhere, maybe you wanted to just be able to make lots and lots of steel for whatever reason, maybe you just wanted to collect base resources, maybe you just want to be far enough the tech tree to experience trains. The game does a great job with the tech tree in order to realize the progression, but it doesn't give you a need or urge to go and do it. This is genreally the role of the biters, but if you play the game with defai;t settings or nerfing them the game becomes easier. It isn't that motivating to start or to play when there isn't something there to make you fail if you don't do something. Atleast in my opinion. Single player takes a lot of patience and self devoation to move yourself along. Depending on the world you load, you can play the game for a while or in little to no time.
MODS:
Mods like bob's and angels, as well as 5dim and Yuoki really change how the base game works. To the point that it makes
the core game look VERY VERY Easy, this is not an understatement. Far from it. In bob's + angel's you have to harvest the ore, crush it, and then smelt the crush ore after removing the stone from the crusher. Tons of stone bi-product.
There are so many mods out there, that people have started doing modpacks.
Some mods are very overpowered while others are very indepth and worthwhile to learn. One of my favorite mods recently is the Yuoki Trains mod, they add a bunch of reskinned trains that are super expensive to make, however are not really worth it unless you are looking for cool looking trains. In such a case of upgraded trains, please refer to 5dim's train mod which adds upgraded versions of the train cars that have more storage.

I'm seeing a lot of reviewers who played the game for 1 hour and said it was too easy. As with most RPGs or MMOs for that matter there is  a sliding scale of difficulty that begins to ramp up the higher you get. I think this is to give you an easy arena in which to learn the class you've chosen - but I had to start being careful in dungeons in the lvl 18-20 realm.
I could see this game being repetive but I'm quite surprised to be honest at how fun it was. I've spend 1k hours playing PoE and more than that in D3, and this felt pretty familiar. Combat feels crisp, it appears that there is some depth to the crafting system (too early to tell), and a card system ("talismans") that kind of works like the cards in Warframe. Art is great, and personally I love playing as a tiny girl with a bigass gun. A lot of the mobs do look like they were lifted straight from WoW and D3, and in fact it almost feels like that is what Tirion was going for...the perfect mashup of those two games.
Despite the somewhat derivative feel, it still feels unique enough to where I anticipate logging a few hundred hours, and definitely getting into the end game to see what that is about. I'll update this review after significantly more time playing it, but for now I give it a solid 7/10. It's free, and from what I can tell so far there aren't any mega-game-breaking benefits only available through real money transactions. No reason not to try it, especially for the ARPG/MMO fan and those who like Blizz games.

After having played games like Torchlight 1/2, Diablo 1 through 3, Path of Exile and the likes, I find myself looking at Devilian with an overall feeling of "meh" attached to it. The game isn't terrible by any stretch, and if you find yourself burnt out on other ARPGs, then sure this might be up your alley.
But Devilian's flaws aren't in its presentation or even in how it tries to mix up the formula. The meat of the game, the combat, feels fairly clunky. Skills feel robotic and just lack the flow that you'd find in other games of the genre. The customization options are weak, the classes are unoriginal, and even the skills feel a little too "inspired" by the games that came before it.
On the positive note though, the "MMO" feel of the game does create a feeling of living in a populated world, and feels reminiscent of classics like Mu online. This both plays to the game's strength, but also caters to its weaknesses by forcing incredibly quick respawn timers on quest mobs.
It's a shame, because I was legitimately looking forward to this game.

BASICALLY:
Medieval Engineers is a wonderful game for anyone who is a big fan of middle age time period. It can appeal to almost any gamer, whether it being architecture (really cool structural integrity too), a survivalist (fun and immersive survival mode (more on that later)), and great potential on the PVP side of things. If you want to build medieval castles, villages, kingdoms even- this is the game for you. The game has both building and survival modes. Survival mode will immerse you into a role; build your kingdom, recruit friends, make enemies. Theres a couple issues with this, however.
BIG CONS:
1. EMPTY WORLDS
- Since its in EA, you could give them a pass. But currently, theres next to no animal life at all. This can make everything seem a little boring at some points of time, but half the fun of EA games are waiting for new exciting stuff to release :D
2. NO MULTIPLAYER POPULATION
- While you can find one or two servers with active players, its not a lot. This isnt that big of a deal because singleplayer can be really fun, but multiplayer is good for roleplayers, PVPers, or if you tend to get lonely.  Find a multiplayer server if you can.
3. BUGS
- Do not buy this game expecting it to be bug free. This is probably one of the buggiest survival games I've played- but it is still playable, and almost every weekly patch comes with its own set of bug fixes.
BIG PROS:
1. GENRE
- This is one of the best medieval building/medieval survival games you could buy.
2. ROLEPLAY
- Even if your not into roleplay, you will find it hard to not roleplay if your on a server. And thats good! :D
3. ARCHITECTURE
- Really cool, somewhat realistic building. Theres structural integrity, which means you can't just build stone cubes and expect to live in it. This keeps buildings true to medieval architecture.
OVER ALL 7/10:
- Bugs are really bad in this game, they can screw you over. If there were a normal amount of bugs, it would be an 8/10.
- Imense potential; Good ideas,  Good development team, etc.
Very good developer support. Gets updated weekly

In Medieval Engineers, you can build whatever you want. A village? A castle? That part of Lord of the Rings? Yup. You can recreate all of those in this game with a wide selection of building blocks. There are also decorative blocks to make the inside parts feel less empty.
Once you've built something, the second part of the game comes into play : Destroying it! You can build catapults and trebuchets to obliterate all of it in spectacular fashion.
What I like a lot about this game is the constant updates every Tuesday, that add various things and fix annoying bugs.
The Steam Workshop is also a great part of this game. You can see what others have created, such as castles or even floating islands.
Performance wise? I get around 60 frames per second on max graphics on a GTX 1070, which is very satisfying.
In a nutshell, I would totally recommend this game.

To truly appreciate this game in a fair manner one has to compare it to something in it's own price range. This game costs 2,99€ on steam at the time I write this review. 2,99€ is roughly the same money I'd have to pay for a kebab or a bowl of noodles at our local chinese diner. Both worthwhile products in my opinion.
With that in mind, the game has a higher actual value than a meal in my opinion since A: you enjoy it at least a little longer and B: you can even replay/re-enjoy it (which would be fairly disgusting with the food I imagine...).
(because I think that's what I'd usually do):
- The game DOES offer some limited control customization, like, binding roll, yaw and pitch to different joystick axis and allowing to invert them as needed, along with a few select button functions needed in the game... actually there ARE just a few functions so I guess I could say 'all of them'.
However the game does not recognize all buttons and/or axis on joysticks and controllers, some clearly different axis are registered as the same, some buttons aren't recognized at all while some multiple buttons are recognized as the same. HOTAS systems are the worst, as the game seems to randomly recognize roughly 10 or 11 buttons wildly strewn about both devices (I had to use a Hat on the throttle unit to fire minigun and missiles because triggers and releases on the stick weren't working).
, in order to play with mouse and keyboard, the game asks you to first unplug every controller and restart the game (quite the pilgrimmage for me...).
- The game is really really loud and it doesn't offer any way of adjusting volume to the user's needs. It's a small issue since you can simply reduce the games volume in windows' volume mixer, but nonetheless annoying.
- Which, as I previously stated isn't that bitter since this game has the price tag of two big bottles of Coka Cola... and that stuff is unhealthy anyway...
The game has 7 short levels, one being the tutorial, one patrol (plain dogfight), one escort, one fleet battle, one bomber swarm intercept, one ground base attack and one space shipyard attack mission. All of these were fun but still ultimately sadly short.
"Story" narration and general writing of dialogue for the short video sequences was outright horrible, and ultimately almost nonexistent.
- There are three playable weapons in the game, heavy-hitting dumbfire missiles, Fire-and-Forget homing missiles and the fighter's autocannon. The missiles fulfill their purposes well (one being against larger ships, the other for fighters of course) but the autocannon has proven to be sadly pointless as it's damage output is too low to compete with the dumbfire missiles while it's bullet speed is too low to actually relieably hit fighters with it. Sad because it's (at least in my opinion) the coolest looking weapon.
- The gameplay is very simple and easy to master which provides a quick, short time enjoyment for which the game was obviously made. Simplicity isn't necessarily a bad thing after all.
- Designs of fighter jets and and also some of the larger ships are quite cool, even in their simple technical execution some of these are superior to ones seen in some other games.
- Nicely chaotic aerial combat. A few large vessels slugging it out among each other while you fly around between them hunting fighters, large numbers of enemies and allies in each battle, anti-air fire from larger ships or ground emplacement looks rather nice and
the most positive thing about it in my opinion:
Destroyed enemy planes or ships don't just explode, they will fall/sink to the ground as burning smoking wrecks... really really cool!
Okay I'm done.
If you like a quick uncomplicated piece of fun for the price of one kebab, if you like dogfighting in a decently cool sci-fi setting that lives without the classic laserguns and energy shields (also cool =D), if you don't mind possibly fiddleing around with controls or unplugging a controller and if you're fair enough not to expect too much from a game at such a price...
I recommend it =)
-> I've seen far worse, more expensive games being highly rated and sold a lot for smartphones. This is fair.
