Air Guardians is more of a demo concept than a true 3rd person airplane shooter, but with realistic (yet playable) physics that's more X-wing or Wing Commander than Babylon 5, huge furballs (dozens of fighters at a time), large ships shooting at each other and you, and some decent combat mechanics, it can be basis of a decent game, just not in its present form.
You are the anonymous squad leader of an unnamed faction fighting against "Global Security Forces". Your aircraft has 3 weapons: gatling gun, seeking missiles, and dumbfire missile. Dumbfire missiles are great against ships and bases and bombers. Seeking missiles are against fighters. There is no ECM/chaff... any missile locked onto you must be evaded. On the other hand, your ammo's unlimited... Feel free to hold down the firing button so you pop missiles continuously if you want.
There are only 6 missions. Yes, SIX, total. Tutorial doesn't count as that just familiarize yourself with the controls, which are simple enough.
The dogfights are fast and furious alright, as you try to spam missiles in the direction of the enemy so the seeker can pick up on the enemy, no lock on needed. Hitting bombers and ships are easy enough... start from far away, reduce speed, spam the dumbfire missile while your crosshair is on the target. Simple enough, right? Obviously, the enemy will be shooting back... a lot. Lots of AA turrets, missile launches, it's sure as heck exciting as a shooter.
But there are a LOT of UI issues, like dark crosshair at night. Yes, there is a night mission and a space mission too. Shooting things without a crosshair is mostly luck. There's also no enemy health bar, which is sorely needed for ships (both friendly and enemy). There's no "coupled" flight, i.e. you can control 3 axis independently if you got the right joystick / gamepad.  There's also no skipping over the mission intro (i.e. "Why we fight!")  And not possible to invert the throttle input (the two triggers on Xbox 360 controller, so I ended up LEFT trigger being full throttle/afterburner, rather than right trigger) while all other axis are possible to invert. Finally, the radar doesn't zoom out far enough to point you back into the action, as it only indicates air targets when there are also ground targets.
There are also some visibility problems, or perhaps level design error, as I saw one section of the ground rose out of the ground like a solid white wall.
All in all, Air Guardians is a nice little adrenaline shootem up that's not far removed from arcade games, but having only 6 missions is almost inexcusable, even for an indie title, and the UI issues prevented it from earning even a begruding recommendation.
HINT: For the final mission, your actual objective is to destroy all the ships in the "shipyard"... and you need to do it QUICKLY lest you get overwhelmed by the bazillion fighters launched later. Hold down ALL THREE triggers so you triple-spam the target. Good luck.

If a roguelike met space hulk, this would be their mean offspring. It's a very unforgiving squad based dungeon crawler. The robots on the ship want you dead, and they are very good at it. You need to recognize each type of enemy and learn to deal with them. You can, with some luck, find equipment to help you out. But first and foremost, you need to keep your squad healthy. Learn how the enemies move, learn how to cut paths through the ship, and make sure to cover the entrances to the rooms you're in. It is a very bleak game. You're not gonna find health packs all over to heal your squad, but at the same time you are invested in them. There's multiple classes, each good for different roles, and together they mesh to make it survivable. Losing a squad member hurts, and you will be fighting to save a squadie if he gets cut off from the rest. I do wish that firing was more free line of sight, ala space hulk, but it's all tile based, which offers a different strategic element, though I find it works pretty well with the constricting corridors you often find yourself in. Playing the tutorial is a must. There's not a lot of clicking to be done, as most controls are done with the keyboard, and if you don't play the tutorial, you will not know what keys to use. I almost wish they had just completely removed the mouse from the controls. I think it just confuses people more than anything. Graphically, it's retro. My only real gripe is that I wish there were death animations and corpses left from your squad members instead of them just dissapearing. If you like roguelikes and you like tactical gameplay, and you don't mind (prefferably like) the retro presentation, it's a pretty fun game. I feel like there should be more depth to it, more classes offering more weaponry, etc, but it is what it is, and what it is is a pretty solid, cuthroat scifi roguelike with squad management. Just don't give up after you get murdered the first couple times.

I have edited my review after trying some recommendations for game play made to me. I do enjoy the game play of this game. It reminds me of ye olde days of fallout 2. If you have no idea what that was you wont like this game.

Overall, I love this game. It delivers on the promise of managing a shelter, fighting for survival, tactical combat with very different approaches to the dead and the living. Given that it was made by a tiny, indie team on a small budget, this ambitious game delivers.
I did wait for the Reanimated update to start playing, and I think a number of earlier complaints have been fixed.
What I like:
I like the dual game of managing the shelter and then going out and exploring the world and engaging in tactical combat, almost like a role playing Total War game.
Set in the modern world!! A nice break from high fantasy for the genre.
Good opportunities to role play, with fairly interesting characters.
Combat is fun and tactical. Approach to fighting zombies and humans is very different. And the noise meter is a good system that adds a nice cost and trade-off decision to firing each round of a gun.
Maps are quite well designed. They capture the feeling on Walking Dead and other zombie shows - the world is your oyster, go around, scavenge, pilfer, but be ware. Around every turn a zombie or 10 could be hanging out, or you bust into a supermarket only to find half a dozen aggressive looters already there and they don't want to share.
The feeling of resource scarcity is real - you are generally always low on something, whether it is fuel, antibiotics, bullets, etc. They did a pretty good job of making enough systems where you feel a constant urge to go out and risk life and limb to find more of something.
Good writing and humor - item descriptions are fun, and some maps visually tell a story without any dialogue. There is a faux-twinkie factory, and an ominous church filled with dead inside. I am sure there are more like it!
Cons:
Though much more stable than previous versions I guess, I still get a few crashes and bugs
Characters feel a bit shallow. There are a good amount of them and probably more I haven't found, but I do wish they had more depth and other branches of dialogue, and more interaction across them.
Interface is very clunky - especially the inventory. Splitting items is a pain. Trading items between team members requires a special move, instead of being just built into the inventory. Reloading and unloading guns is done oddly and you can only do it in certain screens or menus.

Let me start with this, I have owned this game since it came out because I love the concept of it. I started playing at the initial release, but I did not get into the game because, quite frankly, I was overwhelmed by its complexity. I tried again a couple months later, but still did not get into it. I saw that the Reanimated edition was released and finally dug into the game, giving it the time it deserved. I can now say that I love this game and am 100% addicted to it!
This game is complex, difficult, and so SO rewarding. It's been said before, but this game is basically Fallout 1&2 plus X-Com plus Walking Dead. And this combo works so amazing! Sure it is not perfect, and could use a little more polish, but the game is so much more than the sum of all parts and is one of the best gaming experiences I had in years.
The negative reviews on Steam seem to all complain about the morale system and/or the bugs. I can't really speak to how the game was before the Reanimated edition, but I will say there was only 1 bug that I ran into. It was a dialogue bug that happened during a random encounter, where the guy I knocked out was talking the same text as he said when the fight started. I hit him one more time with my bat to kill him and that solved that problem... I didn't see any other bugs, which is impressive considering the scope of this game.
As far as morale... this is the end of the world! It is supposed to be difficult to keep a group together. I struggled through at first and had to make some rough choices about whether to kick people out of my group or not (which I did). But as you progress, it is possible for you to make things work. Overcoming these obstacles is so much more rewarding.  The people that complain about morale are essentially saying the game is too hard, the end of the world isn't meant to be easy and I wouldn't have it any other way.
In closing, don't let the negative reviews keep you from trying this game. At the least, download the demo and dedicate enough time to it so that you understand what this game is all about. Once you do, you will find a gem of a game that you'll love and find nearly impossible to put down.

First things first. My game hours are misleading. Not to say that I don't play the game- but I am one of the unfortunate few that has a loading issue. 9 out of 10 times when I load the game up, it crashes when it gets to 89% and I'm assuming the problem is on my end. So what is my solution?...I leave the game running in the background all the time. It's not to rack up hours or look like my life revolves around Factorio, but because I love this game so much, that when it loads, I don't want to struggle to get it running again, so I leave it running 24/7.
There is no story, really. You are some random space travelling engineer who finds himself crash-landed on this surprisingly Earth-like planet, and you are simply engineering yourself back into space.
You'll use robotic arms, conveyor belts, even flying robots, to move materials around various machines that craft the stuff you'll need to build a rocket to escape. Sounds very simple eh? Well it is...you can "finish" the game without ever needing the help of google. The fun, however, lies in optimization and maximizing output from your machines with minimal input.
You'll find yourself doing math in your off-time, trying to figure out the best rations to manufacture the item of choice. You'll ask yourself if you're smelting enough iron...of course you're not! DOUBLE IT! Once you've doubled it...TRIPLE THAT!
This game is like crack. You just need a little bit more. One more optimization. One more circuit factory....one more smelting array....just another little hit, to get you through today, until you can get back to it tomorrow.
Buyer beware! If you are easily addicted to games, then Factorio will consume you. It will bring you to your knees, and you'll be willing to shovel money at the Devs (who are absolutely amazing btw), for just a little bit more.

Paid DLC in a benchmarking application. Apparently that is a thing now. That paid DLC is 33% of the cost of the entire application. I hate this industry. 3DMark is the quintessential benchmarking tool, but they have seemingly abhorrent business practices.

Several 3DMark updates and many Nvidia Graphics driver updates later, these issues appear to have been solved. I still think they issue lay with 3DMark, but it's hard to say.
The bottom line is that I can now run back-to-back tests and the Time Spy benchmark without any issues. I figured that my problems with it would likely be fixed, so I'm glad to say it was. I'm back to being able to recommend 3DMark for stressing your system and testing to see you are getting what other users are getting from similar systems.
Has gone from an very reliable gaming benchmark to a bug-ridden POS.
I have 3DMark's benchmark results from 2009, and I'm pretty sure I used it even before that. I suspect I've bought it in some form at least three times now. I've liked it that much. Not so much, now.
I tried the free version of the DirectX 12 Time Spy and got exactly one successful run in a dozen tries. Even "better," after installing Time Spy, none of the other benchmarks completed any longer. I had to delete and reinstall to get that functionality back. With the "old" version, it's no longer possible to run two benchmarks in a row. I have about a 3 in 4 success rate running any single benchmark and getting results. (It hangs at the computing results part without ever displaying the gettting results pop-up.) I have a 0 in ∞ success rate in getting a second or subsequent test to complete.
I guess I still recommend it, but Futuremark, you really need to fix your crap.

This game is fun... brutal, unforgiving, permadeath fun.
My first play I made it down four floors, but after the second floor, a feeling of hopelessness and dread started to set it.  My team was injured... two guys with a point each of health.  Armor was low, and ammo was starting to run out.  As I dropped down to the next floor, I was praying for helpful goodies in lockers.
Meanwhile, I was getting a feel for the amount of strategy and thought needed to succeed in the game.  Planning ahead is key, as is gaining a tactical advantage.  Managing supplies is vital.  It's all very challenging, and satisfying.
As I moved through the third floor, using flanking positions and crossfire traps to take down my foes, I came to the realization that it was already too late for me this game.  In many games, even classics like Half-Life, there's a trusty health pack or armor kit just around each corner.  It's all a bit too convenient, really... playing Steam Marines opens your eyes about things like that, and for me at least, has brought understanding that you don't always have to have the easy outs to get through a messy situation and have fun.
It's okay to lose... and you will.  It's okay to feel like you have no clue what you're doing... because you learn as you go.  It's okay that the game is a real challenge... after playing for a few hours, you probably wouldn't want it any other way.

I have to admit, I wasn't impressed with Sniper Elite V2. It lacked a decent story and had limited gameplay. Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army is what Sniper Elite V2 should have been. It’s just so much better killing hordes of zombies instead of a few sparse groups of Nazis. The same weapons are present (+ a few new ones I think), and the same equipment is available. Gameplay is identical to Sniper Elite V2 which fits in nicely to the survival genre. The enemies are more varied, some are suicidal, some are over-sized, some are extremely fast. There’s a good diversity to fight, and plenty of weapons to use (mostly rifles of course). The rifles don’t differ that much, some hit harder, some fire faster, but all of them kill zombies effectively. The bullet cam returns with it’s amazing x-ray kill shot  mode, this time with a decaying zombie corpse!
There’s a single player campaign which is fun to play, but the co-op campaign is where you get your real money’s worth. Enemy density is determined by how many players are in the match, so 2 players means a challenge, and 4 players means prepare for a massacre :P It really is fun to battle the zombie apocalypse alongside friends. The levels are linear, but quite large to allow different options and vantage points for all players. With only 5 missions, the campaign won’t last long, but Sniper Elite difficulty will have you coming back if you’re thirsty for a challenge.
A great standalone game that was worth the pre-order, and something that I‘ll be playing with friends until that ♥♥♥♥♥y elite difficulty has been beaten.

Dead State has fantastic potential! After putting more than 100hrs in, I felt I had genuinely beaten a zombie apocalypse!
If you're heading into Dead State with a Dead Rising/Dead Island state of mind, don't. Dead State is a 'survival simulator'. It's more about 'what if' than 'wouldn't it be cool if...' and right from the get-go, it's all about doing what needs to be done to keep you and your team alive.
It has a great RPG system to it, but you don't level-up by smashing skulls. Instead, you gain EXP by saving survivors, scavenging for supplies and making the best decisions for your team.
With all these 'how will you die' survival horrors, it's actually refreshing to see a deep simulator where your objective is to make it!
After playing the 1.0 build, I've noticed quite a few updates that have ironed-out bugs and added even more gamer ideas. Double Bear seem like a great developer and Dead State will only get better from their loyal support.
Enjoy the apocalypse!

*Recorded hours is bull, I've played MUCH longer than 2 hrs*
So far, the game is LONG and HARD. Straight off the bat, you'll be hit with a minus ## in morale - don't worry, just keep going out and try your BEST not to get your guys KO'ed. If you see a red skull show up next to a character, HIGHLY SUGGEST that you reload (game autosaves everytime you enter and leave an area) - red skull means infected and will NEVER go away.
Love the tactics that can be used in the game, tons of loot EVERYWHERE, there's quite a bit of realism, like the hacking mechanic in the game, and though annoying, panic and horror does make battles harder or easier (depends on which side gets hit by those "run for your life!!" character freak outs).
Pros:
- Dead State uses a REAL map from Texas (the only area that seems made up is "Splendid") for the game map.
- Lots of different types of enemies.
- Sound alerting the undead/infected is a plus for realism.
- Large number of built upgrades (as well as equipment modifications).
- Unlike a lot of zombie games, there are TONS of recruit-able allies.
- There's a vote system (once Vic gets back).
- Can pick lock doors, disarm security alarms, or simply kick the door in.
- And a powerful yet unstable psycho character can join you (sad when I lost him).
Cons: (a lot need correcting and fixing)
- Typos and spelling errors EVERYWHERE!
- Tutorial mentions that you can sneak up on enemies (FALSE).
- Animals and Crawling infected are far more likely to KO player than those standing up! (WTF?)
- Feeling of being forced to build places (allies want it, don't get it done by #day, they leave).
- Boyfriend infuriated you didn't tell him about girlfriend (not spoiling) even though you are NEVER given the option TO TELL HIM (add the option, makes zero sense to not be able to tell him an him getting infuriated cause you didn't say anything!!).
- Turn Order (top right of screen) - Understand when the enemies you're fighting are in the turn order display, but SERIOUSLY cycling through EVERY SINGLE ENEMY ON THE LEVEL? (Big Con!)
- Characters in Panic/Horror can make losing pretty easy (both pro and con).
- Areas do not respawn loot & enemies (realism is a pro) but expects player to remember if area is cleared completely or not (# of times visited and days since last visit is ok, but having to remember what is cleared an what isn't can get annoying and wasteful since Time isn't on our side).
- Allies' Moods feel broke - It gets frustrating & annoying when despite your efforts, the "moods" don't ever seem to change (Morale is oddly separate from this).
- Cannot pick skill & stat point use for Allies. Though it adds to challenge, it still blows that the skill & stat points for allies is out of the player's control, this just forces a player to not bother with the pathetic allies, keep the important ones at home, and pray the allies that go out with you don't focus on a skill you don't favor (more of a con than pro).
- And Todd. He prays while we act. He thanks god instead of us. Seriously tempted to commit Wrath on him....
Despite all the cons in the game, frankly Dead State is STILL a good game. There's a lot of stories in this game based on the characters you befriend, and those you just outright want to body slam through a wall. Feels like Final Fantasy Tactics meets The Walking Dead - both very good games, and Dead State feels like a mix of the two.
Yeah there's a lot of cons that I listed, and not many pros - but most of the cons are personally (my opinion) what needs to be fixed, changed, and corrected by the developer of Dead State. Once those are taken care of, the pros will undoubtedly outnumber the cons.
The game's graphics aren't spectacular, but the visuals matter little when the gameplay is experienced.
To the Game Developer of Dead State - Please take note of the listed Cons, most are errors, typos, bugs, and others are simply game mechanics that need adjustments.
This game could be awesome, COULD BE (has the potential), but right now its just a good game. I've barely explored the map, gotten many tough battles, and made quite a number of interesting allies.
Honest Opinion of the game: 7.5/10.
If most of the listed cons are fixed, changed, or adjusted, it could easily become 9/10.

I've left my original review below for archive purposes, but I'm changing it to a positive.
Every single one of the points I mentioned below has been addressed by the developer, which, to be honest, would be enough on it's own to yield a positive review because that puts him on a level of responsiveness above any "AAA" dev I can think of.
It's now possible to remap controls and joystick axes, and you're left with a relatively entertaining arcade style flight shooter. It's pretty fun and there are no longer any game-breaking bugs or feature deficiencies that I can find.

Aircraft move quite fast, so I found it very hard to get into a dogfight or bring my cannons to bear, as we'd just zoom past each other unable to chase each other every so often. The proximity (homing) missiles work though.

The game is something of a mix between the more casual/party fighter games like the Naruto Ultimate Ninja Storm series or Saint Seiya Soldier's Soul and more technical/mechanical focused games like the Soul Calibur series or the Street Fighter series.
It allows for a lot more combo focused and mechanical freedom than you'd get out of a party fighter, but not to any level of a truely mechanical or technical fighter, and while the characters have more depth than in your party fighter games, there's less characters to use (Which may be because this is the first in the series, and does have nearly double the amount of characters from the first Naruto Ultimate Ninja Storm game) and there is a greater emphasis on doing more than just your party fighter button mash affair.
In comparison to the other anime party fighters, it's not nearly as fast as the Cyberconnect II games, or as power focused as the Dimps games, but meets a nice middle between the two of them.
Which pretty much sums up the game, it's at best times a nice middle, and at worst times a game that pleases nobody to any great deal. Party fighter fans may find it too slow. Technical fighter fans may find it too shallow. Fans of both may find it wortwhile. Fans of one or the other should be weary. Fans of One Piece should probably just get it already.

This is a relaxing game, more easy and casual-friendly than milestones of the genre like Recettear.
The story is simple and dumb, but fun. Graphic and sound are top notch.
That said it's pretty clear that it's a parody with tons of references to more famous games like Half Life, FF and tons of anime and american series: it's a nice title to take a break from more complex games, nothing more and nothing less.
Forging weapons is fun, but it tends to get pretty repetitive: you just need to assign the right smiths (statswise) to the right place and choose the best weapon type according your customer preferred stats and weapons and then basically wait for the weapon completion, gaining more money and fame by making heroes level up with your weapons.
Smiths gain exp and level up their classes, starting from a class specialized in only one of the four different stats (Atk, Mag, Spd, Acc) and progressively unlocking better classes specialized in more stats at once. During the game part of the challenge is managing your smiths' class change in order to not waste exp and cover every stat efficiently.
Comparing this to most of the management games I found that there is no economic pressure whatsoever because while the salary of your employees tends to increase quickly so do your gains and the shady agent 46 doesn't ask you money regularly, but just on certain events.
This, unfortunately, tends to be a lot more rewarding for the safe and slow grinding strategy (which I don't dislike) since you can gain a lot of money and a reasonable amount of exp by making and selling the same good weapons to the same heroes (even when they have reached max level) making you reach one of the two ultimate classes (the ones specialized in every stat) with most of your characters way before the endgame.
The game world is pretty simple, consisting of 4 stages with 3-6 different places each, some places can be explored by your employees to find relics and rare materials to research and craft new weapons, some can be used to buy basic materials, some can be used to train and some to send your stressed smiths on a vacation.
The training and vaction prices and events for each place change with the season, while the items for each place are always the same and follow a pretty linear tier progression meaning that the last area unlocked is probably the only one you need to keep exploring because it usually has strictly better items.
Your smiths can also level up their merchant and exploration skills providing more rewards from exploration and some extra cash and discount while selling/buying.
Your little shop can be improved by adding a variety of stat-boosting decorations and your smiths can gain temporary status effects that improve/lower some stats and there is also a prize to win each year for the best weapons crafted, these are minor aspects that are not very impactful gamewise, especially at the beginning, but are nice additions.
Overall Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! is a good mix but tends to become easier and less complex the more you advance through the story, since having smiths that can do anything or a max lvl merchant pretty much takes away every hard micromanagement choice; however this is not intended to be an endless game so when you reach this point you can pretty much rush to the ending.
The game achievements are the standard ones: craft 25 daggers, craft 50 spears, do this quest that you probably need to do anyway to advance through the story (0 effort required), so they are bad and will require multiple playtroughs/some extra time spent on grinding.
PS If you find yourself liking the game and you want a challenge I recommend buying the DLC.

When it works, there's clearly the kernel of a decent game in here. It's clearly received less attention than Space Engineers, but there's still definitely something interesting and unique here.
The building system is very flexible (especially compared to Space Engineers), letting you actually create believeable structures rather than cubes with 2m thick walls. THe destruction system is also really, really nice - buildings seem to collapse realistically, and walls splinter and form rubble in a hugely satisfying way. Structural integrity is satisfyingly frustrating - if you don't pay attention, buildings can collapse under their own weight.
All that said, it's still clearly an early access game. There's virtually no AI to speak of, and the netcode is comparable to Space Engineers (dodgy af). To be expected, I suppose, in a game with a physics system as elaborate as this, but still frustrating. There's also some very iffy performance issues - again, to be expected in early access, but getting 0.5fps in the middle of a field on a GTX 1070 is rather frustrating.
Overall, not bad at all - even if you just download castles from the Workshop and lob weights at them with a trebuchet.

Hard to say anything that hasn't been said by everyone else, but this scratches the OCD organised optimisation itch like pretty much no other game out there. If you like the idea of starting with nothing and ending up with a sprawling automated system of finely tuned production where everything is about finding that next bottleneck, fixing it, and then working on the next level of complexity, just to rip out half of what you've done when you find a different way of doing it that would be about 20% more efficient, this is the game to play.
Sure, there's monsters you shoot, and with the recent updates you can turn them from being "minor inconvenience" to "pain to stay alive", but the game shines in the way the complexity is steadily added from simply "mine stuff and turn it into other stuff having transported it on conveyor belts" to managing liquid production, using wires that turn stuff on and off with logical conditional statements, making new bases and building an automated rail network to send large quantities of stuff over large distances, then robots capable of carrying stuff through the air, then ... etc etc, every time you get a bit further you get faced with new opportunities, new problems, and new complexities to incorporate into whatever spaghetti network you've alread got.
It genuinely takes a long time to get through a game to completion, and even when you feel like you've basically seen it all some of the mods add huge amounts of additional layers and tiers of complexity (such as the Bob's mods collection).
Summary
It's like a dynamic and evolving randomly generated puzzle game mixed with a colony builder, where a single playthrough can genuinely take tens of hours (the higher level achievement for speed play is to complete within 8 hours of game time, which gives you some idea of how much there is to do). Replayability is mixed (lots of settings you can change, map is randomly generated, but essentially you'll still be doing the same thing), but I've come back to it time and time again to try doing things differently or have more aliens attacking me or less resources to work with and so on.
Very highly recommended

Summary: A unique idea wrapped up in a solidly presentable and well-executed package, this game gives players just enough room to make this game anywhere from an entertaining comedy to a miniature tragedy. It's short, it's effective, and it's free. Why not give it a shot?
seems to be called "friendzone simulator" or "Emily Is a ♥♥♥♥♥" in a lot of reviews, but my interpretation of the game leads me to believe that it's less of a "friendzone simulator" and more of an engaging while still ultimately puppeteered opportunity to see the effects of one's actions.
Whether or not the player ends up "in the friendzone" (read: rejected) is tertiary to the fact that the player never has the chance to end up with Emily in the first place. Allegations (whether you believe them to be true or not) of her being a manipulative and overall selfish, insensitive or harmlessly uninterested person aren't what keeps the player - or rather the main character - from developing a romantic relationship with her; it's the character's inability to express his/her feelings towards Emily and the subsequent awkwardness and uncomfortable emotional pressure that it puts on their relationship that forbids them from ever being more.
Constantly, the character (it's important to understand the distinction between the player and the main character in discussing this game) is so close to saying something that would hint at his/her romantic interest in Emily, and yet every time those words are retracted and inklings of those feelings withheld. It's not Emily "friendzoning" the player, it's about the player failing to make any sort of move towards Emily. Consequently, any romantic or sexual encounters that the two may or may not have had may come across to the main character as a natural indicator that there's something more to the relationship, but because Emily is led for years to believe that you're her friend, her supporter, and
a potential partner, it mucks things up. Sure, some of the scenarios play out in a way such that it seems that there was a clear mutual attraction, but the problem is, the main character never takes that step. From the player's perspective, there is no clear way of knowing that Emily ever has any romantic interest in the main character. But similarly from the player's perspective, it's obvious that the main character has a romantic interest in Emily. Those types of relationships where one person wants one things while the other person wants another are very hard to make work. It's no surprise that they end up losing touch with one another. No matter how you spin it, the main character (not necessarily the player) does not once communicate his/her feelings towards Emily, and so what's romantically sown is romantically reaped: nothing.
Some players will be heartbroken by Emily and the main character's eventual fading disconnect, while others will say good riddance to be done with a friendship that becomes a chore. But the reality is this: sometimes friends drift apart, and if neither person in a relationship tries to make it romantic, then it will (almost) never become more than that.
isn't the most complex or stimulating games I've played, but it fulfills a niche that I've now realized is pretty underexplored. It's not easy to create a twenty minute experience that feels like it spans five years, but the developers here managed to make it work out pretty well. Reflecting on friendship and the consequences of actions and inaction,
is an experience well worth the time and obviously well worth the price.

They say what doesn't kill you makes you stronger. In Steam Marines, even the things that kill you make you stronger. And there are a lot of things that are very good at killing you.
As someone who hasn't played a bunch of roguelikes, this games is brutally difficult. I have often immediately regretted certain tactical decisions, and hung my head in shame as I ended my turn, resigning my squad to a swift and gruesome death.
The procedurally-generated levels, combined with the ability to completely demolish walls (I have a strange compulsion to destroy every wall I see) and carve out your own path gives this game a great deal of replayability. You don't memorize levels to make progress, you learn to plan and make better decisions. You will learn when to lure or flank the enemy, and when to shove the enemy off your ship a la Harrison Ford in Air Force One.
And when you get too frustrated, there's always hope. Maybe you'll get a giant metal exoskeleton you can use to exact fiery flame-thrower vengeance on your unwitting foes...
A very brutal rogue like that rewards tactical thinking for your squad.

About Steampunk, look yourself the snapshots, it's very light, so don't really search that in the game.
About about random range and diversity, it's here, enough to make a play enough different to another, and to keep the surprise which is an important element of the gameplay. But if my experience of Early Access is still valid, and additions hadn't changed it deeply, then the range of variations isn't huge like some of the biggest Roguelike. Overall its key words are, very fun Roguelike, light play, good depth, team, Spacehulk/Alien.

This is a very fun game.  It feels a little clunky at first until you get used to the gameplay and mechanics.
You basically have to manage a growing number of survivors who have gathered at a high school.  You can upgrade and build new facilities, venture out to scavenge for supplies and food, even restore care or get horses.  You also have to make decisions over disputes between survivors and try and keep everyone happy (or kick them out if they just don't fit).  When you venture out, combat is turn based; you need to try and stay quiet if you want to avoid too much attention from zombies.  You can essentially "herd" zombies away from places you want to loot by making noise elsewhere.
Overall it's a solid game imho.  Not sure where the negative reviews come from (maybe game has improved a lot since then) but if you like turn based combat/resource management/survival etc then give this a go

I bought this for $0.99 during a Steam sale, not expecting much. And to be clear, the graphics are a little sloppy, the game-play is straight out of God of War, the "plot" is B-movie fluff, and there are no Steam trading cards for this title. On the other hand...
Marlow Briggs is AMAZING! It completely embraces the cheesiness of its premise, and delivers absurdly over-the-top action on a scale unheard of in most video games. Through it all the protagonist delivers a ton of action movie one-liners and amusing meta-commentary on the number of puzzles involving spikes, swinging blades, and fire. Instead of long, boring cut-scenes, we get cool "freeze frame" moments, with the camera swooping and panning around the frozen tableau as Marlow Briggs defeats an army of giant bugs, or cuts a helicopter in half, or survives the explosion of a cruise-ship-sized mining vehicle. It's also nice to see a black guy as the protagonist, with no one else in the game making a big deal out of it.
There is nothing new or original in this package, so don't expect it to change the definition of gaming. What you DO get is a fun, amusing, and action-packed game at a criminally low price. I HIGHLY recommend Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death.

Graphics

A beautifully rendered world, extremely satisfying levels of destruction, grand animations, and an easy to understand interface. Battlefield: Bad Company 2 has it all.
Gameplay
9
At times, it feels like there are some frustrating balance issues. But those are few and far between. Bad Company 2 is a fantastic game to pick up and go to town with. You'll find glee in causing buildings to crumble around you, planting that charge of C4 on a tank and blowing it up, nailing that perfect headshot from across the map. However, where Bad Company 2 really shines is when you log on with some friends and get coordinated. Communicate and work together to outgun, outflank, and outdo the enemy team.
Story
4
I'll be honest with you. If you are playing Battlefield games for the story, you're going to be really, really disappointed. While there is a storymode here, it honestly isn't worth much of your time except as a glorified tutorial. The characters do give a few good laughs though.
Multiplayer
10
As mentioned earlier, Bad Company 2 really shines when you play with friends, but even alone you're going to have a blast with this one. Hours and hours of fun and destruction await you, with several different modes of multiplayer available to choose from. Be warned though, if you join up this late in the game you're going to face some very, very good long-time players.
Replayability
9
You're going to keep coming back to this one. The peak of the Battlefield series so far, it never gets old racing out of a building as it crumbles around you, covering your team on a withdrawal from an overrun area, or being at the front of a charge to capture a point. Don't miss out on one of the most enjoyable Battlefield experiences yet. The only struggle here is that most your friends will probably have moved on to the new battlefields.
Overall
9.2/10
Though not as popular as it once was (due to the new battlefields) Bad Company 2 still stands at the top of the Battlefield mountain. The Frostbite engine really shines in this iteration. Multiplayer is fast-paced, brutal, and spectacularly fun. Don't like those trees? Mow them down with your LMG. Don't like that building? Blow it up. Your team being overrun? Call in an artillery strike and give them some relief. All in all, an absolute must have for any Battlefield fan.

Summary: A unique idea wrapped up in a solidly presentable and well-executed package, this game gives players just enough room to make this game anywhere from an entertaining comedy to a miniature tragedy. It's short, it's effective, and it's free. Why not give it a shot?
seems to be called "friendzone simulator" or "Emily Is a ♥♥♥♥♥" in a lot of reviews, but my interpretation of the game leads me to believe that it's less of a "friendzone simulator" and more of an engaging while still ultimately puppeteered opportunity to see the effects of one's actions.
Whether or not the player ends up "in the friendzone" (read: rejected) is tertiary to the fact that the player never has the chance to end up with Emily in the first place. Allegations (whether you believe them to be true or not) of her being a manipulative and overall selfish, insensitive or harmlessly uninterested person aren't what keeps the player - or rather the main character - from developing a romantic relationship with her; it's the character's inability to express his/her feelings towards Emily and the subsequent awkwardness and uncomfortable emotional pressure that it puts on their relationship that forbids them from ever being more.
Constantly, the character (it's important to understand the distinction between the player and the main character in discussing this game) is so close to saying something that would hint at his/her romantic interest in Emily, and yet every time those words are retracted and inklings of those feelings withheld. It's not Emily "friendzoning" the player, it's about the player failing to make any sort of move towards Emily. Consequently, any romantic or sexual encounters that the two may or may not have had may come across to the main character as a natural indicator that there's something more to the relationship, but because Emily is led for years to believe that you're her friend, her supporter, and
a potential partner, it mucks things up. Sure, some of the scenarios play out in a way such that it seems that there was a clear mutual attraction, but the problem is, the main character never takes that step. From the player's perspective, there is no clear way of knowing that Emily ever has any romantic interest in the main character. But similarly from the player's perspective, it's obvious that the main character has a romantic interest in Emily. Those types of relationships where one person wants one things while the other person wants another are very hard to make work. It's no surprise that they end up losing touch with one another. No matter how you spin it, the main character (not necessarily the player) does not once communicate his/her feelings towards Emily, and so what's romantically sown is romantically reaped: nothing.
Some players will be heartbroken by Emily and the main character's eventual fading disconnect, while others will say good riddance to be done with a friendship that becomes a chore. But the reality is this: sometimes friends drift apart, and if neither person in a relationship tries to make it romantic, then it will (almost) never become more than that.
isn't the most complex or stimulating games I've played, but it fulfills a niche that I've now realized is pretty underexplored. It's not easy to create a twenty minute experience that feels like it spans five years, but the developers here managed to make it work out pretty well. Reflecting on friendship and the consequences of actions and inaction,
is an experience well worth the time and obviously well worth the price.

This is a narrative based game, and it presents you with options to take. None of these options really mean anything in the long run, only minor details will be mentioned/referenced. It is to the point that these choices do not even really need to exist; there are no branching paths, no different results, only one narrative and thus crippling this game's replayability significantly.
There is a major plot twist towards the game's third act which significantly alters the entire narrative, for the worse, as it depends on stretching suspension of disbelief to the breaking point. The graphics are pretty, and the voicework is okay, but none of that can really save this game from its faults. A hard game to review. It features beautiful hand-drawn locations that you need to go through to challenge the bosses. The bosses are the real meat of the game, all six of them having different patterns to memorize and different achievements to get for beating them in special ways. However, the locations you need to go through to get to them are boring, as beautiful as they often are - as other people have said, it often feels like a (sometimes annoying) walking simulator with some very light puzzles and a great soundtrack. Thing is, you also move really, really slow, which makes getting through these areas even more boring.
Additionally, the game is REALLY short - I explored everything and tried for some achievements (until I got tired of the light RNG some of the bosses have which can really ruin those achievements) and played the game for almost exactly 4 hours; at least 2 1/2 of those hours were spent just walking from point A to point B, only 1 1/2 I actually fought the bosses.
If you are interested in norse mythology and want to see some beautiful hand-drawn scenery together with some epic boss battles and good music, then the game could be worth it - just be wary of the length and how repetitive it gets really quickly. Also, only get it on sale - the game is absolutely not worth 15 € for the length it has or the content it features. I'd say 10 € or below is okay.

This game proves once again — to make an immersive game there's no need to have an AAA-game engine. The most important thing is the story. Here you have the Dead State, where story unfolds before your eyes, and you really feel how you become a new leader of a small community during apocalypse. Yes, most dialogues become repetative soon, but in the mornings you always have some situations happening, and you need to make decisions which affect your gameplay.
You need to keep your small society happy, fed and safe; you may set tasks on job boards, and recent game update made it so that NPCs are actually animated basically, and it adds some immersion too.
Pros:
- Interesting random situations, good decision-making game
- A great mix of Fallout/Wasteland2/Fallout Tactics/XCOM and even... The Sims :) Turn-based combat and real-time movement, when time is running only when you want it to run, makes gameplay run smoothly, at your own preferred pace.
- Good dialogues, not very short, and not too long — you won't get bored reading them
- Immersion is great
Cons:
- Some repetativeness in NPC dialogues
- Some UI issues
- I had couple of glitches and CTDs while I was playing, but fortunately there's a quicksave and autosave function
- Background music is great, but it is repetative
Future suggestions, although the game is in it's final state, I see that devs still actually change some things:
- It would be great if there was some voiceacting involved :)
- More randomness to the radio? Dynamic news?
- Ability to send additional scavenge parties without the leader?
- Loot balance? I'm on my day 31st now, still can't find any DVDs for recreation room, while I have lots of DVD players :)

The slow-mo hits are cool, it's a creepy and stressful game, as well as EXTREMILY difficult sometimes. I won't spoil anything but... that... friggin... church.
I think that covers the good, now for the not so good; the MP40 fires too fast, SVT40 fires too slow, STG44 is too weak, M91/30's (Mosin Nagant) front sight is actually a Kar98k front sight, and the M1903's stock looks like a hybrid between a No.4 Lee Enfield and an M1917. From what I can tell, none of the scopes are accurate to real life. I find the special infected can be quite annoying, there is a serious lack of stealth for a sniper game, there is a serious lack of sniping for a sniper game (rarely go beyond 100m. Rarely go beyond 50m for that matter), one of my biggest gripes is there's no FPS option thus no aim down the sights option, and my last issue so far is I've been playing for roughly 2 hours now and it seems to be the same thing over and over:
*SPOILERS* Fight a wave that instantly knows where you are. Fight another wave that instantly knows where you are. Fight another wave or two in the same manner. Find a safe house, restock on supplies, maybe change firearms. Fight a wave that instantly knows where you are. Fight a wave of jogging skeletons that instantly know where you are, fight a sniper who can jump better than spider man, fight another wave that instantly knows where you are. Safe house. Somewhere along the line is the friggin church. Maybe I'm just bad at 3rd person shooters, but I tried about a half dozen times to beat that friggin checkpoint with the MGing tank nazi, and I'm only on marksman (Normal).
Draw your own conclusions. Want action? Perfect. Want realism with your shooting? Keep looking, or check out Red Orchestra.

I'm at a loss with Steam Marines. The game has promise and I might recommend it when it's finished, but so far the game is just lacking that special umph to make it a great experience rather than a mediocre one.
In Steam Marines you start the game looking over the tutorial, end up confused, start up a game and die... horribly. After 2 or so games and tinkering with the classes I started to get a grip on things. You choose a squad of 4 marines at the beginning of the game and each class has a different weapon and a different skill tree. The skill tree is interesting but basic, each level you get to choose a passive or an activated ability. I never did use the powers much as they take multiple points of Action Points (AP being the resource you use to move, shoot etc.) and it always seemed better to just fire regularly.
The gameplay is a slow tile-based tactical slog through a ghost ships with robots and other baddies crawling out of the walls before attacking. This can be very frustrating as a wrong move and lack of items to restore AP can lead to dead marines very quickly. Furthermore, the random dungeon generation really needs some touch-ups as rooms with no doors or walls placed on top of each other make it impossible to move without breaking down walls and you need to do this to create proper tactical spacing.
At the end of every level you're rated on your performance and if you're a careful player like me you'll most likely end with a negative score even if all your marines survived the level. The score seems to indicate that this is supposed to be a fast-paced tactical RPG but the gameplay itself rewards slow and methodical movement. It's frustrating to say the least.
I'm not saying there isn't fun to be had with this game but in-between bouts of frustration, lackluster UI, boring music and a retro look that works but still needs a little work done (dropped items currently don't show up on the map) it just isn't worth the full price. With some polish I'm sure this gem will shine but right now I just can't recommend it.

In reality this is the difficulty of the game trying to force the player to have some ambition, to get into the feel of a roguelike where you trying to fight your way out of a dire situation. Review for early access version:
As someone who frequently gets
convinced to buy early access games, I was incredibly impressed with Steam Marines. This game feels like playing a full fledged game and while if you look closely you can spot the rough edges, it generally doesn't affect gameplay. Even better than that though is the fact that the developer is constantly active with the community working to fix any issues that crop up and discussing future implementations. As a personal example, I reported a minor bug that I noticed. He responded within 3 hours saying not only had he found the problem, but he also fixed it. If every early access developer put this kind of effort in, it wouldn't be nearly the crapshoot it currently is when buying early access games. If you want proof of developer involvement just look at the forums for this game, he is constantly posting.
On the play side of things, this is not a game that will appeal to everyone. You control a squad of four marines progressing through procedurally generated "decks" of a space ship. There are a lot of gameplay mechanics reminiscent of the XCOM series in that every unit has a limited number of "action points" to use for moving, attacking, healing, etc. Once you have used all of your points the computer takes its turn moving the enemies about in the same fashion. Each of your marines has a different class/weapons and it is up to you to use them in a way that utilizes their strengths. With the exception of a brief tutorial that introduces just enough of the mechanics to kill yourself, there is very little hand holding in this game. Let me be clear though, there is a big difference between accessible and dumbed down. This game is most certainly accessible and honestly, pretty intuitive; it is not at all dumbed down. It will not stop you from accidentally throwing a grenade right next to a teammate, wandering around dying because you went the wrong way, or even wasting your points on accidental actions. This game will never ask you "are sure you want to (insert random action here)".
If this sounds boring in any way let me disabuse you of that right now. This game is incredibly intense in a on-the-edge-of-your-seat way. If you ever start to feel relaxed, it's probably because you are staring at the menu screen after getting your face melted by a robot. Turn based means you get as much time as you want to choose how to lead your marines to their death, it also means you have to sit and watch as the AI exploits your mistakes to bring said death about even faster. As you progress through the game your marines will earn experience that translates into more perks and better stats. You will find yourself becoming more attached to your marines the longer you survive, making it that much worse when they suffer perma-death. The reluctance to enter a new room or turn a corner is heightened by the fact that the game has only one save file that is constantly updated so there are no second chances. You can find survivors along the way but they will be lowly privates with none of the awesomeness of your fallen soldier. Unlike some procedurally generated games there is a definite (and achievable) end goal which is perfect for people like me who need something to work towards besides a general "do good...".
If any of this has sounded interesting I would recommend getting this game. Whether or not it is worth the list price is something you will have to decide for yourself, for me it was. If nothing else, watch for the game to go on sale or try to win one of the free keys the developer offers on his site

note: I played this with an Xbox 360 controller.
If you liked God of War, you will probably like this. It has a bit less polish but the game doesn't ever take itself seriously. There's 4 different weapons, 4 different powers, and probably 9-10 combos for each weapons. There's no chaining, no real reward for doing combos. Getting hit doesn't interrupt your combo, but it will push you back in most cases making you sit in a recovery time (which will probably run out the combo timer). It's closer to an arcade beatemup than a cuhrazee game.
The very last weapon you unlock has great weapon feel. It's too bad it was the last one because I really wanted to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of more enemies with it. The base weapon has a pretty mediocre feel, the second weapon has nearly no response, and the 3rd has a pretty cool aoe hitbox, so I'll let it slide.
There's puzzles in the game, but none that are of any difficulty. However, they're "new" feeling enough to not feel boring.
I laughed a few times in the game but for the most part it's a pretty cliche "an ancient evil awakens (literally)" storyline. It's not absurd enough or meta enough to really hold my interest too much though.
The graphics are pretty well displayed, you can tell it's a console port though. It almost feels like an Unreal engine style game graphically. The animations could have some improvement. When Marlow is sliding down a mountain or snow, his model hardly reacts to the ground. It's like he's on a Slip-and-slide. It feels a bit rushed or on a budget, maybe. I don't know any background information on the game.
In total, I think it was a good arcade style time waster, but I wouldn't go in expecting any sort of depth to anything about it, be it combat, story, or art.
Overall it gets a 6.3/10.

I didn't play this game for multiplayer, online, verusus or anything else. All I wanted was to re-experience (at least a large portion of) the storyline, just like in Naruto's fighting games.
The combat system is exactly what I wanted, and the characters look absolutely amazing. The cutscenes are great, the events transpire just like in the anime with just as much action and suspense. Every fighter has virtually the same default combo but a lot of variety in their special and ultimate attacks, diversifying the gameplay tremendously. They even enlarged the endowments of every woman in this game. Although that was probably just to sell the swimsuit dlc pack, I don't mind at all and I would have gladly paid up if the game didn't feel so absolutely pointless.
That's right, without a cohesive storyline to back up the fights, the game just feels completely hollow. It can't get by on being competitive and balanced like the games you'll see in EVO and no one's going to take it seriously since it's just an anime fighter. One Piece already has a huge volume of story to back it up, so why only include one story arc? Repeating it FOUR times from the perspective of other characters comes off as desperate padding.
I'm miffed by the pricetag (so I picked it up on sale half off just one month after it released and skipped buying the dlc), but after finding out that this game is a shell of my expectation I'm glad I dodged the bullet of paying full price for this.

New life has been breathed into this game! I played it a little bit before the new director (Tim) joined the team. Over the past 5 months there has been a hiatus on updates so the team could do a complete ground-up rewrite. The new version with planets and land claims adds much more focus to team play and pvp. Where before the game was a basic sandbox with no real goal, now Houses can make alliances or got to war. Areas can be claimed by players and shared with other players in their House.
The game still has a long way to go. Many features have rough edges that need to be refined. There are some mechanical blocks that still need to be added to the game. The dev team does a great job of informing players of updates and changes in the weekly update videos every Tuesday. If anything goes wrong in an update you can be sure the dev team will roll out a hotfix to solve the issue.
I've observed some very promising behaviour on the multiplayer servers. Complete strangers will play together and work to accomplish a goal, like building a watchtower to guard a village, or constructing a wall around their area. However, as with all sandbox games there is the problem of griefing. Players will join random servers just to wreck stuff and see things break. The developers have said they are looking at way to add offline protection. It is good to know they are aware of the problem and are already working on solutions.
Unlike Space Engineers, another Keen Software House game, there is a suprising lack of "Clang" (weird physics bugs and breakages). You can build contraptions out of rope drums, catch blocks, and other mechanical blocks. Even on multiplayer servers it's no problem to have functioning siege engines rolling around the world and launching projectiles. There is sometimes a noticable drop in sim-speed, especially when a wall or tower is collapsing, but optimizations in future updates will alleviate that.
If you enjoy multiplayer sandbox games I would highly recommend Medieval Engineers. Find a group of friendly players and make a House on an active server and you will have hours of fun ahead of you.

When I began the game, I got the sense the main character was on a journey to heal himself from the pain of watching his marriage and wife decay due to her dimensia. But then the game insults this idea and the main character by pushing infidelity constantly. But maybe that is the point?
While many people on the reviews I've seen don't like the conspiracy arc of the story, I was more interested and bothered by the game's push to get the main character to cheat on his sick wife. And in my opinion the conspiracy stuff was a red herring. Fluff to make the game seem more intruging than it really is. The true intent of the game is to see if you would selflishly cheat on your sick wife. Perhaps I pass the games test as the ending I chose was to keep the ring on the finger and keep the marriage intact but it was clear to me that the game really really wanted me to break those vows for your female partner on the radio that you speak to throughout the game. 60% of the dialogue choices leaned towards infidelity.
This game is also something you wouldn't play more than once. Running is slow and there isn't much else to do after  playing it through once. In my opinion this game would have been much more successful as as movie than a videogame as it's mostly just walking around and looking at stuff. There is no real challenge.
In conclusion I think this game is pointless. The red herring story is there just to keep you going but is ironically not as interesting as the story leads it up to being while the relationship that builds between the main character and the woman on the radio is designed solely to see if you are cuck enough to cheat on your wife.

I truly enjoyed this game, but I am on the fence on whether or not I'd recommend it to most gamers. The visuals, setting, and overall aesthetics are pleasing to the senses as they urge you to long for a world you didn't know you wanted. The characters and their story tugged at my emotions and I'm not typically one to get suckered in by emotional things. The pacing felt focused and measured... for the first half... then all the good this game sets up winds down in a dissatisfying manner.
There are 3 acts to this story. Act One will grip you and not let go. It holds some of the best moments for me in story-driven games. So much happens in the first few days of the game.
Then the second Act (which tends to be longest, like in most films, books, and plays) is sped through as if in a montage of grand events.
Then Act 3 suddenly happens and all things are resolved. I didn't even have time to process all the first 3rd of the game.
So, there's a few gaffes with the game's story and pace. But, besides that, there's a lot to take in with this game and it is an experience I would repeat.

Some people call this a walking simulator, they don't understand the purpose of the game.  This story is about the growth of the characters involved, and while I will admit the ending is anticlimactic, it is still one of my favorite games of all time and one of the first that I recommend to non-gamers out of my library.  It is less focused on the gameplay and more focused on the way that the story evolves.

Dead State is a game of good intentions marred by unpolished content and occasionally flawed execution.  When it works, it's a delightful experience reminiscent of the original Fallout and other such games with an interesting world and endearing characters.  Collecting loot from locations, rescuing survivors and interacting with them, upgrading your shelter, and equipping your characters all prove to be engaging stuff.  The first 30 days are great fun as you struggle to explore a strange and hostile landscape.
That said, the game ends up with several critical flaws. It's unfortunately buggy and will crash on you quite frequently, the UI is occasionally frustrating to sort through for important information, and the combat is underwhelming due to mechanics that become imbalanced in the mid to late-game. The game just steadily begins to run out of steam after the first month as it gradually runs out of ways to challenge the player.  You'll mostly be sitting around as you wait for the game's endings, which themselves don't do much to really resolve the player's emotional connection to the characters and story.
Dead State is a game I cautious recommend.  It tries to be the Zombie RPG we all wanted 10 years ago and succeeds fpr the most part, but in doing so it feels exactly like an unfinished Iso-RPG from 10 years ago.  Dead State isn't perfect, but I guess it manages to be "good enough".

Dead State is clunky, buggy and slow near the end. It's also one of the best indie games I've played this year. A post-apocalyptic zombie game where fighting zombies is the least of your troubles, your task is to keep a shelter of ragtag survivors afloat. This means keeping it secure by building/maintaining your wall and posting guards. Keeping your food and water supply going by looting abandoned buildings (or unabandoned ones), building a well and gardens, and raising chickens. Trying to keep your food refrigerated (and stop your survivors from rioting) by keeping a steady supply of fuel for the generator. Dealing with the other surviving factions, either through "diplomacy" or force. And so on...
There is a fair bit of combat, but for most battles, it's a matter of chugging through and killing everything so you can loot the map. In most cases, either your party is properly-equipped for a combat scenario (in which case you will eventually win) or it's not (in which case you will lose, probably quickly). This is a big reason the game feels slow nearing the end: you know you can kill everything, so now you need to chug through and do it. This is especially true for the zombie maps, since a "hard" zombie map is just one with a lot of zombies on it. Human enemies will wipe the floor with you in the early days, but by the end game, there are only a few encounters in the game that will give you any real difficulty. Even some of the scariest-looking ones are actually quite easy with decent equipment. So it's the shelter management aspect where the game shines.
In Dead State, you have a great deal of control over all aspects of the shelter's management. You're not only responsible for meeting those basic needs (food/safety/electricity/morale) and assigning work duties, but also internal and external diplomacy. You choose which survivors to recruit, how to deal with other groups of survivors, how to deal with the various cliques in your shelter, and what to do about criminals and other crises. There are a lot of different ethical choices to make that don't boil down simply to "plus karma" or "minus karma" like many other games. Is it more wrong to turn away a survivor that you know is useless, knowing they will die, or to let them in and risk starving everyone in the end due to lack of food? What about attacking other camps for fuel to keep your shelter from falling apart? Does it matter if they are "bad guys"? What counts as a "bad guy" and are you sure you aren't one? :)
Anyway, despite the bugs I thought it was worth every penny. There is a free demo available, which is the full version of the game with a limited number of days, and if you like the demo, you can carry your save over, so if you're curious there's no reason not to try it out.

A decent enough piece of Software, unfortunately completely useless for actual comparison. The scores vary wildly, newest drivers are flagged as "not verified" for months and the Developers clearly don't understand how the current generation CPU and GPU features work. Compared to other benchmarking software (Unigine Heaven, Unigine Valley, Ashes of the Singularity, Prime95, Cinebench), I would not recommend buying it at this price.
Charging 30 bucks for something this broken should be a crime.
In Detail:
- Physics simulations don't use all available cores or all available CPU time. You see it stuttering, however it barely reaches 17% total CPU usage. This leads me to believe that they use a physics engine that does not have parallel computing in it yet - something most major physics engines now have.
- DirectX 11 tests are horribly gimped. So badly that your GPU will actually underclock since it has nothing to do.
- DirectX 12 test (TimeSpy) uses an Async Compute implementation that is tailored towards Nvidia cards.
- All tests look like they were designed to promote the results of a specific brand or vendor in order to get you to buy the product - even if other benchmarks show it as performing worse.
Paid DLC to unlock full features. That is just unacceptable.

It could have been much, much better, but its just one of the few games in this region of time.
The Korean War is sort of a forgotten war in history, and its good to see a game about a forgotten war and learn about it. I can see why this game has mixed reviews, but it really has some features that will stand out to the ordinary strategy player.
The grand campaign would be bland without some of the features included that are almost exclusive to the Theatre of War series. One thing i particularly enjoy is the information in the game is consistently kept. The soldiers under your command can be promoted, awarded, and kept track of at all times. Its amazing and i hate that this isnt seen in most grand strategy games now days. The battles in the game are quite challenging on both sides, but quite frankly they get boring. There literally are only a few maps that will randomly generate when you try and defend a region or attack one, which you can imagine can get quite tedious.
The combat is pretty well done, realistic and challenging to a good extent. People can get surrounded and flee the battlefield due to low morale, that is something that you rarely, if at all, see in video games. Tanks and most other equipment cant be repaired, equipment is scarce, it feels realistic. Some of the combat is a little slow... i remember i sent an infantry squad into a building and it literally took 11 seconds to realize there was a guy with a ppsh in the corner of the room. Oh, that brings me to another point, where are all the submachineguns on the american side? A lot of weapons from Korea seem to be missing from the game, but it really isnt that big of a deal. The submachineguns are kind of a game changer, though. While the US only gets rifles and carbines and MGs, the chinese, russians, and koreans, get every bit of it. Huh, odd. It's a little unbalanced.
You can go to the editor and create your own campaign, which does kind of provide some extra things to do with the game. Make larger campaigns, battles, everything, it's really cool. I did find something on the missing weapons i spoke of.  When looking into the game editor, there are apparently a lot of weapons that arent used in the missions or the campaigns. The Patton, Pershing, T-54, and a ton of other stuff are in the files but not in the missions. It kind of makes me feel like this game is unfinished, unpolished, just not complete in some senses. It has good combat, good strategy, but can be very tedious at some points with the same units, maps, ecetra.
If you enjoy strategy games, have patience, and enjoy games like Men of War and Wargame, this may be for you, try it out and try out the original Theatre of War!
If you like combat, but dont have the patience for doing tedious things just to make a single soldier a colonel or try and get 10 kills with one tank, try something like Men of War, or Wargame, both of those are pretty awesome.
If you are new to strategy games try something like command and conquer or age of empires, both are pretty awesome combat RTS games.

"Is this game P2W?"
It USED to be P2W during Alpha and closed beta.
Trion worlds removed the dungeon Stamina system that basically limits the number of dungoens you can run per day and they also remove the stat bonuses that items in the marketplace gave you so now all clothing in the marketplace are just for vanity/transmog/glamour. :)

As a One piece fan, I naturally got this. I do not prefer the style of the Pirate warriors series. Here we go:
Likes:
+ Love for one piece: moves are true to the series, the characters look nice, and are rather unique to play as.
+ Adore the battle system - haki vs DF, the cool ultimate attacks, nice character damage system, and the tag-team battles.
+ Stars the same awesome Japanese voice cast
+ Decent PC port
Dislikes:
- Short story. While this is not a major turnoff, a few more battles without reusing cutscenes would've been better. Also, could have made it a more coherent story - switching to different playable characters as the story progresses.
- Small health bars. You die way faster due to the insanely high damage the AI does. While I understand 3 admirals vs. Luffy is supposed to be tough for Luffy, I can't understand Akainu getting thrashed when he is clearly supposed to win without breaking a sweat in the story mode.
- Need gameplay tweaks: while there are many gauges, the gauges deplete super-fast and take forever to recharge. Require a better combo system (limited combos=spamming), and for such fast paced gameplay, faster movement while moving around helps.
Nitpicks:
- Although true to character, Sanji won't attack ladies: does little to no damage to them. This makes him not to choose him a lot although he is one of my favorites. Similar with Law...why would he lose HP when he activates room? Is that even a thing?
- Gameplay is smooth. Nevertheless, 60 FPS could've been neat.
- Wanted mode could have been more compelling with unique fights. While there are some good ones like use only Enel to fight Luffy, the repetition of fighting the same opponents can get old fast. The dynamics of the fight won't change with some added conditions either - almost at all times.
Overall, it is worth your while, particularly if you are an acolyte of One piece. I hope there is a sequel, and they improve a lot to bring this series on par with the popular Naruto: Ultimate Ninja Storm series, or even with the Dragonball series. This one certainly shows loads of potential to be great!

Even then though the average battle lasts 60 seconds or so even with full 3v3 while picking a pre-made pirate crew takes ~20 seconds. You quickly grow tired of using the same crew since you win 3v3 battles with 10 or less moves (3 moves to KO each opponent). If you want to do what we are ALL wanting to do and set up a HUGE fantasy custom fight, well that's impossible. You can pit Akainu vs Aokiji and expect to fight forever since both should be "evenly matched" (reference the 10 day fight in the series) but the fight lasts once again less than 60 seconds. It really bothers me there's no way to do something so simple as to increase your stats for a specific fight to have that EPIC BRAWL and immerse yourself in your character. Heck, you can't even change the DIFFICULTY?!?!?
The story mode is severly lacking and it feels like a "tutorial" and less like playing a game. Once again, largely IMPORTANT / MAIN battles last 60 seconds or less and side / non-important battles last 60 seconds or less. I'm fighting the Admirals... I don't want to be able to lose / win the fight in 60 seconds and I want it to be a challenge. As you progress through the story mode everything feels broken, rushed, and mashed together. It doesn't flow comfortably. It would have been so easy to take it in a direction that felt right and not let you "choose path battles" and etc.
They WAY overdid this cut scene and gameplay instagram filter saturation they layer over EVERYTHING. It in no way feels right. All the colors are so saturated and the stupid lines get in the way of the art and it greatly distracts from the game play.
This game honestly plays more like a demo because everything feels rushed, there's no fight customization other than "infinite life" or "infinite burn gauge", and the game has no "goal" and the "Wanted Versus" modes have teams and descriptions of who you are "hunting" that doesn't even make sense because they have such a LIMITED cast. Many of the support players SHOULD have been main players. Vergo, Dragon, Gol D. Roger, Tashigi, the list goes on and on of really key important players people would have loved to play.
I would pay 20$ for this game, MAYBE 30$. I heavily regret paying ~80$ USD. As much as I love One Piece, I can't and won't reccommend this game to anyone.
Stephen Hawking runs better than this game.
