Vanilla Bad Company 2 is great. The gameplay - nearly five years later - is still entertaining, and with the hardware requirements no longer near top end, the game runs great on most modern systems. The campaign is laid back, and the characters all have unique personas to them.
The real meat, however, for Bad Company 2 is the multiplayer. Even now you can still find servers for the base game filled with players at all hours of the day. Multiplayer continues to live on, even as we see Battlefield: Hardline take center stage.
While vanilla Bad Company continues on strong, its expansion Vietnam is now in the stage where only at certain times during the day are there players on the various servers still active today. Yes, you can still get a game in with Vietnam, and yes it is as fun as hell (I think I just got PTSD from my time in Nam man (humor intended)). Certainly you can still find games for Vietnam, though not as much as the base game - whether or not it is worth the money for both is entirely up to the buyer.
Battlefield: Bad Company 2 and the Vietnam expansion is definitely worth your time and money if you have not already picked up the game. Should you already own the game, then it is worth a reinstall just to take a trip down memory lane. Recent additions to the Battlefield franchise can feel lackluster, and considering the price tag for both Vietnam and the base game when compared to newer titles with their large price tags and their emphasis on Season Passes, it might be time to appreciate some good old games once more.
Battlefield: Bad Company 2 ladies and gentlemen; it's still got plenty of fuel left in the tank, even in 2015.

Bad Company 2 is a more than acceptable instalment in the acclaimed Battlefield series. The game features a solid, enjoyable campaign that visits varied locations and harnesses an abundant range of weapons which raise the quality of what could otherwise be a stereotypical, conventional and ultimately dull set of missions. Movements and gunplay is fairly smooth and rarely descends into frustrating territory. Locations pop with colour and life, and there's a bona-fide sense of realism present throughout the environment, even when the mission you are completing is anything but.
The real highlight and the most popular aspect of Bad Company 2 is the immensely popular multi-player mode. With it's vast maps, unique and diverse arsenal of weapons and great team mechanics, Bad Company 2's multi-player triumphs over its counterpart and frequently compared franchise Call of Duty in many respects. Teams feel more close-knit and dependant on each other than most other multi-player games and locations feel more expansive too. Moments of tension and anticipation, speculating what your opponents will attempt next are nail bitingly pleasant. Making tactical decisions and planning your movements requires more brain-power and strategizing than what may be expected, but when your plan achieves success, the feeling of jubilation is unmatched. It really is a game mode most enjoyed with friends who enjoy planning out their moves and attempting to execute them with precision. And with an addictive levelling up system, you'll find it hard to pull yourself away.
Bad Company 2 is a great game and is a genuine classic in the shooter genre. With it's gradually decreasing popularity thanks to the newer instalments in the Battlefield franchise, it's a smart idea to purchase this while the game's community is still thriving.

I truly enjoyed this game, but I am on the fence on whether or not I'd recommend it to most gamers. The visuals, setting, and overall aesthetics are pleasing to the senses as they urge you to long for a world you didn't know you wanted. The characters and their story tugged at my emotions and I'm not typically one to get suckered in by emotional things. The pacing felt focused and measured... for the first half... then all the good this game sets up winds down in a dissatisfying manner.
There are 3 acts to this story. Act One will grip you and not let go. It holds some of the best moments for me in story-driven games. So much happens in the first few days of the game.
Then the second Act (which tends to be longest, like in most films, books, and plays) is sped through as if in a montage of grand events.
Then Act 3 suddenly happens and all things are resolved. I didn't even have time to process all the first 3rd of the game.
So, there's a few gaffes with the game's story and pace. But, besides that, there's a lot to take in with this game and it is an experience I would repeat.

Lots of fun!!!!!! This is an amazing game, who will provide you with countless hours of fun, as long as you are ready for facing the complete unknown. The first thing to remember about this game is that you have to remember that a lot of it being fun is due to its "old style", "retro style", game, so don't expect things to come as easily as they come in modern games, where you can control everything just using your mouse ... this game requires you to really understand it and learn how to play it, and that means that the first times that you play you are probably going to loose, a lot! So, be ready to die, die, and die, as many times as it takes until you understand the gameplay. If the game doesn't look appealing in your first try, consider playing a few more times, since the easiness of dying can make you feel kinda blue when u are beginning. One of the key aspects of the game is memorizing what each class of soldier can do (leader, grenadier, etc.) and understand how to use them ... for instance, if you are not careful the grenadier will most likely get your other soldiers in a friendly fire ... also, you need to pay a lot of attention to how many moving points each soldier has, since a single mistake usually means death. What is fun about this game is that each scenario is completely random, so each start is almost like a fresh new start ... details, like paying attention to ammo, to doors that have bombs on them, or learning when is it worth to break down a wall to move to another room instead of using doors can mean the difference between life and death ... game rules as well must be well learned, since "simple" things like reloading means using all the action points available for that marine ... learning how to fire at enemies is also interesting, since you can only fire in straight lines (exception to the grenadier who can cause collateral damage around where his shells land), so it is almost like playing chess only with pawns and towers ... the guard mode can be pretty useful if you positioned your marine in the correct line of fire, or useless if he is looking to the left and the enemy is coming from the right ... and no, although in guarding mode, he won't turn and shoot the enemy ... in essence, I think this is a game where you spend the first hour learning "how to play" and counting how many times you already died ... however, after understanding the gameplay, it is fun, definitely! Due the random nature of the game you can find yourself suddenly surrounded by enemies or just exploring room after room and getting credits and more ammo ... what is going to happen? Nobody knows, each game is unique, and they are worth a shot ... however, if you are expecting an easy to play game, this is not a good idea ... it takes  time, strategy, memory and the ability to cope with defeat ... just like in real life!

I've never written a review before, but this game deserves one. The game has everything I would expect in a post-apoctolyptic world: starvation, a battle with morale, interactions with survivors, and of course fighting and killing zombies and looters.
I believe the best aspect of this game is interacting and rescuing survivors. Each survivor has such an in-depth storyline which creates an emotional attachment with the gameplayer. You're forced to make such difficult, yet rewarding, decisions which impact the entire game's plotline.
One controversial aspect of this game is the turn-based fighting. Now I may be in the minority with this opinion, but I think the turn-based fighting adds originality to the game. It makes the game memorable and stand out from all the other zombies game.
Another part of the game which is a challenge is the balance of morale. Your survivors are scared, depressed, and alone in this zombified world, and they look to you, their leader, to keep their moods up. If you fail at keeping your survivors happy, they will leave your shelter, steal food and weapons, or even mutiny against you.
This game is brilliant, and the latest patch made it even stronger. DOWNLOAD THIS GAME -- IT'S WORTH IT.

Bought Dead State on sale.  Wanted to get it based on the demo and that it is squad based.  However, given the comments didnt want to pay too much.  Even in the Demo saw how annoying bugs could be.
Overall, I have to say a resounding thumbs up for the game though.  It is exactly what I wanted and hence however many hours in I am through the game I felt it fair to let others know who like me have been on the fence.  I like squad based tactics and so I am really most interested in the scenarios for getting supplies.  I like the combat and even enjoy just turning up while I fight is already going on and watching two looter groups fighting it out with each other, attracting a load of dead guys and then being overrun by them.  I then clean up and take all the loot!  Excellent fun!  I also enjoy the tricky encounters, usually where better armed looters/militia control an area and arent interested in parlaying.  Surprisingly I have also enjoyed running the shelter and developing my character in order to do that.  Admittedly the shelter begins to run itself after a time and you get so much food and luxuries that you could hold out until armageddon but it is a nice touch.  Havent got the lab yet but everything else is done.
So why wait until on sale?  It is still bugged.  It is a little annoying to see your guys walk through a locked door!  Or right through a car.  Also frustrating to not be able to get to loot which has been placed in a position that is inaccessible (rare though).  Early on (possibly demo) it was real annoying to have killed a guy taken some excellent loot only to get back to the shelter and it had gone missing and no I didnt forget to pick it up.  I think the worst faults, so far at least have been in the hotel  in Austin.  Great idea, real enjoyable combat, difficult and demanding.  But moving between floors is a real pain.  Could it not have been made a bit easier?  You will find it almost impossible to move up or down unless your players are in the right position but you cant move your players to get into that position.  Having one person in the right place should be enough then an automatic move.
If you enjoy squad based tactics (old school xcom not the new) and you woul like to try something different then this game is worth getting, you just need to work out what price you are willing to pay for it.  I got it at £14.99 and that was fine for me, under a £10 get it no questions asked.

In the modern zombie apocalypse, you take shelter with several other survivors in abandoned school to fend off zombies and not-so-altruistic survivors.
The zombie-infested modern world is depicted very nicely albeit brutal, where you can see how humanity quickly goes back to being medieval.
Will you stay humane in this maddness to people around you, or become one of the predators yourself, preying on the weak and abusing everyone around you just to survive that another day?
You can do all that and more in this very unique RPG game with turn based combat, strategic and planning elements and lots anf lots of dialogues.
It is really hard to compare this unique game to anything, except that it has been heavily influenced by older RPG titles like Fallout.
All in all, this time spent reading about the game is better be spent playing the game yourself, have fun!

I really love the art and humor of the game, but ultimately I cannot recommend it. At least not if you are looking for an actual engaging business sim. After less than a minute of playing the game, it struck me how much it already seemed to be setting itself up for a mobile game, by which I mean the F2P waiting game variety. I was hoping that I was wrong and that things would become more interesting, but they really don't.
There are no real strategic decisions to make in the game, and the decisions that are available are of very little consequence. For the most part, all you are doing is this:
1) Tell your potatoes to make a weapon
2) Wait while they make it (you can easily imagine purchasing a speed up with "gems" here on mobile)
3) Send one of your potatoes to town to sell it.
4) Wait while they sell it (again, you can imagine the gem gimmicks on mobile)
Same thing applies when you're applying buffs to a weapon, or sending a potato to purchase materials. Ultimately what Holy Potatoes feels like is a game that was very much intended to be a F2P/mobile game with in-app purchases, but has simply removed the in-app purchases and sold itself as a commercial title.
I can recommend the game for its charm, and perhaps as a game to kill time when you are waiting at the doctor's office, but I don't think I can recommend it as a very good sim on PC.
Using my own rating system below, I peg the game at a 3.
7) A classic, essential, and/or must-buy game that is worth full price.
6) A good game that is worth the full price.
5) A pretty good game worth checking out--especially if discounted.
4) A fairly good game, but I'd recommend buying it discounted.
2) Only worth checking out if you are dangerously curious.
1) Avoid at all costs.

I really enjoyed Firewatch from the opening scene. In a few short minutes I was quite attached to the main character and his life - his relationship. The setup reminded me a lot of the opening scene of UP.
The game can best be described as an adventure game, although interactive story is probably a better description. There are no puzzles to solve, but there are a large number of variations in where you can take your own story, and the dialog options reflect that.
A lot of the choices you make in the game don't affect what happens next - but that doesn't make them less interesting. In real life, a lot of choices we make are not rewarded or punished. We make them because we feel they are the right choice to make, and we live with those choices. The game felt a lot like that for me. I know I didn't have to clean up the beer cans left on the ground, but I chose to. The game didn't acknowledge this. I was not rewarded for it, but it felt like the right thing to do.
The ending to me felt right. I know a lot of people have complained about it, but I think you pay attention to the way the story is told throughout this game, it will feel right to you too.

I recommend this game with a few reservations.
First, it's not for everyone.  The game can be very repetitive.  Managing a group of survivors and locating resources to build and feed everyone sounds fun, but what it amounts to is little more than going from one area to another, clubbing everything to death, and putting all their food/fuel/ammo in your inventory.  Then doing it over and over again.
Second, the combat is not very good.  I found it poorly paced.  There is a very basic early game, middle game, and late game, but the jumps between them seem don't transition well.  It's all based on armor, really.  Having better armor suddenly makes you immune to so much damage.  Combat pretty much boils down to doing the same thing over and over again, with very few interesting mechanics.
Third, the game is not paced well.  This goes hand-in-hand with repetitive.  There are very interesting storylines and elements, but there are large bouts of nothing followed by sudden bursts of activities, particularly close to the end where there bouts of nothing become longer and longer.  The game could use a BIT more activity/story.
With all that said, this game is interesting, fun, and contributes to the genre in a much needed way.  The devs are actually patching/making improvements, so I consider that a strong plus as well.  Some bugs remain, but they're definitely working on it, and I didn't run into any major issues (although a few annoying bugs were present).  I enjoyed leading my group through some tough situations and exploring post-apocalyptic Texas, meeting new people, and exploring a variety of environments.  There is some difficulty in building morale/food stores in the beginning, but this is actually fun and contributes to the difficulty of the game (something that is lacking at a certain point).
One final word.  The game has some political (ridiculous conservative/Texan stereotypes) elements to it.  If you're sensitive, you probably won't enjoy this game.  It was  bit heavy handed at times, to be honest. now that the bugs are out of the way, time to start talking about the main parts.

I have held off buying Dead State after seeing some people upset over what they felt was the game leaving Early Access too soon to benefit from the Winter Steam Sale.  I have been watching the game for a long time but decided to wait until it went on sale to pick it up.  It seems like Doublebear has been doing steady patching, while maybe not to the level some people want, updating none the less, so when it went on sale I went ahead and decided to pick it up.   I love turn-based games and RPGs and Zombie stuff so it I figured I would roll the dice and drop $20 on it and see what I got.
So far with a couple hours under my belt I am really enjoying it and I haven't ran into any bugs.  The UI is a bit frustrating at times and a couple of times I wasn't sure what I needed to do for stuff like swapping inventory.  A quick glance at the manual resolved those issues.  The game can be counter-intutive at times but counter-intutive isn't the same thing as game breaking bugs.  During my play (I admit I haven't spent a lot of time yet) I have enjoyed the game play.   It does feel like XCOM with Zombies instead of Aliens.   Yes the misses will frustrate you sometimes, but that is the genre.  The game isn't "easy" but it isn't "unfair" either.
People can fuss over if Doublebear released the game too soon as a greedy move or not.  I don't know what the game state was back in December when it launched, but currently the game is very fun.  Games can always spend some more time in the oven to enchance them, but then again at some point the game has to leave Early Access (though I have a few that I seriously doubt ever will).  But at the end of the day, is the game fun?  Yes it is.  Is it a AAA title, no.  Is the price fair?  Once again that is subjective.  From my couple hours of game time, I can tell you that I wish I had picked the game up eariler, regardless of the sale.  The normal asking price of $30 is a bit high for a indie title, but I believe it is mostly worth the price from what I have seen so far.  I have gotten less enjoyment for double the money.
Game prices are all over the place these days for Indie titles so I honestly don't know what a good price point is for games anymore.  That said I based on what I have seen so far and what I have read the game should last at least 30-40 hours, so I think it is a fair value.

So in closing is the game great?  Time will tell.  Has it been fun so far?  Yes it has.  Have I seen any bugs yet?  None that I can tell, un-intitive user interface design, yes, but bugs not really.   Of course I have just begun the game so that can drastically change along the way.  If it does I will be sure to update my review.  But at this time I can say that I would pay the full asking price for the game, much less on sale.   I think the game is good.  It isn't super, but it is fun and fair.

Dead State I would say is now in my top 5 best zombie games around, even though it is still in the early stages. First would say while the game is out of Early Access, there are still quite a bit of bugs and glitches but I have not come across any game-breaking ones and the game does have an ending. But the game is still being cared for by the developers and still getting big patches and fixes every other month or so.
Now that's out of the way let's start on the game. Dead State is a survival focus RPG where you play as a created character who survives a plane crash and later wakes up in a school with other survivors. The school is your main base and so the main focus is to help build it up while also going out to find supplies and other survivors to join you. It is cool that your base does change when you build upgrades and the March patch now let's survivors roam around, giving it more life-like. The only thing I do wish is more stuff you can do in the base or also the look changes based on the survivors you recruit (mainly them bringing in personal items to decorate).
The gameplay outside the base is similar to games like Xcom or any squad based RPG. You go out with a max of four people and when you arrive at locations, you mostly just look for supplies while fighting off the undead and hostile living. A nice thing is you will have to use different tactics when fighting zombies then living, since the undead aren't as smart and can be dispatch faster. However the good thing is they keep it bit realistic in the sense that taking on one undead or two is easy, but taking on a big group can be deadly. The equipment in the game while plenty, sadly they are not random in stats like Diablo. Also many survivors you recruit will have different skills that can be useful both on and off the field.
Speaking of survivors, Dead State is one of very few zombie games that actually get this right. By right meaning every survivors you recruit is a "person", a unique personality that can change on how you treat them. You will also get events involving them that also give them more of a background. Course another nice thing is nobody is safe, since the game does have permadeath on party members (though if your main character dies it's game over) that does affect morale. However if you have somebody that does get on your nerves, you can easily take them out on scavenging, kill them, and come back claiming they got eaten by undead. Also by them not being safe, they can also get infected if you're not careful. Luckily getting infected doesn't automaticly mean death in this game, as long as you have antibotics you can fight off the infection. So in a sense unlike other zombie games where other survivors are either as lifeless as the undead or there fates are already sealed, this game does them justice by actually making them people trying to survive with you.
Good:
-Plenty of survivors that join you, each with thier own look and personality
-Lots of areas to explore
-Realistic equipment
-Good amount of content and length
Bad:
-Still good amount of bugs
-Combat can drag on little too long
-Interface and menus could use some work on

I wanted to like this game, really. I don't often rate games as bad, and this one isn't really that bad but it leaves alot to be desired.
First of all the Korean War, the Forgotten War; In mainstream culture you see alot of WWII, Vietnam war, and Modern Warfare games and movies. As a fan of the history of war, I was always bothered by the lack of WWI (though we're seeing more) and Korean War games. I was delighted to find a Korean War game on sale and bought it almost instantly, despite the mediocre reviews.
Upon starting it up for the first time, I jumped into the campaign. After about 5 minutes of gameplay, it feels like Men of War: Assault Squad 2 (not sure about the other Men of Wars, i've only played the second). This game is slow. The maps were pretty, and had ample room for combat, but the combat was oh so slow. I wasn't expecting Company of Heroes or anything, but something a little more like Men of War would be exceptable. I enjoy long range combat but I felt it was a little exaggerated. My primary complaint was AI pathfinding. I'd send a squad in one direction, and they'd move straight there. This might be okay in an open field but if there's a mountain in the way, they'd climb up the damn thing until they got stuck.
I also didn't care for the UI at all, I felt it pretty "clunky" for the lack of a better word. When moving units, i'd appreciate it if the formation button didn't reset everytime you select something else. During the campaign (and tutorial) I felt what you were told to do was pretty vague. Now, I've played games with vague instructions but this was pretty bad.
I didn't care for the game. It's not terrible or unplayable, but I think there is alot of room for improvement.
I was pretty bummed out that this as the only Korean War game, but I suppose it's just not as interesting or well known to the masses.
If you were a fan of Men of War or any of the other Theatre of War games, by all means give this a swing (when it's on sale).
5/10

Steam Marines will definitely appeal to a small subset of people, but not to a general gamer audience and certainly not to me (and I love roguelikes!).
To not die within the first couple of floors of Steam Marine, you must play extremely cautiously. Open a door; set up the rest of the squad to guard behind. Look around the room; set up the rest of the squad to guard. If there are enemies, kite backwards while setting the rest of the squad to guard and maybe get some pot shots in. Failure to do any of these things risks the chance of some ranged bot popping out the shadows and taking a marine from full health to dead/near dead in a single turn. You have a rough idea of where enemies are from hearing their footsteps, but you have no idea how the rooms and doors are connected until you actually pop your head in and turn about.
The marine health/enemy damage ratio is so very low, so there is no room for error. Trying to run and gun, or even advance to a forward position and burst an enemy down, will get you killed very fast.
This demanded precision is frustrated by the control scheme: every  of the many actions has a mapped key, with NO context sensitivity. While I'm used to games like this, the learning curve is still a little steep, and the memorization will be a turn-off for many people. This frustration is compounded by the fact that there is no undo, even for benign actions with no impact on the immediate turn, such as guarding. Did you just hit the wrong key at a critical turn and accidentally fire at nothing, or guard into a wall, or use an item you didn’t intend to, etc.? All your hours and effort is wasted now, your run is over.
If a repetitive, boring, and cautious slog through a hardcore dungeon where small mistakes will waste hours of work sounds exciting to you, this game is for you. Again, I’m sure there are some people who will enjoy such a neurotic challenge, but this experience is not for most.

In short: Not a very good roguelike game. Why not? Steam Marines is one of those games that believe tileset graphics are enough to make a good roguelike. The style is indeed lovely but the UI is clunky and the setting uninspiring. Do you like turn based strategy? Do you like knowing your death was your fault and not because of RNG? Then play Steam Marines.
Too often difficulty and randomness are confused. In Steam Marines it is clear that while the levels are procedural and enemies don't spawn in the same place you are supposed to think a turn or two ahead. The position of your marines, whether you blow a hole in the wall or if you remembered to reload the turn before all play a part in your success.
It took me over 20 hours to beat the game on normal and none of those hours were from grinding or wasting my time. Every moment was something new I had to think my way past. Yes the game has permadeath and when you lose your squad you start the game over but the pressure is on from start to finish. Being complacent means you can die as easily on the first level as the last.
Beyond the game getting better (its still in alpha) the developer is active on the forums, talks about game design and what he intends to do in the future. This is the kind of Early Access game you want to support.

A thoroughly disappointing sequel for the diamond in the rough that was Sylvio 1.
The game basically takes away anything that made the first title thrilling - you no longer have to track down voices in the static or anything else because the game conveniently signals their presence via glowing orbs which you can see across the entire level.
The combat system (which admittedly was flawed) has been removed altogether so there no longer is anything you actually have to be scared about; save for some EVPs which quickly get tedious as you simply switch the forward/backward buttons on various speeds to get the info you want. Riddles likewise are no longer present - at best, you pick up some code for a lockpad from an EVP, which is automatically entered when you approach the associated door.
The world design is equally disappointing: Whereas Sylvio 1 had you walking through the expanses of an abandoned amusement park, Sylvio 2 sets you into an ocean with a few dozens islands, all of which look like glorified Unity tech demos. The interior design of the few "dungeons" you get to explore generally is not much better, even if each of them has its own little theme.
And then there's the ending. Without wanting to spoiler anything, it takes the many questions Sylvio 1 left open, gives you a good slap in the face, and leaves aforementioned questions open.
In all seriousness: If I had to take a guess, I would say that Sylvio 2 is one of those titles whose kickstarter failed, and which still was pressed out anyway despite of a notable lack in time and resources. Which, given it's really decent predecessor, is just a pity.

Original Sylvio was a game that came out of nowhere and charmed me with its very unique approach to horror-themed action adventuring. Being centered all around the EVP (Electronic Voice Phenomena) it went against the usual horror expectations - focusing almost entirely on terror, unease, tension and it was almost exclusively audio-based in how it evoked these feelings. Rare (and, to be fair, clunky) encounters with "enemies" weren't horrifying and didn't make you jump. Most things usually made you stop, slowly back away while trying to comprehend what you're seeing and hearing. And while the action adventure elements with those rare action parts and physics-based puzzle solving, or the open map exploration weren't always good and felt clunky, they added something very special to the game. The game wanted to be much more than it could, being a budget one man team product, but what it achieved was still good, unique and memorable.
Imagine my surprise at the fact that Sylvio 2 ditches everything but the basic audio analysis and exploration.
Sylvio 2 project is very different from the initial concept the developer was, sadly unsuccessfully, pitching at Kickstarter. Video analysis is still here, but it feels more like the audio analysis+visuals. Granted, original pitch didn't promise it to be much different, but it also seemed to focus only on video, while the end result still keeps the audio analysis, now with spectrograms, the way it worked originally and, as such, video feels almost redundant and there to bring more conventional horror ideas in.
Which is my personal biggest disappointment, which might instead feel like a huge plus to some people. While game still avoids any conventional horror jump scares, there's now much more focus on the visual side of horror of the kind that makes me want to look at the screen through the fingers (I'm easily impressed -_-). A lot of it is still creative and unique, but it's no longer slow, tense and all up to your imagination in these moments. It's much more in your face, even when it's static and not jumping into the camera.
And I feel like this change of focus also bleeds into the story of the game which overexplains everything by the end. Where original was vague, weird, obscure about the things that happened and why they happened, this game ends on something that just made me go "...really?" All the little stories are still interesting, and piecing them together is interesting, but the overall feel of the game's narration is just messy.
Oh and while you still piece things together and analyse audio and visual recordings, the game just breadcrumbs you through everything with visual "go here" pointers to every single point of interest. Which feels... clumsy. Sure, it solves the strange issue original had where new messages could pop up in places you went to and you would just walk in circles without clear understanding on what else you can do, and it was bad. But just putting markers on the map, always visible through walls, feels just as bad if not worse and kills quite a bit of the mood.
Which is not to say that it's not there. The mood is still top notch when you filter out all these huge issues mentioned above, and music is as fantastic as it was in the original game. Sitting in a dark corner, trying to figure out what you just heard mumbled in the static is an experience that no other games try to do, and I loved it as much as in the original game. Which is why I'm still glad I've played Sylvio 2. But... it feels like this is the first prototype, and the first game was the proper release, while, surprisingly, it's the other way around. I can understand the possible reasons for why it happened, but they don't change that I simply feel disappointed about Sylvio 2.
If you've never played the original game - give it a go and if you want more, definitely play Sylvio 2, just don't expect it to be a worthy sequel. If you just want so ghost story spooky horror and can ignore ugly visuals, you might actually enjoy Sylvio 2 as well, so feel free to give it a go.

Absolutely terrible.  Everything that made the original game feel unique and interesting has been stripped down to a boring cycle of walking to glowing orbs, waiting for a clip to play [you don't even actually use your mic to record voices, they just automatically happen when you stare at the orb] and either walk to the next orb that popped up or do the same scan minigame from the original.  The big "addition" to this sequel is videos you can scan through, but they are much, much worse than pure audio for a few reasons.  First, most of them are actually just audio tracks you're trying to scan back and forth at different speeds to find voice snippets anyway, but instead of having the waveform in front of you so you can tell what parts to check, you just have to scan through the whole scene.  Secondly, the ghosts all over the videos are not scary or even interesting.  Actually seeing so many ghosts without any pressure is like a bad monster movie where they wave the terrible prop in front of the camera in broad daylight.  Finally, a lot of the notes you're trying to get from the video clips are just invisible silent tags that unlock without any indication of what you're supposed to have learned.
On to my biggest problem.  There is no potato gun, because there are no puzzles.  There are things that seem like they're puzzles, but they aren't.  You'll learn a 3 digit combination from a ghost, but when you go to the lock afterwards, you just click on it and it vanishes.  It's functionally the same whether you get the location for a key or just another floating orb you stare at until you learn the name of a ghost to interview.  Most of the areas are just apartments with bad wallpaper, and the overworld is a joke.  In the first game you spent a good portion of the first level fixing up a car and used it to explore the overworld.  In Sylvio 2, you just click on a boat, plug in some coordinates [a new set gets told to you by a ghost for no good reason every level] and click on a bed to skip the travel time.  The design of the overworld is an endless foggy ocean spotted with giant black coils of very unhealthy looking poop.  You climb on some poop heading for the floating glowing orb until you get teleported into another apartment with bad wallpaper.
The voice acting seems to be done by the same lady who was in the original game, and she does a fine job with what she was given.  There is barely any other voice acting in the game, again comparing poorly to the original which had the lengthy audio logs from the kid who was killing crows or whatever.  The story is terrible, mostly shuffling you along one too-obvious 'tragedy' to the next without any depth to the characters or situations presented, and the main character seems to instantly lose all interest in the ghosts she's interviewing the moment one of them bafflingly spits out another coordinate to feed into the boat's GPS.  I wish I could say it was all made up for by the completely stupid ending, but even that was too insubstantial to be interesting.
In summary, this game is a pale shadow of its excellent predecessor.  Sure it's less frustrating and confusing, but for all the wrong reasons.  Give me an interesting but flawed concept over a laser focused snorefest any day.

Sylvio 2 is an odd duck when it comes to video game sequels, its common for the sequels in this medium to be improvements in pretty much all respects. Sylvio 2 is an improvement to 1 in some ways, but in other’s it’s a bit shaky.
Sylvio 2 is much more of a pure adventure game this time around, gone are the spud gun, malevolent shadows, and awkward platforming of the first game. It makes for more of a linear experience, especially because all ghost phenomena is indicated by orbs of light now that guide you to them, but the ghost gadget mechanics have been improved on with the addition of the video camera, which adds even greater creepy atmosphere to the game. And said atmosphere as just as great as the first game, with you now exploring abandoned apartment buildings and the like. The soundtrack also maintain the first’s quality.
The overworld this time is a bunch of islands in a huge lake that you navigate by boat. This honestly feels like padding, especially because you can skip the long travel times by sleeping in the nearby bed in the ship’s bridge. The islands tend to either have the subterranean buildings you to need to go to progress, strange symbols you can collect, and bodies that grant you keys that gives you access to doors in the ballroom area. I think it would have been stronger to have the game be set in a singular building, but that would probably complicate the ending. And let me tell you about the ending…
The ending is one of the most torn I felt with a videogame ending in a while, because while on one hand it’s a huge jarring genre shift with very little foreshadowing from either game to the point it feels like its almost a joke, it actually gives you a good explanation of what was going on in both games when there really wasn’t a clear definitive answer. It’s also ridiculously conclusive.
Ultimately Sylvio 2 is still a flawed game like its predecessor. Its ghost hunting mechanics are great and I’d like to see more like it in other games, but the ending and some of the execution (Namely how the ghosts' narratives could have been stronger) kind of bring it down. It’s still a really nice atmospheric horror game worth playing though.

Sylvio 2 changed up the gameplay from the first game much more than I had expected. The overall map design and transitions between locations/areas just sometimes don't make sense. I sometimes get the feeling that there are cut-scenes missing.
However the ghost recording videos look cool and the performance of the game is great. It will probably run fine on most integrated GPU's.
The game itself works fine, but some bugs remain related to the settings as of now (resolution detection, vsync and quality). The issues can be worked around, but will for sure annoy people.
I think basically everyone who liked the first Sylvio game, most likely will enjoy this game too. But there will be polarizing opinions about if the changes made to the games formula, are for the better or worse. I kinda miss the platforming, weird combat and obscure puzzles. But maybe I'm just being nostalgic, because those things also frustrated me the most about the first game. Anyway I enjoyed Sylvio 2, has an even better spookier atmosphere than the first game.
Note: I played a full playthrough of a pre-release build (I'm one of the Patreon backers), and a partial playthrough of the released game.

The tubular design is an innovative and interesting if risky design choice. In order to get away with disorientating gamers with a quirky interface it really ought to have been first order of business to offset this with superlative controls. No cigar. Controls  ought to have been remappable and user friendly from the outset. Who in their right mind hard maps the movement control to the arrow keys so that right handed players have to discard the mouse to use them? Mouse camera control is a miserable experience. The UI is an absolute nightmare. With so few buildings what the hell is the point of a rotating menu? Just open up a menu and click or better still just a row of small icons at the bottom of the screen. The ever present build queue menu is vast and takes up way too much screen real estate expecially when trying to move with your mouse can so easily open the wholly unnecessary and clunky rotating build choices. Why no indicator as to where buildings have been plopped so they can be laid out accurately?   As it currently stands it is a clunky uninntuitive nausea inducing mess. There's undoubtedly a good game buried under this abysmal UI, and I'm sure its possible to acclimatise, but life's too short and I simply can't be bothered to overcome such unneccessary irritations in a game whose quirky design should have made ironing out these issues a top priority

If you played the first game in the series, you probably know it was considered a flawed gem. Sadly Sylvio 2 continues this trend.
So the core mechanic is the use of EVP - you have a machine that allows you to 'decode' messages from the dead. And you are an investigator in this phenomena. The controls for this machine in game are not the most intuitive, and the game presents little in the way of tutorials or hand holding. However it does lead to linnear follow the dots decoding messages.
The open world exploration has been 'upgraded' as well. You now have a boat and a navigation computer that you use to navigate between islands.. And the islands all like giant floating poos. This part of the game is actually pretty boring in all honesty and I could see this as being a deal breaker for some. At least there is bunik to sleep on so you don't have to travel in realtime.  Maybe for part 3 we culd have a jetpack instead?
Maybe I have not played far enough in, but the combat also seems to have been removed. As that was not very well done in the first, this may be a good thing.
So if you like genuine indy horror games that rely on decent atmosphere, okay story telling, and decent audio then this is worth the low asking cost. But it is not an outlast, resident eveil or amneisia killer by any means, If you don't like slow paced then do not buy this. Also if you are hearing impaired, this game relies heavily on audio cues so be warned.

Honestly, a pretty ambitious game. Developer obviously tried some things that are really big, but they just don't work as well as a player would like. Does fall flat in a couple of areas - async multiplayer is very shallow. Without any adaptation from the enemy, it feels like you're playing against a simple AI that falters the first time their build plan is interrupted. With no fog of war and no control of you're iubes, there's no need to really stray from managing your base. the view in game rarely leaves my base. And since the progression of units and tech is pretty limited, there's not much in the way of countering opponents strategy - its all about pumping out maximum food to make maximum units.
Cool map concepts keep games fresh. The units AI is pretty good. Visuals are fun even if combat is underwhelming. The multiplayer king of the hill concept is really awesome, and can only be done with async multiplayer which is somewhat hollow in an RTS by its very nature.
Overall would recommend at a lower price point to at least experience some awesome ideas, even if implementation isn't as compelling as it could be. It feels like developers bit off more than they can chew. Love the ideas & would love to see more.
I was not provided a key or compensated for this review.

I was reserving my review until the planet update came out so here we go…
More than a simple update, what we had here is a whole new start for the game, under the lead of a new team leader, and I must say that it definitely took a step in the right direction.
Before this update/relaunch, what you had was more a sandbox than an actual game. It really looked promising as the building mechanics were very interesting and game many creative possibilities.
Now, they have introduced these mechanics inside a multiplayer environment where factions, wars, siege and territorial domination are involved and I must say that it is already very interesting.
Don’t get me wrong, as it is now, the whole thing is no more than a preliminary draft of what we will have in several months, there some bugs and many fundamental gameplay mechanisms still have to be implemented/changed but it is already very fun.
It is also clear that the team is very active. Not only that, but it also listens to the community and actually answer in the forums, this is very encouraging.
So, to sum up, this is still not a polished and flawless game, don’t expect this, but there is a huge potential and I believe that the development will be very fast paced form now on.

In my opinion this game is pretty amazing as it is. The game engine itself is built by keen software, which is a lot more than most indie companies even try to do. The engine itself is what takes the most time in almost any game’s development process. The only other indie company I know of that makes its own engine is tale worlds.  Look at games like Ark Survivor Evolved which rake in huge profits and then demand more money for additional content before the game is even finished and it’s ran off of an already built engine for game designing. This game is still being updated and produced without requests for additional funds and the content is great. Yeah, it takes time for them to make the updates but if you knew anything about game design you’d realize that content in a game this detailed is time and labor extensive. I’m an aspiring game designer myself so I’ve learned to appreciate just how much work goes into these games and the fact that this game has one of the best physics engines I’ve seen for a game and some of the nicest graphics for an indie game based on its own engine I’ve nothing to complain about. Yeah, it has bugs but so does every early access game in existence because guess what we’re paying to alpha test the game! It’s not like it’s a finished product slapped with a full price tag and told that it will work 100%. Triple A titles do this to us all the time and when it has bugs they patch them after release and you’ve already dropped 60-80 bucks on it! Just look at Rome 2 total war, Battlefield 4 and almost any other triple A company’s games when they come out fresh from the cooker. Let's start by saying this right now. "If you do not have the patience to play through the game, even through it's tutorial mode story campaign, then you shouldn't waist your money on this game. I'd wait for patches on the AI difficulty to be MUCH easier before buying this game. Even look up some gameplay somewhere before buying it. Hell, wait for a price drop. I don’t care. Certainly not worth a huge chunk, especially if you’re paying with Canadian currency..."
Now then. Honestly, this game had a lot of people hyped up for it early this year, I myself included. I mean, look at this game. It's a Good Looking Next Gen One Piece Fighting Game. But, it didn't get the best reception with its delay, even leaving a lot of people in the dark, questioning how controller support could be messed in such a way. Months rolled by, people got very salty for being divided more and more, day after day, from the console versions getting more attention. But, it's finally here now, and the PC master race can finally try to catch up to those that got the game on the original release date. Now that I finally got my hands on this game, and playing it for a few days since then, let’s see what I think about it.
The story mode is the only mode you can play at the start, and it actually does a decent job of telling you how most of the game’s mechanics work so you will be ready for actual fighting. It does its job, but it’s not a good job, mostly because the interface confused me because I couldn’t see or remember what button did which. It’s especially bad here because the game doesn’t really punish you or reward you with doing the actions or moves it displays for you. It just moves you forward on its own, and expects you to be ready. That’s bad for new players especially, because I even see people playing this game, complaining about spam... And, having no idea how to “block.” The game play mechanics here feel rock soled, and even do as you’d expect them to, but there are times where tracking just says, “Oops! Sorry pal! I didn’t mean to turn your attack into a 180! I’ll try a 120 next time! HAHA!!”
But, the tutorial campaign is fairly decent, with enough length to test your initial patience, and once you complete it, you can finally get the other modes such as: Free Battle, Online, Flag Battle, and Wanted. I really have to say this here too, I hate the training mode in Free Battle, because of a very outdated set up. I know, It’s an anime fighting game, it’s meant to be a novelty and archaic in design, but it’s 2016. You should have more options than this. Even Smash Bros has more options than this. There’s no legit way to train yourself into learning the game’s moves and combos, and other techniques that it really doesn’t bother to teach you. That too I also hate, because it’s a very dated design philosophy.
Now we’re in the meat here with Wanted mode for single players. This is where a lot of the complaints for Burning Blood comes from. This mode lets you play as chosen characters, or a preset team of characters to complete an objective against another set team. These missions can be easy, depending on what you choose, but they can really, REALLY spike up in difficulty because of the AI fallowing you very precisely, or preforming moves that you never learned to do through the tutorial, to the AI having insane stat buffs like more damage and health, and even depending on the conditions (If they aren’t very vague to you when you read it), It can be unforgiving to the point that it’s unfair... I’m looking at you Kuma... And the difficulty also extends to Flag Battle’s computer AI battles as well, as they have a very high chance to get buffs that ONE SHOT you.
You do however, get handsomely rewarded for beating them. For beating Wanted Battles, and for winning Online Matches, you got a decent chunk of Berri, the in game currency, to buy more characters to play as, and buy more support characters to use alongside them. That in my opinion is a plus, because it kind of helps you feel like you’re progressing, but a big minus as well as you don’t get use it for anything else, which is a crying shame. Most other, more popular fighting games let you earn a lot to unlock a ton of content. I’m just disappointed that it’s not in THIS game.
My biggest, most personal complaint about this game, is that the online modes feel very empty. It might be because it’s new, since it’s only been a few months now since it’s console release, and only a few days since the PC release. The net code is pretty much decent, but it’s not great, so I’d wait on that too before spending money.
Final words? I’d recommend it just to have it if you’re a fan of One Piece, and you want something to really pass the time with, with friends or neighbors, your nakama, your yankos, or even your Ivankovs. Just try not to get too competitive if you simply don’t have the patience to wait for people to mess up before you do anything.

I really wish Steam would release a "Neutral" rating sometimes, because this game is both a wonderful fan-service to the anime, and yet it is quite possibly one of the most fustrating online experience I've ever had.
The game plays like most similar titles where you have a 360 stage to duke it out (think Ninja Storm 4). Experiencing the game as your favorite One Piece character, mashing out their flashy moves and watching them beat their long time rivals is a thrill any One Piece fan will appreciate.
For a game locked at 1080p @ 30fps, if performs decently, though not ideal or even acceptable to some PC gamers. The port feels "okay" but the lack of any real graphical options is something to take note of. It feels like the publisher just didn't bother to put in any real effort to maximising the game for the PC.
The first few hours of single-player game play is very much enjoyable and the addition of the "Wanted Versus" helps give the game a little more longevity in that aspect. The "campaign" mode, if you could call it that, starts out nice and easy, but will ramp up the AI difficulty (and I really mean, RAMP UP) exponentially after about 2-3 hours in. If you aren't fond of fighting games where blocking & side stepping are crucial to the gameplay, then avoid the gamer rage by avoiding the game for now.
The meat of the game to me was the Ranked Online part of it. It is for the sole reason that I made my decision to purchase this. The netcode for it is actually pretty decent, it handles the overall matches well for most part and doesn't just drop you out of a match when the connections starts to stutter.
HOWEVER, the player base is still really small and the match making system is just terrible at time. Being matched with a more experienced or higher ranked player I can handle, what I couldn't handle was that the game doesn't care if you're match with someone with over 500ms ping relative to your location. This causes extreme, EXTREME input lag for more than 50% of the matches I've played.
Some combos are nearly impossible to pull off, inputs do not register for over 0.5s, side stepping is a 50-50 chance and button mashing doesn't seem to do your default attack combo sets sometimes.
I'll still keep playing because I am a huge One Piece fan, and also cause I want to feel like I got my moneys' worth since I can't refund it anymore.

I've 'completed' this 'game' 3 times now, and each time I discover something new, something that's better, something that I did 'wrong' before. Always learning, never mastered. If I had to compare this to something it would be minecraft. Remember when you first mined that iron ore and smelted it? But, thats where it ended. Way back then i thought, "I wonder if i could automate this so I could sit back and not have to mine anymore". Obviously, this could never happen. Then came Factorio. You want to automate mining ore? You better or you won't survive the next 100 hours of you grinding for that one rocket launch. You will automate everything you can, because if you don't, you'll never reach the pure ectasy that this game delivers when everything connects and flows like a metal river. That is what is so good about this game. That moment. That moment when you see your construction come to life. It breathes, and pumps, and tingles, and wriggles out. This game is a national treasure.
TL;DR: Buy it, you'll lose sleep, no regrets

Now it's been sometime, I'm posting a new review in place of the old one back when it was still in Early Access.
I've been very interested in this project since it first appeared on Greenlight and have been following it's progress. It's a turn-based zombie survival game where you manage a shelter and have to deal with many harsh situations that may happen based on the survivors you have as not every survivor is as steady minded as you could imagine. Some look for love in the wrong place, others are mentally disturbed (due to what has happened and the situation you are in now) and you can even recruit animals to the shelter which give their own moral bonus, but also eat into your food supplies too.
All the characters in the shelter have their own personalities. Some can even point out new locations where there would be a large storage of weapons or food based on their life before the disaster struck. Some can be very likable like the Loving and helpful Renee or others will be blunt and emotionless like the officer, Vic. There are multiple endings and hours of replayability with the many different dialog trees. I have not yet completed the game, but I have gotten far into it and built everything in the shelter, of course trying to gain enough food and fuel on each excersion to keep moral up becomes difficult with more people.
Now I'm not going to say the game is perfect. There are still bugs in the game and issues where bodies will share the same square, however the dev team are still working on this game and want to make it the best experience for all of those like me who are craving for a zombie survival game where you are responsible for the survivors and all the survivors have varied and interesting personalities.
If you are still uncertain, I'd suggest playing the demo to get a good feel for it. It has that wonderfully nostalgic feel of Fallout 1 + 2 as well as Wasteland.

I'm only about an hour in so far but MAN is this good! If you've never heard of Sylvio, I strongly suggest you play the first one as it is an EXTREMELY underrated game. I played the first one on PS4 early this year and just absolutely fell in love with it. I bought Sylvio 2 as soon as it went up for sale this morning and I played it a little bit this evening.
The graphics are not fantastic or anything but they work really, really well with this type of game. The fun in Sylvio is basically walking around with a recorder and recording voices in the static. Ghosts and whatnot. Then, playing those recordings at 6 different speeds (forward, fast forward, slow forward, backwards, slow backwards, fast backwards) to pick out hidden voices that will give you story info and clues. Using the information and clues you move the story forward, etc. In Sylvio 2 you do the exact same thing only last time it was just audio...this time it's audio and video. You record ghosts and play back the video. It's actually quite addictive.
The game has many locations but I've only been to three so far (I just arrived at my third location). This game has a similar open world structure to the last game only this time you are on a boat and each location is an island that you visit by punching coordinates into a computer.
I'll update more when I've played more of the game but so far, this is definitely an improvement but more of the same at the same time. I couldn't be happier with it so far. Do yourself a favor, if you are thinking about checking this one out, I do highly recommend the first one. Maybe watch some videos online to see if it's something you would be interested in. Medieval Engineers, although in early access and only being on the shelf for less than a year has enough content to keep me entertained for hours, if it's putting on a podcast and building a huge castle for 3 hours, or downloading other castles from the Steam Workshop and tearing them down with custom build catapults and trebuchets,
or maybe trying to survive wave after wave of barbarain attacks at night, and rebuilding in the day. I still have fun doing it.
It's core elements would be:
*Build as much as your computer can handle
*Epic, softbody destruction
*Old, over looked genre setting (atleast for a sandbox building game)
*Semi regular updates adding bug fixes, new blocks, ect.
*Workshop support
*Mod support (mods can also be found from the Steam workshop
*Major replayability (I come back to this game pretty regularly and when I do it's for hours on end.)
*Massive planets you can walk around completley with out loading screens (granted it would probably take you a few hours.)
*Different factions to compete with friends
*Mutiplayer, allthough in the interest of full disclosure it is fairly buggy and can end with the game crashing.
Yes, this game is glitchy, buggy, it may crash for placing a block wrong, but playing it since it came out I have seen more and more of those bugs go away and the physics engine get more stable.
But this game has been out less than a year and is still in early access, yet it has more content and is better crafted than most the early access games on Steam combined.
If you're like me who can't get enough of sandbox building games and can look over a few bugs for the meantime then you'll love this.

I've been playing Medeival Engineers since day 1 of launch, I've been following and playing Keen House Software's other game Space Engineers since the Alpha stage, that means I've had plenty of time to play and get to know the games of KHS, and from what I've seen is massive dedication to the games, (One of the first devs to bring weekly updates every Thursday) listening to the players and changing the game to suit everybody, (planets were never going to be a thing in SE or ME, yet the devs managed to put them in after massive fan feedback.)

(edited 25/07/17) I was in the kickstarter for this game (July 2012, it hit twice it's goal), getting the occasional update. Every time, Id read the reviews, is it worth playing yet? Answer: no. But I get an update saying "massive updates and patches", so decide to give it a go.
Is it ready yet? No. But the devs have called it a day, with no more updates ever, so it's time to play. It's been another 2 years since I last tried it, and again, I see massive improvements from the last update, but it's still incomplete, 5 years on.
128 hours of play and I can say it's a good game, but it's many, many faults make it still a poor attempt.
So ambitious, it tried to be so many things and fell short on all of them. So many unaddressed problems, so many remaining bugs, so many crashes, so many poor design choices.
But if you can look past all that, if you have the fortitude to navigate the clunky interface, if you remember to save many, many times, if you grind until you take a break to watch ninja warrior because that's slightly more entertaining, it does have a nice storyline, it's got interesting characters, it's got plothooks, it's got arcing ramifications for branching choices and it's very pretty (the music, even after 128 hours, I still didn't get sick of).
It had so much going for it, but it was a huge ask. I don't know why they gave up, one or two more updates would make this a great game (money? time? boredom?)
THE BAD
It looks great, but it's got limited camera control.
The menus are physically seperated and you need to move your character to different locations to access all your information.
The NPCs wander freely about the base, making it difficult and time-consuming to track them down when you want to talk to them (I ended up with 30 of them, many wearing identical armor)
I had a murder on the base by an NPC, I had 3 people give a brief statement, then I accused and sentenced someone. IT WAS NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN. (I had 2 cops on the base, and no-one even bothered to examine the body or crime scene).
It crashes. Alot. The ending (which was pretty weak) crashed many times. I don't even know if I saw the final 'ending' because it kept crashing (I'll just presume I did.)
Time to get to the good stuff. You need a fair few NPCs to really get the game going, but then you get bogged down on the minute (such as having to click on every item seperately to get it into the car trunk).
Speaking of the car trunk, it can only hold 200#, even after modifications. And no-one knows how to design a horse saddlebag.
No replayability. You could play in a different way, but the overall game doesn't change and the length of time it takes isn't worth it.
THE GOOD
When the NPCs start to interact with each other, it's great.
Some of them are a little stereotypical, but at least they're colorful.
It's like a zombie 'UFO: Enemy Unknown', but they didn't get around to adapting all the useful features.
It's like a 'Baldur's Gate', but the character development peters out halfway through.
One more update could make this game great, but I'd rather hold my breath for HL3.

I've decided to write a review for this game to try to curb down the negativity around this game. I've read many reviews that claim this game is awful, unplayable, so full of bugs that it's not enjoyable and after playing 75 hours of it, I will have to disagree. I'm not saying it's a perfect game or doesn't need more work and polishing but it is still a pretty damn fine game on it's own.
Now as far as bugs go, I've encontered a few but not nearly as much as other people claim there are. There was one instance of a zombie disapearing and being unattackable while still existing on the map and attacking you on it's turn and every once in a while the game crashed. But other than that I've been pretty much bug free.
What I enjoy about this game? An intresting story/setup where being the leader of your group of survivor of a zombie apocalypse isn't just about mowing through wave after wave of zombies and calling it a day. Taking care of your shelter and your people can be just as fascinating. The combat while not super deep has some interesting layers with positioning, noise making and panic mixed in the simple but effective turn based combat. There are some nice RPG elements added that give some replay value and I absolutely love how you can influence certain events/characters simply by the way you treat them. I also enjoy looking at the shelter evolve with time both from upgrading it but also from smaller things (food in the pantry for example) and wish there was even more of that in the game.
My biggest complaint with the game as it stands is how unbalanced it is. Maybe I've just played that type of game too often or maybe I'm too "efficient" for what the devs intended but after only 30 days in game all shelter upgrades were built. At day 45 I've discovered what looked like most of the locations. And because of the perks I took I had enough fuel and food to not have to care about it for another 3 months, I had enough antibiotics to be able to shower my people with them, my fence was nearly indestructible and I had enough weapons and armor to have everyone equipped, even characters I knew full well I would never take in the field and even then I was throwing weapons and armor in the recycler despite not really needing any more parts. My overall morale was so high that I think people were happier than before the zombie apocalypse. And now I had to just pass each day until sopmething else happened. And it became a bit boring at that. So I decided to make another game where I would put myself restrictions on how much and how fast I would do things. Every day I would only go on one outing for one location only. Doesn't matter that my inventory is not even half full, doesn't matter that I'm still at full health. It sure made the game go at a slower pace and makes it longer before I'm done with everything but I find it disapointing that I have to put myself these restrictions instead of the game making me take hard decisions on what I need now and what will have to wait later. (think X-Com for instance)
I also have other small issues with some desing decisions (like the inability to advance to clock until after everybody is done working) but again overall it is an enjoyable game with a good concept that I hope the devs will keep polishing and making better with time.
Oh and for replay value I hope one day they come up with different maps so that people who played the game don't already know where everybody is or where important things are.

After following the development of this game years before it's actual release, I have to say this is probably the most disappointing zombie game I have ever genuinely followed. And I don't just mean that from a "it's not what I expected because I bought into the hype like an idiot" point of view - this game is filled to the brim with content "spread too thin" and is incredibly lacking in depth of any kind.
~~~
It's one thing to have a great idea, concept and writer.
It's another thing to not actually deliver a good game to go with any of that. It is also another thing to wittingly cut your development roadmap short with what you once called "placeholders" now becoming the final product.
I wanted this game to turn out as amazing as the portrait painted for it. I really did. I hyped this game to a lot of people. The developers recieved plenty of constructive feedback, and for the most part, seemed hopeful in fixing these issues as they promised to eventually do over time. I played and re-played the game throughout it's early access on steam. I gave it a positive review, talking about everything I loved about it.
It was something that had so much potential, and so much of that was wasted in possibly the laziest release of all time.
I thought it was a mistake when I looked at the store page and saw that it was out of early access, but apparently, it wasn't.
You see, the game was nowhere near the true "final release" stage when they started saying it was going to leave early access. Neither the much-needed polish or balance/bug fixes had happened at that point. There was a long laundry list of stuff that was yet to be changed or added. However we just ate up every statement that more was to come with some kind of huge update they were going to put out with the full game.
As expected, we all held our breath. Then the game released. The "massive update" was really just some UI features and terribly minor bug fixes. So much stuff was still very, very wrong with the game.
Pathfinding, which has been a "rough draft" and improperly done since long before the
is still a complete disaster, and it doesn't take too many hours of the game to see how poorly the movement system runs in practice.
There are noteable spelling and grammar mistakes in the UI and dialogue that are still there to this date, and almost all of them were reported over a year ago.
Notice how the NPCs at home base are just kind of there and don't actually seem to be doing anything rather than walking around their token job area? Animations for working, emotion and social interaction were in the works - but apparently dropped just to rush the release.
, certain developers and staff couldn't take the criticism and decided to flag a few negative reviews they felt weren't "honest" enough and then threw fits on social media for the backlash. But that's none of my business.
They removed an ending [Spoiler: The Cure] entirely on the grounds of "It would have been too much work to get it going," despite having the characters involved extremely hype the idea to you as an achievable goal already in the game. And then they never bothered to redo the NPCs involved in the ending quest, so even today a player can accidentally dedicate way too much to this super-disappointing questline for no actual reward.
While we are at it - they also took 'balance' as a reason to write it off, which doesn't make sense since it was originally an ending, and tried to back that one up with "well what if it wasn't an ending". You and I both know that an ending was your original intention. That objective was widely regarded as an ending well before it was scrapped. So using "it was never intended to be an ending" as an excuse was extremely sleazy. I wouldn't have bothered including this as part of the review had you just fessed up to not wanting to dedicate time to it (or had a change in heart for the story lore).
And what did the game do to off it in final? Replaced some text. Threw in an apology from one of the NPCs for getting hopes up. I have several science buffs (including the immunologist) and medical professionals who showed interest in the subject of a cure, and we were basically told that a paragraph of text somehow made up for one of the most anti-climatic story checkpoints in gaming history, all because the developers didn't want to do the work to get it working properly (or add in a scene where the cure fails and all hope is lost) for that matter.
I digress, it's not my game and the developers don't owe me anything for playing it, but it just shows how you gave up on making it great as everybody involved once desired.
The game still looks unpolished. It still plays and feels like an unfinished game. The animations lack depth. Enemies with over-used models. The vast majority of NPCs you interact with don't even have names, and are stuck with "Looter" and "Survivor" as if the devs planned on going in there later and changing them.
When you see early screens of the game, you see people sitting in stools in the lab, tinkering with machines, while a character flings her arms up in the air while raging about somebody being a problem. You see characters moving their arms as they talk, showing emotion. You see life. You see a game where you can show what's happening to a friend and they will understand what is going on in the scene without you explaining it.
That's not the game now at all. Everything is lifeless. Sloppy idle animations which never made it past said adjective. Everything relating to emotion and conditions was reduced to text and labels. Even in the very minor "live-action" parts of the turn based game, it still feels like it's turn-based because everything is still attatched to their simplistic animations and use of the tile system.
I'm going to summarize this to boot.
Obvious pros and cons:
+Good writing.
+Good story.
+Awesome, in-depth characters.
-turn-based gameplay is clunky
-Lack of polish
-Broken story events that don't recognize a previous descision when it should
-Lack of attention to various characters (Jodie Hopkins as an example)
-Extremely empty list of events in the time before the endgame
Borderline points:
=Long storyline (but didn't have the intensity to match the hours)
=Mediocre amount of weapons and content to use outside of characters
=questlines can have a lot of detail and options, but on the flipside, some don't
There is such a heaviness to your home group characters ingame - every quest, everything you build and do is built off of your cast of characters. There are no "filler generics", every survivor in your camp is unique and written individually, and all contribute something different. Which makes me hate that less than half of them have more than 3 or 4 "story events" involving them, because the ones that are actually fleshed out can contribute so much to the story while others add so little.
This game is the poster child for products that spread themselves too thin. I understand that exit-stage early access titles are almost never as good as they made them hyped at the start of development, but this is well beyond "just scrapped ideas". While I found the characters and choices entertaining, literally everything else felt extremely under-developed and nowhere near completion.
That's my blunt review for now.

While this game has a few imperfections I find it to be one of the best games I've bought. It's refreshing to play a game that doesn't star yet another white guy with ambiguous motives. You play an every man trying to rescue his lady friend and defeat a flamboyant and merciless guy hellbent on destruction. I think one of my favorite aspects of this game is that, while the story could have been nothing due to the game mechanics being fun and tight feeling, it actually paints a really compelling picture. You can tell via the voice acting and writing that Marlow really cares about his significant other and vice versa. Other larger budget games often attempt to make you feel something when it comes to romantic interests/sub plots but this is one of the first that actually had me invested in their relationship.
The game mechanics are great. I really enjoy the fixed camera despite it being something that I haven't liked since Silent Hill 2 and it allows you to use your other thumbstick (I use a PS3 controller) to roll and evade making the combat even more refreshing. The difficulty also doesn't let up despite your character getting better weapons as you progress which keeps the game fresh and non-repetitive.
I think the only negative mark I've found so far is that due to the fixed camera, there will be times where you make a move the game doesn't fully anticipate and the camera will float into space, causing you to restart from your last checkpoint. This has only happened twice and I can see how it could happen based on what actions I was trying to accomplish. Aside from that minor issue, the game is solid and it cost me less than a croissant.

This is one of those heartbreaking games where you really, really want to like it.  I'm glad that I only paid a fraction of its cost, though.  That is to say, I paid a fraction for the bundle, and all of them seem to have just one flaw that wrecks the game - and TW3 is merely the least annoying.
The first one was a nice proof of concept: military simulator without any of this 'ballancing' garbage.  A Sherman is inferior to a Tiger, period.  But its age makes it clunky and somewhat dull.  TW2 was a vast improvement - except for pathing, which was lousy.  Because the missions are not timed, all the panzers who cannot cross the bridge at the German spawn point stay there until you get bored and turn off the game.  A flaw that makes it impossible to complete a mission?  Fail.
So there is TW3: Korea, which isnt bad.  It feels small, like the Korean conflict in Red Dragon - a handful of Korean tanks and a few platoons v. a similar American force - and if you win, their entire division retreats?  And the flaw in TW3 is that you can no longer select individual personell.  This is huge because that platoon of useless infantry could spare 3 guys to go man that 57mm and take out the imperialist tank - except it cant.  Unless there is some 'break formation' command I havent found - the interface isnt exactly intuitive, so it may well be.
So, yeah, 7 bucks for the bundle, which essentially translates to 7 bucks for TW3.  Its a fair price, wouldnt pay more, though.
