I wanted to like this game so much. There are just too many faults with it and after experiencing the game crash for no reason on my 3rd mission in the campaign, I'm definitely sure this game is bad.
For starters lets talk about the actual battle experience. There is nothing more pleasing to me than slugging it out over range with tanks/fixed guns. So satisfying watching the shells streak across the map. What is NOT pleasing is when a tank of mine decides its going to go it alone and run around in circles. That's not cool, I didn't order him to do that...
When I'm trying to get my infantry into a better position and the only formations are either 2 a breast or complete line formation. Really? Infantry can't be moved into more advantageous/different formations? Nevermind the fact that infantry organization is just plain stupid. Selecting a squad is a miserable experience, even getting them to go together is a challenge. If I select a squad to move to an area maybe 3 of them will go and 4 of them will hit the dirt and start crawling. Which brings up another issue. Why can't I tell my infantry to get up, hide, run, crawl, etc. Kind of annoying but  not as annoying as formations.
When setting up units before the battle starts its impossible to place them in defending positions correctly. Why can't I position my tank to face a certain direction? Why can't I place infantry on a hilltop inside the deployment zone? They're still in the deployment zone but forget being able to place them anywhere outside the main defensive barriers. Or even splitting them up! I started a defensive match where 3 units were located in one dugout and 4 units of the same infantry squad were in another dugout. I wasn't allowed to take them out of the dugouts without them being the same distance from each other as if they were in the original dugouts. This is hard to explain but it means no matter where I placed that squad the two groups were always at least 50 yards apart.
Then there are issues where the game seems to freeze for at least 3 seconds before humming along perfectly as if nothing happened. I'm not sure what causes the frame rate explosion but it usually only occurs once per match.
This game has the feel of being a 3D Close Combat set in Korea. It feels promising, but it falls severely short of its goal. I'm not sure if the developers are still working on this game, but if they are they really need to take another look at some of the fundamental flaws.

The third installment in the Heart’s Medicine series has finally came out as fans have waited in bated breath: Heart’s Medicine - Hospital Heat. Opening up to Little Creek Hospital on fire as we see a news reporter on the scene. Soon greeted with scenes where Connor is getting some kids out, also showing one of the important characters, Chance saving Sophia, and Allison coming in by helicopter. Building up to the point where just as she has an entry to the hospital, she is knocked through a hole. Leaving us on a cliffhanger and thoughts on what events led to the hospital catching on fire.
We start straight off from what the second game ended. Allison is still in her internship as we get to see more departments of the hospital. Where you had The Ward, Pharmacy, ER, Radiology, and Surgery departments in Time to Heal, you get new ones: Pediatrics, Pathology, Burn-Unit, Maternity Ward, Intensive Care, and Psychiatry. This also goes away from Allison needing to work her way up to a department and instead focusing on family, a love triangle, and revenge. Not only focusing on Allison’s problem with mother issues and seeing her teenage self but also the others. We even have a department solely focused on a flashback for a character we barely saw but has a role in explaining why things are happening in the hospital.
While I did say you do not need to play the first installment, as little is brought into the second game, I still stand by it. But you should play, or at least watch someone play it, the second installment Time to Heal. It not only starts right after the events that took place in the second game but also mentions a lot that happened. Even actions that did not seem would come back and bite someone does and you would not know the events why unless you see the story in Time to Heal. You will not get the whole story on why some things are being mentioned and some of the tension.

As with the previous installment, the gameplay helps drive the story. Getting a segment before and after with possibly something story related happening during your shift. Patients will have a steady flow, increasing in difficulty as you progress, as you need to correctly assign them and see what they need you do. Once you do, and queue up the item or click them for a specific action, Allison’s speed is integrated as she picks up the items and treats the patients. Depending on the item, which can need to be restocked, need two parts, or need time to be prepared, you will see there are levels of interaction. Some do not, but others will need you to do some touch input like doing a slider or a minigame. If you do these actions fast enough, you will get a quick time bonus for assigning, treatment (and if you chain, a chain bonus), and checkout. With the score based on how many hearts you score with your patients.
However, there are some new features they added. What came as a surprise is that the hearts over the patient’s head is determined on what they need rather than the set amount of hearts everyone had in the previous game. Some can have three hearts and it is super easy but then someone can come in with what seems like a million hearts and need a lot of help. This in turn makes the game easy and hard at the same time. It’s easy to get 3 stars this time around as some will be more impactful on your score than others. And with the more hearts coming in indicating that they need a lot of help less patients will come in. But this also means that it is harder later on.
It does make it more about time management for sure. To balance out you needing to constantly transfer the patients, they also added that a patient will need multiple treatments at one station. So keeping this in mind, going to having multiple people waiting on their treatments and waiting to be assigned can be stressful. Juggling a way to get all the quick bonuses, or just get to them before they start losing hearts, as you try to treat everyone else and get items is very stressful. It can even be more stressful with challenges. It is not as big of a deal unless you have certain ones. One of them being the challenge where you need to do a minigame to get a certain amount of hearts collectively. Where I remember it being slack and giving a couple extra in Time to Heal just in case you fail, in this one you have to get all of them correct. And while yes you do not need to quick treatment everyone to get three stars, it can still be stressful coming from how important it is to get golden hearts.
The items you can buy to make them wait longer or more patient becomes more important here. It might not seem like it, especially when you see it was not so much in the previous one, but you will find out. It can get brutal and you need the help you can get. Especially the item that sends a patient to gain hearts and be willing to wait.
The challenges also changed. Of course the story based ones will be different and the ones based on minigames need to be all perfect, but the challenge levels are different. Each department containing the same challenge for the most part. Instead of going for like a regular day that has a special condition, like someone helping you throughout, this one goes for predictability almost. Every level (some almost every) having: a janitor challenge where you need to clean up various spills (they do mix this up towards the end), a pure Oliver the guinea pig finding one instead of finding a lot of them during a shift like usual, one where your score deteriorates, a pure minigame one as you earn scores by how well you do as it throws minigames from that department at you left and right, and a Delicious Emily level where you serve customers in the hospital canteen. This is interesting to see this as it is different and seems new at first. But once you see that it is the same thing over and over it isn’t. It also does not help that you see that a fair amount of minigames act too slow that the maximum hearts you can get indicates.
The minigames are still my favorite. Keeping the level of interactivity the previous installment had as the minigames persist through the 10 shifts. Each having their distinct audio as you do it and different levels of difficulty. With a specific one being heartwarming as a rare surprise can happen. I do appreciate how no old minigames were used. And man, there is one minigame that has you adjusting hospital beds that they actually programmed to move outside of the minigame that I thought was cool. So if you change the position of one, you will see that it reflects what you did in the minigame once you get out of it.
What will happen after the hospital is burnt down? With a next installment promised, who knows what will happen!

Heart's Medicine - Hospital Heat is the 3rd game in the series.  It is a Time Management Game themed in a Soap Opera Hospital.  The gameplay is moving patients to different areas on the screen, and completing minigames to earn hearts.  Earn enough hearts in the level to advance, and complete challenges to earn gems.
The gameplay has not changed since the previous title on steam (Time to Heal) and is similar to the Diner Dash and Delicious games if you have played those games.  The gameplay is more challenging in this game of the series, but nothing drastic that will make most people notice.
Once again, the story is the shining star in this game.  The developers must have noticed that the 2nd game of the series got a lot of attention because of the story, so they again challenge the tear ducts on this one even more, and they do it from the start of the first act.
The gameplay again is nothing to brag about, but the story is what you are going to tell you friends about.  They might call you a filthy casual for playing this type of game, but you and I both know, the story is real and are looking forward to the next game in the series.
I would suggest playing the 2nd game of the series (Time to Heal) before this game as they are some slight references to it and is available on Steam.  The 1st game of the series is not available on steam at the time of this writing.
Achievement Quest: Easy 100% that can be done on 1 playthrough.  Earn all the Stars and All the Games and you should be fine.  Make sure to use the heart boosting stations early, so you don't have to replay levels.  The Vincent achievemnt can be a challenge.  I got it in the last act.

For the uninitiated, "Crazy Otto" circa 1981 holds a special place in arcade history as the game that would eventually become Ms. Pac-man after being acquired by Bally Midway.  When I first saw this appear on the upcoming releases list, I was floored.  After 35 years, the "prototype" version of Ms. Pac was going to be an actual product that I could purchase and play on Steam.  I couldn't have been more excited!
Unfortunately, "2016's Crazy Otto" as it's being called by developer Extend Mode isn't exactly the game I was hoping for.  Yes, there are striking similarities between their version and videos/gameplay of the original that can be found on YouTube and other streaming sites.  However, anyone going into this thinking they are getting the
Crazy Otto arcade ROM from decades gone by will likely be disappointed.
Fortunately though, that's where most of the negatives effectively end with this version.  2016's Crazy Otto is a very capable Ms. Pac-man clone that both looks and plays the part successfully.  The graphics, sounds, and gameplay all capture what the Pac series (and it's seemingly endless number of derivatives) felt like in the early-mid 80's.  Of course, this version of Crazy Otto changes the formula up quite a bit to provide a different experience and challenges.  These changes include "bonus fruits" appearing in different positions, power pellets replenishing, and character positions not resetting (game keeps going) when Otto dies.  These help to differentiate Otto from the plethora of other Pac-man clones both past and present.  They've even included a multiplayer mode that looks pretty fun and frantic, especially if you can gather up 7 other people (and controllers) to play locally.
Sadly, there doesn't appear to be an online MP component that would making sourcing people to fill those 7 spots all the more easier.  During my time with the game, the controls have also become a slight point of contention.  While mostly serviceable, they can feel a bit slippery and imprecise when playing with the analog stick on an Xbox 360 or Xbox One gamepad.  Support for the D-pad (which seems to have been omitted) tends to clear this up, but more recent official Pac-man titles seem to do a better job with analog stick inputs than Otto does.
Nonetheless, 2016's Crazy Otto does enough things right to warrant a purchase from both old-school and newer Pac-man fans alike.  While us classic arcade gamers are not quite getting the
Crazy Otto with this release, we're getting a game that borrows enough from that title, while adding quite a few interesting features that change the gameplay just enough to make it feel fresh and fun.

I've followed this game's development with great interest.  How is it, after more than 36 years, no one has ever tried a multiplayer PacMan?  Other than a "your turn, my turn" approach....
As this game demonstrates - there are enough characters, even if you just stick to the orginal arcade titles.... PacMan, Ms. PacMan, Baby PacMan, and PacMan Jr. - and the four ghosts....  There you go - 2 teams of 4.
Well, this obviously isn't PacMan.  It's Crazy Otto.... it's not even the Crazy Otto that became Ms. PacMan. It's its own thing.  PacMan is well... a PacMan - and he (along with the rest of his Pac family) fight Ghosts.  The old-school Crazy Otto was some sort of PacMan-like-thing with legs, and he (or it) fought ghost-like fruit-like thingies....  This game is all about Ducks and Dinosaurs.
The controls could use some tightening, and I really hope to see a Super Otto at some point, who can eat eat to unlock doors and grow to Super Sized and just eat through walls and whatnot...  Also vertical warp zones would be great (top to bottom).
Overall, I support and promote it because it takes a third-of-a-century old game and tries something brand new with it.

I bought this game on impulse thinking it was actually related to the Crazy Otto game that Ms.Pac-Man was originally, but don't let that fool you, this is NOT that game
This is a local/online take on Pac-Man where you can have up to eight players control the dinosaurs and the Otto family, up to six dinosaurs and four otto "people"
This game feels like a pure rip off of Pac-Man, (right down to the color of the first 4 dinosaurs matching the ghosts) but with varied mazes and a suprisingly interesting approach to the formula, this feels as though it's almost like an homage/rip off hybrid game
But don't get me wrong there are problems with the game, the main problem with the game is the controls and moving. I never imagined that a game maker could mess up WASD and somehow make the "input detection" feel a bit off or delayed, but this game somehow managed to mess that up, not to mention I payed 7 bucks for this game, and after playing the game for a few minutes, I feel as though a better price would be 3 dollars or 4 dollars at most
What was most disappointing tho is that you can't do a single player game as the "ghosts"
To conclude this review of Crazy Otto, the game is a fun and unique take on the Pac-Man formula, but has it's problems and it needs to be addressed/patched, just don't expect much for the single player content and note that multi-player is where this game shines. This game is overall an ok game, but I would NOT pay 7 dollars for the game and wait until the price goes down, and in genreal, expect something unique and nice, but nothing that's groundbreaking or drool generating

I was really excited when this game came out of Early Access- I like me some turn-based combat, and I'm a big fan of zombie survival as a setting.
Sadly it didn't really all come together, although it's not a complete flop- I think 4/10 is a fair score.
The game is spoiled by a combination of weird design choices and horrible bugs.
Design: The armour system makes no sense. No sense at all. If you wear the heaviest armour, you are literally invulnerable to all damage. You can wade into crowds of zombies, or even humans armed with assault rifles, with 0% possibility of death. Goodbye suspense. Also, boy o boy is the combat pretty boring if you're waiting for a dozen zombies to drag themselves over to you, and god forbid you start off with the wrong team-member in a crowded area- get ready to skip turns until it's the turn of the guy in front.
Bugs: I let a few patches go in and decided to give the game another chance. I spent about an hour clearing out a block of houses and looting. The last zombie on the map got stuck in a closed doorway to the room I was in, leaving my team stuck in a bedroom for eternity. This kind of thing is not uncommon. Also, if you aren't able to design a multi-floored building without having players stuck in combat with enemies on different floors that they can't see, stick to bungalows. (I cleared the entirety of the hospital one zombie at a time without ever being able to leave combat)
So yeah. Nice try, but pretty much ♥♥♥♥ed it up in the execution.

I followed this game through it's development and I'm more disappointed in people who created it than in the game itself. A good writer is just that - a good writer. Albeit even being merely good is not enough to create a complex branching CRPG script. On top of that  you also need a good artist, a few competent programmers and a talented game designer to pull everything together. This game have had none of the above, except a good writer. I doubt it could have passed as 'OK' even in late 90s-early 2000s.
After my 4th attempt ended in a similar 'I don't want to go through this anymore' fashion I uninstalled the game and decided to recap my experience with it, perhaps this will save someone couple o' dozen hours of their life.
To boot, the only character you can build from scratch is your protagonist and you can influence a handful of others, some for a bit, others a lot. The key word is 'influence'. All NPC characters have predetermined skill and stat progression preset and, once recruited, they will slowly levelup on a daily basis regardless of their state or occupation. E.G. on day 2 NPC will gain +1 medicine skill regardless if he spent all that day murdering zombified and hauling loot, unclogging crappers, being treated in the infirmary or not doing anything at all. WTF? I expected having a mishmash of different people and then shape them accordingly to their tendencies, personality and community's needs over the months that pass ingame. At this early point my immersion crashed so hard that it never recovered.
Every other system in the game works exactly the same.
1. The county is littered with parked cars whose owners didn't make it to them, you can drain their fuel, loot their luggage, but you have to repair a broken car at your base to be able to drive one.
2. I had to make a screenshot of the ingame map and use Paint to write notes on it to track places i've been to and looting progress, so yeah, no tooltips, no tracking, no useful dynamic in-game info so consult PDF manual before every fart if you don't want to shoot yourself in the foot.
3. You receive harsh morale and stat penalties if you don't make it back from your looting trip before nightfall because... well... because. Albeit threre is no ingame way to know how long it will take to get anywhere. You just go to the world map, walk in a straight line until your ingame clock shows that you're at a point of no return (count what time of the day it is yourself) and cut out a piece of paper of this length and use it as a ruler on my monitor. Feeling ridiculous yet? There's more
4. You didn't make in back in time. Boo-hoo. You are now fatigued for the whole day instead of being able to sleep a couple more hours. Day starts at 8 a.m. Get your♥♥♥♥♥out of the bed. NAOW. Okay, someone else can lead looting squad out, that nosy sheriff, for example, he's basically my lieutenant-in-command now, right? RIGHT? Nope. Uhm... why am I playing this, again?
I could keep going like this for hours, since there are no actual pros to counteract all theese shortcomings. I was hungry for a game like this, I eagerly waited and then convulsively barfed every time I tried to take a bite.
TL,DR Overall game design is plain HORRENDOUS, from combat to character progression. It's basically a linear zombie apocalypse novel that came to be as a game because of studio founder's 'making a good oldschool RPG can't be that hard' attitude. Has zero saving graces as a game. Wasted money.

If I were more willing to save time, I would have wrote a review condemning the game's length and amount of Monty Haul gameplay - because you have to scavenge SO MUCH in this game. Of course, this means going around to all the various places in Central Texas, dodging every zombie and murdering every looter to fill up your backpacks with as many ramen noodles and luxury items as you can carry. TIMES INFINITY. I wouldn't mind if there was more to interact with in the world (and there really needs to be more stuff to do to break up the monotony of scavenging all the time), because having to loot gets so damn boring after a while. I ended up skipping entire days towards the end of my playthrough because I was really sick and tired of having to go out and ♥♥♥♥ing pick up the groceries. And I hated not being able to delegate this task to the two or three people sitting around in the shelter once all the improvements were built. This mechanic, while it fits in really well with the world falling apart and even adds an 'Earth Abides'-style flavor to the proceedings, drove me up the ♥♥♥♥ing wall and onto the ceiling, down the wall on the other side of the room, and back. Like a really angry hamster determined to get out of his cage.
So why didn't I just quit the game and play something else?
Here's why - this game has some very, very interesting storytelling. When people talk about this game being a spiritual successor to games like Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines and Arcanum, they're talking about the solid storytelling. Brian Mitsoda (he worked on Bloodlines and Arcanum) and two other people made this game, and Brian did such a damn good job with the writing that I kept going despite hating what was going on with the game. And that storytelling is what held my interest throughout the entire game - I nearly could forgive all the monotonous scavenging if it meant more lovingly written, well-researched bits about how the world fell to the zombies, about astronauts losing their♥♥♥♥♥♥on the ISS, interactions between survivors, between militia groups, between the outside world and the little emotional ecosystem going on in the shelter. Those moments were beautiful and fun to experience.
I really had to fight to finish the game, both inside the game and outside. The scavenging took such a mental toll on me, but the storytelling kept me coming back for more. I don't doubt that this is going to be a cult classic among RPG enthusiasts, easily joining the ranks of the great RPG games that don't work all that great but have such wonders to show anyway.
You know what? To hell with it. I recommend this game, but  only if you bring several audiobooks or your backlog of podcasts to go along with it. If you don't, the monotony will drive you crazy (unless you're one of those mutants who runs around in a field to beat up slimes so you can grind your way to one-shotting Sephiroth at the end, in which case there is no hope for you). It starts out strong and ends strong, but everything in-between moves so damn slowly I nearly quit several times. You've been warned.

Though the game definitely has its shortcomings, it still provides an enjoyable experience; especially to any die-hard One Piece fan like myself.
The main problem revolves around the lackluster story mode where only one particular arc is explored through multiple perspectives. The idea seemed interesting at first, but once you played through the first two segments you've pretty much uncovered the whole story. The remaining three segments provide some new details, but they also re-tell and re-show everything you saw previously. Even the cutscenes. It ends up being a repetitive experience that, though entertaining at first, becomes bothersome eventually. It also doesn't help that you can beat it within 2-4 hours as well.
The game also has shortcomings when it comes to its difficulty. Most of the time my fate in a battle against the computer was decided on the first few seconds of a match, where the CP would knock out half (sometimes more) of my HP within a few seconds before I could even do anything. I eventually learned how to survive longer, but not without restarting every single match like a million times before I figured it out. The game has a fairly steep learning curve, to say the least.
Yet even though it can be difficult, it is also pretty easy to cheese with the right characters. I was able to dominate CP matches by spammhing certain moves with (2 years ago) Luffy and (Strong World) Ace over and over. I haven't played online much yet, but it's only a matter of time before players find these characters and move combos to spam against other people. The game definitely has balance issues.
Now even though it has all these shortcomings the game is still pretty enjoyable. The story, though repetitive, still showcases one of the most awesome arcs in the One Piece narrative. The art is pretty awesome; I found myself taking screenshots quite a bit, especially during the ultimate attacks. The gameplay elements, like haki and logia types, stay faithful to the rules of the One Piece universe. It was cool to find out that Luffy has a natural advantage against Enel, for example, or that Akainu beats out Ace. This may seem like a minor detail, but it was one that I very much appreciated. I enjoyed my experience with the game, even though I wished it could have been better.

------ Now on to the actual review ---
This game is probably one of my favorites. Artistically, this doesn't really try as hard to create something unique and deep as Braid or Hotline Miami, but just on many levels it was more satisfying to me personally. This game is not for everyone: it really is basically just an exploration game with very little additional gameplay. But unlike "To The Moon", the gameplay is not annoying, and I feel that this really took advantage of the interactive element of gameplay (whereas "To the Moon" may have worked just as well, if not better, as a movie).
One of the most interesting things is how the developer really involved the player in the narrative. In the beginning, you make choices about how you met your wife, and these choices come up later in dialog. Also, while some choices are made, the character acts on their own based on those story choices--in ways I wouldn't, but the fact that I had made key choices made me feel complicit and emotionally attached. Even beyond the intro, this carries through--what is said during dialog and small actions in solving the puzzles are referred to later. All these things create a real sense of presence.
They also accomplished this by using various techniques to keep players from backtracking and to keep them moving forward. For the radio, they made it very easy to respond while doing other things (I only wish I could use the map and radio at the same time), and there was a time limit on response. This caused me to fairly quickly make a dialog choice rather than carefully choosing one. It was awesome because the dialog became more natural and less strategic. In addition, they only allowed the game to be saved to the save file it was started with, preventing backtracking. Overall, this helped to make the story feel unique and special to me. Normally I would backtrack and reload to optimize the outcome, with this, my choices became my life. None of the choices were particularly significant in a global sense, but they really added to my feeling of ownership.
What I liked:
- I love the outdoors and hiking and have visited many national parks. They really got everything right. Furthermore, I love how the trails were branching and yet subtle and didn't always follow the map--just like in real life. Hiking really felt like hiking, so I was really amazed by this.
- Art: they have a really great minimalist art that really goes with the nature scene
- Adult plot elements. I don't mean violence or sex. I mean the dialog was consistent with an older person, and the themes of alcoholism (subtle--it was a constant undercurrent, but never really called out), abandonment of the wife, the discussion over messed up fire-lookouts, flirting, etc. This dialog really sounded like two adults.
- Interaction and feeling that I controlled the story (see above)
Things I didn't like
- The nature of the game meant that I was mostly alone, but they really went to extraordinary lengths to prevent direct human interaction. Sometimes that really didn't make any sense. I understand this is probably due to budget, so it's forgivable, but it was still very annoying.
Overall, I highly recommend this, especially to people who love nature and the outdoors (but are going to stay inside playing video games instead).

Air Forte is an educational game where you and up to three friends take control of little airplanes and collect floating tokens that match a specific requirement for each mission. The missions are either number missions (e.g. collect tokens showing multiples of 3), word type missions (e.g. collect all the verbs) or flag missions (e.g. collect all the European flags). The main story is framed as a children’s comic-book with crazy jungle characters and a flying ace hippopotamus. Along with the surf-themed music the whole package is quite cute.
As with all games, Air Forte is not without its own flaws. Probably the most frustrating is the debatable answer to some of the missions. The number missions are quite clear however the choice to lump Central and North American countries under the category of “North America” or European and Scandinavian countries all as “Europe” can be a little confusing. Worse still are the word games. Some clever instances will get you thinking: boot is a verb and a noun. But it is not rare to find that you are one token short and there is no reasonable answer from the leftover possibilities. While I am willing to accept that maybe I’m not smart enough to win, I find issue with the fact that the rationale is never explained.  That is, the game is ‘educational’ in content, not by the fact that it actually educates the user about anything in particular.
The game itself has a story mode that is quite short and can be finished in a single sitting if you are determined. Play for any longer and you may find that the endearing soundtrack starts to get a bit tired.
Technically, the software works smoothly on the whole. Unfortunately, driving the software with the controller is not supported. Navigating the menus must all be done with the mouse but once the game is started, it supported my gamepad just fine. Another issue is that (as of v.1.53) Steam integration doesn’t work properly. If you haven’t read the discussion board posts, the steamwraper2.dll needs to be renamed to steamwrap2.dll for achievements to work properly.
Despite the problems with Air Forte the chipper presentation and overall feel-goodedness of the game does help it to rise above its own flaws. While the appeal will certainly be limited for adults, it didn’t stop me from sinking a number of hours in getting the achievements and even convincing my better half to join in a few rounds of co-op.

First of all, I received a free 3DMark steam key from the package of Inno 3D GTX1080. It activates both Steam and download version of 3DMark. So thanks to Inno 3D, I got free stuffs and that makes me pretty happy.
I don't have 3Dmark 11 so I cannot make comparison of those 2 version but as Futuremark suggests, 3Dmark is more reliable than version 11 you probably need only this version to benchmark your hardware.
3DMark contains several demo scenes which are pretty the same as game scenes but with less hardware bias and better utilization. Since it is only a benchmark tool, it doesn't have to be running smoothly on low end hardware. It doesn't use the technologies that mainly used in games which may reduce the GPU utilization or multi GPU configuration. The good thing is that the GPU performance it reflected is very close to the raw power of GPU. However the bad thing is that in games, there is an increasing possibility of results varied. For instance, in 3DMark, dual GPU config could probably reach 1.8X to 1.9X the performance of single GPU, however in games, you can only expect 1.6X to 1.7X, sometimes games even doesn't support multi GPU config.
Taking the benchmark tool aside, it has a stress test feature allowing you to test your hardware stability. If your hardware passes the stress test, you can expect it can handle daily use without any problems like  BSOD or GPU temperature issues.
At this time, 3DMark only support DX11 benchmark, Timespy(DX12) and VRMark are on the way here. I will update this review as they come out.

As of this writing, the Planets (more like Planet) update dropped, 0.3.1.
After nearly six months of hiatus, a lot of things have changed.
Under the management of Tim (deepflame), the company has, in my opinion, turned the entire game development around.
The game is moving to a sane patch schedule:
Every week: Alternating between bugfixes and new minor content (like blocks)
Every 6-7 Weeks: Minor feature release (like mechanical blocks)
Every 3 months: Major feature release (not sure what this entails, but probably on planets scale)
Now, on to the new features:
Planets:
- This is more like a single planet, but can be fully modded for any size or features, just like in Space Engineers.
- Contains ruins and other neat easter eggs.
- Yes, you can walk all the way around a planet!
Survival research system:
- Yes, survival is actually playable now. The default world is still creative, but survival does work. You can now gather resources, including rock on the road, and use them to build components to build blocks.
- You start out with nothing. You no longer get starter tools. Minimalist survival experts rejoice!
- Building increasingly more complex blocks requires advancing in the research system to unlock higher tiered blocks and tools.
Female Engineer:
- This may be concerning for some players, like "why spend time on a female engineer when there are more gameplay elements that should be worked on first?"
- In my opinion, having a female playable character in the vanilla game is important for gaining playerbase. People want to have a character that represents them. Gaining more playerbase is always good for a healthy game. People want to play as a character that they feel represents them. For example, I'd prefer a non-bearded model myself.
- Mods can handle this, and there are some already, but it's not the same as having the vanilla game support it. Many players only play a game for 30 minutes or so before they decide whether they like it or not. Having that choice up front, without having to learn the modding system, will help people feel more comfortable with the game.
Claim Blocks:
- You can now claim square areas with a claim block. This protects your area from unauthorized building and mining inside the claimed area. Note this does not protect against normal attacks.
- Taxes: You have to pay taxes (in the form of resources) to maintain the claim block and keep your area claimed.
Banners:
- This is, in my opinion, one of the most immersion providing features to this game. It's well known that in medieval times, banners of the Lord or King who owned an area were on display, and carried into battle. One common example is Cross of Saint George used during The Crusades. Now you can make your own banner and show off to enemies who you are before you destroy them!
World Map:
- This is my most favorite feature.
- The map shows you not only world features, such as mountains, trees, and roads; but also player constructed buildings and rough player location. The map updates dynamically based on player creations (but not voxel changes).
- The world map is automatically generated based on the height map used to construct the planet. This means planet modders don't have to do anything special to create a map, it will be created on its own.
Fast Travel:
- Used in conjunction with the map, this allows the player to quickly travel around the planet, subject to customizable limits (can also be turned off completely).
- Analogous to the Jump Drive in Space Engineers.
Contextual Menu:
- They are still a work in progress, but they are vastly improved over the old clunky interface.
There are so many more features and fixes.
As for function:
- Multiplayer has improved quite a bit, and at least for servers with 16 players or less, is actually playable.
- Yes there are bugs, but they are working quickly to stomp them out now.
- UI is still clunky in some places (like inventory), but more improvements are coming.
- There are issues placing blocks, particularly when trying to aim them to place.
Summary:
- Has the game improved? Tremendously.
- Is it perfectly playable? Of course not, it's still alpha. That said, it's
playable than before.
If you are concerned about EA games and aren't impressed with what you've seen so far (why?), then hold back and wait for a few more updates.
However if you are as excited as I am about where this game is going, and what is in the game
, then pick it up!
Under Tim's leadership, this is really turning out to be a fantastic game. I hope Space Engineers gets the same love and guidance as Medieval Engineers is now getting.

Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! is a highly addictive game with great cartoon-ish graphics, a nice soundtrack and the ability to progress.
There is a bit of waiting around to be done and I understand people comparing it to a mobile game. You click on your potatoes to send them on a job, wait a few seconds till they finish then send them on another job. Its a game where you have to grind to get anywhere as when you unlock a new shop you'll only have one area open which will have the same four potatoes asking for the same kind of weapon until you've sold them enough to unlock another area with four different potatoes... Asking for usually similar weapons.
It does make you think though. Each customer has their own unique likes and dislikes, each Smith Potatoe you hire has different skills which you have to max out and change about. You have to pay attention to what kind of weapon you are making and what skills you are putting into it so that you can sell it to the right potatoe and make the most money possible. There are other mini-quests that pop up, you have Legendary Spuds who ask for special weapons that usually need you to have your Smiths at a high level to make and there is time management and money management in there. I mean you have to send the Smiths out to explore to get certain materials, yet you need to always remember to have enough money to pay them at the end of the month and you also need to keep them happy.
So yes it isn't the hardest game in the world but it also isn't as easy as some reviews have made it out to be. You can easily play this game and do something else (I caught up with non-potatoe related TV programs whilst playing) and its really easy to lose track of time playing it. Highly recommend it.

Sometimes the character you're moving stands completely still and glides across the floor.

SPOILER
The 'end game' happens after day 80, however there is only enough interaction between NPC's in the shelter for 60 days (at least that's all there was for me). So there will be this long boring gap of pretty much nothing happening after 60 days.
/SPOILER
The melee and ranged are completely unbalanced. It got to the point that there are human enemies in the game that can 'only' significantly get hurt by critical hits of high tier ranged weapons. So invest in Ranged 'and' melee.
The car guzzles 'way' too much gas even with all the upgrades. Don't bother with it.
I'll leave it at that for now.

"When the final modern human closes his eyes for the last time, a profound sadness and sense of loss will flash before them, and they will feel around their back for the weapon that did them in and remove a dagger made of apathy."
To be brief, Dead State is an indie game that delivers a human narrative in the face of a world shattering disaster.  You play one of the few remaining souls willing to attempt to hold things together by running a shelter.  The primary goal as a player is to manage resources, over all morale and moods of individual survivors.  These three facets are mostly achieved by exploring the areas outside of the shelter to retrieve everything from antibiotics to toothpaste.  This task will frequently involve dealing with the less threatening slow moving zombies but the larger threat is from looters and other hostile groups that will shoot you for your shoes.  There are other faces outside of the shelter that will hold conversations, often these are survivors who you can offer a place to call home, but there are others about as well.
This game is not a fast paced charge into hoards of the undead.  It is a cautious march forward in the direction of hope.
--Reanimated Update--
I can no longer recommend this game after the Reanimated update.  They've made the slow moving outdated combat even slower.  The only interesting part about the game is the character writing and how the stories between survivors evolve through the course of the game.  However, getting to these events is now a tiresome chore that sap all replay value out of the game.  According to the dev's forum posts they have no intention of changing this as they have been defeated by the difficult engine they chose to make their game with.  It's just not worth it after Reanimated.

I was very skeptical about this game at first, especially when I saw the review and metascore (yikes). It was a game I kept my eye on simply for the fact that it was based in the Korean War, a war that we havn't seen in a game before (but if there is a game that is based in the Korean War that anyone knows of then please, tell me, I would love to get my hands on it). ToW3 has some problems in it, and some things I wish it had, but for the most part, it isn't that bad of a game. First with cons. The UI system is very awkward, and a little confusing at first, and sometimes I dont know if I'm using it correctly or not. The AI pathfinding isnt good. When I tell the AI to move somewhere they will simply go in a strait line toward where I tell them to go, so if I tell the AI to go to a place that is beyond a mountain. They will hoof it up the mountain to the point where they can't walk anymore, literally, they will keep going to the point where they can't go anymore. Although the addition of the Soviets as a what if scenario was good, I wish there was more factions. Specifically the British, South Koreans, and Chinese. Besides that, the game seems to be fine to me. It is a very realistic game, there is no running into a fire fight like in CoH. You need to plan before you attack. I also love the scenarios that you can make with the campaign and mission editor, it adds a lot of replay value to it. I also have to praise the sound and scale of the game, it really is awesome. So lets review:
Pros::
-Pulls away from the usual WW2 and modern day strategy games with a conflict that has never been covered before; The Korean War.
-Very good sound quality, and massive maps.
-High realism that will provide a good challenge.
-Campaign and mission editor which offers a good amount of replayability
Cons:
-Bad AI pathfinding.
-Wierd UI system. (Or I just might be clueless on how to use it)
-Wish for more factions that were involved in the war (British, Chinese, and South Koreans)
ToW3 Korea is a game that pulls away from the WW2 and modern day settings in exchange for something different. It's a fun game for someone who wants good realism, but some bad glitches can push people away from the game.
ToW3 Korea: 8/10

If you are looking for a challenging and realistic strategy game then I recommend TOW 3: Korea. If however your more into simplistic and fast paced RTS then this may not be the game for you.
What the developers aimed to bring to the public is a well made realistic strategy game which is able to reflect warfare in the mid 20th century. This game enables players to not only fight in a battlefield conflict but also micromanage your army layout as you lead either american or north korean forces to victory!
Pros - this game is highly realistic in terms of challenges faced by an army involved in conflict along the Korean peninsula. This game is not a game where you can charge your platoon of men towards entrenched enemy forces, they will be cut down. this is not a game where you can send one tank without support into an enemy line and expect it to survive. this game is realistically brutal and that is how the developers wanted the game to turn out. this is not a game where you can rush the enemy lines without careful planning and preparation where you consider which units have the High ground, which units are able to see enemy positions, wether your units will be vulnerable to mortar or arty fire. so ignore any negative reviews that are shorter than 5 sentences.
Graphics- for a game which came out in 2011 the Graphics are fine, they are not top of the line but who cares?
Cons -  Micromanagement and understanding what each action does can be complex and you may not realize your making a mistake when you perform an action. the UI seems to lack an ability to explain what buttons do what and I recommend the player have a few practice games to fully understand what actions are available before they take part in the Campaigns.
When I mention micromanagement I really do mean micromanagement. during the campaign you can choose how you upgrade each units experience and even choose which units receives medals. before each conflict you can personalize your armies from a much larger pool of available forces.
the micromanagement itself isnt the con, rather the large learning curve a player is thrown into. (its a challenge at first but once you understand what your doing its worth it)
Another Con that I have found is the Victory conditions of a battle
For some conflicts all that is needed is that you place troops in the target town without any nearby enemy units and the battle will just end. To me I feel like that this is a drawback to the gameplay feel of the game. even if half the enemy forces are still present and in fighting condition but else where on the map the battle will just end.
To me if the developers had included the feature that these forces who potentially were cut off from their reinforces either surrender or attempt to fight their way out. rather then the assumed "they just retreated and regrouped with the main battle force who then left the region"
If you are serious about a realistic strategy game then this is it, I am yet to play multiplayer. but from what i can understand form playing against the AI it would only be short from epic.
So for my recommendation. if you are a FPS player and only dabble in RTS games then you are probably better off with much simpler and faster paced games like Company of Heroes. However if your seriously into strategy games and wish to challenge yourself or your familiar with games such as Hearts of Iron, Wargame, men of war and you have enjoyed them then i seriously recommend you at least consider looking into purchasing Theatre of War 3: Korea

This is a review of an early-access game. This game has not technically been "released" yet. You are paying to playtest and report bugs/problems. In return, you get a copy of the game when it's released. I have given this game a thumbs up because I think it has potential, not because I think you should buy it. If you don't want to playtest a game in development, DON'T BUY THIS GAME.
As I said, I think this game has potential But right now, the word is "simplistic." And in this context, that's a bad word.
The gist is, you get a squad of four space marines of various classes, and you fight through several decks of a derelict space ship. Every turn, each marine gets a certain number of action points. Moving one square costs one action point, shooting costs one action point, turning 90 degrees costs one action point, reloading your weapon costs all your remaining action points.
That gets very frustrating, very quickly, but I could live with it. what I CAN'T live with is the aiming mechanic. You can only fire at an enemy that is DIRECTLY in front of you. So if the enemy is four squares north and one square west, your first shot is going to cost three points (move one west, turn north, fire). Not only does that make the game difficult, but it also makes it very frustrating.
That on top of the fact that realoading your weapon ends that marine's turn makes this game (for me) essentially unplayable in its current form. There are a lot of nifty ideas in this game, but for now that is preventing me from enjoying it.
But take heart! This is a pre-release game, so it will be getting better. I can't say for sure that the things I don't like will get fixed, but I am optimistic that Steam Marines will be a fine game some day.
EDIT:
Just started playing this game again, and I'm enjoying it thoroughly. Reading my review above, I can't say that any of that has changed (though unchecking the option for "facing costs AP" was a big relief), but it seems that it matters less. Another problem that I had before was that it was hard to see. Once a marine looked away from a wall (for example), I seem to recall that there was no placeholder graphic to remind you "hey! There was a wall here!" Now walls don't disappear when you're not looking at them. I could be remembering wrong, but if that was a problem before it no longer is.
This is now a game that I will whole-heartedly recommend.

Played about an hour so far and progressed through the tutorial and first 5 levels of the game, but at this stage I think that's all that is necessary to review. Nice pixel-art style graphics and a well chosen score set the mood for this broody journey through a space ship taken over by killer robots! If you are looking for story it seems that's all you're getting, but the gameplay is so engrossing you'll forget that pretty quickly! Add in the fact that once your squad members die they're really gone for good and a wiped out squad means game over and it's really easy to get pulled into this game. Fiendish difficulty and a steep learning curve help to keep you forever on your toes whilst playing.
As far as the early access goes it seems to be a fully functional game, with a lot of room for expansion. For example there are currently 4 possible squad member classes (that cover quite a range of skills), maybe half a dozen item drops (but the varied effects show that there could be many more yet to come), and from what I've seen a small selection of enemies with pretty basic AI. That said I think this Alpha will probably entertain me for at least a couple more hours (especially if the difficulty keeps ramping up as it has been). I imagine the beta and full release will have many hours of gameplay due to the procedurally generated levels and possible squad configurations and tactics.
My only gripe so far is with the control scheme and UI which sometimes make it difficult to work out exactly where you're at (which squad member you're controlling, ammo, etc) and makes it all to easy to make costly mistakes. It would be nice to see some refinement in this over the next few builds as it slows you down in a game that is already requiring a lot of thought before each move.
I would definitely recommend, especially at it's current low price, currently very good, only going to get better :)

This is one game well worth the (cheap) price of Early Access.
Loosely based on the Warhammer 40,000: Space Hulk board game, Steam Marines gives you 4 marines in a ruined steam-punk spaceship, tasked with reaching the elevator to the next level amid a swarm of angry robots.  The game works on a turn-based system with action points that players of XCOM will be very familiar with.  Once you've exhausted the action points on each marine, your turn ends, and all nearby robots get to spend their own action points to move or attack.
Marines can move, attack, activate consoles, pick up loot (and believe me, you'll need a lot of it to survive), guard certain fire zones, or even bash down walls to create new paths.  Destructible environments make this a very dynamic game where you're never safe from the impending march of the machines.  Robots WILL come bursting out of the nearest wall when you're least expecting them - ruining your most careful positioning.  And positioning does matter quite a lot, particularly with some enemy types that are shielded from the front, forcing you to split your forces and flank.  Randomly generated levels provides endless replayability to perfect and level up your squad.
I could go on about this game, but for how cheap it is, and much more is yet to come (it's only in alpha and already a blast to play), this is a no-brainer.  For gaes like it, take a look at Bionic Dues, XCOM, or Space Hulk.

For $3 at the holiday sale, your turn-based itch can be sufficiently scratched by this alpha.  My only critique at this time would be to allow attacks in more than just the four directions (up, down, left, right).
Full release review:  See above.  Also... insanely hard.

[Original Review] I'm a pretty big One Piece fan, and I was interested in Burning Blood ever since it was first announced. I'm sure you can imagine my delight when they finally announced they would be releasing a PC version. Well, the excitement kind of dissipated when the launch of the PC version got delayed by like three months, but now it's here and I've finally gotten to spend some time with it.
First, elephant in the room; Yes, this is a straight up console port with resolution and frame rate caps. (1080p 30fps) The fact that it's 30 fps will no doubt be a deal breaker to many prospective buyers. Honestly I'm a pretty big fps snob but I'm hardly bothered with it in this game. I won't say it feels smooth, because it certainly doesn't, but it really doesn't feel like that big of a detriment to this game like it would in say, a first person shooter. I can at least kind of understand the technical reasoning why the FPS cap is in place because of animations and all that, but I'm a little more perplexed on the resolution lock. Even other straight console ports like Storm 4 could be ran at 4K through the config file, but this game's config file doesn't seem to change anything. A shame, because games with this art-style tend to benefit greatly from a higher resolution, even if you're only downsampling.
Other than that, the port has generally been pretty solid for me. There does seem to be a save bug in the game where your progress just randomly gets deleted. Unfortunately I have no idea where the save data for this game is located so backing your saves up seems impossible. I guess we'll just have to hope Bandai doesn't forget about this port and finds a fix.
Now, onto the game itself.
Burning Blood has basically all the essential modes for a fighting game. Training, free battle, online, etc. I haven't gotten a chance to try the Wanted modes yet, but I have completed the story mode. (Paramount War mode I think it was called) And hoo boy, yeah, the story mode in this game is hot garbage. There's basically four campaigns based on different characters during the Marineford arc. Luffy, Whitebeard, Akainu, and Ace. You can complete all these campaigns in like, an hour. The cutscenes are pretty faithful to the source material, but I skipped most because the music accompanying them sucks and in general the cutscenes are really rushed without the build up from the anime and manga. Also, I'm not sure if it's an issue with the port or the localization for this game, but there's quite a few typos that I noticed. It's not a huge deal mind you, but it does make this look like a slapjob of a localization effort.
Graphically, the game looks... fine? I'm not sure if it's just because it's 30fps and I'm not generally used to that, but this game has kind of a motion blur effect that I'm not particularly fond of.
Now, the gameplay. Right, so, after all these years this is probably the closest One Piece has had to a proper fighting game. It's insanely simplistic, but I was actually quite surprised at how many mechanics the game actually has. Granted, most matches will probably be won by whoever is able to trap you in a combo and spamming X the most, but still. It's more complex than I gave it credit for. There's even some cool ties to the series with certain fighters. Ace vs Akainu for example puts Ace at a disadvantage because Akainu's magma overpowers Ace's fire.
There is a pretty solid cast of characters in here too, and more being added later through DLC. I haven't tried everyone yet but some characters are legitimately super fun to play as. You can just feel the power of Whitebeard as you crack the air and send opponents flying, and some characters like Law even have cool gimmicks where all of his specials can only be used inside his "Room" ability. I feel like these are where Burning Blood shines, and where, as a One Piece fan, I can appreciate it the most.
So, verdict time. Here's the thing, One Piece Burning Blood is undoubtedly the best OP game to date in my opinion. (not that that's saying much tbh) But at its current price of $50, it's really hard for me to recommend at that price. (Keep in mind if you didn't pre-order the game, you're already being locked out of some content.) Even with the huge roster of characters, and a surprisingly stable online, I don't think the average person will see much more than 15-20 hours of gameplay from this title, regardless of how big of an OP fan you are. For $50, I would say hell no, wait for a sale. For $25? Then we're talking.
Also, I'd STRONGLY advise people not buy the dlc for this game right now. There are some new characters being added with them, but most are costume swaps for other characters. For half the price of the initial game, it's just not a very good value really. Again, as with the main game, I recommend waiting for a sale. It's going to be 50% by the time the Holiday sales roll around in December, I guarantee you that.

The benchmark tool 3DMark is only recommended for people who are interested in their hardware and the power/performance of their computer. It is extremely useful if you want to overclock your hardware and to determine the gain in performance. You can use it too to test the performance of your tablet or smartphone. Simply it does what it should do.
This tool has a nice and clean surface. It’s easy to understand and you’ll have always the overview. 3DMark supports many languages including English, German and French. Also there are many settings but the software shows you what these settings do so it’s friendly to beginners too.
There are many benchmark tests for different types of PC’s in this software. For smartphones and tablets, basic notebooks and home-PC’s, mid-range PC’s, high-end gaming PC’s and multi-GPU systems and overclocked PC’s. You can also customize your run in the advanced settings. You can lock the FPS, choose the resolution, antialiasing mode [MSAA/FXAA] and much more. After your test you can compare it online with other users. There is also a test that shows you the stability of your PC.
One feature is that you can save your results and load them to compare. That might be useful if you upgraded your hardware and want to see how much better your PC after an upgrade is.
Like the most games on Steam 3DMark has achievements. If you want to earn them all legally you have to spend a lot of money to buy three or more GPU’s. But there are also funny achievement. For example submit a score that contains 666/1337 or over 9000 in the extreme test.
3DMark is a very useful and worthy benchmark tool if you are a hardware enthusiast or just want to see how much power your PC has but especially for these, who want to overclock their system. But you should have knowledge to use the results. If you are an absolute beginner in the PC world you can’t really use 3DMark meaningful. For all others get it in a sale for $05,00 or use the free version but $25,00 is too much.

Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! is a highly addictive game with great cartoon-ish graphics, a nice soundtrack and the ability to progress.
There is a bit of waiting around to be done and I understand people comparing it to a mobile game. You click on your potatoes to send them on a job, wait a few seconds till they finish then send them on another job. Its a game where you have to grind to get anywhere as when you unlock a new shop you'll only have one area open which will have the same four potatoes asking for the same kind of weapon until you've sold them enough to unlock another area with four different potatoes... Asking for usually similar weapons.
It does make you think though. Each customer has their own unique likes and dislikes, each Smith Potatoe you hire has different skills which you have to max out and change about. You have to pay attention to what kind of weapon you are making and what skills you are putting into it so that you can sell it to the right potatoe and make the most money possible. There are other mini-quests that pop up, you have Legendary Spuds who ask for special weapons that usually need you to have your Smiths at a high level to make and there is time management and money management in there. I mean you have to send the Smiths out to explore to get certain materials, yet you need to always remember to have enough money to pay them at the end of the month and you also need to keep them happy.
So yes it isn't the hardest game in the world but it also isn't as easy as some reviews have made it out to be. You can easily play this game and do something else (I caught up with non-potatoe related TV programs whilst playing) and its really easy to lose track of time playing it. Highly recommend it.

"Why do I even play this?"  I asked myself this after encountering another glitchy door before going into combat with a pack of armed looters.  Character walks through a closed door right into their arms- Why.
Dead State is, for the most part, "finished."  The places are all there, most of them work, and there are a few things that make the game neat to play.  But that's about it.  For a text-based game, I'm entertained for a while.  But, something doesn't feel right...  The glitches, the static characters standing around doing nothing in any room at the base, the mundane grinding process, the fact that once I can't even assign a job to everyone I've brought together...  Well, there's the problem.  The game doesn't feel "finished."
Once your character is good at leading, negotiating, and fighting, all that's left is finding the people you would actually want to have around- that is if you make it that far.  The game's combat system is cruel, unforgiving, repetitive, and I hope you don't mind bodies stacking on top of one another so you can't loot one of them. It's super disappointing to see this game "released" in the state that it is now, having watched development from the very start.
This end product is rather boring.  Don't get me wrong, I can enjoy it, but more needs to be done to iron out the problems, more animations need to be added, and for God's sake, there needs to be a variation of death poses.  Everything I kill ends up laying there like it's planking- in some cases, forbidding me to loot the corpse, and we CAN NOT have that in a completed game.
Dead State may mostly be finished, but it isn't, and if they don't bring the updates to fix these problems and to "modernize" what feels like a game from 2005, I'm unable to recommend it to anybody at the price they're charging.
If you want this game badly enough, wait for a sale.  I wouldn't pay more than $14 for this in the state that it's in.  It just isn't up to par with more modern titles.  It's pretending to be a classic in 2015.
I'm sorry to those of you who support the game, and it's development team, but it appears that Dead State has been abandoned.  There are still numerous bugs, and there has not been a release of any editor tools to improve gameplay via Mods.  This is both disappointing and shameful; the least that this team could have done was offer to stick around for a while, but it's pretty clear they only sought to fulfill their Kickstarter obligations and jump ship.  They were never in it for the community.
Dead State still feels like an incomplete game.  It still has its vintage C-Grade game graphics, and still fails to fulfill the full level of immersion one would expect from a game posing to be one purified Turn-Based RPG in style.  When comparing this to other games in my library, such as Wasteland 2, Arms Dealer, Kenshi, Project Zomboid, Space Engineers, and others, Dead State left Early Access before it was finished, and the Development team rushed a
edition, That means they decided to upgrade the game after it was released, showing you how much they care about the very principles of "Early Access," wherein you actually get things done before putting out a game.
The very fact that these developers left their community and game to rot is simply disgraceful; it's as if they're relying on pure name-recollection to keep a fanbase (Example: "Oh, it's the company behind Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines! The game was okay, maybe this'll be better."), which means they either don't care about their games or they don't care about you.  Seeing a game left in the dark like this is dishonorable.  You don't leave a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥production sitting around, you fix it so it works for your customers or you lose your customers.  Bottom line.  I can tell you that I will not be giving Double Bear my business again.

This is ok way of making a fighting game for One Piece. I'll split into categories to determine if this makes or breaks it for you.
Story:
Don't bother if you want a good summary of the main story because that ain't happening here. It covers one part and their is no variation in cutscenes except for a few. You want a good summary of the main story without filler? Get Pirate Warriors 3 instead, it gives the details you need and its not far off from the original source.
Score: Painful and a waste of time. Its best to skip cutscenes after you finish Luffy's story.
Gameplay Mechanics:
So far its easy to get used to once you get the tutorial down. And yes tutorial text box is useful because the move set in the pause menu is cryptic, meaning they don't show which button does what. That aside, the combat is reptitive. You can change up a bit but a lot of the time you SPAM to win. Defenses are definitely different in variety just be warned that pressing the RB button to avoid damage you must be stationary and a lot of the times it doesn't work when you move. Flash Counter or Flash Block have to be timed at the exact moment you get hit and that can be a pain to activate frequently. Counters are useless far away.
Score: Limitations would have been nice, instead they make the blue meter for just the RB command. Other than that the fighting is very similar to the show but just know your not in for a AMAZING fighting game. As for different body types, the speed wins the most but if you pull off the heavy set guys be prepared to enrage your opponent. Playing this with others is not always gonna end up with happy results. Game modes are severly limited though which is a shame.
Roster:
Their are plently of characters but their are many that aren't playable (Except Lucci who ends up as DLC). Luckily majority of main characters from each Arc are playable.
Score: This is how you should start out the first fighting game for this series.
DLC:
A lot of it is overpowered and some costumes do have different special attacks. There's not much to say here.
Score: Would be nice if a lot of them did the same damage as the originals.
Overall:
This game is reptitive and has character balancing issues but it still can hold up for a bit. Its a pain to get every character because you need to grind that money out in order to get them. But Im used to that because I played Naruto Clash of Ninja Revolution 3 (The Wii fighting game that actually is the perfect Naruto game, I highly recommend it!) but it won't please others. Its nice that the roster has a bit of everyone from different arcs but disappointing when they leave some out. Story is absolute garbage and you rather get Pirate Warriors 3 instead to get a much better summary and stuff that matters! Is it worth buying? Wait till the price drops, as a lot of people are not satisfied and you may feel like the combat is nothing worth your effort. But if you do buy, just make sure that your getting a fighting game that it has some problems. There isn't much to say about this but its still a competent fighter. Enjoy it while you can and keep it if you want to play with friends. Its highly recommended to play more of it online.

Simply put it's the best Battlefield there is. 3 and 4 try too hard to emulate CoD. They made it fast-paced, light, flashy; then they simply plopped overpowered vehicles down on certain maps and left it. Bad Company 2 offers legimately competitive multiplayer. Vehicles are more sparse and serve a tactical purpose. The firefights felt weightier and more based on tactical positioning. Because of this, teamwork becomes crucial, especially on maps with fewer players. Almost everything in the game is destructible. It gets explosives a huge utility boost. It makes games more dynamic and interesting every time. Overall, it's just a solid game. Even the campaign is more interesting and fun than 3 and 4. The multiplayer is where the game shines. however. Rather than add in all of these new features and flashy messages, they kept it simple and incredibly polished. Great tactical action, classes make sense and all feel incredibly useful, fantastic mid-sized maps with a combination of close quarters and open field, weaving in a few vehicles where they feel appropriate. It's a shame, the direction Battlefield is going. DICE really needs to just look at their roots, and see why they became popular. Battlefield 2 was fantastic and Bad Company 2 just took the best parts of Battlefield 2, the best parts of Call of Duty, and made magic.

The first thing I thought upon playing the first five minutes of this game was that Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! heavily reminds me of Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale, another game about selling weapons/items to adventurers.
Now depending on what you want in a "management" game, I would choose between this game and Recettear.
Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! is a game where you are a potato man, who's looking to forge weapons to sell to heroes/heroines. That's it. You forge a weapon, pick a main stat, and sell it to those who value the weapon type (sword, wand, daggar, axe, etc) and main weapon stat (Attack, speed, accuracy, and magic). After a few hours of playing, I've found the game to be...lacking. You can explore planets to find materials, in which to use to research newer kinds of weapons. Along the way you hire smiths to help you in forging these weapons. This game also goes along the lines of games like Game Dev Tycoon.
Earlier I mentioned a game called Recettear. I admit that Holy Potatoes has a more-appealing art and sound style, BUT! Recettear is just more fun. Recettear is a game in which you also sell weapons, but there's another side to the game where you can take weapons and items you forge to go on a mini-game of exploration in dungeons. It's a bit of a side-action game to the game's management skills. Also, if you are not a fan of anime or japanese voice acting, Recettear isn't the game for you.
Overall, I would recommend this game, but maybe wait until it's on sale.

Dead State is a survival/horror RPG with strong base-building elements set in the zombie apocalypse. (Think Fallout Tactics but open-ended with a strategic/resource management layer). As the elected leader of a small group of survivors, you must go on runs for supplies, locate and rescue other survivors, allocate resources and gradually build up your shelter from a bare-bones school into a fortified complex. You must constantly deal with not only the hordes of walking dead, but perhaps more importantly, the living, who in many cases are even more dangerous.
Everyone you find has their own story, their own motivations, priorities, and attitude towards life and what is happening out in the world. As your shelter and group grows in size and reputation, people will eventually begin coming to you, leaving you with a choice as to how to deal with them. Letting in everyone may seem like a good idea, but eventually you will have to deal with the personality conflicts that arise between certain members of your group. Threats to your survival will arise both from the outside and from inside the shelter itself, forcing you to make tough, black-or-white decisions about how to deal with them. Food shortages, supply shortages, morale problems, and epidemics of disease are daily specters. Do a bad job in dealing with these issues, and other strong-willed members of the group may decide to challenge your leadership, putting you at risk of being thrown out of your own shelter.
Combat is squad-based, turn-based, and tactical. Traveling to any of the game's many scattered locations to scavenge for supplies invariably results in hostile encounters with the both walking dead and rival groups of hostile scavengers or survivors. Each member of your group has a specific set of skills that may make them suitable as a melee fighter, ranged combatant, or combat medic, and it is up to you to equip and assemble your squad with those things in mind, using whatever weapons, armor, equipment and medical supplies you have managed to scrounge or manufacture. The pros and cons of various weapons and armor, the layout of external obstacles and the internals of buildings, and proper noise management all play into getting your scavenging team in and out of dangerous situations alive and, hopefully, with backpacks full of badly-needed loot.
The game does have some interface and gameplay issues, and there have been alot of reports from users about crashes as well as glitches and bugs ranging from annoying to game-breaking throughout the game's release history. Personally, at 60 hours/50 game days in, I have not encountered anything more than a few minor glitches that, while annoying, have not seriously impacted my gameplay, in addition to a few isolated crashes. Luckily, the devs wisely included an automated bug-reporting tool with the full game that will allow you to notify them whenever there is a crash. I would advise anyone who buys the game to backup your save files just in case something catastrophic happens. I will admit that the game could use a few more updates, in my opinion, but more in terms of things to be added or modified rather than fixed outright. Overall I feel that the basic mechanics of the game are solid, providing a compelling and realistic simulation of trying to lead a group of survivors through the zombie apocalypse. I definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys open-ended RPGs or turn-based strategy games.

Steam Marines is a game about how hard it would be if you were responsible for protecting a ship from robots and/or aliens, but you forgot to pack a map.
Steam Marines is a roguelike (pedants be damned) mixed with "classical" squad based tactical gameplay, hitting a good balance of both genres.  The core of the game is about managing a team of 4 Marines are you move through a procedurally generated ship, combating a variety of enemies in turn based combat.  You clear the ship room by room, exercising the best tactics you can to conserve life and ammo so you can make it to the next floor.  There's an AP system in place, so on your turn, you move your squad around as far as your AP will let you, and then it's the enemy's turn, exhausting their AP, etc. so positioning and attention to detail is required to make sure you don't leave a Marine stranded in a bad position
I've never strayed past normal difficulty, but even there the game can be pretty unforgiving.  Death is permanent, and often swift.  Ammo is limited and so is inventory space, so you really need to scrounge carefully and decide on what to pack when you move between decks.  I've had games that were rougher than others, but never once did I feel as if the RNG was the sole thing that screwed me over- in most of my games, there was something better I could've done to avoid calamity.
Despite being an early access title, I wholly recommend Steam Marines.  Even in its current alpha state, the game is a lot of fun and tactically challenging, and as an added bonus, the developer is really active with the Steam community.
What I paid for it: 10 bucks.
What I would pay for it: Upon completion, 15 bucks, easy.
