Growing up, I played a lot of flash games. I remember games like Sonny, Pandemic, Kingdom Rush, Fancy Pants, Gemcraft very fondly. Seeing a game so heavily inspired by Pandemic, I was pretty keen to see how much Plague Inc had changed and improved on, since it's a full release rather than a free flash game. Honestly, I'm a little disappointed.
Maybe it's an unfair comparison since they're very different genres, but Kingdom Rush's full version felt like a great standalone game with charming visuals and a good amount of content delivered at a fast pace. Plague Inc feels like Pandemic alright, but not demonstrably better in terms of gameplay. Sure, there's a lot more variety but not in a tangible or fun way... just "look how many achievements there are".
The different "plagues" are unique, sure, but the core gameplay loop is very repetitive. Early game is extremely tedious, "good" builds are hard to deviate from if you want to guarantee a win and the "clicker" aspect of the game is the only thing keeping your eyes on the screen as the simulation part happens. For a strategy game, it's very casual and one-dimensional. I don't know, I feel pretty mixed on Plague Inc: Evolved as a product. It's not a bad game by any means, it's just... only barely better than its inspiration in terms of gameplay.
Plague Inc: Evolved does have a relatively good UI and serviceable presentation, as well as a LOT of content, so if you really enjoy the gameplay loop of clicking on bubbles and doing slightly different builds based on the difficulty level, plague you're using and "modifiers", then you're going to get a lot of time out of this. I just started getting burned out after completing all the main stuff, but I enjoyed my time for the first 8 or so hours.
In conclusion, Plague Inc: Evolved is fine. It's Pandemic with a much prettier aesthetic and a lot more content. I'm a bit less enthused on it than I expected, but I could see someone getting a good 20 hrs out of it. I recommend buying it on sale if you're unsure.

A surprising amount to this game considering the price.
A fairly traditional J-RPG, with a turn-based / ATB mix system similar to Grandia, where the time bar fills up, and time pauses when a character reaches the action stage, allowing you to enter a command.
The Level up system is like Final Fantasy 13's EXCEPT with a lot more freedom & customisation; instead of levelling up, you earn skill points that you spend on a series of skill trees. You pick one of (trying to remember the number...) ~6 classes, which each gives different stat bonuses & moves, depending on the character in question. Once you complete the path of ~25 'nodes' you can pick another class to continue on. After completing 2 classes, you then pick from the original group again, except the classes are now Rank 2, and have new stat & skill rewards for the tree.
Also, every fifth or so node will give you the choice between 1 of 2 rewards, so you can actually vastly change your party as time goes on - I had one character receiving only Attack & HP boosts to the best of my ability, leaving a slow and powerful guy who's next to impossible to kill; I also made 2 characters focus on All-hitting attacks with high speed, so they can continually barrage the enemies with solid amounts of damage. The 4th character I focused on a range of magic abilities, so that powerful healing and damage could be carried out against more physically-oriented enemies.
Enemies roam about on the field map, the standard 'don't want to battle, don't make contact' system; dungeons are broken into squares, with all the enemies per square acting as one unit - you make contact, you fight all the enemies on the screen as one. There's room to exploit this to find certain enemies for items, which isn't necessarily a bad thing.
Story-wise it's pretty standard, 'Save the world from a thing, slowly learn more about it' - it nicely frames the gameplay, and has some nice characters; nothing exceptional, but it all tends to work within the game's desired atmosphere. I've only finished one chapter, so it could develop far more than I've seen. I should add that the chapter end wasn't too hard-hitting or notable - indeed, I only noticed because of the achievement popping up!
I'm not sure if it would get worse, but it has a few issues regarding simple grinding to break the flow of combat - once you unlock the battle arena you are immediately treated to a fight against several groups of weak enemies that yield a large amount of skill points, crafting parts and money in one go (enough to power through multiple nodes early on); there is no restriction to the number of times you can do this, so with each character having a Hit-All move, this can be quickly rushed through several times, granting far more rewards than it deserves to...were you patient enough this could probably see a person reaching end-game strength within a couple of hours, potentially. Obviously this isn't that bad, just don't do it - or do it,if that's your bag. Some people would probably call this a bonus feature.
Graphically it is what it is, nothing really goes against the visual style you see. Some breaks and odd parts in various dungeons, but really nothing bad enough to warrant discrediting the game for it.
Waffle waffle etc etc. It will at most be a few £s, and it's definitely worth it if the above sounds acceptable to you - I got it for 99p in a sale, definitely glad I gave it a shot; for me, it rivals a few chart J-RPGs I've bought in the past. It does the genre proud, at a time when it's mostly fading into obscurity.

Despite what others have to say, I think this is a pretty solid CC game. It's not as good as Invasion Normandy (which, IMHO, is one of the best games I've ever played), but it's still enjoyable. I'd recommend it to fans of the CC series. If you're new to the series, I'd wait until this goes on sale.
I agree though that the pricetag is hard to justify. I guarantee that the reviews for this game would notably go up if they dropped the price by $10 - $15. I doubt the same amount of resources that go into a AAA title (or a fresh indie) went into this game; espeically given that most of the aspects of the game (and probably large swaths of the code) already existed and weren't built up from scratch. (It would be interesting to see the source code for CC:V and compare it to this one.)
I know others have complained about the lack of graphics updates, but I'm happy they didn't change any of that. That's essentially what makes a CC game feel like a CC game. If it ain't broke, don't fix it.
Playing as the British, it is HARD. (For me, that's part of the appeal.) It reminds me a lot of Battle of the Bulge in the early missions playing as the Allies; where you take it up the rump from the Germans on a regular basis. I feel like that's an ok comparison to the difficulty? The Germans primarily have Tiger and Panther tanks, which presents its own set of challenges. These things are BEASTS and extremely difficult to take out. (Moreso than in the other installments.) Volley fire from the flanks with multiple anti-tank troops is the better method if you don't have any tanks. If you do have tanks, going head on isn't going to work out very well for you... The front armor on Tigers feels somewhat impervious. (Which... Is kind of how it was in reality.) As always, the allied tanks feel like they're made of the finest Chinesium.
This part will sound like complaints (one part definitely is), but they're just something to be aware of for those who have played previous CC games.
There's been some changes in the AI. Just like all other CC games, the tanks never really go where you want them to. Now, they'll randomly try to punch through a hedgerow and get tracked when a road was right next to them. Your drivers are idiots, but now they're even bigger idiots. With commands, there's a lag time that wasn't there before. Your troops may or may not take their sweet time getting somewhere when you tell them to move fast. They've pretty obviously nerfed mortars, but I think in Invasion Normandy they were a bit overpowered. (the 60mm's definitely were.) Now they're closer to what they were in Battle of the Bulge. However, they also seem to be less accurate now as well. Not that they were ever overly accurate, but you'll be able to tell a difference from previous installments.
My biggest complaint about the game is that the customization of the units you can deploy isn't there anymore. With Invasion Normandy, this was my favorite aspect. I'm surprised they didn't keep that in. Instead, your bound to what is a mostly confusing system of what you can and can't switch around. It's a bit... Obnoxious? I don't really see the point of this change.

Heavily inspired by FTL, March of the Living is an Oregon Trail roguelike journey through midwestern America in search of a safe haven. Anyone familiar with zombie movies, TV shows, or comics, especially the Walking Dead, will easily enjoy the themes, stories, and tidbits that saturate the game. Zombies shamble along ala George Romero's classics, raiders will harass you, cannibals will try to eat you, and there are some moral choices to make that will affect the outcome of the game, if only slightly.
I found it quite immersive. Between the soundtrack, appealing art style, and overwhelming sense of loneliness and trepidation while on the road, there was that exhilarating anxiety at every encounter. About halfway across the map, things gradually became much more difficult. Even on easy, in the second 'sector' it was a constant issue. Managing hunger, fatigue, ammo, and supplies, and hoping you don't run into anything unfortunate.
RNG is a major factor to this game however. The 'XCOM-like' combat of battling percentages, which can be frustrating but I don't find this an issue in a game like this. It's a 'rogue-lite', RNG comes with the territory. Combat is pausable just like FTL and you can plan your attacks. Controls can be extremely clumsy sometimes and you can get mixed up with who you have selected; accidentally moving the wrong person or targeting the wrong zombie. Unlike FTL, you are responsible for every action your party members do. I feel there needs to be some automation to an extent. If you get caught up and aren't paying enough attention, one of your members might be staring down a zombie with an empty clip while it bites them. I found it too difficult and frustrating to play without pausing, something I really enjoyed from FTL. If bitten, your guys can become infected, hurting them daily. I thought it was a nice touch.
Replay value is on the higher side. Between the random events, choices, and difficulties you face, there is enough to keep you going at least a few runs.
These kinds of games are a dime a dozen, but since this one built itself off one of the best/my favorites, adapting it for a familiar, zombie infected, post apocalyptic journey, I would recommend picking this up. You'll probably get a good deal of time from this game. I don't like paying full price, having been spoiled by Steam sales of yonder years, so I would've gotten it on a sale. 50% off or higher (which it is now), absolutely buy this.

This game is not for everyone. Watch gameplay before deciding whether or not you should purchase it, as I did.
The facts:
- A beginning-to-end playthrough on one of the characters lasts about 4-5 hours (there are 4 playable characters in the main game, with 1 additional in the DLC)
- RNG plays a considerable role throughout the game. More often than not, it will be up to chance whether whatever decision you made was the correct one or not, or if you will be made to fight, or if you will lose any items or people upon fleeing. I'd say it is fair however.
The pros:
- Addictive for the first playthrough.
- Appeals to roguelike, text adventure, and zombie loving sensibilities.
- Runs at 60 fps on a potato.
- Simple survival mechanics. You need to eat, you need to rest, you need to loot to obtain ammunition, food, and medicine, encouraging you to take risks when in cities or in random events.
The cons:
- Even the easiest difficulty is too hard (don't get me wrong, there's nothing wrong with a game being hard when that is the objective, but when a game has scalable difficulty, "easy" should mean "easy").
- Feels kind of incomplete to a degree. When you are playing you will likely find yourself thinking often
- None of the characters have very fleshed out or captivating stories, with the exception of the DLC which I do highly recommend as it has a very interesting plot.
- There is a text based fight at the climax of the game wherein it is impossible to deduce what the right choices are. You can actually be killed and lose the game in this fight which is incredibly frustrating after spending four hours getting to that point.
Again, I will strongly suggest that you not be put off by my criticisms and watch some gameplay to see if you might like it. I'd say it is pretty addictive at the outset and worth checking out if it is on sale, but eventually you will likely get annoyed at the difficulty and unfairness of certain elements. Ultimately, I don't regret purchasing it but it is not for everybody.

"Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop" is a management tycoon game, reminiscent of "Game Dev Tycoon" with a non-serious tone painted on it. But it lacks the meat, the intricacy of a management simulator and boils down to a mindless clicker by the mid to late game, making your purchase feel questionable at best.
Let me explain.

The game kicks off as you take control of a Potato Smith, Patata by default whose grandfather has passed away and now you have inherited his Workshop. Agent 46 ,
the first character introduced to you in the game will teach you the basic mechanics of the game. The goal of this game is to create various weapons and sell them to heroes to earn $tarch,
to progress through the story.
The game is a hit or miss as it resembles and plays like a mobile or tablet game rather than a PC game. So this review will be my opinion on this game and might not be the same as yours so have some starch on hand to dilute the salt.
The game is fairly simple in terms of gameplay, in order to create a weapon you must have the materials to create it and then assign your Smiths to a specific workshop to increase a weapon’s stats which are Attack, Speed, Accuracy and Magic. These weapons are then sold to heroes who act as your customers. Every hero has their own stat preferences for their weapon and will pay more as well as give a higher grade for a weapon with stats which matches their own specific preference. The better the weapon the more experience the heroes will gain to level up and the more starch you get.
However, here, its gameplay is where the game falls apart. Unlike Game Dev Tycoon or other management simulators your actions are very limited i.e. placing your Smith on the station which corresponds with their highest stat. Furthermore, regions which you eventually progress through cannot be revisited meaning that you can't level up your heroes whose region you have already cleared. The same is the issue with research. For research to be carried out to unlock new weapons you need materials, many of which are region specific and without being able to revisit those regions completion becomes a hinderance.
As for the Smiths, you start off with three of the, and can get more as the game progresses eventually attracting "Legendary Smiths" and "Legendary Heroes" to your workshop. Most if not all the Smiths are references to popular media making them unique and lively. Their short bio reflects on their counterparts and adds character to them even if most have negeligible dialogue.
The efficency of your Smiths depends on their happiness which gradually decreases by overworking them but can be built up by sending them on payed vacations or having your potato dog supporting them on their station. As you progress the game you unlock new areas and eventually move to different regions while upgrading your workshops to meet the higher demand of the new heroes.
There are tons of various events which happen from time to time ranging from Aliens granting you knowledge, earthquakes, to choosing to turn the TV on or not. There are also the yearly Hammer Awards which rank the weapons on their stats. The 3 judges can be bribed to give you a better chance at winning the awards but you might get caught and get disqualified. However, the events do not change and once you find the beneficial choice for the specific event it becomes needless and the Hammer Awards aren't anything special as well, for the late-game even your mediocre weapons outclass the best so you feel no need to put in effort.
The cartoonish graphics complement the game's demeanor. The characters and weapons are distinct in appearance have a certain charm to them. This makes the world of "Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Workshop?!" interesting while remaining simplistic. Just as the setting of the game encapsulates its direction, the story albeit bland and over saturated with jokes also follows the same essence. However, the humor is lacking and will leave a cold silence in its wake. So in its writing aspect the game falls short.
"Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop," is all in all a fun game for your first hour or so, but subsequent playthroughs and the mid-late game get boring as the game ends up being repetitive. For 15$ I would not recommend this game at all. It suffers from simplicity which it tries so hard to accomplish making the game have no clear direction, resulting in mediocrity, much like this review. The only reason to pick it up would be for completion or trading cards but the former, completion, isn't possible as the player can't 100% the game due to the fact that there are DLC achievements, which aren't worth it due to aforementioned repetive nature of the game. For those of you may bring up this point, I spent the 30+ hours on the game to complete its story for a fair review.  Whatever the game makes up in its appearence and tone, crumbles through its gameplay.

"The Shelter" was a well thought out concept, but executed poorly. You get very little, if at all, dialogue changes from allies. Allies in "The Shelter" are pretty much just nice looking statues. At some point in the game, it becomes a literal waiting game whereby you just pass up days because every location has been scavenged, all the upgrades built, and no new shelter crises arise.

The iconic benchmarking tool to test optimizations you've made to your gaming rig.  Use your score to make improvements to your machine, compare with systems with similar hardware configurations or just brag to your friends.
I like that there are many levels of difficulty from low end smartphones to 4k desktops.  The results of each run are saved online for easy comparing.  Very useful for finding bottlenecks and a must for overclockers.

It really dows give you an idea of what needs to be upgrades or what is adequate for certain tasks. Whether your CPU or Graphics card is underperforming and what types of games and graphics settings yout hardware can handle. For example, my CPU gets prettymich 24fps on the firestrike ultra physics test, but my GPU gets around 5fps on its graphics test, meaning that its time for a GPU upgrade.
Really worth the buy if you have replacable hardware that could do with an effective stress test

How to play Factorio:
- Mine and carry ore around yourself.
- Build machines to mine for you.
- Build belts and robotic arms so those ores get smelted automatically.
- Build science labs and supply them with science packs you made yourself.
- Research factories.
- Build those factories to make science packs automatically.
- Build factories to make belts and robotic arms automatically.
- Build factories that build factories automatically.
- Panic when you get swarmed by angry locals.
- Set up automated defences.
- Research and build little robot drones that can construct and repair your ever growing facilities for you.
- Use robots to automatically mass-build more factory factories so that you can then automatically build more robots.
- Seek out fresh ore patches far from your base and bring the goodies back via an automated train network.
- Spend hours tinkering with things to make them faster, more efficient, and just bigger to meet an ever increasing demand for resources. ("The bureaucracy is expanding to meet the needs of the expanding bureaucracy.")
- Wonder where whole days of your life went. (I played for hours before it was added to Steam.)
- Just when you think you know how it all works, try some mods and discover exciting new impossibly complicated supply chains. (I recommend the "Sea Block" pack.)
If you've played modded Minecraft, and love the automation aspects but hate the fact that modded Minecraft is a poorly-performing crashy mess, try Factorio instead!

I recently purchased this game as I am a long time fan of the close combat series.
PROS:
1-Very realistic. In fact the most realistic war game I have found so far. Infantry have experience, can fear and surrender      if not supported by tanks or another flanking squad etc...  They can gain experience if they are kept alive from one battle to another...
ALSO, if one team gets surrounded, they wont receive resources any more, and their ammo and fuel will deplete from one battle to another if you dont support them by sending another team to clear the road for them.
2- The operation and campaign need a good strategy in order to win the operation/campaign, BOTH in the tactical map phase( where you can see all the maps) to move your teams from one map to another, AND in the map itself where the battle begins
3- High level or replayability : You can play the game for like a thousand hour and not get bored, because you can play as both the Germans or the Allies,  It has many campaigns to choose from, many operations and many single battles. You can set the difficulty as well. BUT MOST IMPORTANTLY is that you can create your own custom scenario and campaign!  Example Select the difficulty you want, the maps you want to capture/defend, location of resources, the squad you want etc...
You can also play online if you need,
CONS:
1- The AI needs to be smarter, sometimes he rushes into you and capture victory locations, but some othertimes it just sits back defending without capturing enough victory location,  AI needs to be more aggressive.
SO ALWAYS play as the attacker if you want a good challenge, because the AI is good on defense and counter attacking, but not so good on offense.
You can play as the defenders, but then you need to select a weaker team than the AI opponent, because the AI is not smart enough
I strongly recommend buying this game :)

The reason I bought this game is because I played the free version, loved the game, and wanted to check out the additional contents as well as support the creator. If you played, the online version and don't find it to fit your taste then this game might not be for you.

-Enjoyable RPG gameplay

-Original storyline
-Multiple minigames
-Some pretty good in-game music
-Additional content to free version
Cons:
-Some dialouge cutscene glitches(No impact to gameplay)

Though I love the idea of an FTL-style zombie survivial game, this game suffers from three main drawbacks.
First, the combat isn't fun. On top of being a generally boring design, multiple aspects of the combat make it difficult to get the survivors to do what you want them to do.  For example, let's say you get in a fight with 4 basic zombies and 4 strong zombies (faster and more deadly, and thus should be prioritized).  Your survivor will try to shoot them in the order they appear in the HUD, which is usually basic zombies first, followed by strong zombies.  If you specifically command the survivor to shoot the first strong zombie (#5 in line) and he kills it, he will then default back to shooting the first basic zombie (#1), forcing you to pause and repick his target every single time.  When you have 3 survivors and it is not clear who is targeting what, it becomes a madhouse where more than half the fight is spent paused ensuring they are shooting the things you actually want them to shoot.
Second, the zombie apocalype narrative is often poorly executed. Frequently, it is clear that the developers had a specifc functional result in mind for a scenario, but failed to attached a believable storyline/theme to it. For example, the developers wanted a situation where you have the option to fight an unspecified number of zombies to get a random reward.  The scenario they come up with for this involves your survivors happening upon a building and having a guy tell you that he will give you a reward up front if you will go an kill a group of infected for him down the road. In reality, what idiot in a zombie apocalypse would agree to fight a bunch of infected without asking "hey, what's this reward you are going to give me? I'm not gonna go fight a zombie hoard if all you are gonna give me is a pack of matches." The game is absolutely rife with these kinds of situations, and it completely destroys your immersion with the narrative.
The final problem is an extension of the second, namely that the poor scenario writting leads you to incorrect assumptions about how they will turn out.  For example, I got to the final location in the game and needed to get by some infected. Before this scenario, all of my survivors were fed and well rested. One of my survivors suggests she scout ahead, another suggests we get a car, and my last option is basically to bum rush the zombies.  I have my survivor scout ahead, but she doesn't come back.  I wait for five hours, but she doesnt return, so I give up on her. Now, you'd think that my survivors might have been able to rest or at least take shifts in the 5 hours of safety that I spent waiting, If not, you'd think I would now be given the option to take my other survivor's suggestin of finding car.  At the very least, you'd think I'd have the chance to rest up and eat something before bum rushing the zombies, given the 5 hours I've already be able to wait with no danger.  But no, I am forced to immediately charge the zombies with all of my remaining survivors exhausted and starving.  I have not played March of the Living since.
All in all, its not a bad game and there is fun to be had, but you have to be willing to put up with some notable issues.

Very clearly inspired by FTL and seasoned to taste with a dash of Oregon Trail, March of the Living is an excellent narrative roguelike that will kill as many hours as you do the undead.  The premise of the game is that your chosen survivor is on a journey to get from A to B for their own particular reason.  You'll have to overcome rotters (zombies), maintain your supplies, and deal with an abundance of random events as you plot your course across the vast regions that are between you and your goal.
The game's mechanics are very simple, though, this does not mean that it is easy.  A single rotter bite can infect you which, for the most part, is a death sentence.  Combat is real-time with pause and you can quickly be overrun if you're not careful, especially once you have several survivors that you're simultaneously controlling.  Scavenging is always a mix of excitement and sheer terror as you have the potential to find great items and large supply caches but always run the risk of attracting a dangerous horde of rotters.  The random events that you become engaged in every couple of minutes are text-based with multiple choices for you to select, and as far as I have experienced, are very plentiful.  I have yet to run into the same event and I was just eaten alive on my third playthrough.
I highly recommend this game to those who enjoy narrative roguelikes as long as pixel graphics and basic mechanics do not turn you off from a game.  As long as they do not, March of the Living is a great game that may be one that you keep revisiting for years to come.

It's not often that you'll come across a game as odd as Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death. It's a budget title from ZootFly, famous for their Ghostbusters demo they released a few years before the actual game from Atari.  On paper, its a generic action game. You play Marlow Briggs, you work on a rig?..., bad guys come after you, you get infused with the power of the jungle, now you can fight the bad guys.
But Marlow Briggs, to experience Marlow Briggs, is entirely different thing all together.
Imagine, almost to a fault, a Sony all-stars mashup. Imagine the world of Nathan Drake's Uncharted, invaded by a mildly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Kratos, who is guided along his journey by the “Aku-Aku” mask from Crash Bandicoot, roll them together like a Katamari Damacy ball and you have Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death.
This game, is for lack of a better definition a B-Game. It's story doesn't rival any of the before mentioned games, and it isn't trying to. Marlow is a clever mix, cherry picked from the finest parts of other games, and created it's own awe inspiring game.  It's fun, the action is constant and enjoyable. The story is simple, but the characters are interesting. Marlow is a tough, but soft hero, imagine a Keith David meets Sidney Poitier. He's a character who can be kind, but shake some sass if he has to. He's followed by the Mask of Death, who like the Aku-Aku mask follows the player around, providing the comic relief and instructional help.
The action is non stop. It just keeps blasting right around you. The gameplay is almost exactly like God of War or DMC, hack and slash, mowing down enemys left and right.
For $5.00, or if you've purchased it during the summer sale for $0.99, Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death is a fantastic game. It has the polish and action of a AAA title, not a budget title, and could serve as the perfect black sheep to the family of Sony games that inspired it's creation.
A must buy.

A very good idea which unfortunately wasnt executed well enough. therefore I can not recommend it to others.
The game was released before it is ready, probably due to sales season.
In an early access you expect bugs, but in the (finished!!) version the amount of bugs were immense. I am not going to list all, as there are forums for these. but I will go through some bugs that ruined my experience below.
Good sides,
Turn based, tactical combat (not great as there is not cover system etc, but decent)
Survival (in the first few weeks you really have to fight for each chocolate bar and manage parts and morale) later on they become irrelevant.
open world and a big map.
Graphics
Graphics are old but i like it anyway, I am not after shiny textures. Gameplay matters for me.
Audio
Audio is unfortunately quite poor as music variety is quite limited and static, and there is almost no voice in the game. Characters on levels communicate with subtitles over their heads, which you can easily miss if you are looking elsewhere. There is no message log (like in fallout). There is a combat log which could use some improvement. Sounds effects are below decent.
Gameplay.
Pathfinding and AI in general is terrible. My characters kept sliding to their destination often through walls. Enemies can also sometimes shoot through obstacles. Enemies can knock down your entire squad without a direct line of sight, using a single granade. (maybe they have thermal vision, which isnt implemented in the game :)  )
Interface could really use some polish. there is almost no info on statuses, just an icon which doesnt tell you if that character has reduced strength or perception, etc...
Armor in late game is too strong both for you and your enemies. Assault rifles can have problems without critical hits. Zombies are only a threat during first weeks, later on they become a joke, which destroys the mood for a zombie game.
Minor bugs are somewhat ok.
However, after hours of battling 10+ soldiers/mercs with full armor and assault rifles (to combat is slow, which I like as it is expected in such a genre), to crash to desktop on the last soldier is not fun. dont know about others but I have had so many CTDs. (dont tell me to update my graphics driver, or restart my computer)
The quests are also quite poorly made in the sense that the choice you make earlier is not reflected to the next day and people in the shelter complain (or are sick) as if you made the other choice in the crisis event a few days ago. quests dont get ticked off, or people in shelter keep saying the same things over and over.
The game is based Looting and keeping your people safe/well fed/ healthy. However in order to loot large maps I had to return to them 10 times.
I dont want to sound so harsh (although I probably did with all the critism). it is  a small company and I appreciate that they try to bring old turn /squad based RPG back to life.  it was just an unfinished product with a lot of bugs released earlier than it should have been. if they lack manpower, they should have waited a bit more to polish the game.

Colossal Kaiju Combat Early Access Review
I will preface my review of CKC by stating that I am a huge fan of fighting games and kaiju, but this game is easily accessible to people who are not familiar with either. This review will not touch on much, since the game will always be a WIP.
VISUALS
The game's four monsters are mostly simple in design. You have a hammerhead shark, a radioactive dino and it's robotic doppleganger, and then a fire-stone tiki golem. Each one looks pretty good, if you are looking for hyper realistic visuals, that is not the goal of this game. The characters are thoughtfully designed to show off their unique personalities and origin, and this comes through in their animations (which are updated quite regularly around community feedback).
PLAYABILITY
Like I said, the game is a work-in-progess, and things are always changing and evolving. So, I will not point out flaws  that exist in elements that ~1% of their man-power has been focused on.
Controls/Player Feedback- This game is controller ONLY. It supports basically any wired gamepad you may already own (Dualshock 3/4, XBOX 360/One Cont). I use a Razer controller, and it works perfectly. Inputs on the gamepad will either result in attacks (punches, kicks, laser beams) or defensive maneuvers (running, ducking, jumping). Each character has ~15 attacks, not counting weapons and charging (a high risk football-style tackle), these attacks perform similarly to a degree, but can be chained together very strategically. You can make risky attacks that will reward you with high damage, but leave you vulnerable for a longer period of time, or chain together many quick-weak attacks for guaranteed damage.
Menu/Presentation- Menus are barebones, again not something they have put any serious time into yet.
HUD/User Interface The HUD looks pretty cool so far, you have remaining health represented by a # value. Energy or other resource represented by a yellow gauge, and green shields that represent your defense cells (no function attached to these yet).
If you are a fan of fighting games that can be played casually or competitively, CKC is a definite recommendation.

Dino Dini’s Kick Off Revival – Steam Edition:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

In 1989 the original Kick Off was released, one year before the World cup which was held in Italy. It was a frantic year and just about everybody had become experts in football - who’s going to win and why, etcetera and etcetera. Well, we didn’t want a bar of that! My friends and I were (eight in total) in a world cup tournament every Saturday in front of my old Atari St. As I write this I can see ourselves screaming in my small bedroom. So when I saw this game I decided it was time to revive my old skills by giving Dino Dini’s Kick Off Revival a go!
Dino Dini’s Kick Off Revival is an arcade Football game, but if you are into Football management, this game will probably not be for you.
Apart from the fun memories this game brought back, it’s bloody hard to master! The reason behind it is that you have one button mechanism for shoots, passes, headers and to those long sliding tackles which create interesting patterns when you reach half time and totally crazy at the end of the match. The other hard aspect to get used to is the analogue stick on your gamepad (by the way, you must have a gamepad to play this game); you’ll have to learn not to push the stick all the way in the direction you want your player to go on the field - you’ll lose the ball every time. By mastering this, you’ll be able to execute slow dribbles which will help your team greatly. I personally recommend that any old or new players to go through all the tutorials (it will help you a bit) and practice well before playing your first game. Otherwise, your national team might receive the thumper of a life time by an unknown team. I can’t believe Gibraltar flogged France in a friendly match! I can hear people saying that the French national team is not what it used to be, but THAT bad? - I don’t think so! This game is all about developing your skills in order to win a match. I must say, that I would have liked to have a better layout in regards to the practice session, as it is a bit confusing right now.
The gameplay is very fast and challenging even on the amateur difficulty. Your players can be booked or sent off if a tackle is deemed too aggressive, but the offside rules don’t seem to be implemented. In terms of free kicks, corners and penalties it comes down to how well you use the stick and the one button mechanism.

In this current build, you can play a friendly match, the European Cup and an online game and be part of the leader board. Personally, I didn’t experience an online game at this stage which is all to do with the time zone (that’s my guess).
Graphically, it’s a big improvement from the 8bits graphics but it could have been better. You must own a Gamepad to be able to play this game. As I mentioned above, this game isn’t going to be easy to master and if you manage to find yourself in front of the net, make it count! Also, we need more content, such as leagues, more cups, and maybe polishing the stadium up a bit.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Fun, fast and challenging gameplay
-	Single and online modes
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Requires a steady bit of practice
-	Needs more content
-	No trading cards
If you are looking for a challenging Football arcade game, this one is for you!
6/10

I grew up playing Kick Off and Kick Off 2 (KO2). I tried all the other footy games that came and went.
KO2 has stayed with me so I was waiting and waiting for for Dino to create a new game.
I've followed the development of Kick Off Revival (KOR) since it was first announced. Thanks to Dino streaming on Twitch just about every single day for the last year! He's a man on a mission. The Twitch sessions have been really interesting, entertaining and intriguing. A community of followers (Kormunity) was formed by regulars who hold a goal of the month competition, regular tournaments and offer support to new players.
So last year I accidently bought a PS4 just to try KOR for myself and Its been the only thing I've played on there since.
Some people will come to KOR wanting a straight remake of KO2 and will initially be disappointed. But... there are some similarities
* its a football game
* its very fast
* the ball is not glued to your feet
* its has a top down view
* there is only 1 button
* it has aftertouch
* it was created by Dino Dini
* it takes some getting used to
* its difficult to score a goal
* you need to practice
* you need to practice
* its rewarding
* it feels great when you score
The main differences
* analog input
KO2 and most 8bit/16bit games only had 8 directions and it was all or nothing.
Like most modern games KOR uses a Gamepad/Joypad. This basically means you can run or walk depending on how far you push the stick. This takes us older gamers (KO2 addicts) some time to get used to.
* you can play online
* there are some features missing (dun dun daaa)
There has been a great deal of work done by a very small team to deliver the game to PS4/Vita/Steam. BUT its being actively developed and improved. Content (Teams, Game Modes) will follow. This for me makes the game interesting. Follow the development streams, get involved with the "Kormunity" play the game and practice!
After a bit of practice the game feels good. Once you are in the zone its very similar to Rocket League (minus the cars) Some of the goal of the month entries are amazing!
Core gameplay is really great. Having control of everything is wonderfull.
Playing "Triple A" football games after KOR makes my arms ache its like I'm rowing a boat in custard.
Anyway its a bargain so grab it and stick with it.....and PRACTICE!!!

Instead of notification, a temper tantrum was thrown on Twitter. The target of that tantrum removed the videos promptly, but the company lodged a DMCA anyway.

The target of the publisher’s anger is a jerk and should be called out, but misuse of copyright to attempt financial harm outside of actual copyright infringment is misuse of copyright and the publisher deserves to be called out and other consumers made aware of this kind of behavior.

The hand-drawn animation and graphics presented in this game caught me off guard most of the time - always love me some classic 2D. Jotun has bit of Shadow of the Colossus feeling with the main focus on beating the bosses on the spotlight, and somewhat Rayman Origins vibe for moving background-wise. The achievements are what drove me to complete the game. Plot is well done, too; you'll be told about the beginning of Thora’s journey, and then you'll discover more as you go (mainly after beating the bosses), until comes the resolution. Something that's truly punishing at times is when you died with that gigantic
font on your screen, but at the same time that could drive/motivate somebody else to accomplish it even more. Despite all the failures in every single first try, the results were all worth it thanks to the achievement. Though, I haven’t tried the Valhalla ones since they could be too hard to beat without your powers since it can depend on your skill and persistence which plays the main factor.
The walking part can feel too long and boring, especially with a pretty big-sized map (I'm talking about the exploration maps, not the boss ones). Thora’s combo variation isn’t also more than 1-2 swings, though they might not be much expected since the weapon itself could be too heavy to do ninja-like variation. But the graphics personally paid off, along with the feel of accomplishment. There was also a feeling of impossibility to beat the boss with
a double-edged axe, pretty much requires you to do trial-and-error to beat each bosses if you wanted to do it without using your powers.
The musics are catchy in my ears as an OST lover, mainly during boss fights with their boss HP adaptation; the closer you're beating them, the music will get tenser and tenser. I also adore the voice actings presented in this game, although I couldn't judge it further since they used Norwegian that I am not mastering.
All in all, the boss beatings are the definite spotlight in this game. If you are one of those art appreciator (and don’t mind with all the long walks you have to do), I can recommend you to check this game out. Pretty mixed, I gotta admit. But I don't want to ignore the beautiful graphics, is all. Recommended when it's on sale.

Lo Pan kidnaps Marlow's woman and leaves him for dead by having an ancient scythe weapon lodged onto Marlow's chest. As Marlow travels to save his love, he gains more weapons and abilities to waste Lo Pan's army and the nightmarish oversized insects and phantoms that get in his way.
I'd recommend playing on Easy, because enemies tend to take a lot of hits before they die on Normal.

Still slow as hell.  The situation is you start out as a peasant and get to build a castle and siege engines.  For reasons that will be explained later, I never got so far as building the more advanced items.  Lack of an in game tutorial is still an issue, although there is an online one if you dont mind streaming it.  To start, you have to gather the basic resources to make some simple tools and workstations.  The tools help you gather resources faster and to build your fort.  I recommend keeping it simple at first, just a box with a door.  You will need to research better wals and so you will need to craft a research station, which can be built at the workstation.  Hence the need for a tutorial.The first thing you will notice is you will begin to starve to death frequently, and you need metric♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of food to fill you up, Im talking like 20 pumpkins.  I suppose the crafted food would be better, but again, I never got that far.  I built a small fort only to find out that doors are some kind of mythical super tech that you have to research once you have metal mining up and going.  So again, I didnt get to it.  Now normally I would give a game more than a couple hours on a re-review, but honestly, the framerate was giving me a headache.  I'm talking 5-7 frames a second on a quad core processor with a fairly new video card.    Coupled with the fact you cant trurn the food 'feature' off made it mildly unpleasant to re-review this title.  It's not a bad game if you can overlook the warts.
Gameplay -
Probably the most important tech to research is farming.  If for no other reason so you can make bread, A simple recipe that fills you up.  Only requires wheat which you can find growing wild.
I recommend waiting to start building your first castle until you find an iron deposit, preferably near a forest.  Its a bit of a pain to find iron as it is quite rare.  Making it a strategic resource.  It can be found by looking for large areas in the grass where the grass looks dead.  Its yellow and red instead of green.  It took me about an hour of running around to find a deposit.  Once you find a spot, dig down anywhere from 2-10 blocks and you will find an iron deposit.  You can tell because the stone will be rust colored instead of white.  Once you have a deposit, you need to site your castle.  You can of course put yoru castle on top of the iron deposit.  The deposit I found is in the side of a mountain so thats not the easiest thign to do, so I started the castle about halfway between the mine and the nearest forest.  If you have barbarians turned on you may want to rush developing better weapons.  Sword and crossbow come in handy, especiialy the crossbow if you have your defences set up so you can shoot the barbarrians attacking your gates.
All in all, It is a good game, and I would recommend it if not for the serious lag issues.  I've heard all the excuses about it still being early access, but seriously, the game has been under development for at least a year and the issues keep getting worse not better.

Demise of Nations is a great addition to the steam library. I am a person whom invests most of his time into work and other life committments, but I also love the grand strat genre which creates an obvious conflict of interest since grand strat game sessions turn into gigantic monolithic time sinks. So if you are like me, then this is definitely one of the games you need to be looking at. It honestly feels like Civ-lite. You could play this game on a potato, and the pacing is ideal for a person who can't afford to live at their PC. Sessions can last anywhere from 30 minutes, to 5-8 hours depending on how you set the game up.
The game comes with a "free" map. Keep in mind that each map essentially functions as a different game. The free map is more dressed down like RISK. The DLC maps are $3.99 a piece and contain map modes that more closely resemble Hearts of Iron (Modern maps), and Civilization 3 (Demise of Nations: Legacy). The ease of modding and the potential it has to produce increasingly more sophisticated and balanced incarnations of the game make it a pretty exciting prospect. Especially for a free game.
There is no limit to the replayability. There are DLC maps that include random map gens, with an absolute ton of features and settings that can be modified to make each session unique. I find myself playing this game more and more in place of Civilization 5 simply because I can scratch the "itch" without needing to waste entire days of my life making progress.
Multiplayer is a blast. I would recommend playing it with friends. The diplomacy and general "flow" of the game make for some pretty funny/tense rivalries and stand-offs. Depending on the people you're playing with, it can easily become a backstabbing simulator in all the best ways.
My only issue with the game is that the AI is pretty dumb. AI nations even on the hardest difficulty can be pushovers. I find that they're simply "resistance" while the (real) player Empires get going. I would prefer if the AI were smarter, and it seems to have trouble adapting to the different game modes. Like in some of the Legacy maps, for example, the AI nations lag behind you because they don't seem to fully understand how to develop resource tiles and balance their economies. I suspect these issues will be changed in subsequent patches as the game is still very new.
All in all I would recommend trying DoN out, and honestly it would be well worth $15 if they were aiming for that kind of price point. Considering you can pick up the Legacy maps for $3.99 each (which is where the real fun is if you're a civ fan), it's an absolute steal.

Short review: Fallout meets State of Decay - buy it ;)
Long Version:
Dead State is all about the apocalypse feeling after a zombie disaster. You have to build your little shelter, gater other survivors and keep them alive as well as happy. At the same time there is a rough "bigger" story, which you can follow to different endings.
Good points:
.,Exploration of the state, with random encounters and mostly different maps.
.,Fallout like character creation of your own survivor, including different skills/attributes and the improvements of these (including perks).
.,Many different weapons/armors and other equipments.
.,A great variety of survivor characters, which create a good part of the atmosphere, together with the radio DJ and the messages you can find throughout the game. But beware, some may work against you, they have their own personalities ;)
.,You can - up to a point - play an really evil style as well as a normal or even good and helpful guy.
.,Long playtime
.,Base building, weapon modding etc.
.,great humor
Indifferent points:
.,Combat - It mostly works fine as it is, but naturally could use some more options
.,The late middle game can drag a bit.
,. There could be more dialogues/interaction with the survivors, since it is one of the strongest parts of the game, i can´t get enough of it.
Not so good points:
., Not an optimal balancing.. zombies become kinda less dangerous, when you have better armor, same is with weapons - you won´t use most of the melee weapons. At least i don´t.
,. Still much room for improvement regarding the handling of your fellow survivors/items etc.
,. Many (mostly smaller) glitches still in the game (sometimes characters "float" or zombies stand on the same tile etc.).
Nothing gamebreaking though for me.
So, in the end, i have my fun with it, even if it´s still a bit rough on the edges. A very overlooked zombie rpg/strategy gem, which really didn´t deserve some of the negative review trolling it got.
Hope to see much more of this game!

Dead State, is a great game. It uses an isometric view, turn based combat and base building/management NPC interaction system.
The plot has so far been excellent, with well written background stories for NPCs. The dialogue, and the interaction really makes you feel like you're dealing with the daily problems of life in the apocalypse. You must scavenge for supplies, repair your base, and upgrade it, But you have to deal with the people you care for as well. Keeping up moral, finding personal items they need, while assigning them tasks and job schedules around the base.
The interface at first seems abit clunky, but took me very little time to get used to it. The sound & graphics, while not cutting-edge, are done very nicely. One thing I'd really like to point out, is the areas you visit while looking for supplies or running errands. Every map area, tells a story if you look. Very impressively done, for example I was looting a local neighborhood and every house every block, you could see the damage or the carnage and piece together what happened there. A car slammed into a power-pole, the trail of blood as the driver tried to escape to a house... The door smashed, his body half devoured in the doorway ! Just little stuff like that seriously adds to the ambience, and feel of the game's setting.
I also would like to point out the leveling and skill system, is well done. You really do get the feeling that each level is really going to help you survive. You don't have to reach level X before you can survive on your own ; each of level you gain does give you the sense of accomplishment. And so far most skills, that I've gained/used have a purpose, have a use that just might keep you out of the hands of the Dead for just another day...
The bad... The game does have some bugs. I haven't really experienced anything to severe, or to frequent to prevent me from playing on. So far I crashed once, loading a save-game. Just once, and reloading the game and reloading the save went fine on the next attempt. I know there are some odd dialogue mix ups that others have had an issue with ; But so far I have not.
Over all, a well done game that is enjoyable.

I really wanted to like this game, but in the end I can't recommend buying it in its current state even after multiple patches.
+ Combat can be tense in the early game before you get good weapons/armor because you don't want to attract too many zombies or human enemies all at once. Note emphasis on "early," see below.
+ Base management can be fun, especially once you get lots of survivors who then start interacting with each other which can lead to interesting crisis events. Probably the best part of the game.Seems to clearly draw from Suikoden, what with being able to recruit lots of characters to your home base who have vignettes and even being able to build a suggestion box to read often humorous suggestions from them.  Until you get a lot of survivors the base is pretty dead though.
+ Can scratch that loot tick before you get tired of looting. Nothing like opening a single container and seeing a ton of nice loot.
- The game still has a lot of bugs including ones patches claim to have fixed (see: certain stairs in the hotel only working after rejiggering your whole party position so you can use them, enemies especially zombies clipping into each other while moving and merging into one tile, etc) which can make playing a chore.
- Combat breaks very quickly after the early game. You start finding armor that lets you ignore damage, quickly making zombies irrelevant and humans who don't have guns higher tier than the armor you're wearing irrelevant until eventually you have such good armor there are no longer enemies that can threaten you without critting. This cuts both ways and eventually the only significant way you can damage certain enemies is on crits, especially the really annoying ones with riot shields who you should basically not bother with if you aren't critting them with weapon types they're least resistant to. You can find and craft various gas grenades that trivialize combat against human enemies who aren't resistant to gas, which is like 90% of them including the top tier ones since you just blind or even knock them out and then pummel them while they're helpless. A zombie game where zombies quickly become irrelevant because your armor is so good they do nothing to you and humans become almost irrelevant soon after has serious issues.
-The interface is one of the worst I've encountered in a long while. You spend a lot of time looking at inventory screens, and because of that what might be minor problems in another game or taken alone quickly add up to become frustrating. There is physically no way to drop an item you realize you don't even care enough about to recycle (see below), you have to dump it into a container somewhere on the map. If you want to move things from the car to your base's stash that don't auto stock, you have to first move it to your main character and then move it into your stash (hope you invested in strength!). You have to move things one by one from character inventories to the trunk in the field because you can't move things from multiple characters inventories like when you trade between characters (another interface issue because you have to actually select it as an action on the field by right click cycling through other options instead of just pressing "I" when you're not in base). I can go on. Again, these might be minor issues in other games or taken alone, but since by this games nature you spend so much time messing with inventories it adds up very quickly. The idea of getting loot in a game with a large emphasis on looting actually became a chore that I began dreading.
- You can recycle things you don't want into "parts," one of the resources in base management once you build a building. This is just completely ridiculous. First of all, once you build a recycler, you no longer have to care about parts because you can recycle trash items into more parts than you will ever need. This is a game partially about resource management where you can build an easily accessible building that lets you ignore one of the resources. Let that sink in. The other issue is it encourages you to pick up every piece of garbage you encounter so you can turn them into parts encouraging the most base loot hording behavior. This is already annoying if you're a lootaholic in games like Elder Scrolls series, but compound it with unfun messing with inventories and you can see why I never wanted to see another inventory screen in this game again. They nerfed this building at some point in beta and its still ridiculous. Guys you don't need to try to make every bad idea you come up with work, just delete it and move on.
- There isn't really any story until extremely late in the game. I'm talking like 80+ days in. That might appeal to some people, but by like day 30 I had my base pretty much set up and no longer had resource issues. That left 50+ days of basically going through the motions for the sake of it. Resources quickly become irrelevant when you get good transportation so you can bring home hundreds of pounds of materials home in a single day from no longer challenging maps. Lets not even talk about recycling.
- I don't care about graphics in RPGs but if you do... play another game. Not much going on in the audio department either.
I don't want to keep going because again, I really wanted to like this game. I think they have made an admirable effort considering their situation and resources. But that the people behind it made an admirable effort doesn't mean you should buy a game, and in its current state after beta and multiple patches I can can only recommend this game to extreme fans of the genre who are also extremely forgiving. I like to think I am in that category most of the time, but this game in particular soured me.

I've just finished my first playthrough of Dead State and I definitely plan on replaying it at some point in the future. In short, I'd say that it's definitely in my top games for 2014.
The game is a bit of a curious mix of survival games (think resource gathering in something like This War of Mine) set within a framework of a RPG playing quite like Fallout 1 and 2. After a brief intro sequence you are soon aware that the zombie apocalypse is happening and you are soon put in charge of a shelter in a Texas town called Splendid. It's your job to make sure any survivors (you will find many who you can invite into the Shelter) living there can, well, continue to survive. You talk to people, solve conflicts, assign jobs. And then you wander out into the world seeking resources.
The game is viewed from a top-down perspective with a camera you can spin around.
There are a few different gameplay actions you do during the game. As described above, the Shelter is your base which you need to improve. This is done via a Job Board where you can assign tasks to your fellow survivors such as building things, be a doctor, or come with you out into the field to get supplies.
This is all dependant on the game's RPG system where you can invest points into various skills such as Ranged Combat, Leadership, Medical skill etc. All survivors you meet have their own set of skills (which you don't have any control over, but will continue to grow over the course of the game) which make them suitable for different tasks.
There is a base management aspect of the Shelter. You need to keep it stocked with food, gas for the generator, luxury items and medical items. There is a morale stat for the Shelter depending on how well you do.
The survivors also hang around the Shelter where you can talk to them and get (fairly brief) bits of their stories. You can also ask them if there's anything special they'd want from the scavenging hunts. Someone may favour whiskey, someone else a cigar. This will raise their mood. If a survivor's mood goes down, they may end up leaving you.
Also, each morning there are little interactions, situations that arise in the Shelter. People may be arguing, someone may need to talk to you about something etc. Sometimes there are Crisis Events which is regarding bigger decisions in the Shelter. The characters involved will agree or disagree depending on your choices.
The writing for the characters is very good most of the time. It's down to earth and believable most of the time. There are a few exceptions but mostly the writing gives the game a real human feel which is exactly what a game like this needs. You can also find "data items" which can be found in the world and decrypted so you can read them. These items vary from the Dead State equivalent of Twitter messages, medical reports, personal letters, message board discussions etc, mostly about the outbreak of the zombie virus. These are *fantastic* and present a real nice backdrop to everything that's happening.
I also have to give the developers kudos for including characters with a form of mental illness. Too often in games do they treat mental illness as just being CRAZY! But Dead State does it seriously even while it may not dive too deeply into the subject either.
During the day, you're most likely out scavenging with your party (total of 4 members including yourself). This is done via a worldmap travel system (again fairly similar to the older Fallouts). There are many locations to find in the game, all with varying resources, allies to recruit and enemies.
The combat system is very much like Fallout. It's turnbased and may feel rather slow and clunky to some players. The combat system feels at its best when fighting against humans, it can get pretty exciting. Most of the time, the zombies are a non-threat. Individual zombies are weak and easily taken care of. Any danger that they pose comes from the being in groups.
There is a noise-level system in the game, and the zombies are attracted to noise which creates a very interesting dynamic. If you get into a firefight with some humans, you can soon count on the fact that zombies will start to move towards the location of the gunshots. This creates a great an additional layer to think about during combat.
You can also use this to your advantage, luring groups of zombies into a bunch of human enemies by throwing firecrackers for example.
Dead State is not a AAA game by any means, and it may look really crude at first. The character models in particular look fairly boring. However, when actually playing, one notices that locations in particular are quite well done. It's not high end graphics by any means but all locations manage to convey a sense of place really well. Whether it's a shopping mall, a neighbourhood of houses, a resort. They work really well actually. Animations are also pretty well done though it feels like it could've needed a few more.
Nothing special here. The music works well and does its job. It sounds relaxing at the Shelter (except when conflicts arise) and creepy when exploring. Given how much combat there is in the game, the combat music quicky wears out its welcome unfortunately and starts to grate after a while. Sound effects feel pretty "stock", nothing particularly exciting.
Much drama has been made about the buginess of Dead State and, indeed, I did run into a fair amount of bugs and polish issues. Mostly it seems to be certain story events and such happening out of sequence at times. There are many small annoyances also such as difficulty traversing stairs at times. It feels a bit janky at times, moreso the longer into the game you get. At least that was my personal experience.
I had about 5 crashes throughout my nearly 50 hours with the game, I'd say that's pretty good actually.
It also has some pacing problems. The game is pretty slow to get going, mostly due to there being few followers at the start and not much to "do with them" so to speak. It feels a bit empty. The game shines during the middle when the Shelter starts filling up, people start talking to each other and things start happening. And then the energy goes away again toward the end of the game where you've collected all the stuff you need basically. It feels more like a waiting game then for the end-game to set in. I think the game would've done well to be "condensed" a bit, especially at the end it can actually get a bit boring unfortunately.
All in all, I *highly* recommend Dead State if you know you like the types of gameplay it offers, It is extremely addictive, I found it very easy to play through just "one more in-game day". The writing is mostly great and give it all a nice sense of purpose. Like I said above, this is one of my top games for 2014, no question.
However, the bugs may annoy you depending on how sensitive you are to games feeling a bit broken and janky. The devs are gonna be actively patching the game so you may want to wait a bit before taking the plunge yourself.
All in all, highly recommended!

Dino Dini's Kick Off Revival has taken a lot of stick over the last year after the PS4 release,  In my mind, largly due to a misunderstanding of what the game is.  This is not a football simulation.  Kick Off Revial tries to capture the essence of football in an arcade style game and put the player in full control of what happens on the pitch.
This means the ball does not stick to your player.
Passing direction and power is not assisted
You can run in any direction
Height of kicks and shots is player controlled.
All of this manual control mean that practice is needed to gain an understanding of how to use it efficiently.
But once you do, the fun really begins.
You start to pass the ball around your opponent, crossing from the wing and heading the ball home, or perhaps you intercept a clearance outside the box and fire a topspin shot in to the top corner?
Low shots, high shots, curling shots, lobs - all are ppossibe once you learn the finesse required to control the analog stick.
And this is the key difference from previous versions of Kick Off, and where I believe the issues arise for Kick Off players.  Running speed, direction and shot/pass power are all controlled with the single analog stick.  This takes time, patience and practice.
Yes, game modes are limited but the developer is hoping to add features over time.
This game was made with local and online multiplayer in mind.  Play another opponent and the game really does come in to it's own.  Enjoy playing someone at your level or wonder how that player who seems so much better than you does that crazy shot and try to figure it out... or ways to stop them.
For me this has been the main pull of the game, online multiplayer and competing with players that seem almost god-like on the pitch.
Aspire to compete with them... and keep playing them to learn their techiques

Referee - yes there is a referee but not actually visible on pitch, no linesmen either - shame really. In essence, I have an Xbox controller plugged in and a competition pro plugged in. 2 Player option is greyed out? Cannot figure out how to configure keyboard controls - if at all possible. The game needs some refinement ie options for controller and definately some instructions for controllers - how to change formation etc. So would I recommend the game? Yes, because of the price its an absolute bargain - for people that have played and mastered kick off 2. I don't even know where to begin with this game. It was amazing when I played it on newgrounds and it's even better now. Crystal Story 2 is the kind of game which you might consider "casual fan" before realising you've invested hours upon hours of playing it and trying to get everything. It's the type of game that beats all odds and exceeds your expectations.
Story: ++++
The story of Crystal Story 2 isn't anything really unique. You've probably seen it before. Unlikely hero in a strange world finds a party of friends, travels the world and beats the ultimate evil. However, the developer acknowledges this and instead of trying to glorify it, he has fun with it, plays with various cliches and over-used tropes and ends up creating a very entertaining, fun story which...miraculously...even manages to surprise you at various points in the game. I won't give anything away but get ready to laugh, cry and go "Awww" in the most unique "cliche" story you will ever experience.
Characters: ++++
Not much can be said about the characters. They're your usual teen party that saves the world from the evil demon. You have the spiky haired, half-dragon protagonist, the over-excited rogue/thief, the broody emo and the over-emotional teenage girl. Throughout the game, you'll meet other characters as well, some of which were in the original crystal story as well. If you play that first, they're fun to run into and talk to, albeit, somewhat weak in combat.
Although each of the main characters fills a specific anime trope, they all have debt and never feel hollow or uninteresting. Each time you stop in a town, you get to speak with them in the inn and explore their personalities a little more.
The game takes itself seriously but not TOO seriously. The characters perfectly reflect this.
However, their team dynamic is the real focus here. These characters would be decent at best if solo. But seeing their interactions together is what makes this party so interesting. You can see they developr real relationships and have fun together. Their relationship is better developed than that of many high-budget JRPG parties out there.
There's also a robot side-kick you unlock after reaching Crystalia, the capital of the world. However, he never leaves Crystalia so he's as good as gone after you leave the place. His purpose is to tell jokes and change the character names. The jokes are puns. Hear at your own risk.
Gameplay: +++++
The gameplay is rather typical. Turn based combat, various classes to pick for your characters, explorable environments and a variety of mini-games to play through-out the game. And yet, as simple as that might seem, it actually becomes rather complex and fun once you unlock your second class.
The characters get stronger as you play by acquiring SP (skill points) through combat and then spending them. This replaces the typical level system with a much better and way more fun class system. Each class has 5 levels and each level has a pre-set amount of stat spheres you can unlock with SP to make each character stronger. When you reach the final stat sphere, you unlock a secondary level 1 class. This repeats until you max out 2 level 5 classes where you can choose a 3rd level 1 class. This however happens either very late into the game or with a lot of farming so you won't ever be overpowered unless you are ready to grind.
In addition to the main quests, the game offers a variety of side-quests and mini-games as well. You can collect trading cards in the world and then play a rather addictive card-game at an inn. You can look for loot in fishing ponds. You can do bounty hunts before and after the games final boss. You can participate in various arena battles and get stronger. Or you can just♥♥♥♥♥♥back and enjoy the music from the inn's jukebox. There's no rush. The game makes it obvious it wants you to have fun and decide for yourself how you want to progress and when.
*(Note: For any fans of the thief class, you should know that stealing in this game is also very rewarding. Some could argue it's actually essential to unlock everything but you can go through the game without worrying about it.)
Customization: +++++
The game has a very rich customization system.
You have a weapon slot and 3 armor slots (which are practically for both armor and accessories). You unlock the armor slots as the game progresses.
While this is straight-forward enough, the real focus of this system is actually in the upgrade system of your equipment. You can upgrade literary everything.
All items have levels and stages. Most start at stage 1, level 1. You upgrade their levels using money and scrap metal (which you can either buy, steal or find by killing enemies). Then, you'll be prompted to upgrade their stage using a crystal. So now you have an item stage 2, level 1 and you can upgrade it further.
This system is flawlessly designed.  Your items will never feel useless or weak because you can always upgrade them.
In addition to this, there's also an in-depth crafting system. What this means is that you can use your loot to create even better loot. Essentially, you'll be using it to craft your starting gear into stronger gear. So instead of using 2 slots, one for an MP trinket and another for an HP trinket, you'll combine them into 1 item and free 1 slot.
Other than equipment, you can also craft items such as potions, elixirs and bombs. This process, however, becomes almost mechanical after a while since you'll never run out of the ingredients required for these items.
World: +++++
The world is actually surprisingly large and rich considering the price of the game. You have a variety of towns, dungeons, secret locations etc. and you'll never feel like they're repeating themselves. There's also a lot of end-game dungeons which are practically the climax of the game. Even more so than the final boss. And, of course, there's an extra chapter after the main storyline ends which adds even more to an already surprisingly large game. I honestly can't believe how rich and well-made this RPG is.
The overworld is also well designed and feels nostalgic to old school RPGs.
One thing you might consider a drawback is that the towns feel practically the same. A hand-drawn background of whichever city you're in and a menu with which you can access the inn, the shop etc.
Once you reach Crystalia, the inn is replaced by a palace but that's about it.
The real difference between them is that later towns have more items available in the stores. However, after a point you won't actually care about that. Eventually you'll return to Crystalia every time since it's the only town that has your robot sidekick in it as well as scrap metal for sale. The arena and the card battles are all the same throughout all towns. The only reason to return to older towns would be to complete the bounty hunts and after that, you'll not be seeing them again.
Not much else can be said about the world. It's vast, it's fun to explore, it feels great to be in it.
Soundtrack: +++++
The soundtrack fits this game perfectly. It has everything. It's reminiscent of the bit era of music but it goes beyond that.
Each area has a unique track to go with it both in the exploration and in the combat segments. This means that you'll never get bored, hearing the same track over and over again.
There's also specific themes that are made solely for the story segments.
In addition to all this, you can also use the jukebox present in every inn and listen to whichever track you wish (only requirment is that you've progressed far enough in the story).
Honestly, this is the type of effort I wasn't even expecting from a game of this price. The music is practically a selling point in and of itself.
Achievements: +++

Dead State is a very unigue, one-of-its-kind, single-player RPG set in a zombie-apocalypse environment. The hand-drawn animation and graphics presented in this game caught me off guard most of the time - always love me some classic 2D. Jotun has bit of Shadow of the Colossus feeling with the main focus on beating the bosses on the spotlight, and somewhat Rayman Origins vibe for moving background-wise. The achievements are what drove me to complete the game. Plot is well done, too; you'll be told about the beginning of Thora’s journey, and then you'll discover more as you go (mainly after beating the bosses), until comes the resolution. Something that's truly punishing at times is when you died with that gigantic
font on your screen, but at the same time that could drive/motivate somebody else to accomplish it even more. Despite all the failures in every single first try, the results were all worth it thanks to the achievement. Though, I haven’t tried the Valhalla ones since they could be too hard to beat without your powers since it can depend on your skill and persistence which plays the main factor.
The walking part can feel too long and boring, especially with a pretty big-sized map (I'm talking about the exploration maps, not the boss ones). Thora’s combo variation isn’t also more than 1-2 swings, though they might not be much expected since the weapon itself could be too heavy to do ninja-like variation. But the graphics personally paid off, along with the feel of accomplishment. There was also a feeling of impossibility to beat the boss with
a double-edged axe, pretty much requires you to do trial-and-error to beat each bosses if you wanted to do it without using your powers.
The musics are catchy in my ears as an OST lover, mainly during boss fights with their boss HP adaptation; the closer you're beating them, the music will get tenser and tenser. I also adore the voice actings presented in this game, although I couldn't judge it further since they used Norwegian that I am not mastering.
All in all, the boss beatings are the definite spotlight in this game. If you are one of those art appreciator (and don’t mind with all the long walks you have to do), I can recommend you to check this game out. Pretty mixed, I gotta admit. But I don't want to ignore the beautiful graphics, is all. Recommended when it's on sale.
