Potatoes, such elegant creatures. With their joyful smiles and innocent lifestyle, what would
drive them to require weapons?
Well, let me show you...
Holy Potatoes, A Weapon Shop has been described as nothing more than a waiting game. Much
like a facebook or web title, but honestly, there is a lot more to it than just that.
Taking insparation from games like Game Dev Story, Weapon Shop De Omasse and Recettear: an
item shop's tale, Daylight Studios have pushed their way through Steam Greenlight and come
out with a relaxing and fun title that had me hooked for hours!
At first you meet with Agent 46, now here's a guy with something to hide... I wonder where
I remember him from? He says that he owns 99.99% of the Blacksmith Shop. Something
about an agreement with your Grandfather who owned the shop before you inherited it. You only
see him when he comes to collect his cut of Starch, that's the currency of the game, and
continues to increase each time. I haven't found out what happens if you don't have enough,
but I could guess he would either give you more time to give him his cut, considering he failed blacksmithing school and needs someone to turn a profit in the shop, or just pull his silverballers and make a holy potato.
Luckily, your Blacksmith Shop doesn't come completely empty, you start with some workers that resemble Potatofied (Yeah, I'm making that a word) Potatofied versions of Lara Croft, Hulk Hogan and the Comedian Russell Peters. All with their stat specialisation of Strength, Speed and Accuracy. When making weapons, they can be moved around to help at the different forges or sharpening stones to increase the stats on the weapon being made, but make sure you have an adventurer to sell it to that likes those stats or you won't be making any money... starch... gems?  Actually, Potato Gems would have been a totally awesome premium currency, except there is no premium currency or micro-transactions in this game! Good Job Daylight!
You need to look after your smiths, sometimes they can get into a bit of a funk and need a holiday. Off they go, all expenses paid for a day or two of rest before coming back to work. They can also be sent off to buy or search for materials, training or sent off to research new weapons to make. Where do they go to research? The bookcase of course! Then through the purple portal behind it. Who knew?
If you take a look at the Adventurers that you want to sell to and their location, you can make a couple of weapons with their prefered main stat and only make one trip to sell what you have made. Early on, I made a few mistakes as you can't sell to the same adventurer twice in one visit as once they've bought a weapon, they're not there to sell another one to, so mix it up!
Making weapons is easy, first, click that Forge button, check your buyers, Move your smiths to the prefered stat stations, click that Forge button again and make a weapon!
As the smiths are making the weapon, they wave their arms all about. I don't get it, I thought they'd need to use the hammer or hold the weapon at the grinding stone or hold it in the forge, but nope, they wave their hands in the air like they're at a rave!
You can also boost the prefered stat on the weapon by selecting it and hoping that the gods are on your side. A good stat boost make for a more expensive weapon and keep Agent 46 from mashing you. You can also pay for more experienced potato smiths for a huge increase early on if your employed smiths haven't trained up enough.
After making a few weapons, you hear a sound outside... No, it can't be... a Potato Dog? What the hell? are there Potato Birds? Potato Fish? Hipotatopotimuses? You can't be serious. Ah well, he seems to make the other smiths happy, so lets give it a name.
I'll call you  Waggleton the Third! There we go!
There are many potato dogs like you, but you shall be mine! Oh, a Finding Nemo Reference, how cute.
Splas Splash, Splash Splash? Wait? What? Dogs don't go "Splash Splash", Oh you little...
Then it just runs around barking and whining, annoying all the other smiths in the shop and eating food.
Oh, look at how happy he is, he has a mountain of food, until he eats it all and repays you by taking a dump in his food bowl. That's grattitude for you, "Oh, I eat all my food and now that it's gone I'll dookie in my bowl" that's real nice. And being a Potato Dog, shouldn't it be mashed potato instead? I dunno, I have a feeling I'm thinking to much into it.
Holy Potatos a Weapon Shop is a fun, relaxing game that passes the time well and has enough depth to keep you interested and wanting to make "Just one more weapon" or do "One more thing" before leaving the game. And to me, that's what making a fun game is all about.

Holy Potatoes! A weapon shop! Is full of cute graphics, spud humor, and addicting gameplay for those who love the simulation genre.
It may seem at first to be a really repetitive experience, but the game keeps growing in depth.
You start out as a young potato learning that your grandfather has passed and you inherited his weapon shop. Well, you own 0.01 percent of his weapon shop. Who care, you have a cool new occupation, wait you don’t know anything about making weapons? No worries, blacksmiths do all the work. Blacksmiths like Lara Craft. Who knew a spud raider could be so perky?
Each blacksmith has a finely tuned skill they start off with and those create stats for weapons for “heroes” Yup, like bandits, pirates, gladiators, and snipers. Totally the hero type, if you know what I mean spud.
Each blacksmith’s specialty goes to an attribute. Attack power, Accuracy, Speed, and Magic. But as you progress, the game starts to open up, as you can upgrade your shop, hire more blacksmiths and work your blacksmiths skills until they master everything.  It takes time, training, but worth it. You’ll learn tricks along the way, learn which “heroes” like what weapons and what stats are within reach.  Take a look at the training tree, there are lots of reasons to re-assign job titles in order to become a weapons master. There are tons of little details in this game that shine, from random decision making about where or not to turn on a tv that is outside of your shop to saving kids from bullies, to random statues to put in the store, it’s quite the adventure.
Always be on the lookout for the annual weapon awards, here if you win, you get cash bonuses, and maybe get some starch into the judges hands for a little positivity in your direction. Yes, starch is really the currency, and yes, I LOVE IT!
Once you start gaining reputation Big time heroes start looking for you, they will request very specific weapons and give you lots of bonuses. Plus the interactions are hilarious and full of spud puns.
It’s a fun story, a well put together simulation game, and I found myself losing track of time while playing this game. I say it’s well worth the 14.99, and if you dig fun music, great artwork, and Lots of potato jokes, it’s a must have.
It's fun to a certain extent. If you liked Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale, this will not compare but it's close enough. I wouldn't say it's worth $15 though. Definitely $10.

Bad Company 2 was hamstrung on consoles, but plays great on the PC. The maps are not exactly designed for maximum player counts, but it still plays well enough. It is worth it if you get it for cheap on sale and you feel like some Battlefield on Steam.

What can I say about this game that isn't gonna take up a whole lot of room? To save all the hapless text that bores the stuff out of you, yes, I DO recommend this game if you're interested in an FPS game. I'm not gonna say this game is flawless in every conceivable angle, because obviously this is not the case. From my experiences of playing this, I should point out a few things that you should know going in:
1: This is a game that plays by its own twisted sense of reality. This is a rule you can pretty much apply to every game ever. While Battlefield: Bad Company 2 acts generally like any old FPS game, there are many things that seem to more or less break the fourth wall. For example, the spotting system has flaws with which you can see the enemy behind cover for a few seconds in the form of a red triangle above their head. This can lead to exploits involving players getting shot just as they leap from cover if not outright getting killed through smoke, garage doors, or rubble. Also worth mentioning is that many weapons function awkwardly from a more common-sense means of use which may seem suspicious. For example, the bolt-action rifles have uncanny hipfire accuracy that is almost reliable. That's not to say there isn't an extreme, though, if someone has "overdosed on Ritalin."
2: This is a TEAM game. It is highly important you keep this in mind, because I've been through countless matches where my teammates/enemies do little more than camp in the deployment zones without playing the objective and snipe, attempting vainfully to pad their K/D. K/D is only half the battle in this game. It's good to balance trying to get kills/assists, playing the objective, and scoring points by helping your teammates do the same. The four classes each have their own support gadget (Ammo Boxes, Medkits, Repair Tools, and Motion Sensors) - use them wherever it is most advantageous. While you can get an ace pin going 0/98 by playing total support (*cough* medic *cough*), someone on your team still has to bear the burden.
3: This game is nearly, if not, five years old right now at the time I originally typed this. As a result of EA and DICE having released
Battlefield 4, the game feels less populated than it once was, which is a damn shame. The game released after BC2 is billed as a sequel to the 2005 original Battlefield 2, but it just feels like a watered down BC2 in retrospect. I wanted to like the game, but it just didn't feel the same, and I kept looking back to Bad Company 2 because EA and DICE just seemed to... get it more on the mark, in my opinion at least. True, it does have quite a few flaws, and some rigs may not be totally optimized for the game even if they are technically able to run the game itself, but it has a charm, and I guess I have a soft spot for this game myself. Maybe that's just my ability to adjust to its crap factor, though. I dunno.
If there ever is a sequel to Bad Company 2, I'd be interested to at least look at it. But I'd be praying it's not gonna look like
Battlefield 4. BC2's own sequel should look like the other Bad Company games; maybe touch up the graphics a little if they feel they should, but besides the point. It should also play like those games as well; maybe nerf a few weapons or snap that bolt hipfire anomaly. That is just my opinion, though, and obviously I have to see it for myself to believe it can hold true. But the route EA DICE went
makes me doubt if they could make a game that is nearly as good anymore.
That being said, I like this game. Will you find enjoyment in this game, too? Probably. Probably not. Obviously it depends on your taste or if you even like FPS games at all. But check it out when you see a sale pop up sometime.
EDIT: Don't get me wrong. BF4 is pretty good.

You'll walk out with loads of intel that would've taken you hours to get any of the other ways.
It's a fun game for a few hours and worth it for the nostalgia but everyone out there who is saying it needs a remake is dead wrong. The elements of Covert Action have been done in dozens of other games in more modern implementations. Deus Ex: Human Revolution does a lot of this stuff very well. Then there are the Splinter Cell games, Alpha Protocol and the newer Fallouts that all share some elements with Covert Action but have done them in more modern ways. And I suspect that Sid Meier is aware of that since it's one of the few games he hasn't seen fit to revisit.

A wonderful game! I can't believe this was released in 1990! It has great graphics, depth, and functionality for the time period. Reading the 60-70 page manual is a must. If you can commit yourself to that, there's a very immersive game waiting for you.
What I really like is the subject matter. You are Max Remington, the world's only free-lance spy. So good, you only work at the direct request of the American President. At his request, you'll investigate vast conspiracies, uncover clues, find the culprits, and arrest them before they can commit their devastating crimes. An intriguing premise (if not the most realistic), but what really makes this game stand out is it was made at that special time where the Berlin Wall had fallen, but the Soviet Union had not yet collapsed. As such, your enemies aren't the KGB (though the KGB has a presence) but other international terrorists. It's really fascinating from a historical perspective.
I hear that Sid Meier himself was not pleased with his game overall. He said that the game of having combat with enemy agents detracted too much from piecing together clues to solve crimes, and vice-versa. From this experience he created the "Covert Action Rule," where a game should not divert its attention. For example, in Civilization, if a unit fights another unit, you don't switch to a RTS game and fight out the battle, you just resolve it and move on with the Civilization game. To Sid Meier I would say: "You overestimate this 'flaw'!" Look at how popular the Total War series is, which does exactly what he describes! Personally, I don't think the combat game detracts from the 'solving mystery' game at all. It wouldn't feel like a real spy game if you couldn't break into hideouts, photograph evidence, and capture criminal masterminds.
If you can stand playing old DOS games and have free time to commit to learning the game, I wholeheartedly recommend it. I wouldn't expect a remake to ever happen: we're just too far away from Cold War politics for a game like this to work in the modern Global War on Terror-era.

Close Combat: Gateway to Caen is an excellent Close Combat game that details Operation Epsom, a British plan to flank German positions at Caen to basically create a short cut into the city, whilst at the same time taking down German defenders at the Odon river. Historically, it was a costly battle for both Axis and Allies, and technically the Allies won, as German defenders committed all of their armour to close the gap, essentially wasting their fuel and vehicles on re-establishing their positions on the river Odon after the initial British attack. The British, as said, paid a high price, as they were up against veteran armour 'fresh' from the eastern front, that chewed up British armour like nothing else. The battle could have gone either way, and so the 'what if' factor is perfect for a game where you can play both sides.
Gateway to Caen takes some getting used to if you are a veteran of the CC series. Unit scale is back to somewhat smaller, and unit choices per battle when playing the grand campaign are somewhat more limited. This is by no means a bad thing as you are finally forced to truely consider what you field when. When playing the campaign, as troops grow tired you HAVE to rotate them out every so many battles, or they eventually panic/surrender, no matter what their quality.
Units included in the game are, amongst others, 2nd & 12th SS Panzer ('Das Reich'& the infamous 'Hitlerjugend' fanatics), The Royal Scots Fusiliers, the 46th Highland infantry brigade, 9th RTR and 43rd Wessex Infantry division.
The main campaign is pretty well balanced: Generally speaking the British forces outnumber the Germans with what they can field at any given time, but the Germans often outgun the British with their heavy armour and 88mm Flak batteries. German troops do consist mainly of 'ad hoc' defenders initially, making for a pretty steep start when playing Germans, despite the prepared positions and the big guns.
On my YouTube channel, I dedicated a series to this game, playing the main campaign as the Germans, check it out here:
I recommend this game to anyone interested in World War 2 gaming and the Close Combat series in general.

Strap in kids, and grab your Gas Masks. This is, still, one of the best virus games out there.
The customization of the plagues you create is amazing and almost endless. You won't win every time, even if you follow a guide. I named one of my plagues "Trump" he was a parasite, and he infected the world before any symptoms happened.... then went on to make everyone insane and suicidal. I thought it was great.
Cons would have to be the RNG of some messages not showing up, few bugs here and there but nothing game breaking. just minor annoyances. I could see a few ways of updating the game to nerf the cure bar a little to make it so there isn't only one way to beat the game with a fungus. And lastly, there isn't much of the game, it's more like an App (considering it started as a mobile game I could see why.) I would like to see more content, maybe more ways to stop the cure, a more in-depth look at the virus, maybe customize the virus' looks... Who doesn't want to see a neuro worm with a top-hat and monacle?
In conclusion. I give this game a solid 7 out of 10. Highly recommend.

The most powerful unit in the game is the "Troop transport" that can shoot units 2 spots away, even cities, go figure???
Another thing is the trade screen.  Here you can set up trades and have them repeat each turn. Except that it does not work right.  If you set up a trade for 500 food and you sell 100 food then next turn the repeat option is only for 400 food so you have to do it again anyways. jotun is a masterclass in atmosphere, presentation, artwork and mythology. if you are remotely interested in norse mythology - you will enjoy this game. you don't need to be a lover of boss battles or difficulty to enjoy this game; i don't consider myself to be one of those people and i enjoyed it nonetheless, and the difficulty was never to frustrating or felt impossible for me.
jotun is the story of thora, a viking warrior who died an inglorious on the high seas. in order to reach valhalla, the gods have given her a second chance – she must defeat of the terrifying Jotun, giants determined to stop her from reaching valhalla.
i loved the addition that thora spoke in her native tongue, and the dialogue translations that ran across the screen were always powerful and a nice addition. the artwork is phenomenal - the hand-drawn style really brings everything to life with vibrancy and color. boss battles are the main focus of the game, but the levels in between reduced that huge focus and were never boring or uninteresting, despite thora's slow walking pace. the visuals were always enticing and wonderful and never were uninteresting or seemed like a continuous repetition of what the player saw before. the boss battles were tense and gripping, and did well to make usage of only two major attacks modes, and the additions of god powers served the player well.
the practically only problem i think anyone would have with this game are the achievements. if you're the type to 100% every game you ever encounter, you may dislike this game. achievements are difficult and meant to be difficult, and requires a complete mastery of god power timings and how to use your move set efficiently and effectively.
tldr; jotun is completely worth its price tag - even if you don't enjoy boss battles, if you're into norse mythology or breathtaking visuals, you'll find a home here.

I knew I was going to spend some time with ths game when I found myself zooming in on the map so I could see the details, read the spraypainted graffiti on the wall, and try to figure out just what story was being told with the scenery in a house that was no more important to the storyline than holding three zombies to fight and a little bit of random loot.
I like strategic games, I like building games, I like RPG's, and I really liked the Fallout series of games. Any game that is going to give me a dog companion (a perk available in the game) to face the post-apocalyptic future, zombie-filled or otherwise, is going to get my attention. A shelter filled with unique occupants with interesting backstories, single player combat that I have to worry about more than my current health to survive, and wanting to see what new thing happens tomorrow is going to keep my attention for a while.
IF you prefer FPS/realtime over turn based games, cannot stand bugs in games, or want the latest and greatest in game graphics think twice before buying this game.
IF you like games where you go back to earlier saves to try something different, unexpected "monkey wrench" challenges to your plans, and games that tell a story I think you'll like this one.
It is a travel around an area map in search of locations for encounters kind of game that has base management, personalitiy conflicts you must settle, and a humor to it.
Combat, which is turn based, isn't deep but its' different. Worrying about allies panicing, how much noise is being made, and if a combatant you thought dispatched and done with will get up again to attack you as a zombie are things I haven't had to deal with in combat before. It IS a zombie game full of zombies. Slow, simple, easy to kill one. Trying to balance noise that attracts more of them against the noise made killing them isn't as easy. Neither are the human enemies you come up against, some of which can be quite challenging the first time you meet them - especially if you are underarmed or underarmored. The variety of weapons is pretty extensive. I have three hundred hours in it and I have not tried them all with their different kinds of attacks.
This is a game I have enjoyed coming back to and seeing what was improved on in every patch and update. I am willing to put up with bugs to play a good Alpha or Beta game. Why anyone would want to go back to waiting months for a patch that tries to fix everything instead of an incremental improvement/feedback loop I will probably never understand. As often as this game has been updated to fix the remaining bugs and incoroprate player suggestions I'm sure I will be playing it off and on for some time to come.
Think you'll enjoy it. I did.

So basically you are a potato smith in a potato universe. You are taking over for your deceased grandfather, who was a great potato smith. You get to name your smith, and I being the creative person I am (sarcasm) named him potato. You own his 0.01% of the weapon shop. Agent supposedly owns the other 99.9% and he claims that your grandfather and he had made this deal. The following may be a spoiler: Agent seems reluctant to talk about himself, your grandfather, and the past. I haven’t finished the game yet but I’m suspicious of agent.
So anyway, your mission is to craft many weapons to sell to heroes around the universe. Each hero has a preference of the type of weapon and what stats he likes. There are four stats: attack, speed, accuracy, and magic. You can also research new weapons and that gives you the ability to craft that weapon. Once you move onto the next universe, you cannot research weapons in the previous universe, so I suggest you research all of them before moving on.
In the beginning, you start off with 3 employees. Later on you gain/hire more. The staff can gain experience for crafting, selling, and exploring and level up. Each member can boost a skill that they are assigned to. Once they reach max level, they won’t gain xp anymore and you have the option of changing their skill (attack, speed, accuracy, or magic).
The story line is really interesting and enjoying. The dialog is great. You know how some games you want to skip the dialog? This isn’t one of them. I really love all the puns and music references. I also love the characters’ personality. There are trivia and random events that keep the game engaging.
I think this game would make a good mobile game. It’s the kind of game I’d like to play on the go. If it were available for mobile or some other handheld device, I’ll get it right away.
The graphics are wonderful and clean. I love looking at it. And the colors are perfect. Not too bright or dark. I don’t know how to explain it but the graphics, colors, and game play are seriously wonderful.
I did have some trouble with lag and freezing, usually when I change areas (ie from shop to map) HOWEVER I’m not sure if it’s from the game itself or from my computer. And I’m really suspecting it’s from my end but I’m not 100% sure. But this doesn’t hinder the game or make it unplayable, and it sure isn’t a brother (not like dota lag/freeze). You can easily ignore it – it isn’t annoying or a pain.
In summary,
Graphics 10/10
Color 10/10

Game play 10/10

tl;dr
Anyways, this game is pretty simple for an RPG. It's a turn-based battle system where you can choose between attacking with your weapon, using skills, items, and delaying your turn.
When you defeat enemies you get SP and most often items/gold, too. You use this SP to buy permanent stat bonuses for your character from their class "line." It's not a branching tree with different skills to choose or anything like that, it's a simple line with occasionally a choice between one stat boost or another and some skills down the line. Once you finish the first class line  you can choose one of the other 6 class lines for "Level 1." So if you were in the Slayer I line you'd get to choose to start Thief, Trickster, Elementalist, Healer, or Guardian I line. After your second line you go up to the 2nd class line so you'd have a choice between Slayer, Guardian, Healer, Elementalist, Trickster, or Thief II. Rinse and repeat. Keep in mind that you're not likely going to have access to the previous skills of any class for a character if you bypass it. So you might want to choose your classes based on which skills that class will get, but you don't get definitions of the skills until you're committed down that class line.
Don't worry terribly much about stats, because those can be balanced with wearing certain equipment that you can upgrade with Scrap Metal and gems you come across. Scrap metal can be found in battle, stolen from some enemies, or later on purchased in a shop.
There's more to the game, but I don't want this review to be too long so in short there's a lot to this simple game. You fight monsters, you focus on how you want your character to level up, you can play minigames, fight bosses, grind all you want, and play through the game at your own pace.

I am torn on this game.
On the one side I love zombie survival games with scavenging and trying to keep alive in a setting where all the odds are stacked against you. The world is nicely presented through the writing, allthough, in not too long you will start to see events play out that you've experienced before and it starts to feel a bit dry. I also love that there's contextual use for certain items and skillsets for the other survivors should you happen to have the appropriate ones with you.
On the other hand, it's easy to grow tired of the unceasing slaps that the game doles out to you when  the dice do not fall in your favour, and yes there seems to be quite a bit of dice rolling behind the scenes in this game. At one point I had two survivors who were both starting to feel the wear of travelling and needed to rest. When you're in a city you can search for a safe space to rest in, which sounded like a good idea at first. The catch is that when you search for a place like this you run the risk of running into zombies, but I thought little of it as I had only met zombies rarely while doing this.
First attempt I ran into seven zombies. With two survivors and little ammo left I decided that it wasn't really worth the trouble and fled. The game decided that doing this was to be punished by losing my other survivor. Even though the zombies only appeared from one side of the screen. You can never flee an encounter without risking loosing one of your partymembers or loose gear. Aside from the events where the game asks you if you want to approach something, it is never an option to refrain from combat with the undead without some kind of repercussion, which I find forced and ridiculous.
Searching for a second time led my main guy into a gaggle of five more zombies, which at that point I HAD to flee, which lost me my best weapon. Searching for a place to rest a third time ALSO led me into a group of undead, but at this point my main guy was so tired of trying to find a place to rest he simply died of fatigue on the spot.
Aside from that I've had survivors instantaneously die from hunger right after travelling because the health meter takes a hit immediately if you allow the hunger meter to fill up, instead of gradually taking damage after it's filled, which would avoid those annoying events alltogether.
Or the events where you roll the dice and either things go well or you get to nominate one of your party to either take a slight hit or get fatally wounded. An example of this is an event where you come across a point where a road has been blocked by a fallen tree and loads of cars. You get three choices in this event; Navigate between the cars, climb over the fallen tree or skip the whole issue alltogether and go through the woods.
Having played a good few zombie games and seen a rather large number of zombie movies I figured moving in between the cars would be bad as there would most likely be undead still strapped in the car, and climbing over the tree sounded like an event where one of the survivors would fall off. So I headed into the forest to go around. No dice, it was full of undead. So I decided the tree was the least dangerous of the two remaining options. The survivors I sent up and over promptly fell off the tree and hurt himself. In a second game I came across the same situation and decided to go for the cars. And Lo and Behold, there was a zombie hidden among the cars who grabbed my survivor and bit him in the foot, incidentially the same guy who fell off the tree in the previous example, so maybe he was just a plain unlucky guy.
I wouldn't mind these outcomes so much if there was a hint towards how successful either of these actions would be in the text, but no such luck. The game throws the dice behind the scenes and either saves you or dooms you in the process.
Luckily, the survivors, aside from the few paragraphs you get about them when you initally meet them, turned out to be pretty faceless up and until where I've played so far. This meant that everyone in the party aside from the main character, served as risk sponges, item mules and a means for safety in numbers. I'd have loved for there to be little snippets about the characters in your party and how you get along with them, the partymembers weighing in when something happens, ANYTHING just to have some kind of impact when the random dice decide that someone needs to die.
I on the other hand found the game not quite my cup of tea for the reasons described above.

neg: (so, it could use a little more work... these are mainly notes to the developer here from one indie dev to another. Like I said, the game is already cool and interesting and worth supporting.)
- when you're alt+tabbed out of the game it needs to pause the game and turn off the sound. It's pretty annoying that the sound and music keeps playing when I'm trying to do something out of the game.

(Open up FTL and look at their UIs to see what I mean. They even have add a slight glow to a lot of UI elements. It might seem kind of dumb, cause players wouldn't focus on most of that stuff. - I'll just be straight with this point and say the maps looks terrible. For example, FTL maps are gorgeous. I hope the maps here will get some actual graphics eventually. I wish Steam didn't have a binary score system, because this game isn't that bad.
That said, even though I'm going to give it a couple more tries, I think there are more negatives than positives here.
I like the loot system overall. It's nice that ammo and food just stack without taking up space, and I like that people barter and that some people "collect" otherwise crappy loot, making you actually think twice about throwing away glasses and bobbleheads. I like the map system and that the random encounters are frequent, varied, and that they can have different outcomes.
I don't like the combat. If all you have to do to avoid getting wrecked is to move, why can't there be some AI for your buddies to move out of the way once in awhile? Having to control them just as much as your main guy just makes it that much harder to keep him alive. I also don't like the difficulty "curve." I was having a very successful run until I got into one fight in the second zone where suddenly I had no reaction time to move my guys out of zombie range. My main guy died before I realized he was even in danger, and he had a Semi-Automatic Pistol, so shouldn't he be attacking at least as fast as the zombie?
Areas where improvement would be nice include smaller map "zones," since the random generation just makes for weird routes and like fifty places per zone that you just ignore. Another thing would be an "empty clip" option in the management screen. If you find a better weapon than the one you have, your precious bullets are stuck in the worse gun. Some variation in barter values would also be cool. A guy on the road with 5 handgun bullets to his name wouldn't part with them as easily as the defined trading post that has 30 of them. Finally, I got a car. I had to have a certain character in my group and had to fight off a group zombies, but getting the car fixed up did absolutely nothing, so far as I could tell. It doesn't even appear on the side of the road when you stop or anything. Are you planning to update that, or what? I should at least be able to move across two points on the map at a time or get trunk space for items. What was the point?
Overall, I like the game and would have recommended it if it weren't so frustrating.

This is one of the best games I've ever played.
This game is from the era of Microprose games that expertly combined mini-games using a cohesive big picture to give them context and motivation. Its siblings are Sword of the Samurai and Pirates! (the modern remake of which is available on Steam as well, at
, and also highly recommended).
You play as freelance spy Max Remmington, contracted to the CIA, and your job is to foil terrorist attacks before they can occur. You do this by gathering evidence against the members of the conspiracy through wiretapping, stakeouts, infiltrating and searching their hideouts, or simply following them in your car. Once you have the evidence you need, you pounce on them and bring them in. The trick is to let the conspiracy progress far enough that you can implicate everyone involved without spooking them and sending them to ground, while still preventing the attack from actually happening.
How you approach the case is totally up to you. You could wiretap the local cartel hideout in the hopes of catching some encrypted message, then take it back to the CIA office to crack the code. Or you can infiltrate the hideout yourself, plant bugs, photograph documents (with your super spy camera) and slip out before the guards notice you. When it's time to haul in the bad guys, you could go in with guns and grenades, or you could go with a high-speed car chase.
Each conspiracy you thwart gets you one step closer to identifying and capturing the leader of one of the terrorist factions involved. The overall, eventual goal of the game is to wipe out every one of these organisations by arresting and convicting each leader.
This game is dated in its interface and graphics, but otherwise stands up remarkably well. When I say this is one of the best games ever, I do so with no nostalgia goggles on - I first played it 15 to 20 years AFTER its release in 1990, as abandonware. I've bought it now for the first time.
The one flaw in the game that jumps out is that the number of different encrypted message texts are rather limited considering how many cases you need to play if you want to capture every single terrorist leader. After a while you recognise the texts fairly quickly, which makes cryptography quite easy. Still, you'll be tens if not hundreds of hours into the game by the time you reach this point.
Note also that you will need to read the PDF manual, as this game predates in-game tutorials. It's well worth it, however.
edit: I see Steam doesn't actually include the manual yet, which is inexplicable to me. It's worth tracking down. At the very least, you will need the controls, which I've found at
edit again: it turns out pdf copies of the manual and technical supplement (which is where the controls are) are actually included in the Steam\steamapps\common\Sid Meier's Covert Action. That said, my technical supplement is apparently "Handbuch.pdf" and is entirely in German. Not as helpful as if it were in English, but it's a start! ;)
Overall: highly, highly recommended.

[TL;DR]
NOTHING NEW HAS BEEN ADDED.
IT IS LITERALLY THE SAME GAME AS FROM 2001, EXCEPT IT COMES WITH THE PRICE OF A BRAND NEW GAME ($40) WHICH, BEING RELEASED A YEAR AGO, IT IS NOT.
IT IS STILL A GREAT GAME, JUST NOT AT THIS PRICE. WAIT FOR A MASSIVE SALE (LIKE 75-90% OFF).
I bought this as part of a Humble Bundle, so my frustration is not completely about the price, but I will address it in a bit.
My biggest concern is that, even as a fan of the original series, this company (Slitherine) is attempting to call this a new game... it's not.
It had been mentioned in another review, but it is also quite apparent when playing, that it is the same engine, the same assets (although 32bit, which i think is a lie because it looks the same as the 15 year old CC:III), and the same artwork. It has been a while since I played CC:IV Invasion Normandy, but I recall that the maps in this game are taken from CC:IV.
Normally I wouldnt have a problem with all that I mentioned above, afterall I looked at this game from the perspective of being an update/remake of a game that I loved. The problem is; they didn't do a damn thing to update it. NOTHING.
The strategic map was taken from the older games. The RPG-ish elements of having command and soldiers throughout multiple battles/campaigns was taken from the older games.
Absolutely nothing has been done to this game to separate it from the old games, which again, being a huge fan of the old games would normally be OK. Except for one huge thing...
THE PRICE. Now being that I paid $10 for this in a humble bundle, I don't feel like I have been swindled. But I can sympathize with those that paid $40.00 for this game thinking that it was some new iteration of the CC series.
This may be hyperbolic, but, Slytherine should be ashamed of themselves. I can only imagine how many people have been tricked into buying this game at the price of $40.00.
$40.00!!!! Let that sink in.
I will wrap this up by saying this... I paid $10 and sent almost all of the $10 to charity. I gave slitherine one cent.
One cent is about how much effort was put into this game.
That may sound really harsh, but again, I am a huge fan of this series and I am going to continue playing this game, but not without constantly feeling lucky that I didn't pay full price for it.

Lup is yet another game in a line of shovelware released by publisher Back to Basics Gaming in an attempt to rake in quick money using steam trading cards. While I cannot say for certain whether it is a Unity asset flip (where a developer purchases cheap models and textures off the Unity Asset Store and attempts to "flip" it into a shovelware title for a profit), the possibility certainly exists given how the player character is an undetailed 2D sprite and most of the world is low-polycount 3D models that look like they came from several different artists.
This game is a bog-standard shovelware platformer in which you control a poorly-drawn sprite with a gun that fires lag-inducing particle effects, whose ultimate goal is to run through a handful of forgettable stages, avoiding lag-incuding particle effects shot from various enemies (most of which look like turrets taken from a stock Unity asset pack). Getting hit simply reduces your health by a wildly varying amount - most enemies do little damage, but some will kill you in one or two hits seemingly at random - and causes knockback in a random direction. There are also pits and "lava", which range in lethality from "tiny amount of damage and a ton of upwards knockback" to "your sprite has gotten stuck, please wait 50 seconds to die".
There are a whole bunch of game mechanics that simply don't matter, from picking up ammo boxes to upgrade your weapon (which seemingly does the same amount of damage regardless of upgrade level) to picking up coins and green orbs that as far as I can tell do absolutely nothing but increase your score.
I should also mention that the game's in-game menus do not work properly. There is no way (at least, that I know of) to return to the title screen from inside the game, nor is there a properly working "exit" button on the title screen - there is an exit button, but it doesn't actually do anything when clicked.
Lup can be finished in as little as 20 to 25 minutes in a casual playthrough. I have 8+ hours in it mostly because I have made poor life choices and chose to speedrun it as a way of increasing the visibility of shovelware on Steam.
Overall, this game is garbage and I would recommend that no one purchase anything from Back to Basics Gaming - even for the trading cards.

Take an evil role of a plague. Be bacteria, parasite, virus, or another disease and bend the future to your vision. The main goal of the game is pretty simple – exterminate the human race. But the game offers more...
Would your disease be the one which eradicates human race? Will your pathogen write down in history as the one which almost decimated mankind but didn’t have the endurance to finish the job? Would you like to turn people into zombies, vampires or slaves? Well who would’t like that! The game offers this and more through 10 disease types, some would say why so little. Still there are many ways you can choose to develop your unique disease. Or as it seems at the first sight, after a while you will see the repetitiveness.
You can obtain DNA (or RNA) points which allows your sickness to develop in many ways. Endurance in extreme conditions, imunity against antibiotics, new ways of transmision via air, water or animals; symptoms doing all the nasty things you would like to avoid in real life and more. This is I would say main feature of the game, because other parts aren’t so engaging for the player. Clicking on bubbles which pop up a lot on the world map is the part of the game where you will spend time the most. Maybe it‘s nice to see the map indicating how your disease is spreading, but the bubbles become irritating after a while, but you gotta keep clicking on them because of the progress! This is what makes the game after a while very repetitive and after 20 minutes you will see everything what you can do in the game and the rest is pure grind. So I see why there are a lot of events, out of which some are rare, but most of them also repeat reguralry. If you kept reading to this point you ask why should you buy the game? I would say it’s not some blockbuster, but still it is entertaining from time to time.
✪
– Your virus or another kind of plague can mutate and develop. Main feature of the game is fun, but still I miss larger scale, so large you don‘t know what to choose. Even though the lack of DNA points makes you carry out tough decisions.
✪
- The game offers various events, which are sometimes realistic, sometimes funny and rarely important.
✪
- Turn people into zombies, rise apes against humanity, or choose one of 20 other scenarios making the world different place from the one we know now.
✪
Offers a nice diversion from static singleplayer. There are two possibilities, you can cope with your friend on wiping out human race. Or you can compete! Who kills the most, wins.
✪
– As I said before this is not a game which you‘ll play for hours and hours. Just a while before you get bored, still it’s not an obstacle. I would consider this game a daily quest.
✪
– Maybe you will not like this, but it’s a mobile game originally and I don’t see a big difference between this and a mobile version. Maybe I had too big expectations.
✪
– Once you start a game there usually isn’t much to do than to wait for DNA points or another special action according to the type of plague you chose.

This game deserves a chance. Expect a few hours of entertainment. It’s not an AAA title, it‘s not an ultra amazing game, but it is fun and the price suits the product.  Over average simulator.

I enjoyed my time with Firewatch. I love the art style and the voice acting was amazing.
As an adult gamer in my 40s, themes such as mortality, fidelity, depression, loss and the stresses of life resonate far more with me now than they would if I was 20 or 30 years younger. While I was certainly drawn in by the suspense of the game's narrative, the only fear I felt was the idea of actually living in the protagonists' shoes and facing losing my own wife. That, my friends, is called empathy. And if you can create empathy, then you're a damn fine storyteller.
I've seen criticisms about the game's length and it's value. While I certainly understand that $20 means different things to different people, I've never fully agreed with the benchmark of hours per dollar equating to value. With Firewatch, for example, my time playing the game came in at around four hours. But my time thinking about the game afterwards has easily tripled that.
Similarly, criticisms of the game's abrupt ending puzzle me as well. While it's true that games and stories on other mediums often follow very clear, complete arcs, life doesn't work that way. Things happen unexpectedly. Lives end abruptly. We're always planning for a tomorrow without realizing tomorrow is never a guarantee. After losing my own father both abruptly and unexpectedly this year, I can attest to that.
In the end, how you feel about Firewatch, and how much you are able to appreciate its story, may depend greatly on you. If you lack the context of personal life experiences, then the maturity of these themes may be lost on you. For those players, maybe all they see is a "walking simulator". (Personally I think that descriptor is overly-reductive, and says more about the person using it than it does the game they're playing.) But for anyone like me who has had to state some of these things in the face in my own life, the game is far more than just the sum of its parts.
I highly recommend it.

A great JRPG, but only for fans who're fond of the formula. If you do no like Final Fantasy, or others in this genre, then this game is not for you. The game runs smoothly, and the glitches are small, such as dismantling a talisman giving an amethyst instead of a sapphire. The story is present, and not horrible, but able to be skipped. It has a few easter eggs buried in here for those who look, but other than that the story is a basic JRPG one, saving the world from ancient disaster, all that kind of stuff. Playing the original browser game is uneeded to understand the story, although they do make some jokes for those who've played it.
Combat is good, with higher level enemies and bosses needing a fair amount of planning to defeat. Most fights aside from the bosses are able to be avoided, and grinding is not needed until the post-game, if you play your cards right. Plus the battle arena makes grinding coming down to mostly skill. The boss fights are somewhat sub-par to FF standards, but the final boss meets this just fine. For the price, it gives a few hours of enjoyment, plenty of side quest bosses, plus a very challenging post game that really pushes you.
In terms of tips, the battle area x is great for gaining levels and items post game, plus the stat boost items when using dice. Never use alchemy for equipment other than weapons because you can find those as drops, and use the alchemy deconstruction on the start and last stat boost equipment to rack up as much scrap needed to upgrade weapons as possible. Pray to RNJesus for dice and other rare gear early on, Hold off from buying items in bulk until you get the 25% discount in the water temple, get only what you need until then. The locked blue chests contain rare cards, and the key is hidden in the final level, so don't stress yourself looking how to open it. Save rare items like elixer brews and rocket burst bombs for the final boss fight. Don't be afraid to have a charactor take a different class for a level, as gaining important skills, like buffs, is important since every charactor learns different spells from the same class. Debuffs can fail, and its best to use one with a speedy charactor who can cast them in rapidly to hope one lands on the boss (speedy thief is best for this). Finally, your weapon level decides your ultimate, so you cannot get the achievements for using them until they're level 2 or above, and you unlock the final one at level 4,

-Stylized graphics and art design, doesnt have to be top notch HD to be very charming and loveable
-Overall an immensely enjoyable experience
My only problems, which were just nitpicky things that didnt really affect my experience:
-The level-up screen is a bit laggy if you're on the Main Map area, but it's corrected immediately as soon as you go into a town to level-up (My guess is that it just opens a new window and leaves the Main Map animations/environment still loading and active, thus as it tries to do level-up animations it's just doing alot at once)
-You can't delete a save file, which may seem very minor, but i have 1 save i play on and i accidentally saved in another slot, and i dont like seeing the unused save file XD
-When you want to craft a weapon it doesnt tell you the stats of the item, only the effect, but i can see why if you can just upgrade an item with scrap metal you dont necessarily care about stats, only the unique buff
All in all, for 3 bucks or however much this game costs, its a great buy and tons of fun. Im kinda sad i bought this on sale, i wish i could have given the developer(s) the full price XD

I've played this game for over a year now, starting way back when it was limited to a 7 day run.  In that time, it has grown and evolved immensely.  If you've played games such as Fallout 1-2. Brotherhood of Steel, or the Final Fantasy Tactics games, or even any of the X-COM franchise, new or old, the isometric view and turn based combat will be familiar and nostalgic.
The game is not a graphical powerhouse, and was never intended as such, it is much more focused on the story, on the myriad and drastically varied group of people thrust together into a desperate survival situation.
Every one of the more then 40 characters is unique, from the first handful you start out with to the dozens more you can find and recruit over time, they each have their own desires, demands, and (in some cases) psychosis.
The zombies, while an ever present obstacle, aren't the real threat, but then, they really never are.  From as far back as the first forays into the genre, (Night of the Living Dead, Dawn of the Dead, etc,) the zombies are a foe, but not the major threat.  The major threat is, as always, other people.  The dead are easy to predict, simple and direct.  Your living foes, the duplicitious, under handed, cruel, desperate or just good old fashioned bat crap crazy other survivors of this world of central Texas are where the real challenge lays.  They are, by their very nature, completely unpredictable, and profoundly deadly.
Over all, this game, while it certainly does have its rough spots, is absolutely worth the money.  The dedication and detail that the development team has put into this title shows through any of the realtively minor remaining bugs, and will likely provide many hours of enjoyment.
UPDATE:
The Reanimated rerelease, update, add-on, what ever you want to call it, adds a lot more polish and even a small amount of new content for no additional price.  While it was a game worth picking up a year ago, it still is, remaining a rare gem of the early access system.

Dead state is a convoluted little game.
Overall, it is obviously competentenly made, but it is also obvious that over the course of development mistakes were made and nobody quite bothered rectifying them.
The problem with this is that all the glaring little errors that managed to escape scrutiny appear late in game, precisely by the time it has you by the balls, you are having the time of your life, and naturally you are expecting the situation to escalate, but it doesn't. Instead, it just folds up like a house of cards.
All of this looks like a result of a terrible lack of oversight, and in too many areas.
Well, since I'm no professional gaming journalist, let's just make an obtuse little list.
So here we go, in no particurlar order:
Balancing issues - there are precisely three tiers of armor in the whole game. One is, to put it mildly,♥♥♥♥♥♥and has all the usefulness of a wet tissue paper. The other excludes zombies from the list of viable threats completely. Finally, the third one is a ballistic vest and and any other armor with a better defence rating. You put those kevlar sunday suits on, you never have to worry about anything ever again, nothing can seriously harm you anymore, which instantly turns the game into a glorified mall looting simulator. Everything else can be worked with, but if you're making a combat-heavy game and then take any thrill out of it, you aren't exactly gunning for a favorable impression. And you can get the goddamn vests fairly early in-game, too. I've got my first three around day 18 or so, and that's not that far into the game at all, and I didn't stumble upon them either - an NPC directed me there.
Speaking of the loot, Dead State is a damn good looting simulator. There are all sorts of neat little locations you can shamelessly rob, tons of people you can liberate from their stuff, and in general it is very satisfying to haul bags of freshly stolen military rations back to your hideout. Or at least it would be, if you didn't have to wrestle with the inventory every time you have to do that. If you are trying to haul a serious load, you will have to click a gajillion times though at least three menus. And you will end up having to do just that, because, as you progress through the game, your character roster will expand and expand and expand, even if you suffer losses, there will be ample replacements, and all those buggers will want to eat, if nothing else.
Hovever, the interface problems don't really end there. For example, you can't really view character stats and inventory on the same screen, so often you have to backtrack between two different tabs to see what exacly you should be arming mr. New Guy with so he wouldn't blow his♥♥♥♥♥up or. All of this would be acceptable if you were dealing with a game lke  W2, where new party members are few and far between, but nope, no dice, there is a huge roster of potentially available characters and you will have to rotate them from time to time.
There are also a lot of smaller questionable design decisions, and them being lacking is often apparent in the late game - for example, the way zombies cannot pose any threat to you no matter the numbers. You are never risking getting bum-rushed, mobbed, dragged to ground and eaten, when facing a big group - not any more than during a one-one fight, which kinda goes against the conventions of zombie genre, because them shamblers are supposed to have strength in numbers. But no, as far as the game is concerned, there is very little practical difference between a fighting a mob of zeds and fighting them mano a mano.
Speaking of which, balance issue notwithstanding, the combat system leaves a lot to be desired. It would be acceptable in a 20-hours game, but, once again, the deeper you get, the more obvious its lack of depth is and it's not going to get any better, because the few options it can offer are laid out in front of you from the beginning.
Finally, the plot. Without getting too much into details, I was pretty disappointed to learn about the ending. While execution was par the course, there  was much more promise to it. See, there were all sorts of little breacrumbs with omnious hints here and there, but it turned out they've had zero relation to the plot itself. In addition, it appears that some content was straight out cut, and the threads were just left there hanging.
There's also an issue with the bugs ranging from mildly annoying to game-breaking, but discussing those is pointless. Indie studios like Double Bear can hardly afford quality QA, and whatever the reason for game being the way it is right now, the bugs can at least be fixed. Bad design is forever.
In general, Dead state is a game you can nitpick for a long time, but - credit where it's due - only because Dead State is a big game with a lot of effort put into it. There is a lot enviromental storytelling going on, the sound meter makes you think and use the situation to your advantage, since both living and the dead can react to you making a ruckus, there is a lot of characters with unique interactions, quest lines and personality qurks, the management aspect is interesting and adds another, much needed layer of complexity.
Problem is, though, for each and every one of these points there is counterpoint. The areas get duller and duller the further you venture from your starting point, the noise gimmick becomes meaningless because there is little combat difficulty to speak of, so you can just shrug and go in guns blazing, the character interaction is shallow and only manages to grab your interest by juggling characters around and never focusing on any of them - and that's actually a good thing, as this is a cardboad cutout fest worthy of the worst Bioware games, management aspect looks interesting but never delivers, because you won't ever find yourself starved for resources or even operating at a loss, and so on and so forth.
I guess it is worth its money, since I've got my 60 hours of entertainment out of it, but it's not worth the disappointment you will inevitably experience.
And that does the game in.

What I think about this game:
March of the Living Review:
March of the Living is a “you're ♥♥♥♥ed” simulator: whichever character you choose, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. You're given an objective and you have to set out on a randomly generated spider-webbed path, dealing with zamboozles and the living, all while juggling items and your own well-being. With each kilometer traversed your character (or party) will become fatigued and hungry, meaning you'll have to take less-than-opportune snack, potty, and nap breaks along the way. Since it's zombie country now there's a helpful gauge indicating how close the zombie growling is to you and, if it gets close enough, you'll be thrust into that weird FTL pause command strategy gameplay. You'll encounter sometimes as many as six zimbompos, and when you have a party of your own things can get crowded real quick. It's hard to tell pixels apart in the mosh pit but you can select actions outside of the fray using little character profiles on the top right.

Nice basic art style. Reminds me a little of Lone Survivor. The story decisions I had to make frequently gave me pause, as there is always a chance of getting badly hurt no matter how innocuous the situation at first seems to be. The tactical fights started off small but in time can get rather pitched and frantic, and I don't even have a full party gathered yet. A good 2D game if you want some excitement in your combat. Only a couple hours in and I'm eager to see how the character tales progress.

Jotun is a beautifully hand-drawn, top-down, exploration and boss-bashing game with some puzzles thrown in for good measure. Scandinavian Mythology is not often presented so well. Unlike those fussy gods, I'm impressed.
The artwork is something Hayao Miyazaki (Studio Ghibli) would approve of. It's one thing to make a game look good. Making it feel good is something else. Immersing a player takes artistry and talent, and the folks at Thunder Lotus Games have plenty of both. I won't say I couldn't put it down, but every time I picked it up, it transported me to another world.
Jotun's audio is as thoughtful as it is soothing. I love the warm voices, and the softly rolling Old Norse language stirs something in the Norwegian half of my cold, black, critic-heart.* The music changes appropriately with the environment, and the Jotun grunt satisfyingly when you give 'em the ax.
[PROS]
Choosing to subtly portray the protagonist as a female rather than a male was a stroke of genius. Thora's mighty braids and antlers won me over immediately.
There is no tutorial, but I think this is due to a desire to keep the player in the story. The controls aren't difficult to figure out (check the options for key mappings), and I love that I don't have to RTFM.
Exploration rewards have been hidden around the landscape, helping to alleviate an otherwise linear progression. At first, I was disappointed to see no representation of Thora's position on the map, but after playing for a while, I began to appreciate the added challenge and immersion this provides.
The camera slowly follows over the landscape, without being obtrusive or letting the action out of frame. Some of the negative reviews I read led me to believe otherwise. From what I've seen so far, they've fixed any issues they may have had, but sometimes you still have to be in just the right spot to see everything.
Save locations are plentiful and when you've completed your primary quest and are done exploring an area, you can quickly teleport back to Ginnungagap ("yawning void"). What a great name. I think I'll write it again, Ginnungagap.
Although I haven't finished it yet, I'm estimating around five hours of play once completed. Not bad for fifteen bucks.
[CONS]
Must I smash everything with my ax? I know that's the Viking way, but it 'd be good to see a little thoughtfulness pay off. (Why did I cut that eye-flower? Why? Bravely run away!)
Speaking of the combat, it takes a little getting used to. While the hack and slash is rather limited (consisting of one quick, light attack and one slow, heavy attack) each god bust you discover unlocks a new power. I don't honestly consider this a 'con', but it did garner some player complaints.
If you return to Ginnungagap, leaving an area incomplete, you may have to redo the puzzles in that area when you go back again. This happened to me with the constellations in The Northern Sky. I accidentally took a wrong turn and left before finishing, which left me having to solve the constellation puzzle a second time to complete the area. I want my five minutes back! I could've made a sandwich...
[The Vedict]
Overall, Jotun hits what I crave, so perhaps I'm a bit dazzled, but the Steam reviews seem to agree this is a fun game set at a reasonable price. I'm expecting great things in the future from Thunder Lotus Games. They appear to have done their research and provided one of the most authentic looks at Scandinavian lore ever set to a video game. It reminds me of my favorite teacher reading us those big, richly illustrated books in kindergarten. It deserves a Caldecott Medal. I can't wait to see what they come up with next. In the mean time, the free Valhalla Edition is set to release on September 9th, and promises, “an epic boss rush mode with even fiercer versions of the already challenging jotun.” This tells me the developer loves their game as much as I do, so I give a Solid 9. Well done.

I'd like to begin saying that I'm biased towards this series, seeing how I've played every installment since the first.
To me this is the optimal WW2-tactical game. What got me to like this series was how it got you close to the action and provided you with an efficient interface to command your combating soldiers. To me every battle I've played has been a mini *insert-your-favorite-war-flick-here*. Before long the battlefield is scarred by explosions and fire, the dead and dying are piling at the victory points and you are sitting by the keyboard ruing for Fritz or Cambell who's lying in ambush trying to capture that Sherman/Tiger-tank off-guard.
The strategy portion of the game is as it's been since it's inception and as always to me a distraction, I find the heart to be in the battles. Each battle can range from 30-60 minutes so set aside some time if you choose to play the campaign.
The system is impeccable, with only minor changes here and there from the previous games, and as always a wonderful historical accuracy. The battles and missions who are just based on history are noted as such.
The interface is the only main concern I have. But this may be because I'm so used to the bottom-centered interface after years of playing that I'm unable to get to grips with the changes. I haven't played so much yet so maybe after a couple of more hours I'll get a hold of the new setup.
Every battle is a story and if you have the time to dedicate you'll not be sorry. This is if you have a little interest for military history and good strategy games, but who doesn't? Now I just hope they'll start porting the classics too, I'd like to play The Russian Front and Invasion Normandy again, this time with support for multiplayer via Steam. Get to it!

This is a pretty shaky thumbs up from me.  Demise of Nations: Rome is a turn based strategy game set during the roman times.  You control several units, and have five resources that you have to manage.  As the game progresses, you research things like unit upgrades, buildings, and terrain upgrades.  The basic scenario starts out with Rome at war with a neighbor, and all other contries are neutral.
This game needs improvement.  During your turn, it gives no indication of which units need to move.  When you click on a space with an enemy unit as an action, it moves your unit there and only attacks if the enemy unit is still there.  There is no option for resource icons.  The game takes forever to run it's course, and the aforementioned flaws make winning annoying.  The tutorial, though improved since release, leaves much to be desired.  Capture the Flag mode is thouroughly broken.
The multiplayer isn't much better.  It takes coins to create a game, which take forever to regenerate.  Half of the time the game isn't created, and a fourth of the time the created game is unjoinable.  Server times are dismal.
The game has some pay content, mostly just extra maps and a generator.  I haven't seen the need to spend money on this, but the generator has promise.
But still, this game has potential.  It's still in early access, and Noble Master has done a good job of responding to bugs and likewise problems.  It's a fairly easy 100%, although the dev has said he might add more acheivements.  Plus, besides the extra maps, it's free.
With some improvement, this can be a great game.  I give it 6/10, so long as the Dev keeps it up.
EDIT -- 6/10/15
After about a month of development since I posted this review, this game has truly improved.
The tutorial is much better.  The We Go system is much better, and many of the single player flaws I mentioned are fixed.  Resource Icons are there, which makes it a lot easier to manage your land.  The new acheivements have been added, and some of them are quite difficult.
There have been some other changes too, but I found that playing this time arround was much easier than before.
New Rating: 8/10

You want opinions, well, here they are.
- The character interaction between the people at the shelter is fantastic.
All the characters have different likes and dislikes as well as personalities.
Some might be kind and helpful, other might be psychotic and one or two might be complete sociopaths who care for nobody besides themselves.
You also get to interact with them in a meaningful way at times, meaning you can at certain points steer them into choosing paths (for example there was one who asked me if they should be a better shot or a better harvester).
-The map. It's HUGE, there are so many places that you can visit that it's almost overwhelming at times. There are different types of locations from an abandoned gas station to a two story hospital and a nine-story hotel.
-Leveling
It's not your usual type of leveling, you don't level up by killing but by the goals you finish to better the shelter. For example, bring home 100 food and/or 50 luxury items. These can be mixed and done at random. One of my favorite is 'decrypting' data-discs by basically solving an anagram.
-The shelter/basebuilding
It's nothing fancy but it gets the job done. You have certain things you can build to improve the shelter, such as a sturdier fence or a car to be able to travel faster on the map. It's nothing extraordinary but it's effective and does what it's supposed to.
-Combat
Very simple and disappointing. However, since there are more than one faction (besides the zombies) you can now and then run into different groups fighting each-other and decide to either jump in and start killing or wait out to see who's the victor and then attack them.
Now for the bad parts.
-Bugs, bugs and more bugs
Some bugs can be annoying, such as not being able to loot certain stuff while others might be somewhat game-breaking (as event not triggering or not being able to fix broken things in the shelter). This is something that can and should put most people off from playing the game as of now since if you spent 40+ hours just to have everything break down and then make you wait til there's a patch that fixes it.
Because of the bugs I can't recommend this since I can't even finish the game due to CTD's at the end fight.
I would give this game 7 carrots out of 4 bears holding 20 poker-cards.

Dead State needs some serious rebalancing in the early stages... I'm all for gritty and realistic, but when it seems more than half the looters you encounter on your first day have guns, and you don't, it negatively impacts initial enjoyment as you watch your characters getting blown away in 2 shots, before you even land a single melee blow on the looter...
Additionally to this, the tutorial is virtually pointless and the manual does not give much more insight... Dead State lacks 'hover over' tool tips for character conditions, once again making early play arduous whilst you're trying to figure out what exactly is going on...
Dead State shows considerable potential, but IMO it feels as though it still requires alot of work before reaching it and I would not recommend buying Dead State as is...
If you don't mind your survivors getting blown away at the drop of a hat on your first day, while you're still trying to figure out the basics, then Dead State is almost certainly for you however...
**** ADDED AFTER 31 HOURS OF GAMEPLAY ****
Kept plugging away since I had paid for it and, once you actually manage to get a little armour and some better gear, Dead State actually starts to become quite enjoyable..
That is until you start getting better and better gear, at which time it becomes almost too easy... Zombies can barely inflict any damage and even gunfire is of little concern, only reiterating my previous assessment that rebalancing is required, not just in the early game, but even in the later stages.
The longer you play, the more bugs you will also encounter such as 'misplaced' enemies (sprite in a different location to where they are physically recognised by the game), to-do tasks that are never completed, unusual inventory management and item stacking anomalies and game events that do not seem to trigger correctly.
BIGGEST ISSUE NOW : after nearing the 30 hour play time mark, I am now encountering regular random CRASHES TO DESKTOP. There is absolutely no reason for this, as everything has been running fine until close to 25+ hours when I first started encountering CTD issues.
It's my suspicion that the more your explore, recover and improve your compound, the more unstable the game engine becomes, which would fit in line with what other people (and some professional reviews) have also mentioned.
Once again, even having invested 30 hours into Dead State, I would NOT recommend it in it's present release state and it requires considerable further work before it can be considered to be truely 'finished'...
It is my opinion that THIS IS NOT A FULL RELEASE GAME IN IT'S PRESENT STATE - IT IS LITTLE MORE THAN A LATE-STAGE PUBLIC BETA, THAT PRETENDS TO BE A FINAL RELEASE.
It might take a bit to click, but beneath the old fashioned layout and looks is a deeply enjoyable and sincere game.

I’ve been wanting to play Jotun for over a year but only recently, when the game was temporarily free, I picked it up. I like what Thunder Lotus Games was trying to do: explore Nordic mythology and fight giant bosses? Sounds great.
Boy was I disappointed. Boss fights might be the only interesting aspect of the game. The rest is unnecessarily long, slow, and content-less.
- Bosses are challenging, especially as the game progresses. Odin took more than a few tries.
- The guy in the well (Mimir) creeps me out. - the attention to detail here is fabulous. Great job.
- Good variety of God powers. The number of charges per power also seemed fair.
- You don’t come across Nordic mythology very often in video games. Especially not a game that delves deeper into the stories behind the Gods.
- The word Ginnungagap makes me giggle.
- My biggest issue with Jotun is the lack of content. There is just too much empty space. I understand that the big maps make you reflect on how small your character is in comparison to everything else. However, there is just so little to do. Additionally, your character only has one speed (without the use of God powers). Super slow. I found myself frustrated at how boring it was to explore each map. I enjoyed the different gimmicks (snow, lava, etc) but it just wasn’t enough to make each level interesting. This game would have been more fun if only the bosses were included, which is a huge shame.
- Inconsistent with the quality of graphics and animations. Some things look amazing, while others just sloppy. For example, when you drink from Mimir’s well, the detail on both the graphics and animations are fantastic. On the other hand, when you hit dwarves with your axe they hover back and after a brief delay throw their arms up in pain. Maybe this was done for comedic effect, but I thought it looked terrible.
- When you character attacks, she is rooted in place. Additionally, her attacks in general are also quite slow. When you combine these two elements, it makes combat very static and stutter-y. It doesn’t pair well with the fact that you are expected to move a lot. For these reasons, I didn’t enjoy the melee combat, but I guess that is a matter of taste.
Overall the game is very… dull. Your character is slow. Melee attacks are slow. Even opening gates is unnecessarily slow. Too much map to explore with too little content. Shame because the boss fights, God powers, and mythology were interesting. I do not foresee myself playing Jotun again.

TLDR;
Rating: 8.9/10
If you lack the time to put in many hours into a game, but want a decent action rpg with a cool cartoony style, you've come across the right game. In under 10 hours you can likely complete the game 100% including getting through the post-game Valhalla Mode (Boss-only).  In order to get get all achievements though, likely going to take you about 20 hours total. I would add this game on your wishlist and wait for a 50-60% off sale. It's totally worth it at that price.
---
Overall Rating: 9/10
Gameplay: 10/10
- Battle System (Action RPG) is intuitive and not too complex. I really enjoy the variety of the levels and the mythos explained throughout the story. Some of the gameplay elements are very unique and creative. My favorite levels being the Winter level with snowstorm and the Sky level with the lightning.

(-2): Although the mythos is cool and the MC is a good example of a strong female, her backstory doesn't leave us enough to feel emotionally connected to her character. Art: 10/10

- Textures are lovely and likely due to the art direction, this game will age well for the rest of time.
Controls: 9/10

Sound/Music: 10/10
- The music and sound effects are beautiful and immersive. I never found a single moment where I was bothered or irritated by the choice of music.
- Love the voice narration between the MC and the "Gods". Absolutely amazing work!
Length: 7/10
(-3): Honestly, for my situation where I have little time to begin with, the few days I played through this game was fantastic. Emily is Away is, right after Undertale, the most touching and personal game I have ever experienced. With the nostalgia it presents to everyone who used Windows Messenger back when Coldplay, Blink-182, and Harry Potter were the biggest things on our minds, it already allows millions of gamers to relate to the main character. All of the references it presents in the form of Easter Eggs (all of which you can figure out through rigorous trial and error) are absolutely hilarious! My personal favorite is the Undertale reference, although John Cena and Doge are not far behind. Now onto the story. Emily is Away begins with something any high school  student can relate to: chatting up your best friend/crush on a messaging app on your PC, just before attending a graduation party. I'm sure we all remember those feelings! Beware your choices, however, for Emily will remember your words and decisions! As the years progress and you have your annual chat session with Emily, you realize just how made for each other you were. Every interaction feels natural and personal. I truly believe that everyone can relate to the main character in just about every way imaginable. From naming the character and giving him a personalized username to being able to freely pick the choice that best represents how you, the player, would act in any of the given situations, Emily is Away allows every unique person who decides to download and play this god-like game to truly feel emotions they haven't felt in years. I must give one warning, however. Player beware: you may contract carpal tunnel if you play this game as much as I have. Although, I cannot deny that this ailment was entirely worth the time I have spent playing this masterpiece. I give Emiliy is Away a 10/10.
