Well made little indie game that is flying under the radar at the moment in my humble opinion.
March of the Living for me is a mix of Oregon Trail and FTL as far as gameplay goes, along with some more rng/rogue like aspects mixed in. The look of the game reminds me of the original Police Quest and Kings Quest games, with the 8-bit, blocky look and the quality writing instead of voicework. If you like FTL or Oregon Trail i would suggest getting this game asap, you should have a good amount of fun with it. The theme and setting is also very "Walking Dead'ish" also.
You will die alot, fail early on,etc.. things will not be easy for you and any companions you find along the way, make you're decisions wisely though, they can have big impact on things.
You pretty much go from each area/city and go scavenge, shoot zombies and make tough decisions when you come across someone or something. You have to keep an eye on you're health, how tired you are, how hungry you are much more. And as I mentioned above, the choices you face are a HUGE part of this game to.
If a game that has aspects FTL and Oregon Trail in it, along with a walking dead style setting interests you then give this a try ASAP. I think most people will enjoy it, but at the same time I could see it being a bit to tough for some and also the graphics might be unacceptable to some people who list graphics as the most important aspect of a videogame.
For me though this has been a nice pleasent surprise and I expect to play many, many more hours of this game!

Marlow Briggs is a rather unknown game but become recently popular due to its low price and word of mouth advertising. And, I have to admit, it's actually damn fun to play.
Marlow plays like some sort of Devil May Cry or God Of War, but where these other games usually take a little break inbetween the action packed moments Marlow moves full speed ahead. There's hardly ever a dull moment in this game. You move from one crazy action packed scene to the next, with usually just a few seconds of breathing room before hacking away at the next group of enemies.
This game isn't extremely long, about 5-6 hours, which is more than enough. After finishing it you're probably done with it anyway. It's fun for a first playthrough, then you'll just delete if off your PC most likely. It doesn't have any replay value. Which might actually be the reason why it's just non-stop action.
The graphics look good, the voice acting is decent and the gameplay solid.
Marlow Briggs is something you just have to play if you love action games. Especially considering the price these days.

A combination of old-school (some would say antiquated) turn-based RPG mechanics and survivalist simulation. All over the map in terms of balance and characterization, and the UI is shameful across the board. Over the long haul, however, Dead State's charms begin to manifest.
It will take awhile before the game starts to get going. A safe bet for the first-time player is that you'll be about 10-12 hours in before the first character conflicts kick in and you start exploring places more spectacular and atmospheric than deserted small-town main streets and suburbs. Story content is gated by in-game days and it takes about a week (each day an hour or more of gameplay, depending) before things start to really happen. If you can't devote that kind of time or don't have the patience (and not everyone does!) then it's a take-or-leave game. It squeezes surprisingly little from its premise otherwise (there is SO MUCH you could get from a hardcore RPG set in a zombie apocalypse), and clearly marks itself as an earnestly made first game from a new developer. I would say that if you're into 90's Interplay classics, have time on your hands and really, really love zombie fiction, it's worth the $30. Otherwise? Wait for a few patches or get it on sale. But it's worth the look if you're into turn-based RPGs.

Holy Potatoes! is a neat looking game.
The game is a blacksmith/weapon shop simulator where the accent is put on crafting the best possible weapon for each customer. Customers have preferences, in weapon type stats, and the stats of the weapons crafted can be influenced in real time by placing your potatoes on different spots (even if it doesn't fit their profession, that way you can maximise the stats) and random events. The higher the weapon's stat, the more the client will pay and the more fame you get from a sale.
The game opens up to weapon research, temporary event and contracts to take advantage of, unlock of new areas to exploration, new clients to sell, as well as HR (or should I say Potatoe Resource Management?).
In short, it's a nice little game that seems simple at first, but that hides a great deal of depth when you really start looking into it.

I wish to show this little game that is a few expensive, even with the -13%. It's the last version of the Close Combat Series, and i think the first one on Steam. It's about World War 2, and if you pass through the 2D low graphics, it's a very, if not the best, realistic simulation of battles. When they are shot, men don't run: they hide and they get fear, when they are hit, they are wounded or directly killed. With the right click on an unit you can give several orders like fire, launch smoke, run, walk, sneak, defend and ambush, with very different effects on your men or on ennemies, also you have infantry, leaders, tanks, guns, machineguns, mortars, anti-tank support, flame-throwers as units and airplanes/mortars/guns as support. And there is a lot less, if not at all, "mouse skill" like still in total war, where fast clicking can help a lot. Here all is in position and orders (with still a random factor).

If you can get used to the extremely dated graphics and UI there really is a great strategy game underneath. Some control issues, and some non sensical reactions from your soldiers can be frustrating, but there is little else on steam that has the old school quality that a Close Combat game brings to the table. It does feel a little over priced for a game that is originally this old, but if you make it passed the dated exterior succesfully you will get plenty of hours of play from the quality beneath.

I am not normally the type to write reviews, but I feel that Dead State is worth a break from the ordinary.
I have been playing since early access (First Seven Days release) and gone back for multiple playthroughs with each patch release right up until full release.
End result, over 300 hours played on this game and I dont feel I have wasted any of them.
YES, there are bugs, some of them are immersion breaking, some are annoying, but nothing OVERLY game breaking. The Devs are incredibly quick to respond to any new bugs found and are continually consulting the player base to find and eliminate bugs as they happen. To me, this is incredibly satisfying as I know my opinion as a consumer is valued.
As to the game itself?
If you are looking for a pulse-pounding thrill ride as you slaughter increasingly tough and varied monsters in graphic ways with an assortment of zany and idiosincratic weapons....
Look somewhere else.
Dead State is a htoughtful game that encourages you to plan ahead, from catering to the needs and wants of your fellow survivors to deciding when, where and how you and your team will fight.
Sometimes it is better to sneak through an area, get what you can and get out quietly.
I found I was investing into the fellow survivors, thinking outside the game to better understand thier motives and how best to make them work. A sure sign of good writing (Although you may not believe it simply from appearances)
Finally, if like me, you have played more than your fair share of RPG's (especially from the 90's and 00's) the isometric viewpoint, the turn based combat and even the JRPGesque base and NPC collection will tickle all the nostalgia bones and keep you coming back for more.
tl:dr?
A great game that may still seem a little rough around the edges, but a must have for any RPG and/or Zombie Survival fan
It's everything that made Pandemic good, and more.

Firstly, Dead State is a diamond in the rough.
Let me say that I don't relate to people who fiercely defend titles and developers where the products are incomplete or have problems.  I've seen fans who jump onboard and immediately shout down anybody who has negative criticism of the game.  I pay for (and expect) quality, and really struggle with the new era of gaming which puts the public in the chair of tester.
Having said that, I really enjoy Dead State.  A *lot*.
It was formally released early December (about a week ago), and there are still a pretty wide range of improvements that could be made to the game.  The thing is, even without them, the game is fun.  It's quite immersive .. insofar as it pulls you into the story and the concerns of your survivors.
A lot of games try to achieve immersion these days - but they have some kind of false idea of what immersion means .. making a game grindy and laborious may be exactly how it feels to chop down a tree in real life - but you soon get bored and realise it's just a game.
What Dead State throws at you is relationships and a foundation of morale and needs that drives them, and then lets you try and survive in an open sandbox in Texas.
Scavenge, deal with zombies, deal with friendly and hostile survivors, try to satisfy the needs of your community - those are the basic imperatives of the game.
People interact with you, there are branching conversations - a very significant amount of dialogue.
On the downside is that some elements feel a little unpolished.
I find the combat to be fun and tense, and the environments you nervously scavenge through to be beautifully drawn .. but the combat mechanics themselves feel a tad simple and unpolished.  People have complained about lack of stealth, cover .. and yeah, I agree - there are some of the tactical systems in the game that could use a second look.
What would that achieve ?
It would take a GREAT game and make it a WONDERFUL game.
Game is still very good in it's present state, I recommend it.

Holy Potaotes! A Weapon Shop?! Is a mix of management simulation and role-playing game. With light-hearted humor,  you manage a weapon shop that employes various craftsmen to make weapons for adventurers throughout a variety of lands.
While the game looks like a variant of something like Game Dev Story, it is not by the same developers. Gameplay shares some similar aspects and so does presentation.
In Holy Potatoes!, you'll hire freelancers to improve your weapons, level up your craftsmen in various abilities, cross-train their abilities, send them to explore unlockable regions for materials and relics and enchantments, reserch new weapon recipies, and use your advanced weapons to level-up the adventurers of the land.
I streamed this game for four hours (see below) and a sentiment I kept finding myself sharing is that this feels like it would be more at home on a mobile platform. By which, I mean that on a mobile platform, it has just the right level of depth and complexity for that environment, but doesn't meet the standards you'd generally have for a game to keep you tied to your desk. I don't want to sit at a computer and play this for hours at a time. I want to play a bit of this on my tablet while in bed, before falling asleep. Daylight Studios appears to be a mobile developer, though this also seems to be their first game (and PC only, at this point). I can only assume this is going to be ported to mobile, where it'll feel more appropriate.
Speaking of hours at a time . . . this game takes a very long time to ramp up. In the four or five hours that I played on stream, it wasn't until the very last few minutes that I finally unlocked most of the aspects of the game. It is easily a couple hours of gameplay before you even open the ability to research. The pacing just seems glacial. Like its meant to be a "wait an hour, then come back and press a few more buttons and wait a few more hours" experience.
Overall, I had an okay time and I didn't mind the non-stop cultural-reference puns. I am not sure I will play this again, though. I also think that $15 USD is steep for what it offers.
this is the style and pace you enjoy in your gaming, I would recommend picking this up on a sale. If you're not sure how you feel about this type of game, then I'd wait for a
sale. Otherwise -- and despite the overall craftmenship of this game seeming very good -- I just can't recommend such a slowly paced (and eventually very repetitive) game at this price. I look forward to giving it another go on mobile, when (surely) launches on iOS.
Ultimately, while not a bad game, I would not actively recommend it. If Steam had a middle ground
ranking, that's what I'd give it.

Jotun...a beautiful but ultimately hollow game.
I really struggled whether I would recommend this game.  It has so much going for it-- beautiful hand drawn animation, a story steeped in Nordic lore, a haunting, melancholy soundtrack.
And yet, sadly, the game never becomes greater than the sum of those parts.  Despite the beautiful art, the worlds feel empty.  The lore is leaned on too much without expanding upon it or making it the game's own.  But what ultimately drops Jotun from the promised land is its gameplay--
The game is simply boring to play.  There is zero depth to the combat.  Dodge, light attack, heavy attack, and a few limited 'God Powers' you wield scarcely.  The enemies are DOA.  They're simple, repetitive, and at times too cheap.  It's almost like the designers created this beautiful game and kept putting off improving the combat until, before they knew, the game had to go out.  So they jacked up the enemies damage numbers and called it a day.
Ultimately, I'm going to recommend this game, but only if it's on sale.  It's a short game with no depth, but the Art and Music make it worth a purchase.
It's one of those games you'll think after beating it, 'What could have been?'

Myths of Orion is a beautiful hidden object game with a fluid gameplay, a surprisingly grim storyline, and lazy hidden object scene design.
Despite its sci-fi sounding title, Myths of Orion: Light from the North is actually a typical fairy tale fantasy hidden object game, with a surprising story approach: our tale starts after the big evil sorcerer already won and devastated most of the kingdoms. As a daughter of a young enchantress, the protagonist’s task is not exactly to stop said evil but to ensure that he cannot cause even more harm by re-acquiring his books of power.
The game’s biggest selling point is its astonishing visuals, but I fear that the developers put too much effort into the graphics, because the genre-defining hidden objects scenes are suspiciously rare and rather weak in design. Therefore, it is up to the traditional point ‘n’ click gameplay and the conventional puzzles to carry Myths of Orion, and for the most part, they do a decent job—although, as usual for Cateia Games, the backtracking reaches epic proportions, but thankfully the map reduces this problem to a mere nuisance.

My biggest complaint lies with one specific aspect of gameplay. Throughout the game, you acquire "god powers," which assist you in combat (through healing, increased speed, damage mitigation, etc.). To activate these, you cycle through them and then hit the "god power" button. However, the icons that indicate which power you're about to use are up at the top-left corner of the screen. That, and you have enough of them that it takes some time to cycle through them to get to your preferred power.
It would be nice to either 1) have some graphic show up near your character when selecting a power (think Shulk's Monado Arts from Smash 4) or 2) use the right stick on the controller to bring up an "ability wheel," so that you could just flick the stick in a particular direction to activate that ability. I think either of those would help out a lot.
Overall, though, this game is really cool, and definitely worth a try. And I don't even mind that I bought it like a week before it was free.

Reviewing the game after finishing my first playthrough with the starting character Greg after two attempts.
First found out about this game from Many a True Nerds Let's play and knew it was my kind of game.  March of the Living is a roguelike with simplier management than FTL.  Instead of a whole space ship filled with crew members and different rooms to control and keep from blowing up, the March of the Living is in charge of a small group of surviors trying to get to safety at the end of the map.  The player will have to keep in check the survivors fatigue, hunger and ammos and weapons.    From the three walkthroughs I had played, I ran into different companions and the story itself changed accordingly.  I encountered different events though some quest objectives are the same.  I had a really fun time crafting a narrative out of the gameplay and would recommend it for anyone who wanted to be in charge of a small group of survivors and let the narrative of their journey playout.  However for players who expected this to be completely like FTL, then they may be disappointed as the systems in place are not as complex.  There are no different races or different beam weapons; It only has pistols, shotguns and rifles which is completely fine in the context of the game itself.
The only criticism I have is that there's an optimal marching position for the survivor group.  You don't want to be on either end of the screen as zombies can attack from both sides so you want to have the survivors in the middle.  But every time you rest the group is reset to the left of the screen.  It would be nice to have a button to get the characters go back to a predetermined position like how in FTL there was a button to return the crew back to their respected rooms.  But with that said, all the improvements in FTL were not implemented until many patches and Advanced edition after.
Overall it's a fun little game with a surprising amount of replayability.  I just surived with Greg, and now I've unlocked another protoganist with a completely different story and there are two more stories after that.  Mix and match all the different companions in the game then I would say there's a lot of fun to have for only 15 dollars.  Considering a movie ticket this day would get a 2 and a half hour of entertainment, I already had over 10 hours of play so I felt I like I got my money worth.
All things considered although this game is similar to FTL, I would say it's more like Sunless Sea with it's emerging narrative.  FTL barely had a story, while I was more invested in the plot and the clues sprinkled to what caused the outbreak.
It's definitely a simple little game with a lot of depth in it.

Some people will write off a game based on graphics, and that is quite a shame. Even with simple pixel graphics this game achieves a good amount of intensity and stress-inducing moments, as any good survival horror game should. I would even go so far as to say those simple graphics manage to set quite a dire mood themselves. The BGM is awesome and the sounds are sufficiently gruesome. The splat of my first survivor dying...
The game play is great; as more zombies begin showing up the ability to quickly and easily pause to direct multiple survivors, reload and make offensive/defensive choices is very handy. The massive amount of choices you are given grants the game tons of replay value (a single play-through isn't "short" by any means either). I've seen others say they struggled with the controls but i found it quite easy to get the hang of.
My favorite part is the random event feature, where you are given multiple options that not only determine the moment, but the entire progress in the game going forward in that every decision counts. That one point of damage or ration of food can make all the difference. Being kind to the right person or shooting another right off the bat can have great or terrible consequences.
I haven't run into any glitches, and only two extremely minor combat functionality complaints. Great game right out of the gate. It's a bit early to rate it maybe, but at this time i give it a 9/10 score. I look forward to discovering where this well written story goes next!

For those who are looking at this game because they loved Space Engineers:
Think hard before buying this one. In fact, if you're going to buy it, read up on how to play a little bit first, then buy it and dive in so you can get a good taste before you hit the two hours mark. That way you can return it for a refund if you don't care for it.
This game is simply too rudimentary and clunky if you're already used to Space Engineers—it feels like this game was branched off from SE and then it was never able to catch up. The survival mode is sorely lacking in polish, but if you are a  creative mode-only player then you won't mind. The controls are inexplicably awkward for a SE veteran. You'll have as much stutter as on a SE planet, and there's no space mode to save you from it here.
This game can still shine for you depending on what you're looking for, but the odds are against it so go in prepared to eject and perhaps you'll be pleasantly surprised.

This is... uh... well. It's a game, yeah, but... the title is... well, uh... How do I put this lightly? Ha, that's kind of a pun. Light. Heh. Because the game's name is Shmadow.
Shmadow. ♥♥♥♥ing Shmadow.
Shmadow? Really? REALLY now? That's what you're going with? Shmadow? Of all ♥♥♥♥ing titles you're gonna name it like you're naming your Sonic original character? Is this named after your fursona, Shmadow the Shmedgehog? This is by far the stupidest title I've ever seen. If you named the game "Black Ball Assault" we would've gotten the same idea. The idea that you made a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game and dared to charge real money for it.
Well, what is Shmadow exactly? Besides the stupidest sounding word I've heard since "twug", which is apparently short for "Twitter Hug", Shmadow is a little PSchee game on Shteam. Shmadow, according to the developer, is a portmanteau of "shoot-em-up" and "shadow". Because that's what this game is, summed up in a word. Kind of.
It's got the basic building blocks of a shoot-em-up. You move around the screen, aiming your nonstop barrage of white particles around with the mouse to hit all the black things coming at you. Like an interracial porno. The little white circle is you, the good guy. The little black circles are the bad guys, because they're black. You need to stop them from mugging you, or banging your wife. Or voting.
You can acquire power-ups and charge up special attacks to help you take down the bosses that'll randomly appear. They'll be made of a fancier gradient, and shoot bigger balls at you. Very fun sounding, I'm sure. Maybe not so bad for a dollar or two.
But Shmadow plays like a fancy version of Asteroids. Only instead of jagged triangle shapes they're just big black balls. There's no structure, bosses just kinda drop on you randomly and in no particular order. Things are just kinda flying at you from all directions, and your only real purpose is to get points. It's like someone's final project for their Flash class, but they waited until the last minute on the character design and just said "♥♥♥♥ it, we're doing circles".
"Inspired by light and shadow", yeah right. "Limbo-inspired graphical style". Sure, buddy. And Shmadow the Smegma is actually a knockoff of Shmonic the Smegma. Totally not original at all. You got it, buddy. Whatever you want us to believe.
It's shmallow and dull. There's not even an interesting hook to the game, unless you think a black background with a white circle as the main character is a totally killer art style. You could easily google "Asteroids" and find a free version of it to play online, which would probably entertain you about as long as this does. I've played better on Flash game websites. I'm not even knocking it for being arcadey, I've played some really fun arcade-style games. It's just not fun to play, it's not shmatisfying at all. If I waved around a flashlight in a dark room for a few minutes I would've had about as much fun as I did playing this game.
What I find most offensive and off-putting about this game is that the name probably came first, and then the game. I can totally see someone sitting at their desk, thinking of the name "Shmadow" and saying "Oh my God, thish ish the funniesht name I've ever come up with, I better make a game about it right now". Was Shmadow really the best you could come up with? Really? I shudder to think of what names didn't make the cut. Were there worse names? Is it possible to have a worse name than Shmadow?
There's a lot of better things you could do with a dollar and some change. Like use the dollar as a little scoop to scoop the coins into your mouth. At least then you're getting your daily required copper and zinc. Important nutrients for a growing body. And maybe if you're lucky one will get caught in your windpipe and you'll get the rush of choking to death.

A twin stick shooter, wherein you play as a ball of light, fending for oneself amidst the darkness.
15+ minutes
Arcade / Twin Stick Shooter
5/10
There’s not a whole lot to this game; you play as a ball of light in a world of shadows, except for the background, everything in the world is dark. You illuminate your surroundings with your bullets and with the ball of light that serves essentially as your vessel. Plenty of random blobs of darkness hurtle toward you like asteroids, and will darken, and even blackout the area until destroyed or passed. Occasionally you face bosses, whom will drop various power-ups.
That’s really all there is to the game, and that’s the trouble with it; I want to like this game, but there’s just not enough to it. The shadow gimmick remind me a bit of
(though the art isn’t nearly to that caliber), and it’s kinda a neat one, but there’s very little to the gameplay. There’s no levels, or end boss, you just play for a high score; and while that’s not necessarily a bad thing (both the original
and
are twin stick shooters that do just that), the gameplay isn’t gripping enough to compel me to aim for a high score. The levels and enemies are randomized, so that at least helps mix up the gameplay a bit, but it’s still not enough.
I want to be able to recommend this game, but I can’t. After playing it for a mere 15 minutes, I’m probably not ever going to touch this one again. It’s not bad per se, so much as it’s not enough. Still, I only paid $0.50 for it, so it’s not like my wallet is hurting from it. But if you need a twin stick shooter, you’re better off buying
instead. It’ll cost you a bit more than this game, but it’s well worth it.

Wow, have I really used this program 8.9 hours?  Geez.  I guess you should listen to me then!
I absolutely love this program.  I didn't pay full price for it (bought a Steam code online), and I consider it to be a great value for the price I paid.
This software thorougly tests out your hardware.  And, the BEST part is that you can review your results online with their great website (results open in your default browser automatically).  The website not only shows you exactly where your score stands next to all results, but it can even show you how your results compare to others with the EXACT same hardware.  I found out that many people with my graphics card have a slight overclock, so I downloaded MSI afterburner and I experienced the same (improved) results as they did.  Plus, the results helped me to see how my CPU was holding back my GPU.  I eventually upgraded my system, and thanks to the "hardware search" feature on their website, I could see how much my score would improve before I even bought the new hardware.  I would say that this is one of the best applications of this program: deciding how to upgrade your system.  As someone who is relatively new to building his own system, I consider this program to be a must-have.

There's a good variety of cars but the tracks are pretty samey, with no good gimmicks or unique features and some frustrating invisible walls. The drifting mechanic is also pretty weird and stiff if you're used to Mario Kart, but I got the hang of it eventually. Races aren't too hard if you keep buying and upgrading new cars, though it should be mentioned that there's zero rubberbanding, which is both a blessing and a curse. If one CPU driver pulls away from the pack he can be impossible to catch, forcing a restart if you want gold. Most races are basic time trials or eliminations, but there is one neat one called Evade where the track is covered in mines, and the last place car is eliminated every 15 seconds. Those races are more about driving carefully than fast, and they can be pretty intense. It's not a bad game, just an unpolished one. I got all the way through it but I wouldn't recommend it unless you are dying for an arcade racer right now.

Its a cooperative aerial view shooter with a large amount of varied equipments to fit to different play styles, situations and roles within the your four person (or less) team. The goal of the game is to simply, to cross the map while surviving the a swarm of spiky hungry aliens that think space marine will be their next meal. It has two short comings (for me at least only two) are that the game is a bit short, it has 10 levels or so that can be replayed 2 or 3 times in a single week before getting stale. With all this said, remember its not a cheap game, its a free game- so get it, RIGHT NOW.

I should begin by saying I've never played any other game like this before. I know they exist, but I simply didn't care enough to try one. Well, with this one I knew about the development process a little and I followed it's progress as best as I could while it was being finished. I voted yes on greenlight the moment I saw it was finally on there, and continued to follow news about it. Finally, a release date was revealed. While the price made me cringe a little (I typically buy on sale) I knew it would be worth it simply to support the developer and of course, the publishing studio Creaky Corpse (The folks responsible for the Dead Frontier MMO, which I've put a considerable amount of time and enough cash to buy a used car or two into over the last 3+ years).
So, when I logged on Steam on the release date and bought this game I felt proud of myself, that something I had helped to succeed in my own limited way had made the first steps towards making the big bucks and hopefully launching a career for the developer. I downloaded, opened the game and... put that ♥♥♥♥♥ on idle for 2 hours so I could claim my free bonus gift on Dead Frontier for buying it. Now, don't be too hasty in your judgement. I was genuinely excited to try this game, but simply wasn't feeling it yesterday. I felt like it today, so after getting home from work I started it up and actually played. And it's fun. It reminds me of my childhood, when I would play the handful of games I had access to using my Super Nintendo. The way it looks reminds me of those earlier times, where no one gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about graphics or appealing to entitled kids who need everything spoonfed to them. The way you have to play does too.
In March of the Living, you figure things out on your own or die trying. And even when you have figured things out, prepare to die some more. You follow the story, powered by random events that will alter the outcome based on the way you play. Now, with a limited amount of options you're not usually going to do the things you as a person would do in that situation. That's okay, because no dev team could put in options to suit everyone. Even the folks that work on the more recent fallout games can't do it, and they must have huge teams and even larger budgets. The combat is another frustrating mechanic, until you realize that you can pause, plan your attack, then resume the game without a problem. After learning that, small herds are easy targets provided you haven't run out of ammo or been hit too much to risk melee combat.
This is what some will view as "too difficult" and that blows my mind. Once you figure things out, it's all smooth sailing until you get screwed by the RNG. However, the RNG is also the games strong point. Any story, no matter how good will get boring after enough repetitions. With March of the Living, your chances of things playing out the exact same are ridiculously slim. And with about 150 events (I saw maybe 12 in the time I actually played, which is likely 40-45 minutes) it will likely take a lot of tries to see them all. Oh, I should mention that if you die then you have to restart as there's no way to save progress (at least, not that I've discovered). That's the one thing that genuinely annoys me about March of the Living.
TL:DR - If you're not an entitled brat, and don't care about graphics and all that crap, and don't mind a bit of frustration then this is probably a solid choice for you. Final approval rating: 8/10.

Was having fun with the game for the most part. However issues cropped up slowly, driving me to question how much fun I was really having. So long story short it just tragicly falls short of being a really good game.
The map is far too big for the difficulty it boasts, specially when you get a quest at the very end of a sector only for it to be 3 inches from the start of that same sector, meaning you have to backtrack ALL the way back to the start, with now no means to resupply on the way there and then back again.
Combat is fairly broken as well, on both sides that it's too easy to win, and too easy to lose. You can wipe out 6 zombies with 2 shotgun shells if you herd them together. Or you can use the old faithful beat, retreat, repeat, with a hammer. However noting that the second you get grabbed, you may as well save yourself time and quit the game, look at the clock, see how much time you wasted, and question if you actually had any fun. The game has no real way of dealing with being grabbed, and for some reason, if you have a gun equipt, you have no way of firing the gun either. All you can then do at this point is watch as a single zombie slowly kills you, with no means of fighting back, or breaking free.
The same can apply if you get infected and somehow live. every day you lose a single HP, with no means of a cure, which makes me question; why is this mechanic in the game at all? why not instantly kill you and save you time and false hope.
Speaking of false hope, why is it that i can have 2 companions, yet the second my starting character dies, its a game over? What happens to them? Do they instantly die from a rampaging plot device? Why does the game not continue on from their point of view?

I have two real problems with this, for starters, there's no real customisation with this game. Weapons are given stats by your potatoes according to how skilled they are in certain areas of weapon smithing, but occassionally they can decide to simply not work for short periods making your created weapons not have anywhere near the stats you wanted, and there's no real way of changing this. Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death is a fast-paced third person hack'n'slash game by Slovenian developer ZootFly which didn't catch a lot of attention among PC gamers at its release. Making use of pretty much all of the popular clichés, the game is filled with mindless over-the-top action, tons of explosions and hilarious puns without ever taking itself seriously at any point.
The story proves this instantly: Your girlfriend translates ancient scripts for a rich company mogul somewhere in Central America. You visit her and she explains to you how her boss is up to no good because he wants to perform a ritual that would make him a powerful god and ruler of the world. So you try to take here with you back home, which her boss obviously doesn't like, so he gets you killed with an ancient scythe, not knowing that it is imbued with power that resurrects you and summons the Mask of Death, your new companion on your path to rescue your girlfriend and stop the bad boss.
The game is based on ZootFly's own proprietary, multi-platform engine called ZEN, which doesn't really provide any PC graphics options other than resolution, fullscreen and brightness. That's a shame because the game could've definitely used some AA, which would make the colorful and detailed enviroments look even better than they already do.
While the level design as such is pretty linear, which tends to get boring after a while in a lot of games, ZootFly actually managed to add quite a lot of variety to it. Throughout the game you will encounter combat arenas, puzzles, deadly death traps, quick-reaction minigames, turret sequences and even some top-down shoot-em-up action. This sounds like a weird mix of gameplay elements but is incorporated extremely well into the game, so you never have the feeling that it is out of place.
Combat and controls are exactly like what you would expect from a game like this. Throughout the story, you get access to 4 different and upgradable weapons, each of them with a variety of combos to deliver maximum damage. Additionally, by defeating the ancient gods of fire, earth, water and wind, you unlock their devastating ground attacks, which can help you out of tricky situations or simply cause widespread carnage when facing many of the varying enemies at once.
The puzzle elements in the game mostly consist of moving blocks on trigger platforms or flipping switches to open doors and while they never are overly challenging they actually provide a welcome change to the otherwise extremely fast-paced gameplay, so you can take a short break from all the action.
Usually, with a low-budget title like this, the soundtrack and voice acting are two of the things where the developer tries to save money. Surprisingly enough, the soundtrack is actually pretty decent and, paired with the level design, builds up a really good atmosphere. While the dialogues are a bit cheesy at times, the voice acting itself is good and fits perfectly to the game characters, especially to Marlow and the Mask, who are constantly teasing each other verbally. That makes for some hilarious puns even in the weirdest situations. For example, while you are climbing a stone wall that is about to collapse and kill you, you are arguing with the Mask about who is whose sidekick in this game.
With around 8 hours of playtime for the story, the game provides an extremely decent bang for the buck and if you want to test your skills further, you can give the Challenge mode a shot where you replay the minigames from the story to achieve better scores and times to rank up in the online leaderboards.
Marlow Briggs and the Mask of Death is cheesy. It's mindless. It's over-the-top action. But that is exactly what makes the game so enjoyable and so much fun and it's great to see some developers going bonkers with their games without trying to be serious, dramatic or mature. If something like this is right up your alley, make sure to check the game out!

Single-Player Review:
I like it when I can play a good military shooter. Bad Company 2 delivers on 3 fronts to make it unique, and those are story, characters, and the guns. But first the problems. I'm going to get right to it and say that the game design is not nearly as good as in the first Bad Company, and the game shoves far too much bullsh*t at you, cuasing you to die, reload the checkpoint, and repeat. It gets tedious to the point that I started not wanting to play the game. Until you finish a level. Each cutscene that you are delivered to offers the great story that comes with the Bad Company name, and it takes us to all sorts of interesting locals, from the jungles of Bolivia to an in-airplane shootout. But the story wouldn't be nearly as good if not for the characters. Sarge, Hagaard, and Sweetwater are back, and are as funny as last time. In 2, everyone has something to say that is either funny, meaningful, or just good plot dialogue that works. Even your character, Preston Marlowe has quite a bit of voice time. But on to the reason quite a few play FPS games for, the guns. There are a plethora of guns, with all sorts of attachments you can find. And being able to swap them out and carry 2 primarys lets you play however you want, allowing a freedom of sorts.
Score: 7/10

BC2 appeared to have everything going for it: Strong reviews, amazing visuals, comedy, and I was already a fan of other Battlefield games. The single player campaign started out really well, recreating an amazing atmosphere which had eluded me since way back in CoD2. But after this, my experience was ruined by poor design choices at every turn.
Reasons I didn't enjoy it:
- BC2 is far too close to being "on rails". There's no freedom; you're always being micromanaged, and there's far too many of these jarring fade-to-white transitions where your control is taken away. At times, it's mere seconds of gameplay before you reach an arbitrary point where control is yanked off you yet again. This isn't only frustrating but repeatedly breaks the immersion.
- There's little sense of what's going on half the time. Like the story, the characters motivations are unclear, unengaging and convoluted, and you often can't repeat cutscenes if you try (there's no saved games, just a single autosave slot). It takes 6 hours (almost the entire game) before the opening events (the only intriguing part of the plot) are finally dragged into the context of the story, if you could even call it that. Often a mission will abruptly end, then you're whisked away and dumped into another location with little to no explanation. This would usually happen just as I was finally starting to enjoy it.
- Usually, games (and gamers) have an ideal balance between freedom and hand-holding. By combining linear maps with poor mission design, BC2 astoundingly manages to leave you feeling both neglected and restricted simultaneously. Sometimes you're playing "guess whether to obey the dialogue or follow the checkpoint", since they often conflict and you die if you obey the wrong one. Frequently, the mission design relies upon the auto-save, setting you up to fail with unforeseeable ambushes and insta-death. Certain sections will be repeated over and over, making it more about remembering where the enemies are scripted to appear, rather than about skill or the dynamic fun the Battlefield series is known for.
- The AI is highly inorganic. There are glaringly disjointed "patrol" and "attack" modes, with unnatural transitions between them. While your squad is "stealthing", they can banter loudly within stones throw of the enemy, in plain sight, and not be detected. And yet, the entire enemy force will hear you pull the pin from a grenade, instantly entering attack mode and shooting you before you can even throw it. In "attack" mode, the enemy ALWAYS and INSTANTLY knows where you are, even when you're hidden by a wall, and they ALWAYS prioritise shooting you rather than your squad, even when your squad members are closer to them. It's particularly frustrating when multiple helicopters will follow you, a lone soldier, all over the world while ignoring all other targets.
I miss the scenes in HL where you could sit back and watch AI battle AI just for the entertainment value, not knowing how it's going to turn out. If necessary, you could step in and tilt the scales back to your favour. In BC2 your team are invincible, so you just ignore them.
- Your squad is useless. All 3 of them could be shooting at a single enemy for 2 minutes and hit nothing, but if you fire one short burst in the enemies general direction they die instantly. Combined with the fact your squad can't even serve as a diversion (see above), it's very rare they help you at all. I saw them kill maybe 10 enemies in the entire game. You don't get that great feeling of comradery other squad games offer; you just feel alone.
- There is no strategy to BC2 whatsoever. The enemies know where you are (see above), and you know where they are thanks to your mini-map. In most missions, you can't flank because you must walk exactly where the game tells you and
the game tells you. One time, walking as little as a couple of steps off course gave me "10 seconds to re-enter the combat area or fail". Now, I wasn't being unreasonable by walking to the edge of the map or anything - I was trying to cross a shallow trench towards the objective. But instead, I was forced to go into this deep and indefensible riverbed to have enemies spawn almost right on top of me, and like a rail shooter it was very obvious and jarring. This is pretty sad to see in a Battlefield game, since Battlefield was one of the first to do large free roaming maps. There's no reason to force you artificially through an obstacle course (not all the maps do).
- There was a similarly awful case where taking a step ahead during some expositional dialogue, I got "enemy mortar is spotted in the area, get back to the combat zone in 10 seconds or fail". But literally 2 seconds later, suddenly that enemy mortar never existed and it's where I had to go. This was only once, but it's just one of many examples of how the game forces you to be in correct position to watch anything it deems entertaining at all times. In doing so, it loses any semblance of an organic battlefield, thus discarding the required atmosphere to make said event entertaining in the first place. I found myself missing Battlefield "multiplayer" with bots, of having reinforcements roll up from unexpected directions and change the situation dynamically.
- The comedic banter could have been BC2's redeeming feature. I really love this kind of thing in other games, but in BC2 I missed almost everything they said, because (1) for some reason the dialogue volume is turned down in the options by default. I didn't realise this until the game was half over, but (2) turning it all the way up didn't help that much either; it's still too quiet, and (3) they tend to mumble away in the background during firefights, so you're distracted and/or can't hear them over the noise anyway.
- The story lacks any trace of dramatic punch. The sad scenes don't feel sad and the climaxes are underwhelming. Some good ideas are let down by poor execution, like failing to pause for emphasis, or insufficient sound effects and music. The characters are so whimsical that it's hard to understand their motivations or emphasize with them, which is part of the joke, I guess? It's difficult to tell.
- There are too many poorly executed scenes like "we have to get to that vehicle over there" when you're literally standing in arms reach. Even the very impressive and atmospheric opening sequence had "cut the engines so the enemy can't hear us" when you're literally 5 meters away and can hear them talking at normal volume. This would have been funny if it were on purpose, but I don't think it was, unless this game is too subtle for me to discern the cliché from the parody? In any case, it was rarely funny.
Final thoughts:
To my great surprise, I really struggled my way through BC2 with only a few fleeting moments of enjoyment. I took refuge by trying out "Crysis" and I noticed a stunning number of conceptual similarities, yet found it significantly more fun. I ended up finishing that before BC2 and in less sittings, even though it was twice as long.
BC2 shows all the hallmark signs of what happens if you translate a game literally from its design document without any of the flexibility or refinement required to make it all fit together seamlessly in a way that's fun. It's as if each of the components were created by talented individuals, then assembled by machines concerned only for checklists. Ultimately, BC2's only untainted qualities are the graphics and the sound tech (which are AMAZING). The end result is a largely soulless and superficial single player experience.

You can get a review of the features from different places. These are my impresisons.
Is the game perfect? No.
Is the game very good? No.
Is the game good? Maybe.
Is the game fun? Maybe.
Let's get the elephant out of the way early. Dead State has a host of issues. Combat is simplistic. The zombies aren't really a threat. There are numerous bugs and I have experienced numerous crashes. Certain game concepts are poorly explained. The UI can be rough in places, especially dealing with inventory. You can't eject people from the shelter. Areas don't get monster respawn. Enemies are always in the same place on every game, limiting replayability. The list goes on. So there are many legitimate reasons why some people may not like it.
Yet I enjoyed it for a while. The game feels old-school, almost in an original Fallout sense. It plays slowly and methodically and you have a chance to really get to know the world. Issues and situations are thrown at you, sometimes with no easy answer. It has that "one more day, one more turn" feel that most good games have. I always have something to do, explore, build and always a new situation to handle. The person who is bit - do I get them out of the shelter because they're using up all my antibiotics? Or do I do the merciful thing and keep them here? How do I handle an abortion issue?Does a woman's right to choose outweigh the necessity of repopulating the human race? Do I go fishing for food or do I try to scout that new camp to find supplies to reinforce our wall? Combat at times is difficult and after a fierce fire fight you can feel tired, not elated, but it's always nice to get the spoils of your victory.
This is one of the first Kickstarter games I backed and I don't regret it because I wanted to see a game like this made. I had some fun playing it and it piques my imagination. There are many areas where the game could be improved and maybe that will happen and maybe that won't. If it does, Dead State may become a very good game. If it doesn't, I still got some enjoyment for my time spent with it.
So why the negative review? The game is just simply too poorly balanced and too buggy to recommend. Combat is horribly unbalanced - you'll want one type of weapon and one type only because it's so vastly superior to everything else. Zombies are so easy to beat that they present no challenge whatsoever. A zombie game where you aren't afraid of the zombies is not a good thing. Bugs abound everywhere, including some show stoppers that won't let you finish the game. The NPCs that you meet aren't really interesting and their stories don't really go anywhere. The only threats are other humans and most of those interactions are exceptionally simplistic and almost all end in firefights. So between the balance, the bugs, the dull NPCs and the simplistic combat, after the first few hours you've seen everything the game has to offer.
Simplistic combat + unscary zombies + few tactical options + bugs + simplistic NPC interactions  = unhappy Blackadar. It's too bad too because this game was close to being very good. It just needed another 6 months of real polish before release. It didn't get it.
Long story short, you MIGHT have some fun with this if you're old school like me. But eventually you will probably tire of the bugs, balance an bad NPCs and you'll toss it away. I stuck with it to the bitter end, including an ending that required console commands to get past game stopping bugs, but that's because I'm a glutton for punishment. So I have to give it a thumbs' down. Go give your money to the Shadowrun games instead - better stories, better settings, better combat and better balance.

Great old school rpg fun. With all the baggage that entails.
Zombies are boring but the conflicts that all disasters create between people are interesting. Dead State understands this, and that's why it manages to remain captivating despite the overdone subject material.
It's a turn-based rpg and you travel the post-zombie-apocalypse wasteland in search of loot to bring back to your shelter. There's loads of combat, base building, and managing the personalities in your base. The combat isn't anything to write home about, but it's on par with Fallout 1 & 2.
The writing is really great, and one of the best parts of the game is reading through the dialogue you have with the people at your shelter. There's tons of opportunities to be a truly disgusting person without being stereotypically evil.
Like all great old school rpgs, however, it's got its fair share of bugs. Don't get me wrong though, it's very playable - there's nothing game breaking - but slight annoyances can add up if you're sensitive to that sort of thing, you little babby. Save often and keep multiple saves to avoid headaches. Graphics are fairly dated, too - although the character portraits are quite pretty.
I've played about 26 hours of it and it's definitely super impressive, coming from a small indie studio.
More like this please. Maybe with a robot apocalypse next time.

I like to go in blind, so I started out with in survival mode with everything at whatever defaults the devs thought best. Here's my experience so far:
I awoke in a rather picturesque field of grass and flowers next to a cart. I pushed the cart and it moved easily, which seemed like good news, but I'd save that for later. I immediately headed for a forest I saw in the distance as that looked like a good place to start my search for useful resources. Arriving at the edge of the forest I immediately grabbed the axe I had conveniently been provided and chopped down a tree. The tree fell on me and I died.
I awoke again next to my trusty cart and headed in a different direction. This time I wandered until I came across an abandoned house. It wasn't the most interesting thing I'd ever seen, so I wandered back toward the forest. Noticing my growing hunger, I looked around for food and saw an unsuspecting deer. I tried to get the deer. The deer ran away. I searched some more and found some mushrooms. At this point I was quite hungry so it seemed worth the risk. I ate the mushrooms which turned out to be nothing more than edible mushrooms.
I wandered back to the tree I had chopped down and tried to pick it up. Apparently a 175kg log wouldn't fit in my backpack, so I chopped it into smaller pieces and carried them back to a relatively level area in the field to start building some shelter.
The game is absolutely not done, and a cursory glance at the forums will show you a definite weak spot in project management, resulting in a somewhat unstructured and chaotic release cycle. To their credit, they specifically list Project Manager as an open position, so I think they're aware.
The bottom line is this game is fun in its current state, and promises much more. If you like survival, building, medieval times and being crushed by falling trees, this game is absolutely for you.

I went into this one with very low expectations, and it was better than I thought.
This game has abundant minor issues and feels a bit unfinished.  It's got clunky hitboxes and glitchy hit detection; it's possible to drive right through stage walls in some places.  Collisions behave really oddly.  Powerups aren't too useful.   There's not too many pre-programmed tracks, either.
Also, there's a highly overpowered mechanic called Drift; sliding around curves filles a boost gauge that can be activated for a major speed increase at any time; with a bit of skill, high drift cars will spend half of every race in turbo mode, and low drift cars will be left in the dust.  This limits your car choice options.
However, there's positives, too.  A variety of game modes keeps things feeling fresh.  Races are fast-paced and don't drag on.  There's a fully functional track editor.  Vehicle handling is actually pretty okay.
As a MAJOR plus, computer AI does not feel cheaty - Cheating AI is my major issue with most other racing games.  The game is fairly low challenge, but a large part of that is because the devs weren't seeking to add artificial difficulty with rubber-banding or any such rubbish.
The verdict: There's fun to be had here, as long as your expectations aren't too high.  Fly through all those tracks with drift, buy a bunch of upgrades, snag a ton of easy achievements, and it makes for an enjoyable afternoon.

As a fan of Mario Kart who is forever looking for a good pc clone, this game got me excited, but I don't think I will ever play it again. If this was a game still in development I would be the #1 fan and avidly follow it, but as it is it just can't be enjoyed.
First of all, the controls: pressing up will give a constant speed to your car, while left-right will change its angle. That's all. I wasn't expecting something super realistic from a toy car battle game, but I really need some more variables under my control if I must feel that I'm responsible for my results. To be fair, the cars have stats like "handling" and "grip" that you can improve by buying upgrades, it's just hard to imagine where they could be possibly used. The few times some physics seems in play it feels totally wrong. For example when it rains it's hard to turn, but it doesn't seem like water on the floor... more like water got into my keyboard causing it to malfunction.
There are a few powerups, but they could be condensed in just two: "hit the car behind you" and "hit the car before you".
And I was always winning first place without even thinking what I was doing. The problem is not that the game is too easy, but that the player is not responsible for the result. If the difficulty was increased, you would always lose rather than always win.
There is little content. I played for one hour always going to the next challenge, and I think I only saw three different tracks. To add a bit more variety, there are four different modes: a normal race, a solo race against the clock, a mode where every 15 seconds the last car gets eliminated, and a fourth mode that is just like the third, but with random mines on the track. None of them got me involved.
Besides all these problems, for some reason the game just isn't fun. The developers clearly tried to replicate the mario kart formula, but that isn't enough. It looks like they completely skipped the part where you tweak the game until you find a combination that makes it enjoyable.
I really don't enjoy writing a review that is so negative, I guess I hope they read it and decide to go back working on this project (maybe as a new game). What I can't understand is that the big work seems already done. The graphics are cool, and the engine works, what's left to do is the fun part.
I'm not bitter about this because I got the game in a bundle I bought for something else, but I certainly don't recommend you pay 9,99eur for it (or any price really).

If you are a fan of The Walking Dead and want to get a good view on the post-apocalyptic world of zombies, and enjoy FTL, then you should give this one a whirl, I managed to make it to the second map where I met my end to a group of bandits on Day 10... shoulda just ran.
Combat with Rotters/Bandits may be a bit confusing at first, when in doubt, pause and plan your course of action as in the later stages one small slip up may be your end... sometimes it may be best to run, there's no shame in that.
Every decision you make will have an effect on how the game progresses, good or bad it will come back and either help you out with a food ration, or a bullet in the knee and ultimately boils down to how the game will end should you survive.
The scale of difficulty is a pretty steep one but once you got the basics down you'll be able to progress further with each new game think smart, think of what you would do if you were in that very situation. The map is randomly generated with each new game so you won't get the same scripted event most times.
Very minor bugs, clicking on your character in your party can be difficult on the fly but that can be compensated by pausing and laying down your battle plan.
The big bug I came across was where I found the little girl and her dog Rex, and escorted her back to a cottage, Chloe's Apartment for Greg's story never showed up, which resulted in me having to suicide and start a new game.
But all in all, it feels great and it's a nice change from the usual zombie games popping up nowadays, sound and scripts for events are very well done with a few bugs that can be tweaked, graphics are pretty sweet and brings back the feel of old retro games but it's not for everyone. Take a chance on MOTL, you won't regret it.

Oh boy, this game is a bit of a mess, and really hard to review, so hard in fact, it took me over 10 days to do it. (Sorry for my inactivity btw)
Let's get to it, Vanquish: The Adventures of Lady Exton (That's a mouthful) it's a platformer that needs some serious polish and better coding, because, as I played it, I found it a mess. I hate platformers, but I can admit that the Marios and the Megamans are some really good games, but this one is just...
You play as Madam Lady Exton, a beautiful woman living in a steampunk era, who mysteriously wakes up in a cell, after the two seconds it took to break out, she finds that her parasol has a gun, which isn't strong enough to kill anything, and that it's her duty to... to... to what? I must've missed the story, because I haven't found any, Exton is just killing innocent annoying robots and that's it, after 10 levels there's an underwhelming boss, and between that you go through underwhelming levels.
Obviously, it's a platformer, you jump on platforms, and you shoot thingies until you reach the end of the level, quite simple, so how do you screw this up? By programming it in under two hours, the controls are floaty, it seems like an ice level all the time, and the jumps have a small but noticeable delay, which gets old fast, the top of the screen is solid, so you'll crash your head on it frequently, and when you do, you can't do the double part of you jump, and you'll plummet to your death.
The enemies are more annoying than difficult, they clutter the screen, making it impossible to avoid damage, and any damage cancels your jump, removing all momentum and killing you with gravity. You do have a really generous health bar though, but your gun deals next to no damage, taking over 10 shots to kill an enemy, which the levels are full of, too full. So it takes a lot of time to get through one, and it's just so unrewarding, you just reach a balloon and go to the next level, 30 times, that's it. And the background moves back when you go forward, and that's worse than it seems, it actually nauseates me, and gives me a very bad headache.
With some polish it could be good, maybe increase the damage, remove the ceiling, and remove some of the clutter of some levels. But I'm not a game designer.
The art style is actually good, really good even, everything is well drawn, the enemies are a bit too simple, but it's overall good, the background looks nice and Exton herself looks good as well, the animations are a bit on the lazy side, they aren't really fluid and nice, but it can be forgiven.
The music though, it's the best part of the game, it's just ear candy, it loops quickly, but it's really good, the composer did a great job. The sound effects on the other hand... There's just one, the gunshot, other than that, none. Which makes the game quite awkward at times, because of the silence.
Overall, my opinion of the game could easily change, but it won't for now, because I haven't heard of the developer for 4 months, so they could've very well abandoned it, but I'm none to judge.
I don't recommend the game as is.

Dead State stands alone as a Zombie TBS Rpg, mostly because there aren't any others. The game's core is great, the concept is spot on, and Turned based strategy is, in my opinion, the best mechanical base for a zombie game. The final product isn't as good as I hoped it would be when I first read about it two years ago. But I still think the released game is enjoyable, if short of the potential the setting and style could have provided.
Issues
Dead State uses the Torque engine just like Age of Decadence, its not that pretty. Better than 2d pixels but it also lacks the "retro charm" some pixel games capture.
There is very little scripted content like what is found in Age of Decadence, I enjoyed that content in AOD and wish some of these engine utilizations made it into Dead State.
Its psuedo open world, you really have no choice in where you go or stay only in the order of actions. This is the biggest issue I have with game. There is very little emergent content, and NPC interactions are very limited. Its either friendly will join you, or shoot first ask questions later. If you shoot first you make everyone sad though.
UI is clunky and this is a title you should read the manual for, otherwise you will be complaining about follower item management in the forums.
The good
Its a zombie tbs RPG!
Classic zombies, ie walking dead style. No sci-fi exploding, mutuant jumping zombies. Could use more of them on screen at once IMO.
All the classic themes are present. Gather supplies, fix up your shelter, defend against zombies and bandits, or be a bandit.
Good selection of weapons, items, skills, upgrades, etc. You can build a self sustaining fortress, but you can't leave and live in a house of your choosing.
This is a great base and I'm excited to see what/when mods get ahold of it.

As far as indie releases go, these guys got it as smooth as anyone on release day. There are bugs, which are getting squashed. So far none of them have really bothered me or my game and im really diving it this game. One bad patch came out and was quickly rectified, which happens to the AAA devolepers too. I wouldnt really hold it against doublebear.
The game itself hits my sweet spot of gaming. Turn based, rpg, strategy gaming with base building. The closet analogy game released recently would be Wasteland 2. So its easiest to compare them and would be relevant to most gamers too:
Dead State (DS) has base building which i love. Wasteland 2 (WS) doesn't have this, and the way that game was made makes it seem like it SHOULD have been in there. The way the second half of WS was written it seems like it should have been included and it to me it felt like a great chance to extend that game was ignored.
WS was too campy in my opinion. It made far too many referential jokes and nods and what not to the previous game and the genre in general. I felt that was a mistake. DS tries and succeeds in maintaining a better immersion in the zombie filled world and takes itself seriously. So over all DS beats WS in its game world.
On the negative side DS needs to be balanced still. Combat goes from wildly hard to wildly easy. Not long into the game only a few characters can mow down a battalion of zombies with little effort. That being said, the inclusion of so much fighting other humans can be tricky. You will find in the long run, its the living humans that are truely the real enemy in the game. But im sure as the patches come, feed back is gathered, and balance is achieved, this won't be a negative for long.
Graphics are passable for the game, but they bog my machine down way more then should. If you have a low end machine you might run into problems with graphics on anything other then lowest settings. My machine is middle of the road and i have to run middle of the road graphics. While comparative games generally run much better. This is probably an optimazation issue, which of course, tends to get taken care of in patches. From the already released patches it seems like they are trying to get this ironed out.
There plenty of stuff to find and loot in the game. Much of it though is not anyting more then having the words FOOD and LUXURY ITEMS written on a holder card and given different names. While they may be 1000 items inthe game, 900 of them are functionally identical, but the fact i can horde up toilet paper and candy bars makes the game feel more immersive then it really is as far as loot is concerned. I almost wish the game made a distinction though between toilet paper and tooth paste and it didnt just all end up as one pool when you bring it back. But that would probably have made the game turn into a consumables stockpile sim, which i might like, but i bet most gamers wouldnt. So I accept the way it is, and be happy enough with it.
I would have liked more base building features. Base defense battles (which may or may not be included but i have yet to see one). More weapon and armor types (though honestly there already a lot, but i just would like more).
My biggest gripe is the lack of documention of some things. I find data items before I am told how they could can used, so i spent a long time trying to figure out why i couldnt access them in the library. I also got confused when unlocking blueprints inthe workshop had the same icon as the actual item construction. So i did blueprints and couldnt tell know could build the item, i thought it just made more blueprints. But fortunately the devolpers watch the forums and answered in minutes (literally minutes) and i got it sorted out. But its a good sign the game is complex enough to not be instantly figured out, but i would have liked better tutorials/documentation.
If you read this whole review, you will know i am whole heartedly recommending this game. This game had me up til the sun rose the day of release playing it. Its probably been 2 or 3 years since a game did that to me. Thank you to the devolpers for making this game!

BC2 appeared to have everything going for it: Strong reviews, amazing visuals, comedy, and I was already a fan of other Battlefield games. The single player campaign started out really well, recreating an amazing atmosphere which had eluded me since way back in CoD2. But after this, my experience was ruined by poor design choices at every turn.
Reasons I didn't enjoy it:
- BC2 is far too close to being "on rails". There's no freedom; you're always being micromanaged, and there's far too many of these jarring fade-to-white transitions where your control is taken away. At times, it's mere seconds of gameplay before you reach an arbitrary point where control is yanked off you yet again. This isn't only frustrating but repeatedly breaks the immersion.
- There's little sense of what's going on half the time. Like the story, the characters motivations are unclear, unengaging and convoluted, and you often can't repeat cutscenes if you try (there's no saved games, just a single autosave slot). It takes 6 hours (almost the entire game) before the opening events (the only intriguing part of the plot) are finally dragged into the context of the story, if you could even call it that. Often a mission will abruptly end, then you're whisked away and dumped into another location with little to no explanation. This would usually happen just as I was finally starting to enjoy it.
- Usually, games (and gamers) have an ideal balance between freedom and hand-holding. By combining linear maps with poor mission design, BC2 astoundingly manages to leave you feeling both neglected and restricted simultaneously. Sometimes you're playing "guess whether to obey the dialogue or follow the checkpoint", since they often conflict and you die if you obey the wrong one. Frequently, the mission design relies upon the auto-save, setting you up to fail with unforeseeable ambushes and insta-death. Certain sections will be repeated over and over, making it more about remembering where the enemies are scripted to appear, rather than about skill or the dynamic fun the Battlefield series is known for.
- The AI is highly inorganic. There are glaringly disjointed "patrol" and "attack" modes, with unnatural transitions between them. While your squad is "stealthing", they can banter loudly within stones throw of the enemy, in plain sight, and not be detected. And yet, the entire enemy force will hear you pull the pin from a grenade, instantly entering attack mode and shooting you before you can even throw it. In "attack" mode, the enemy ALWAYS and INSTANTLY knows where you are, even when you're hidden by a wall, and they ALWAYS prioritise shooting you rather than your squad, even when your squad members are closer to them. It's particularly frustrating when multiple helicopters will follow you, a lone soldier, all over the world while ignoring all other targets.
I miss the scenes in HL where you could sit back and watch AI battle AI just for the entertainment value, not knowing how it's going to turn out. If necessary, you could step in and tilt the scales back to your favour. In BC2 your team are invincible, so you just ignore them.
- Your squad is useless. All 3 of them could be shooting at a single enemy for 2 minutes and hit nothing, but if you fire one short burst in the enemies general direction they die instantly. Combined with the fact your squad can't even serve as a diversion (see above), it's very rare they help you at all. I saw them kill maybe 10 enemies in the entire game. You don't get that great feeling of comradery other squad games offer; you just feel alone.
- There is no strategy to BC2 whatsoever. The enemies know where you are (see above), and you know where they are thanks to your mini-map. In most missions, you can't flank because you must walk exactly where the game tells you and
the game tells you. One time, walking as little as a couple of steps off course gave me "10 seconds to re-enter the combat area or fail". Now, I wasn't being unreasonable by walking to the edge of the map or anything - I was trying to cross a shallow trench towards the objective. But instead, I was forced to go into this deep and indefensible riverbed to have enemies spawn almost right on top of me, and like a rail shooter it was very obvious and jarring. This is pretty sad to see in a Battlefield game, since Battlefield was one of the first to do large free roaming maps. There's no reason to force you artificially through an obstacle course (not all the maps do).
- There was a similarly awful case where taking a step ahead during some expositional dialogue, I got "enemy mortar is spotted in the area, get back to the combat zone in 10 seconds or fail". But literally 2 seconds later, suddenly that enemy mortar never existed and it's where I had to go. This was only once, but it's just one of many examples of how the game forces you to be in correct position to watch anything it deems entertaining at all times. In doing so, it loses any semblance of an organic battlefield, thus discarding the required atmosphere to make said event entertaining in the first place. I found myself missing Battlefield "multiplayer" with bots, of having reinforcements roll up from unexpected directions and change the situation dynamically.
- The comedic banter could have been BC2's redeeming feature. I really love this kind of thing in other games, but in BC2 I missed almost everything they said, because (1) for some reason the dialogue volume is turned down in the options by default. I didn't realise this until the game was half over, but (2) turning it all the way up didn't help that much either; it's still too quiet, and (3) they tend to mumble away in the background during firefights, so you're distracted and/or can't hear them over the noise anyway.
- The story lacks any trace of dramatic punch. The sad scenes don't feel sad and the climaxes are underwhelming. Some good ideas are let down by poor execution, like failing to pause for emphasis, or insufficient sound effects and music. The characters are so whimsical that it's hard to understand their motivations or emphasize with them, which is part of the joke, I guess? It's difficult to tell.
- There are too many poorly executed scenes like "we have to get to that vehicle over there" when you're literally standing in arms reach. Even the very impressive and atmospheric opening sequence had "cut the engines so the enemy can't hear us" when you're literally 5 meters away and can hear them talking at normal volume. This would have been funny if it were on purpose, but I don't think it was, unless this game is too subtle for me to discern the cliché from the parody? In any case, it was rarely funny.
Final thoughts:
To my great surprise, I really struggled my way through BC2 with only a few fleeting moments of enjoyment. I took refuge by trying out "Crysis" and I noticed a stunning number of conceptual similarities, yet found it significantly more fun. I ended up finishing that before BC2 and in less sittings, even though it was twice as long.
BC2 shows all the hallmark signs of what happens if you translate a game literally from its design document without any of the flexibility or refinement required to make it all fit together seamlessly in a way that's fun. It's as if each of the components were created by talented individuals, then assembled by machines concerned only for checklists. Ultimately, BC2's only untainted qualities are the graphics and the sound tech (which are AMAZING). The end result is a largely soulless and superficial single player experience.

It is a difficult desicion to whether give Jotun a thumb up or down, since the game is very prominent in both its con and pro.
As you can see from the trailer, the appearance of this game is aesthetic and like a piece of delicate art. Some Vikiing mythology lores are weaven into the game as well, immersing you in the background.
However, as an action game, Jotun is not suitable for everyone. The handling and response are very poor, the heroine moves and attacks at a rather low speed with considerable delay both before and after you press the button. (Perhaps the designer wants to simulate the way real viking warrior behaviours in battle, but since there's no other fast acting classes in the game, it only ruins the player experiences.) The heavy attack is practically useless, excpet for solving puzzles, because it takes about four time the frames of a normal attack and inflicts substantially four times the damage while giving enemy the chance to escape. Another problem is that the hit box is inconsistent, that means, by one gesture of the boss, you can damage him by chopping his hair, but after he changes into another gesture, your attack does not even count for hitting the position which is supposed to be his leg.
With these factors combined, the boss fights (which is the emphasis of this game) become very painful, at least for many non-hardcore action player.
The exploration part is also boring. Although many other reviewers mentioned the map system being unfriendly, I have nothing against it. The main problem is that the maps are vast but empty. In each of the maps, you basically have to repeat the same thing a lot of times to solve the puzzles.
Jotun is a beautiful game to look at, but not a solid game to play. If you really like the aesthetic presentation, watching a playthrough video may be a good choice.
