One of the many games that could use a neutral sign, instead of just thumbs up or down.
The value of this game depends on your needs as a gamer, and on your age too.
I've got it from a bundle and I'm happy I didn't pay the full price, but at the same time I'm happy to own it, because sometimes I just want to play a casual, easy game just to relax for a bit, and this is especially good at it.
In fact, this game is even too easy if you're an experienced gamer as me, and probably even as an average one, but you know, sometimes you don't have the mood to get into simulators or hard games, and just want those 30/60 minutes of relax with an easy and fun game.
Thanks to the good graphics and catchy soundtrack, playing this game is fun and puts you in a good mood.
You've got a good selection of cars which you need to purchase with the money you collect by playing, and a positive thing is that they really feels different and there's usually one to match your preferred play style, or even to match the needs of certain tracks. You can also upgrade some aspects of them, but at a certain point you'll have to buy a better one anyway.
The game spreads into many levels of increasing difficulty, each of which has 6 tracks to play. The game mode can be any of the few that the developer created, like normal races, elimination, time attack and so on.
The variety of the tracks is decent enough to me: they can have one of the few backgrounds available (like kitchen, garage and what else), and each has an assortment of different tracks available, and I guess you play at least once for each game mode on each track of the campaign.
To beat your enemies you have to play well or you won't have many chances, unless you use a car that's so much more powerful, but that obviously cannot be done on the latter tracks. You can also collect power ups and use them at your will, and you can find both attack and defense ones. The last thing is the boost, which can be used only when it's full and can be refilled through a powerup or through jumping/sliding.
This game comes with online/local multiplayer, and even with a track editor with Steam Workshop support, so there's a good amount of toys to play with.
Other things worth noting, that cannot be found so often even in mainstream games, are a replay system, and even a photo mode.
It may sound like such a great game from this description, and in fact the potential is there, but there's also many things done wrong here.
The main problem is the engine used: Unity. Once again, it can deliver a game quicker than using a better one, but the problems it gives to the users are too many, especially on bigger projects.
Super Toy Cars suffers from the usual performance problems that all Unity games suffers, although here they aren't as bad as in other games, but in a racing game, a framerate stutter can lead to a loss of control of the vehicle.
This is an arcade racer so that's less important, but since I can play GRID2 in full HD, with 16xAF and 4xAA, with all settings to High and some to Ultra at a stable 60fps with the graphics you all know, I know that the very simple special effects used in this game (fake env-mapping for example) and the simple models should run smoother than it does, especially since this game is more suited to kids, and you usually don't give your kids the most powerful pc you have around to play with.
The physics are also quite bad which, paired with really weird track objects bounding boxes, it can lead to moments of frustration.
You may want to cut corners sometimes, because the game seem to push that strategy with a lot of cars that slides while just steering, and the fact that you obtain boost by doing so, and that you even have a button on your gamepad just for sliding, but the objects put on the track have strange bounding boxes which sometimes are smaller than the objects themselves, and sometimes are bigger, which leads you to hit your head into invisible walls that just shouldn't be there.
The cars also becomes less controllable at times, especially while jumping and when the framerate stutters. Weird behaviors can also be observed while hitting other cars or any other object in the game.
Other Unity-related problems are lack of support for dinput and older xinput gamepads (needing you to use x360ce), some weird audio-related glitches and general stability. The game didn't crash often (like twice so far in-game), but it crash on exit for some reason, like other Unity games that I have (no profile data loss anyway).
I can't comment on the multiplayer as I could never find anyone playing this game and I don't have anyone to play with here.
I can't comment much on the track editor either because I don't have time to learn how to use it, but I can comment on the fact that I hoped it would be easier to use. One little thing the devs can do is to add some tooltips on its GUI so that you can easily know what each button does, but I guess it won't need a lot of practice or a lot of reading to get used to it.
The whole in-game shop is also looking like it was rushed, because you just can save up to power up your current car and you'll be able to win so many races, which leads to you save enough to buy a car powerful enough to win another 1/3 of the game. You can basically win the whole game with just 3 cars, and by that time you'll have enough money to buy the rest of them with their powerups, but that's probably because the game is easy and therefore more suited to kids.
In fact, I see this game like a little gem for kids, as they can play a game that is easy enough for them, play local multiplayer or online with their little friends, and spend additional time using the built-in track editor to make their own track, that can be shared on the Workshop for everyone to enjoy (or hate).
I have to thumb down this game because for my age and likings, this game does too many important things (for me) wrong and it's also too easy and short, but it would probably be a thumb up if I were a kid or if I had kids.
I also know many people of my age that just can't drive serious racing games, and this game may be good for them too (lol).
There's many other arcade racers out there which does things right, like Little Racers STREET, so consider the alternatives before buying this, unless, as I said, you need a game for your (young) kids.

---This review is of April 22nd. I will be updating it as patches are released.----
One of the biggest qualms I have about this game is the combat. The combat is atrocious as you have to manage every character in a small window of time.
or reload or move out of the god damn way, so you have to control every aspect of that and gets incredibly annoying. Not to mention right off the bat you are only armed with 20 bullets, a pistol and a hammer and are expected to fend of 5 zombies every so often (5 zombies don't sound like much, but take into account that you can miss a shot, fleeing can result in losing items AND members, and resorting to melee can increase your chances of getting bit and INFECTED, causing you to lose 1 health per day. As far as I know, being infected is a permanent debuff). This is especially annoying when you're scavenging a city and a group of zombies just happen to pop up on every scavenging attempt. You lose ammo and supplies faster than you can find them.
Another problem is with the hunger and fatigue bar. The hunger bar increases WAY TOO FAST compared to the fatigue bar. Paired with the amount of food you find, it almost makes it incredibly difficult to make it through the game with a full party. You might as well solo the game or bring at max 1 person if you want to maintain your food storage.
Additionally, losing health in this game is ridiculous. Finding health packs are hard as it is and don't help when they only heal you 1-2 and occasionally 4 hp at the most. This game wears you down, and many random events can screw you over if they choose to. For example, you can choose to search a cabin and then a zombie pops out of nowhere and infects you. There goes -2hp and another -1 hp every day. Want to avoid the crow swarm? Then duck. Oh wait - there goes -1 hp. Calling the bluff on that crazy guy at Chloe's house? Well darn I guess the gun was loaded after all: -3hp.
Lastly, there is just a lack of... "stuff"? There is a lot of writing in this game, which is good, but the scenery and art is minimal. Just the same pixelated forests and city landscapes over and over and over. There are very few items in the game which you actually need. You only should carry ammo, health items, food, a melee item, and that's it - everything else you sell to buy those items. No crafting or making armor or anything - and in the case there is an event where an npc does need a junk item, well guess what? He gives you one of the four important items or a stupid crossword book.
This game is incredibly unforgiving. Not in a Dark Souls "you-need-skill-to-play" kind of way but more like a "wow- developers-was-this-really-necessary" kind of way. It's okay and has a lot of potential, but the developers really need to ask and give the community what they want in terms of balancing and content and implement them in future patches.
I'd give this game an overall score of 6/10 but would not recommend.

This game is amazing. In the following 48 hours after I bought this game, I played it for 38 hours. Weekend well spent. This game sucks you in and you lose track of the time very quickly. You'll swear you were playing for 20 mins...nope, bam, 4 hours gone like that. It's extremely addictive.
As for the game itself, it's a factory-building game. You mine resources from the ground, manually at first but you quickly build machines to automate this. You lay transport (read: conveyor) belts to transport materials around, build power stations to power the whole thing, build turrets and weapons to defend against aliens, and expand your factory to research upgrades which allow you to...expand even more, ad infinitum. This game is a perfectionists nightmare because you'll find yourself repeatedly expanding and rebuilding your factory as you figure out more efficient ways to process and build things. The methods you use in the early-game just won't be enough to cope with the massive megafactories you'll end up with 100 hours into the game so for anyone who likes optimisation, this game is for you.
Modding support is great, multiplayer works and it playable but very laggy. Constant updates keep this game fresh and exciting, and I can't wait to play another 20 hours at the next lan party!

Furnaces smelt iron, Mining Drills mine ores, but at the top of the list where things are more complicated there are no tutorials. How do you program a logic robot? Fun game. Campaign is standard "bad people are trying to conquer the world" fare, but some funny quips and fairly good gameplay make it an enjoyable experience overall. I'd give campaign a 7/10. However, you should not buy this just game for the singleplayer.
Multiplayer is where BFBC2 really shines. I used to play on console (hence low playtime). I was delighted to see that there are still a few servers running. The upgrade system is very straightforward and the difference between guns is actually noticeable. Ranks go from 1 to 50, but it takes a good amount of time to progress through them. Vehicles are also cool and mostly balanced. The map design is very good and each plays differently, aside from a few recycled assets. Some things I don't like are a few overpowered upgrades only available to high ranking players (Magnum Ammo and Vehicle Alternate Warhead, specifically). Also, games are almost always won/lost by a landslide. In addition to this, there is no mechanism to prevent base camping. Some games your team literally cannot move from spawn. I'd give multiplayer a 9/10.
Bottom line: If you like multiplayer and can put up with some annoying tactics, this game is great. However, if you're a singleplayer person, you probably should not buy.

Update: I still haven't beaten the game, but there are a few things I'd like to add to my 10-hour first impressions. The positive recommendation didn't change though.
Characters still feel bland. The dialog is, for the most part, very generic and there are many characters in my shelter that I barely know, and didn't even bother to get to know their names. Part of the problem here is that, what makes them special (eventually), comes by way of them taking the initiative to talk to the player about their problems or ideas. Those events trigger at different times, and not very often, which means that most will probably remain forgetable for a long time. This system is fine as it is, but I believe there's much room for improvement there.
As I found more people, and as I invited them to the shelter, the game became significantly more interesting and I became much more immersed in it. In the morning of each new day people will talk to the player making requests (like not working today), suggestions and other stuff. There are also crisis events that trigger rarely and result in a meeting between the main characters forming a makeshift, small council to discuss an issue. The role of the player is as the leader of this shelter, so he's expected to have the final word in these matters. There will be some moral dilemmas along the way which at times made me really feel responsible for these people well being.
As for the difficulty, I described it as escalating quickly in my first impressions, but after getting good equipment and weapons, along with leveling my character with a focus in combat, that difficulty curve quickly peaked and now is taking a big dive. Combat is way too easy now, especially against zombies. Apparently the main character can't get infected, which, along with the fact that they can no longer do any damage even if they hit me, makes them just an annoyance. Other humans still pose some challenge from time to time, but it's rare. I expect another spike in difficulty soon, otherwise I'd have to say this game has severe balancing issues. In terms of shelter management, even with a character build not meant to excel at that, it has become easier lately as well, though not as much. Raising morale, getting enough antibiotics to keep infected survivors alive, and getting fuel are the main causes of tension. It became incredibly easier after getting a horse, and I expect it to become even easier with a car, so again, I expect events to trigger that will put more strain on resources soon.
As for bugs, I found quite a few. I recon many are supposed to be fixed soon, but at the time of writing, there will be some glaring small issues that indicate lack of polish. The only really bad ones were crashes, which only started happening recently, but twice in two days, in which I lost some significant progress. It's my fault for not saving, but an auto-save feature would have been very welcome.
One thing I'd like to test is its replayability. I want to create a new character that is all about running a shelter, managing people, leading them in combat, but not being a good combatant himself. That should make the game harder, and I like the idea from a roleplaying perspective, although I don't know if a second playthrough can be different enough for that to be fun. On the other hand, I'd like to beat the game first, but I have no idea if I'm close or not.
So there, my opinion of the game improved dramatically because I got totally hooked as time went by. I recognize how hard it must be to balance the tension between the combat and shelter management parts of the game, and for the most part, it does a very good job at it. The text below was written much earlier into the game.
---
This "review" was written at around 10 hours of gameplay (so pretty early in the context of this game). Up to this point, my experience with the game has been positive. Here's a quick rundown of my experience with it. I've seen many comparisons with other games, so I'm going to frame this in comparison with them.
- Unlike TWOM and XCOM, this one plays from the point of view of a specific character that you create in the beginning.
- The character creation is fairly simple, but allows for many different playstyles. From looking at the options available, I see that you could play the main character as ranged, melee, shelter manager/leader, or a mixture. I don't see options that would allow secialization on a stealthy gameplay though, which is disappointing. There's 4 general stats (analogue to Fallout's attributes) and around 10 skills with perk choices built into the skill progression system that allows for even more customization.
- There's a shelter stage, and a combat stage that would be familiar to XCOM fans, although unlike XCOM, they play the same. In the shelter stage you walk around the shelter talking to people, assigning jobs / upgrading facilities / creating items by interacting with an object, getting or storing items by interacting with a container.
- Just like State of Decay, you have to manage the resources of the shelter, in the forms of food, morale, antibiotics, fuel and the mood the specific characters.
- When you leave the shelter, you'll see a map whose mechanics will be familiar to anyone that played the original Fallout games, with random encounters and all.
- The gameplay in the remote locations you find is close to the original Fallout, with the difference that you control your party members as well during combat. There are many little new mechanics that I like, for instance, if an ally is blocking your way to an enemy, you can swap positions with him by spending two Action Points (also useful if you want a character to shield another). I found the combat part to be very unforgiving and difficulty ramps up quickly while you'll be scrounging for bullets and other stuff.
- I found many issues with the text, sometimes being cut off or being hard to read due to lack of contrast with the background, but those instances aren't too bothersome and not game breaking in any way.
- The narrative and cast of characters up to this point seems bland. Little of it made me care for them, which I think is a failure in this department, as I think this is important for this game to truly shine. This is one thing I don't want to judge so early into the game, but I would expect to be more immersed in the narrative by now.
Summary
I'm having a lot of fun with it. It's fairly nostalgic if you played Fallout, and the mechanics seem to be well designed. Graphically is not very polished, and doesn't seem very unique from an artistic perspective (like TWOM is) which makes it look very generic, but the mixtures of RPG, turn-based tactical combat and resource management mechanics of the game are its greatest assets. I'll update this later on, but this is my first impression of the game. I'd recomend it for anyone that played the original Fallouts and XCOMs, but I doubt this would grab the attention of less patient gamers.

I played it before release and have played about 15 hours after release. This game combines a lot of great elements that I love to see in games. I really wanted to recommend it, but no. At release this is more like a game that's ready to enter beta testing. The development team is still working hard on it, but it's nowhere near release ready. There are many known issues that have not been patched, some of which will cause crashes to desktop, like double-clicking at the wrong time.
There are unfinished features and overall a lack of polish. The trading/inventory management is extremely awkward. Tutorial messages will popup at inappropriate times if you breeze through the tutorial too quickly. Pathfinding is still very bad in spots. The main character frequently paces back and forth when doing commmon tasks like going to sleep to cycle a new day.
The tactical combat is very basic. There's no crouching behind an object for cover. Allies block movement. Characters and enemies occasionally stack in the same square which stops you from attacking/interacting with them properly. It's not terrible, but it's  nowhere near the level of X-Com or Shadowrun.
I would recommend this game if the price tag was $15 instead of $30.

Take the customer and shop aspects of Recettear, add the managing aspects of both Game Dev Story and the various time management games like Diner Dash, blend in a lot of humor. Now shape it into a universe full of Potato people, bake it, and then drown it in puns, references, and silliness.
And you might get something like Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?!. That, or a grand ol tasty mess.
Holy Potatoes jackets you with picking up the legacy of your grandfather, the ol spud. Once a renowned blacksmith, you begin rebuilding the family legacy as you hire a variety of blacksmiths for your shop to create weapons. Each blacksmith starts good at a specific weapon stat (attack, speed, accuracy), and they work together to forge a weapon.  Send your smiths out to sell weapons and buy supplies at various towns and dangerous areas. Have them explore and locate rare materials you'll need to research new weapons. Send them out on vacation to relax, as a stressed smith is a bad smith!
You earn $tarch, the world's currency, which you need to pay your blacksmiths, pay rent, buy supplies, do research, and upgrade your shop. A smith can only do one thing at a time, so you need to balance making weapons, selling them, researching, and many other things. Various events will effect both your smiths and your weapons.
Overall, the game is extremely fun and humorous. It doesn't rely on references and humor to be a fantastic game at its core, but it definitely helps.
If you can't stand a sack of puns, though, you might avoid it.

Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?! is a game about running a weapons store/blacksmith in an RPG universe filled with...Potatoes
The world seems cute, loaded with potato puns along with simple yet good graphics, but with only a few things to do in it no amount of looking pretty and cute dialogue is going to redeem the fact that in its essence it's a waiting game.
That's right, there's no real simulation or management here(Thanks steam tags!), with you just sending your potatoes out to do things and then waiting for them to come back. Or alternatively, telling them to make a weapon and then waiting for them to finish. The large part of this game is waiting for things to be done so that you can tell them to do more things...And then you wait some more.
This may be fine and well for a timewaster game on an iphone, but it just does not cut it for an actual PC game. You sit and wait for your potatoes to be done and you are occasionally thrown a random event which is a reference to an older game with two options which can both be a success (Minor, barely noticable effect on a single potatosmith), or a bad event which will give you a slight bad effect on a single potatosmith. In the end, you can just skip most of them and you wouldn't lose out on anything. It relies purely on it's 'humour' of gaming references and potato puns to be interesting, which does not make for a good game.
There is simply no gameplay to be had. No real managing your store, or figuring out what to do best, just telling your spuds to go do stuff and then waiting for them to do it. I would say it is closer to an interactive screensaver with pretense of being a game than it is to actually being a game - Sad too, as I was hoping to find a good management game
With a price of 15 euro, I would say it is severely overpricing itself. If it were in an app store, for maybe 5 euro/dollar I could see it succeed, but at this price and on a PC it has no chance at all. If you are still curious about it, pick it up at a sale, but don't bother with it full price unless you are a very patient person, and you do not mind not having anything to do.

The presentation is very nice. Music is well done, items and characters are decent, The game itself doesnt have much going for it. There are no real decisions to be made, no deadline, very little managing. Just keep clicking and you will progress. It is your standard molbile game at the end of the day, but at a steep price.

Along the way you may have all sorts of random events that can occur, from workers getting sick to sudden price hikes. Simply put, it's very hard to find the blemishes in this tycoon simulator. Shmadow is very simple but quite original at the same time. The game is a side scrolling shoot em up where you are a light mote using your light to fight against the darkness. The game has fog of war, and your mote and your bullets reveal an aura around themselves. As you are damaged your mote gets smaller, the healthier you are the bigger your field of vision.
The game is very challenging, at no point playing this game did I feel like "well with this power up it's game over"
Power ups do not last long so you are never over powered. The bosses can be quite troublesome, and the fact that you can't see obsticles until the last moment make the game very punishing. That said, it can be played casually and is very enjoyable, a good little time waster. The fact that the game is very straight forward (I played it the first time without even reading the controls, and I figured everything out as I went) but still has enough content and challenges to keep the most hardcore shmups players engaged.

I wouldn't call it exactly "FTL-Like" as others have. It's rogue-lite in the sense that you select your character/class, and traverse a procedurally generated world - but that's where the similarities end.
The shooting mechanics are much more simplified. You're typically either aiming for the head, or the body. Some weapons ala shotguns have additional modes of fire, such as burst shots. Definitely nowhere near the range of FTL's weapon selection, or in-depth damage system.
The difficulty is a long shot away from FTL levels, being far easier, and more forgiving of mistakes - you can take that as a good thing, or a bad thing.
You're not under any active time pressure from an ongoing hunt, or anything like that. Backtracking is A-OK.
The random events are enjoyable, but the encounters are on the boring side. Move, shoot, move shoot, repeat.
It's a good title, but I wouldn't recommend it as an "FTL but with Zombies" game. It's a lot more like a good sprawling story/exploration title. Fans of the rogue-lite genre may find it too easy.

Shmadow is a fun little twin-stick shmup game with tough bosses and power-ups to help you through the game. One of the special things about this game is that it features 4 player LOCAL co-op(Xbox and Playstation controller fully supported and required for co-op), something that is not often done in video games these days. You can play this game with your buddys on the coach while drinking root beer and eating Oreo's.
But on to the actual substance of the game.
You are a ball of light navigating through the dark with the help of your bullets to light the way and destroy all that goes against you (which is pretty much everything on the screen except for the background). You can get power ups after defeating bosses you encounter. These bosses can be very brutal, from slowing down and speeding up time, to bombarding you with lazers and drowning you with bullets. All while trying to avoid or destroy black blobs that damages/kills you opon touch.
There are three difficulties: Casual, Normal and Nightmare. These names don't lie. Casual is fairly easy with some practice, Normal is what you would expect and Nightmare is for those who enjoy getting pwned (I know I still say pwn, I'm stuck in 2007). The game also features a leaderboard for each difficulty.
And the music in this game is fairly decent. Goes well with the game.
For the core price of 2$, I personally think this game is worth a checkout.

Word of warning -- TownCraft is abandoned and no longer receives updates. Developer moved on to new titles (Objects in Space).
TownCraft is a casual sandbox/crafting game in which you build up a tiny settlement into a village then a town. You start with nothing and slowly gather and craft the resources needed to build and expand, eventually hiring travellers to collect resources for you.
It's easy on the eyes and rather slow-paced with very little in terms of actual difficulty. You can't die, can't lose buildings, and worst case scenario your workers leave if you can't pay them. I have not run into a fail condition so far. There are randomised quests but none of the ones I have seen had any real time limits to them anyway.
There are a lot of items to gather and craft, however it feels like this was just the start, like more items were to be added -- which never happened as the game was abandoned over 6 months ago. Even before I discovered the game was abandoned I felt a certain lack of depth to the game. Sure, there are crafting combinations to discover, but there's little really to motivate that and it's easy to build up a town and craft everything there is in the game.
I can't say it's all bad though. For the few hours that played the game I enjoyed myself. Still, I can't really recommend purchase because the game feels shallow and now that it was abandoned there is no hope for more content. If you already own it it's decent for a few hours, if you don't own it there are better games to buy instead.

Super Toy Cars feels like a game that escaped out of early access with a reassuring smile and a lot of fundamental issues unaddressed.
As I was playing through it I kept having to double check that it was indeed fully released and not still undergoing development, with so many prevalent bugs and a general lack of basic racing necessities popping up as if I had somehow been slipped a beta build in place of the final game. But Super Toy Cars is indeed "finished", or at least unlikely to receive any major future updates, so we're left with the game we've been given and it's a rather disappointing end result to something that started off with such promise.
Super Toy Cars wants to occupy a space between kart racers and somewhat more realistic arcade racers, with the handling and track designs of the latter and the zany power-ups and silliness so often associated with the former. In reality it adheres almost entirely to traditional arcade racing, with the inclusion of power-ups being rather unnecessary and pretty useless on the whole. There was rarely an instance where launching a missile or dropping an oil spill gave me any noticeable advantage, occasionally being a slight annoyance but usually something I forgot was even there.
I think a lot of this though has to do with how spaced out racers inevitably get over the course of a race. After the first lap I would often be so far behind or ahead of everyone else that there wasn't any chance I'd be able to hit someone with a power-up even should I want to, and even in the rare instance I was in the middle of the pack it so often felt like I was the only one driving. It's a mystery to me how so many racers can exist on such a small track and remain largely entirely separate from each other, but it definitely makes the game feel rather isolating when the only reminder that you're racing against someone is the fraction in the upper corner of the screen.
Again this is linked to another issue in the game, that being how unbalanced the different cars are and the laughably inept AI racers the game pits you against. Drift is by far the most important stat in the game, so much so that it means cars with a high drift rating will almost always be far and away the best vehicles in the game, rendering all but two or three cars impractical to try and drive. After only a few races I'd settled upon the Panther and found myself dominating every race despite driving like an absolute madman and crashing into things on a near constant basis. If the game starts out easy it trickles down to a virtual void of challenge, as I blew through race after race wondering if I had somehow been caught in a loop and wasn't actually moving forward in events.
Keeping with the trend of every issue being intrinsically linked to another, that feeling of consistent repetition is the result of an abundance of redundancies in track designs and event types. There are only twelve tracks in the game, and at least half of them feel almost interchangeable with one another, with the others being iconic mostly for their backgrounds and not any interesting track layout. The handful of different event types again double up on each other, with checkpoint and single lap time trials feeling nearly identical and the only alteration between elimination and evade being the obnoxious mines placed along the track. There's already a noticeable lack of content in Super Toy Cars, but having so much of it feel so similar to each other and stretch on so long somehow seems worse than if the game had just been half as long.
The monotonous grind of repeated events robs the game of any sense of progression. You aren't looking forward to new tracks because there aren't any; you aren't looking to improve your skills because the AI is never challenging you. There's no desire to buy new cars as so many are useless, and upgrades are needless and so inexpensive you can be fully upgraded after only a half dozen races or less.
And then there are the usual hallmarks of unfinished games: glitchy audio, constant collision issues, hitting invisible walls and clipping through solid ones, random frame rate drops, and a rather embarrassingly bare bones online mode (which doesn't even support private lobbies or inviting friends).
I like what Super Toy Cars is going for, and I think with a few more months of development it could have become a lot more than it did, but being ostensibly finished it feels pointless to hold out hope that its problems will ever be fixed, or that it's even in a state that could be remedied with a few patches. I'm not sure if it was pushed out the door early or its developers really thought it was finished, but the end result is still a game that's in need of attention it won't receive.

This game is amazing. In the following 48 hours after I bought this game, I played it for 38 hours. Weekend well spent. This game sucks you in and you lose track of the time very quickly. You'll swear you were playing for 20 mins...nope, bam, 4 hours gone like that. It's extremely addictive.
As for the game itself, it's a factory-building game. You mine resources from the ground, manually at first but you quickly build machines to automate this. You lay transport (read: conveyor) belts to transport materials around, build power stations to power the whole thing, build turrets and weapons to defend against aliens, and expand your factory to research upgrades which allow you to...expand even more, ad infinitum. This game is a perfectionists nightmare because you'll find yourself repeatedly expanding and rebuilding your factory as you figure out more efficient ways to process and build things. The methods you use in the early-game just won't be enough to cope with the massive megafactories you'll end up with 100 hours into the game so for anyone who likes optimisation, this game is for you.
Modding support is great, multiplayer works and it playable but very laggy. Constant updates keep this game fresh and exciting, and I can't wait to play another 20 hours at the next lan party!

I'm a sucker for the arcade racing genre, so I purchased this game early on (it might have been early access, I don't remember now), and I pretty much immediately wrote it off.  More than anything the chunky hit boxes and punishing reset mechanics made for an infurating experience.  That said, I'm glad I re-downloaded and gave it another shot.  It's still not perfect but it's a whole lot better.  In some ways the racing experience is among the most satisfactory of the arcade racers I play (among them, Bang Bang Racing, Mini-motors EVO, Little Street Racers) because it feels like the AI cars neither cheat nor are handicapped in an unrealistic manner.  What remains imperfect are the hitboxes on some areas of some maps, which occasionally will find you stuck on parts that should clearly be traversable. Also, the heavily-mined elimination maps in career mode are almost hair-on-the-tongue annoying, at least if you're the sort that tries to get first on every map.  I would rate myself as mediocre at this genre, for what it's worth, so if you're an ace at driving games, this might be too simple for you.

I've put about 4 hours into this game, restarted several times due to bugs, which have since been fixed, and enjoyed the time put into it. Not all smooth, but in the time i've owned the game i have seen progress going in a good direction. I'd recommend it if you're into the strategy/survival thing. Things are of course likely to change due to the whole early acccess thing. Below is what i liked and disliked.
You start off with 4 characters, and each day they can do either 1, 2 or 4 actions, depending on whether you feed them that day or not, as well as what the action is. Some things, such as building or hunting, use more than 1 energy. If you have extra food then you get two extra actions, or you can play it safe and stockpile that food for a rainy day. Not that rain is int he game yet, but ya never know.
Building stuff seems to take too long, at least for the energy spent to build compared to how long that same amount of energy takes to gather. If it takes 2 minutes of gathering for 3 out of 4 characters to end their day, but 10 minutes of building for the 4th guy to finish its a rather boring day.
I like the hunting system, chance to fail, chance to succeed for several days worth of food, or chance to succeed but lose the hunting tool... great system! Also love how the guys try sneaking upon the prey.
Wood chopping with an axe: I'm a bit torn on this one. Its a 2 energy investment but takes several minutes to complete. Timewise i can have the other 3 people eat, each do 4 gatherings for the day and still wait on the wood guy to grab the last log or two. I'd like to see an option to assign someone to assist in log carrying, using 2 energy for the tree cutter and 1 for the assistant, but it cuts the carrying time in half (since both take 1 log at a time out of the 6 per tree). Wood gathered per tree remains the same, just grab it all faster and end the day faster.
They gathering system is nice, though i'd also like to have the random option back, with maybe a 25% chance they grab an extra item for doing random.. instead of 8 sticks maybe they bring 16 for example. As it is the hand gathering is already 1/3 as efficient as hunting or gathering with tools, so late game the women will be a lot less useful compared to the men. Perhaps even leading us to starve one out just to save on food, after all, if she isnt earning her keep...
Research for the first few items is a bit too expensive. Once you unlock tools and get the stations built gathering isnt so bad, but i kept running out of wood with the campfire burning it early on while trying to save up for the first few items.
We've been getting bug fixes frequently and new stuff implemented. The dev seems to care and be putting time into fixing and improving the game. Fun game so far, i can only see it getting better in the future.

Ok, it is never easy to write a good Early Access Review. The basic rule is to review the game features. not the bugs, because these should be squashed sometime during the alpha and beta test phase. but Ok here we go.
The game has a sandbox and a survival mode. in sandbox, it is basically build for free, your character can fly, great for the creative mind and for learning the basic mechanics of the game.
In survial mode, your character needs to eat to stay alive. food can be found in the form of berries, muchrooms and you can hunt game for a nice chop of deer meat. Jummie.
Besides starvation, the other ways of dying are being crushed by a falling tree or any other heavy object, killed by other players or AI (PvPvE). There is an option to play off-line and without barbarian bits as well if you don't like that aspect.
To build your castle in survival is a very rewarding but time consuming process. for example a single foundation block takes 20 stone and 10 wood chips to build. you can carry 10 wood chips fine, but only 1 stone. It would take for ever to build a castle without some form of transport.
This is where the engineering bit really comes to life. I started really enjoying the game after building my first cart that is pulled up the hill using a drum and rope. after chopping down some trees or gathering stone in the quarry, I simply fill the boxes on my cart, go back to the scaffolding site and haul the cart in with the rope spindle.
If you are up to being clever enough to build things like this, or cranes or other medieval construction mechanics, this game is for you!
Also, every now and then save your game under a different name. build a Trebuchet or catapult and demolish your work. Big fun, then load your backup save game and continue building.
Remarks: Make sure you have a decent computer! my I7 laptop with GeForce GT 630M can barely run the game. Also I had to downgrade my graphics drivers to Nvidia driver version 355.98 because of a lightning error that occurs with later drivers. Performance improvements are normally done in a later development phase, but until than the game has heavy physics and graphics demands.
Another thing is the learning curve. There are many tutorials on the web, but due to the many updates these are out of date quickly and some times they are not representing the latest version of the game any more. It often takes a lot of efford and asking on the forums how a new feature works. Again, tutorials and hints are normally implemented in the final stages of game development.
For an early acces game, It is at the moment already very playable en enjoyable and it has all the potential to become a great game once finished. Therefore the game has my recommendation!

To fans of complicated games such as Dwarf Fortress and Aurora, Factorio is a very safe bet. For others unfamiliar with these games, it's still something definitely worth checking out. I originally discovered this game through Steam family sharing as a family member had picked it up, but quickly felt the need to buy it myself - partly because I wanted to support the awesome work by Factorio's devs, but also because I absolutely needed to keep playing while my family member played their own games - it's just so addictive.
As for the actual content, this game is like Minecraft's redstone took way too much caffeine. You have to gather resources, refine them, research new ways to gather and refine, and so on and so forth. You start out just gathering a couple of resources to make an automatic miner, so that you can automatically fuel your furnaces, so that you can in turn create another automatic miner. You laugh to yourself that this is overkill, who could possibly need 10 mining drills? That's so much ore! But then suddenly it's wednesday morning and you've been playing for 72 hours straight and you have 300 mining drills and are burning down all the forests to pave the way for the new "overkill" furnace park where you've planned to make 500 furnaces and the baby is crying and your wife has left and taken the dog but you just need a few more oil rigs, man.
Overall, a solid 10/10, would get divorced again.

All 3DMark did for me was confirm my suspicion that I have a Mid-Range Gaming PC. With that in mind, I see that it will be useful gauging overclocked hardware and future upgrades. I'm not an expert on benchmarks,  but I have no complaints. I bought it on sale and I thought it was a pretty good value for what I got it for.
Just got green circuits running.
Never had any issues with testing my hardware with this tool. I would happily recommend this to any person who wants to test the true power of their hardware in this realistic but taxing benchmark.

3DMark is benchmarking software which serves to allow you to put a number to the capabilities of your computer. In it, a series of scenes are rendered by your hardware, typically beyond the reach of all but the highest end of computers, and you can find out how many frames per second it performs, and how it performs relative to other computers. It's a fun little distraction, and that's all there is to it. Choose a price point to where you think it's worthwhile.
I will say, for achievement collectors, this thing has some of the most arbitrary achievements I've seen.

This is a great utility for stressing your hardware, and overclocking. Paired with MSI Afterburner, This can help you fine tune overclocks by seeing if you can run the benchmark a few times through stable. I would reccomend this software to anyone with a new peice of hardware, as it gives you a great sense of what you can do with it. As I got it for 5 dollars (I think?) on sale, there is no reason not to buy this when the prices get low. Solid 9.5/10 from me.

In case you all ask: I didn't try this game out just for the hat. I just wanted to try something new.
And, well... this game gave much more than I expected it to give.
It's a great four-person co-op game. You and three other players take on the roles of a Marine squad dropped into a colony overtaken by an alien infestation. This takes you on a campaign consisting of seven missions, watching your squad in top-down view kick♥♥♥♥♥
The controls are the simplest, but that doesn't mean the worst: you move with WASD, aim with your mouse. It's bare minimum, but that's very intuitive and aiming is made a lot easier by this.
There are four character classes: Officers, which use powerful Vindicator shotguns with huge stopping power and also increase the abilities of their squadmates, Special Weapons who use heavy autoguns to mow down enemies, Medics who tend to the team's health and Techs who are able to use tools better than others and perform hacks. The game offers two characters in every class, each one with different abilities (for example, between the two Medics, Faith is faster and a better Medic overall, but Bastille is tougher, better at combat, and gets a bonus to using adrenaline shots). This not only allows you to choose a character of the required class that will suit your playstyle, but also puts a hard limit on the number of duplicate classes a team can have (since there are two characters of each class, that means - go figure - up to two of the same class). Something a LOT of modern class-based games would use.
In terms of weapons, you get only a handful at the very beginning, and unlock more as you gain experience and level up. However, standard weapons are usually the most useful and reliable, with only a few really neccesary unlocks (such as a medigun. Yes, a frikkin' medigun. Which works just like any TF2 player would imagine it to work). This makes resetting your levels for cosmetic "promotions" not that painful, on the other hand.
The game gives you a variety of enemies to fight: other than the standard Drones, Rangers and Mortarbugs which attack at a distance, Boomers which are basically walking suicide bombers, Shieldbugs which require flanking and teamwork to hit their weakpoints, and Parasites which can infest and kill a marine very quickly, unless the Medic takes care of the victim.
The official campaign, while very short, has a high replayability, and the game also offers the fan creators development tools to create their own works.
Unfortunately, despite its high quality, the game isn't too popular. You might find maybe 20-25 dedicated servers and 5-10 lobbies at any given moment. Speaking of the lobby option, it doesn't show you the ping of that particular one. You're forced to connect and then use the "ping" console command to check it. It's kind of a waste, but that's a technical problem that could be easily fixed, and doesn't really matter in the long run.
Overall, this is a very, very good game. I highly recommend it to any survival horror fans, as well as shooter players and co-op gamers. It would be a sin to not at least give it a try.

I saw a few YouTubers play this, and knew right away I'd have to give it a try. Eagerly downloaded and hopped in, confident my first run would be a decent one as I'd seen some gameplay already. Things started out great, or so I thought, then I got killed on Day 2.
Loaded up a second run, and made it to day 8 and the second area in what was easily one of the funnest, most tense, interesting hour and a half of game I've had in a while. The ups and downs had me on the edge of my seat, and I was forced to make tough decisions the whole way through. Finally met my doom on a pitch black night facing a rotter the likes of which I'd yet to encounter.
While people will and have compared this to a certain highly popular rogue-like, I think the game stands very well on it's own. The inspiration is surely there, but in my limited time with the game I feel like I will enjoy WotL a lot more than the excellent but story 'dry' FTL. Combat in the former is far more robust and polished, and can be a bit fiddly in WotL, but as a whole I do really enjoy March of the Living. Before purchasing this game, you have to realise this is an INDIE title made by a small team with a small budget. It cuts some corners, it's not as polished as the bigger titles. Can you live with that? If yes, then it's a little gem of a game.
It's a turn-based zombie apocalypse fallout-esque "loot the world" RPG. Like scavenging? Like old-school "dumb slow" zombies? Like exploring stuff and building up your home camp? This is it.
At the moment of this writting, be aware that there are still quite a few bugs in the game, but most of them are minor or can be overlooked and the game is still enjoyable. However, the devs have been very visible and present and it's obvious they are working on those right now; expect many patches in the weeks to come.
It's not a tactical combat game; the combat is not as integrated as some dedicated game like X-Com. Don't go in expecting a ton of tactical combat options, as almost everything is organic, and battle is closer to chess than an actual firefight. Movement and positioning are as important as the type of equipment you bring to the table, and personally I like it that way; there's no artificial game effects, everything is part of the way you handle your squad. Getting swarmed by zombies? Pull back and use a choke point. Getting mowed down by human enemies with guns? Move behind cover and force them to come into melee range, or pull them into the nearby pack of zombies, etc.
The rest of the game contains a lot of dialogue and decision-making. Dealing with your ever-growing pack of survivors keeps you on edge, as you never know what kind of event is going to pop up each day, which keeps the world interesting. Exploring the map and finding a new zone full of goodies to bring back to your base camp is an awesome feeling, like finding a treasure room each time, and random encounters run the gamut from new allies to just a few random zombies to bandit ambushes.
The maps were nicely crafted, and have this sense of "events past", you can almost read the story of what transpired at the location you are visiting, with the crashed cars and the blood streaks left by the zombies that must have dragged the screaming occupants out, etc.
All in all, a nice game that will only get better as the devs fix the bugs. Its premise is also quite unique, and I'm giving this 100% of my support, as I want more games of this type to exist.

You've probably played a lot of zombie games over the past few years, the market is flooded with them, but trust me when I say Dead State is worth your time.
Taking the idea of old-school turn-based RPGs and giving them an undead twist, DoubleBear has created a game that insanly fun and just the right level of challenging.
If you are in any way a fan of either zombies or surivial games, then DS is going to have something to keep you interested. Instead of being rewarded for mowing down hoards of zombies with impossible weapons, you gain your experience by improving your shelter, helping survivors, and picking up whatever small creature-comforts you can while you walk across a large and dangerous landscape looking for food, weapons, and any friendly faces you can come across.
Dead State is by no means a perfect game, but it's one that I find myself coming back to quite a lot. Even now, bugs are being fixed, features are being added, and everything about the game is improving. I can not urge you enough to give this game a try, even if your taste in zombie games has gone a bit stale.

A disclaimer, I haven't played the steam edition of Firewatch that I own, mainly because my laptop at the time could not handle it. As of now I've played the game multiple times, but exclusively on Playstation 4. I felt secure in purchasing the game twice because I adore this company and like to offer my support, but also because Firewatch has become a very personal game to me.
In May 2015 I lost my aunt, who I was very close with. She died after a long battle with dementia and mistreatment in a nursing home we would not have placed her in if given the choice. I was there by her bedside when she died, around a week before my birthday and moving into my first apartment/starting my first job. I had very little time to grieve for her, and after helping my grandma and family watch over her and help her, issues facing people with and families effected by alzheimer's and dementia has become a very important thing for me. Because of the fast pace at which my life was changing, I bottled up my grief and went on with my life.
My boyfriend introduced me to Firewatch later that year, telling me that it was coming out in the upcoming year and he knew it would be something I'd love. I watched the website and news regarding the game like a hawk, eager to see more about it. When it went up for preorder, I immediately bought it on steam. Once I realized that my dying laptop would struggle to even boot it up, I preordered it on my PS4. It may have been silly, but I believed in this game.
The day it came out I was incredibly excited. And then, almost immediately after starting the game, I had to stop. I was unaware that the protagonist had a history with dealing with a similar issue, watching helplessly as a loved one succumbs to dementia. I broke down on the spot, every bit of grief that had been kept inside came swelling up all at once. I pressed on, and found that the game was not only therapuetic, but everything I had wanted it to be and more. It has become one of my all time favorite games, and I'll still play it every so often just so I can wander the forests and mountain paths. It's very soothing if you've had a stressful day.
The gameplay is solid, though there isn't much to it. You walk around the park and interact with things, it's one of those games that are narrative driven rather than anything else. I liked throwing things around the watchtower at the start of each section.
The graphics are beautiful, stunning to look at wherever you go in the game. The only issue I ever had was if the environment was too dark in the caves, it made manuevering through it a bit difficult at times. This wasn't a frequent issue, and mainly a problem with my television settings.
The voice acting and character writing is fantastic. You get a real sense of who these characters are and their motivations and dreams through the game. You start to really care for them which, surprisingly, can be a difficult goal to obtain.
The story was seen as controversial when this game first came out and, while I understand why, I thought it was perfect. I was ready for a round of park ranger the simulator, but what I got instead was *SPOILERS* lonely people who fall into conspiracy theories, only to be jarred back into reality and the fact that sometimes things are a lot more simple than what you may hope for. The soundtrack at the climax really holds the moment up well, and I was forced to sit in stunned silence as everything sank in. This was very divisive for many people who wanted an ending more fantastical, but sometimes reality just ends up this way. Endings in the real world can be sad and plain, unremarkable, regardless of the journey you took to get there.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I know that many people avoid "walking simulators" but that term is often used negatively and I personally wouldn't attach it here. Firewatch is a narrative driven experience that has moments of adrenaline mixed with moments of serenity and is something I'd love for all to enjoy at least once. I've played through the game multiple times and I expect to continue doing so for years to come.

This is one of those games where a polar yes/no system doesn't exactly cut it. Personally, I couldn't stand this game any longer than I played it, but I know for a fact there's just enough here to warrant someone having a good time.
Let's get one thing out of the way immediately: This game immediately wins in the design department. The beutiful, hand drawn aesthetic paired with an appropriately cinematic score make Jotun look and sound excellent. In game sounds are a little hit and miss, but the majority is put together compotently.
Outside of eye candy, this action portion of this is mostly delivered through tight boss battles after a couple levels of exploration. They're well made, make sense intuitively when it comes to mechanics, and do a great job steadily introducing difficulty as time progresses. There's a fine line in difficulty that goes from "motivationally frustrating" to "table flip" that this mostly stays in between. Any treads outside of it come from external factors.
And then we reach the point where everything falls apart slightly. There's several mechanical design aspects that scream amateur, particularly in the adventure part of action-adventure. Before you reach the game's fantastically put together boss battles, you have to go through two levels of exploratory areas that provide background lore for the source material and ways to discover upgrades through flat health bonuses and powers. I don't have another way to describe these levels as dreadful. Certain scenery requires different attacks to progress, but have similar markings on them. The levels are sprawling and slightly confusing in layout, but the only map you have has no indication of where you are, and is in the pause menu. The majority don't even have combat and are more about enviromental hazards with spotty hit detection. I could go on and on. These poorly executed exploration pieces are what killed the game for me way too soon.
It doesn't help that the tutorial level doesn't do a good job of explaining the main gameplay loop. The pattern for the game, as presented by the first half, is do two levels of exploration, find the section's unique ability, maybe some other upgrade, then fight a boss. The tutorial level has you fight a mini-boss in the middle of one level and fail to signpost that there might be something beyond the path it makes you take, and made me end up missing the first ability of the game.
I want to love this game, as it should be right up my alley, but the simple fact is the majority of it is not fun. The boss battles are great in spectacle, everything looks and feels great, but there's too much time spent where I'm thinking "please no more." Maybe i'm expecting too much, maybe I'm just bitter, maybe I'm just an idiot. I'm honestly hoping I'm wrong and that it picks up past the first few stages I saw, but I'm not patient for that.

that there are health- and power-ups to unlock, and that there is a map for this purpose -- visible on the floor of Ginnungagap, and when you press escape in any other zone -- goes a long way to making otherwise bland gameplay and infuriating boss fights a little less bland and infuriating. Unfortunately, none of this is made clear, and reading the map can be a bit of a mystery at first, too. Hopefully this little review will help others clue in to how things work a bit earlier than I did! I also recommend going over the keyboard controls as a way of discovering the actions you can take.
At any rate, the art, music, and narration are
, and the subject matter is intriguing. I suspect that this isn't really my type of game, but I'll give it a cautious recommendation.

Emily Is Away is a re-enactment of AIM back in the day, including the nostalgic Windows XP noises.
This game made me pull out my old Windows XP to play The Sims on it.
You start off with a nostalgic Windows XP start-up sound, and you are greeted by a menu that looks like the screen on Windows XP where you sign in. On the right is where you get to select your chapter. It obviously starts off at Chapter 1 (2002), and as you progress, you will unlock more chapters, up to Chapter 5 (2006).
During these chapters, you have a conversation with a friend named Emily. In this conversation, you will be required to select a sentence to say to Emily, press the keys on your keyboard, and expect a reply. Depending on the sentence you choose, will cause an action in the future, like who you will get together with, who your friends are, what your job is, etc.
This is a game I couldn't exit (with the nostalgic Windows XP shutdown sound) without having the desire to come back to. And it's free! So why isn't it in your library yet?

I was raised on Re-Volt, Crash Team Racing and Mario Kart
Do you now what all 3 of those games have in common? They are all interesting with a fair bit of replayability
Re-Volt made you feel like you were handling actual toy cars, in addition to having an impressive selection of cars/tracks
Crash Team Racing was just the best. Small-ish selection for cars and tracks. But the power-ups and the sheer uniqueness of the entire game made this a gem
Mario Kart was the great grandfather of kart racing, and had a fairly large track selection and had plenty of multiplayer mayhem
Does Super Toy Cars do this?
Yes. For about an hour and a half. Then it gets *really* dull *REALLY* quickly
The number of tracks described in the description is slightly wrong, or at least pretty misleading. They mean there are 12 tracks TOTAL, and there are 4 different locations TOTAL. It doesnt mean "there are 12 tracks in 4 locations for a total of 48 tracks" Moreover, the tracks are very simple affairs, nothing really unique about them at all
The cars are meh. Between the hitboxes being helariously random (as they collide with the track funkily, making drifting a chore when you clip a tube wall wrong, or get bumped out of a drift by a guy 3 feet away). This also makes ramming quite literally a hit or miss situation
Also, each car has stats that determine how they run. The only way to see these stats is to go into the campaign mode and memorize them, as you cannot see the during "quick race" or "multiplayer" modes. But again, unless if its an extreme stat (insanely high or low) you will not notice a difference. Without fail the high speed models (formula 1 car generally) will have a piece of cake for the races, where as the more maneuverable or more weighty models get lapped constantly with very little balancing
The powerups are lame. There is not much really to be said about them other than they feel weak because of the funky physics on the car's part. If a car gets hit with an 8ball (a very powerful weapon) it kind of gets spun a little... It also has the annoying feature of replacing your powerup whenever you drive over a new one. Making sure that you cant save them for when you need them
So in summary, I would give Super Toy Cars a 4/10
Its not a bad game, just a game done poorly. Pick it up if its on sale for 4 dollars or less, but dont expect much
TL:DR VERSION
Ok racing game gets boring quickly. Spend 10 dollars elsewhere

as well as a comprehensive written review:
Super Toy Cars tries to bring their influences of the micro machines series to the today's era. Sadly, the effort is mostly in vain.
The graphics are ugly, especially the edges are very rough, even with 8x MSAA activated. The screenshots shown above are highly post-processed and do not represent the ingame graphics. The sound design is plainly bad. While the music is good, the few tracks get repetitive very quickly and the sound effects are incredibly hideous. The gameplay overall is also subpar. The cars, while feeling distinct from another, all are floaty, act unpredictably in terms of physics, the sliding mechanics requires you to hold a button, which feels unnatural and there are also very few tracks in the base game. However there is a track editor, thus this problem might be solved by the community.
Overall, I would not recommend Super Toy Cars. If you are desperate for an action-racing game and are looking for a couple of hours of enjoyment, maybe with friends, Super Toy Cars could be it, since there is not much other stuff out there. But it's no Mario Kart, Blur or Micro Machines.

I do not like the idea of writing negative reviews on games. However, I cannot recommend this title in its present state. This one has been out for some time, and it is still very poorly allocated. The memory allocation makes the game almost impossible to run. I have a GTX970 video card, and a 4690 Intel processor, as well as 8G of ram. The game is not running worth a darn on it. It continually freezes up (usually after every single block placement while building), and then crashes to desktop, saying that there is sufficient memory for all the tasks running. The only things running is the Steam ap and the game. When the problem is posted on the discussion page, the devs do not respond. The only response I have seen is the statement that the individual's computer is not powerful enough to play the game. And this for a fairly high-end rig.
The construction inventory, to be fair, is fairly extensive. However, it lacks some fairly vital and basic items. For instance, you can place statues around the castle courtyard, but there are no doors of any kind. No drawbridges, nothing. So either you cannot leave the keep, or the enemies can just walk in. I can see this oversight for a short while, but for any length of time it is pretty game breaking.
As a multiplayer game it has some serious potential down the road, provided the devs actually (eventually) respond to, and address the issues in-game. But that time has not yet arrived. And as long as they ignore these legitimate concerns from their customers, the game is still fairly unplayable. As a single-player game, which the store page insists that it is, there is nothing to do but to build the architecture. No serious NPC's exist or are slated to ever exist as far as I can tell. That is not all bad. As a castle-building simulator, it could be fun for some people, and I would eventually be willing to recommend it at that time, provided the problems are addressed.

It's pretty much a much improved version of "The Oregon Trail" with zombies. Only took us 40 years to get it. Nothing else I really wanna add to the things the devs did right, it's a really fun game. Setting reminds me of Walking Dead, the music reminds me of The Last of Us.
My only complaint is the lack of a "continue" option. When you die, you die. I personally hate pouring an hour into one life just to die suddenly from *reason x* then have to start over. For those who want the bragging rights of beating a hard game, good for you. Everyone else who just wants to finish the game, good for you too, but unless this is added, I'm capped out at 6 hours and will probably uninstall.
Those 6 hours were worth my $13.49.

The actual game itself is good, mechanics in place are good, although some things need some tweaking in my opinion.
Fatigue/Hunger: These drain too fast, it gets to be quite a hassle to have to sleep/eat every 5-10 minutes of gameplay. Food is not plentiful enough to sustain large groups.
Combat: You simply do not loot enough bullets to use guns consistently, which does seem concerning because of how clunky the combat systems can get with melee. Having to simultaneously control up to 6 characters in a live melee situation feels clunky when using more than 1-2 characters (micromanaging attacks, grapple countering, etc.). A time-based turn system like in the Monster's Den series would be better suited for combat in my opinion.
I also feel that combat is rather repetitive, with such high chances to get into encounters while searching, and since combat is rather clunky, it does detract from the experience.
Inventory seems a bit small, but with more characters and more playthroughs, I guess we as players can know which items are useful and which are useless.
There are parts that I do like, such as not being able to go back to a previous save in the same playthrough (although I do wish we got a save slot for each of the characters!), which truly puts weight on your decisions.
Do not get me wrong, the game is good, but I feel as if these issues hamper it from delivering the optimal gameplay experience.
An "easy mode" (which would probably be the regular mode, with how it is now being the "hardcore mode") as suggested with all of these improvements seems like the solution.

Ok so I have now played a good couple of hours on MoTL and Figured I needed to elaborate more in my review so I'm re-doing it.
Most of it's functions are used on your mouse so it's not got a load of controls to get you flustered. It's an easy to learn and challenging game with multiple outcomes and ways to get through it based on the choices you make. It can be difficult to get into at the beginning but would like to share a few things to help you out a little more when you start off, as not to be completely screwed.
1st, try to use your hammer to start off with, this will save your ammo till you need it and help you grasp the fighting a little better (You can press space bar to pause to plan your moves) I find it best to attack one and run back after your first hit before going in for a second.
2nd, rather than making it your goal to get to the quests as quickly as you can, try to hit as many areas on the map as you can on your way to the quests, each stop you get a text box come up and sometimes these can help you get supplies.
3rd, DO NOT FLEE. Try and kill every zombie that comes for you using the method above, if you flee, you risk chance of loosing something you may need later on.
4th, If someone wants to come with you, allow them. You can use these to either help you fight zombies, or you can use them as a distraction so they get eaten whilst you pick off the zombies.
Lastly, when you're scavenging, always hit the 60 minute search, If you're heard by the Rotters and you kill them off, you can still potentially find items.
Doing this I've managed to get as far as Day 13, through to the second map area. Getting out of the Grapple is a bit difficult at times, but other than that, you should be good.
Hope this helps you to enjoy the game and progress a little Further :)

X-com in a Zombie holocaust.
You're either completely sold on that premise or don't know what Im talking about. If you're in the same group as I am, and hearing those words makes you go "OMGOMGOMGOMGOMGOMG", then the game was made specifically for you in mind.
This is and indie labor of love devoted to a very specific game mechanics that lots of old school gamers like myself find lacking in todays "PEW PEW" marketplace. People in that group probably know who they are and can accept the quibbles of low budget games like this so long as the broad strokes work, and they do for the most part.
Like many criticisms have likely pointed out, the game is definitely unintuitive in certain areas, inventory management being the one that immediately springs to mind. However, in fairness, many of the criticisms I see people saying certain things aren't in game when in fact they are, such as Group inventory management at base, attacking diagonally (must have a two handed weapon). However these features can be lost in the somewhat clunky interface.
Basically, the idea of an old school base management turn based RPG in a zombie holocaust either sells you on it's own, or it doesn't. If that premise whets your whistle, you'll likely be able to look past some of the quibbles of indie game design in favor what they did right, which is quite a lot. You'd also be able to look past the unfortunate release timing of the game which puts in smack dab in the middle of zombie mania in pop culture, when in fact at it's inception that would have made it a much more original concept.

Now that I've put in a few hours (12) in the game, I can make a pretty comprehensive review on this title.
First off- Dead State has rough edges, surely, but overall, it's an enticing zombie survival game, with emphasis on squad and shelter management, improving your abode while trying to weather out the apocalypse. You'll set up your base in a school in a fictional Texas town, trying to make ends meet without succumbing to the horrors of the zombie apocalypse, which is not limited to the shambling dead. The game makes good use of the setting, providing a few differing factions and splinter groups set up in the ruins of the world, each striving to survive- sometimes at the expense of others. You won't be getting many warm welcomes, and most of these will turn out to be ambushes, so that the thugs in question can loot those canned pineapples from your carcass.
Thankfully, not all of Texas is going to meet you with guns blazing- sometimes, diplomacy is the way to go, and investing in the skill trees can net you surprising results, varying from avoiding armed confrontation with hostile groups, to negotiating new location information, talking depressed survivors into fighting for another day or even recruiting some of the tough-as-nails survivors to join your growing community. Naturally, characters of nominal importance are the only ones you can actually recruit- you can pretty safely discern hostile troops from their lack of name, and the ubiquitous looter gear they're armed with.
After 12 hours, I can safely say that I am glad I backed Dead State- it's proving itself to be pretty much all it boasted, albeit with a few rough edges. I find myself playing 'just one more day', trying to meet up daily demands and the missions on the To-Do list. You're free to explore the end of the world, utilizing your own judgement and goals, although it does pay to placate and bribe your growing group of survivors every now and then, just to keep everybody happy, healthy and ready to eke out a meager existence in a world filled with ravenous undead, trigger-happy looters, gun-toting militias, renegade cops, mercenaries and just ordinary people trying to survive at all costs.
Pros:
- Solid tactical gameplay. Aside a few odd glitches in the 1.0 (multiple enemies occupying single tile, some impr. weapons losing their ammo charges- pepper sprays, nail guns and the like), you can pretty much plan, and execute raids on the many locations in the game, sometimes taking an active part in offense, sometimes defense, and every once in a while, just playing both hostile survivors and the zombies against each other.
- Stealth versus guns-blazing approaches- you're free to use your own judgement in how to deal with each location, but the game will most likely toss a zombie or two on maps where you announce your presence by three rounds rapid.
- Varied locations that, although using same buildings from time to time, are still distinguishable from each other.
- Emphasis on Survival, instead of shooting one thousand zombies. Stealth, planning and a bit of cloak and dagger can get you in and out of many situations where most games would provide you with one option- violence. In Dead State, violence is usually the last, least desireable option.
- Different characters with various backgrounds, motivations, likes and dislikes, which are factored in the daily business of your Shelter. Some are nearly joke characters, while others have to cope with the tragedies arising from losing their loved ones to the zombie plague.
- Good range of skills, weapons and choices for improvements on the home base
- Great concept art, character portraits
CONS:
- Still a bit buggy. Expect they will sort 'em out in the future patches, but be ready for clipping foes, misplaced pepper spray and nail gun magazines, one or two zones where Turn-Based-Combat trigger is broken and the fight will continue, despite no active hostilities. One shut-in recruitable survivor dialogue which should end up in violence, does not.
- The game really doesn't give you a heads up that initiating hostilities towards obviously hostile survivor groups first can lead to a MASSIVE negative morale in home base. You see a crazed shooter, you better have them initiate combat, or suffer the consequences.
- Static game zones: Sadly, once you've cleared out a game zone, there's nothing left to do there. And you can't mark these looted areas off your map, but have to rely on your own memory.
- No way to mark vital resources on the map, like discovering and making note of a sack of concrete mix you'll need later for HQ upgrades.
- Some of the menus are still a bit difficult to navigate/ too small to read on higher resolutions.
- Survivor inventory management in the HQ is a bit tricky to locate, but once you pick up on the drop-down menu on the upper left corner, you're set. Also, ammo dividing can be achieved with the CTRL-click on ammo stack, after which the portion allocated can be moved to the HQ stockpile, and distributed to your survivors.
- No real soundtrack or voices, sound effects that stick to mind.
