Full discolsure: Ironcast isn't a game I expected to get into when I first saw it. At first glance, I thought it looked too odd for me to like. I mean, there's mechs, a Steampunk setting, and everything is packaged in a match 3 game. But at the same time, it piqued my curiosity to the point that it went onto my wishlist and eventually my library when it went on sale. This was further encouraged by people saying that this was like a Steampunk FTL, and you can check my review of that to see how much adore that game. 38 hours of gameplay later, I would like to apologize to the devs for doubting them; this game rocks.
So what is this game about? In a clockwork nutshell, it's about an invasion of Britain by the French involving Steampunk bipedal mechs called Ironcasts. You play as a fair number of pilots that you can put into different mechs, upgrade your Ironcast with better weapons and defenses as you go, and slowly uncover the story as to why the French invaded. And this is all packaged in a match 3 game.
But hear me out, because I can tell some of you are rolling your eyes at the idea. Here's how it works: the match 3 mechanic is there to fill your ammunition, energy to power your shields and drives, coolant to make sure you don't overheat and kill yourself, and repair points so you can fix your subsystems when they get damaged. It may seem the the two concepts wouldn't mix, but once you start playing, the three genres of match 3, Steampunk, and rouge-lite feel more natural than you think. In fact, they go together like tea, crumpets, and dapper costumes.
The music is nice, but it's not something I really focus on in a game where I'm trying to survive, espcially with the sounds of Steampunk machinery and futuristic sci-fi weapons going off in my ears. The soundtrack is memorable when you have a moment to listen to it, but it won't be the first thing you notice in the heat of the moment.
Now it's time for me to address the number one complaint people seem to have with this game: the RNG. Honestly… I don't think it's really an issue. The Almighty and Fickle RNGesus is so common to the genres of not just match 3s but rouge-lites as well that it seems pointless to bring it up. In my opinion, people who complain about RNG in games like this may as well complain about ice cream being cold. But to be fair, the RNG CAN be unfair sometimes, and you might be put into a no-win situation. But so can games like Nuclear Throne, Enter the Gungeon, or heck, FTL. So if the idea of RNG in a rouge-like/lite doesn't appeal to you, you probably shouldn't play those kinds of games.
All that being said, Ironcast is an enjoyable game and one that I didn't expect to like. But I gave it a chance, and I'm so glad I did. Props to the developers for creating this, and for putting up with me on Twitter, haha!

I'm not too sure what to think of Ironcast. It's a "match 3" type of game where you take 3 turns at a time connecting "gems" of the same color to increase your ironcast's stats.
I've been looking at a new take on these games, mainly adding an RPG aspect to it like the "puzzle quest" series. But as it tries doing something different, it removes some of the fun aspects of both matching and RPG games. Once you die, you have to restart from scratch. Sure you get a few unlocks and global upgrades whenever you die, but it never feels like you're making any real progress. The matching aspect isn't that bad, but it lacks the satisfaction of stack combos other games provide.
So it's hard for me to both recommend and not recommend this game. There are better games like this out there, but none of them have any steampunk mechs.

I actually like this game, even though it is a rougelite reliant on RNG, because:
- When you hit the level-cap and have understood the game well, only the first few battles are RNG-Heavy.
- If you strategize well, you will have consistent progress throught the game
- If you understand your strengths and weaknesses at each stage of the game, you know which fights to take and which to shun.
What I really dislike about the game, is that:
- It really feels like a strategy game that is well balanced, but requires the RNG aspect to not be too short or feel boring quickly (could easily be fixed by creating a better mechanic)
- While leveling and not having the level-based passive bonuses, the RNG-aspect is even more important for success.
- The weird way the roguelike aspects are coded leads to the loss of all campaign progress (of a playthrough) if it freezes while inside a battle (happend to me, well geared, prefectly ready to destroy the final boss (like seriously, I could absorb all his damage for 2 out of 7 turns because of shield strength and had the strongest weapons in the game)), which is super frustrating after having sunk 2 hours into a playthrough!
- Still not bad enough to not be recommended, but be mindful of the grindy aspect and necessity to learn underlying dynamics and mechanics of the game to be consisten.
- Don't buy it if you want consistent strategy!

Considering turn based games have been around for decades, it's hard to explain why this one stuffs it all up so horribly. On the surface this has a lot to recommend it; recource gathering, base building, missions and more besides, and no doubt that make might for a fun game. But the combat system is so irredeemably awful it makes getting into the game a tricky notion.
The typical action point system only comes into play once you're in combat so you're free to run around until then, but once you enter combat, good Lord does the game go south. For a start, you can't attack on a diagonal, which makes precisely no sense. Square on fighting is the order of the day. Secondly, there's no way to bring up a list of key commands so if you need to change view for instance, there are no on-screen icons to do it (a staple of these kind of games surely), you're kind of stuck. The whole game lacks that kind of simple clarity. Thirdly, it's too easy to batter someone on your team (why does the game allow this without at least a simple 'are you sure?' check?).
As a result, once you enter combat it turns into a farce of repeated misses with whatever weapon you have equipped (early in the game you equip a weapon which doesn't show on your character who then gets advised to equip a weapon by everyone he meets before going outside - top work!), shuffling your characters around to try and get to the right square to attack and then using all your action points hitting your own team. It's just rubbish from top to bottom.
It might get better and I'm certainly going to persist playing it as it seems to have genuine depth, but it's frustrating and counter-intuitive to play. I was hoping for State of Decay meets X-Com but this falls far short of that lofty aspiration.

Game delivers exactly what it promised: Team-based, 3/4 tactical zombie survival / base management in open world environment. There's a lot to sink your teeth into with this one. Basically you lead this bunch of survivors and every morning you get a quick briefing of things / place to explore before setting them to work and you and your scavenging party set out to find some resources to survive another day.
Throughout your travels you'll come across other survivors, some good, some not so much. But its you against the zeds so every live body helps. There's lots to explore and different modes of travel, and the shelter will requires lots of upgrades to turn it into a haven amongst all the chaos around you. There are items you need to collect to improve survivor's morale throughout your travels, in turn they will give you advice and mark locations on your map for you to explore. The overland map presents lots of random encounters during your travels, some good, some bad.
The shelter is what it's all about. You are constantly struggling with the other survivors to turn this little elementary school into a bonafide ZA haven. And it has all the ability to do it, with 2 floors and multiple rooms you will have everything you and your survivors will need to survive the nights of Splendid if you plan accordingly.
Combat starts off appearing simple but as you get more followers and more weapons you can then start to have very tactical battles, with different status effects and AOE biological weapons to help keep the battle in your favor, making impossible-looking battles into 3-round wipe ups if you're careful. Both ranged and melee are viable (I stick to melee, this is a ZA)
The maps run from classic overrun parks and hospitals, to dark scenes of lost hope, to some really...unique scenarios that I wouldnt have expected. Games like these are what makes all the risk of joining an EA worthwhile. Would highly recommend.

I am a Man of Constant Sorrow
Full disclosure: review copy provided by developer/publisher!
Zombies: I know 'em, you know 'em, even your grandmother knows 'em (though she probably remembers when they were bug-eyed Haitians under a voodoo spell). Personally, I haven't been bitten (teehee) by the zombie bug: they're boring whether they're shambling, running, walking; they're boring whether they're stupid, learning, or ending John Leguizamo's career. “OOOO, METAPHORS! WE'RE THE REAL WALKING DEAD -” Shut the ♥♥♥♥ up. It's tired. It's old hat.
But I really dig this game. REALLY dig it.
March of the Living is a “you're ♥♥♥♥ed” simulator: whichever character you choose, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. You're given an objective and you have to set out on a randomly generated spider-webbed path, dealing with zamboozles and the living, all while juggling items and your own well-being. With each kilometer traversed your character (or party) will become fatigued and hungry, meaning you'll have to take less-than-opportune snack, potty, and nap breaks along the way. Since it's zombie country now there's a helpful gauge indicating how close the zombie growling is to you and, if it gets close enough, you'll be thrust into that weird FTL pause command strategy gameplay. You'll encounter sometimes as many as six zimbompos, and when you have a party of your own things can get crowded real quick. It's hard to tell pixels apart in the mosh pit but you can select actions outside of the fray using little character profiles on the top right.
As you travel you'll hit cities (distinguishable on the map because they look like skylines), and you can scavenge for more supplies... they're like reliable oasises. You'll grab health, ammo, items to trade with barterers, and weapons.
This is a procedurally generated, RNG-y affair so it comes with the usual pros and cons.
Pros: every journey is going to  be a little different.
Con: ♥♥♥♥ you, did you think you were going to find a crab apple or something to eat? Enjoy a long, agonizing, drawn out death.
The writing is compelling in that FTL way... lots of encounters and scenarios, lots of characters to meet and unlock, lots of deaths to die. And it's not about the destination,  it's about the journey. You're going to die an AWFUL lot, and sometimes it's just going to be straight-up NOT FAIR... but you'll persevere, in the end. You'll come back to this one because it's exciting to see how long you can hold it together, how different situations can be defused (or ignited), etc. Biggest gripe I have is the fatigue/hunger bar drops SUPER quick... but that's just me. There's also a flee mechanic in case you decide you want to cut and run from an intimidating fight... if you're alone you're liable to lose some ammo or food or an item, but if you have a party member or two you can pretty much say buh-bye to them. Of the five or six times I've fled with a party member in tow they ended up lost except ONCE, never to be seen or heard from again. Maybe that's just my RNG, I don't know.
What I do know is this is a fun one if you're looking to fill in that Organ/Oregon Trail/FTL void in your heart.
And that cover art? Brilliant. There's a zambly with maggots writhing in the sinews of his torn corpse and it is radical.

I played Franchise Hockey Manager 2 (FHM2) for a while and then got Eastside after so this is a comparison between the 2.
Pros:
- New rosters available (if created by a modder). You dont have buy a new game to get new rosters.
- Ability to shop player (This is available in FHM4)
- You can decide what each player means to your orginization, like if he is a core piece or fringe player. You also get prompted with interviews or actions to take if a player has a bad stretch or whatever. These are pretty rare but kinda interesting
- In-game visuals are fun to watch sometimes and are very customizable. You can watch every second or none at all.
- Overall more enjoyable than FHM2
Cons:
- Less historic rosters than FHM2
- You will get a 'email' on basically anything that happens in that league and 85% are not relevent. I have not found a way to filter them
- The "player rating" feature isn't very useful. Basically any NHL player in the NHL will get rated 6-10. Obviously if you put a AHL player he will score lower. I wish it was based off of their skill level or contract size. If a top player in the leauge like Ovechkin doesn't do much, he should score worse than a 4th liner that has similar game stats.
- Each day is broken into 3 sections; morning, evening, night. This means there is 3 clicks and simulations that take place each day, and if it's after the trade deadline and all your guys are healthy you have to click a million times to sim to the end of the season. Not a big deal just annoying when there is little to do, and there is a lot of times when there is nothing to do.
- Player stats are sort of confusing. There are no defined offensive and defensive stats, which makes it hard to figure out who is a better player in a trade. Thinks like "Determination" and "Work Rate" and "Anticipation" are difficult because I don't know how important they are. Should an offensive player have a high Anticipation? Or is that a defensive trait? If a offensive player with a high Work Rate is rare, is he worth keeping? Is it more important than high wristshot or stickhandling?
Tl;dr - If you like up to date rosters and a new game (and possibly new features) every year or so, get the latest FHM game. If you just want to mess around with a cheap hockey manager game and have the ability for modders to make up-to-date rosters, get this game.

This game has been in "Early Access" for an eternity. I bought it early hoping I could support it and make it better, but it's never come even close to being a decent playable game:
- Poorly optimized. Crashes often on a pretty good computer, and even when it doesn't crash it's super laggy.
- Glitchy. Character often gets stuck at random spots. Even in the pre-set environments, like the pre-loaded castle, there are tons of spots where you just randomly can't move.
- Interaction with objects is fairly useless. Again, even in the pre-set environments, the objects like catapults and drawbridges are purely for show.
- Gravity is useless. There are no calculations for structural integrity, so you might as well play Minecraft.
- Build tools are very rudimentary. Again, even Minecraft has more variety than this, and is a playable game to boot.
- Graphics suck. There are no other skins or textures in the base game, much less an ability to choose between them in the same castle. Everything starts to look the same after a while.
If you want to design and "build" castles, just use Google Sketchup. If you want to play in a fortress of your design, play Minecraft or any of the dozens of other games out there in the same vein. This one just felt like a giant waste of time and money.

Absolutely amazing game. It literally is everything I ever wanted!
The game's visuals are extremely beautiful to look at and the soundtrack definitely enhances the entire experience massively. This game is perfect for people who are fascinated by the unknown depths of the sea. Did SOMA or Subnautica catch your interest because you thought it was interesting to see how the deep sea looks? Well, this game is definitely the right one for you.
It tells a linear and unique story with the help of a bunch of likeable characters, each one having their own individual personality. You are the commander of a submarine and it's your task to go to the bottom of the sea, though you'll find that there's a lot to discover and take care of while you're on your way into the creepy and unsettling darkness and I can assure you that I spent half of my entire time just going "WOAH WHAT IS THAT?" "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥" "Dude, that's awesome" "Oh my god this is beautiful"
The game does an amazing job of delivering the exact thing you'd expect from the endless ocean. The developers found a great way to play around with the fact that you are indeed incredibly tiny in comparison to the vast size of the ocean and it's inhabitants, and the constant threat from all sides. More often than not will you find yourself in a situation where you hear stuff or see a torpedo warning, only to go into full-alert-mode as you panic and start to look around to try to get a grasp of what's going on around you.
That, combined with an amazing soundtrack, strong visuals to underline the experience, and some extremely unique ideas/concept will definitely make your playthrough memorable.
The game isn't perfect however but this is the first game of the developers and I feel like (based on the critics) they already worked to polish the game!
The controls can be a bit tricky at first but I assure you that you'll find yourself dashing through the ocean and destroying pirates in no time! Once you get a hang of it, you can pull of some very interesting maneuvers and use it to your advantage for...well...things like quick in-and-out combat!
Another thing that I personally didn't like was that a few mechanics aren't properly used. You'll quickly realize that you don't really need to manage your oxygen and food and the entire "economy" resolves around looting the same object and selling them to eventually buy ammunition, new guns, new ships and food. It's something , sure, and it works too, but I feel like there could be some improvement. I don't think it hindered my enjoyment in my playthrough however.
And the last thing I'd criticize about the game is the ending which felt a bit off. It wasn't bad, but definitely felt like it didn't fit. Once again I don't think that's a big thing in comparison to the overall experience I had.
A quick overview of the pros and cons
Pros:
+Stunning Visuals that are used to their full extent to bring the colorful and unique world to life.
+A truly amazing OST that captures the intensity of combat, the creepiness of the depths, the elegance and epicness of enemies and places and...of course...the feeling of exploration and adventure!
+A lot of unique and interesting concepts that you'd expect from a deep-sea game.
+Characters with distinct personalities to tell the story and bring the cast to life.
+A stunning world to explore with no pressure to follow the main mission. Take your time and watch how pirates blow traders up, how battleship protect the capital cities with a whole broadside and their torpedoes, stare in the depths and ask yourself whether you want to continue or not if you're as scared of the depths as I am!
+ A handful of Submarines to choose from and to upgrade. New subs through the game AND old subs don't become obsolete. Bought a big ship with lots of guns and HP but ended up swapping back to a smaller more agile one 2 hours later due to new enemies. Once again. Once you bought them, you are free to swap ships whenever you want.
+ Customizable Weapons of the Submarines. Burst guns, Blast guns, Jack-of-all-trades guns, you name it. And you aren't bound to just one but you can use them all and swap them mid-combat! Same with torpedoes.
+A unique gameplay element due to the switch between 2D and 3D perspective. Honestly, it's great!
+It's a good submarine game. Cmon. How many submarine games are out there? And how many of them are actually good?
+ 10-20 hours of gametime depending on how much time you take for exploring or looting
+ A fair saving system that allows you to manually jump back to the last checkpoint
+ A lot of interesting lore inside of them game and even more on the official website!
Cons:
- Tricky controls at first might end up making things a little bit difficult or awkward at first
- Can be a bit grindy (I myself didn't have to grind at all but you might end up needing to grind for a tiny amount of time)
- There are very few bugs (I did run into 2 of them but none of them were game-breaking and with the help of the checkpoint reset I didn't lose more than 5 minute for both combined. So don't even worry about the bugs! Just squish em)
- The very very very VERY end felt a little off. Literally just the last 5 minutes of the game though
- Some mechanics aren't fully used. Trading/Economy feels rather shallow and the homebase is just kinda there. Nothing really ruins the experience though. At least that's how I felt.
Overall just a great game. Definitely worth the 20 bucks for me, but for those who are unsure....5 bucks on sale....you can't do ANYTHING wrong there!

Diluvion is one of those games I want to love, but it will only let me like it. Beginning with the art style and design of the subs, the devs clearly took time and effort to create an engaging and detailed environment despite the rather simplistic environment models. The particle effects are quite well-done, and result in a murky and mysterious underwater world that sets the mood nicely and puts the player on edge from the very start of the game. It’s possible to spend hours exploring the various areas and become lost in that aspect of the game. It’s truly unfortunate the story and quest line are linear, as the real beauty of a game like this lies in exploring the world the devs created.
Although it is possible to master the basics quickly, the game requires forethought and strategy to successfully navigate the various hazards including the environment itself. Air and food are the most precious commodities, but other materials are nearly as important. And as noted the environment itself
The game offers a sub to fit most any taste, whether one prefers a vehicle that is fast, spacious, or heavily armed. And while the environment models are pretty plain, the subs are nicely designed and animated, and most importantly "feel" different at the helm. Controls are fairly intuitive and responsive, and the physics give a real sense of mass and inertia.
The quests, while fairly mundane in nature are still engaging and fit in with the story. Once a player is familiar with the in-game economy, it's easy to build up cash for upgrades and gear. The game uses schools of fish as sort of a guide to quest objectives, but the system has its problems. If you start from the preceding quest they are reliable, however if you have to take a detour - for air, food, or other supplies, or simply get attacked on the way to the next quest, the fish disappear. If a player does not start at the preceding quest location, the fish try to guide you from quest to quest starting at the very beginning of the game... Also the explosion of fish that accompanies saves can be a hindrance. The game saves when a player enters a certain area, every time the player passes through and these are the only saves available. So if the player is attacked near one of these spaces, it’s possible to have your view of the fight pretty much eliminated by the flashy save animation that fills your screen with fish. Ditto treacherous passages with strong currents – you didn’t really want to see where you were going when we were trying to tell your game is saved, did you?
Combat becomes repetitive very quickly, and although this game has a lot going for it, enemy AI can be quite frustrating.  Enemy subs are typically not very challenging so the game seems to compensate by employing what I like to call the ♥♥♥♥♥ Protocol - game ending torpedoes that come seemingly out of nowhere (apparently they have unlimited range), NPC subs that are engaged in a fight to the death suddenly reach an accord and turn on you once you get close enough, and enemies that won’t commit to a fight, staying close to the edge of range, launching the occasional torpedo and then retreating again. This is the worst as a player can’t ignore torpedoes and live long, but trying to engage can be wasteful of food and ammunition. Imagine you’re walking along and you see a little dog sitting in a yard. The dog doesn’t bark at as you walk by, but as soon as you pass it gives you a painful nip on your ankle. When you turn around, the dog is back in the yard, but as soon as you turn around again, another annoying bite. And this goes on until you finally turn and force a fight, or make it to one of the very few settlements that actually has patrol subs on station. It feels like a cheap way to extend game play without adding any additional content, both the time and materials wasted on these meaningless encounters and the extra grinding necessary to replace consumables.
Overall, though, the game stand on its own merits as a great effort and worth checking out – if only the game world was larger and more geared toward exploration, and the story line was tailored for the same...

I've enjoyed this a lot.  At heart, it's a puzzle-solving game, which I really like.  Coming from an old-school computer programming background (think switches and lights) it's something that resonates with me.  Nicely written documentation that could easily pass for actual data sheets.  The chips available, although fictitious, are very much like some of the PICs and microcontrollers available in the real world.  The way all the puzzles are tied together via e-mails between the company owner and the employees is great fun, as some of the employees are just as odd as some of the "computer people" I know personally.  This isn't something you'll play through in an hour or two.  Once you get into some of the more complex puzzles, you may have to walk away for a bit.  The answer will come to you one day in the shower.  ;)  Many of the design goals can be accomplished by brute force, but can you optimize parts count, power consumption, and programming efficiency...?  Going back and "tweaking" designs once you finish is almost as much fun as playing through the first time.  Highly recommended if you have a technical mind and enjoy quiet, contemplative games that make you really use your head.

Puzzle games in general have a reputation for being casual and simple, but this title is what I would call a "hardcore puzzle game". There is a lot of depth, with a huge manual, many systems to master, and several approaches to each puzzle. In addition to this, it has a great sim aspect. It is based around designing what I think are called integrated circuits and writing assembler style code for the microprocessors. Emails, product sheets, and specifications for your fake job that you paid money to have are extremely detailed, adding to the game's character. Optimizing your puzzles to top the excellently presented histogram style leaderboards and creating your own puzzles or simple arcade games in the sandbox mode adds significant replay value. Strongly reccomend, but the learning curve is tough so make sure to get help from the community if youre new to programming!

This is a truly great puzzle-fighter RPG. (Think: Puzzle Quest, Puzzles & Dragons, Might & Magic Clash of Heroes).
Basically: you play a victorian steampunk mech pilot who fights other steampunk mechs and the occasional steampunk armored train. You fight by matching colored gems to get resources (ammo, coolant, fuel, scrap) and using those resources to keep your shields up, fire your weapons, and so on.
The game really unfolds as you play: it has a sort of roguelike element, in that there is permadeath if you fail a mission, but when you restart you will have unlocked more powerups, more pilots, more mechs, and so on. This keeps things pretty fresh, and the core mechanics are addictive and compelling.
The good: Tough, fun, clever, occasionally gorgeous game. The characters are rather diverse -- the first pilot is a lady (literally a lady, she's of high birth) with a steampunk robot arm, and the unlocks are quite varied.
The bad: Random, unfair at times, the mechs themselves are bland-looking.
Overall, this game is a hidden gem and I recommend it highly.

takes the established match-3 formula, wraps it in a Victorian England steampunk setting, adds rogue-lite mechanics, and serves the result with a pinch of RPG mechanics.
In the game, you control the commander of a Steampunk mech, the eponymous Ironcast, defending the British Empire from a French invasion. You guide your armor through battles by collecting resouces (e.g. ammunition, energy, coolant) that power your Ironcast, its shields, drive or weapons. Those weapons you collect or craft after your battles. The game offers different (unlockable) starter mechs, with pre-set strengths and weaknesses, which – on a good run – can lead to you controlling a devastating war machine. On a bad run, however, things can go south very quickly. If you happen to meet the wrong enemy for your setup, your run might be over pretty suddenly. For some, this might be a major annoyance, others will love the random rogue-lite aspect. Not all your efforts will be utterly in vain when you fail your run, as the game offers a meta progression system that mostly offers stats increases to your Ironcasts. So failing time and again will make the game somewhat easier.
The game's presentation is solid, with an intriguing theme carried out adeptly with regards to the graphics. For me, the music could have been more memorable, and the story presented in a more enthralling manner – although the writing isn't half bad either.
If you enjoy both playing match-3 games and the (sometimes unfair) difficulty of
might be just the right thing for you.

Dead in the water.
( An early access review of Dead State(2nd attempt))
by Merit Coba.
Imagine you are in a restaurant downtown and you are invited by the waiter to come over to the kitchen to help the cook select the ingredients for your dinner, tell him how much you want and describe how to cook it.  You then return to your table. When the waiter arrives with three plates, he puts one plate down and then tosses the contents of the plates on top of the others. What do you get?
On the 31st of October a release date was announced for Dead State: the 4th of December.
This means that the game must by now, writing early November, be in a state to be sold after some minor tweaking and polishing.
Is that the case?
Now on the upside this game has many things to commend it.
For one is that they made your character's improvement part of a goal system instead of  the usual experience system.
Next to that you can kind of improve you other party members by assigning them jobs and at times influence their progress through dialogs.
Also commendable is the way they give the game a kind of flow. At the start even a single zombie is a challenge for your group, let alone a group of them, but after a while zombies are no longer a danger but hostile people, those with guns and armor.
Another great idea is how the zombies can kill your party members and enemy humans and make them zombies to. One of the craziest encounters is  when your party runs into a shootout between two gangs while zombies attack from all sides.
At the core there are good ideas but this game is far from finished and beset with many issues. Here is a random list.
The game lacks a general story line, it is either not there or just not finished. There is a kind of conflict brewing between the militia at one hand and the military at the other, but  when I tried to talk to either side I was told to get lost.  There were some small incidents, like the military asking me for supplies and a proclamation from the militia, but  this didn't seem to open up more dialog.
Storylines are broken. An example is the one of Fiona Parks, a girl who is devoted to you. At some moment I was approached by Davis, one of the survivors, telling me how sorry he was about what Fiona did. I had no clue what he was talking about and Fiona was fine. This went of every morning until at one point it was announced that Fiona had killed someone. She duly got a trial(in which she supported the side that demanded her death), then a minute later she was reported to have killed again, was put on trial again and banned. Since then the Davis conversation happens every morning. (At least it makes sense now.)
Most zombies don't roam but just stand around so you can take them out one at a time, mostly by attacking them from behind.
Groups of zombies or people stop being a danger because you can kill them one at a time by bashing on a locked door that is out of their view, which will then draw in your enemies one at a time(and the door will be restored to full points when you reload a saved game, so you can repeat this until all the enemies have been taken care of). That way you can gang up on one of them and thus take down stronger enemies that would normally wipe your party out.
(One tip: give Vic a shotgun. And if you can get the combat shotgun he becomes an unstoppable force. In fact after a while you are pretty invulnerable.)
Unfinished maps, empty maps, maps that don't work, doors that don't work properly, invisible barriers, barriers that you can walk through(the Coleman side entry).
Dogs can only be attacked from the front and the back and sometimes not be shot at.
Fifth party members showing up unexpectedly.
The chicken and egg issue: to build your chickencoop you need to find a chicken, when you do it gets slaughtered when you take it home because you don't have a chickencoop.
Some quests are broken(Aggro asks you to get Alan, but he never shows).
There is a quest for swapping food for medicines, but you can't get food from your storage, although you can fish for fish. I did so and took the fish with me to this deal. Then the deal was made, but no exchange happened yet I got a message that the deal went really well.
The game doesn't keep a record of the locations that you already visited agains the locations that other survivors tell you about, so you get a message that they marked a  new location on your map, but nothing shows because you already discovered it.
When fully upgraded the fence can't be repaired(unless it is completely destroyed I guess).
Some upgrades on your shelter are described not to function.
Some items have no icons.
The storage of your shelter is bugged for sometimes the tabs won't work. This seems to effect mostly the ammunition tab and this might have something to do with creating ammo
The radio you can create to assign jobs doesn't work.
Ammo you can create yourself and it only costs you a one time price to give you access to an unlimited supply of them. So in the end you can just bang away as ammo isn't an issue(this might by intendend)
On and on goes the list of issues.
I was amazed about all these issues for people seem to think well of this game, so I checked the game agains steam several times and even have reinstalled it from scratch. I even tried to see I could download a recent upgrade from the double bear website, but they just point me to steam. Maybe steam is hosting a old game or  perhaps what I describe is the current state of the game.
I suspect the latter as I see in the forums many of the issues being mentioned.
Maybe the game is remarkably patched by the time it gets released but based on what I experienced above and based on the price I still give it a thumbs down.
No doubt someone is going to say that what I say is not true, so what I would suggest is that you just look around on the forums that talk about this game and, if it is available, download a demo.
I hope that the game developers finish the game properly.. it certainly has it's merits.
I have another review here which shows pictures so you have also visible proof of what I am saying.

EDIT 4/22:
In what way is this game hard? I've got 72 pistol bullets, 124 shotgun shells, and 36 rifle bullets. I'm throwing away first aid packs and old rifles. Juno is running around like Michonne decapitating zombies from behind with a machette while they chase around the other guys. Of course, I'm a little short on food, so we'll probably all starve to death. But, hey, it's always something.
Having played for two nights I can say this:
- The combat interface is good. It could be improved with some tweaks, but a few people are claiming it's unplayable or something, which is stupid.
- The combat is more tactically complicated than a lot of people are giving it credit for, especially if you want to conserve ammunition.
- I definately did get to the point where I was "I just want to get to the next city and loot it" while at the same time I was getting tired and worried about making a mistake and killing everyone. The key to a turn-based game is that "just one more turn" feeling. If I want just one more turn, it's good.
=====
EDIT 4/21:
I'd note that I did end up playing the game until about 2:00 last night. I still can't give it 10/10 becuase there are some clunky things about combat. The main one is that you have to go into inventory to switch weapons. There should be a click button to cycle them, or something like that. But, the game was interesting enough that I played through that minor frustration. Given combat is over half of the playtime, that is pretty good.
I ran into repeat events, but not often enough that it felt tired and I'm pretty sure they weren't duplicates in one playthrough. The game did stop responding once and I had to kill it from the task manager. But, the "continue" button got me back to the same place and the game didn't become unstable after that.
It doesn't presently have the diversity of FTL. But, FTL didn't have all of the features it has now when it was first introduced. Also, a lot of what kept FTL fresh were updates and mods, which this game seems like it could also accept pretty easily.
=====
All the elements deliver. The game requires a lot of strategic thinking, resource management, and tactics. There are about 12 significant variables (it depends on if you think of inventory and weapons as one consideration or one per character), all of them are intuitive, and they are all recursively intertwined. No two elements (hunger and fatigue, for example) can be managed separately.
Like most games of this type, it has a steep learning curve and you're going to die. Probably, it's going to be after slow resource attrition leading to a TPK encounter nowhere in particular. I suppose that is theme appropriate.
Although it is roguelike, it doesn't feel like FTL. This is more the equivalent of "The Oregon Trail" with zombies.
If the type of game and the theme are your taste, it's better than it looks. It's worth $20.

March of the living is a new indy game on steam . You take on the roll of a survivor trying to get to his x wife and hopefully be reunited with your son.
Along the way you'll bump into random encounters that can help or hurt you. As well as other survivors, gangs, infection, and of course lots of zombies.
The game has a lot of simularities to FTL. The map system will be familiar to anyone who has played FTL but the map feels way larger. The random encounters where you get to decide to "help" someone that might turn into a trap, avoid them, or start a fight. These tense choices are really where the game shines.
While moving across the country you will be forced to scavenge for weapons, ammunition, food, and medical supplies to increase your chances of survival. If you run out of ammo you may find yourself fighting a horde with a melee weapon. If you get hurt infection may kill you.
The games graphics on initial impression are going to turn a lot of people off. This is a shame as the game itself is actually amazing. Hopefully folks will take the time to look past the graphics and give the game a shot.
All in all I enjoyed the game and believe its worth picking up if you like games similar to FTL.

This is the best of the Hockey management games out there. It's a lot better than Franchise Hockey Manager (which isn't saying much really). So if you're a hockey fan and have to have a Hockey GM simulator, then this rating probably doesn't apply to you.
Me, I'm a management sim fan more than a hockey fan. And I can say EHM is nowhere near as good as other games of the type.
It's one of those games that you play, and you're sort of burning out because know you're working a lot harder to view and accomplish the same things in this game than you would be in a better structured game. Like you can't customize lists, as far as I can tell. Data isn't displayed on screens where that data would be pretty useful - like setting up lines involves a lot more clicking to view your different players, at least for me, than I would like. Sometimes the 'sign free agent' ot other buttons stop working or things are greyed out, and you don't know why but you know that continuing to the next day, for some reason, will fix it. If you go fullscreen and click out of the game, you just might not be able to get it visible again when you click back.
There's a lot of little things like that. Not game breakers by themselves, but added up they tire you out as a player and drain the fun. It's not intuitive. It's work.
My dislike isn't just because I'm not a hockey fan. I'm not a Racing or Cricket fan, but I like Motorsport Manager and Cricket Manager because they are really well put together. World Boxing Manager is another one, even though I don't follow boxing. EHM might be a great game under the hood, but the fact gets hidden underneath a slow sim speed, a number of minor, irritating bugs, and having to click way too much.
If you're a hockey fan, this is worth it. Not worth anything like $20, but worth it in a sale. If you're just looking for a good management sim, EHM isn't worth the time.

This game is for anyone that enjoys playing sport sims and loves hockey. A long time ago, I played a game called Sub Culture. It was was my first brush with one of those free-roaming space sim type games, except underwater. God damn was it hard, but I loved it. Though I preferred Freelancer, Sub Culture was a big part of my childhood.
Diluvion immediately reminded me of that game, though it is smaller in scope and has a fairly linear questline. It's also a lot darker visually, relying heavily on its music score for atmosphere and bright lights in the abyssal darkness to guide you. Aesthetically, Diluvion is a treasure. The abovementioned contrast and music, as well as its Jules Verne-esque submarine and structure design, and vaguely hinted-at supernatural elements create a very memorable experience.
Following what appeared to be a golden age brought low by greed and war, humanity has been punished by the gods, driven beneath the waves and sealed in by an impenetrably vast ice sheet. One goddess, Lun, took pity on us and hid a gift at the deepest part of the ocean, which, if we are worthy, we may be able to reach. This part is the Endless Corridor, a place sought after by explorers and feared by the superstitous dweller priests.
Through three major areas: The Forgotten Fjords, the Sunken Coast, and the Abyss itself, you will complete a series of quests, battle pirates, scavenge wrecks and trade at capsule-towns and stations for supplies, ammuntion and valuables to sell, purchase and upgrade new subs and a home base, and fight some pretty difficult bosses.
The game is fairly combat focused, which isn't out of place for a "space sim", but given that there aren't any sidequests to speak of, in the end it feels a bit more like a pipe shooter with breaks for scavenging in between. This isn't bad, but the design of the environments belies the game's relatively short length.
Operating your sub is fairly involved. You can adjust throttle up to three speeds foward or reverse, as well as go into temporary overdrive forward, turn, raise and lower your depth, and aim your sub's scrap cannons in any direction, though the actual coverage of your turrets depends on your current sub. Early on you also get access to torpedoes, which act like the missles in a space game, requriing you to first obtain a target lock. In towns, and certain other areas (including on occassion, the wreck of a pirate sub you just took out) you can pay to hire new crew from your sub, who can be assigned to your helm, sonar station, guns or torpedoes and improve the performance of each based on their stats.
However, your sub's supplies are a constant concern. You have limited air, which can be reflled for free at any town, but you also need scrap for your guns (which doubles as a currency needed to upgrade your sub), torpedoes, food for your crew, (which if it runs out, you can't assign crew to stations), and repair kits. Indicators for each of these are displayed on your hud while sailing about, so keep an eye on them. Also be aware that unassigned crew will work on repairing any hull damage.
Though some reviewers have complained about the controls, the short length and the supposed "virtue signaling" of the ending (Seriously? What is wrong with you people? The message of the ending is important!) My biggest issue is with the incredibly inconsistent difficulty. While battling the pirates can be challenging if you are undergeared, the boss fights, and also the corridor fight prior to the final boss, are hilariously skewed against you, to the point where I needed to use cheat engine to finish the latter.
I can remmoned the game purely based on its aesthetics, just be aware it isn't balanced very well.

This is, in fact, a wonderful game, but I didn't accidentally hit the thumbs-down. I'll explain.
The good: realistically, if you *love* submarine games, if you *love* games like X3:TC, X: Rebirth, Endless Sky. and want to see a submarine take on the whole thing, then yeah, pick this game up. Stop reading reviews and pick it up- if your alternative is doing nothing to fulfill your lust for games like the above, that is. If you *love* feeling alone in a universe too distraught to be concerned with your safety or well-being, this game is for you.
The meh: controls feel like you're going through gel but that was clearly a design choice. A lot of people won't like this. Also, it has full controller support- USE ONE.
The bad: Let's start with the really bad. This one's a sin. The item storage DOES NOT WORK. Do not trust it! It will delete itself if you so much as look at another item storage. Solution: get a giant boat and never bank. Secondly, in 2 hours, I've had 3-second lock-ups three times. To the credit of the devs, it stops time during these lock-ups and always seems to recover from them, so that's cool. They often occur during saving, which is automatic and not your choice- which is cool...EXCEPT IT FILLS YOUR SCREEN WITH LAGGY GREEN FISH. Now, don't get me wrong, I have a decent computer. I run Elite: Dangerous on high (not extreme) with over 60fps but those green save fish, man... This game is not new, the devs were made aware of these problems a long time ago.
Some minor issues: okay, lemme explain something. Your sub has 2 life resources: food and air. Air, you can't live without. It's refilled in a couple ways including visiting stations. Simple. Goes down with time. Now, food, works a bit different. If you don't have food, all that happens is your crew goes on strike and refuse to leave the living room (which is fine by me: that's where I like them! When they're in there they repair my boat and yes, they'll do that during a hunger strike). So, instead of buffing the engines or the guns or whatever, they repair the ship. Cool. And to save on food, you might just keep them in the living- NOPE. If there is food, they'll eat it. If there isn't, they just won't do SKILLED labor. So forget about having a massive crew unless you're like me and keep food-starved personnel to repair the ship and take on risky points of opportunities (that's a thing, too. You can risk your crew's life in an 'event' to resolve the event. I like this - there are other ways to end the event that other people prefer, such as ones that like their crew, but not me- no sir, I'm a slave driving homicidal maniac). So yeah, the whole crew thing and not being able to store them or 'turn them off' is weird even though I can just not carry food.
Also: why is everything on my map but home base? You just kinda memorize that in 3d space? That's weird, fam.
The "to be honest": I'm gonna end up with like 30 hours played in this game, I'm sure. That has nothing to do with my review. My review reflects the level of polish this game has. At 1 hour in, I sat down and thought about if I wanted a refund long and hard (40 seconds) before I continued. I decided that because this game was so clearly for me, it gets a pass on my "don't release unpolished, unfinished games if you don't want me to chargeback" rule.

In this game, we are a pilot of humanoid robots belonging to the army of the fictive Great Britain in 19th, and fight against the invasions from the continent. The game system is a combination of match 3 puzzles and turn-based RPG; we have enough time to think and decide.
A game turn consists of a battle phase and an enhancement phase, and the boss battles are forcibly occurred after several turns.
In a turn-based battle phase, we need to gather resources, such as ammo, energy, and coolant, by match 3 puzzles, and then, select commands, such as fire weapons, expand shields, and boost drives. There are several types of victory conditions: simply defeat an enemy, endure the attacks of enemies several turns, collect special gems in a puzzle board, and so on. We get some moneys and experiences according to the results of battles.
In an enhancement phase, we can repair our robot, grade-up the weapon, shields, and drives the robot, and improve the skills of our pilot. Because the moneys and experiences are limited, we need to select the combinations of enhancements suitable for our tactics.
The battle balance is relatively tough, and a single defeat in battles immediately brings game over. We need some experiences that our well-grown robots and pilots are destroyed by unmerciful invaders in a flash. But the joy of developing robots and pilots and relatively short play time encourages us to try again, and enables us to complete all battles some days in a future.
Because I’m familiar with European history, I also enjoyed the ambience of game world. However, the problem is that the game story is described from only the British side; the music of boss battle is an arranged version of “La Marseillaise”. I’ll pay an additional charge if the second arc from the French side is on the sale.

This is an excellent concept for a game. On the surface it appears to be a typical match-three with a dueling mechanic, but it is so much more. As it is a rogue-lite, death will end a run forever. However there is progression over the (many) failed runs that you will experience.
In terms of gameplay, the missions are varied enough as to not be boring, but it could stand a few more variations.
There is a distinct difficulty curve in that the second part of the game is notably more difficult and I've yet to finish the final boss after ~100 hours and almost just as many runs.
Suggested for anyone who can stomach repeated and heartwrenching loss.
Update: The final boss is possible, just took me 109 hours :)

TL;DR--I've nominated this game for the "Haunts my Dreams" award, since whenever it crosses my mind a wave of regret and flashbacks flows through me.
Pros:
Steampunk mecha and tanks with death rays and shields, and extremely apropos British flavor
Clever story background explaining why you're stomping around in a steam-powered bipedal engine of destruction
Simple to learn yet hard to master use of "match 3+" for effective action during each combat turn
Neutral:
Most revealing parts of the clever story can be largely missed if a relatively small number of the missions either don't get randomly generated or simply are not chosen
No "save scumming" with this roguelike, you get killed and that's it for you, start a new campaign buddy
Cons:
Roguelike random generation of missions, enemies, and rewards compounded by random generation of field for "match 3+" mechanic largely determines whether you will win or lose even if your skill and tactics are top notch
Random enemies are often extremely more powerfully equipped than you can possibly be from the very beginning of the game, even during supposedly easy missions
The devs got all my money for this game because a dear friend of mine who lives some distance away had just started playing it and was very enthusiastic.  Because the description sounded interesting, I bought the whole package including the DLC as it wasn't too expensive and I wanted something the two of us could talk shop about when we visited next.
I nearly immediately regretted this decision.
Not sure whether to take my opinion seriously?  If you check my profile you will see I have slammed in many many hours, and have all the achievements [which means all the global unlocks].  But that is solely because I am an extraordinarily stubborn completionist.  I've gotten to the end of the campaign five times, out of which I pulled 3 victories.  So I consider myself approximately as competent at the game as it is reasonable to expect a player can become.  And I still have gotten my♥♥♥♥♥kicked before the second campaign mission begins.  NOT JOKING--the run I got the "kill yourself by overheating" achievement was during that first mission, and NOT on purpose--the board just wouldn't drop me the matches I needed to actually perform any useful actions and I ran out of coolant just before trying to shield myself to avoid getting killed by the enemy's attack their next turn...
Upgrades for your pilot, mecha special attacks, and weapon/drive/shield slots are also entirely randomly generated each time you level, and far too often are "choose one of 3 things that all suck and are a waste of your time".  Devs, since so much of this game is random, when someone plays it enough to get global unlocks of useful upgrades, why don't you just let them pick when they would like to get those?  Or run a skill tree or something?  I mean, a little balance might help the player deal with the "four days until the final boss, fight a couple of light scouts that turn out to have Mark V* equipment in all slots and 2000 health" nonsense without throwing their mouse at the screen.
*All equipment runs from Mark I to Mark V, and increases both in damage resistance and effectiveness substantially with every step.  It is possible, but extremely difficult, to have all Mark V gear for the final boss fight.  A well upgraded player will have 1100-1200 health at the final boss.
I also took Katherine Chapman nearly every playthrough after the first, a DLC pilot whose special ability increases the number of rare blueprint drops that happen.  One of my five "all the way" trips with her, not ONE. SINGLE. RARE. happened the entire campaign; I lost that one because I just didn't have enough scrap to repair my hull AND buy parts to upgrade so I could actually fight effectively.
Not spoilering this because everyone needs to know--you NEVER have enough scrap to repair your hull AND buy parts to upgrade so you can actually fight effectively.  A constant sense of desperation and doom will hover over you most playthroughs unless you have an unlikely string of lucky reward drops for winning missions and leveling, destroying any enjoyment you might have otherwise experienced.  And playing a game should involve some enjoyment; the tooltips basically are the devs shrugging and saying, "Oh well, if you lose just keep playing, eventually the global unlock bonuses will help you."  Translation:  because you enjoy ramming your face into this brick wall so much, keep doing it, and sooner or later your face will get tough enough that you can make a crack in it...
Also, protip:  "Survival" missions are a trap.  Their only purpose is to make you waste all your accumulated and desperately hoarded scrap to repair yourself afterwards.
The money isn't the issue here; save your mental health and play something else, almost ANYTHING else.  Devs, seriously, if you can't deal with the game theory required to fix the awful balance issues, just rename this game or at least change the description to make it clear it is for masochists only, normal gamers need to have a hint to avoid the soul-destroying experience you have created.
Verdict:  HELL no.

An enjoyable game, however, you should be aware of a rather odd bug caused by some dev choices:
The game quietly attempts to connect to a variety of Amazon Web Services. It will try to do this infinitely, as long as the game as running, even if the attempts are blocked.
I'm not exactly sure what data is so important that it needs to try forever, but if you're like me and manage your own firewall configuration by hand then you'll find that these repeated attempts to "call home" will cause the game to stutter and lag unbearably.
When asked about the issue, the devs first stated that their game does not have any code which would communicate across the internet. They have since clarified that they're using these AWS instances to track user metrics and "difficulty data". I've asked for an option to disable this tracking but I received no response.
Regardless, a fun game, it just seems a little shady and harkens back to the days of Wild Tangent and other "phone home" games.

3D Mark is a de facto industry standard for simple benchmarking of gaming PCs. It will test your PC hardware and give you a final score, this score then can be used to compare your "rig" against others (3DMark keeps all user tests in a online database) or compare to yourself as you test different hardware configurations. The concept is simple: the higher the score, the powerful your configuration. It is useful too when you want to upgrade your PC, you can check online reviews of a new video card and see how much you can upgrade by comparing the 3D Mark scores.
It also has some nice features, like storing your scores online and even a few achievements. The online website also has lots of information of almost every video card and CPU available, you can see stats, prices, scores, and even compare them. Highly recommended for the gaming/PC enthusiast, keep in mind regular users/gamers will not find much here.
Excellent and practical for testing not only your specs, but also for you to check whatever overclock setting you decide to run on your PC. Give it a try!!!

The game's released. It's been a rocky launch technically.They probably rushed it a bit too fast, but it's pretty solid. If you have the patience to put up with bugs and glitches you will find a good game here. The developer seems intent on stabilizing the game in that regard.
It's an interesting mix of survivalist group management and turn based tactical resolution. My biggest complaint is that gun combat mechanics are VERY weak once you start fighting militia and rogue soldiers. It's the exact same run-n-gun AI from the early game except these guys have assault rifles, body armor, grenades, and a firm desire to expend all that in killing you.  Consider carefully before starting a campaign in Ironman mode.  The game keeps you on rails to start with limited options, but that opens up as you go.

I remember reading about this game months ago, and then kind of forgetting about it. After completing a game of Wasteland 2, the turn based RPG bug bit me again.. totally reminding me of FO,FO2, and Jagged Alliance of days past. I searched steam for some more, and rememberd Dead State.
Ive put some decent hours into Beta Patch #2 so far and I really like where this is going. Its got all the elements of past turn based RPG's (ie. combat, micromanaging, strategy, building) and more. You wake up as part of a group in a school, which becomes your "base". You have to stock that base with food, weapons, etc.. from surrounding areas, all while looking out for zombies and bad guys. Along the way, more can join your group and you have access to all the group for job tasks or scavenging.
You dont level up by killing anything, you level up by completing "shelter goals". Some of the goals include gathering so much food, med supplies, luxuries, etc.. I thought this was a neat way to gain more skills for your characters, totally away from the norm of killing for skill. I like it.
Im on day 25 or so on beta patch #2, and I'm coming to the point where I may have taken in too many people at once, so each day ends up being a search for food more than anything, luckily there are "fishing spots" to walk to and test your luck harvesting fish. In fact, I see the potential to have hundreds, if not thousands of locations on the map along with encounters because of the way the map scren and travel works.. this could be a pretty content loaded game moving forward.
My Jagged Alliance heart wants to see more specialized firearm variants, as right now, they seem to have one firearm per ammo type. This may be wishful thinking, but would be pretty cool moving forward. I know its the zombie apocalypse, but cant that dead soldier just be carrying a MK17 SD variant or something ;)
I'm sure others will complain about the "graphics" in some cases, but for me, they dont matter as much.. these games are about the adventure, the open world, the choose your own tasks, the story.. you make it what you want to survive. The true turn based RPG thrives non-linearly, and this game certainly has that potential.
All in all, the game is well worth the purchase, even at this early access stage. I think we are in the middle of a turn based RPG game renaissance, and I couldnt be happier about it.  If you like this sort of game, micro managing little pixel squads of people, and, well, the zombie apocalypse.. get Dead State now, you wont regret it.

Age of Cavemen is a time management building sim set during the days of cavemen and dinosaurs. You set up a base building various buildings that range from food production to axe towers that can defend your base from other players.
It's very similar to other games like Clash of Clans and Age of Empires: Castle Siege. Build, attack, and wait. That's right, wait. Age of Cavemen uses several walls to hinder your progress. From resource limiting to build times. The wait times start low enough, but quickly extend from seconds to minutes to hours to days in very little time. You can of course purchase premium meteorites to speed those times up.
The game can be enjoyable at times, and I actually enjoy these type of games. Except, this game is very, very buggy. Troops can become stuck on walls, premium meteorites can magically disappear, attacks that you should have won will crash or freeze the game randomly and at least one achievement is bugged. It's very disappointing as the game could really shine if the bugs were fixed.
In its current state, I can't recommend Age of Cavemen..
Update Patches: After various updates, the game has become even more unplayable to the point where the game will no longer ever connect to the server. At this point I'm giving up on this game ever working in any form.
More Update Patches: Things are improving with each new patch and while there are still bugs remaining, it has become much more playable.

NOTE: I have to say that I played a sizeable role as one of the game's event designers. As such, this review may contain elements of bias, but I will try to be as honest as I can, from my perspective as a gamer. I played more hours than you can see through various dev builds pre-Steam, so I'd like to say I've seen much of what the game has to offer.
March of the Living has some similarities to FTL: Faster Than Light, an excellent game which was openly admitted to be a large influence. As one of four playable survivors, your main goal is to pass through three zones, each gradually increasing in difficulty, and reach the end sector, picking up other survivors and supplies along the way while dealing with situations and quests as they arise in each sector. All this is done while managing your supplies of ammunition, food and items, whilst balancing health, hunger and fatigue. It's a fairly simple concept that, for the most part, works pretty solidly. At least during my playthroughs, I tended to find a considerable amount of supplies as I was rather thorough with scouring the map, but you'd be surprised how fast that can go when you have several party members.
The combat isn't the most complex model out there, but it works well enough. You can control up to six party members in real time, with a pause option for sorting through each character's actions. This makes sure it doesn't get too overwhelming. There are four main weapon types, which are melee, pistols, shotguns and rifles respectively. Each character has their own preferred weapon type/s, though they aren't restricted by said preferences, so characters aren't completely useless when using gear they aren't skilled with. You'd be well advised to keep one melee weapon on hand, but with the limited inventory space... eh.
You'll find both human and zombie enemies, which do have some subtle differences in colour palette and attacks. The former tend to be infinitely more dangerous however, so be wary. Rushing into a fight with a trio of bandits isn't wise if you're going solo, after all. Playing smart and knowing when to flee will come in handy. I personally found using the pistol's uncanny ability to headshot fairly often at short range to be a workable strategy throughout, though that may be changed. In a prolonged fight, you may cause enough noise to attract other zombies. This is most likely to happen in cities, but can happen out on the roads too. It'll eat through your ammo if you let it.
It's... not really a good idea for me to judge the quality of the writing, given the circumstances, but I do find that it is more than adequate for the purposes. There's much which could be done with the setting, but hopefully it can be expanded upon with mods or with future intervention from the devs themselves. I will say though that it's easy to add in custom events by following the simple structure shown in the games .XML event files. Notepad++ and a bit of practice/study of the given files makes it a breeze.
It's not the most visually spectacular game out there, but that's a by-product of the art style more than anything else. It works fine, and can be edited/added to easily enough. I found the music to be a nice touch, suiting the atmosphere of the game. It might get grating after a while, but that might also be because of the amount of time I spent listening to it pre-release during game testing... Of course, this is all replaceable, or will be in due time.
If I had any complaints, it'd probably be with the map's random generator, but the settings for that can be changed fairly easily. That's a running theme with the game, incidentally. Everything can quite easily be changed if you look through the files and edit some variables. Tailoring the experience isn't too difficult at all.
Overall, I find the game to be rather entertaining. It's not perfect by any means, but it's defintely competent in all the right places. It's a simple enough concept that pretty much anyone will grasp the main gameplay mechanics within a few minutes at most. The game as it stands is reasonable on its own, but it also functions works well as a base for expansion by enterprising players. I can't wait to see where the modding community takes it in the future.

Assembly Language + board layout + RTFM.  You know that Australian guy on youtube who hates solar roads (see EEVBlog)?  He's in here too.  :)
Instead of playing Shenzhen I/O, you could buy a breadboard, and a few components and maybe an Arduino or rPi or a demo board and play with real-world components.  And you should!  But if you aren't sure, or you have no idea what all that stuff is, this can help you get your feet wet for pretty cheap.  Also this doesn't use any girly-man C compiler like Arduino, or sissy LInux operating system like rPi - this uses ASM.  That's not sexist either - regardless of your gender, if you code in ASM you are a stud!
I bought Shenzhen I/O on sale and figured this has everything TIS-100 has plus some.  Correct game: Check!  Correct price: Check!
Then I openned it up for 1 minute, saw the RTFM references, shut the game down, and printed out the manual and never had time to look at it for at least 6 months.
And the whole time there's the LITTLE DEMON ON MY SHOULDER saying "ASM?  Are you kidding me?"
So there's a time and a place for everything.  [For PHP that time would be "never", but for ASM apparently my years of programming experience and hand porting one processor to another purely in ASM still had some room for this game to be played.]
It's not _really_ ASM - for anyone who knows the difference, you might get a slight pain in the back of your neck when you notice some of the differences.  Those differences are extremely slight, and can actually be appreciated for what they are.  The game does not take you all the way down the binary rabbit hole (at least from what I'm able to tell after 2 hrs playing).  But it's a start.  Also the amount of ROM available is cleverly the # of lines of code you can see without scrolling!  Very cool game design!
This game will give you the sick thinking that comes with ASM.  By sick, I mean, writing code that's almost as bad as PERL, you'll have trouble reading it later, you'll wonder why you added 3 and subtract 7 with a label in between.  It all becomes very cryptic.  But the ideas that lead you to this monstrosity - that's where the beauty lies.  You wind up making some convoluted mess that actually works, and is optimized so much it won't make sense without drilling into what happens at every step.
--->>> Usually though, the best solution proves to also be the most elegant - and seeing that elegance immerge is something very beautiful. <<<---
What really blows me away, is how perfectly designed the puzzles in this game are.  The amount of space for your code is just enough to squeeze out the functionality you need.  It's really very impressive.  The effects of very minor changes can also affect battery life in unexpected ways - just raising that kind of awareness, I think, is a very cool feature.
When I was a kid, I learned a sort of equivalent to ASM on a TI programmable calculator.  Shenzhen I/O could be thought of as modern equivalent.  You can take it as fast as you like.
<mumbles something about "It's SOOOO RTFM!"...>

I've always been a bit disappointed by Zachtronics games because they feel more like home work than puzzles.  I really like puzzle games, my favorites are Enigma, Fish Fillets 2, Toki Tori 1 and 2, and Talos Principle.  Something about figuring out the solution in those games gives you an Aha! moment that make you feel clever in a way Zachtronic games do not. Zachtronic games are going through the steps to get to the end result, I have played deep into all of them and they just get longer and more complicated, but they never seem to require you to figure anything out, which would give you that Aha! moment.
They do have a nice moment at the end where you are watching your completed thing and see how it functions just the way you'd imagined.  It's an almost artistic sense of movement, and maybe the choices you make in the game are artistic rather than logical.  In creating the sandwich maker for this particular game, I made in extremely inefficient, but made sure every step and loop still had a purpose.  I think my code might actually make a person smile who had played the game, but is that the game?  I've played hours hoping it would get more difficult on its own, not that I would make it more difficult.  Each level just takes longer.  And at this point I'm thinking, why don't I just code my own programs and then at least I would have something when I was done with all this work.
Also, these are a lot of the same feelings I'd had after playing TIS-100 and I might have stopped buying these things then, but I was partly attracted back by people celebrating the solitaire mini game in this game, but it is no good.  I don't think the designer really understands what makes a solitaire game good.  It is just much too easy.  and it is possible to lose by random chance.  (i don't object to the latter in solitaire at all, but in comparison to free cell, which is almost the same game, you can't lose by random chance AND it is more difficult.)
The best part of the game is the little news snippets about tech problems in the near future, like self driving cars being stuck in a loop.  They are quite clever.
I might end up going back and playing a bit more of the game and updating the review if my experience changes, but I have logged quite a bit of time already.

This is the game for people who played TIS-100 but wanted more than just the programming.  This is also for the people who played TIS-100 and thought it was crazy difficult.  Shenzhen I/O expands on the idea, and adds depth and character to create a new game.  The game is less "alone" than its predecessor since you are working as part of a fictional development team and get ideas, input, and encouragement from coworkers.
This gives a little bit of the feel of how actual microcontroller development works.  Sure, the components are fictional, but they borrow from real-world problems.  If you like tinkering with things and figuring out how they work, this is a game for you.
Solitiare with a mini coding game.

The natural progression from TIS-100, Shenzhen combines the pseudo assembly programing, but adds the additional challenge of routing and placing components onto a (limited) board as well, taking the complexity to another level. And really, that's what elevates Shenzhen to the next level compared to the other, more abstract zach-games. The restricted solution space forces you to come up with more clever solutions to solve the problems, without overwhelming you with possiblities.

It reminds me very much of some of my favorite old AAA games, but it's hard to decide which one I keep feeling nostalgia about. The underwater world reminds me of Crimson Skies by FASA if it had involved subs instead of planes. The way the world slowly opens up into a larger sandbox and the story introduces one to new content in an efficient way, feels kinda like Freelancer (but no robust trading yet).
I don't know of anything quite like it. - It's a casual sub combat game with target lead indicators (if your sonar is online) telling you where to fire to hit moving targets, a la Freelancer. While on sale I HIGHLY reccommend picking up the edition with the Manta sub, because its 40 inventory capacity is delightfully OP for amassing wealth early on, not to mention how cool it looks when firing off a frontal cannon assault.
Overall, I'd easily feel happy paying $20 for this.
The optimal gameplay in order to prosper in this world (in my experience) is a mix of bolt-cannon and torpedo combat duels with pirates (solitary at first, then roaming in packs in the second zone), punctuated by frequent docking with loot-containing wrecks below and above you, and a common routine of visiting wandering merchants to sell high, and visiting one's home base to buy low..
Hearing two bandits duking it out is always fun, since you can sweep in and clean up on the loot.
It's combat, it's exploration, and it's more taxing on my computer than expected, but became fun & fluid on the lowest graphics setting. VERY VERY worth the sale price for gamers who like Freelancer-esque experiences even when they are simpler in scope.  8.3/10 so far.

Despite the occasional flaws (that are mentioned a lot in other reviews), and an overall feeling of the game that is slightly under-developed, Diluvion manages to deliver the authentic experience of an early 00's open-world exploration game, and that makes it definitely worthwhile if you long for that feeling that most of today's games lack.

That being said, you should bear in mind that back in the day "industrial standards" for the games of Diluvion's scale were very different from today's anticipated "AAA" games quality bar - it's far from being "polished", so to say. If that doesn't stop you from exploring its limits and dealing with loose ends that poke from here and there, then you should give it a go - grab it on a sale (like I did) if you're somewhat uncertain.

Oh, and don't forget to bring a controller - you'll need one.

I really had looked forward to picking this up based on what I'd heard and waited for it to go on sale. Now I wish you could return games after playing more than a few hours, because this is a game that wears thin over time. I really do think this could have been a great game with some more forethought.
The main problem is it's too RNG dependent. How well you do on a playthrough depends a lot on whether certain blueprints, particularly rares, drop, as well as getting certain active talents (the ones that collect all of one color from the board in particular, or talents that increase coolant). And while you can grind to smooth out how hard this hits you, the upgrades per level are so miniscule as to be almost laughable.
The difficulty curve between matches ramps up ridiculously given how quickly you can accumulate upgrades - and is particularly harsh if you make it past the first boss.
Some of these problems could have been mitigated by the addition of a few basic systems - selling items you no longer need, having a store to buy some basic items. The ability to have an option to control costs would be particularly welcome, as that is most of what makes this game difficult (though a combat slider would be an options as well). I'd already decided I don't like roguelikes and this has turned me off of roguelites. I want to be able to play the game the way I want to - I'm not willing to grind forever and repeat the same levels over and over when I could just go play another game that's more satisfying and rewarding or lets me have control over how I can play the game.
Also, for a game that makes you play the same parts over and over, you think there'd be an option to automatically skip all text you've seen before. Otherwise I'm just hitting skip skip skip. Cmon developers, why are you pushing the work onto me? That's an easy fix.
Also, for a game that's a matching game, there's no competition with the computer. Is it making other matches behind the scenes? There's no way for me to block the computers actions. Also, most matching games have additional rewards for long matches or for matches that result from gems dropping - while I know that the second doesn't work the way they've designed the matching here, I miss both of these systems. The gold standard for this game is migh and magic - clash of heroes, and this just comes up short in comparison.
I'll keep out an eye for a sequel that addresses these concerns, otherwise I don't think I'll be buying it.
