Beautifully and atmospheric game ruined by bad game design. they should stick to an exploration game instead of the dark souls-esque thing theyre going for..

The Good;
• Visuals: Jotun is a beautiful game. The backgrounds are stunning and amazingly well drawn and it is obvious that a lot of love and care went into it.
• Animation: The bosses in Jotun are wonderfully animated, and actually remind me of Don Bluth's own works, such as Dragon's Lair and Space Ace.
• Music: While it's nothing bombastic, Jotun has some beautiful music that fits the areas you traverse, many which are quite relaxing to just sit and listen to.
• Setting: Jotun is the first game I've played that follows Norse mythology as close as it does, and is the most accurate I've seen a game get to it.
• Presentation: This game does a FANTASTIC job at presenting areas and enemies to you. The scaling of some bosses, areas, and even the great serpent Jörmungandr are nothing short of impressive.
The Bad;
• Slow moving character: It takes quite a while to get from one area to another, even with the speed ability you get later.
• Invincibility Frames: More specifically, the lack of them. There are none, not when rolling or taking damage. This makes fighting multiple enemies especially frustrating. With bosses, it's difficult to not get hit.
• Exploring: While it should be fun to explore each area and see the sites, most of the time it's a chore that just bores you, especially with how long it can take. It also gets quite repetitive, with a lack of true variety to keep you entertained.
• Fighting: It's not fun. You have two attacks; your normal one which you can swing twice, and a power attack. Both are incredibly slow and leave you wide open for enemies. You can't combo with your normal attack either.
• The Map: While the map shows you the layout of the area, it lacks the icon to show you where you are, thus forcing you to pay extra attention to where you go and to constantly check it and mentally map out where you are at.
The Sub-par;
• The Story: While the story isn't bad, it's not really great, either. You don't get invested in the character, and while it's neat to learn her backstory, it doesn't invoke any emotion in you either.
Final Thoughts;
Jotun is a decent game that's great to experience for the first time, and get wowed by the backgrounds and scale of the bosses, but it's not a riveting experience that you'll want to return to, unless you want to get all the Achievements. Experienced gamers who like a good challenge may enjoy it, but average gamers may want to give this game a pass, unless you want to see the visuals for yourself.
I give the game an overall score of 6/10.

I found the mythology that Jotun teaches fascinating, but the gameplay infuriated me. To start with, navigation is far more difficult than it should be. You try to find your way through abstract maps that often don't explain how you are even supposed to get from one place to another or lie about paths that don't exist. There's no marker representing you on the map, so navigation becomes even more difficult as you try to figure out where you are at the moment before you can try to figure out where to go next. The boss battles also take far too long. Every attack chips from a massive health pool. Making boss battles drag on far longer than they deserve. If you're looking for satisfying gameplay, look elsewhere. If you're looking for information on Norse mythology, look up a video on Youtube, so you don't have to grind through sub-par gameplay to find it.

Just finished doing 100% achievements, here's what I think after having experienced pretty much everything:
Pros
Fun action and platforming (must use keyboard and mouse, controller not precise enough)
Hooking around feels good when you get the hang of it
Challenging yet not frustatingly difficult
Awesome music, even after all these hours I'm not tired of it
Great art style, world and lore
Cons
Room layout and ennemies become repetitive after a few hours
Hard to see spike balls and traps can be frustrating
It's rare, but sometimes when entering a room you will get damage from a hazard immediately with no time to react
Overcosted black market items prolongs the length of the game artificially
Overall I'd say it's pretty good if you like action platformers. If you are mainly a rogue-lite fan you may be dispapointed by this aspect of the game.

This game is outstanding. The devs did a great job of walking the line between nostalgia and progress. It has a really unique combination of style and gameplay features that I really like.
The pixel-style really suits the simple goals of the levels. You jump, hook , and shoot. Pretty basic right? Not so fast. The coordination between hook-shotting around and platforming blends really well with the shooting. It feels familiar and comfortable, and like nothing you've ever played at the same time.

The platforming is fast-paced, the art is just delicious, and the structure of the rogue-like elements are the first time in recent gaming for me that I felt they added more than they subtracted. Love it.

Nice game considering a small studio. I can say that Diluvion delivers a very nice package as you navigate through the sea, discovering the dangers of the deep while following the story.
It has a set of nice elements and they all work, except for the camera that has it´s issues only when you position your sub on tight trenches and you really force it to go on a way it shouldn't, like going sideways on these tight places because you got hit, then things get confused, but nothing that comes even close to make the player give up the game or stop playing for a while.
But other than that issue, the game runs perfectly fine... no bugs that I could see, absolutely a smooth ride for me. The game just works very nice.
So you have 3 maps, each one deeper than the other, and you will do some quests to know what´s going on and how to proceed the story... Once you complete the objectives, you can proceed to the next map, and once you reach part 2, you can get back to part 1 of the map in case you need. Dont think it´s a short number of maps, because they will keep you navigating for hours and hours, so I can surely say their sizes are totally OK.
The game has a crew system that needs to evolve to become more important, but it works the way it is, and you can upgrade your team by using tokens on them. So each member has abilities and charge you the price based on them to join yout crew. Once paid, they´re with you, no more charges.
The crew needs food to keep working, so you gotta explore and kill enemies to get food. I cant consider it a grindy game because not a single once i had to stop the adventure to farm any item. Even the farm is related to the quest, so that wont be a problem.
A lot of times you´ll see pirates, so disable them and get the loot, as you need scrap metal for your cannon (they are your bullets), and you can also get torpedos from them, or buying from market places.
The developers found creative solutions to depict the deep sea, and you have many beautiful parts, and lots of places to explore. To each map there´s a boss, and they´re nice, but you will "suffer" a bit to get to the last one, because the last map is the total darkness.
-- CONCLUSION
I chose to be more detailed on my review because this is an indie game, and as there are a lot of trash today, I thought it would be better to give the clearest idea as possible so you wont think this game sucks, because it doesnt at all.
Go get it... it´s worth the price!!! I´ve spent 27 hours and it was well worth it !!!!

Diluvian, what is it? First off it is and RPG of sorts where you are the captian of a submarine. Not the modern nuclear submarines (though IDK what these things really are supposed to tun off) but old sci-fi or Jeules Vern esq submarines. In fact the entire world will very much remind you of 20,000 leauges under the sea or maybee a little of Sea-Quest meets Sunless Sea. You travel around a world represented by three zones trying to make a living and upgrade your submarine and overall gameplay/progression is much like the older space RPGs (Freelancer). There is no surface, only the deep in this game which is a little odd at first but it grows on you and fits with the game's lore very well. I cannot say much more about the game without possible spoilers, but, if so far it sounds like your cup of tea then give it a shot. You won't regret it.
In short Diluvian is the an interesting twist on an old tried but true genre of video game that has not seen much (good) action in a long while. It is still currently in development, but, doest not still feel like an alpha build. You should not get it and expect regular updates as the crew working on it is but three gents. Despite it's size though the team is very responsive and will help you work out any problems you have. It is well worth the $20 though for at least the first playthough and if you don't like it after that... Well it'll still have been a fun 10 hours.

What is Diluvion:
An arcade Style submarine deep sea exploraion game in an open 3D underwater world and handdrawn 2D interiors all inspired by Jule Verne Fantasy with minor micomanagement for crew and inventory.
What Diluvion is not:
Its not a submarine simulator at all and If you are looking for something like Aquanox, there is no "real cockpit or bridge" and combat is 3rd person based. you always have your submarine in front.
The Game:
Diluvion's world is based on 3 underwater maps where a simple but intresting story is leading you around. In the beginning you can choose from 3 different submarines : a combat sub, a trader sub and a scout sub.
they come in diferent style and have limited armor, wepons, cargohold and speed for their "class"
There are 4 Main Stations on your sub: the bridge, gunnery station, sonar and depending on your type of submarine the torpedo room. then there is also a cargohold that acts as your inventory and the crew room for not assigned crewmember. if it comes to steering your vessel i recomend the arcade version where your sub alwas follow your mouse pointer (similiar to mouse steering in War Thunder arcade air battle). in simulation mode you steer your submarine with keys and your view with the mouse. i didnt try set up a gamepad but there are control settings so it might work.
While you constant need to watch your amount of oxygen (can be increased with extra O2 bottles) there also is food to keep your crewmembers at work and Scrap Metal/Torpedos for your weponry. once you get more crew they can be added to the different staion so you get a boost to like weapon reload or sonar range etc or if they stay in the bunk they will autorepair your sub. sometimes you find repair kits as loot or at vendors but those have an anoying side effect: sadly there is no setting at what amount of HP/armor your kits get used so they will be instantly used (only if you have free crew)  once our subs gets damage even its just a couple HP.
During your travel you sure need to "ping" alot around with your sonar to get a rough view of your surrounding and discover hidden/sunken/abonded stations and wrecks for loot and to "see" underwater citys, friendly and hostile vessels/objects. Every "Object" that can be entered, like a station or subwreck etc, has a "docking port". when you are in range you can shoot your "docking harpoon" at it and pull yourself closer (quite awesome and frustrating at times). Once you get the hang of it all, let the atmosphere catch you while traveling around on your underwater adventure and beware of some sure creepy areas.  oh, and watch the dive limit of your sub or it get crushed.
So far behind all that deep sea explorarion and sub combat, Diluvion is a rough gem that still needs a bit of polishing here and there.
-Missing some crew portraits for assinged crew members
-rescale of the questlog and undock it from the map
-rescale and better inventory management (not that there is so much different stuff to manage but i hate scroll bars there)
-would like something like mousewheel zoom in/out when docked. autozoom/scale isnt that optimal.
-repair kits need some "use at X% hp" setting
Diluvion is such an amazing and beautiful game totally worth the £15 pounds

Basically, the game is a micro-controller simulator. You try to achieve tasks by wiring chips and writing microcode for them.
If you know nothing about programming and basic electronics, I'd suggest you stay away from this - later puzzles get really brain-breaking even for somebody who does.
If you are a professional in the area - most likely stay away, too. First - there is no need to bring your work into your entertainment. Second - it would probably be too easy and primitive for a pro.
But if you are somewhat in-between, like me - a high-level developer, for example, or a programming and electronics enthusiast - then, by all means, do check it out. It's a lot of fun and, also, a good, simple enough, sandbox to just have fun.

An amazing game. The game itself is simple to learn yet nearly impossible to master. Essentially a point and shoot arcade game, it is the Alien game that was never made. It barely works oin my computer and yet my friends and I can't stop playing it. There is nothing like fighting off swarms of aliens with your friends on Skype listening as you get seperated and your medic gets torn to shreds. But the mission comes first as the tech/engineer marine still has to be escorted to the bomb. That heartbreking moment when the badass, minigun toting, and cigar smoking heavy weapons experts yells "Go on without me!" and runs into and alien swarm cursing and spraying his minigun/flamethrowe/chainsaw. Yes, you read that correctly you can get a chainsaw. Also, you can get a sentry gun. They take time to set up but a sentry gun can easily turn the tide of a battle. Need I say more? Okay, the only thing this game is really missing (for now) is new content. The campaign is short but brutal, depending on the difficulty. There are levels in the game, however having a max level (25) marine on your team doesn't help that much. Sure they get access to better equipment, but a good trigger finger and a keen eye will help far more. After all you do get a sentry turret at level one and, excluding the chainsaw, might be the most overpowered weapon in the game. Ammo is also incredibly scarce throughout levels so bring along friends, they can give some extra firepower when needed or when friendly-fire is enabled you can take for the cost of a few bullets and one meat shield.

Alien Swarm is a surprising experience. It's a very challengeing experience on higher difficulty and right at the beginning of the learning curve. The high difficulty will force you into good teamplay, or you will only encounter death and loses. The game is fast, atmospheric and punishing for mistakes.

Pros:
Good production values (art direction, music, sound design, voice acting)
Fun way to learn about basic Norse mythology
Short
Cons:
Attacks are so slow to come out that it doesn't feel like you're playing a capable warrior. Mitigated by being able to cancel animations by dodging, but that only prevents the game from being too frustrating to play at all.
Character's move speed feels slow.
Story is undermined by the above. Hard to suspend disbelief about your character's background when it doesn't feel good to play as her.
Shallow combat mechanics. It's very obvious when to quick attack vs. heavy attack, and heavy attacks dominate most the time because dodge cancelling almost entirely shifts the risk of whiffing and being punished to just whiffing and missing some damage output. And the opportunity cost of getting in 1-2 quick hits vs. one heavy hit again favors going for the heavy hit.
Most levels are boring, due to only using 2 of:
1. Enemies
2. Puzzles
3. Environmental hazards
It's fine to use one element at a time in the early levels, just enough for players to learn the mechanics involved, but later levels should combine all three, and up the intensity. One of the last levels (Tree) is just navigating a slightly confusing level while occasionally dealing with an environmental hazard. For how far it is in the game, the player has already learned the underlying mechanics involved (especially since the Lake level was similar but better executed). A shorter, more intense level would have been better than what we got, and that goes for most levels. Compare with Braid, where every level explores a different/new game mechanic, and moves on before it gets stale.
Not enough unlockable shortcuts in the level design, resulting in boring backtracking at times.
You should get your life/powers refilled upon entering the hub, but don't.

Ironcast is a great match-3/TBS mecha game set in a steampunk universe.  It runs great, bug and crash free.  I got a good 60-70 hours of play out of it before I hit max level and completed the game for the first time (I'm not the fastest gamer out there).

I had a good time playing Ironcast and would recommend it to others.

Ironcast describes itself as "Puzzlequest meets FTL in this Steampunk Victorian era roguelite.", and as the reference to Puzzlequest implies, Ironcast is a Match-3 game and gameplay is also turn-based. The objects that you are matching on the board are known as 'nodes', and these affect your Ironcast in terms of available ammunition (purple), energy (orange), coolant (blue), or repair tools (green).
Your Ironcast can only hold a limited number of each resource at any one time (i.e 9 ammunition, 10 energy, 20 coolant, 10 repair), which is where part of the games strategy comes into effect. When I first started playing this game I was selecting as many nodes as I could fit into a match, however after watching others play the game I soon realised that this may not be the best way to go. Only collecting the amount that will fill your maximum meter allows you to not waste resources, and also allows you to strategically position other nodes on the board.
I have heard complaints of this game being repetitive, which it is, but as far as I am concerned all Match-3 style games are (or certainly all the ones I have ever played). It is the additional content in this game - the global unlocks, the gameplay strategy, the attacking targeting system, the workshop, the choice of commanders/Ironcasts, etc., that give this game longevity.
I am only 3.5hrs in to this game currently, and I have unlocked one new commander and one new Ironcast to use in battle, and will continue to work my way through obtaining the rest of the currently locked content.
If you are a fan of the Puzzlequest style Match-3 games, I see no reason why you would not like Ironcast. It is surprisingly strategic (as it took me some time to work out), and the global unlocks give you a reason to continue to play after each death on the battlefield. I would definitely recommend that you give this a try if you are normally a fan of this genre.

Ironcast mixes Match-3 gameplay with Victorian steampunk battlemechs, the titular ironcast, in an accessible and entertaining format.
By way of matching similar color nodes the player powers their ironcast's systems, allowing them to move and raise shields or fire various weapons. These matches, the longer they grow, also grant increasing amounts of experience points that enable the selection from one of three randomly chosen abilites upon leveling. Some of these abilities are tied to particular systems (drives, shields or a particular weapon slot), while others are installed as an enhancment to the ironcast or are a buff for your ironcast commander.
This game mixes in some very rogue-lite elements by dropping various craftable system schematics that can swing your play strategy from offensive to defensive, making evasion more appealing than damage absorption, for instance, or vice-versa. Similarly, there is an overall experience measure, accumulated from play-through to play-through that allows for a global leveling system, granting various minor buffs to make future games easier.
The art is effective at creating this alternate Victorian steampunk world and the sounds and music are pleasant enough.
The  unlockable ironcast commanders are rendered with portraits, incredibly wordy backstories that make no difference in the overall campaign, each having a unique ability that can significantly change one's approach to play. Just the same, various ironcasts, each one obviously designed to match up to the abilities of a particular commander, are well rendered, each also possessing a particular quality that sets it apart from the rest of the pack.
Missions are accessed from a map of southern England. Three are offered up as options to the player, drawn from a fairly limited pool of missions. Mostly they are either destroy X number of enemies in Y number of turns, or simply survive Y number of turns, perhaps while collecting crates that spawn in the Match-3 board in the center of the screen.
There is a back and forth of dialog at the beginning of each mission with a dispatching officer which lends some context to what you're doing and why, but it's irrelevant to actual gameplay and are, fortunately, skippable. The campaign itself is a two-act affair, punctuated with over-sized boss fights at the end of each act. Success in the final fight is often a function of which schematics have dropped during play and the luck of the Match-3 draw, so to speak.
There are two DLCs available for the game, but each merely contains an additional ironcast and commander. It's disappointing that new campaigns weren't added or at least more missions with more varied structures and goals. Even at a buck, I can't recommend either of the DLCs.
Ironcast presents a casual and entertaining adaptation of Match-3 play that allows for a strategic depth that might appeal to a more serious gamer. Adding in the attractive Victorian steampunk dystopia and the unlockables makes for a fun, budget friendly diversion.
If FTL and puzzle quest had a steampunk baby, you would get ironcast

I love this game. It starts off with an intro cinematic that gets you pumped to play it, from its music that puts me in mind of veteran favourites, to the wonderfully designed characters and ships.
The gameplay consists of the titular character boarding a pirate ship, and exploring each of its rooms for treasure and special abilities. There are room hazards to avoid, lots of pirates based on sea animals and birds to defeat, and special boss fights after you've successfully completed a run of ships. You can find traders within the game who will sell you potions and food to restore health, or maybe an ability that will turn your blasma pistol into a tri-shot device.These are bought with gold found from exploring the ships, but do not carry over between runs. Special skull tokens are found at the end of each ship that you can use to buy items and abilities from "the black market" which will give your character permanent upgrades.
You will fail a lot, but the game actively rewards you for playing. Even if you fail to complete a run, you will still earn experience points that go towards levelling up - as you level up, you unlock ability cards that you can apply to your character, that will make them a bit hardier next time!
Note: All of this is found within the gameplay - there are no microtransactions, nothing shady.
The unique parts of the platforming are the use of a hookshot device that pulls your character towards rings hanging in the room, and a time-altering device that slows the action down. As I got better at the game, I found myself using the hookshot almost exclusively to move around - it is so much fun to zip around on the rings, but it takes some practice to be able to do so without injuring the player character.
It is frustrating! Gygaxian traps will have me swearing out loud because I didn't spot the faint tells of their presence. I got stuck in a room last night that I could not escape, simply because I was not good enough at using the hookshot to climb out of a giant pit. I was able to laugh that one off because it was so ridiculous, every time I shot up, I would get propelled into a spike and fall back down again.
I particularly like the inclusion of relics and lore - I was able to uncover secrets in the game based on the descriptive information attached to these items, and I adore the fact that the identity of the main character isn't known - they are simply "Flinthook".
I nominated this game for the Better Than I Expected award, because it has been so superb. The music is stuck in my head all day, and it is a joy for me to come home to play at night before I go to bed. I cannot rate it highly enough; one of my very favourite games from this year.

I dsicovered the armed with wings series by pure accident and I played the games since they were released on

It was right up my alley. The boss fights,the atmosphere,the enemies,the five main weapons of choice you could pick. (One was endgame.) Quema Tormenta

Surprisingly fun game, not sure how/when I got it but I saw it in my library and gave it a go.

This is still early access as of when I'm writing, so these things are to be expected, but I'll say them just so nobody says I didn't mention them (I have good things to say below this stuff!)...
...The story / campaign is a bit short right now (I'm guessing it will be longer when the game is done; this is the fourth/fifth(?) game in the series and the dev's skills have gotten much better, so I'm guessing he's continuing)
...And there are a few bugs.  Notably, enemies who are currently dying are still deactivated when they move offscreen (so they don't finish dying until they come back onscreen.  This isn't game-breaking, but the dying enemies are still solid, so you can run into them (they probably shouldn't be), and they won't trigger "completed when all enemies are killed" events (eg, on the level where you have to go down before ceiling spikes get you, I hit an enemy off the top of the screen and had to jump up to trigger the door opening event).
Those things aside (hopefully they're already in the works)...
...This game's combat is very fluid, graceful, and dynamic (much better than the first, and even the third game in the series; both are flash games).  It has a very solid, well put together combo system (at least for the default character; I haven't used the lord much, so not sure about him...the default character's looks and moves are so awesome I just don't care about the lord XD).  The combat is what this game is about!  Look at the preview videos!
...Even though it's early access, the game already has LOCAL multiplayer support (coop and pvp).  Hopefully online multiplayer later?  This game could be pretty interesting with a matchmaking system and public tournaments!
...It has a fair selection of different weapons and mods for them...I haven't unlocked them all yet.  I would say they take a bit too long (too many points) to unlock compared to the length of the game, but the game may be longer when finished (who knows).  You can also unlock them in survival mode (probably faster than normal game).
Basically, if the combat in the preview videos looks good to you, I highly suggest this game.  If it doesn't, maybe not your thing.
Just a note for the dev if he(?) sees this; I think your current art style, character designs, and character personalities are all fantastic.  As far as what I think is lacking...probably just the stuff I already mentioned at the top.

Updated 1/24/2015:
TL;DR: Dead State remains quite combat focused, and while there is a lot of interaction to be had much of it may not be seen in a single play through the game. For a strategy RPG created on such a limited budget by a small team I consider it to be an entertaining experience that was well worth my time and money, and look forward to seeing what Doublebear does in the future.
Dead State remains an entertaining experience, but although it is released it still has some balance issues. Late game there is practically no reason to use the apocalypse armor over the Advanced Tactical Vest, which is a required component of the apocalypse armor. Combat can be rather enjoyable, but for experienced players it may be too easy. That being said, I've seen numerous complaints on the forums that it was too difficult, so I suppose they've struck a reasonable balance. I'm looking forward to the release of Iron Man modes, and although the game has passed the 1.0 mark Doublebear continues to flesh out the experience and address issues in the game itself.
If you're new to the strategy RPG genre and are looking for an experience that can be completed without a lot of combat this is probably not that title. Conversely, if you're adept at playing Strategy RPGs and want consistent end game challenges, this is also not that title. Doublebear has managed to create a fairly engaging game that revolves around both combat and crisis events and ally management. Unfortunately for the experienced player, they may never lose any ally and therefore won't have a problem getting so much morale that they never experience the darker aspects of the title. Meanwhile those who aren't able to manage the combat portion of the game may well lose so many allies that they have a hard time keeping allies.
I enjoy Brian Mitsoda's writing style, and overall I found Dead State to be a very entertaining experience. That being said
Dead State is shaping up to be a really enjoyable zombie survival RPG, and while it has tactical combat, the primary emphasis is going to be on the survivors and their personalities. Making sure that everyone has some semblance of normalcy in their otherwise upended lives and navigating the perils of the post-disaster world will eventually entail a lot of the experience. As the game stands, a lot of it is about the combat. It makes sense that they would want to expose the most replayable aspect of the game and get users opinions on it, and while it does strongly resemble the Age of Decadence on which the game has been built AoD has varied enough options for tactical combat that Dead State has a solid foundation on which to build in that regard.
As of right now (6/29/2014), the first seven days is all that is open to players for exploration and testing, but in the not so distant future plans are to open up more content for eager fans who want more. While I have only played through the first seven days twice I am likely to wait on that update before I dive back into Dead State. While the combat and potential choices in the first seven days is appealing, I'm rather more interested in how the game unfolds with regards to various factions and additional allies. At the end of the day, the first seven days is a fun tactical experience released to acquire feedback on aspects of the game that are still able to be changed. The game will revolve largely around the shelter and keeping your survivors from killing one another or hating your leadership enough to fracture your group into factions that each pursue their own agendas.
If everything unfolds in the direction it seems to be heading, you could potentially apply a variety of the shelter aspects to another type of disaster and the transition from zombie apocalypse to plague or famine or the destabilization of the magnetic poles and ensuing havoc EM radiation would have on unshielded electronics and minus the scavanging expeditions where you had to bludgeon people to death with a baseball bat things could feasibly progress in a similar fashion.

I was really looking forward to Diluvion, sadly it's the victim of careless development. Numerous times throughout my playthrough I asked myself if what I just experienced was a bug, feature, or just laziness.
-Repair kits are wasted constantly when not in combat and when they are not needed, making them a waste of money and time to try to use.
-The game doesn't track conversations across saves, so dying or loading the game results in every conversation popping up all at once.
-The ship auto-assigns crew very poorly, sometimes a 4 man crew on my engines adds 100%, other times it adds 10%, because the game doesn't know which crew to put there and I can't pick specific members.
-Enemies respawn any time you dock anywhere, meaning even though I already killed pirate band X, I now have to kill them all again on my way back to town. I spent a very large portion of the early game consistently running out of ammo.
-Some enemies just become hostile, seemingly for no reason. The Atlantica, a massive battleship that sits outside one of the game's leading faction ports, decided out of nowhere to start blowing me to pieces once as I undocked.
-The drone enemy in the game is at least five times faster than you, and its pathfinding makes it just ram you then spin around the hull of your ship, making it nearly impossible to aim at. Three or four of these at once quickly becomes a hassle rather than a fun combat experience. By the way, I didn't finish the game. At 13 hours I entered the leviathan area with at least ten drones and a few other enemies all attacking at once, where your hull goes from 40 to 0 in less than three seconds. It's definitely possible, but only by cheesing it and staying far enough away that they never see you and just firing torpedos ovre and over, which by the way the enemies don't attack you for doing.
-The "limited edition" Manta sub is really cool, however for some reason its crush depth doesn't upgrade properly, in fact only the starter sub upgrades properly, meaning by the time you reach the endgame it's the only one you can use.
-The angler from the demo was left in the game, which was a fun way to end the demo, but a really dumb way to punish players who don't know that docking there is an instant and guaranteed death (especially since it's not near a save area). Did I mention that your crew directly TELLS you to dock there?
As a final note, throughout the whole game I had virtually no repair kits and barely enough torpedos, but as you go toward the leviathan you get put through several relatively easy fights that net you nearly 100 food, 90 torpedos, and like 20 repair kits. It feels cheap and defeats the purpose of trying to stockpile things up until that point. I guess it makes sense to get such a ludicrous amount of torpedos given that the next area has to be cheesed with them just to get through, and after cheesing my way along for fifteen minutes and dying only to find out you start the whole thing over, I gave up on this game.
Final verdict: It seems unfinished. It's as simple as that. Not a lot of forethought was put into replayability either given how long the game is and how unrewarding the progress is. It would've been infinitely more fun if it was randomly generated as a rogue-like rather than the lame story that just seems to drag you through terrible fight after terrible fight.

Diluvion as it stands is an intruiging start to what can be a content-thick, lore and character driven adventure. At the moment, the game ended before I wanted it to but that is more so a positive statement than negative. I really fell in love with the world and gameplay.
Positives
+The lore,environment, and story are mysterious and engaging
+The asthetics range from beautiful and wonderous to pure nightmare fuel
+The soundtrack simultaneously makes the world feel alive and tragically lonely
+The gameplay is unique and challenging
+You truly feel rewarded for mastering the mechanics of the game
+By the second gameplay zone you truly get invested in the stories of the world
Cons
- I wanted more lore and dialogue
- I wanted more game-time
- There is an apparent lack of variety in money-making strategies
- The objective of the story was clear but could have been developed more
Many of the criticisms from the major review outlets have either already been patched out or are in the works to get patched out per comments made by the developers on the game's subreddit. Most of the Cons are also just consequences of being a small indie studio. This game has had a fantastic start and has serious potential in future content. Definitely worth a playthrough - it can be as quick as you want it to be but there's no shortage of sub-battles to hunt for if you're looking for more.

Excellent programming game. Beautifully designed and imaginative challenges that demonstrate the standard uses microcontrollers are put to. The physical boards vary from puzzle to puzzle and seem to be designed to constrain the tendency to work around the limitations of the components by just adding more of them and shuttling signals between them. You'll notice this more keenly if you're someone who tends to come up with verbose solutions involving components pinging each other. Also, the setting of the game (working in Shenzhen, emails from your colleagues) is well written and also enjoyable. After each product, the email conversation for that product continues and is a fun read after the intense product development session. Its clear from the debugging tools provided and all the polish in this game that it was made with a lot of love.
Absolutely gorgeous, fantastic game, well worth it if you enjoy programming!!

Ok, FOR FIRST TIMERS, if you've never played any of the previous Armed with Wings games, I'd recommend checking out AwW: Culmination. It's free and on your browser, plus it's a good place to start and to get familiar with the feel of these games. Secondly, if you've played the previous AwW games but aren't so sure about this one, play the AwW:R survival mode demo on Newgrounds. It's a nice introduction to the gameplay and it's pretty much like a try-before-buy type deal.
Now to the game itself.
It's great so far, but it's missing a couple elements the other AwW games had such as side characters and an upgrading system. The game seems pretty lonely, honestly. Even though I just play it for fun, it's like the only thing you really do in the game is kill things. No other characters, just you and the monsters/Vandheer. Story stuff doesn't happen often as of now. I know the story will probably get more development, but as of the day I'm writing this, there aren't really any characters/personalities here. I'd suggest improving on that factor by taking from the 3rd AwW installment. There were charactes... not that you really got to get attached to them considering they didn't get the most screen-time since the space between stages was relatively short.
Another thing it seems to be missing from its previous installments is a hub world. This could be a chance to add some NPCs or side characters to talk to which could come of use to you as you use them for various things such as upgrading or shopping.
I mean- he is a Lone Warrior, but c'mon. He's gotta have some friends.
Now, the art style. OOOOOOOOOOH the art style. I love it so much. I've toyed with the idea of shadows/silhouettes as characters/environments since before I played the first AwW, but holy crap you did it way better than me. I commend you, good man.
TL;DR, get the game if you love killing monsters and solving puzzles with a unique and creative art style to drive it home. Can't wait to see how this game turns out! I'm absolutely confident it won't disappoint. Keep up the amazing work.

This is one of those niche games that most gamers probably wouldn't like but a certain demographic will obsess on.
If you're a NHL or hockey fan. If you've ever played fantasy hockey. If you obsess on your favorite team and what would make it better. If you ever wanted to blow up an eternal loser like my Canucks (:sadface:) and rebuild the way you'd want to see it. This game is for you.
I've probably played this game more than all other games combined in my life. I've spent literally tens of thousands of hours on this game since it's inital release in 2004 and it honestly hasn't changed much since then. There's been some tweaks here and there in the game's 13+ year history but it's still essentially the same text based sports management sim now that it was then. As someone who loves sports sims and I've played most of then, NHL Eastside is the absolute best and deepest one I've ever played. You control every aspect of the playing side of the game. Transactions, waivers, minor teams, drafts, personnel, strategies, contracts, scouting and free agent signings.
The most engrossing thing for me has always been developing young players and working them into your system. Under your guidance players like Connor McDavid, Patrik Laine, Auston Matthews and other prospects can either flourish or flounder in your system.
I'm not sure if casual fans will enjoy it. But if you're a hardcore hockey, sports strategy/sports management games fan EHM is a peak experience. Even today 13 years later, I still get the urge and thrill of spending an evening obsessing on this game fairly often.

Great game, definitely worth it. That said, if you're not into planning, thinking, math, or troubleshooting, then you're gonna have a bad time.
I only have two complaints.
The fluid system is a nightmare. Construction robots can easily create mistakes when laying pipes from blueprints (which reflect placements, not final behavior), and if you get the wrong fluid in the wrong pipe then that corruption will move through your refinery as you're tearing out and replacing the tainted pipes. In complex setups, it's tedious enough to troubleshoot that you're better off deconstructing the whole thing, but you end up losing all the resources in your facilities and pipes. It's either that or mouse over every corner or ground pipe (which don't always show the icon), tear out the tainted pipes, then check every other pipe again after the corruption has moved from one place to another (it will until you've torn up everything anyway).
The ratios are critical - if you produce too much of a resource then the whole system will just shut down. With belts, backed up resources are fine (unless you're still working with loops), but if you fill up your facilities or storage tanks with a fluid then the other two will stop producing; this is solvable, but annoying.
The train tutorials are pitiful, and the signaling system is frustrating. The mantra of chains on entry to intersections and regular signals on exit doesn't seem to actually work in game, or even the tutorials. The provided explanations don't show much, and answers detailing how they should work are never given. It's bad enough that belting resources across a continent is preferable since that's at least movement, as opposed to a train sitting there erroring out "No Path" unless on manual.

I had some decently high hopes for this game. I am a Kickstarter backer and thought the concept looked great and was excited to see what they did with this game. Sadly, I have just been disapointed with the game so far.
As gameplay goes, it is buggy (but as a unreleased game this is expected). It is a turn-based system. The basis for who goes where is a blackbox and unclear if/how you approach will let you have the first turn or last turn in a mob. This can create an extremely annoying start to a fight. It ruins the strategic element from time to time and has made me walk away from the game on more than one occasion. There are two types of enemies in the game 'looters' and 'zombies', however, the only real difference is that 'looters' have items. Other than that they follow the same mindlesss horde approach to a fight. This makes, what should be the palette cleanser of combat just more of the same. The game feels to "be on rails" and there is, as of now, zero replay value to be had. While there is an expected main story it doesn't feel like there is going to be much in the way of meaningful choice in the end. Then there is the fact that the game is not intutive and has 'hidden' controls like the quick save and quick load which can ruin your game if you accidently hit it outta the blue. << 09/26/14 UPDATE >>
So the game has hit BETA state and the first patch has been released. I've also become a bit more active in the game's forums and learnt a couple things that I'd like to share with potential buyers.
First, the game is meant to be SHORT. In game time is estimated to be about 3 or 4 months. This is worrysome when you consider that it'll probably take you less than 2 months to kill and loot EVERYTHING in the rather small area map you get to explore. This would mean that you'd spend a substantial amount of time either idle or simply dealing with repetitive task like assigning jobs or going to auto-gather locations.
Talking about locations, a lot are on the small size. In most cases, you get to explore an area with only a couple of enterable buildings, which further decreases game time.
Combat is still pretty straight forward and rather easy. My biggest worry hasn't been zombies or hostile survivors, but loot capacity. Once you know where you can find a good armor and a decent weapon (usually melee), you can go there almost straight away and get kitted out. Unless they substantially change how combat behaves (specially remove the player's ability to run behind an enemy and begin combat, thus always getting the first shot), I can't see it become challenging. Even big groups can be split appart by causing noise, which usually leads one or two members straight into your ambush just around the corner.
Can't really comment much on the game's story as of yet because a lot of the script and dialogues have not been implemented or are currently not working, but even though it does seem to be shaping up to be an interesting zombie survival story, the presumed lenght of the campaign worries me greatly.
I'd still recommend the game to any zombie fanatics out there, but be sure to know what kind of game you are getting into.
All in all, I would recommend you go check out Project Zomboid before you buy this one, because even though the graphics are worse, it's got the survival aspect nailed down MUCH better than Dead State, and survivor AI is also in the works there.
PD: There's no plans of allowing modding to the game either, at least from what I've seen and read.
<< 14/03/15 UPDATE >>
Well, after waiting for a good while for some kind of patch or content update I find myself abandoned by the developers. There hasn't been any major changes since December and from what I've seen, the Devs already said that the planned "expansions" have been called off because the game didn't sell well enough. What does that mean? You'll get a few more patches that fix what should have been functional on release day and perhaps a few more game mechanics that also should have been there on release day. Then, it's game over for Dead State.
I am angry at myself for thinking that this could be any good. I've been following this since Alpha and I should have known that this team could not pull off such an ambitious project. Ambitious because it was something new, not because it was something hard to do. Honestly, with dated graphics and game mechanics that seem out of the 90s, how could this game take them two years to make? And don't get me started on the ending and the plot holes and so much other stuff.
Bottom line, Dead State brings nothing new to the party. Combat hasn't been improved. Its boring, repetitive and cumbersome (when it doesn't bug out). The story is lame and the characters - while they have a few moments - are blanks that say their lines (the very few they have) and stand around in your shelter doing absolutely nothing. Music is nothing to be remembered. The rest of the game mechanics - specially the survival aspect - are badly implemented, break immersion or simply make no sense.
What more can I say? I've been warning the devs about these faults for a long time on their forums and I was always met with blind optimism or simple denial. Now we are 3 months after release and it's exactly what I thought was going to happen: A disaster.
To any possible customer:
You want Combat? > H1Z1 / DayZ Standalone / DayZ Mod
You want Survival? > Project Zomboid
You want story? > The Walkind Dead by Telltale Games, S1 and S2

Updated for Reanimated Version:
It took me several attempts to get into this game, but am now hooked. I'm at about day 15 and am happy to report that the writing gets better and all of the features I was looking forward to start to open up quite a bit (shelter upgrades, new survivors, interesting but tough choices, and personality management).
I am a point and click guy, but will admit, there are times the combat can get pretty tedious. There are some layers of strategy that can be satisfying (ie; using the noise meter and zombie hordes to your advantage to take out looters) BUT you really need to take time in between battles to manage your inventory before heading out on another run. They do, however, alleviate some of the micromanagement by automatically stocking shelter items each time you return.
Your survivors will randomly need to take some time off due to sickness or other reasons, so you will have shuffle your scavenger party every once and a while (this is a good thing). Your survivors also level up, but at a slower pace than your main character.  And while you can't allocate the points manually, you can occassionally suggest areas you would like your other survivors to improve when they do decide to level up (which is fine, I guess. It goes along with the concept that you can't control everybody at your shelter. You have to mange personalities through dialogue choices and finding items in missions).
For me, the UI wasn't as intuitive as I was expecting when it comes to information and inventory management...but that's a tiny gripe.
Aside from those gripes and small pathing issues, if you give it a little time, the game does get interesting. It's certainly worth 20 bucks and has more depth than I thought it would. The demo will give you a good idea of gameplay mechanics, but as I mentioned, it really picks up from about day 8-12.

First of all, I want to say that this is a pretty good game. I don't prefer turn-based games, but for a turn-based game, it's not bad at all. A little bit basic, there doesn't feel like there's much meat to it, and maybe that's just because I'm so used to my games having voice acting in them or something, I'm not sure. It's true that it's only essentially a Beta version of a demo, so of course it's not that developed - and I understand that, that makes sense.
That is one of my main problems with this game. You are,
being lied to by the developers. It used to be they had the word "demo" plastered everywhere, all over their game summaries and descriptions and even in the early-access disclaimer thing. Now, you can't find the word "demo" anywhere, and on top of that, the limit of them informing you what you are actually purchasing for $25 are only these two sentences:
"Dead State is currently in Early Access - purchasing now will eventually unlock the full game for you at final release, and in the meantime you can playtest the first seven days of the game (ongoing feature updates are planned)."
and
"Dead State: The First Seven Days is an early, WIP preview of the first week of Dead State's gameplay - an opportunity to prepare your strategy for the full game and help us test and polish the full Dead State experience."
To the layman? Who only skims the description because, let's be honest, a good majority of people? Only skim. This looks like it is saying "For now you get the first 7 days, but maybe as we go along until release, we'll be releasing more days." -- Because
People, I want to be very clear:
Now, to my actual gameplay review:
The game is alright. I know it seems like I couldn't have played enough for very long, but believe me, I got enough time to play that I know exactly what the game is about and how it works.
In all honesty? It's kind of like a Zombie Apocalypse version of Pokemon Mystery Dungeon. There are some tweaks here or there, obviously, but generally speaking it's very similar. If you're not careful, you could end up inadvertently shoving a character in the middle of like 8 zombies at once, and though that's a true danger in most zombie apocalypse worlds, I have a hard time believing my other characters would take about 8 turns before saving him. That was literally the first thing that happened to me when I went into the game. I literally quit and started over again because the game gave me absolutely NO warning that something like that could happen.
Now, maybe it's just me, and maybe it's just because it's been a
long time since I played a turn-based game last, but when I played this game, I got absolutely NO instruction on how to play, whatsoever. And again, maybe it's just because I'm a moron -- I definitely can be, from time to time. But when I first played, I had no idea what was better - was the knife better? Or was the bat better? I had no idea, because I had no idea what the difference (in this game) piercing damage was in comparison to blunt damage. I mean of course most people assume piercing damage DOES more damage, but honestly some basic gamers may not know that, and they're not very clear about it.
On top of that, I had absolutely no idea that, when I started, the zombies were all gonna get 2 fighting turns in a row and I was only going to get 1. I also didn't know that even if the screen was clear, they could still appear later, around corners and the like - again, I know that SHOULD be generally common sense, but I've been spoiled by all of the other open-world games out there, and I'm used to a goblin being around a corner before I even get around that corner. I've played so many various games that I NEED to be told the rules in a game like this, I can't just predict them, because I've just played so many other games with so many other rules.
Also, for the record, the graphics are pretty bleh. Even for an early version of the game. I mean it's 2014, we expect quite a bit more out of games these days, even top-down turn-based ones.

It's a given that in the Rogue genre, almost everything is random and your endgame comes from unforgiving mistakes at first and bad luck at last. Ironcast is no different, and after about 20 games, I was only able to confront the boss once, and died a glorious death "so close to beat him".
Is there any winning strategy in this game ? I'm not sure. What I've learned so far, is that Defense is key to survival. If you let your guard down, you will suffer. Oh boy, yes you will. So Defense and Energy Upgrade are a must, but be wary of Energy cost, since some Defenses requires 3 Energy et other ones 4 Energy - this might not seem a lot, but when you are 1 Energy short, you pay a big price in Health, that will later transfer in Golden Bars in the workshop - those precious Bars you need to upgrade.
What about Weapons ? Whatever your choice, you need one to be used against strong armor and little to no movement (single shot with high damage), and one against fast movement and little to no armor (multiple shots with low damage). Splash damage can be good, as long as you are not in a mission where you have to preserve any component of an enemy Ironcast - just check the splash damage is under the current opponent Defense level.
One note about Cooling. It's used for Weapons, Defense and Movement. Even if the initial reserve is fairly high, if you use them a lot, you'll be short soon, and working a machinery without Cooling is like setting yourself ablaze.
On my own, I like to play the first character (Defense and Movement bonuses) with the second Ironcast (Energy weapons) and play like a tower (almost no movement). I usually bet on upgrading Energy reserve up to 12, Defense then Weapons (same ones, but better if available) ; and on the abilities offered each time you reach a level : Cooling + Defense + Golden bars bonuses. My only weakness is that at a certain point, my weapons might not be up to the task.

In simple terms, Britain and France are at war over a valuable new source of energy. They are using mechs called "Ironcast" which have proven to be more sturdy and longer-lasting than tanks and light vehicles. You command one of these Ironcast, and it's your job to gain resources by matching colored block on the grid below that symbolize various components, and use these to command your unit to attack, repair, defend (shield), and walk (evasion) each turn.
+ Very strategic gameplay where you are constantly thinking about the best combination of tiles to destroy, and the best way to use your resources to both do the most damage while also taking the least amount of damage possible.
+ Unique turn-based mechanics where essentially each turn you are able to match up to 3 chains, and then are able to attack / defend / repair until your resources run out, although you may want to keep some for next turn.
+ The upgrade system is quite honestly amazing, you can research new guns, gain passive abilities, defensive abilities, and a wide variety of perks for your guns, shields, and so fourth.
+ Great background music / soundtrack
+ Wonderful graphics / art-style, I especially like the weapon animations and the very clean UI in the center where you match the tiles and choose your attacks.
+ Challenging enemies to face especially if you choose the harder missions
+ Difficult but exciting boss fights
- (This may be a positive to some) but when you die it's essentially "Game Over" and you can not go back to your last save, you must restart and lose all your progress. You do earn little perks and unlock new characters / ironcast to use, but it can still be sad as you don't always know what you will be facing or how difficult the enemy will be. (sometimes the odds are stacked against you)

Normally I would not recommend this because it's a fairly middle of the road game that does nothing impressive and gets a lot wrong. However, since there aren't many games in this genre with submarines it gets a pass.
Pros -
-Nice atmosphere.
-Nice music.
-Submarine maneuvers well.
-Last boss fight is exciting and done well.
Cons -
-Story is poorly written and poorly presented with plot threads dropped with no satisfactory resolutions.
-Docking mechanic is extremely shallow and offers little gameplay but you'll be doing it a lot.
-Targetting even with a maxed out navigator is finicky.
-Biomes lack diversity wich makes the world seem dead (no sea creatures).
-Enemy diversity is nonexistent. You'll be fighting submarines and only submarines (except the last boss).
-Final zone feels unfinished.
-You never really feel like the Captain. It seems like your helmsman makes all the decisions regarding where you go and what to do.
-Occasional bugs that stop the main quest from proceeding (fixed with reloading the previous checkpoint).
Pick it up on the cheap if you're hungry for a shallow undersea adventure but if you aren't then pass on it. Your life won't be any worse for not playing this.

I struggled to decide to not recommend this game because I had high hopes for it and was not disappointed in many regards.
The combat, exploration, and player control of how your sub functions (weapons, class, crew, etc) are the games strongest points. And it does these quite well.
But, in every area it does well, it also could improve a lot.
Some examples of this:
The controls are decent, but I found operating the sub with a keyboard and mouse to be quite difficult and navigating menus and locations with a controller to be quite difficult. This prompted me to switch between the two quite frequently, which I did get used to. It's just a bit of a hassle.
There will be some occasional and extremely minor SPOILERS from this point on, nothing really story related.
The combat for all intents and purposes is great. But I feel like there is a lack of interesting encounters. There are only two "big" encounters before the end of the game and you don't actually defeat either of them, you just disable their weapons (also small note, the second encounter involves you helping to retake a ship for a faction, yet after you complete this, the ship remains hostile permenantly although this might be a bug).
I expected the ocean to have a bit more biodiversity, but everything other than the crab with the battleship on it that was in the trailer and a single late game non combat encounter was a man made ship or one of the constructs guarding the end game area (I guess you could call these creatures, but some of them are lootable and have scrap and stuff). Point being, I expected more sea monsters and whales and squids, but there are little to none.
The game has so many features that are extremely cool, but near useless or not well implemented. Some examples:
Also, small but SPOILER heavy complaint: The characters finally get to the end. They are pretty well developed and have good chemistry.
And what do these characters do after not shutting up the entire game? They have no reaction. Any other time, they'd comment on every little thing, making me have to ignore torpedos coming at me just so I can see that whatsherface feels sad otherwise the notification won't go away. But all this achievement and wonder and they say nothing.
I did have fun, however. I was just largely let down with it. It's one of those games that clearly has tons of potential, but poor design decisions make it miss the mark.
The $20 price tag is even a decent price for it. It could be beaten in a weekend and you could have a lot of fun with it. But it just doesn't live up to what it so easily could be.
I will be looking out for more work from these devs as they do have talent.
Also, the preorder sub is literally an already in game sub with slightly better stats and maybe a unique texture.

Note; I talk alittle about everything in the game in this review. If you want to be surprised to what this game has, then skip to the end.
I suppose I'll begin this review by saying that my experience with this game went flawlessly. Through the 18 hours I spent on the game, I experienced 0 bugs, errors, or crashes. Everything played out how it was suppose to, and in this day and age that is a great feat to say about a game.
Now, I heard of diluvion back when it first came out on kickstarter, and I couldnt wait to be able to play it for myself when it finally came out. And I can honestly say it was definitely worth the wait.
I didn't encounter any bugs in the game with my playthrough, and if I did, they were too insignificant for me to remember them.
Thoughts about the game;
Submarine piloting is perfect. Theres alot of "bad" reviews from people who've only played the game for an hour saying "this game sucks the controls are bad". Its a SUBMARINE, and in this game, it pilots exactly how you would expect a submarine to pilot. (you know, you adjust the throttle to increase/decrease speed, and only use the directional keys to move left/right/up/down) So in that regard, I would suggest looking up a gameplay vid of the submarine piloting BEFORE you buy, in case that kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥russles your jimmies.
Atmosphere of the game is really spot on with what to expect when you're underwater. Fog clouds your vision of the distant horizon, so it really gives it that feeling of the unknown whenever you travel anywhere. The "sealife" you encounter is mostly an aesthetic, but there are a few moments in the game where that isnt the case
Its technically randomly generated in a few ways. Throughout the game your main currency is "scrap", however scrap also functions as your ammunition for your basic weapon. In certain towns you can find shop keepers that sell various goods in exchange for scrap. And throughout the game there are randomly generated wrecks that hold scrap and other various goods. Alot of the game is spent searching the ocean floors for these wrecks to salvage scrap from them to buy what you need, and I honestly I like it. You might have to scavange ALOT to get what you need to progress, but most of the time it isnt just as simple as going from point A to B. Thats when the combat comes in
If this game was a sandwich, the wreck salvaging would be the meat and cheese, and the combat would be the bread and mayo. You really can't have the game be complete without both of them together. Combat is simple; aim your reticle with your mouse over enemy subs, and shoot the !@#% out of them. As I mentioned, your scrap currency is also your ammunition for your basic guns. So it becomes a case of "should I try to fight this guy to get what he has, or run away to conserve my scrap to buy things at the shop?" Through the game you get crew members, and you can assign these crew members to certain stations in your sub to enhance the abilites of that part of the sub (guns, ship intergrity, torpedoes, and sonar) However, having a crew member not assigned to any station will give your ship a passive heal over time. More people, the more healing you receive, but the worse your ship performs in the 4 sections I mentioned before. so basically, be prepared before entering a fight!
Finally, the 2 "fuels" you need to stay on top of, and the story. While going through the game you have a "food meter" and an "air meter". Your crews needs to eat, and if they aren't getting fed (as in, you run out of food. duh) they leave their station on the ship and sit in thier beds not being of any use to you. So scavange food from wrecks, or buy it from vendors, whatever it takes. Additionally, your "air meter" slowly goes down while you're travelling around, and if it runs out, bam you die. Thats it. Sub just blows up and you restart from your last save point. When you enter a town, it automatically fills all your air tanks. You can also purchase more airtanks from certain suppliers as you go through the game, so you can travel for longer periods of time without visiting towns. Now, about save points....
VISITING TOWNS AUTOMATICALLY SAVES YOUR GAME, AND THATS THE ONLY WAY YOU CAN SAVE YOUR GAME. Around towns and certain vistas, there's a giant orb of green fish that encircle the entrance port to the location. All you do is enter this circle, and your game is automatically saved. I might be wrong, but this is the ONLY way to save your progress in the game. So keep your eyes out for them. Also, you can find maps for these locations as an item, inside these locations when you visit them. When you acquire the map item, the location will appear on your world map so you know how to get back later. Theres also a compass you can access via keybind that shows the direction you need to go to get to a location, but it only shows that location if you have the map for it. So get exploring.
All in all, the only problem I really had with the game was the final area of the game doesnt have alot of things to find/explore. The other areas had PLENTY to find and discover, and the final area doesnt have nearly as much. If you get there, or have gotten there already, you'll know what I mean.
Also, this deserves its own little section. The ending sequence of this game is hands down, the greatest ending to a game Ive ever played in my life. Do yourself a favor and experience it for yourself. Watching it in a video or playthrough is not the same as being there yourself.
Tl;DR - This game is beautifully crafted in every aspect, and truly captures what its like to be an undersea explorer in charge of your own little submarine. Its not too difficult, but at the same time it isnt a walk in the park. Controls are what to be expected of when piloting a submarine, but if thats too much of a bother for you, I suggest looking at a video showing the controls before you buy the game and then make a bad review of it with 0.5 hours saying "controls are bad, game suck". As for bugs, I didnt experience a single bug in my 18.7 hours of play, so idk. Maybe I had good luck. You might love this game for its unique adventure you can't find anywhere else, or you might find it "boring" because there isnt an explosion or gunshot happening every 0.5 seconds. Ether way, its only $20. Definitely the most fun Ive ever had with $20.

Flinthook is pretty great for what it is - a run'n'gun roguelite with fun movement mechanics. If you don't like permadeath and you don't like frustrating, challenging, one-more-try gameplay, probably look elsewhere. There are a lot of persistent upgrades to balance you up to the game, but even with a bunch of perks (which are unlocked in random packs, AFAIK) some of the randomly generated ships are insane.
The game is fast-paced, but will punish you if you jump in without thinking. All the hooks are laid out in a way that you can take them in a smooth path, and avoid damage if you time it right. There are myriad enemies and environmental hazards that make this game as much about damage avoidance a la bullet hells as it is about glidey platforming.
Not the best roguelite I've played but certainly captivating. Pick it up on a discount at the least

I had been waiting for the game to come out for a long time when I bought it. I was immediately entranced by the graphics and music, but was worried that the gameplay might not live up to my expectations.
It blew me away.
The controls are tight and work very well together. Again, I was worried that my Steam controller might not work well, since it only has one joystick. I usually have to use the keyboard to play twin stick games due to the trackpads being hard to use, but I was once again pleasantly surprised. All the aiming is done with the movement joystick - you hold down a bumper to stand still if you want to fire while not moving. Genius.
And then there's the hook. Again, you use the same joystick to aim the hook, and can stand still while doing so. Zipping through a level using the rings hanging from the ceiling is one of the most satisfying feelings in the game, and I usually equip plenty of hook perks because of how useful it is. You even need to use the hook to attack certain enemies. More genius.
Every shot you fire has weight and the animations are astounding. Granted, it can get a bit grindy, as you have to level up to unlock more perks, which are the only real way of boosting your health and other stats, but the secrets and lore make up for it - you discover something new every playthrough.
Mechanics are amazing but simple and just the idea of being a space pirate is awesome. 10/10.

Rearmed is a great purchase for fans of the series and newcomers alike. The combat is smooth and dynamic with several possibilities, combining some of the best elements from previous games. The art is fantastic as always and the levels are often a mix of desolate wastelands and intricate structures. There are a few puzzle aspects, but they tend to provide a break from combat rather than an alternative to it. As you progress through the game, you unlock new weapons and abilities (of which there are about 100) that make the game easier for different playstyles.
The game has 40 levels in its story mode as well as a few survival maps. There are 2 difficulty settings beyond "Normal," for those who want more challenging content after completing the base game. There is also a local multiplayer with the option to challenge a friend, playing as any of the 3 characters currently available. The developer has hinted about adding a 4th character at some point in the future.
I would easily recommend this game to any veterans of the series, and the $8 price tag is definitely worth it. If you haven't played an Armed with Wings game before, I encourage you to try out some of them, such as Armed with Wings 3 and Culmination, before buying it. The style of Rearmed is very similar but it vastly improves on most of the other games' mechanics. You can play all of the original games on the
website.
Also be sure to join the Discord community! It's a friendly place with about 200 active members that you can get into

Armed With Wings: Rearmed is a stylish action/platform/puzzle game with an extremely high amount of polish for an Early Access title. The most direct gameplay comparisons I can make with this game are "They Bleed Pixels" with its directional-based combat system, and "Super Meat Boy" with it's 'just one more try' bites of gameplay, on top of the challenge they both provide.
Combat in the game focuses on properly analyzing your foe(s) for openings, then chaining free-form moves (determined by directional input in tandem with Light/Heavy attack) into combos to defeat them. Spacing and timing are key, especially when there is more than one enemy to contend with. Animations are fluid and impactful, and very stylized. Combat is challenging, and can punish button-mashing very quickly, which makes it all the more rewarding when you emerge victorious. The only thing to be wary of is that the game is a bit slow in explaining combat mechanics in-depth, which may or may not be a negative depending on if you are someone who prefers experimentation over hand-holding. (I prefer experimentation, myself.) It will tell you the tools you need to survive, however, it won't just throw you to the wolves.
When you die in the game, your points are allocated automatically into an unlock system that unlocks weapons with various stats (Speed, Damage, Blocking, etc), and Boosters, which change how your weapons perform. For example, the first booster you unlock adds 2 hits to your normal combo chain, which you can equip via the menus to suit your playstyle. This serves to add a lot fo replay value, as there is also Survival Mode to test your combat prowess, as well as a local VS mode to test your friendships. ;)
The puzzles in the game involve the use of an Eagle which accompanies the player throughout the levels. It can move objects such as switches and weights to open doors, distract enemies barring your path, and pick up out-of-reach health globes. It can also move into areas unreachable by the player, which is used in clever ways to break up sections between combat.
Platforming in the game is unique, as well, in that there is no dedicated jump button. Instead, the player character jumps automatically by leaping off of ledges, making timing important for crossing pitfalls.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes a challenge, anyone who likes a minimalist art style with a beautiful aesthetic, and anyone who likes feeling like a total badass ninja. This Early Access game is already excellent, especially for the asking price, and I only see it getting better as the developers have been very active in responding to feedback.

First of all, here is my review for the original game.
I liked the game. It was a standard top down shooter, with a halo theme. The sounds felt adequate. Shooting enemies felt enjoyable. There is a heriarchy of various enemy types. Some were easy to kill, others were not, some were a few high threat. The gameplay felt seamless. Non-stop action and plenty of weapons to choose from. Overall it was fun, but there were a few drawbacks (which you can read about in the review above).
This game is more of the same, with most of the drawbacks fixed. The major difference between this original and this game is that here you also fight the "forerunners". I haven't played halo games outside of halo 1 and 2, but i do know a thing or two about what has been happening to the franchise. Basically, in the original trilogy, you basically 2 other enemy factions to fight - the covenant and the flood. The reboot (Halo 4), introduced a new faction - the forerunner.
In the original you only fight the covenant. In this game you fight both, but primarily the forerunners.
Now, the game is pretty much the same thing. Except the levels became longer. There is at least a gurantee that they will last for 5 minutes. There are a total of 5 missions, each having 6 levels. It takes 3-4 hours.
The scorpion (tank) controls were fixed too. Before, these controls were like this - imagine a dot in the center of your screen. Draw lines to the north, south, west, east, up to 8 directions. When you press W, you go north for example, relative to your screen. I hope you get the idea. It was very hard to control that thing. It's sort of strange because the same system is used for movement of your character, but it just doesn't work when using it on a tank.
Now, pressing W goes forward relative to the direction your tank's front is facing. A and D rotate the tank. S makes it go backward.
There is one problem with the game though. The 5 mission that the game has. There are only 4 really. The fifth one requires you to earn gold stars in the 4 missions before it to play it first. Personally i hate the concept of stars, and i think that the level should be accessible to all, regardless of the stars. I wouldn't mind if 1 mission would make up 5% of the game, but here it's 20%. They are locking away a pretty sizeable piece of content.
