Factorio is a game perfect for those who like to build, to think, and who are addicted to the freedom of creation. You start on a randomly generated world and have to hit rocks to get your first resources. But the game opens up into something more when you unlock the factory and begin the ever-evolving process of automation. Research, robotic arms, conveyor belts, turrets, weapons, and armor can all be made in a factory and as soon as it has the required materials it starts producing.
At first, the automation is simple with conveyor belts going from mines to the factory and a robotic arm to supply it. Soon, however, the complexity spikes as the more advanced items in the game require finished products as part of their construction. You'll find that the resources around your starting area may not be enough to meet all your needs and they are finite as well. Factories and most buildings also require power which will need an infrastructure all its own. The end-game consists of a complete train network, loaded and unloaded automatically by those robotic arms, which connects to your various outposts harvesting the materials your massive base requires to keep up production.
It isn't all smooth sailing in your building of an industrial empire though, you'll be opposed by the various alien spawns around the map which launch waves at your base when it grows (there is a pollution mechanic that controls this). On the other hand, going out with the weapons, armor, and vehicles you can research and build to clear out these nests of aliens yields a resource used in high-end gear. There are also various levels of turrets you can use to ward off the waves and walls can be built as well. Yes, even your defenses can be automated.
You "win" the main game by creating and launching a rocket to space, a task that requires an enormous amount of materials and components, but at that point it's mostly an excuse to build more things than the end of the game. There are additional ways to play the game as well, including multiplayer, or changing the amount of resources, alien spawns, and types of terrain when generating a new map. Mods are supported and the developers have done a lot to assist modders over time. The graphics are in 2D but are actually rendered from 3D models and fairly decent for such a small studio. The developers have also come out with a steady stream of free updates since releasing the game and clearly care about it and their community.
Overall, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you have some free time and enjoy base building games or supply chain management puzzles then you will definitely enjoy this game. There are a number of games that know how to make it fun to destroy things but very few that also know how to make it fun to create things. Factorio is one of my favorite games of all time because it does both well. If you're not balling on a budget then pony up and support these devs, they've definitely earned it.

When you inevitably lose, that just brings me back to my first point: losing to progress is bad design.

When I first discovered this gem of a game, I immediately fell in love with the sweet art style and the Minim characters. But boy, was I in for a treat: the story is just as sweet and wonderful as the art. The story is, in essence, about the pilgrimage of Mii, a minim, to find his partner Mo who has gone missing. The puzzles are just right - not too hard - but keep in mind that I HATE puzzles - so I was really happy with the tips system. If you want hard puzzles, this might not be the game for you. The developers did a great job in keeping the tediousness down with one exception: at one point you need to keep a hamster fed in order to go up and down a mountain. Having to constantly go through three steps when the milk ran out was annoying.

I'm posting this review for a friend who has already played the game through a review copy for Just Adventure provided by the publisher. From what I've read and played so far, I'm interested in playing more.
The word minim derives from the Latin word minimus, meaning "least" or "smallest."
Meet some Minims: cute little creatures who resemble a kind of gourd stood on-end with two eyes at the top. The Minims is also the name of a new adventure game for Windows and Mac (previously released on iOS) by indie developer beyondthosehills.
Story

The game's story is imaginative, well-written and touching, with some humor thrown in for good measure. There are three Minims in The Minims: Mii, his wife Mo and, briefly, Mii's Elder Minim.
One day, Mii discovers Mo has gone missing and sets out on a journey to find her. This occupies the balance of the game (which is relatively short; I knocked it off in a single afternoon).
Mii discovers that he not only needs to find Mo; he is told by his Elder Minim that he must make a choice: to follow his inner path -- which is located in his mind -- and be transformed forever, or choose to return to his old life as if nothing had happened.
Mii is also told that Mo has already made her choice. How could he choose anything but to go on? (I didn't have the heart to choose "go back," so I don't know what happens in that case). He is then teleported into his own mind, which turns out to be quite an interesting place.
During his mind-journey, Mii visits curious, unusual locations inhabited by some rather odd characters. Each one aids Mii's progress in some way; however, this being an adventure game, he's also obliged to do things for them.
Puzzles

During his travels, Mii must solve a variety of inventory-based puzzles. Most aren't particularly difficult, although one refused to budge for me no matter what I tried. Even the game's generous help system was of no use, and I ended up solving it by accident. I found this a tad frustrating, but it's the only trouble I had.
Navigation and Mechanics

The developer has given point-and-click navigation an interesting twist. The game also offers 360-degree panning, and you can look up and down as well.
Even though the game is played in 3rd-person, Mii doesn't always move when you do. There are times he'll wait for you to check out an area of interest and return to him afterwards. In these cases, you're often able to shift your view around and see him standing in the distance.
The camera will also pan on its own to show you various things. I particularly enjoyed the camerawork used as Mii traverses a very long, very high bridge. It's quite cinematic.
The Minims can be played either windowed or in full-screen.
The game offers no user-initiated saves. It does let you return to the beginning of each chapter once you've played it. If you need to leave mid-chapter, you're taken back to the point at which you left the game. If you start a new game, the slate is wiped clean.
Graphics and Sound

The Minims' quasi-cartoon visual style is colorful and quirky. I think it's quite appealing.
There is no spoken dialog in the game; instead, bubbles filled with text appear over characters' heads, which suits the game nicely. The music is very well-done, as are the ambient sounds.
Conclusion

The Minims is generally quite pleasant and relaxing to play. It has an imaginative story with characters and locations that are fanciful and charming.
If you're looking for a point-and-click adventure that's practically stress-free (albeit somewhat short), The Minims is for you. Kudos to beyondthosehills for making such a sweet, enjoyable game.
Grade: A-
+ Great story
+ Pleasant and relaxing
+ Appealing, quasi-cartoon visual style
+ Music and ambient sounds are very well-done
- Somewhat short
- No user-initiated saves

Diluvion is a 3D deep sea exploration game which lets you control your own submarine. Does it explodes to success or sinks to the absolute bottom, let’s find out:
Diluvion is set a post-apocalyptic world where the world has sunk into oceans after a great flood and humans are forced to live deep down in the depth of the seas in their submarines. You are given the job of captaining your own submarine and recruiting and upgrading your crew and ship. There are whole cities buried deep beneath the seas and you have to explore them and fend off enemies using your submarine’s guns and torpedoes.
You explore the depth of these dangerous waters in a 3D perspective of your submarine while you switch to a FTL like 2D perspective when you’re interacting with your crews. This crew is one of the most important parts of your submarine and the management of this crew at important stations is crucial to the battles in Diluvion. For example, employing two members at your gun station will help you reload faster and so on. This crew also needs ample amount of oxygen to survive which makes sense considering the backdrop of the game. The game can also be dauntingly difficult at times if you run out of resources at an important time and the game makes sure that you pay for your mistake with its infuriating checkpoint system.
You can save your game when you find some green fish which are most prominent in major settlements while the game also saves when you recruit a new crew member or discover an important location. But this system can easily make you lose hours of your progress just because you couldn’t find the damned fish. The UI of the game is also all over the place and kills the overall visual elegance of the game single-handedly. The AI of the game can also tend to be sometimes silly and hand themselves over to you without putting up an actual fight.
The story of Diluvion is interesting and the lore present here is really fun to explore. The crew tell interesting stories of their own and you will often come up to strange places which are just awe inspiring. You can also buy your own home base later on in the game and then upgrade it in RPG style which helps in your future endeavours. You can also upgrade various parts of your submarine to increase its hull and armour which increases attacks, defence and the ability to venture farther below in the depth of these waters. You also have the choice to choose from the few submarines you are given at the start.
While Diluvion is pretty much a linear game with quite a bit of handholding, it gives room for some really interesting exploration. But all of this is let down by a really bad UI and control system which holds Diluvion from truly achieving what it aspires to be.
The best part of Diluvion is its amazing visuals. It nails the isolated environments of the depth of seas and the steampunk design of its ships and cities. More often than not you will come across some real marvellous looking ships and cities which have been consumed by the waters and they look haunting.
The hand drawn 2D perspective when you switch to talk to your crew members also lends itself to the visuals and is done neatly. Most of the exploration in Diluvion is also made interesting due to these visuals which shows an unique world and tells a story of its own. Effects like explosion and other things are also done well and they are distinguished well from their surroundings.
While the main soundtrack itself is average, what propels Diluvion to another level is the use of sound effects. These sound effects make the whole exploration prospect much more isolating and daunting. Overall, Diluvion has an amazing sound design which lends perfectly to its visuals.
Diluvion is a game that presents a unique world and provides interesting lore to go along with it. But is hugely let down by its UI design and the frustrating checkpoint system it has. It is in dire need of some polish and the price might be a little steep for some people but if you can look past the problems, you will find a gorgeous world that begs for exploration.

Flinthook has amazing game feel. Grappling around and shootin’ dudes feels awesome! It feel great to find loot and relics. The soundtrack is catchy, the sound effects click, the graphics are stylish, the animations are crisp and it all fits together into a retro-platformer aesthetic that is to die for.
I’m happy to see that the core gameplay is as solid as it looked during its earlier days or development :)
However, despite adoring the above, the way Flinthook handles runs and a rouge-like system is where to brakes come on.
Runs can take up to 30 minutes [for the first areas] and death means you lose everything except levels that net you some less-than-helpful useless slot-based powerups and an obscure alternate currency. This currency is the only way to add permanent upgrades.
I’m on level 3, but have to grind level 2 over and over to get a shot at getting ~14 tokens to use on one small upgrade. I had the same experience with level 1, trying to get to level 2.
It felt tough to hit a wall that early, especially with all sorts of fantasies about I’d miss out on if I put it down.
Things also ramp up in difficulty pretty fast. Occasionally I walk into insane platforming rooms and just think to myself, “Well, there goes 1/3 of my HP”.
Bosses also take progressively more time to just get to. It starts with beating 3 levels in a row and then a boss and moves to [where I’m at] 5 much tougher levels and then a boss.
Patrice Bourgeault also did a stellar job with the soundtrack, but a bit more variety for level music may have been nice. Although, this is likely just a symptom exaggerated by the boredom of grinding.
If Flinthook moved at a faster pace, had more item/blaster/upgrade variety and was more forgiving with deaths it could’ve easily been a smash hit, at least in my books.
Still, I’d recommend it. Flinthook is charming and smooth as butter and I do have some doubts that the reason for my concerns about advancement may be due to just a lack of patience. The game feels high quality enough to make some of its downsides sting more but I would love to see that game supported and its developers take on new challenges in the future =]

I've completed all the problems from the main/original campaign. The only other Zachtronics game that I have played is TIS-100 and that will be my benchmark in this review (since Zachtronics games are quite different from other types of games).
~ Gameplay ~
By far the most intimidating thing about Shenzhen I/O is the 40+-paged manual. However it was a pleasant surprise to discover that most of the pages are just "filler." The only pages that we need to read to begin playing are those in the Language Reference and Parts Datasheets sections.
Compared to TIS-100, Shenzhen I/O is actually enjoyable! The problems that we solve serve a clear purpose, and sometimes we can even see our programs in action! For example, when we are asked to create a program for a gardening robot, we can actually SEE our program in action as the robot executes our code.
In the early game, most of my gameplay involved tinkering with the components and code, trying to understand the nuances of the game. Towards the end, I found myself spending most of my time away from the code and thinking about the problems instead.
~ Story ~
We play the role of a young enginner in the near future (around 2024) who is forced to move to China to find work. Despite the initial culture shock of a dystopian society, we quickly find ourselves surrounded by a dynamic cast of coworkers, including other expats facing the same circumstances.
Over the course of the campaign, we discover the nuances of their characters, including their hidden insecurities and grandest ambitions.
In my opinion, cast of Shenzhen I/O feel just as alive, if not more so, than even some characters from story-based games!
~ Visuals/Music/Ambiance ~
The interface is mind-blowingly good, especially for a puzzle game (or perhaps I've simply been traumatized by TIS-100). Everything feels smooth and satisfying.
~ Last Thoughts ~
I think that this is a great game for everyone. Try a few levels and see if it awakens the engineer within!

Shenzhen I/O is a puzzle game that requires programming (a mock version of assembly language) to solve each level, with a level mechanic near identical to game developer Zachtronics's previous game, TIS-100. Shenzhen however is a more shiney, soulful version of its predecessor, which was based on a computer you discovered from the 1980s of which you unravell the previous (now mysteriously dead) owner's story. This game's situation is quite different in that your tasks are simply just your job. Shenzhen places you as a tech engineer who has moved to China, for some reason, working for a company called Shenzhen, where you log into a mock operating system with an e-mail inbox, with levels presented in the form of e-mail chains containing specifications to build circuits for. Amongst these e-mail chains are colleague banter which I can't say is particularly interesting or entertaining and would rather it was just 1 e-mail to get to the point, or better yet, no e-mails at all and just a task listing instead. The feel of an office environment for a puzzle game actually makes the goal of each task motivation seem as simply 'the company wants to make it' not 'you're solving a problem/puzzle'. The products you're building circuit boards for can be completely uninteresting, such as a sandwich maker and a fake haunted doll audio mechanism. These levels can take many hours, sometimes days to solve, and with the more dreary products at the end of it, it can be hard to press on.
That being said, the puzzle solving itself is challenging, though requires a lot of patience. There's no hand-holding here, you're pretty much on your own. I find myself pacing around the room thinking of ways to approach things and some levels can go on for several days in my case. I can't say I have this amount of patience for any other game. It feels very rewarding when you complete a level successfully, that is until you are presented with an online score comparison at the end of each level. I hated this in TIS-100. To spend so long cracking a puzzle and to be shown that you've made a comparably inefficient product compared to the rest of the world can be annoyingly anti-climatic. How many of these players simply Googled the best method anyway? We'll never know but the score board doesn't care and there are the numbers right in your face every time. If you're a competitive person however, then you should be alright with this.
Like TIS-100, there is a PDF manual to lay out all the syntax and special in-game devices that you need to know about. The syntax itself is very similar to TIS-100, however a couple of handy commands were removed, such as SWP, though a couple of new ones have been introduced. That being said the very basic language syntax made sense in TIS-100, which was based in the 80s, feels remarkably out of date for a game meant for the present day. You cannot enstate everyday programming features such as variables, methods, functions, proper looping techniques and arrays. The code often becomes spaghetti code with 'GOTO' style (JMP) commands that no programmer would even dream of using today, and 'IF' (TEQ etc.) style conditions that intertwine with each other due to a simple proceeding + or - that could actually be triggered by more than 1 conditional line. Things are quite limited, too, such as just 1 or 2 integer storage module per circuit to work with, limited lines of code available, limited room for circuits and wires on the panel, can all cause frustration and reduce creativity. In fairness however the developers can be appreciated that some limitations are necessary, or the puzzles would be too easy, but I feel that relying on language oddities to make the coding run more efficiently is all slightly unnerving.
All in all the game is worth it if you're up for a challenge. This is not a fast-paced game and you have only your own brain to rely on. Much of your hair will be pulled, but can all be very rewarding once you crack a level. The player situation of a person simply doing their job is rather unappealing but can be overlooked to access a great experience. I'm 40 hours in and suspect I have at least 40 hours more until I reach (if ever) the end! This is definitely worth a go.

Well, I guess it's time for me to finally give my opinion on this title.
Please note that this review was written at the time of version 0.15.34, so the future product will look drastically different compared to what I talk about in this review.
This will not involve the dev team's right-wing political views (Outside this sentence or two). While I don't mind that they're right-wing (Heck, I'm happy for them in this day and age of TRIGGEREDS), that doesn't matter for the sake of this review; what matters is this game.
Factorio is a top-down sandbox game where you build an automated factory from scratch and don't let it (Or yourself) get destroyed in the process by angry bugs. That's the basics, but the game is far more complicated than that.
Gameplay:
Factorio can best be equated with a Firaxis RTS: Easy to learn, but difficult to master. Unlike Minecraft (At least in earlier versions), the player can access a single player campaign which can be used to learn the ropes of the early-to-mid game. Enemies will generally remain near their nests, only coming after you if your factory's pollution (Or yourself) gets near them. There's also nothing demanding you build in a certain manner. Want to spread your buildings out and wall them off like an industrial park? Make one huge fortress that constantly expands as you go? You can go either way and no one will call you out for it (I know I'm gonna be called out for this review's opening though... -_-).
The only main issue with Factorio's style of gameplay is it's rising complexity. Items like trains and robots require vasts amounts of resources and research. Regardless of your build style, you'll have to eventually create a Rube Goldberg-style assembly line just to make a single piece of THE SCIENCE! needed to advance. If you want to drive the pain train home even further though, you can enable a sort of 'hard mode' that makes things far more expensive to build.
On a positive note though, it's recommended that you don't hold back when you build. It's encouraged that you tear down or fill in what you need to in order to ensure your factory functions smoothly (AKA, have fun being an environmentalist's nightmare).
A freeplay mode also exists, allowing you to dabble with all the techs, practice building, design a dream factory, or even make your own little railroad without worrying about your resources. If these three modes aren't your cup of tea, there's also several puzzle modes, ranging from shuttling resources from chest to chest using conveyor belts to making a certain amount of items in a certain amount of time.
Graphics:
While I'm not usually one for dull muddled colors (Blame Fallout 3 and the 2000s in general for that), I enjoy this game's dieselpunk/sci-fi aesthetics very much. Machinery is animated, from the flailing bits and pieces of steam engines and assemblers to the opening and closing of the doors on railroad cars at a station. Just about everything has numerous frames of animation that help make the game feel a little more alive.
Up close however is where the game begins to show its early release colors. EVERYTHING is sprite-based, and as a consequence, if you zoom in you WILL see the pixels on everything around you. Trust me, it's not pleasant. On top of this, once you play enough times you will probably start to get tired of seeing the same grasslands and deserts over and over again.
Performance:
The game generates a world millions of tiles wide, meaning you have a lot of ground to cover if you want to run the place dry of resources. However thanks to the game's sprite-based design (Much like Sonic Mania) the game is capable of running at a steady 24/7 60FPS. The only time the game will stutter is during an autosave, of which three are kept by default at all times.
Final Thoughts:
Overall, I say that Factorio is still a great game for those with a knack for base building and strategy. The game has limitless hours of action, strategy and puzzle-solving, and because it's still in development, there's more to come in the future. If you want something lower-end and cheaper than Minecraft, then Factorio might just work for you.
Then again, I'm just another average gamer. Take this all with a grain of salt.

Not having played many Match-3 games before I had this lying in my collection for many months before just recently dusting it off and trying it out. And WOW! Great fun! A nice mixture of Rogue-alike systems, Match-3 and turn-based combat.
The story is simple: in a steampunk setting France is invading the British mainland - and it is you job to stop them. You do that by controlling a steampunk mech (an 'ironcast') through ten missions before finally confronting the main boss. Until then you level up (gaining HP and special abilities), improve your ironcast using salvaged equipment and try to gather as many resources as possible for the big end fight. In the end you want as much manpower (reduces the final boss' HP) and scrap (=money to upgrade your ironcast) as you can get.
The missions range from simple battles against one or more enemies (one after another), salvage missions (bringing down enemies without damaging specific parts like for example the shields or weapons), collection missions (collecting crates while fighting) and survival (survive for a given number of rounds). Sometimes these missions are pepped up with having your cooling system damaged or requiring you not to stop, or having to fix your jammed weapons before being able to engage the enemy. There's also trade missions (non-combat) where you exchange one resource (scrap vs manpower) by negociating with potential allies.
You have to power your systems with the elements you match in a match-3 style. Per combat turn you can perform three matches and as many other actions as your resources (ammunition, power, coolant, repair tokens and abilities) allow. You can match as many neighbouring elements of the same color as you like (not just rows or columns) as long as your line doesn't intersect itself. Using special tokens you can chain different colors, and there's power ups, scrap (i.e. money to upgfrade your ironcast) and - for some missions - special crates you have to collect.
Using your resources you power your shields (damage reduction), weapons or drivers (evasion), and you need coolant tokens as you activate these systems. Shields and movement can be activated up to three levels (for increased protection) and then loose one level each turn. So you have to constantly refresh them to keep them up. You can target specific systems (weapons, drive or shields) on the the enemy units, of which there are basically two types: tanks and ironcasts. They differ in that tanks have armour (damage reduction by %) and ironcasts have shields (absolute damage reduction per hit - rendering some weaker but multishot weapons useless against more powerful shields).
Once you die the game is over and you next game starts, the missions and level-up bonuses are choosen randomly (you have a choice, but the selection you're offered is mainly random). Also: no saves or anything. So it's a rogue-like of a sort. But after each game your XP get added to your global score and you can unlock new commanders and ironcasts models (each with specific abilities), bonuses or additional abilities. So even if you don't beat the boss (or even reach it) you still get a feeling of continuing progress which is good to overcome the initial frustration (especially if you're not too good at games like this).
All in all it's a great game, with a charming story and art style, solid gameplay and well worth a few rounds. I only wish it would be available for Android, as it's definitely the kind of game I'd love to play on my tablet, too.

Ironcast strikes the perfect balance between story and excitement that I feel all modern puzzlers should strive for. Ironcast is played out in a Steampunk Victorian England where players duke it out in huge mechs. Players link together nodes of specific types in order to do things such as power up their weapons, repair their mechs, and boost up shields as well as other tasks. For what seems like a basic ‘Match 3’ puzzler, there is an incredible amount of depth here. Each pilot and mech has unique stats and can further be customized through purchasing equipment and using augmentations. This game is addictive, punishing, and something totally fresh. Each battle is a total blast to play and delivers the same action and intensity as a tournament fighter or shooter while also giving you the depth and strategy of an RPG or TGC.
Fantastic game.

There's potential for a good game here, but it's marred by poor design decisions and overreliance on the RNG. It wouldn't be so bad if you had more than one life (no-one thought to equip the ironcasts with ejector seats?), but as it is if the board doesn't generate the right colours then you're forced to start the whole game over no matter what tactics you use. The game likes generating missions it's objectively impossible for your vehicle to complete - such as not damaging a particular enemy subsystem despite the fact that the ironcasts only come with weapons that damage all systems. The missions where you're asked to negiotiate with someone for resources are also frustrating since the only way to 'win' them is to find out the correct answers by trial and error.
Avoid.

Service to the Queen in steam-punk Victorian England is, much like in our own alternate world, cruel, bitterly unfair and ultimately unrewarding. And yet, it is so very satisfying to combat insurmountable odds and emerge victorious, no matter how small that victory is. Ironcast manages to create a very deep risk/reward system out of a "match three" game, as well as an original setting reminding fondly of Douglas Adams' humourous melancholy in Dr. Who, and Alan Moore's Victorian England in the League of Extraordinary Gentlemen. The only thing missing is more single-player campaign content, and possibly a board-game with cardboard cutouts for the marching Ironcast and all their upgrades.

This is the last great battlefield. It has tight gameplay, well balanced classes, fantastic map design, and multiplayer that necessitates teamwork. It even has a pretty decent (but spectacular) single player campaign, which has a pretty generic and bland story, but hilarious characters. But the multiplayer is where this one shines. Although there can only be a max of 32 players per match, the map design and squad system mean that battles still feel "big" like they were in Battlefield 2. The ability to respawn on a squad member keeps you in the action, and keeps the battles very fast paced. (Note squads groups of up to 4 players, and with proper teamwork and communication squads working together can be very effective.) The vehicles in Bad Company 2 are not as prominent as they are in the "main" battlefield series, but they do exist and are quite useful. No jets, however.
The most important thing in this game is how nearly every building, wall, and peice of cover is destructible. It means that no battle in a map is evert going to be quite the same, and you can destroy terrain tactically. You can even level the forests to make sure that the enemy attacks have no cover. Due to ability to wreck nearly everything on the map, Bad Company 2 stands out from nearly ever other multiplayer first person shooter due to this. Also, there is a large and active multiplayer community to this day, which stands as a testament to the game's lasting appeal.
To summarize, this is the pinnacle of the battlefield series, before EA started crapping out generic re-hashing of the battlefield series ever 1-2 years. It is worth buying at any price (though I am a little annoyed that I bought it at half off, only for it to go to 75% off the next day). The best part, this version doesn't require Origin. So, take a leap of faith and but this one, you won't regret it.

This game has enormous potential.  It's incredibly fun to play (at first) as the movement/platforming is extremely smooth.  There's lots of satisfying pep & pizazz when getting hit, killing enemies, opening chests, etc.  Just in general the game feels really good and the roguelike systems are all excellent.
That said, it only hurts even more when upon playing for a bit longer one realizes that this potential has been squandered due to massive oversights by whoever was in charge of seeing the project come together as a whole.
Graphically, the game is gorgeous pixel art.  It is also designed in such a way that it is almost always difficult to parse traps & other things from just scenery.  Overall the contrast between entities is far too low and at some point it all sort of just blends together into a yellowish-brown blur.
More bothersome than the graphical choices is the fact that the game's control scheme is flatout unacceptable.  By the time you beat the first bounty, you'll probably have a nagging feeling like perhaps the default control scheme somewhat flawed.  Ok, no problem.  It looks like the devs have acknowledged this problem & introduced a second control scheme choice post-launch.  The alternative "Pro" controls are a little better, but not good enough.  By not learning from their first mistake and failing to realize they were not any good at knowing how their own game should control, they missed a perfect opportunity to implement fully rebindable keys.
I have many other issues with this game which have continued to build up as I put more hours into it.  That said, were the major issues stated above resolved, most of the other problems I have with this title could be considered not to be a big deal as they wouldn't destroy my recommendation.  Until that time, I cannot in good faith recommend this product.

Overall, this game is fantastic. And highly recommended.
There are some cons, but the pros far outweight them. This is one of the best feeling platformers out there. I will mention all of the cons and some of pros. That's a good problem as the list of cons is small enough to say them all, but for a list of pros, I would miss some.
- MUSIC. It's honestly great, but feels repeditive fast with very little variety.
- PHYSICS. The game feels awesome with mouse or gamepad. Tuned to just feel buttery smooth and right. Grapple hook looked alkward to me in videos, but feels surprisingly smooth. Makes you want to swing around all over the place if you have to or not with just the right amount of lock (a small amount).
- CONTROLS. Custom controls shoudl be standard with all games. There are two controler schemes, with no other customization. One puts aim + move on the same stick and uses classic platforming controls for jumping. The other lets you aim and move independently with twin stick. There is no further customization. I'd really like to mix and match a lot. Another huge annoyance to me personally is being forced to used analogue over d-pad. I like d-pad so much more. But movement (maybe not aiming) is absolutely something that should facilitate users preference. Unless d-pad was used for other functions, which it does not seem to be. In summary, needs custom controls and d-pad enabeled.
- ENDLESS: Hits your max health every level. I understand ramping up the difficulty, but this way of doing it feels cheap and subject to random finds. Maybe there's a minimum it reduces it too, but I still don't feel that's right. I know it will reduce it below 100. I'm glad endless exists, but feels cheap enough that I'm not interested in this part.
- BOSS GAUNTLET: You must beat 3 levels before the first boss fight. The next 2 bosses increase this count by 1. At 3, it feels right. But once it gets beyond that, it feels like a somewhat artificial way to increase the life of the game. The levels are short. So I like some of this, but think it becomes too much about half way through. I'm finding myself less encouraged to keep playing, but if I never play again, the game was still more than worth it.
- BOSSES: 4. I've beaten half. Would prefer not increasing level count and adding another 2 boss battles. I have only seen half the bosses, but that's only because of the "Boss Gauntlet".
- DIFFICULTY: Just right. And with a minor persistant progression, it make it more accessable for those struggling when you trade skilled play for grind. Best of both worlds.
- DAILY / WEEKLY CHALLENGES: Should have a countdown timer indicating when the next restart is. Very small deal, but would be nice. It is nice that these challenges exist. These are 3 levels, therefor backing up my "Boss Gauntlet" claim above that 3 feels just right.
- STORY: Amazingly good by keeping it simply to inject imagination into the gameplay, but still let the gameplay be the game over the story. Absolutely refreshing by todays over bloat standards.
- CUTSCENES: Get the same one after each level. It's nice. It's short (5-10 seconds I'm guessing), but I'd still prefer be able to press a button to skip after seeing it well over 100 times.
- ART: Top tier.
I'd recommend Rogue Legacy over this. But if you liked that, then I'd highly recommend this. Unless you just want to grapple, then get this first. Simply put The Minims is a very solid point and click adventure game. It isn't the best point and click game but I have played considerably worse point and click games. The story is pretty good, the controls work well, and the graphics are nice. If you like points and click games you should like the game.
The two biggest problems with the game are the length and the difficulty. The Minims is too easy in my opinion which leads to the game being pretty short. A lot of the puzzles are pretty straight forward and thus aren't that hard to figure out. If you ever get stuck you can always use the hint system which should make it impossible to get stuck in the game. The easy difficulty is not necessarily a bad thing but if you are looking for a challenge I don't think you will be challenged by The Minims. The easy difficulty makes the game only three to four hours long so you aren't going to get a lot of time out of the game.
If you don't care for point and click adventure games, The Minims isn't going to be for you. If you like point and click games though and the premise interests you I think you will enjoy The Minims.

beyondthosehills
is a point-and-click adventure game developed and published by beyondthosehills.
You play as Mii, a Minim (yellow limb-less creatures), who goes on a quest to find his wife Mo. He will meet a cast of colorful characters and he will go to varied and weird locales.
As far as adventure games go, this one has a very simple, yet fun and interesting story that will keep you engaged for three hours. It's well written and it manages to keep your attention also thanks to its pacing.
Made with the Unity engine, it is very polished, with detailed backgrounds, good models, decent animations and gorgeous colors. Its vibrant look makes it stand out from other more depressing indie games.
Your standard point-and-click game: pick up items, use them to solve puzzles, talk to characters. The only thing that makes it different is the possibility to rotate the camera in 360°: it's not really a gimmick or a mechanic, just a small feature that feels like a breath of fresh air in an otherwise stale genre.
The game offers a decent challenge while never being frustrating or hard. Plus there is an hint system that can be used twice before waiting two minutes for it to recharge that basically spills out the solution to each puzzle, so you won't be stuck. Ever.
The game feels really empty: the soundtrack is too calm and relaxing for its own good, the sound effects are few and far between, and there is no voice acting.
Overall, this is a surprisingly well done adventure game: even though it's short, the funny story and nice graphics are worth the price alone. Recommended to all point-and-click fans.

First, I will admit I got this game on its free weekend, and I have only done one pass through the game, completing it literally minutes before this review.
That being said... I don't see a reason for another.
While the story of a female viking struggling for acceptance is an interesting one, and certainly the language voiceovers are a lovely touch, the bosses and hazards mostly thematically interesting, the areas very unique in each other... then we get into the gameplay.
The main character seems unable to manage anything above a leisurely lope, and I found myself wondering if I should go the Ocarina of Time path and hurl myself head over heels repeatedly in the direction I wanted to go, stuttery and stupid as it was, which makes for a pretty poor experience through the stages, since there is a LOT of ground to cover, and a lot of it doesn't even feature voiceover or hazards to keep you interested. Just... 'trudge across this bridge, and keep on going, something interesting will happen soon.' The map provided for the pause menu is absolutely no help in this regard, as SOME areas show points of interest, and some do not. On some maps, the apple that extends your HP is marked with a spiral, on some those are just voiceover spots. On some maps they show trees you can slice to make a bridge, on some they don't. And nowhere on the map does it bother to provide you with a marker showing your position, nor enough detail to really determine where you are.
And then we have the... "combat". I'm going to start by bringing up the fact that there are only two real non-boss combat sequences, and both of them are 'swing once, everything in reach of your axe dies'. Which I suppose would be a point in how strong the main heroine is, if she didn't swing that axe so lethargically I wonder if her arms had fallen asleep. Add to this the piddling amount of damage your swings do to bosses, and the basic attack is basically worthless for anything besides dinging terrain. I suppose it is a good thing you have a heavy attack to deal real damage. You'll just need to check in with the boss's secretary, of course, to ensure they don't have anything scheduled in the next week... which should be about the time your attack will finally land. Odin was one of the most devastating bosses to deal with in this game because he very often got bored of waiting for the power attacks to land and would lazily drift away out of your reach to go check his divine facebook while he waited for you to remember that you were fighting and drop your axe downwards. In addition, the total lack of reach on ANY of your attacks, in addition to the large bosses who can obscure a large portion of your screen often turns into situations where your swings overlap the boss's model, but he isn't hittable at that particular part of his anatomy at that moment.
So... in summary. Slow movement, slow swings that you cannot move during, slower still power attack which is your only way to deal noticable damage to bosses, a slow dodge that barely moves you and slow walks to the bosses' arenas. I might be spoiled, because most of the other 'boss rush' games I've played in the past have involved... well... rushing? But the slow pace of Jotun lead me to want to 'get it over with', and I closed the game and clicked 'uninstall' without hesitation.
It's a pretty package, but opening it was a chore, and the contents didn't hold me at all.

Jotun is one of these games where it's almost painful to give it a bad review: The game is positively beautiful to look at, has a more than decent soundtrack, and the Icelandic voiceovers really give it that special type of charm. The boss fights invarably are spectacular as you battle monsters several times your own size, and you'll spend a good part of your time searching for upgrades and scenic viewpoints.
But alas, the gameplay.
Jotun essentially puts you in several distinct overworlds, each (safe for one) has two levels and one boss level attached to it. Each of these levels has one or two mechanics to call its own - in one, you may be making your way up a tree while avoiding attacks by a giant eagle; while in another, you are repeatedly ambushed by large hordes of dwarves. The problem being that you spend each level only interacting with these one or two specific mechanics. Though the levels themselves are comparatively short, variety is something you will direly miss in them.
Outside of bossfights, combat in Jotun is extremely rare - as a matter of fact, I'm fairly certain that only three levels in the game have enemies against which you can physically defend yourself, whereas you otherwise can dodge enemy attacks at best. This perhaps would be forgivable if the highly touted exploration aspect of the game would be more rewarding - you will occasionaly run into monuments or other sights that trigger an audio quote from the heroine, but while these are meant to give some insight into Norse mythology, they more than often leave more questions than they answer (for instance: What kind of messages is Rattatoskr carrying up and down the world tree?). The comparatively slow movement speed of Thora does not help to elate the spirits when you have to jog from one end of the map to the other.
As for the bossfights themselves: They're all over the place. From my personal impression, some of them are almost laughably easy, while others are almost guaranteed to take you several attempts, not to the least because of violently unpredictable RNG elements - meaning that one boss you want to hit constantly teleports to the other side of the arena, while another may make it night-impossible to dodge electric discharges on the ground while at the same time trying to avoid being hit by lightning. Despite of this, most bossfights are good fun, and they definitely are the hightlight of Jotun.
As last word on the game's length: Even if you go out of your way to collect all god-powers, upgrades, and lore tidbits, you'll be through with Jotun in 6-7 hours. If you did not like the game, you'll probably be happy to be done with it. If you, on the other hand, did like the game, you'll only end up craving for more. It's a rather unsatisfying feeling at any rate.

Alright, before I begin, I would like to say that I have been playing the Armed With Wings franchise for years now. It is a personal favorite of mine, flashgames wise. So, when I saw this on Steam, I was beyond excited. Finally, a paid for Armed With Wings, which could only mean that the game will be fantastic. I have always said to myself that if I ever had the money, I would try and donate to the person who created this game series. And now I can support him. So if I seem a bit biased in this review, then I do apologise. Now let us begin the review.
Okay, first things first, the art style. The art style is minimalistic, only being black, white and various shades of grey. This has been the art style of the game series since the first one, and it has always been amazing.
Secondly, gameplay. Very fluid movements, very nicely animated, and overall, very satisfying to control. There is a light, speedy attack and a single hit heavy dashing attack. You can change the direction you attack by holding up or down, which is very useful for pulling off combos. Now, levels are different than the previous games, and this can be a good or bad thing. Whenever you start the game and play, you have to play through all the way until you either die, or beat the last level. As of writing this review all the levels are not available, but what levels there are are varied, and themed differently. It has a sort of platforming style of gameplay, but the platforming is relatively limited and there really is no jump button. You tend to solve puzzles in the level with your eagle, because you're "armed with wings." The eagle cannot attack, but it can pick up things to help you progress. Overall, I'd give the gameplay itself a 8/10, if only because I know not everyone likes the kind of game it is.
Next, is story. Actually, I'm not going to give story spoilers, because you can get most of the story from the first Armed with Wings game which is relatively cheap. It tends to go for the low, low price of free, and can be found on Newgrounds. Basically, play the other games first, they're amazing.
Soundtrack. Love me a good soundtrack. And you know what this game has? A really good soundtrack. Most of the music fits all of the areas really well, and is wonderfully composed. That is pretty much all I got for music. It's really good.
Finally, glitches. There really aren't a whole lot of bugs and glitches(from what I've seen). The only real issue I've found is if you go high enough over an area, you can skip certain events. Those are pretty much all the bugs I found, and it will probably be fixed in the near future.
Overall, I'd say this is a wonderful game, and played my nostalgia like a fiddle. Of course, I did try and be really critical about this game, but Sun-Studios did too good a job when creating it that I essentially had to nitpick to find stuff wrong with it.
TL;DR: It's a fantastic game, and you should at least try out the original flash games.

Not much more than a time-waster, but you get what you pay for. And for $3, it's a pretty decent value.
Mechanically, it's a decent top-down shooter. Not the best that I've played, but I've certainly played worse. There's a rather healthy variety of weapons and items to make use of, all of which feel unique and have their own specific uses. I wish I could say the same for the enemy types, though.
The game pits you against the typical Halo ensemble; Grunts, Jackals, Elites, and some others mixed in for good measure, including some of the Promethean enemies from Halo 4 and onward. The problem is, though, all the enemies feel about the same, with the only major differences between enemy types being the number of hit-points they have. Sure, some opponents will try to change it up a bit by hurling all of their grenades at you, or by playing keep-away with ranged weapons, but not quite enough to keep things interesting. As a result, the game gets repetetive rather quickly.
But, I'd be lying if I said I wasn't enjoying a bit of dumb fun in the time that it took for the game to start feeling like a grind. The weapons are (for the most part) fun to use and it feels satisfying to lay waste to dozens of smaller enemies at once by spraying them with dual SMGs. There's a small array of vehicles and stationary guns to make use of as well, all of which pack a satisfying punch and deliver massive damage to even the larger enemies of the game.
All in all, a fair package for the price. Again, there's little more to it than just shooting aliens, and it starts to get repetitive rather quickly. But, as far as top-down shooters go, there are worse ones out there, and there are certainly worse things to drop $3 on.
If you like Halo, you'll probably get a kick out of this game, and giving it a go won't kill your wallet.

Battlefield: Bad Company 2 holds a special place in my heart. I love Vietnam War movies, games and music and this game just happens to have a Vietnam War expansion pack. It really nails the expansion too. The weapons, the scenarios, maps, music, vehicles...it's all so very well done. The expansion pack is multiplayer only and it's epic!
campaign is pretty "CoD-like" linear most of the time.  There are some sandboxy areas but for the most of time it's your simple corridor shooter.
Make no mistake tho, the campaign is very enjoyable. It's not a serious shooter. It has a bunch of good humour in it, fantastic characters, pwetty graphiczzz and a vast variety of locations: deserts, snowy areas and jungles - I love me some jungles and xmas areas, man.
It's about 8 hours long. Nothing special...no replay value, really. But it is fun for what it is and i guess you could go and replay it just for the heck of it.
is why people play Battlefield. Battlefield used to be a multiplayer only game. The first time it had a singleplayer campaign was back in 2007 in Battlefield: Bad Company. That game is a console exclusive tho.

Multiplayer is just awesome. Everything can be destroyed. Now don't get me wrong, i do love me some BF3 and BF4. I don't hate on them like other "hardcore" Battlefield fans. The hate is childish and quite ignorant to be honest. Nothing wrong with Battlefield 4 (it had a bad launch but it's OK now) and Battlefield 3...nothing bad to say about that game...but back to the point: Bad Company 2 lets you blow up everything! Blow up trees, blow up houses, blow boats, blow up water...explosion! EXPLOSION!

Just like in singleplayer, there are quite a good variety of locations: jungles, forests, xmas, deserts, plain fields. + The Vietnam expansion which adds A LOT to the epicness. Feels like a totally new game.

Disappointment?
Hmm... I really like the visuals and the world in which the story is set. If played as a freeform exploration, it's a joy to play. The care and thought behind the world concept that has gone into the creation is obvious.
The gameplay with regard to the campaign however makes it frustratingly tiresome unfortunately.
If I had known in advance just how much this game is orientated towards undersea combat, I would probably not have bought it. While navigation control isn't hard to learn or manage, combat navigation and aiming is extremely clumsy.
I'm constantly bemused during combat by the physics. Every time I use it, there's a part of my mind wondering just how the flek does the flek maintain enough velocity over the firing range through seawater to be effective in causing any damage. And then there's the lasers. How are they possible? They should be diffracted so much by the seawater to be useless or boil the seawater long before they can reach their target.
It's almost as if all the care and attention to simulate the deep sea immersion has been thrown out the window just to enable physics defying combat options.
This contradiction between striving for immersion into submersible life (excuse the pun) and employing combat using contrived damage delivery methods is what disappoints me the most.
There is also the contradiction of the premise that humanity has been taught an extremely hard lesson about the dire consequences of aggression and yet rather than allow an option to strive for a pacifistic ideal for harmony, the player is forced to repeat the errors of aggression by the campaign combat requirements.
So, I wouldn't say I have been disappointed as such. I have enjoyed playing Diluvion.

One of the better Indie games I've had the pleasure of playing in recent memory. The game description says it all and, in my opinion, Diluvion delivers on all counts: "Diluvion is a 3D deep sea, Jules Verne inspired, exploration game with RPG elements and thrilling submarine combat."
The gameplay reminds me a lot of Rebel Galaxy and, as of this writing, the controls are intuitive using an Xbox One controller. There's a FOV slider that you'll want to make use of, especially if you're playing with a 21:9 monitor, the soundtrack and graphics are polished and well done, and the ~$20 pricetag makes it an absolute steal.

Diluvion is an enjoyable if somewhat shallow experience. The eviroments are really well done and fun to visit, there are only three zones but they all look and feel compleatly diffrent. The combat is solid, but becomes stale rather quickly outside of the three boss fights due to a lack of enemy variety. It claims its an rpg but there are no rpg elements to be found. The story is kind of sloppy and drops a lot of interesting side stories to focus on getting the player to the end of the game. There is claerly a decent amount of lore for the game but it is all in the captains journal, which seems to be backer exclusive. Too bad because the setting is really well crafted, I would have liked to see more. The devs were passionate about the project but it is feels like they had to cut corners and content. Even though I seem kinda down on the game, it is arock solid foundation to build on, hopefully the game sells enough so that we can see the full potnetial of the game realized latter down the line.

Man, I want to enjoy this game. Really, I could enjoy this game... IF...
If the controls were more intuitive. If you enjoy controls that take a long time to master simply for the goal of being non-standard, then it's fine. But I've often felt that controls should FAVOR the immersion. Help me into a story. Not be as realistically irritating as really doing the thing ought to be. It's like flavor text, in that it's striving for immersion, but where it lands is "difficult to feel comfortable with".
If the Combat system had a tutorial or a slower ramp up. While trying to master the controls, you're put into combat. No big deal, you've got guns, fire them. After finally realizing the slow shoot, miss, projectile based combat, I finally killed the first enemy. But I was nearly out of ammo by the time the second one found me. And at that point, my options are "skip the learning parts of the game" or "die". I'm not saying be easy, but maybe ramp up a little softer. Or make ammo refill with air tanks.
If the RPG elements were engaging. Most of the RPG elements amounted to 1) Dialogue trees which have one option and 2) that option is only "move the story forward". I wanted my choices to feel like I was playing a character, but instead it feels more like the "choices unlock goodies" style of RPG where all that can be gained is simply items. And that's kind of lame.
What it has is wonderful. It has the framework of a great game that I would play for years and think about when I wasn't playing. The crew management idea. Fantastic. The under sea exploration? Marvelous, I'm terrified of the deep. But the lack of a ramp up, the controls which keep you from getting immersed, and the bad RPG elements, just make this game kind of a mess. If this were an alpha, I'd give the notes to try making more standard and less creative controls. Streamline the combat so it feels cohesive and not just an irritating part. And finally make the RPG choices be story, not bonus hunting. As it is, this game is too expensive to be this difficult to enjoy.

I’ll start by saying I did end up requesting a refund for this game.  Now, that is not to say this is a bad game.  Overall, I enjoyed the game but there was something missing to make me want to devote the massive amount of time I can only imagine this game will take to complete.  Not saying that this game is Skyrim level depth, nowhere near but it lends itself to exploration and from what I’ve read there is a decent amount to explore.
Mechanically the game is decent, didn’t have the issues that a lot of gamers complain about when it comes to camera angels or mouse issues.  Overall the interface is basic but really leaves me needing more information.  I’d like to know the mechanics without scouring the forums, uses of items and such would be decent, not asking for every nuisance but at least a general break down. Unfortunately, in some ways the game feels a bit like a series of mini-games combined and that is one of the big factors for me getting a refund; potentially there is so much more.
Graphically the game is beautiful, well mostly.  The zones and environment are beautiful, the subs and capsules look amazing but the game starts to fall apart at what feel are unfinished character models and the inside locations.  The two frame animations and the ‘Sims’ like voices are interesting in concept but need a bit more fleshing out.
Story wise, I love the concept of this game, it is everything I want in a submarine meets rpg  / rogue game with the post-apocalyptic style but the issue is that I don’t know what is going on, why or even more about the world.  All the characters have one or two lines and don’t really go into the narrative and seem to just assume I know what is going on.  This is the single biggest reason I decided not to finish this game.
Ultimately, I think this a good game but in a world of good games I had to pass up for conservation of time.  If you have the extra time I urge you to give this a go as I don’t think you’d be overall disappointed.

Overall, this game is fantastic. And highly recommended.
There are some cons, but the pros far outweight them. This is one of the best feeling platformers out there. I will mention all of the cons and some of pros. That's a good problem as the list of cons is small enough to say them all, but for a list of pros, I would miss some.
- MUSIC. It's honestly great, but feels repeditive fast with very little variety.
- PHYSICS. The game feels awesome with mouse or gamepad. Tuned to just feel buttery smooth and right. Grapple hook looked alkward to me in videos, but feels surprisingly smooth. Makes you want to swing around all over the place if you have to or not with just the right amount of lock (a small amount).
- CONTROLS. Custom controls shoudl be standard with all games. There are two controler schemes, with no other customization. One puts aim + move on the same stick and uses classic platforming controls for jumping. The other lets you aim and move independently with twin stick. There is no further customization. I'd really like to mix and match a lot. Another huge annoyance to me personally is being forced to used analogue over d-pad. I like d-pad so much more. But movement (maybe not aiming) is absolutely something that should facilitate users preference. Unless d-pad was used for other functions, which it does not seem to be. In summary, needs custom controls and d-pad enabeled.
- ENDLESS: Hits your max health every level. I understand ramping up the difficulty, but this way of doing it feels cheap and subject to random finds. Maybe there's a minimum it reduces it too, but I still don't feel that's right. I know it will reduce it below 100. I'm glad endless exists, but feels cheap enough that I'm not interested in this part.
- BOSS GAUNTLET: You must beat 3 levels before the first boss fight. The next 2 bosses increase this count by 1. At 3, it feels right. But once it gets beyond that, it feels like a somewhat artificial way to increase the life of the game. The levels are short. So I like some of this, but think it becomes too much about half way through. I'm finding myself less encouraged to keep playing, but if I never play again, the game was still more than worth it.
- BOSSES: 4. I've beaten half. Would prefer not increasing level count and adding another 2 boss battles. I have only seen half the bosses, but that's only because of the "Boss Gauntlet".
- DIFFICULTY: Just right. And with a minor persistant progression, it make it more accessable for those struggling when you trade skilled play for grind. Best of both worlds.
- DAILY / WEEKLY CHALLENGES: Should have a countdown timer indicating when the next restart is. Very small deal, but would be nice. It is nice that these challenges exist. These are 3 levels, therefor backing up my "Boss Gauntlet" claim above that 3 feels just right.
- STORY: Amazingly good by keeping it simply to inject imagination into the gameplay, but still let the gameplay be the game over the story. Absolutely refreshing by todays over bloat standards.
- CUTSCENES: Get the same one after each level. It's nice. It's short (5-10 seconds I'm guessing), but I'd still prefer be able to press a button to skip after seeing it well over 100 times.
- ART: Top tier.

What does it take to make a game that is truly profitable these days? I know, I know... there are many, many good games on Steam and the Indie market is quite saturated. However, it saddens me to see this game with less than 500 user reviews. It deserves more attention, not a profound amount more, but definitely more.
So what is Ironcast? Well its a cool blend of match 3 (or more) gameplay mixed with turn based strategy gameplay. It has rogue-like elements with random system (loot) drops and random perk progression as well as an overall progression which slowly increases your stats for each proceeding play through. It has one hell of a cool aesthetic, which is victorian era Steampunk set in London. You're one of the last surviving Ironcast commanders for England as France has declared war on your nation, and it's your job to protect against the invaders. With multiple characters and Ironcasts to choose from, each playthrough can be rather unique. A playthrough could lead down a walking tank path, with your Ironcast having huge health and dolling out massive damage. Or it could be an evasive, speedy Ironcast that can pump out lots of rounds but is susceptible to direct hits. Each play through can be quite different with all the starting options and random nature of the beast.
The pros for this $15 game far outweigh the cons. The setting is awesome, especially if you like Steampunk, and the art style is superb, it fits the game and gameplay like a glove. Each play through has the potential to be entirely different and has fairly good variety in the missions. The game is absolutely challenging, but this is also somewhat of a negative that I will discuss more in the Cons. The progression system is solid and gives rewards consistently. The combat and puzzle elements are addicting and very, very fun. And lastly, the animation quality and visual effects are just a joy to watch. I'm sure i've missed some things, but those are the biggest pros.
- $15 Rogue-like with high replayability
- Excellent and authentic London Steampunk setting and aesthetic
- Solid progression system with good variety
- Really, really addictive and fun gameplay
- Easy to pick up but diffictult to master strategy systems
- Unflinchingly challenging
- Excellent sound effects and sound design
- Great animation quality and visual fidelity
- Solid customization system
Some of the cons are a bit nit picky, but there are definitely some things that need mentioning. The story is lackluster, but it really isn't what's going to keep you playing a game like this anyway. The mission variety is there, it has decent variety, but some of the mission types seem lopsided against you in a bad way. Also, some of the mission types I found myself ignoring every chance I had, other mission types I chose nearly every time. This could have been better. I would have liked to have had a larger roster of characters and Ironcasts, but this could just be because I absolutely love their designs and just want to see more. Finally, the games difficulty. The game can be downright brutal at times. Just when you feel you're putting together a good run, you could end up with a terrible roll of the dice and lose everything. A lot of the frustration can be chalked up to the random nature of rogue-likes, but it was a serious hurdle for me. Even on a normal difficulty mission I'd sometimes be just blindsided by a terrible turn of events and lose my Ironcast, and death is permanent.
At one point, I was ready to quit playing the game out of frustration. Though the very next game I beat Durant and made it all the way to the Interloper... so maybe I was just being a baby :) ... I died with the Interloper at only 1900 hp.... SO CLOSE! ... i'll get you next time, you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!
- Throw away story
- Mixed bag of mission variety
- Random nature rogue-like can cause frustration
- Difficulty had me boiling at one point
- Would have been nice to have more character and Ironcast variety
Overall, this game is absolutely worth $15. I got it on sale, and I kind of wish I didn't because I feel these developers deserve more support. I'm almost certainly going to pick up the DLC at some point soon because the game has its hooks in me. It has a few down sides and it can frustrating as all hell, but when this game shines, it shines like the sun. Rarely do you see the Steampunk aesthetic and it's always awesome when you do. This game has it in spades and does it flawlessly.
Ironcast is a really, really fun and addictive rogue-like turn-based strategy game that deserves more attention than it's gotten. It's a pretty damn unique mix of genres and is absolutely beautiful to look at and play. If that isn't enough for you to buy it, then pick it up during a good sale and just give it a chance. I truly believe most who play this game, even if you aren't interested in Steampunk, will enjoy what they get. And if you're a fan of tanks like I am, just imagine your own personal, walking, victorian era tank... it gets me giddy every time :)

tl;dr I had a lot of fun with this game, but it's hard to recommend. I don't regret buying it, but I think it's more interesting as a view into what a game COULD DO rather than a succesful execution of itself. The game is not recieving any updates or gameplay fixes. Check the DIscussions page for many repeated grievances with this game.
For a roguelite, there's veeery little mission, equipment, or player character variety. There are, broadly speaking, only 2 different enemy types (mechs and trains) not including 2 bosses, 4 ways weapons deal damage (single-shot, multi-shot, even spread, lopsided spread), and 2 'elements' of damage (projectile and energy). There are 4 pilots and 4 mechs to choose from, but of those, there's a strong player consensus that one of them is best. So yk. ~illusion of variety and customization, ho!~
The game also goes by veeery slowly. It feels like the battle system here might have been great for a long Puzzle Quest-style campaign but was stapled to a roguelite. There are few ways to turn the tide of battle with strategic skill or weapon use once you're behind, and few times to retool your build for specific fights (money is VERY tight), so the seemingly tactical computer RPG-like gameplay mostly keeps the pace (glacial) and leaves the tactics.
So, the novelty runs out very quickly. You will not get much out of this game compared to other, similar ones at the same $15 price tag. You'd probably get more from roguelites at $10 or $5.
Specifics: The Disney Tsumo-style puzzle grid actually gives you more agency over resource collection and board manipulation than you might think. However, there board is tiny (6x6) considering the amount of different colored peices there are (5, not including gimmick pieces) and very few abilities that manipulate the board. There are way more instances of you just not being able to find resources you need versus similar games (Puzzle Quest, specifically) because you only regularly use 3/5 of the resources, 1 of them being used twice as often as the other 2, with the 2 left over being functionally worthless. It's messy.
So, I think the player consensus right now is that it's actually optimal to match as many damn pieces as you can just for the EXP bonuses because trying to control the board over the longterm is hopeless. Which sucks, because it removes what makes the constellation-match (?) gameplay interesting for a resource gathering mechanic, the control: being able to match partial sections of touching pieces that don't clear on contact.
My biggest problem with the game is that the computer doesn't operate on the same board state. So, it feels really unfair that you have to deal with a bad board, and they get to regularly perform double the actions you get to once you're hunting for coolant (the resource you need twice as much of than others). If you thought having to play around the AI getting combos or 4-matches in Puzzle Quest was bad, this is so many times worse. It'd be much fairer if they had to use the same board or their own puzzle board, but they randomly get to perform actions based on rules and math that don't apply to the player and are much more favorable to them, despite both parties acting under identical battle mechanics. There are maybe two skills out of dozens of randomly appearing ones that let you effectively interact with enemy resources. It's B.S.
All these frustrations are framed by a really sparse story about a desperate, near-impossible effort of the British to fight off an invasion of the much more technoligcally advanced French forces. But there are other, more engaging ways to reenforce that tone than by making a very elaborate, slow game of Yahtzee.

Ironcast is a Rougelite Mech building and fighting game with a matching mini game as a means of resource control. It's a unique take on what many writers now refer to as an FTL style game. I preview the game in the video above. Below are my initial thoughts on Ironcast and it's DLC.
A review copy of Ironcast was provided to
by Dreadbit and Ripstone, for that we thank them greatly.
Ironcast is a very well styled game with a steampunk art motif and an incredible amount of character. The gameplay is fun and challenging, with the rougue-lite aspect it feels fresh at all times. Like many of the rouge type games, there is a benefit to all of your future mechs as you more, you gain global modifiers that are consistent from game to game. It's a refreshing and fun game, easy to learn, and has quite a bit of replay value.
I spent quite a bit of time feeling the game was too easy, until I encountered a few losses in a row and realized that poor choices generally equal poor results, regardless of difficulty. Keeping things like shields and movement up and repaired and paying attention to mission objectives is important, I failed to do so in the first fight in the video above and you see my mech get melted. Unlocking a new mech after that made it worth every piece of scrap, very satisfying.
The random aspect I find to be a part of the roughelike genre and I expect at times to run into a nearly unwinnable situation or to get poor resource nodes. The nodes however you can control to an extent by grouping rather than gunning for what you need immediately, that part is less RNG and more of a logic puzzle. The whole package fits together well and plays very smoothly. I enjoy the stlye of gameplay because it allows you to walk away and come back at any time for the most part. I have my 19 month old son around, yet this is playable throughout the day since I'm not concerned with a timer.
I can't find much reason not to reccommed this one. I've seen some gripes about RNG, but that is expected, and challenges are welcomed on my part. I think the art is fantastic, the music while not my taste fits the motif and is well done. There are very few games that play this well and mix so many elements together in such a clean streamlined manner. This is one I will be spending time with regularly, I'd certainly reccomend checking this out, the replay value is genuinely high on this one.
Thanks for watching and reading, check out
for news and reviews!

I'm not a fan of Early Access program on Steam. Often games don't get finished for one reason or another. But sometimes there is a title that catches my eye and I can't help it to give it a try. Armed with Wings is such a case. It's good side-scroller, hack 'n slash game. This is first impressions of the game.
You play as a fallen lone warrior. He awakes in a limbo like place, summoned by a god-looking figure. He is tasked with slaying the King that defeat you. I'm not too far in, but I think it's maybe just a simple revenge story.
Gameplay shines here. The first level is tutorial. It teaches you basics of the game, but it doesn't tell you that you have more than one basic attack.  You can actually juggle in air with the right buttons. The combat is so satisfying, part because of the tight controls, part because of the animation quality. It's not really fast paced like DMC, it's a little bit slower. The swings with the sword feel great and you have to sometimes time your attacks, because you can easily die. All my deaths are my faulth and non of them feel cheap. You have to decide to block or evade. It depends what type of enemy you encounter. I found myself using evade more often, but it wasn't always the smartest thing to do. And sometimes I was too eager to fight and this cost me a life. You have three of them. I thought at one point if a group of enemies are gathered in one place, it would be easy, but I was wrong. They wiped the floor with me. It's definitely doable if you don't rush like me. Here you don't have a jump button and at first it was weird, but once I figure out all attacks, I found the combat still really enjoyable without him.
Life is restore by picking up white orbs. They can be found in different places in the level or you can just chain a few attacks and enemies will drop them. You can even use parts of the envoirment to hurt them. There are rocks on the ground and by hitting them, they will fly towards the enemies and damage them. A neat little idea.
There is slight delay between finishing a combo and start new one. I'm not sure if I like it. It's probably intentional to have some sort vulnerability to keep you on your toes.

Exept the story you can find survival mode, but I was not prepared enough for it. After wave three I died within few seconds.
When you slay enemies, you get points and after you quit or loose all your lives, all of them goes to the unlockables. They are linear, you can't put the wherever you want. They can be sword or a booster. Through my time with the game I unlock three swords with different stats and one booster. From here and the timer on top of the screen comes the replayability. There are leaderboards and a lot of things to unlock, so you can get better and more powerful.
The level design is basic, but there are sometimes different paths to take. Some may even lead you to skip a level and get more points. There are some puzzles here, but they are easy. All include an eagle that follows you around. With him you can also gather healing orbs or distract enemy. All levels are fairly short. I'm not that further into the game, so I can't comment for all of them. I beaten half of the levels and they are total of 30 for now.
The sound design is nice. All moves have great sounds effects, but the music is lacking variety. I only heard two songs – one through the levels, the other was for the first boss battle. They both are really great, but few more would be nice. The track that I heard most is really enchanting. It immerse me into this dark world. Yet simple, but effective to me.
Graphics is what caught my attention at first. When I saw the trailer my first thought was “Samurai Jack in black and white”. I love the simple graphic art style, it's especially suitable for the the tone that tries to achive and it succeed. If there was a single other colour, it won't be the same. And also I mention in the beginning the quality of the animation. It is awesome!
What I saw is really great for an early acces title. It have tons of potential to be more than just great. There are a lot of things to be added – new character, new booster, new swords and new levels. There will be replayability, without being a rogue-lite. When you die, you can start from the beginning or choose a level. What I like to see further into development is more resolution options, few more track and combos maybe, rebindble keys not only for keyboard, but also for controller. I try both methods, but controller is more fun. Since I don't have Xbox 360 controller (which by the way is supported), I had to use third party software. It's promising title, not very expensive and updates come fairly frequently. Just because it's in Early Access my advise is to wait and see how much content there will be. But if you decide to support the developer, it would be great. It have content, but in my opinion it's not worth the full price for now. I'll follow the game and if it comes out of Early Access I will beat it and update my review.

The control scheme is fairly simple, arrows move your character, WASD controls your actions, this is about as ergonomic as you can get, as long as you have a decent keyboard.
